If you enjoyed Furi as much as I did, then I highly suggest that you get this DLC.
Oh, the "extra" is a bundle of fun too...

The Flame's fight is a fairly fun and "new" fight and some of the tricks it had got me by surprise, including the cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bringing in his shotgun for the melee phases and blowing my head off more than once
however, in addition to the undeniable temptation that having "one more boss" had for me, the DLC also decided to give a little treat to people like me (however, that's for people who get it)

"Furi - One More Fight DLC"
(Unlocks a Second Fight)
Biggest plot twist since "it was aliens all along."

Everything I loved about Furi is in this fight. Frantic, fast-paced action, with challenging yet extremely fair difficulty. This guy is pretty tough but he never quite feels ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I beat him on my first try without too much of a problem, which goes to show that he is in fact fair. There were a couple of attacks that despite initially being telegraphed well, another projectile was snuck in and got a bit of a cheap hit on me, but those moments are really few and far between. This is still a very enjoyable fight, and a fairly lenghty one, too. Took me a little under 10 minutes to beat him on Furi difficulty.
The Flame has a lot of really cool and interesting attacks, some of which you'll be familiar with, others you'll be pleasantly surprised with. The vast majority of his attacks are very well telegprahed and you're always given enough time to react to everything. The arena you fight in is very interesting with how it changes in certain phases but I feel like you aren't given enough of a warning when it does change since I did fall down a couple of times in its transition.
On Furier however... This guy will definitely give you a run for your money. I got a game over on him and right before beating him I almost got a second one. Much like the original boss fights on Furier difficulty, in certain places it adds a much needed extra challenge while in other places it's getting borderline unfair with attacks that you can't really see coming your first time around, but it's not that bad, really, and you do learn his patterns really fast.
The boss is really nicely designed, well animated and has some really cool tricks up his sleeves, though I did encounter a few minor glitches like what seemed to be occasionaly missing dialogue and in one cutscene his model disappeared for a moment. Aside from that it's really well polished and feels right at home with the rest of the bosses in Furi.
If you still somehow end up being disappointed with the difficulty of this boss however, you do get a nice little surprise once you beat him.
In conclusion, if you liked Furi, without a doubt get this DLC. For $4 you definitely get enough content here to justify it and what's in it, is definitely enjoyable and worthwhile as fan of the original game.

Do not hesitate, buy it now. This is the first time in over a year I truly enjoyed playing a video game.

-If you enjoyed Magicka but you're like me and not into magic-fantasy stuff, this is a sci-fi version of Magicka with guns.
-If you enjoyed watching Starship Troopers (SST) like I did when I was a child then this is definitely for you, and people like you are why we were at the Bug homeworld within a few days and nowhere close to the Illuminate and Cyborg homeworlds. Lol.
Seriously this game hits the SST vibe really hard from the first movie with the humorous propaganda and overall vibe. Add in the bugs and you have a pretty close analogue to a modern SST game if playing the bugs. The meta game is also more fun that I originally though, I'm now choosing the front closest to the home system to fight on so we won't risk having to defend ourselves. Most people are hitting the bugs as of this post during the first war and we got to the homeplanet like 2nd day of release, and the Illumanati systems are about 1 notch further along than the cyborg. I think lots of people think like me and are playing the Cyborgs to simply shore up that weak spot but it's also an advancing front so we are advancing on all 3 fronts. Maybe in the next war cycle the devs will adjust numbers and make it harder to progress.
All the kit in the base game works fine. In fact I just bought the DLC megapack and only used one of the items tonight, I still mostly use the base-game stuff. Everything has it's use, it will suck most of the time if used inproperly. While the DLC are not needed if you enjoy this game they give you more options to further tune your play style to a specific situation but you are not missing anything critical just by being in the base game. Typically DLC are a neg to me but this game does it right, the new stuff isn't OP nor is it useless/cosmetic-only.
On to criticisms. Aiming is made for controllers, so your character always starts aiming in front of them and you have to sweep to your target. You get used to it within a few hours of play, no problem. It's a minor annoyance we cannot have the crosshair always on to see where we are aiming though, this is just a bad oversight of the port from Playstation. The random 'funny' deaths are only funny if you play this game lightly. When playing serious and the game decides to land a pod 10ft away from the beacon right on you instead that's not funny at higher levels. The game is designed with a poor camera system too, the camera hovers in the middle of the entire squad, spread out too much and you can't see enemies at the edges before they run into your guy. This forces a squad to stick together, but this forced closeness also causes lots of accidental deaths from friendly fire to drop pods landing in such close quarters etc. This is by design, this game is made to be difficult and for you to die. Having a low-death count is not necessary, it's just a sign of skill.
Overall besides a few minor negatives I would call Helldivers GOTY material since we are close to Christmas. All year 2015 nothing entertained me like the recent PC release of Helldivers. Entry price is $20 and you will have everything needed in-game to be a top-shelf player if you do your part. The $40 pack with all DLC is worth it, otherwise you have to pay $25 for all the DLC in a megapack after buying the base game or like $45 for all the DLC individually. If $40 makes you balk then just spend the $20 and call it a good enjoy the game, that's like the price of 3 footlongs from subway.

The downside to this is you don't get the same "layers within layers" of the puzzle box like in Room 1. I sortof missed the delight when a new part of the box would open or change in a unique way. The concept behind Beatbuddy is smart - it's a platformer (taking place underwater so you have free-form of movement) where there is a constant beat of music where by doing certain actions on the beat makes your progress through the game much easier. You don't need to have the precision of a musican, fortunately, as the game is very generous with beat-matching mechanic as well as frequent checkpoints and health drops. Add in that mst of the music is from the emerging Electro Swing genre, and the game works in concept.  Puzzles are generally of the right amount of effort and complexity, with a decent learning curve to all the various moves, enemies, and obstacles in the game.
The major problem I had with the game is that the levels are on the long side - 30-40 minutes, and while the backing song does change with the various sections of each level, you're listening to the same basic music over and over again.  And as this is a bass-heavy track to keep that beat going, it does wear on you over long periods.  The graphics for the levels also get a bit weary.  But as noted, the game wisely has lots of self-saving checkpoints so playing brief segments is possible.  The game is definitely worth your time to play through, though the type that you should keep your eye out for a sale to get.

A fun action adventure game with a few puzzle elements. The game has a cool art style with hand drawn environments in a 2D world. The levels themselves are fairly large, but have multiple sections in them usually containing puzzles that then allow you to progress to the next sections of the level. The best thing about the game is definitely the music and how it syncs to the gameplay, and how everything just moves together. You can definitely tell how they really wanted to integrate rhythm based gameplay into the game and it works well.
In most of the game, you'll play as Beatbuddy himself, opening up paths to progress and also solving various puzzles that usually require you moving a device to another area to open doors and so on. But in other parts, you'll be in a vehicle with a companion doing the same thing which keeps the gameplay fresh.
The only downside I found, was sometimes the movements can be a little clunky and frustrating but that's mainly in the vehicle parts and not so much when you're just controlling Beatbuddy himself. This viewpoint is only from playing with the controller however, so I'm not sure if the mouse and keyboard gameplay is any different or better.

That's probably the strong point of this game, the synchronization of the animations with the soundtrack itself is just perfect. To be honest the game is not exactly nothing out of extraordinary, in my honest opinion, it's good at most but like I said, the soundtrack turns Beatbuddy into something much more enjoyable. The game takes about 5-6 hours to complete and each level has several chapters. There's checkpoints spread throughout the levels in which you save your progress. Overall the levels are pretty well designed along with the background artwork. Most of the game involves bashing walls using the "bass plants" which propel you foward and you might change your path by going against mirrors and rotating them in order to go to the right place, there's also times in which you drive some kind of submarine which is actually pretty fun because it moves in bumps synchronized with the beat, other than that is basicly just beating down enemies and moving some kind of devices from one place to another in order to open doors. The game was surprisingly fun for me to play through and relatively short. If you enjoy a good soundtrack then you'll probably have a great time with Beatbuddy, if you're expecting a platformer or something more elaborated, you're not going to get it here.

If you want to play a fun platformer with musical elements, you NEED to check out Sound Shapes on PSN, which does control much better, even sounds better and is so beautiful, it made me cry!

It's good; get it. On sale, it's a steal; get it!
With all the major expansions this is the essential Civilization game, and a great taster if you are thinking of Civ 6.
For those new to the game, the gist of it is this: You start off with just a city and a warrior unit from which you begin building at the 'dawn of time' and gradually expand your civilzation by gaining culture, advancing scientifically, building and using military, diplomacy, building new cities and buildings within those cities, and building enough 'improvements' to sustain an economy which can maintain the above. Because the map is tiled, each tile yields resources; perhaps a certain amount of food, construction, gold, or even another resource such as horses (needed to build horsemen etc) or iron, oil, even uranium (I don't need to tell you what that's for). As you progress you will find that you unlock more and more improvements, more buildings and more units that you can build, and if you play your diplomacy and development well enough, you will find that you can really start to get ahead of the competition; picture tanks versus musketmen - that can happen. Finally there are wonders which can provide a variety of benefits and a boost of culture. Benefits may include a free worker, reductions in costs for various things or even free technologies! Obviously getting a wonder before other people can therefore be of great importance.
Those are the basics and to new-comers that's more than enough to be getting on with and the AI can give you fairly decent games on a variety of difficulty settings. Equally, there are many, many, many map varieties for your prefered experience - you might want a map with no water, on the other hand maybe small scattered islands:
On the subject of customisation; there are many, many different leaders you can play. The game even offers different leaders for a given civilization in some places; each leader provides differences to the civilization and so as you play with any given leader you want to keep their bonuses in mind and exploit them as best you can. It must be said though, personally I don't tend to notice a great difference between given leaders, the most noticeable thing is their unique units, but even those only last so long before technology supasses them. Maybe I'm just not pro enough. Yet, I play casually, and I enjoy it.
The visuals are readable and clear which really helps for longer play times, and the soundtrack is different for each Civ and varies based on the era you are in or whether you are at war or peace. As the Brits, you may even recongise a good bit of Greensleaves in there too. For new players there is also a decent
, essentially a wiki lookup for everything in the game, and even includes larger written backgrounds on each leader and Civ for the historically curious.
Personally, I never really player online or with other people much so I can't really comment on that, but from the time I did spend with other people, I can say that it's an enjoyable experience, even when they march into your territory and refuse all of your offers of peace because, well, they know they are going to walk all over you... or me in this case; we've already established I'm not particularly good at this game.
Another caveat though is that the AI can be a bit temperamental, though this has always been an issue with Civ games and remains one because they can never really act like a human (then again I haven't played at higher difficulties); they might denounce you for no reason, expand erratically, and so on. The final thing to say is that late game diplomacy can be a little... 'off'? Things like World Congress and United Nations - too me they became annoying po-ups every few turns that had little to no impact on the game other than that annoyance and were never really very well explained as to how some people end up with more diplomats than others, more voters and so on. But by that time I have a big enough nuclear arsenal that no matter how much the UN may not like it, I can kill everyone everywhere, like Mr Kim over there only dreams he could.
In summary; it's a good game as a complete edition with all the expansions. On sale the bundle is more than worth it. Civ 5 Complete is a great entry into the 4X genre (4X = eXplore, eXpand, eXploit and eXterminate).

So i may have low hours, but i have already finished the campaign, and have a couple things to say, and recommend for the game. Dying light is absolutly amazing. Great story and gameplay. But not every game is perfect.
Pros:
-Parkour is amazing. Very well done and makes you feel like a badass.
-Endless hours of gameplay. Your definitly getting your moneys worth.
-The story is interesting. Has that kind of effect you would see in The last of us. (going with that because no spoilers)
-Online play is very smooth. Ive never encountered any kind of connection issues or bugs so far.
-Open world.
Cons:
-The game is very slow at the start If you dont have the DLC. For about 1-2 hours maybe you spend half your time wumping zombies with a table leg or a plank or just running from them alltogether.
-Some of the bossfights are insanely hard on your own. Its somewhat annoying because not very many people are playing this game anymore.
-The Bozak Hoard DLC is near impossible to complete on your own
-The Following DLC can be annoying sometimes, because every time you get in your car you will attract maybe 3-4 virals which are very annoying to get away from because they are as fast as your car.
-Lots and lots of bugs. From NPC's falling through the ground to your character acting like hes missing numerous braincells (Jumping the wrong way off a wall, not grabbing a ledge or grabbing the wrong ledge, getting stuck, etc.)
-Be the zombie "goons" Are massive zombies with heavy rebars that can do a ton of damage to you, and knock you down. They spawn on the last 3 nests and i feel this is very unfair for the survivors.
As for the Be The Zombie mode, ive found it very difficult and tedious to win against 1 person when being the zombie. Certain factors are a little bit unfair in the mode. The hunter cant do anything to you while in the radious of a flare except watch helplessly as you destroy a nest, or try to distract them by tackling and slamming which will most likely fail against experienced players. And these are the problems i have with just 1 person. With 4, if they stay grouped up, the hunter pretty much has absolutly no chance of winning. Unlimited UV flashlights, Flares, etc. Can really make the game unbalanced. The hunter also dies way too fast. Surround him with a group and hes pretty much instantly dead. Respawn times for the hunter are a bit too long also. Your gonna be dying alot as a hunter against 4 people. So a faster respawn time wouldnt hurt. Also "goons" Are massive zombies with heavy rebars that can do a ton of damage to you, and knock you down. They spawn on the last 3 nests and i feel this is very unfair for the survivors.
The game also does a very poor job at showing you where to go, this is mainly a problem with main story quests, or even some of The Following DLC side quests. I understand why they didnt put much effort into that part of the game though, because the game isnt based around the main story, as are all open world games. So im not heavily bothered by this.
Overall, the game is very good, but like i said, no game is perfect. Based on the game itself without any dlc, id give it a 7/10. As for the DLC in the game, id say The Following DLC is all you really need. 5.5/10 for the DLC. Would i recommend at full price? No. The game is in too much of a broken state atm. Updates are still coming in, but it seems they only really care for content drops rather then fixing bugs.

One of my favourite games ever!
This game is the adaptation of the Metro 2033 book (Dmitri Glukhovsky), which I also strongly recommend. To make it short, you are Artyom, a young Moscovite man, who has lived in the metro system of Moscow for the past 20 years, since a nuclear war wiped out all life on the surface (or has it?). Some weird stuff is happening in the tunnels near your home station, and you have to report about it to the "police" force of the subway, forcing your way through nazis, comunists, opportunists, bandits, mutant creatures and other scary stuff. (If it's still not clear for you : this is an allegory of post-comunist Russia).
The graphics are beautiful, the sound is gorgeous, the story is convincing and enthralling, the gameplay on point. I love the shooting mechanics, the customization of your weapons, the choice of weapons, the variety of enemies.
Regarding the game itself, there are a few jumpscares here and there, but not too much, it's mostly a sort of psychological horror (apart from sheer blood and violence when fighting) that creeps on you. There are several game modes, which lead you to various playstyles.
You can play it in the easy difficulties, where there's ammo everywhere, and you just plow your way through everything (or try to sneak, fail, and then have to shoot everyone). Or you can play in harder difficulties, where you are forced to stealth your way simply because there's no bullets to shoot anymore.
The only downsides of this game are the limited possibility of replaying (since it is fairly linear) and the impossibility to play in highest difficulty on the first time. Explanation : in highest difficulty mode, you have no UI, and no clues of what key to press to interact with objects, or how to select your different weapons. Meaning that you'll be stuck. So you have to play it once with the hints, telling you how to choose knife/mines/grenades, and then play it in harder, once you understand how it works.
Overall, a great game with a good scenario!

I don't even know where to begin. The art direction, the intense gameplay, the survival elements, the post-apocaliptic weaponry, level design... Metro 2033 is just barely short of a masterpiece. Except for a few minor setbacks such as weak sound design and a lack of story direction, Metro does almost everything right.
For me this is the quintessential post-apocaliptic Russia survival game. The gameplay can be extremely challenging, and the ideas behind all the the game elements were developed with great care. When I play it, it really feels like I'm deep underground trying to fight for my life against the monsters lurking in the Metro. When Artyom begins to asphixiate as his gas mask is cracked, or the filter is running out, the panic begins to set in. I can't tell you how many times my heart was filled with fear as I tried to reload while these monsters swiped at me.
You're missing out if you haven't played this game. End of story.

A good alternative to other post-apocalyptic FPS. I like the atmosphere of the game, which seems to some degree reflect Russian culture. The story is quite interesting, though I think it would have been great to be given more leeway and options to choose for influencing the outcome of the game. It seemed like there could have been just a bit more. The scenery of post-apocalyptic Moscow and the population living in the old subway tunnels is well-chosen. The characters are all quite rough, but rather flat. It would have been nicer to get more info about their backgrounds. The missions are varied and fun. Makes me want to read the original novels. I only think that the sound is a bit simple. Can't compare the graphics of the redux version to the old one since I haven't played the original release, but it's emphasising the atmosphere well, still looking good for an old game like that.
Recommendation for all people who like post-apocalyptic settings! Looking forward to playing the sequel.

Metro 2033 takes place in the year 2033 in a world where a nuclear war has occurred.
The only survivors now are living inside the giant metro of Moscou.
Over time Metro’s stations transformed into citys with their own politics.
In this metro there is 2 big factions the Reds and the Fascists their ideologies are basicaly the same as the one of the USSR and the Third Reich.
And also dangerous mutant creatures are living outside and inside of the Metro.
You play as Artiom a young man who lived  peacefuly in the station of ВДНХ until the Dark ones appeared out of nowhere, their regular attack are threatening the survival of the station.
A friend named Hunter gives you a mission before intering a tunnel to check it, in case he don’t come back after 24 hours you will need to contact Sparta a group composed of the best warriors of the Metro to help you and your station to get rid of those Dark ones.
Hunter didn’t come back so you will need to get to Polis to get there it will not be easy of course, but you will see the rest by yourself.
And I will not talk about the story of Metro Last Light because I don’t want to spoil you the ending of Metro 2033.
Because I don’t want to spoil you the games’ characters I will not talk about each individually I will say in general.
They all looks nice you can easely guess their personality only with the visual, they don’t do things that are out of theirs character and they are interesting not everyone but a lot of them.
This is all.
The game’s graphics are realy good I am not talking about 11K textures resolution but the environment’s composition, god it’s gorgeous if you want to see some amazing post nuclear environments try this game.
I love the musics this is just incredible the feelings of loneliness, sadness and hope that are given only by the main menu music...
The overall sound design is magnificent it immerse you completely in the univers, the sounds of the wind outside, the "cave" sounds in the tunnels, just wow.
So obviously I think that the ambiance is outstanding.
The gameplay is realy good the fighting is realy satisfying in this game.
The game have a lot of weapons and some nice customisation possibility.
It’s interesting that when you are against humans (it’s more rare with monsters) you can do it stealthy and it’s fun to try even if sometimes it’s pretty hard.
The game itself is in my opinion "too easy" even on the highest difficulty I din’t get much problem to finish those two games but it was still a lot of fun and the the fact that you can’t see your HUD  (Spartan mod) is an original and cool idea.
Also you will need to be a little patient you will not fight humans every five seconds there is a lot of dialogue that you can’t skip, if get interested by the story it goes pretty fast and it’s enjoyable to listen but I can’t imagine how boring it is if you don’t get in.
During every loading screens Artiom is explaining where he is going and why, it’s a realy good way to easely keep the track of the story and so be more easely immersed in the universe.
The Metros' serie is a Master Piece the ambiance is amazing the story is good and the gameplay is just a lot of fun. If you want a shooter with an interesting post-apocalyptique story, play Metro 2033.

"A Story About My Uncle" is a  decent platformer with some refreshing innovations. The story is charming, the gameplay is original, and the backgrounds are gorgeous.
However, the game has some serious flaws. The character models came off as cheap and cartoony and seemed out of place. Up until I encountered one of the frog people I felt pretty immersed in the game... but they kind of pulled me out of it. Also, and this is probably my biggest issue with the game, the difficulty comes off as artificial. I like platformers that require quick reflexes and I also like games that require you to think through puzzles instead of just rushing through. This game unsuccessfully mixes the two. Progressing through the game requires a lot of trial and error. I found myself taking a lot of blind leaps just to see if I could grapple to an object in the distance. Some places that look accessible aren't. Some areas are hard to see and only become obviously visible after messing up a few times. So even after getting through a tough area...it just doesn't feel all that rewarding.
Even with these flaws though, there's something about flying through giant glowing caverns that makes the game appealing enough to play. And like I said earlier, the story is quite charming. It's innocent without being childish or trivial. I probably wouldn't recommend it to the average gamer, but for those who enjoy platformers and are looking for something new, I'd say give it a shot.

A Story About My Uncle is the first game from Gone North Games, a small indie studio based in Sweeden. According to their website, Gone North Games was founded by 9 students who have a passion for making games. Since it's advertised all over their website and apparently important to the developers, I'll repeat it here - A Story About My Uncle is a completely non-violent video game. This isn't really an entirely novel concept for a game, but it is unusual I suppose. For better or worse, most games do rely on some sort of violent combat as their main game mechanic. I do think it's cool that games like Gone Home or To The Moon are using video games purely as a story telling medium. But unfortunately, A Story About My Uncle doesn't tell a very interesting story. It is a pretty fun platformer though which is really what this game stands on
The game begins as you, the narrator, are reading your daughter a bedtime story. The entire rest of the game is played out as a flashback as the narrator recounts how he, as a boy, used to play with his uncle at his uncle's house. One day, the narrator's uncle went missing and you soon find out that he was transported to a distant magical world through some transporter device that the narrator's uncle invented. The game is a little vague on the details of how exactly this transporter was invented or how it works, but the narrator of course uses it to travel to this other world in search of his uncle. That's pretty much all the exposition you get. I mean that's it for the rest of the game. You meet some other characters and go to new locations, but the story never really progresses at all. You're just searching for your uncle the whole game. That's it. And then (spoiler alert) the game just kind of ends abruptly at a certain point and the credits roll. Nothing is really resolved and nothing really changes, just "The End". It was very anti-climactic and disappointing. It almost seemed rushed, like they might have been trying to go somewhere with the story, but had to cut a lot of it to meet deadlines or something like that. In any case, I somewhat ironically found the story in A Story About My Uncle to be underdeveloped and uninteresting.
Near the beginning of the game, the narrator discovers some magical super-bouncy boots and some magical grappling tether thing which serve as the game's platforming mechanics. I can't remember what the game actually called the boots and grapple device and I'm too lazy to look it up, but these definitely are what make this game fun and interesting. The boots allow you to jump crazy high and crazy far and the tether allows you to pull yourself closer towards certain parts of the terrain. Most of the terrain in the game is made up of small chunks of floating rock as shown in the cover art above, so the platforming can be kind of challenging in certain areas. Quick props to the graphic artists for this game, I found a lot of the floating terrain and world design to be really interesting from an artistic point of view. Very cool and imaginative artwork.
I prefer to play games laying down in my couch with a controller as opposed to sitting forward with a mouse and keyboard, even while playing PC games. So I'm not sure if it was just because I was playing with a controller, but there were some parts of this game that were really tricky to pull off. And I'm usually quite good at platformers. And that's fine, I enjoy a good challenge, but the difficulty curve with this game was a little wonky. There was one particular section near the end of the game that was insanely difficult, it probably took me 30-40 attempts to finally do it right. And then the rest of the game was mind-numbingly easy. My only other complaint, from a gameplay perspective, was with the level design. It was quite often not very clear where the game wanted me to go next, especially in the later levels where the terrain is separated by great distances. I had to jump around and try to grapple to things trail-and-error style until I finally found something that worked. The difficulty curve is forgivable, but in a linear platformer like this I feel like the player should always have a pretty good idea of where the game wants them to go next.
It is definitely a flawed game, but if you like 3D platformers, you could do worse than A Story About My Uncle. It's got some really cool art design and fun platforming, but it has some design issues and the actual story might as well not even exist. It was also kind of short, I finished it in about 5 hours, but I found that length to be appropriate. All in all, not too bad for a small team making their first game. And as its developers insist, it's completely non-violent, if that's a selling point for you.

Metro 2033 takes place in the year 2033 in a world where a nuclear war has occurred.
The only survivors now are living inside the giant metro of Moscou.
Over time Metro’s stations transformed into citys with their own politics.
In this metro there is 2 big factions the Reds and the Fascists their ideologies are basicaly the same as the one of the USSR and the Third Reich.
And also dangerous mutant creatures are living outside and inside of the Metro.
You play as Artiom a young man who lived  peacefuly in the station of ВДНХ until the Dark ones appeared out of nowhere, their regular attack are threatening the survival of the station.
A friend named Hunter gives you a mission before intering a tunnel to check it, in case he don’t come back after 24 hours you will need to contact Sparta a group composed of the best warriors of the Metro to help you and your station to get rid of those Dark ones.
Hunter didn’t come back so you will need to get to Polis to get there it will not be easy of course, but you will see the rest by yourself.
And I will not talk about the story of Metro Last Light because I don’t want to spoil you the ending of Metro 2033.
Because I don’t want to spoil you the games’ characters I will not talk about each individually I will say in general.
They all looks nice you can easely guess their personality only with the visual, they don’t do things that are out of theirs character and they are interesting not everyone but a lot of them.
This is all.
The game’s graphics are realy good I am not talking about 11K textures resolution but the environment’s composition, god it’s gorgeous if you want to see some amazing post nuclear environments try this game.
I love the musics this is just incredible the feelings of loneliness, sadness and hope that are given only by the main menu music...
The overall sound design is magnificent it immerse you completely in the univers, the sounds of the wind outside, the "cave" sounds in the tunnels, just wow.
So obviously I think that the ambiance is outstanding.
The gameplay is realy good the fighting is realy satisfying in this game.
The game have a lot of weapons and some nice customisation possibility.
It’s interesting that when you are against humans (it’s more rare with monsters) you can do it stealthy and it’s fun to try even if sometimes it’s pretty hard.
The game itself is in my opinion "too easy" even on the highest difficulty I din’t get much problem to finish those two games but it was still a lot of fun and the the fact that you can’t see your HUD  (Spartan mod) is an original and cool idea.
Also you will need to be a little patient you will not fight humans every five seconds there is a lot of dialogue that you can’t skip, if get interested by the story it goes pretty fast and it’s enjoyable to listen but I can’t imagine how boring it is if you don’t get in.
During every loading screens Artiom is explaining where he is going and why, it’s a realy good way to easely keep the track of the story and so be more easely immersed in the universe.
The Metros' serie is a Master Piece the ambiance is amazing the story is good and the gameplay is just a lot of fun. If you want a shooter with an interesting post-apocalyptique story, play Metro 2033.

After Playing 17 hours of this game i feel i have more than enough play time to be able to write a short review on it. Company of heroes 2 is the sequel to company of heroes. The game is a unique RTS that dives you into the frontlines of world war 2. Though this game gets a lot of negative feedback because of the vanilla version of the games campaign I still feel its one of the better RTS games that I have played in years.
Positive: Gameplay is solid for the most part. It seems pretty balanced overall. Has a unique win type of victory point captures, so win are based on who has the most points at the end of the game. Character and vehicle models look great and graphics over all look beautiful. Also like the fact that this is the only RTS i found on steam that has a pretty active multiplayer community. More people play this RTS in multiplayer right now than any other RTS.
Negative: Matchmaking is kind of a long process and can having you waiting 10+ minutes before finding a match. Vehicle Pathfinding needs work. Load times arent good. DLC's cost to much. Ardennes Assault costs as much as the actual game (though you can just buy the 2 factions that come in that pack seperately for 12 dollars. you just dont get the missions). Campaign missions kind of hard even on the easiest setting. Tutorial is not very informative. Random drops after battles sometimes disappear from inventory.
Over all I would say the base game is worth the price. Only if this is the kind of game youre into. Look into it before buying. Its fun and youll have a blast honing your strategy skills to defeat other players. Russians dont like this game as well as others because of the campaign. Its a good and fun campaign but i do agree it does not exactly historically portray the soviet union on how it was and maybe not enough research was done. but if you buy a game made with mostly multiplayer functions in mind, the campaign shouldnt matter compared to what the actual game has to offer. COD freequently depicts america as always betraying its own people as well as brittain, but you dont see us complaining because theyre not accurate and make us seem like monsters. we buy them for the multiplayer. no one buys COD for the campaign, that said COH2 should also be bought with the same thing in mind. if you skip the campaign and just play the multiplayer you would find this game to be amazing fun.
My score, I give it a 7 out of 10. I feel like a 7 might even be pushing it but i give it such a low score because of how over priced most of the DLC is, the fact i feel the vanilla version is not 100% worth its retail price and that a number of issues that should have been fixed a long time ago are not being addressed. Other than that i do reccomend this game and think its a lot of fun for anyone who likes a good RTS.

Sickening how they turned this great franchise into a micro transaction pay to win mess...
The base game is still great. I love CoH more than any RTS. My entire problem is with the way they have turned CoH2 into a huge micro transaction pay to win game where the more you play the better your troops/guns/vehicles are.
So if you buy the base game you get several commanders. I can't remember specifics but the original armies from the first release gave you more options than the Western Front Armies. More commands. Six commanders for the Soviets because I bought the digital deluxe version and got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don't get me started on what I got for my extra $40. Six extra commanders and some vehicle textures, oh joy!
Anyway, it has been a long time since the beta testing and since I started playing retail. More on that a bit later. If I am not mistaken there will be three to six starter commanders for the Soviets (three of those are from the deluxe version I think), the German Wehrmacht came with three to six (again three extra from the Deluxe Edition I think), the Western Front Armies add-on came with three each for US Forces and the German Oberkommando West. I've logged one hundred hours of nothing but skirmish and online multiplayer. Though I tend to play skirmish mode mostly. At the end of the game you get random drops. Since purchase I have got ten Soviet commanders to drop. Nine Wehrmacht commanders. And one (yes, just one) US Forces commander to drop even though I have played mainly the US forces since the release of Western Front Armies.
The problem? When we beta tested you got to picked the commander and their combat options or perks so to speak. With the retail release you don't have that option and even though the two base armies have lots of commanders and intel bulletins that randomly drop at end game the commanders are too similar in my opinion. And the Intel Bulletins are basically improvements to your existing options. So the more you play the better your sqauds/guns/tanks are.
The add-on of the Western Forces gave very little. Random drops are almost non existant because they only have several extra commanders and they are trying to get you to buy them for $3.99 each. And there in lies the problem. Since Western Front Armies went live I have scored one commander and it was a cruel joke. His first perk is a WC51 Military Truck w/ .50 cal HMG mounted on the back that can't even pin down a squad of engineers. Not to mention they (any squad even engineers) can take it out so fast it is completely worthless on the battlefield. Does that sound balanced? Oh, but if I buy the other commanders they have much better options you say? No, thanks.
I recommend buying the entire game if you can get it on the cheap. I regret paying one hundred US dollars for the so called deluxe version. I have bought the Western Front Armies and the British Forces but grudgingly. Like I said I love CoH and since the original CoH I can't play other RTS games because they are just weak. I love the franchise and the game mechanics. I hate the way Sega screwed us loyal fans with this micro transaction BS.

Progress!
The developer has implemented some of my suggestions regarding balance and rewards for playing actively. Now, if you defeat a monster that's a higher level, you get more experience as opposed to the same amount of experience for every monster. There are also chests to open by clicking from which you can gather resources.
There are now multiple profiles, allowing you to start with the other eggs without erasing your save file and also the ability to go back waves so that you can keep beating monsters until your team has enough DPS to fell the boss. It's worked wonderfully and I've done it a few times so I can start getting all of my monsters on the same level.
You can enchant your monsters, which increases DPS individually and has helped greatly in making sure that idle play is a more viable option.
You can also
Keep 'em coming~ I'm working on evolving my other monsters now so I can get enough money to buy a farm.
---------------------------------------------
It's still a bit too early to write my typical Early Access Report. This will remain a tentative thumbs up as I wait for updates because there's nothing inherently bad about the game except for the lack of content... But then, isn't that what the Early Access phase is meant to address?
You choose from one of three starter monsters, each of which start out as eggs. Others are recruited automatically once you defeat them. After your egg hits level five, either by clicking anywhere on the screen a little more than five thousand times or by waiting until you rack up enough idle damage, it hatches.
In order to gain gold and exp you can keep clicking, which does the amount indicated on your stat screen (click strength), or you can stay idle and let your monster do the work (DPS). Your monster always does slightly less damage than you--and that's not taking into consideration how quickly you can click. Thus, the idle option isn't viable at the moment because it does a sliver of damage in comparison to the HP of the monsters, which will quickly ramp up to the quadruple digits and beyond while the damage you can inflict remains below 20.
Your click damage increases as you level up. You can also increase your idle damage by upgrading the monsters you randomly recruit (currently there are only three, which you'll defeat on a loop, and you can only have one of each time), though that takes a ton of gold. To put it into perspective, I've clicked 12k times and killed over 400 enemies, but I'm still 3000 gold away from buying my first upgrade. This is after leaving the game idle for some time.
Only your active monster gains experience. You can tab between them using the arrows at the bottom of the box displaying your monsters.
The music is irritating; a constant loop that I immediately muted. The graphics are okay. The portraits are nice and so are the sprites, but everything else looks very mobile/flash game.
The biggest problem with Creature Clicker in its current state--other than the lack of content variety, of course--is the balance. Your monster will perpetually be behind in level by 2-3 levels than the enemies, which isn't a problem given that you don't take damage, but a more powerful monster isn't worth much more experience. The grind becomes very real because of this: even if you use a monster at level 0 against a monster at level 10, it will still get bread crumbs for exp.
I just ran into my first boss. My starter monster is level 8 and I only do 19 damage.... Yet the fight requires me to do 14k damage in 60 seconds. Not happening. This needs to be patched--and quickly. I'm stuck now; I can't run and there's no way I'm going to put my fingers through that kind of stress because I'm almost certain there's no way I could pull off that feat.
Some suggestions to the developer:
I look forward to updating this once there's more meat to Creature Clicker!

I thoroughly enjoyed The Room and The Room Two. I believe they are both excellent games that do something that a lot of puzzle games don't.
The addition of multiple puzzle areas in each chapter was welcome in my opinion as it adds much more depth to the game world.
However, the game got frustrating and tiring during The Lab section. I felt as if the general concept of the puzzles was just being rehashed without too much deviation. Take the whole "Find a key to open a drawer to get another key to open another drawer" thing for example. I feel like it was reused too often in this game making it pad the gameplay for extra unnecessary length. I would have liked to see more diverse puzzles, but that is my opinion.
It could have been just because I played through the whole game in one sitting. Take that as a compliment though. A game that gets me to play through it in one sitting is a good game. It means it's immersive/fun enough to warrant it.
Another thing I felt was a bit off with the game was the story. I couldn't quite wrap my head around the story about the certain areas and I feel like it could have gone into more depth.
(SPOILER ALERT IF YOU HAVEN'T PLAYED THE ROOM OR THE ROOM TWO)
While I understand how the character gets to these places, (at the end of the first game, you go through a door leading to the first chapter of this one,) I don't quite understand the logic behind the areas. Is it supposed to be telling a story about history? A story about an adventure and some sort of strange discovery? Why are the areas themed in such ways as an (Aztec?) temple, a supposed pirate ship, a room with a fireplace (which i'm not quite sure what to call the table in the center) and a lab? Is there a connection between these places? I couldn't quite figure that out during the game, and whether or not that is a bad thing is up for debate as games such as the FNaF series do the same thing.
(END OF SPOILERS)
tl;dr
The game is good, I enjoyed it, but I had trouble understanding the story and the puzzles seemed a bit repetitive.
Anyway, I still recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzle games. The puzzles are interesting and can be rather challenging at times making the game enjoyable for those who like a challenge.
I give this game a solid 8/10.

A beautiful continuation on its predecessor, with expanded puzzing environments that are a bit of a blessing and a curse at the same time. More environment means wider-ranging puzzles and more pretty things to see and click on, but the developers seem to have dumbed down some of the puzzling in order to prevent the player from getting overwhelmed, while there are some times when the opposite may happen where the player has too much space to explore and no apparent next step in the puzzle. The hint system handles this elegantly and I would recommend anyone playing the game to keep it turned on, since you won't receive any hints unless you choose to, and it's a good way to allay frustration when you've been spinning around the room for ten minutes without finding the next step in the puzzle, which may turn out to be in an area you didn't know there was any interactivity in the first place.
Overall, I'd give The Room Two a 7.5/10 rating - sometimes it's a bit of a pixel hunt and there are unfotunately few if any truly intellectually-challenging puzzles, but it's still a beautiful trip through an interesting world, and even if the puzzles are more of the 'search-and-apply' variety, there's still a sense of accomplishment in progressing through the game.

A positive review with a major caveat: This is not quite the worthy spiritual sequel to STALKER that it is made out to be.
If you're coming from STALKER, as I am, prepare to be underwhelmed. The game is nowhere near as hard as it's made out to be. I played on hardest difficulty + Spartan + ranger mode and never had more trouble than an average map in STALKER (and to the degree it *is* hard it's usually due to poor design, such as sudden scripted rushes of enemies, or poor checkpoint placement).  Anomalies are there, technically, but have little to do with gameplay.  The maps are linear.  The world is also unexpectedly bright--ambient light abounds and it's as if the developers couldn't hold themselves back from placing glowing mushrooms in every corridor. Consequently, though the game was certainly tense, I never felt afraid the way I would exploring a lab in STALKER.

The short:
Artfully crafted, often whimsical, and thought provoking, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a great example of game as a narrative, visual, and audio storytelling artform. The game is short, but is definately worth picking up. There are a few small hiccups (occasionally it can be difficult to figure out how to progress the story) and a bit of a pacing issue in the mine, but otherwise this game is gem.
9/10
The long:
As others have said, this is a short game. 5 to 6 hours for most folks if you don't reference a guide. The closest thing that comes to mind to this title is the wonderfully artful Dear Esther, though this has more interactivity.
The texture work is EXCELLENT and greatly added to the immersiveness of the fairly closed world you have access to. The game is great looking, in other words.
The pacing is relaxed and at your own leisure except for part of the mine, which some folks complain about. Though not hard, the pacing of a portion of it is... very different / somewhat jarring and may detract from the experience for some. One or two other occasions had me not sure how to progress, but generally I could figure out what to do next.
This is a more accessable example of "a game as an artform." If you like games, art, or prefer your games at your own pace and NOT running around pointing a gun at everything, this is worth catching on sale.

While I do commend the gameplay mechanics and the beautiful, detailed environments, I took serious issue with the story. Without giving away any spoilers, I'll say that the ending makes the game far less interesting than the sum of it's parts. Play if you like games like "Gone Home" but wanted more puzzles, don't play if you like games like "Gone Home" but wanted fuller stories.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a short game, but I quite enjoyed it.  It has a wonderful sense of atmosphere: beautiful environments, lovely music, and a mystery to drive you forward.  The story was smaller in scope than I originally thought, but I liked it.
The puzzles were not hard, but they were interesting enough to give me a sense that I was solving the mystery, and I genuinely enjoyed how their investigation system would bring up multiple observations and new questions, rather than just stating observable facts.
My only complaints were some bad framerate when transitioning between areas and some unnecessary backtrack at the end.  My computer only has 4GB of ram, so the game paged memory to disc pretty aggressively, but it settled down once I got to the next area.  The backtracking was not required by the game design, but rather me not knowing where to go after one particular cause-and-effect puzzle.

Played it all the way through in just one sitting, took around 4hrs. I enjoyed playing the game because the way it progresses. However I was not satisfied with the games ending. I also believe that the game should have been longer to allow the truely interesting story continue to expand.
Beautiful to look at ,  and a joy to walk around , but as for gameplay..... well soon gets boring .

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is astounding on so many levels.
Visually, it presents itself almost photorealistically. After completeing the game, I come back, over and over, simply to walk the landscape and take screen shots.
The ambience of the game is reminiscent of the old Phantasmagoria and 7th Guest / 11th Hour games from the early nineties.
Everything in the game looks meticulously hand-crafted and will make your jaw drop. Once the initial load screen has passed, the game seems to never load areas again. There is no quick travel, which upon closer reflection makes a lot of sense, as I feel it would break the immersion. The gorgeous landscapes makes the missing quick travel unimportant anyway.
I absolutely recommend this game. I am looking so much forward to the next project from The Astronauts.

If I am not mistaken there will be three to six starter commanders for the Soviets (three of those are from the deluxe version I think), the German Wehrmacht came with three to six (again three extra from the Deluxe Edition I think), the Western Front Armies add-on came with three each for US Forces and the German Oberkommando West. Saints Row IV [Steam - PS3 - Xbox 360 - Xbone - PS4]: 7.8/10
By a few people, the Saints Row series has been loosely described as the "fun GTA" to me, and I understand the analogy. Not to say GTA isn't fun, but Saints Row adds to the enjoyment by boosting the ridiculousness and humor with a "who gives a ♥♥♥♥" attitude.
This fourth installment is the first of the series I've played so far, and it wasn't long before it became a favorite of mine. Not nearly close to Metroid Prime, Majora's Mask, etc., but it ranks higher than most games I've played.
Your main character, after saving the world from a nuclear attack (I think it was a nuclear attack anyway) in the most awesomest way, became the President of the United ♥♥♥♥ing States of ♥♥♥♥ing Murica. I would say that a ultra-violent sociopath wouldn't be able to get into office, but America is about to elect Trump in. Anyway,♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down when an advanced alien race invades Earth, steals the best and brightest of the species (surely there aren't that many) and blows Earth up. He kidnaps your character, and locks you into a simulation.
As it so happens, that was a mistake. After you escape the part of a simulation where you can't control your body, you end up in a simulated NYC. And BECAUSE it's a simulation (and because one of your friends is a hacker) you not only can corrupt this simulation, but you can gain super powers as well. These super powers are unique to the series.
That's the summary of the plot, but it basically describes the entire plot anyway. The rest of the story mode is simply rescuing your team members and killing the leader of the alien race.
Throughout the story mode, you get to do missions that vary extremely. This is kind of odd, though, because the game gives you super powers only to regret doing so for the rest of the game. This is because half of the actual missions lie outside of the simulations where you're just a normal gun wielding human being. There are fun missions, like using a giant mecha suit, and not so fun missions. I'll get into those in a bit.
By far one of my favorite aspects about this game is the customization. You can be female or male, change the voice, skin color, personality, boob size,♥♥♥♥♥♥size, tattoos, clothes, etc. etc. The voice is an important one, make sure you choose the third male voice, because the cockney accent is hilarious to me. (Obviously you can choose whatever you like I don't care.) You aren't limited with normal skin tones either, you can make your skin ♥♥♥♥ing shiny blue. There are a lot of clothes, tattoos, shoes, etc. to choose from, no issues there.
The weapons are amazing. You have so many awesome and funny weapons to choose from. Awesome normal weapons would be: gold plated duel wielding desert eagles, shotgun, Robocop's guns; awesome alien weapons would be: blackhole gun, other guns I don't want to explain; and funny weapons include the dildobat and the hentaibat. Enough said.
Your super powers are also amazing. The offensive super powers go from telekesis to ice and so on, and they're quite fun to use in different situations. I quite like how there isn't one power that supersedes the others in a way that makes all others useless.
Along with the ability to customize cars (to an awesome extent), you can keep them and all of the weapons in a database for your use at any time. All you have to do is use your cellphone to have a car or gun materialize for your use.
The powers, however, do hinder the game a bit. You have the powers to run 4 times as fast as the fastest car, run on water, and fly through the air. Considering you can do this at any time, why in the world would you ever use a vehicle? You'd have to have nothing else to do to use a vehicle.
There are some side missions that are either dull or frustrating, and they come more often than not. One of the main missions parodies MGS, in that you sneak around under a box rather than killing everyone. That's fine and all, but not only did they do a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job at parodying the series, they made it really annoying too.
The game's humor helps it stand out from the GTA series. While we all know the GTA series has its own humor, this one is far more ridiculous and satirical. Not only am I talking about the dildobat, but also the dialogue. The one wrestler guy who commentated on some of the minigames was hilarious. There were points where the humor got a bit too try-hard and dry, but the overall attitude of the game makes up for that a bit.
There are several types of collectibles in the game. You can collect cars of course, but you can also collect these data things throughout the game that you use to upgrade your super powers. The one thing about those, as fun as they are to collect, there will actually be leftovers without anything to buy. This would be okay if they didn't have room for upgrading, but they did. Why can't I buy an upgrade where my powers didn't have to charge at all? There are also story monologues you can pick up that has a few characters explaining their past in relevance to the game's plot, which can be interesting if you want to know about the characters.
There's this minor annoyance I have with the game's cheats. If you use any of the cheats, the game stops autosaving. Now who in the ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ studio thought that was a good idea? Firstly, what the hell is the point if I can save manually? It just gives me a bit more work to do whenever I want it saved. Secondly, WHAT IF MY GAME FREEZES LIKE MINE DID? ♥♥♥♥ YOU. It really doesn't make sense, not ONLY did you make the cheats yourself (meaning you aren't against cheats in the first place), but I bought your game. I purchased it, meaning I can mod or use cheats all I ♥♥♥♥ing want to.

When I saw that in this game you have super powers and stuff from the start I thought it was a bad idea because it would make the game super bland and give no feeling of achievement or fulfillment and that's exactly what happens in Saints Row IV.  It didn't bother me for the first couple of hours but then it became really boring. I set the difficulty to Hard before playing due having experience from the previous game but even so, it's really easy, especially if you bought Saints Row IV in a sale with a bunch of DLC bundled together that give you additional weapons and abilities, which was the case with me (just throw that exploding ball thing at something and watch as everything explodes around you and your enemies are all dead in matter of seconds).
As someone that always tries to complete all the side quests and optional things in games, I obviously left the main plot of the game aside to complete everything and then enjoy the main dish afterwards but wow- the optional activities you do in this game are extremely repetitive. You do them in order to get upgrade points and such and they existed in The Third too but the difference is that in The Third I ignored all of them and enjoyed the main plot a lot because it was fun, while in this game the main plot is really tedious and running around the city at super speeds, flying, jumping really high, destroying everything with a fire ball and other powers is just simply boring. There are some optional things to "decorate" the game like romancing (by that I mean having sex)  with your crew members but it's completely worthless and does nothing, it's just a very short scene with them saying "oh okay, let's ♥♥♥♥" and then the screen goes black and you are back in tiny ship with nothing to do aside from going into the virtual world again to do more boring side quests that you basically already did.
The humor is pretty mediocre, while in The Third I thought it was pretty funny. I really doubt it's because my taste in humor got more refined or something because it hasn't been that long since I played The Third.
This game honestly feels like it was rushed a lot, if I had to define it in a single sentence I would say it feels like a rushed DLC for The Third. Maybe I grew a little too old to enjoy games like this or something but, I don't know, it just feels so bad and I was so disappointed that I couldn't even force myself to finish it.

Get this on sale, watch a "let's play", perhaps buy the soundtrack - Beatbuddy excels at everything it does, except the "game" part.
Beatbuddy offers great visual design, richly drawn assets and fluid animations.
Beatbuddy offers an exceptional soundtrack that will certainly keep you listening.
Beatbuddy has apparently been painstakingly patched by dedicated developers.
Beatbuddy, however, is broken by design, at least gameplay-wise.
The game seems to attempt to relate its gameplay formula to rhythmic cues and boy does everything seem really nice, in theory, until you actually start to move around. The issue is very simple, and very hard to fix for a complete game.
Automatic actions happen between set intervals, following the beat of the song - but your movements don't. This is partially fixed by the vehicular sections, that set your movements to the beat, although not responding reliably to input.
Dashes, punches and other actions happen in their own time and generate offsetting audible feedback, making controls feel even less responsive than they already are. This becomes clear since the start of the game, as soon as color-changing bubbles and spiked crabs appear.
Obstacles clear their paths within the song's rhythmic call, as you dash through 0.3 seconds later causing annoying dissonance.
Crabs swing to the beat, as you punch them as fast as you can click, ignoring any sort of timing or planning there could ever be.
Vehicle dashes are timed to the second beat! Except holding the button does the same thing, while attempting to click on-beat results in failed half-dashes.
Jellyfishes move to the beat! Move along with them in synchronicity so you can survive! Except they move less per beat than you do, forcing you to either ignore the song or smash your face every sixth beat.
The issues pile up as new elements are added, it seems.
Playing only with visual cues might actually be more helpful than attempting to follow the song.

I recommend this game but not without some big warnings, namely that if you get frustrated easily you should stay away. The dependency on the grappling hook glove is a very novel twist on the first-person platformer; however, some areas are beyond frustrating, particularly the ice cavern level later in the game. In one particular section, I spent well over an hour trying to get past it and I definitely felt my blood pressure rise after continued failures. There are also several areas where the next location is not readily apparent.
Additionally, the voice acting for the most part is horrible, especially by the man and girl who do the primary voiceovers. The voice actors for the NPCs do a good job, especially for the one girl who accompanies you for a while, but she's unfortunately a bright spot in a whole world of vocal darkness.
But even with those negatives, the game as a whole is overwhelmingly positive. It's bright and colorful, focused on the story, non-violent, and gives a significant amount of exploration possibilities. It really is a fun game. But thanks to the difficulty of some areas, you might want to take this game in steps instead of trying to knock it all out at once.

Unless this game is on sale and you're only spending a couple bucks on this, don't bother.
The game wants you to see it as a story-driven exploration game, but it doesn't really do to well on either account.
The story components are all a bit screwy. The script itself is awkward and the voice acting doesn't help. None of the voice acting sounds natural.  The movement of the characters also look rigid and un-natural. The full story just felt uninspired as well; not bad per se but it felt like they just had a vague idea and just built off of it, as is evident with Maggy (one of the three characters in the whole thing) just being a huge stereotype. Overall, the story and all things related to it just make me uncomfortable and detract from the gameplay.
So what about the gameplay? "Eh." Jumping around and grappling from flying rock thing to flying rock thing is fun. There is no getting around that. The big problem is some of the parts seem oddly unforgiving. Jumping from thing to thing is fun, but once you start falling down again and again... Well it loses that simple style of fun flying around gives you.
And although the game is based on exploration, it's super linear. Which isn't too bad until you realize that going off the beaten path just means death. The worst part is they have hidden things in levels to encourage exploration, but once you try to explore that flying mountain you'll realize it's impossible to stand on, once you try to escape the giant creature in the cave by going into the river that's resting under it you'll realize that there was no river. Only lies. And you'll fall through and die.
So what is goo about this game? the environments. They're pretty, memorable, and look unique.  I feel like this is the part they put all their effort into (and I mean all of it) and is the sole reason I can't completely bash this game, because I did enjoy looking at all the different areas. I just wish the villiages/towns were more... Fleshed out. They had some stuff that was pretty to look at, but it had no depth.
So in conclusion, the story and characters were a let down; the gameplay is frustrating, linear, and frustratingly linear in spite of good ideas; and the environments almost make it worthwhile.

Woah!  I'm amazed by Liftoff, especially considering it's early access.  It's a killer training tool for someone looking to get into quads and develop some skill and technique before burying their real gear into the dirt at 80mph.  It works perfectly with the Taranis QX7 - minimal transmitter programming and minimal calibration in Liftoff.  A regular USB cable is all I used, no proprietary dongles or the ilk.  You can also set up a standard controller to work, but be aware that controller joysticks are sprung to center, whereas normally an RC transmitter throttle axis will not be sprung, so you may want to set the throttle range to only use the positive Y axis, rather than having to hold the stick down, away from the center to achieve 0% throttle (it feels strange but it approximates a real transmitter if you don't have one or don't want to set one up.)  There're lots of in-game versions of real world quad setups and approximations for anything it doesn't have verbatim, 150 size, 250, etc., etc.  There's a good selection of courses, with what looks like more on the way from the developers and the community.  It also provides Betaflight style PID tuning.
I'm coming from a year-or-so of doing well learning to fly cheap foamboard fixed-wing planes, but yearning for that pick-up-and-fly-anywhere FPV experience that quads seem to deliver on, so I went through all the sims I could find - Liftoff is the one that does what I need.  It feels like learning to ride a bike, I've been logging a minimum of 30mins of progression every day, and I'm getting really confident surprisingly quick.  At first I was meandering high above an open field aimless and clumsy (incapable of recovery from the slightest missteps,) now I'm zooming right above the ground whipping around obstacles, making plenty of mistakes still, but able to correct for a lot of them and finish laps regardless.  I was really surprised by the tutorial, I expected something rote and boring, but the flight model feels so real and challenging that even though I was only navigating a flat grid-world with flags and gates, I was really able to focus and simply GET BETTER.  The reset after a crash is quick and doesn't feel like utter defeat, and the tutorial videos have decent advice.  Moving back to the other areas after going through the tutorial was a stark contrast - I've never had a tutorial in a game give me that much of a sense of improvement before.  It's a good feeling - I'd credit it to the work they've put into the flight model, structure, look, and feel of the game.  I'm excited to spend more time on a real quad, but for now Liftoff is a good way to train up from nothing while I spend the dark winter nights building a 270 rig in the basement.  I never thought I'd go from zero experience with quads to this confident and comfortable, this quickly!

First off let me say that i have had a rough history with early access games, but there are always a few developers who shine apart from the rest.  Lugus has put soul into this game. its not just a drone simulator. it has a lot to offer. and the developers are commited to adding more.  it has a growing community of friendly helpful hobbyists who just want to see the hobby get more popular. and the developers listen closely to bug reports, complaints and suggestions.  any major bugs i had from updates, are fixed within a week.
if you are looking for a racing game to play on your PS4 or Xbox controller, your immediate experience will be unenjoyable.
if you are looking for an entry point into RC quadcopters buying a RC transmitter and Liftoff should be your first step.
"why liftoff instead of other simulators?"
-well aside from the community, Liftoff has an extensive track creator. Which allows you and the community to create endless opportunity for races.  the blue print map allows for people to go creatively wild. and make environments from the ground up. and FPV racing clubs even recreate their own tracks within the simulator for practice.
-it has a diverse player base of many skill levels. A LOT of people play liftoff, its not hard to find a race or freestyle lobby. the game does not balance player skill, so you will find your self racing with people much faster than you. and even when you get to the point where you feel faster than most other people, someone is going to be twice as fast as that. its easy to caught up in lap times,  racing is competitve so we have to compare our selves to others, just keep in mind some people might have as much as 5 or more years of flight time than you.  its good to follow and watch the better pilots to see how they might approach a problem differently. commit it memory in practice and try to improve your times.

I played Saints Row: The Third about 2 years before playing this game and since I really liked The Third I thought it was obvious that this game would please me, but I was wrong. If you never played a Saints Row game you should know that they're basically like GTA but wackier.
In this game our protagonist is the president of the United States and the planet gets invaded by aliens, who destroy it and create a virtual world for people to live in pretty much like the Matrix. When I saw that in this game you have super powers and stuff from the start I thought it was a bad idea because it would make the game super bland and give no feeling of achievement or fulfillment and that's exactly what happens in Saints Row IV.  It didn't bother me for the first couple of hours but then it became really boring. I set the difficulty to Hard before playing due having experience from the previous game but even so, it's really easy, especially if you bought Saints Row IV in a sale with a bunch of DLC bundled together that give you additional weapons and abilities, which was the case with me (just throw that exploding ball thing at something and watch as everything explodes around you and your enemies are all dead in matter of seconds).
As someone that always tries to complete all the side quests and optional things in games, I obviously left the main plot of the game aside to complete everything and then enjoy the main dish afterwards but wow- the optional activities you do in this game are extremely repetitive. You do them in order to get upgrade points and such and they existed in The Third too but the difference is that in The Third I ignored all of them and enjoyed the main plot a lot because it was fun, while in this game the main plot is really tedious and running around the city at super speeds, flying, jumping really high, destroying everything with a fire ball and other powers is just simply boring. There are some optional things to "decorate" the game like romancing (by that I mean having sex)  with your crew members but it's completely worthless and does nothing, it's just a very short scene with them saying "oh okay, let's ♥♥♥♥" and then the screen goes black and you are back in tiny ship with nothing to do aside from going into the virtual world again to do more boring side quests that you basically already did.
The humor is pretty mediocre, while in The Third I thought it was pretty funny. I really doubt it's because my taste in humor got more refined or something because it hasn't been that long since I played The Third.
This game honestly feels like it was rushed a lot, if I had to define it in a single sentence I would say it feels like a rushed DLC for The Third. Maybe I grew a little too old to enjoy games like this or something but, I don't know, it just feels so bad and I was so disappointed that I couldn't even force myself to finish it.

This game is rediculous in many ways, although that's not uncommon for the Saints Row games.
Like the previous Saints Row games it has humor and lots of it. It's really the main reason why I play them. Many things about the game are completely over the top, but in a way that is amusing. The visuals and great voice acting contribute a lot to this. The characters are all likable and the story is interesting. If you played the previous games it ties back and revisits many of the events that have taken place earlier. As the world of which the game takes place in is more open to unreal and weird things the developers took this to heart and made some truly strange missions and events. These are mostly in the main quests.
It's the 'nature' of SRIV that makes it worth playing. It's generally just fun to play and fool around in. That's good because there are other aspects of the game that aren't so great.
Some things I don't like all that much:
Game balance is a problem.  The super powers are what I blame for this. The 'super powers' are fun at times, but they tend to make the game often too easy, and you gain them quickly. They really should reduce the effectiveness of the powers and speed at which you get them. The game is still challenging at times, but it often feels like you can swoop in and kill all the bad guys in a minute without breaking a sweat. It can be fun to be this super powerful super hero-like person (go and get a good costume to match!) but if you have all these powers and the enemies don't scale to keep it challenging the game can become less engaging. On the positive side, there are some fun mini-games that you can put your powers to good use!
The atmosphere and immersion of the game is also a problem. Things look pretty generic to me. Steel Port doesn't really feel like a place that I want to spend the time to explore. Componding this, once you get super speed and jumping powers you really don't need to spend time exploring. Just race across the map. Again, the powers are fun at times, but it detracts from the immersion of the city. Why steal a car or take time to explore when you can dash across the map and get to your objective so much faster? Furthermore, SRIV takes place in the same 'location' (or map) as Saints Row the Third does. It's pretty much exactly the same. I wish they spent the time to create a new map, like DC. If you played through the Third it makes it that less compelling to explore.
I noticed all these issues while playing, but I felt the story, characters, and just plain over-the-topness of the game kept me interested in continuing to play. They could have made the game even better if they spent more times working out the balance issues to make it more 'passively' entertaining.
Conclusion / TLDR
Overall, my recommendation is to give the game a try. The story, characters, voice acting, and main quests are fun and entertaining. I would stick to the main story quests and the character's personal quests. There are side-missions you can do, but they can get a bit repetative. The city isn't that exciting when it comes to lingering, exploring, or doing things like stealing cars. The powers are fun and convenient, but ultimately detracts from immersion and makes the game much easier as the enemies don't scale to compensate. If you're concerned about getting the best end, what you need is to complete all the chacter's personal quests before the final quest.
I also recommend playing Saints Row the Third. That game is better when it comes to parts of the gameplay that the super powers hurt in IV, and IV is a good follow-up to the Third.
