The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is the debut title from Polish developer The Astronauts founded by former People Can Fly (Painkiller, Bulletstorm) founder Adrian Chmielarz. As an adventure game with an emphasis on exploration and atmosphere without any combat whatsoever, it’s definitely a departure for the designer. The players assume the role of Paul Prospero, a detective with paranormal abilities who comes to picturesque Red Creek Valley after receiving a letter from a young boy named Ethan Carter. It is clear from the beginning that Ethan is missing, but everything else is up to you to uncover. There is no tutorial, there is no hand holding.
The most striking thing about the game from the first second is how gorgeous it looks. You start off in a dark patch of forest, but very soon you’ll reach a bridge providing a breathtaking look at the valley. It makes a strong statement for realism and art being able to co-exist in a single beautiful package. The sense of scale is impressive as well. Even though in reality this is a fairly linear game, it is designed in such a way that it gives the illusion of grand scale. It masterfully escapes that ugly feeling that you’re being pushed down a singular narrow path. This is also reflected in the puzzles and storytelling. You can solve the puzzles in any order you wish and you’ll probably even miss some as well as you go along. However, you need to solve them all if you wish to see the very ending.
There are two types of puzzles: solving a murder and experiencing a supernatural short story written by Ethan that you can find wandering about. Solving a murder revolves around finding a body and several key items and then piecing together the chronology of events which will then unfold before you. It is a really interesting and effective method of storytelling that ensures that the player feels involved in what happened even though he is just an observer. Both the murders and Ethan’s stories give small yet interesting glimpses of insight into the relationships within the Carter family and the strange and tragic events which took place. The puzzles themselves are fairly simple and the narrative is light, but the sense of immersion and atmosphere is very strong throughout. I will also provide a small hint regarding the puzzles which may prevent you from wandering around aimlessly too much. Each puzzle is a separate scene, this means that all of the necessary items and solutions regarding the puzzle are nearby, you won’t find an item in one location that you will need to use somewhere else.
The terrific soundtrack and sound design are also a big part of the great immersion and atmosphere. A haunting piano melody or the soft rustling of leaves in the wind go a long way to establish a sense of presence, you really feel like you’re there yourself. It’s a game of contrasts. Beautiful and serene in one moment, creepy and uneasy in the second. You’re trekking through an idyllic landscape only to uncover abandoned, dilapidated buildings and mutilated bodies. And it all comes together in a refreshingly unexpected ending that will give you pause and provide you with something to think about even if for only a moment.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a truly great adventure game with a fantastically realized game world brimming with clever design that will keep you motivated to uncover the secrets it hides.
8 OUT OF 10 (GREAT)

Highly recommended if you want a change in pace and love adventure games!

I am really not a fan of Two Stick Shooters/Top-down Shooters. But this got my motor going immediately when I first saw it being released on Playstation 4.
I chose to wait, because I was certain it'd be on Steam.
The day arrived. I immediately got the Digital Deluxe Edition. It contains all DLC's ever released so far. And I sure hope there will be new ones.
If you are against such games, try it anyways. You can always use the Steam return and get your money back.
What got me especially into buying this game:
- Hardcore gameplay (really punishing for little mistakes sometimes. Like friendly fire or getting crushed by an ally or even your own pod)
- Customization of your character. (choose your headdress, your clothing, even your gender)
- Stratagem system (I didn't count them, but there's a lot of them. basically pod drops. Calling in air strikes, ammo, support weapons, revival pods, even mechanized robots which you can control. Mini Titanfall, am I right? ;) )
- Weapon upgrade system (level up or gather samples of the planets to earn research points. Invest then into upgrading your favorite weapons and stratagems, which contains more ammo in weapons, or faster deploy of stratagems and longer duration of it)
- Perk system (choose perks like a laser sight, terrain boots (which make you go on a normal pace in snow and swamps which can really save your butt, contained in the terrain DLC), a jump pack, an auto injector which makes you get up faster when knocked down, and so on~)
- Planets with quests (drop down on the planet and do various objectives. Like defuse left over bombs, which you have to uncover with a "sniffer", which is a metal detector. Or find a black box/survivor and return them to the base. Or even arm a nuke, which you have to defend for a certain amount of time, which then goes off to wherever. By the way, the planets are supposedly procedurally generated - means it's a different stage layout every single time.)
- Enemy variety (there's 3 kinds of enemies. The Bugs, the Cyborgs, and the Illuminate. All of them with their own kind of units with different, really mean, attacks.)
- Leveling system (just as other games. You level up and unlock clothing, weapons, stratagems, perks )
What is upsetting about this game:
- Dying because of a stupid reason like when someone joins your game and you get their drop pod on your head. You can still see where it lands don't worry. But in the heat of the battle, sometimes you overlook it. Another reason is getting a full load of an ally who empties his magazine into you. May it be on purpose or not. Don't worry, you can be revived as often as you like, as long as there is at least 1 dude alive and it is not on cooldown.
So basically only the dying part, which WILL happen and often, trust me.
But overall, buy it. Don't think, just buy it. Go into Multiplayer and look for some nice people. It's pure fun.
Thanks for reading.

It started a few years ago on my Kindle, when The Room Two was being offered for free on the appstore. Curious, I snatched it up; I mean, who would pass up a free game? I downloaded it, started it up, and was instantly invested. The puzzles, the envirements, the story is was trying to tell that, even after playing through it several times, I still don't quit understand it. Despite jumping into the second game first, I thoroughly enjoyed it. I bought the first game when I found it on the appstore and liked it as well. Skip to present day, my boyfriend bought me both games for Christmas and I replayed them both. Remastered and on a much larger screen.
The graphics are polished, looking very nice even on low. The music is pleasent and at times disturbing. Some areas I heard whispering, breathing, chanting, one time it sounded like a monster was creeping around behind me, scratching at the walls. While this is by no means a horror game, it doesn't stop the atmostphere from getting to you. The games try to tell you a story; something about dimension hopping, I don't know. It's not entirely clear, being told solely through notes left by someone who knows you and attempts to guide you. As I've said, I've played through both games many times and still can't grasp a complete story. It may be one of those games that's meant to be theorized, or I might be missing something entirely. Even still, not knowing completely what's going on adds to the atmostphere. The feeling of being completely lost.

As for the puzzles themselves, they have a nice variation. You have easy and simple puzzles and then hard ones that leave you circling the room looking for that one detail you've missed. They range from remembering numbers or letters to catching that part of the table that doesn't quite look right and may lead to something. The more difficult puzzles aren't to the point of frustration; I never had to look up a guide on how to do them. If you're really stuck, the game's little hints are often enough to push you in the right direction.
The only real problems the game faces is that sometimes when you click on something, it zooms to what was next to it or the camera isn't quite where you want it to be. It's nothing major, you can get use to it, but something it's annoying when you're trying to see something and the camera's not feeling it. Also sometimes the game make a loud noise like something major happened or seemingly an attempt to spook you. I once opened a cabnet and the game made a loud suspenseful sound like something shocking was there but it was just bugs on display. It's kinda mood breaking to me. The Room and Room Two are both short, although the second game is a little longer. I believe a game purely filled with puzzles are good shorter and think a 6 hour game would just get boring. It may take an hour or so to complete The Room Two depending on how quick you can pick up on things.
Overall, both The Room and The Room Two are enjoyable for those who like point-and-click puzzle games. I highly recommend them both to people interested in an hour or two distraction.

It's a very good simulator. I have found a bunch of minor cons, and a lot of pros. The following are from my personal experience with this simulator (updated after 24 hours of gameplay):
Pros:
- Feels quite realistic in terms of how it flies (not 100% spot on, but close enough)
- Great for gaining muscle memory and practicing manovers
- Lots of tracks, and can be expanded by steam workshop (improvement: entire maps from workshop + a map editor or SDK to allow conversion of any maps (from other games for example))
- Controller setup was easy (as long as you have only 1 controller attached. Improvement: instead of 'Controller 1', 'Controller 2' etc, have names, such as 'Xbox controller player 1', 'vJoy Device 1' etc. Also, make it usable when there's more than 4 controllers attached)
- In-game HUD almost corresponds to what I see in my FPV headset
- The game looks great (improvement: could be more realistic (hay balls don't reflect nearly as much light, the entire environment is static etc))
- Decent training scenarios (improvement: allow using any drone in training, not only the sluggish one)
- Can build your own tracks
Cons:
- Music volume is inconsistent (the default 70% is obnoxiously loud compared to all other sounds at 100%)
- A lot of the settings cannot be changed in the pause menu (audio settings for one, in the menus, it's very hard to set the correct level, as it's not the loudness it's at in-game)
- Slider controls are inaccurate (for example camera tilt angle is a slider, which makes it nearly impossible to use a percise value, please allow manual input. My real quad has a tiny servo for camera angle, and allows for very percise settings)
- Even at fantastic graphics setting, objects tend to pop in and out of view (disturbing specially on the Hannover map, where flying in the park, benches, poles etc just pop into view)
- [minor complaint] When you crash the drone, and break a propeller (so it goes gray), it often times does not reset automatically, even though the drone is practically unflyable. Need to reach the keyboard to reset (suggestion: configuration to edit crash behavior).
- [my biggest complaint so far] There is no exclusive fullscreen. In order to play with DSR from 5K to 1440p (to get rid of aliasing effect for good), I need to set my whole desktop resolution to that. Also, exclusive fullscreen would make this game more resilient to lagspikes (for example when windows telemetry runner starts, I get a lagspike). At least have the option (it doesn't have to be default, and should be fairly easy to implement with unity engine)
- All maps are quite small. Can't do much roaming even in free flight
- No wind simulation (this should be optional)
- When I have more than 4 controllers attached, there are times it's impossible to set the right one. Also, sometimes it seems to not pick the correct controller that I used last time upon launching the game (defaults to my mouse (which has a built-in controller with 1 axis) or one of the xbox controllers).
- Ground is very slippery and strange - without applying throttle, you can turn the drone in any way you want before taking off, even at a 75 degree angle, and take off
- Some checkpoints have awkward hit detection - gates work great, but floating checkpoints can be a real hassle to hit (either detecting too large range horizontally, or not enough range vertically)
- Camera noise is a nice feature, but unfortunately it's too unrealistic for me to use (it seems to have shadows for HUD, which is something I've never seen on my FPV setup. More configuration would help)
- No replays. Your only hope is to use a screen recorder, but that's not very flexible

Flamebreak is a top down action RPG that takes some of the best elements from Binding of Isaac, FTL, and MOBAs and combines it into a game that is very fun to play.  As of this review I have a little over 30 hours into the game and suspect I will have to log another 50 or so until I experience most of what the game has to offer.
The overworld is similar to FTL in which you move from level to level and if you take too long the shadow (instead of the rebel fleet) will push you towards the end of the level.  Combat is very similar to Binding of Isaac only now you have 4 action commands like in a MOBA.  You do have the option to purchase additional skills if they appear at a shop in addition to new items, weapons, and armor that boost your stats.
Please note that this game is not a MOBA so please don’t buy it expecting it to be one.
The graphics are pleasant and combined with an amazing soundtrack help to immerse you in the world - the switch from the overworlds music to combat music upon entering a new level helps to get your adrenaline flowing.
The game is very challenging once you start playing on Hard or Nightmare difficulties (the fairy quest challenge in particular was insanely difficult) although Normal will still present a good challenge for new players.  Also, thanks to this game being a roguelite, a new world will spawn each time you start a new playthrough giving this game immense replay value.
I strongly recommend this game if you have any interest in roguelites.

This game is awesome. Similiar to the game Nuclear Throne, the combat is fast paced and while it involves dodging attacks, it is not a bullet hell like Enter the Gungeon or Binding of Isaac. Instead, you are encouraged to manipulate the terrain and enemy ai so that you are not put in a situation where too much dodging is involved.
Each enemy type has vastly different attack patterns, from ranged marksman who run if you get close, to enemies that block off areas of the battlefield with a laser that track towards your position, to bullrush charging enemies that will eat the corpses of their fallen allies to heal and go into a frenzy. Sometimes there will be more powerful versions of basic enemies in an encounter.
One of the games biggest strengths is that every time you are handed a procedurally generated encounter, the terrain and variety of enemies means that the encounter is a new challenge. This, combined with your character having a basic attack and three abilities all chosen randomly, is what makes the game so much fun to play again and again.

In a single sentence, this game is amazingly fun and I can't stop playing it.
I didn't have much experience in the rogue-lite genre before this, only playing a bit of Binding of Isaac and not really getting into that.  This, though, is a gem.  It's tough, certainly, but not unfairly tough.  It rewards skill, and the more you play it the more you learn the core patterns of both enemy movement and your own skill synergies.  Though you'll die a lot at first, you'll feel like it's your own fault, not because the game cheesed you.
At first you'll be happy to get past the first few bosses, then you'll get further, then you'll beat your first Godplane and fill thrilled, and then you'll start consistently beating your runs, and then you'll start competing for the top of the daily leaderboards, and the next thing you know you'll have spent more time on this little indie game than all the AAA games you bought during the last sale.
It's flat out fun, and it's perfect for short 5-10min coffee breaks or for longer, multi-run marathon sessions.  I've put in more than 100 hours so far and I'm just as excited as when I beat the first boss.  Perhaps the best $10 I've ever spent

Fun and positively addictive combat system. Grinding in this game is one of the best grinding experiences in ARPG. Boss battles are tricky and sometimes incredibly brutal, with an upward trend of difficulty in attack patterns and damage received from the first boss to the very last, which is always a crucial key in boss battles design.
Storyline is straightforward and fluid with epic twists (the most literal sense of 'epic'). Covers most of the important key points that explain what happens in the main series, while also leaves very much room for personal interpretation and possibly retelling.
Character designs are surprisingly intricate and interesting, considering the fact that Falcom had always been set with simplicity in all Ys titles until Ys Origin came out in 2006.
Not much needs to be said about the music. Falcom JDK Band did a fantastic job as usual. I believe the music in Ys Origin is about as well-praised as that of Oath in Felghana. Beyond the Beginning is personally my favorite track.
The only potential problem with the game is everything stays the very same throughout all three arcs, except for character combat mechanics, storyline, and minor spoiler: a true final boss. This can be boring to some people, but not to me personally.
Overall, this is definitely a very solid and highly polished dungeon-crawler ARPG from Falcom, and a worthy title to mark the big jump of the series to Ys Seven. Absolutely a huge Yes from me.

I really wanted to like this game. Unfortunately this game really wanted to hate me. On paper it's everything I like: first-person movement, no unnecessary combat, good art design and music, a mysterious short story with heart. But if you can't get the hang of the controls-- after three hours, I certainly couldn't-- the entire game is nothing but frustration. If I was playing it improperly, the game didn't give me any clue as to what I was doing wrong. Or right, for that matter. If this game wants to be about swinging, why does the main grapple mechanic yank you to ledges you can't grab? This is A Story About Hitting Your Head And Falling A Lot. At least the music is nice and calming... though that makes it seem like it shouldn't be so infuriating to play.
I think the problem is that most of the gameplay environments are tiny platforms suspended at maximum distance in empty space; with no quick way of judging relative depth, perspective, target size or distance, there's no reliable way to know how fast you're going or in what direction, or how close you are to your destination-- moving platforms are particularly hard to judge. Maybe some floating stationary particles in the air, or some kind of on-screen meter would help? The stationary skybox, while pretty, only helps you know what direction your head is pointed. Your body is only a disembodied hand. Speed lines and subtle wind clues are all you get to calculate 3D physics trajectory with precise timing. Checkpoints are the only mercy. At one point, your only friend in the game will taunt you for using your best tool... it's really defeating. If you buy this, just hope you're "more hardcore" than me, I guess.
I've beaten Mirror's Edge on every difficulty and I can finish Jumping Flash without dying so I'm no stranger to first-person platforming-- maybe it's just that those protagonists had visible feet?-- but this game never clicked with me. I'd try dozens of times to pass one checkpoint, agonizingly almost-but-not-quite-reaching the next one, only to land on it the 35th time with no idea what I'd done "right." There are no difficulty options. I got to the final level, tried for a half hour without even seeing the first checkpoint (let alone reach it) and I gave up. This makes me wonder if the game was artificially made more difficult to disguise how short it is. It also makes me think that if you get the hang of the controls and find a good flow, this game's less than an hour long. I would have preferred an easy hour than three hours of nonstop frustration. Or at least some sort of aim assist option. I don't even think it's priced too high... I just don't want to pay any money to feel that frustrated.
Maybe if I played more twitch-based super-demanding multiplayer games, I'd be used to this sort of pixel-perfect trajectory-based movement, but this game presents itself as a child's bedtime story in a peaceful world and then asks you to have the reflexes of a lifelong speedrunner. If your favorite thing about FPS games is rocket-jumping and exploiting glitches, give this a shot. As for me, I can finish Half-Life 2 in less than four hours but I couldn't finish this game at all. So I watched the ending and it turns out I had already guessed it; the developers spoil their own story by getting cute with 'hidden' text and a simple letter-substitution cipher that they show you the key for early in the game. Oh well. (They also hobble the story with some clumsy writing and awkward voice acting, but I assume it's a small team for whom English is not their first language.)
I really appreciate that they tried for something unique and emotional, but in the end the nice art design couldn't hide a super-hardcore frustration-fest with fiddly controls. Make a sequel with a main character who has a visible body and can grab ledges, and test out its difficulty curve on a wide range of gamers before you ship it, and I'll be on board. This game, though, was just too much frustration and not enough fun.

Despite what a lot of the negative reviews are saying, there's a bundled DLC option that gives you all the packs for a discount, which compared to the collector's edition is only about $5 USD more expensive. It's not very visible on the main page, you can find it by clicking on an individual piece of DLC and looking at the related items. I definitely don't think this game deserves negative reviews for having a slightly misleading Steam page (may not even be the devs fault, and they seem to be extremely passionate about this game).
That aside, the game is an extremely fun coop twin stick shooter, reminiscent of Left4Dead and Alien Swarm. I've been playing with random people and I've been having as much fun as I've had with friends (even moreso sometimes). It's unforgiving in its difficulty and it's a pleasure to play. Finding the right load out and strategies for the different varieties of planets and missions is a real challenge. The netcode is rock solid (compared to the cluster♥♥♥♥ that Magicka online was), and the developers seem relatively active in patching and releasing new content (it's been out for a year on PSN and has had two major updates, plus the DLC).
Having a bunch of the content locked behind DLC is a little concerning, but I've bought a few pieces and it doesn't seem to give me a huge advantage over the base content. They're pretty much sidegrades, and anyone who hasn't bought the DLC will have a great and competitive time regardless. The top review (at the moment) cites the tank as something you can't get without buying the DLC. It's true, but the tank is also remarkably useless compared to other strategies. I suppose if you really really want to drive a tank you're stuck for options, but it's by no means a pay to win scenario.

As i already thrown out a lot words lets explain them a bit to get the "Title" straight and right down as that as it is~
Team-based
Helldivers is a very very very hard game if you really lay hands on to try playing it all solo - and i guess that will not really ever happen. Reading that this game is actually created from the devs of "Magicka" let you maybe think "oh this will be funny" but no. Twin-Stick Top-Down Shooter
I guess this words are more explained by themself. The game playes best on a Controller. It is from the Top-down view (Like the most of this kind, like Alien Swarm) and is a really great shooter.
So in my view, Helldivers is really worth playing if you enjoyed Alien Swarm/ Breed or this kind of shooters. If you also enjoyed the Magicka series you might enjoy this lil gem of gaming too. It is simple to understand but hard to play - at least if you play solo. So i recomment this game to play it with friends (at least 1 ;P) and people who enjoyed Alien Swarm or a like. * The mechanics are fun, I had a blast shooting things - it was challenging but not off-putting. I played on the normal difficulty (one up from easiest).
* The atmosphere is amazing, portrayed really well.
* I had lots of fun throughout the whole thing. When I find a game I like I end up tired as I can't stop playing it. There were a few nights where I went to bed a couple of hours later than I should have.
* Perfect amount of scares for me. Some sections had me on the edge of my toes but it really added to the atmosphere and story.
On the down side there are a couple of things that annoyed me a little:
* Check-point saves - I f'ing hate these. In games that have moral choices, and small side quests, these should be mandatory. I do not want to replay sections because I took the path that progresses the story rather than the one with exploration or side quests.
* Moral choices - these aren't apparent, and without saves I didn't even bother. Instead I just watched the "other" ending on youtube. I don't particularly want to replay the game with a walkthrough telling me to take the left path first.
* Some mechanics aren't obvious, I didn't know you could recharge your flashlight or night vision goggles until 80% of the way through the game.
* Game works, F^&k gameworks - turn of phys-x if you have an amd card. On my 390x, I had a locked 60fps with 0.5 AA, tesselation down one setting and phys-x off. Game is still beautiful.
I would give this game a 7.5/10. If it allowed me to save when I wanted to I would have explored alot more and made sure I made the correct moral choices, making it a 9/10.

Summary: Lots and lots of mechanical puzzles (like the original The Room), essentially no dialog. Hints are reasonably good, my biggest complaint is the pixel hunting to find the location that I need to double-click to zoom in on to use (like a small lever or knob). You don't need to have played the original since the storyline is less important, although there's no explanation of the diffraction glass in this game (i.e. the "see through" lens) so I could see it being confusing to someone who didn't play the first.
"I'm following a trail of bread crumbs that have been left out for me"
Before you start on this game, set the screen brightness to 10 in the options menu (it's separate from the other graphics options). The settings are dark, and you might miss some subtle clues otherwise.
There's probably 5 hours of puzzles in the game, more or less depending on how quickly you solve the puzzles. I found it useful in the tougher puzzles to exit the game and set it aside for awhile instead of clicking through all the hints right away.
"Or maybe I'm in Hell. That's okay, I'm not scared of Hell. It's just Heaven for bad people."
The majority of the puzzles are using hidden sliders/knobs/latches/etc so that you can get to the next hidden slider/knob/latch/etc. As such much of the game is linear. The hints system usually gives you a series of three clues, the first being what the next objective is ("it would be nice to get into that cabinet"), what the puzzle involves ("I wonder what the numbers on the table means") and finally a near-spolier for how to solve the puzzle. It doesn't actually give you a solution, but there's enough information to make a good attempt at the puzzle with the final hint. I had to use the hints for about 10% of the puzzles, most of that being when I didn't have an idea what I should do next.
"This is somebody's game and I can't stop playing a game that eveybody else has lost."
One criticism is that the hot-spots for zooming into things are not always clear, and I had to use the hints when I needed to be certain that there was hot spot somewhere there.
Seriously, if you like puzzle games get both this and the original -- they are steals at a few bucks apiece. 10/10

Beatbuddy is a charmer of an action-adventure, where you help a tadpole-seacreature-whoknows thing stop an evil moustached prince from stealing all the music from the land..err sea.
Whilst it's not the most challenging as an action or puzzle game, it does provide a good few hours of gameplay.  Backdrops have an aquatic cartoon feel, perspective shifts smooth and well, but it's the music that's the feature - not just the selection, but the way in which the designers have integrated rhythm into the game.
Much of the flora and fauna in the game both move along with the beat and in some cases provide percussion.  It's a charming experience and it's easy to find yourself stopping just to listen and watch them  all do their thing.  Being in time also helps in moving around and in solving some of the parts of the puzzles.  Even the beatboxing that musically represents the character dialogues fits in well.
On the downside, it's a little short and it's a little easy, but if you want a few hours chilled gameplay, then you can't go wrong.

Is awesome visuals and great music alone enough to sell a game? Not to say Beatbuddy offers nothing else but that was my first thought as I spotted this brilliant looking game. It seems to me often indy games either focus on game play or art and usually sacrifice one for the other. It is an unfortunate decision when it comes to the meager budgets such studios often have to work with. Beatbuddy certainly focuses on the visuals with some amazing eye candy that I can tell was lovingly crafted by a very hard working artist and on top of that it incorporates some amazing music into it as well.
So the game looks amazing and features some pretty good music. But the ultimate question we always have to ask ourselves, how fun is it? Visuals are great but in my experience after a few hours of playing the wow-factor always wears off no matter how pretty the game is. At that point I just focus on the whole purpose of the game, playing it! Steam classifies Beatbuddy as a “Casual Indie Platformer Action Adventure” game. And while it does fit into the extremely generic Action Adventure classification, platformer seems not to do the game justice. Was Echo the Dolphin a platformer? That is what reminds me most of Beatbuddy’s gameplay style. And it is refreshing to see something similar with your little Beatbuddy swimming around the world rather than jumping from platform to platform. If anything its more of a puzzle action game as you traverse the beautiful looking water caves of ‘Symphonia’.
Part of me feels like there was some sort of checklist over in Threaks’ development studio. What does a good action puzzle game have to have? Launch springs? Check. Vehicle sections? Check. Teleporters? Check. Dashing Combat? Check. Collectibles? Check. Open and closeable doors? Check. Moveable walls? Check. While nothing is particularly ground breaking it is certainly full of your typical puzzle elements. The vehicle section seems to offer the only really unique little caveat with your vehicle only being able to shoot in one direction and you have to find these arrow points to rotate you around so you can blast through different parts of the maze. Overall it’s a pretty good set of puzzle game components but I have one annoying complaint. Beatbuddy introduces one element at a time and gives you time to master each element before adding a new. This is a good idea and all but I feel they take too much time introducing new elements. Because of this the first 4/5 of the game feels like little more than a long drawn out tutorial where you master each element and then mix it in with some old element, then move on.
This makes the first few levels feel incredibly unchallenging. Frankly I was starting to get bored but kept plowing through anyway. The visuals and music were almost enough to make up for the slow increase in complexity but the game was really lagging halfway through. Yet when I reached the last level and all the different complex systems were used together, the game was really quite fun. The only problem was I had about 45 minutes of fun after about 4 hours of meh. If the game had kept going, had a few more levels with all the toys in them, I’d have been really really happy with this game. Yet it left me somewhat disappointed when it ended. And the game is really much too short. Even though I was taking my time (flower sniffing as my MMO friends would say) I still completed the whole game in under 5 hours. That seems a bit of disappointing value for the $15 cost of entry even with the great music and visuals. Hell, you know a game might be too short when there’s an achievement for beating it in under 3 hours!
The music system however is really quite good. I actually hope mainstream game developers might take a few chapters out of Beatbuddy’s book here. Each level (or track) has a unique song that flows in the background and changes dynamically based upon what you are doing. It will kick up into full gear when you’re in a vehicle or lulls back to a simple beat when you’re just mellowing in empty water. It is further enhanced as enemies add their own tracks that work into the rhythm of the song. This gives me ques as to upcoming enemies such as snare drums means I’m going to be running into some spike guys soon or a throbbing base drum means there’s a springy thing around. The best use of this is the snail mounted turrets that shoot at you in beat to the song. It’s really quite clever and makes me really feel the rhythm as I try to dodge deadly flying objects.
For the most part I felt like Beatbuddy might be too easy. The game is incredibly forgiving most of the time with your character able to take many hits and plentiful sources to replenish health abound (heck your vehicle automatically restores health after just a couple seconds). None of the puzzles are mind bendingly difficult and only one or two near the end even take more than a few moments of thought to figure out. I almost feel like the developers didn’t want you to have any troubles in seeing their beautiful art/music project and made sure the game did not get in your way. There are a couple places that I got a little frustrated at but nothing so bad as to make me rage quit and generally I was able to figure out a way forward and continued my progress.
While the game seems fairly well polished I did run into a few blemishes along the way. The intro and ending cut-scenes (which featured a horribly annoying beat-bop voice that I just wanted to strange!) had a white border around the hand drawn visuals. And then the caption, in white, bled over the border making it hard to read what was said. Since the voice was trying too hard to be beat-ish I could hardly understand was was said either. Also I found a few places when running from a collapsing ceiling (check) where I would get stuck. The ceiling collapsed down then stopped and locked me in a small box with no escape and I ended up having to quit and launch the game again to go back to the most recent checkpoint. For that matter, checkpoints? I thought we were past that ancient system! Another thing that really drives me bonkers is the camera constantly zooming in and out. I wish they’d pick a zoom level and stick to it, preferably far enough away that I can see where the hell I’m going rather than the tight shots that make it far too easy to get lost.
Also don’t look for much in terms of story here. I think there might have been somebody somewhere with a nice story but almost none of it is portrayed in the game. It feels like it was ripped out of your typical tropes, some army invades some temple, kidnaps the princesses, and you have to rescue them. Also once you finally catch up to the end boss don’t expect some climactic final fight, the ending is more anti-climactic than doing laundry.

Story: 3/10
Value: 4/10
Overall: 6.2/10

This is probably the most lovingly made and beautiful game (art direction not polygon count or any dumb stuff like that) that I have ever seen. Bioshock Infinite was my favorite gaming world before this and I still love Columbia for its Steampunk beauty but this is something else. The effort and dedication put into each level and set-piece is astounding coming from an Indie developer. Also, there is no combat so far so there is more time to let the beautiful setting take you away (unlike Bioshock Infinite where almost constant combat did not leave enough time to enjoy the beauty of the city). Before objectives you can run free and explore the villages and whatnot where every little detail put into the world makes it worthwhile. Also, there is no stress of combat put upon the player so this is a truly relaxing experience. Now for the gameplay itself. The gameplay is simply platforming and grappling hook puzzles that manage to be challenging while not too punishing. Certain puzzles may leave you frustrated at times but when you overcome the obstacle you feel accomplished. However, one small mistake leaves you to die and a slightly miscalculated jump will end your life. Thus, the game becomes slightly challenging. Furthermore, the game is beautifully narrated as a father telling a child a bedtime story and the childhood mysticism with foreign lands and new experiences is beautifully realized in an almost Seussian manner. In the story, I noticed subtle commentry by the narrator on topics such as racism and over-pollution of earth which I found very interesting. Throughout the narration, you feel the narrator pining for love from a father figure, even going as far as to relate to other species, which he says shouldn't be normal, being as they are, frog people (thus the commentry on racism). Overall, "A Story About My Uncle" is an absolutely amazing game from very skilled developers with many endearing qualities and is absolutely worth every single penny and more.

Ys Origin is a Japanese action RPG that is a prequel to it's many previous installations in the Ys franchise, taking place 700 years before the events of the original. You can choose between three playable characters with their own distinctive combat style and skills and each one of them offers a different story perspective. This is also the very first YS game without Adol Christin being the protagonist.
- A good story to introduce you into the world of Ys
- Three storylines with different characters which show you different perspectives
- Different characters also use completely different skills and weapons
- Fast paced and challenging action combat
- Four difficulties with the higher ones being a real challenge
- Decent amount of challenging boss fights
- The option of grinding monsters until bosses become manageable
- Simple and easy to understand controls, best played with a controller
- Clean yet beautiful 2D rendered environments that have a 3D feel
- Character sprites in gorgeous pixel style
- Memorable soundtrack that will stick to you even after you have finished the game (I highly recommend checking out the YS Origins super arranged version)
- Boss Rush, Time Mode, Arena Mode
- 15 to 35 hours of playtime depending on your playstyle
Certainly one of the best action RPGs on steam and despite it's age, is still hella good looking. I recommend this game to any fan of the YS franchise and JRPG fans in general. Also make sure to check out all the other YS games already available on steam.

For those of you not put off by those things, Ys Origin is a wonderul throwback to simpler times. I can't promise you'll enjoy it but I sure did.

I recently reviewed this game for my game review blog, Five Penny Review. If you enjoy this review, please visit my page:
What sets this game apart?
The Ys series has been a popular action RPG franchise since 1987, but has only had limited release in the US.  Ys Origin serves as a prequel to the rest of the series chronologically, but is one of the most recent releases in the series.    While the combat sometimes seems more like a hack-and-slash action game than an RPG, there is a sense of strategy and patience required in some areas, especially boss fights, which maintains a more cerebral element in the game.  In addition, there are some good platforming sequences and simple puzzle elements that add enough variety to keep the game from feeling monotonous by breaking up the combat sequences.
What is the difficulty factor?
This game is extremely simple to pick up and play.  It features the choice of mouse and keyboard controls featuring point and click movement, or you can control your character with just the keyboard when more precision is needed.  Personally, I only use the mouse when I have a slice of pizza in my left hand.  When new powers are unlocked, brief tutorial screens pop-up to explain their use, and most of them feel fairly intuitive anyway.  The game also does a fairly good job of offering direction, feeling fairly linear except for a few brief moments, often due to dialogue from the NPCs.
With that being said, this game is not without its challenging points.  The bosses tend to be extremely powerful, at least until you master the patterns of their attacks.  Even then, they require some precision movement and possibly some level grinding to survive.  For those familiar with the bullet-hell genre, you may find yourselves following a familiar strategy of focusing on not getting hit, only taking attacks when you have the rare opportunity.  The rest of the game is fairly tame, although if you let yourself get impatient or careless you will likely end up dying.  Save often.
Does it use media effectively?
I feel a bit torn regarding the visuals of this game.  The cut scenes use a great mix of 3-D and anime style graphics and are usually gorgeous to look at.  The hand drawn character art used during dialogue is on par with many other games, although the character designs feel a bit stale, like you’ve seen them all used before.  The sprites for the characters have an odd, compressed feel to them, looking more like dwarves than the anime style drawings used outside of gameplay.  The game also uses an odd semi-locked camera at three-quarter view, but the level designs do a good job accounting for this.
The music in this game is phenomenal, playing on both the classical and rock aspects of traditional game music to keep every fight intense.  One thing that struck me was the lack of voice acting in the game, which I feel could have done a lot to enhance the overall experience of the game, especially during some of the longer cut scenes that can break the momentum of the game.
Best moment in the game?
Without a doubt, the star of Ys Origin is the boss fight experience.  Every boss fight seems bigger and more epic than the last, and each one requires better timing and more complex movement to follow its pattern.  Off hand, I really enjoyed the giant centipede boss, Nygtilger, playing as Yunica.  It wasn’t necessarily the hardest boss, but the amount of movement and explosions, coupled with the amount of time you spend climbing on it made it a really fun experience.
Who needs to play this game?
While it doesn’t have as many exploration or story elements as many other games of this genre, Ys Origin’s saving grace are its gameplay and music.  Each character has a very different feeling to its playthrough, including some alteration of the level design and especially the bosses, greatly increasing the playtime on this game.  With scalable difficulty and already difficult bosses, it can also prove a suitable challenge for players seeking it, or to encourage subsequent playthroughs.  Personally, while I enjoyed the game, I am glad I picked it up while it was on sale.  If it sounds like your cup of tea, I would wait for the next Steam sale to roll around to pick it up.

There are more and more games that are tagged “walking simulator” nowadays. Sometimes they are pretty, sometimes they aren’t. Sometimes they have great game mechanics apart from just being virtual tourism, sometimes they don’t. Story-wise, they could be good or bad. I have to say, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter has all of these.
Upon starting the game it felt like I was really walking in a forest on abandoned train tracks. Many games I have played are “pretty”, but usually you’ll notice something out of place, some texture that doesn’t fit into place, something unpolished. Ethan doesn’t have this problem, the scenery is all very realistic and quite gorgeous - it’s quite clear the devs took great care on the quality. If you’re getting this game because you heard it’s very aesthetically pleasing, that’s one criteria down.
Performance wise, I had some micro-stutters (which seems to be a somewhat common issue and is addressed in the main FAQ on the forums). But I’m running it maxed out, and it doesn’t happen often, capping it at 60 fps for me seemed to fix the issue, but I’m not completely sure if that was the only thing. Otherwise, the game has proved to run very smoothly.
The story is really immersive - it’s not quite linear and you’re allowed to to play most parts in whatever order you choose. To get to the endgame, the game makes sure you have to have come across all necessary pieces of information to do so, but before that, it’s pretty open world. It also tells you what you’ve missed, before the end, so you can go back and gather the missing information without wasting time, something I really appreciated in the design.
Now the gameplay -you are actually here to solve mysteries, and you have to carefully explore and observe to do so. I’m very impressed with the way the game lets the player do so - it seems very natural, a good contrast to some very forced mystery games (where you “randomly combine everything in the inventory to try to advance the story”).
I do have some gripes with the game - there are some very helpful things with the controls I could have benefitted from knowing, but at the same time, a tutorial doesn’t seem to fit too well in the atmosphere the game is trying to create. So I suggest new players browse or ask for some beginner tips (not too much in case of spoilers), it did cause me frustration because I didn’t know of some mechanics at all till I had to read a guide. Overall, this frustration lasted for a while in the middle of the game but after getting past that, the game delivered so well all was forgiven!
To be honest one of my favorite “walking simulators” has been Gone Home, or something similar - great visuals and storytelling, some puzzle solving elements. Ethan added on my expectations with greater scope and deeper gameplay elements, which makes it quite a full fleshed adventure/ mystery game in my books rather than just a “walking simulator”, now. So unless you’re expecting a guns blazing, action packed game, Ethan should meet your expectations in many good ways.

Short version of the review.
7/10. Flawed, but still worth the asking price if you like story driven games. (Hint: If you don't like them, do not buy it)
Long version below.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a gorgeous, completely story driven game with some rough flaws, but still completely worth the asking price despite being a measely 3 hours to complete on my first blind playthrough. The atmosphere is fantastic and drives home a lonely, empty setting that is decently fun to explore. However, this game has some very apparent flaws, which despite me enjoying the overall game, stood out.
The game world is large, very large and open. While this gives a feeling of freedom, it can also lead to you getting confused as to where to go next. While the majority of the game is fairly straightforward, they do not lie when they said the game will not hold your hand. So this is less of a flaw, and more of a minor annoyance for players like me who insist on checking every corner, looking for extras (and ironically I missed the sole extra in the game).
This game also suffers a fairly glaring pacing issue, some of the scenes are played out quite dramatically while others are fairly relaxed, without spoiling anything, the third scene in the game plays out as if it were the finale, only to drop you right back into the game world upon completion. More of a personal gripe with me, as it made the ending fairly obvious to anyone paying attention. However the game does a good job keeping you guessing as to whether your prediction is right up to the very end (which is was, but this isn't a huge deal to me).
Finally the mine. this is a minor spoiler, but wholly unimportant to the plot, but none the less if you don't want even the tiniest of spoilers do not read any further. My final score is above, so you don't need to worry about missing any crucial bits of the review.
The mine scene contains an unwarrented jump scare, which completely ruined the entire level for me. The game in no way needed this win/loss state to justify it, as the whole game had been played perfectly fine without it. To me it felt cheap, especially considering how well the game built it's atmosphere up until that point. For some reason the developer decided to make the game Amnesia the dark desent for one level, and it just felt completely out of place.
All in all, I think it deserves the 7/10 and I could easily see mystery fans buying this for $20. A lot of people disagree with the pricing, but in all fairness people will happily pay $20 for a movie that only lasts 2 hours and has no interactivity.

I'll say that this is a very good game, but not my type. I got it on sale and wanted to try it, and I'm glad I did.
Firstly, if you can't sit through a long turn based game, don't waste your money, this isn't for you.
Buuuuttttt, if you can, this game is really great. The whole point of this game is elimination or domination... you vs. the other civilizations on the map. It doesn't get more strategy intensive than this. You must manage economics, infrastructure, diplomatic relations, wars, and even the culture of your civilization all at once. At times it feels like 5 gangsters trying to mug you at once... you punch out 4 and the other 1 shoots you in the face. You have to be able to look at the big picture from early on, or you will just wast your time.
And that's a lot of time. One game can take an entire day... sometimes more. On one hand this game can feel long and monotonous (take breaks). On the other hand, this length gives a sort of epic feeling... like this is all worth your time.
The real gem in this game is the multiplayer. Having all your friends (at least a couple friends required for this) bring their PC's to your house and filling the room with food and soda is the perfect setup for an awesome day. Fight to the death with them as you engage in a satisfying, crushing, and friendship shattering battle of wits. The winner gets bragging rights, and everyone else will be salty for weeks.
So why do I ultimately not love this? Turn based is just too slow for me. I can't do it. I can, however, appreciate that this is a great game. All in all, I'd say 7/10, but would strongly reccomend.

Despite what a lot of the negative reviews are saying, there's a bundled DLC option that gives you all the packs for a discount, which compared to the collector's edition is only about $5 USD more expensive. It's not very visible on the main page, you can find it by clicking on an individual piece of DLC and looking at the related items. I definitely don't think this game deserves negative reviews for having a slightly misleading Steam page (may not even be the devs fault, and they seem to be extremely passionate about this game).
That aside, the game is an extremely fun coop twin stick shooter, reminiscent of Left4Dead and Alien Swarm. I've been playing with random people and I've been having as much fun as I've had with friends (even moreso sometimes). It's unforgiving in its difficulty and it's a pleasure to play. Finding the right load out and strategies for the different varieties of planets and missions is a real challenge. The netcode is rock solid (compared to the cluster♥♥♥♥ that Magicka online was), and the developers seem relatively active in patching and releasing new content (it's been out for a year on PSN and has had two major updates, plus the DLC).
Having a bunch of the content locked behind DLC is a little concerning, but I've bought a few pieces and it doesn't seem to give me a huge advantage over the base content. They're pretty much sidegrades, and anyone who hasn't bought the DLC will have a great and competitive time regardless. The top review (at the moment) cites the tank as something you can't get without buying the DLC. It's true, but the tank is also remarkably useless compared to other strategies. I suppose if you really really want to drive a tank you're stuck for options, but it's by no means a pay to win scenario.

Reading that this game is actually created from the devs of "Magicka" let you maybe think "oh this will be funny" but no. I completely suck at this game, but I always have a good time playing it. I've only recently bandwagoned onto the franchise and while I may never amount to the skill and experience of those who've been playing it since '96 I still enjoy the abundance of awesome/hilarious moments match after match. The joy it provides is so pure and simple yet the game itself has so much depth. It never stops being fun and also enticing to dig deeper into. The map and mode variety is greater than any other shooter I've played.
Though the community is small, it's (for the most part) a joyous one to be among. I've read comments and reviews claiming that the community is hostile and unwelcoming to newcomers and while that might be true for some servers, most of the larger ones I play on consist of people just there to have a good time.
If your interest is soley competitive then you might face some frustration finding equally skilled players to practice against, be prepared for a long learning curve and countless humiliating defeats.  You can also play against bots on any map/mode of your choosing. I for one just enjoy the whole experience, win or lose. It's common for modern games to reward you with progression/loot treadmills to keep players hooked, but Quake Live isn't about that. It's about gameplay that fully engages, challenges, and entertains you at all times. If you can grasp the appeal of that, you'll have a good a time.
My biggest gripe is that besides FFA, Duel and Clan Arena there aren't many (if any at all) servers running other modes. I'm too lacking in experience to enter a Duel, and I'm not a fan of waiting to respawn in Clan Arena, so that means I spend most of my gametime in FFA. I completely understand that with a game that's been around this long the players who've experienced it all will migrate to what they like best, but as a newer player it leaves your options limited. Despite that, I really wish Bethesda would put some money into marketing this game. In an era of countless tactical military shooters Quake Live deserves to stand out. My hope is that when Quake Champions officially releases (with all modern bells and whistles), Quake Live won't be abandoned, but instead garner more attention and remain active side by side with it as a pure alternative. I hope this game never dies.

This game is pretty damn good! I tend to complain a lot, even about games I like. This though.. find much to complain about this. I'll try, though: the soundtrack is really dull, the flash when a fight starts hurts my eyes, some skills are probably weaker/stronger than others, and the game *could* have more content.
That's pretty much it. Otherwise, I love this. I like Binding of Isaac a lot, and this is just as good, though different. Obviously Isaac has more content at this point, after an expansion and Rebirth, but this game is so *solid*. The controls are good, the mechanics are good.. uhh, it's all good.
My favourite thing though is how the items/skills are designed. They're all different, more than just numbers. There's relatively little overlap, every skill is mechanically different and feels different. There's very little overlap (like, say, fireball/frost ball/lightning ball in some games), and they're all useful (though I admit I hate getting a few of them. Screw Blizzard).
Items come mostly in sets of three, get the full set and get a really strong effect (like +50% ability power multiplier, ignore a hit every 11 seconds, get a powerful summon..). The set effects are all different, and nearly every one is good for some build/skillset (I say nearly only because I'm not sold on Phoenix set's flight, yet).
I just love when a game is actually well designed. Too many games slap a bunch of effects and call it a day, without actually thinking how things work together.

rating: not worth playing
The only thing which is fun about this game is to look at it because it looks gorgeous, but it is a bad game, not terrible, but its not worth your time. There are so many other games you could play even if you are someone who plays tons of games.
The story isnt bad as far as I played, but it is also not really motivating or interesting. Whats really weird is how the story is connected to the gameplay. The game tells you in the beginning that it does not hold your hand, which is weird it sounds like they are praising themselves for that, and first that sounds like a good thing but these devs did not understand what holding your hand means.
As the player I did not understand at all why I am doing what I was doing in this game, or what the point of investigating these murders are and especially the game doesnt explain any of its mechanics. The problem about this is that the character you are playing as DOES know all of that. He knows that he has special abilities, but I dont know how to use them and that doesnt make sense. A game has to explain its mechanics, basic ruleset.
Look at Dark Souls, Half-Life 2 or Portal 2. Those game do not hold your hand, but explain and teach the player how to use its mechanics.
The funny thing is this game doesnt even have many mechanics, actually you could call it a walking simulator with a little bit of clicking. Exploration seems attractive at first, but there is nothing to find.
The most weird thing about this game is that I didnt investigate the first murder, because I had no idea what to do, but I also dont have to do it. You can just walk past everything and you might even not know that you missed stuff. And that makes the game pointless to me, if these things dont matter for the game why should I do them?
I cant recommend this to anyone.

I've seen a few flame wars started from this game, so straight out of the gates I will say this game is NOT for someone who wants a long linear or even free roaming adventure rpg.
With that said, if you're looking for a game with a story that you have to wrap your head around and piece together, then maybe this game is for you! I'm a huge psychological anime fan and occult mystery lover, so I fit right into the story telling and the fact that I was a "famous occult detective" that was asked to investigate "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" made it catch me from the opening sequence. Also honestly if you're good at deducing a mystery (like a detective *hint hint*) then the things fall into place and start to give you that mystery solving satisfaction as if you're slowly solving the murder mystery of the century!
Beyond the whole I <3 mystery part,
The game scores an 8 out of 10 with me
Pro's
- Graphics are beautiful, I'm on med graphics and still felt compelled to take screenshots
- The mystery kept me wondering what is the cause? How will it end?!
- Gameplay is a welcomed change from the recent norm. No blaring markers saying "ITEM HERE! DROP OFF HERE!"
- Environment felt stressful and edgy yet mysterious and relaxing all at the same time
- Soundtrack is mysterious as well
Con's
- It is pretty short if you rush it, I can counter argue it with the brain wrapping and speculation you can give it... But it still is a pretty short game.
- Is confusing sometimes, if you are quick to get frustrated or don't have allot of time, maybe consider passing on this one or going in with a guide.
- Still coming out with regular updates and fixes, I feel as though it's a one play game and I may be wrong if they make more stories based around the universe and release it. But once I'm done I don't think I am going to come back unless to re-live the mystery gameplay when I get nostalgic.
- Characters feel distant unless you can get into the story and piece together who they are and what they are doing. Like I said before, maybe not a game for someone who doesn't really piece information together creatively and decisively.
With all that said I really loved this game myself and will be looking forward to more work like this, pick it up and give it a try if you wanna play something a little more on the out there side!

This is probably the most lovingly made and beautiful game (art direction not polygon count or any dumb stuff like that) that I have ever seen. Bioshock Infinite was my favorite gaming world before this and I still love Columbia for its Steampunk beauty but this is something else. The effort and dedication put into each level and set-piece is astounding coming from an Indie developer. Also, there is no combat so far so there is more time to let the beautiful setting take you away (unlike Bioshock Infinite where almost constant combat did not leave enough time to enjoy the beauty of the city). Before objectives you can run free and explore the villages and whatnot where every little detail put into the world makes it worthwhile. Also, there is no stress of combat put upon the player so this is a truly relaxing experience. Now for the gameplay itself. The gameplay is simply platforming and grappling hook puzzles that manage to be challenging while not too punishing. Certain puzzles may leave you frustrated at times but when you overcome the obstacle you feel accomplished. However, one small mistake leaves you to die and a slightly miscalculated jump will end your life. Thus, the game becomes slightly challenging. Furthermore, the game is beautifully narrated as a father telling a child a bedtime story and the childhood mysticism with foreign lands and new experiences is beautifully realized in an almost Seussian manner. In the story, I noticed subtle commentry by the narrator on topics such as racism and over-pollution of earth which I found very interesting. Throughout the narration, you feel the narrator pining for love from a father figure, even going as far as to relate to other species, which he says shouldn't be normal, being as they are, frog people (thus the commentry on racism). Overall, "A Story About My Uncle" is an absolutely amazing game from very skilled developers with many endearing qualities and is absolutely worth every single penny and more.

A sourcemod dating back to '09, a competitive tactical shooter with three classes, each defined by armor, mobility, available weaponry, thermoptic camouflage time, and vision mode. A beautiful world based on not-quite-GitS-don’t-sue-us aesthetic and the (rarely heard) atmospheric soundtrack sell the mood of the game when you’re hunting/being hunted in a game of cybernetic cat and mouse. It's tactical, harsh, and surprisingly fast-paced when you least expect it.
[replace * with u]
When the silence breaks and the fully automatic .50 caliber bullets start flying, you find yourself in a situational rock-paper-scissors matchup. Situational as in there is a hierarchy of “Support beats other classes in well-lit open battles”, “Assault can easily eliminate moving Recons”, or “cloaked Recons will have the ambush advantage in darker areas.” But these rules don’t always hold true. Depending on the lighting a Support can shut down a Recon’s ambush, an Assault can nade an entrenched Support, and a Recon could, well, there are a lot of risky options Recon can pull out of nowhere.
Communication with your team is paramount to success, spanning from enemy callouts, requesting/offering flanking support from teammates, warning of traps/ambushes, using the objective flag to actively mark all enemies in a 50 meter radius, or just hiding in a corner with a friend and talking about mopeds.
Being based on as old of a version of source as it is, there’s a fair amount of jank in the game. Hit registration is ■■■■, made even worse by ping and higher movement speeds. Leaning doesn’t always work if you're close to walls or short fences. Aiming down sight doesn’t exist, you get some zoom and a reticule instead for anything that isn’t a sniper rifle. Recoil is a random dispersal cone after the first shot, really primitive system that can put a bad taste in your mouth.
Some of that jank works for the game when it comes to movement. You’ve got wiggle walking, wall running, and some serious bunnyhopping. The playerbase is a ghost town outside of NA/EU evening hours, joining
is necessary to find out when other players are on.
All this makes it a difficult game to get into with long-time legacy players shutting down the unaware, but if you can get past that there’s a SOLID core gameplay that’ll keep you thinking and guessing. Looking at my friends who’ve played recently, the 22 of us have logged 331 thousand hours on Steam, averaging out to 15 thousand hours each. The game did something right, that or we all did something terribly wrong.
This is more 'Ghost In The Shell' than 'First Assault' is.

Well here we are a few days into June 2012, and the gaming year couldn't be going better.. E3 is in full swing, with publishers announcing their latest and greatest titles. However quite frankly I'm finding myself distracted from all the excitement. Why, do you ask? It's because I have found my personal Game of The Year, and I don't think anything else that could come out right now could possibly top it. You can take your Diablos, your Modern Warfares, your Max Paynes, and you can file them all away for some other time and place. I'm too busy saving the ancient land of Ys from demonic hordes hellbent on the destruction of humanity!
It has been a mere three months since XSEED made their Steam debut with the smash hit Ys: The Oath in Felghana. In that short time their crack squad of programming gurus and translation wizards have been working overtime to bring us more Ys goodness, and this time they've takes us back to the beginning with Ys Origin. This entry in the series is actually a prequel, taking place 700 years before the events of the first Ys games. This of course means that Adol Christin has to sit this round out, however do not despair! This time around we have THREE playable characters to fill out the roster, and each of them brings their own story and unique gameplay style to the table.
If you have played a Ys game before (and I'm sure you have) then you should feel right at home with Yunica Tovah, our first playable character. She's a tough but compassionate young girl who has dedicated her life to protecting the goddesses. Do not underestimate her abilities because although she cannot use magic, she can swing around a massive battle axe as if it were a feather duster. Players new to the series should start with Yunica, as she is very easy to handle in combat. Once players feel comfortable they can tackle Hugo Fact, a magic user who plays out like a bullet hell shooter. The third (and secret) character will unlock once you finish the game as either Yunica or Hugo, and suffice it to say he's only for experienced players.
Of course it would not be an Ys game if it didn't have big badass boss fights, and Ys Origin delivers in spades! As usual each boss has it's weak point and a pattern that you can exploit, and half the fun is figuring out how! Unlike other games that have impossibly punishing bosses, in Ys Origin if you're dying frequently you can simply level up and try again. Also be sure to check out the upgrade menu at save points, though they may seem minor, the right enhancement can save your life. Also be on the lookout for rare cleria ore, as it can be used to temper your weapons.
The music and graphics are of course as stunning as you would expect from a series of such a high caliber as Ys. From the stirring violin strains of the opening theme which give way to choral chants and guitar riffs, you can guess from just that track alone that the soundtrack is something special. And it truly is, with a wildly diverse soundscape of orchestral music inlaid with the finest hair metal that Falcom Sound Team J.D.K. has to offer. Just ad rich are the gorgeously rendered 3d backgrounds and lush sprites that make up the visuals.
After you finish the main quest in Ys Origin there's still plenty to do. A host of unlockables including Time Attack, Boss Rush, and Arena modes round out the package, offering hours of gameplay beyond the main story. If you yearn for an epic story with brutal bosses, complex character development, and a truly hardcore soundtrack, look no further than Ys Origin. Newcomers will find an engaging start to a new series, and Ys veterans will find plenty of references to their beloved series, and even answers to some burning questions that they may have. At a solid asking price of $20, Ys Origin is an unbeatable value. Pick it up today!

YS Origins, a lost gem among rpg's?
Ys Origins is a prequel to a series named Ys which I had never even heard of, which I was suprised considering my love of rpg's. Ys Origins feels a lot more like a very fast legend of Zelda title mixed with a dungeon crawler, as in you navaigate dungeons while solving puzzles and killing a lot of enemy demons rather than a Final Fantasy type game with it's turn based battle mechanics. The game consists of three characters Yunica, Hugo and Toal, the game must be completed once to unlock Toal.
The three characters have very different distinct play styles and abilities which really makes the game feel fresh even though you are revisiting the same areas each time, also each time you will see a different side to an interesting story. The entireity of the game is spent climbing a tower, with your surroundings, traps and enemies varying from floor to floor.  You will solve puzzles while fighting hundreds of demons which will give you experience to level up to get stronger and sp to enhance other abilities.
Along with the three characters the game also contains a time trial mode that times your climb of the tower and an arena mode which you fight waves of monsters increasing the replay value, which you can unlock other versions of the three characters and the main character from the other Ys games.
Enemies are very varied, but every few floors you will face a gigantic boss, the boss's are very challenging needing different tactics each time and extremely rewarding when you finally finish it off.
I really enjoyed playing it as all three characters and will be purchasing the other ys games on steam and reviewing those too.

Live the legend that is Ys in Ys: Origin. Search through a sprawling and multi tiered tower that you may remember from other Ys games for the first time on a quest to find the twin goddesses and thwart demons and outsiders alike. While easier and much more linear than others in the series, this game provides multiple characters with different playstyles and controls the same as modern Ys installments for fast and decisive action. A gloriously atmospheric and rocking soundtrack supports the different zones of the tower while monsterous and menacing bosses bar your path to your ultimate goal of rescuing the goddesses.
The various ways to complete this game depending on what character you pick through their combat style makes this game very replayable if you are a fan of Ys or real-time action RPGs. Through the use of magic artifacts and different weapons you are able to find unique weaknesses in enemies and exploit them viciously. While your equipment is very limited for a Ys game, the items you can pick up are mostly the ones you know and love from other installments as they are recovered from the broken land of Ys here initially.
I never had a Ys game before Oath, but with this, I and II (remade with the old "bump" combat style), and Oath as well in my library I always keep coming back to Ys for another adventure.

Not everyday is a good day to fly. It's raining outside, you're sick, you've been drinking, or you need to rebuild your favorite quad? No worries, fire up Liftoff, have a seat, and get ready to rip. Most pilots will tell you that you need to keep flying to keep your skills up, or you'll go rusty, and have to relearn everything all over again. It's about muscle memmory, timing, and familiarity. Liftoff helps out when you don't have any packs left to rip, or the weather isn't cooperating. Customize your quad as close as you can to the one yu fly with the workbench, tune it up in the ingame BetaFlight simulator, and set your FPV angle. Yhe FPV will also simulate the video noise you get from your headset from flying near large metal structures, behind trees, and distance (to a degree, you'll never lose Video like in real life).  Want to race it up with the community? Get out there and try the prebuilt tracks, or get on the Steam workshop and try out maps that others out there made. Loads of fun without the cost of crashed quads, busted props, and puffed packs.  Grab it and you'll be pleased. I'd like to say this game as such is not bad at all. It is smooth and a decent experience. But its not as good as the hype express makes it out to be. I wish there was a neutral option, because then I would have chosen it.
Pros:
1. Simple with a good learning curve. This means anyone can comfortable play this game, but it takes time and effort to get really good at it. There are however complicated mechanics for advanced movement tricks which you will learn after long practice etc.
2. I didn't encounter any bugs.
3. Community map support. This is excellent. Many maps are crisp, well designed and perfectly playable.
4. Online game play is smooth and doesn't have warping etc at reasonable latencies.
5. Game has fast paced smooth hoverboard type of movement, good responsiveness and is quite enjoyable to play if you enjoy that particular flavour of movement. Some may not like it as it  feels like running on ice(without the sliding).
6. Many game modes with predefined rules. But you are limited to these predefined gametype sets.
7. Nice GUI and menus that utilise Steam API and lobby systems. But very limited options for match settings.
Cons:
1. No proper mod or mutator support. I want to host a local game with friends and bots using regen, low grav or vampire etc. I can't find anywhere to do so. I can't find any place with mods that add these features. Where do I edit the physics, etc of my game? It seems to be impossible.
2. Graphics are absolutely awful. I understand that this was a browser game initially but even then. The player models are all ugly (sometimes neon) blobs. The weapons are bland looking and look too similar when you hold them. The walls are flat, empty and blank in dull colours. Some maps are crisp and nice but there is a lack of texture on the walls.
I know the pros like it this way because they can turn everything to dull shades and see their enemies better but for a normal player who's looking for a good experience and not spending 2000 hours practicing pro skills, its terribly ugly. Many of the maps seem to have the exact same textures and don't seem to have much individual character to them.
In summary I'd say in terms of graphics Map textures are barebone but still reasonably crisp and bright. Player models and Weapon models are absolute rubbish and ugly af.
3. Uninspired weapons. Old time quake fans will burn me at the stake for this, but the weapons really are dull. A shotgun, a rocket launcher, laser beam gun, mandatory energy ball shooter, grenade launcher and 2 machine guns. The railgun is more interesting but thats about it. In my opinion, the guns in Unreal Tournament have so much more character and variety that they feel very iconic. They also look a 1000 times better and more distinct in-game.
4. No alternate fire modes. This is probably a matter of opinion but I like guns with alternate fire modes. It adds uniqueness to weapons, complexity and a new level of strategy.
5. Why do the maps not tell you how many players are ideal for that map? I end up having to guess how many bots to add because apart from the name and a tiny screenshot, there is literally no description for each map.
6. Too expensive considering whats being offered.
7. Playerbase isn't large but you can probably find a game or two depending on your region. The problem is that about 80%+ of players are the people with 1000+ hours in-game. Multiplayer is basically not fun unless you play with friends. The pros who have been practicing for years will destroy new players and it requires considerable practice with bots etc in order to even have a nice challenging and fair game.
Summary: Buy this if you're a quake fan and just want something that feels like the good old days and caters heavily to your nostalgia. I wouldn't recommend this for a new person who is not attached to the characters, weapons or setting. It feels too simplistic. I will probably play this game occassionally but I don't see myself spending a lot of time on it.
Personally, I'd rather play UT2004 or even UT99(GOTYE) over this. They have better graphics, mods, match settings and mutators that can add in pretty much anything that I want in to those games. For something more modern with amazing visuals and maps, I would play Toxikk. I look forward to trying Quake Champions and UT4 later on.

Spent two hours trying to beat the Phoenix (like the first out of six? bosses).
