The very next encounter was a skillshot minigame and I hooked one of the bomb-carrying goblins, blowing myself up in the process.
10/10 would get cancer again.

And here I was thinking Enter the Gungeon was hands down the best balanced, most interesting, and most skill-centric roguelike-like shooter out there. And then Flamebreak comes along and kicks it in the pants.
Flamebreak takes the world map progress from FTL wholesale, but actually gives you smart decisions to make on the map, unlike FTL, with shops generally in specific locations the game will be happy to remind you of in tool tips and consumable items to warp back and forth, enhance shops, etc...
At each node is top down twin-stick/WASD+mouse combat. Your hero will have a random assortment of a weapon and three powers, each quite different, but all functional, leading to quite a few combinations. What you find on the map are stat upgrades, supplemental abilities, and gear sets to try to take these powers and spin them into overdrive. If you have a stun, a teleport, and a melee weapon, then you can focus on weapon attack, powers that bolster stun, etc etc. In another run, you could be dropping mines, summoning minions, and hurling fireballs buffed to 16x their original power if you play your cards right.
Each screen is a short, bite sized skirmish, never running long, never spamming cheesy HP tanks BoI style at you, but always throwing some different combination of enemies and hazards.
Everything in this game works phenomenally well. To describe it makes it sound mundane and boring, just cobbled together from bits you've seen before. And in a sense it is, but the execution skill in this game is second to none. It's easily one of the best in this subgenre.

Beatbuddy... The title suggests this game is all about music and in a way it is, but don't expect something like Bit.Trip Runner, Symphony or Audiosurf here. Beatbuddy is an action adventure where your enemies produce the sounds resulting in a track for each of the six levels. The levels themselves are big and should take you around 30-45 minutes to finish. So completing the game will take you about 5-6 hours. I can tell you that that's more than enough because Beatbuddy just doesn't have enough variety to keep things interesting for much longer than that. True, it introduces new puzzles and enemies in every level that you play, like so many other games really, but for Beatbuddy is just isn't enough.
Plus, the fact that I experienced 2 game breaking bugs made me realize that Beatbuddy is a good game, but nothing groundbreaking. I can understand that a game has bugs, as long as they don't break the game but for a game that's 2D and somewhat linear it's unforgiving. Especially if it's such a short experience.
On the other hand; the levels are well made and have beautiful art so it's not all bad.
My advice to you: grab it when it's on sale.

Half-Life 2: Episode One is the first of the two episodes that take place after the end of Half-Life 2.
After an ending oddly reminiscent of the first game, we are once again left on a cliffhanger after the events of Half-Life 2. This game is the continuation of Half-Life 2, and once again we take control of Gordon Freeman on his unstoppable killing spree.
While Episode One is very short in comparison to Half-Life 2, it still holds the same level of quality in terms of gameplay. The same characters are there, and a few new enemies and mechanics are introduced. None of this is exactly game-changing, yet it does keep it fresh. The story lacks a little, which is mainly due to the lenght of the game.
There isn't much to say for Episode One that hasn't already been said for Half-Life 2. While it is fun to fight alongside Alyx, it doesn't quite make up for the length of it. If purchased through the Orange Box, it isn't much of a problem.
Overall, definitely worth playing, but only as part of the series, and not on its own.

Overall, a very solid game! The environment felt very immersive, even though you're railroaded through the game. Sound is used to great effect, especially in gauging the types and location of enemies. The weapons mechanics provided for a good deal of customization and range of styles—each weapon has its own distinct quality and personality and any of them can be used to great effect throughout the course of the game. There is a sense of stealth mechanics; however, it seemed pretty simple and straightforward: stay in the shadows, always crouch, turn off lights, etc... Ammo can be challenging to manage if you're not careful, but being very mindful of exploring the maps should ensure that you'll always have what you need to complete a mission/area.
I would recommend playing this game at its harder difficulties, as that really adds to the immersion; you'll definitely have to rely on teammembers from time to time to assist in finishing off enemies or else risk running out of ammo. And if you're having a hard time with some of the more difficult battles:
My one real complaint is the lack of transparency in how the morale system works, as it influences your ability to achieve the alternate ending. But what you need to do and how are not at all explained throughout the game. I don't mind replaying a game in order to further explore alternate methods of play or endings; however, it makes no sense for me to do so if I have no understanding of what I should do differently in order to get a different result. However, that does not at all take away from the great story that's told when experiencing this game and would definitely recomend it to anyone looking for a great first-person shooter that's full of action, drama, and especially fear and tension!
Verdict: 4/5

First things first - I had no idea what this game was about when I bought it. It was cheap in a Steam Sale, and I thought 'Hey why not - lol backlog'. However, times are a changing, and it's no longer about buffing that backlog game count, but actually PLAYING GAMES.
Yes, playing games. On steam.
So, having finally gotten around to playing this game (thanks to Steam Roulette), I have to say I'm genuinly surprised by how much I enjoyed it. It's a simple RPG/Adventure game, with some very basic yet effective hack'n'slash mechanics. While it would be wrong to say it's similar to Devil May Cry in the way that the combat is simple, but at the same time a little frantic, it does help paint a similar picture.
The most rewarding part of the entire experience are the Boss Battles. They're old school - patterns & phase based, rather than just being normal mobs with a crazy amount of HP, dealing insane damage. Nope, no spank'n'tank here - these bosses have patterns of attacks, and phase of attacks based on their HP. Classic.
They're frustrating to the point of fanfare when you finally take them down, which is great.
Games tend to skip over the challenge and frustration these days, which means gamers miss out on learning, resilience and fist pumping when they finally topple the♥♥♥♥♥♥that's blocked their way for the last hour. This game doesn't deny you that pleasure.
I feel like I'm not really doing the game justice - if you're still unsure there are 10/11 youtube videos linked to my Steam Account of my playthrough, so you could always check those out too.
Ultimately, give it a go and you might surprise yourself.

A Story About My Uncle was developed by Gone North Games, and puts you in the role of a young boy. Well that's not exactly it, but its something close to that. The story opens up as a father is telling his daughter a bedtime story, a story filled with adventure, and about something that he did when he was young. He has an uncle, a great explorer, who always seemed to find himself in a position of wonder. Now as the story begins you find yourself in a first person view in your uncle's house. This is when the game truly begins as you now step into your younger you shoes, and get to play the adventure story you are telling.
Graphically this game really gave you the feeling of movement. Sadly for me it was mostly falling to my death, but that's alright. So as I was saying, in this game you are going to be traversing your uncle's house and world beyond a portal which will take you through several different environments. To be honest with you, teh environments looked amazing, especially later in the game. The only thing that left me wanting was the character designs. They looked like a last minute push into the game. You have these amazing environments with lighting and contrast, and color, and then when you look at the characters you are interacting with its like something wasn't complete, the look flat, and rough around the edges.
I do have to say that I really did like to voice acting, sure the majority of the characters were talking in strange mumbles, but it made the game feel that much more alive. I also think the narrator, the father's voice caused that warm feeling and show of love as he unfolds the story to his daughter.
The controls in the game are very straight forward, you are going to move, jump, and grapple. There are ways to enhance all of these actions, thanks to the power of your suit that you find before going through the portal, but for the most part you are going to be doing one of those actions.
So you are a young man trying to find his uncle. You are worried because he hasn't sent his usual postcard. You decide to go look for him, and find that there's a suit that fits you like a glove. You then put the suit on, find the workspace that your uncle usually keeps hidden away, and then get thrusted into another world. Ironically this is where your uncle has been jettisoning garbage for a bit. The interesting thing is that the inhabitants of this world are utilizing the trash to create a better world for themselves. There are definite signs that your uncle interacted with these creatures, and it becomes clear that you are going to have to push further into this world if you are going to find him. You will be faced with caverns, darkness, monsters, and more. The majority of the game is spent centered around the grappling mechanic of your suit. You have a finite amount of times to grapple, though later you find that it is possible to recharge mid-grappling session, so that you can actually get through areas.
I have to say that for the most part I really enjoyed this game, though I have to say that by the end of it I was thoroughly done with wanting to grapple. There are just too many times where some of the camera angles that I was getting was giving me a sense of false depth. There were other times where you could see that certain things weren't acting exactly correctly when it came to depth as pieces of a windmill like blade would flip axes. There were definitely some parts to this game that were beyond unforgiving if you deviated from the intended path to get from point A to B, but there were a couple of times where I felt smart having beaten the game at its own game by going a route I'm not sure I was supposed to take.
If you like a game that centers around a grappling mechanic, that has a bedtime story centered around looking for a lost relative, then this is the game for you. If you find that you get frustrated easily if you accidentally have a tendency to double click, thereby exhausting an extra grappling chance, you might have some choice words, much like I did, for this game at times. At the end of the day, this is by no means a perfect game, but there's something about it that was inviting enough that I wanted to know what really happened to the uncle. So with all its little blemishes, its huge dependency on grappling, its still a game that you might want to check out. I give this game a 7.4 out of 10.

I can easily say this is one of the most disappointing games I've played in awhile. Seeing all the positive reviews and what people had to say about this game I was ready to be amazed. Sadly, this game failed miserably to impress and I'm now wondering as to where the praise for this game even comes from.
I'll start of and say what's right about the game. For one, the immersion in this game is top-notch. Every level design feels unique and authentic to what the game goes for. The gunplay is rather nice and different from your normal fps singleplayer style which is a nice addition but it is annoying how weak some of the guns are to the same enemies later on in the game. Graphics are pretty stunning and help to make each level feel as real and organic as possible while giving out that post-apocolyptic vibe. It also has a pretty cool story with a nice twist at the end making it for a real dark and immersive but mysterious experience. Lastly, gotta hand it to them that this game can cause some great scares and overall does give an eerie vibe so the horror elements are quite a nice touch.
As for the negatives, I have a lot to say about this game negatively. For one, this game is way too ♥♥♥♥ing linear especially for an fps with a given world like this. I enjoyed exploring a lot in this game but sadly there wasn't all that much to explore which drove me nuts because of how good the design of these levels and such were but you were so restricted that it was deplorable. Enemy and friendly ai in this game is downright terrible, soldiers will do the same tactics to flush you out over and over and trying to play stealthily really shows the stupidity. There is a severe lack in variety of creatures in this game. Seriously, how many times do I have to fight the Nosalis in a standalone horde mode or just riding on a vehicle? I'm beginning to think this is the only enemy in the ♥♥♥♥ing game at this point. The scripted events in this game are as poor and pathetic as they come because they're never any different from the last. You either get in a vehicle and fight off some enemies, either meet up with some more soldiers and fight a horde, someone saves you and you gotta do them a favor, or you finally get to explore just a little and still end up fighting a horde that is only Nosalis again. I had graphical glitches everywhere and the game ran poorly on my rig which is inexcusable given my rig is capable of running games more demanding then this perfectly fine. The voice acting outside of a couple of main characters is also rubbish and absolutely hilariously bad. I cannot for the life of me take some of the dialogue in this game seriously due to how badly delivered a lot of it is.
This game wouldn't have been so bad to me if it wasn't for the awful scripted horde events that feature the same enemy all the time, the linear areas which should allow for exploration, and pretty bad ai. As much as I didn't really like it and give it a thumbs down, technically it is still a good game that I can see people liking a lot. For me, it failed to live up to expectations and I'm hoping that Last Light fixes a lot of the issues i have. I don't necessarily get bogged down by linearity but the other parts of the game have to be tighter for me to excuse it as such. 5/10

A Story About My Uncle is a great little platformer game that only lasts an hour or two, three. But one that deserves your attention.
Your character's daughter one day asks for a story and you start telling about your uncle you were once looking for, a long time ago. So, the game starts with a younger you, trying to find your uncle.
The story isn't deep, it's even simple, but it's told in a way that it's realistic, you know, like how one would tell a story to his or her child.
The graphics are beautiful, and the attention to detail in the environments is sublime. The characters are a bit off, but fortunately, there are only a handful of characters you'll meet. There are some citizens to be found here and there, but you won't likely see them up close.
These sharacters have excellent voice acting, even if there aren't that many conversations and they all sound like one would expect. No problems here.
Gameplay wise the goal is to work your way to the end of the level by using a glove/device that allows you to traverse great distances. You can attach it to certain surfaces and that way swing across the many platformers you'll encounter.
Sometimes it's a little bit unclear where you have to go to, but by looking around you can usually figure it out quick enough.
It can become a bit frustrating because -although there are checkpoints- there's also a bit of skill and luck involved. It's not always clear how far you're away from a certain object and that ocassionally results in you falling to your death. Thankfully, death has no real penalties and the game doesn't need to reload anything. You're instantly transported back to your last checkpoint.
Later on you'll earn upgrades that allow you to recharge while traveling, the ability to jump, use a jetpack or to use more charges.
There are several worlds to explore, with different settings and physics but in the end there are only a handful of them (not even that I think). There are also some secrets to be found in each level (each level lasts about an hour or so), but I have no clue if it adds anything to the game or story or if they're just there for the challenge of it.
A Story About My Uncle is a clever game with some excellent gameplay mechanics. It could've benefited from a little bit more narration and a couple of extra levels/worlds, but what's there is already lots of fun (mixed with some minor frustrations).

I played the 360 version of this game like 7-8 yrs ago and I pumped a LOT of hours into this game and it still manages to keep me amused. There are two things that make this game so much fun. T-Hunt (preferably with friends, realistic and high enemy density) and Customization.
T-Hunt is pretty self-explanatory, there are a set number of terrorists per map and you'll have to hunt them all down. Sometimes it's easier said than done because most of those terrorists are insanely accurate and deadly especially the infamous SPAS-12 wielding terrorists.
One of the greatest parts of this game is that there's a good amount of customization options for your character. You will gain XP from every kill and then eventually you'll start to gain more ranks and that means more options to customize your character with different armor, clothing and camos. Customizing your character is addicting as hell and it's kinda nice to see what kind of operators other players have made. There are of course those who run with their vomit colored tanktops looking like they are running towards the nearest convenience store getting their latest fix of their favourite energy drink. But hey, who am I to judge? If that's the character you want to create then so be it.
You'll also unlock more weapons and slight XP boosts through the system called "A.C.E.S" this game has. There are three A.C.E.S trees called Marksman, CQB and Assault. The level cap for each tree is 100 but the weapon unlocks stop at 20, after that it's just an XP boost after another. You'll gain these A.C.E.S points for killing terrorists with different ways, for example, killing someone with a headshot or a kill from long range gains you some Marksman points while killing someone from close range or killing someone while blindfiring gains you some CQB points. Assault points are mostly explosives related and shooting through the walls.
AFAIK the PC version is mostly the same except for a few extra bugs, the most notorious one being the sound loop bug which makes the game pretty much unplayable for off-host players. Luckily there's a fix that reduces the frequency of it happening which can be found here:
Overall it's a pretty good "tactical" shooter that still holds up. It's a shame that almost none of the recent games have this kind of customization as this game has. It's a great game to have some casual fun with friends while playing T-Hunt and also getting killed by terrorists with shotguns.

It took a while for it to happen, but games like Binding of Isaac seem to be taking off a lot as a sub-genre, meaning that if you're not a fan of the game's poop jokes or some of the more questionable design decisions it's introduced recently, there are more options for you. Deathstate, Nuclear Throne, Starward Rogue and Enter the Gungeon are some I've enjoyed, but Flamebreak is one that seems to have flown under the radar, which is unfortunate, as I also think it's one of the best.
The game takes place on your typical fantasy world, not long after Pyrion, the top god, has finished making the world and populating it with humans, elves, dwarves, minotaurs, skeletons (yeah I dunno either), and other races. He also creates a group of demigods to help him rule the place, which turns out to be a bad idea as they quickly grow jealous of him being worshiped over them, and team up to kill him before taking over the world themselves. Pyrion doesn't die completely, though, as a part of him remains in the Phoenix, the first living thing he created.
You play as one of many individuals who both aren't happy with this situation and somehow know what to about it: namely, killing the Phoenix to release Pyrion's spirit (I guess anyway, that part's not exactly clear) before challenging the demigods on their home planes.
Every run you can pick from one of three, which will have a different race which determines stat values and what their unique ability is, a different weapon that acts as their basic attack, and two skills which range from fireballs to spawning a friendly turret. Some races are better at using skills, while others might want to stick to just using their weapon - though there are also skills that rely on how much damage the basic attack does, so there's a lot of potential synergies out there. You can also pick out all these things, at the cost of scoring less with the game's unlock system.
You progress through the areas a lot like FTL; one square per turn, which might contain a fight, a shop or a mini-game. There's a couple different types of fights, but they all give an exact amount of money, which is nice. The shops can range from towns, which sell simple stat upgrades and items you can use on the map, to blacksmiths and jewelers, who sell parts of armor sets - basically this game's version of the Isaac transformations, but much more fleshed out. All of them have quite dramatic, helpful effects, so it's well worth it to seek them out however you can.
Combat itself takes place in small arenas that usually contain obstacles along with a few enemies. They're all of the same races you can be, so they'll attack in ways that you could yourself, which is a neat touch. It's typical twin-stick gameplay, with the caveat that you have to manage cooldowns on your skills, and often time when you use them. Kiting is also pretty important, as even the bulkiest races can't take too much punishment, and you generally can't heal in the middle of combat. But there's plenty of time to make your character stronger, and the times I've died it never really felt like there was no way out.
The game's been updated a lot since it came out, so there's some real effort on the part of the developers to add new things and keep everything balanced. I bought it for five dollars, and I don't regret it at all. If anything, it's worth far more.

I can easily say this is one of the most disappointing games I've played in awhile. Seeing all the positive reviews and what people had to say about this game I was ready to be amazed. Sadly, this game failed miserably to impress and I'm now wondering as to where the praise for this game even comes from.
I'll start of and say what's right about the game. For one, the immersion in this game is top-notch. Every level design feels unique and authentic to what the game goes for. The gunplay is rather nice and different from your normal fps singleplayer style which is a nice addition but it is annoying how weak some of the guns are to the same enemies later on in the game. Graphics are pretty stunning and help to make each level feel as real and organic as possible while giving out that post-apocolyptic vibe. It also has a pretty cool story with a nice twist at the end making it for a real dark and immersive but mysterious experience. Lastly, gotta hand it to them that this game can cause some great scares and overall does give an eerie vibe so the horror elements are quite a nice touch.
As for the negatives, I have a lot to say about this game negatively. For one, this game is way too ♥♥♥♥ing linear especially for an fps with a given world like this. I enjoyed exploring a lot in this game but sadly there wasn't all that much to explore which drove me nuts because of how good the design of these levels and such were but you were so restricted that it was deplorable. Enemy and friendly ai in this game is downright terrible, soldiers will do the same tactics to flush you out over and over and trying to play stealthily really shows the stupidity. There is a severe lack in variety of creatures in this game. Seriously, how many times do I have to fight the Nosalis in a standalone horde mode or just riding on a vehicle? I'm beginning to think this is the only enemy in the ♥♥♥♥ing game at this point. The scripted events in this game are as poor and pathetic as they come because they're never any different from the last. You either get in a vehicle and fight off some enemies, either meet up with some more soldiers and fight a horde, someone saves you and you gotta do them a favor, or you finally get to explore just a little and still end up fighting a horde that is only Nosalis again. I had graphical glitches everywhere and the game ran poorly on my rig which is inexcusable given my rig is capable of running games more demanding then this perfectly fine. The voice acting outside of a couple of main characters is also rubbish and absolutely hilariously bad. I cannot for the life of me take some of the dialogue in this game seriously due to how badly delivered a lot of it is.
This game wouldn't have been so bad to me if it wasn't for the awful scripted horde events that feature the same enemy all the time, the linear areas which should allow for exploration, and pretty bad ai. As much as I didn't really like it and give it a thumbs down, technically it is still a good game that I can see people liking a lot. For me, it failed to live up to expectations and I'm hoping that Last Light fixes a lot of the issues i have. I don't necessarily get bogged down by linearity but the other parts of the game have to be tighter for me to excuse it as such. 5/10

If you enjoy playing action role-playing games (particularly those from Japan), Ys Origin is a solid investment.  At first, the level designs and monsters were fairly basic, but this is not so much of an issue as you progress higher up the tower.  The amount of variety in the demon designs and floor designs later on isn't spectacular, but keep in mind this is all going on inside of a tower.  The bosses--I would say--are the only exception.  The level and skill system revolve around finding new equipment and gems.  Although simple in design, there is just enough variety to keep you interested.  The story itself is alright (at least to the point where I am at...), and the characters aren't too bad.  You won't be interacting with them too much anyway.  In order to improve your character's own abilities and the abilities of some of your weapons and other equipment, the game allows players to cash in the SP dropped by defeated demons.  This SP is cashed in at the game's Goddess statues, which also serve as save points.  Generally, the distance between these save points is just the "right" distance.  If you don't know what difficulty to play at, I would recommend the "normal" difficulty setting.  Normal might seem too easy at first, but the game becomes significantly harder later on.  However, action RPG veterans will likely want to bump up the difficulty a notch or two.  If not at the normal price, then consider adding Ys Origin to your Steam library the next time the game is on sale.

Can't really place why Origin stands out as my favourite in the Ys series, but it just does. The gameplay is fast, fun and fluid and the boss fights are challenging yet rewarding. On their own, the stories are jagged and a bit weak. The writing is VERY amateurish in my opinion, but that adds to the charm of the game. The sometimes hilariously bad dialogue makes it feel as though you're playing through an early 90's anime, but the incredible combat makes up for it.
It's a fast paced game but definitely not for everyone. If you're hesitatnt, i'd recommend checking out some gameplay footage or waiting until it goes on sale.

TL;DR: One-eyed monster in a tunnel. 10/10!!!!!
This is what innovation looks like. A Story About My Uncle brings many new and interesting things to videogaming and furthers the genre described as "walking trail" games. I highly recommend this to anybody who tires of consuming the samey, prosaic videogames.
The story, though sparse, is quite unique. It's about becoming a father, of all things. Plot points lay scattered around the long paths. As you stumble upon these nuggets the narrator, a father telling a bedtime story, exposits about his uncle Fred or the given situation. By searching out your uncle, you get a glimpse of person your character grows into. Pretty sneaky.
Controls are tight, if a little counter-intuitive at first. Jumping platforms requires a mixture of spacebar for regular jumps and right mouse button for bigger jumps. It is very disorienting, and I expended a good deal of grey matter mitigating this scheme the entire game. Swinging fom exposed rock like Joey Ramone works much easier, however. Factoring in some rocket boots from the later stages and getting around proved to be fun.
Fun, yes. Miles and miles of fun streching out along corridors textured very much the same. Fun swinging puzzles repeated with tiny variations over and over again. Hmm. My sarcasm button must be broken on this board. A Story About My Uncle paces itself poorly in places. Too often, the reward for solving a challenging puzzle is another puzzle or a small, mute walk to the next row of platforms. A tiny gripe, but I can't count the number of times I'd wished to just reach the destination.
Overall? It's new. It's different. It's Indie. It's rough around the edges, sometimes literally. You could carve glass with some of these pointy character models. However, A Story About My Uncle brings something new to the party and we're collectively richer for it.

'The Room 2' is just as good as 'The Room'. If you played the first game, all you may want to know is that 'The Room 2' is more of the same. Yay! The only differences are: environments are more varied and there is a little more story (but only a little).
'The Room' and 'The Room 2' are the best puzzle games I have ever played and I've been playing them since the 1990s. It's puzzling in its most basic form. There is almost no story being told. Chapter after chapter, you just tackle one big puzzle. In order to solve each puzzle, a number of tasks need to be performed, ranging from solving mini-puzzles to spotting hidden compartments in the puzzle and coming up with a logical way to open them. Solving the puzzles feels exciting and rewarding, and it's just a lot of fun. I think a large part of the reason is that in 'The Room' and 'The Room 2', the puzzles feel very 'physical', as opposed to just seeing a board of some form in front of you like in most other puzzle games. It almost feels like you could reach out and touch the puzzles and solve them that way.
To conclude, a few short additional notes that may help you decide whether to buy 'The Room' and 'The Room 2' if you're still not sure:
- both games are short: about 3 to 4 hours each, so you may want to buy them when they're on sale, although I think the quality of both games certainly justifies their full price.
- they're not very difficult: for me the games were just challenging enough but if you're the sadistic kind of puzzler who only likes being challenged to the point of migraine, you will not find that here. On the contrary, there is a hint system in the game so if you feel stumped at any time, you can click a button to give you some pointers.
- the Steam Achievements are the most basic: one achievement for completing each chapter of the games.

I played Saints Row: The Third and I had a blast from the beginning because of its exciting, open-world gameplay and zany sense of humor. It reminded me of the Grand Theft Auto series, but with much more zaniness. Saints Row IV includes open-world gameplay and is humorous but it is a different type of open-world gameplay. There are clownish weapons, costumes and activities like Saints Row: The Third and it is set in the same city of Steelport. However, the city has changed because planet Earth has suddenly been taken over by aliens known as Zin and led by Zinyak, an alien overlord with a strong British accent.
The map layout of Steelport is the same as in Saints Row: The Third, but the setting is dark with no day or night cycle. Your interaction with the game world is different because your protagonist has super powers and has become one with superhero powers. The super powers are brand new and they allow you to fly in the air from one point to another. You are so strong that your melee attacks can overwhelm any civilian trying to harm you. The city is really a simulation and not the city you knew before the alien takeover.
You can customize your protagonist the way you want like in Saints Row: The Third to your heart’s content and you can choose male or female. New characters have been added to the narrative, including actor Keith David and Roddy Piper. The signs on the streets indicate that the aliens rule the city such as “obey” and “trust Zinyak.” It reminded me of the sci-fi film They Live, a film starring Keith David and Roddy Piper. One of the results of the alien takeover in the simulation is the access to alien weapons such as the Inflato-Ray, a weapon that inflates its target until its hilarious explosion. All weapons can be customized at the Friendly Fire shops scattered around the simulation.
The super powers are quite varied, allowing you to run up skyscrapers and freeze blasting enemies so that you can shatter them to pieces with one of your conventional weapons. The super powers can be upgraded just like weapons can, but you will have to find data clusters gathered around the simulation in order to buy those upgrades. Therefore, the data clusters are the game currency for your super powers. The ability to fly makes the use of motor vehicles less fun since it is a lot easier to navigate from one part of the simulation to the next by flying or super sprinting. Super sprinting makes you sprint much faster than any car at its highest speed.
There is much replay value in this game because of the diverse activities and challenges. You can complete 60+ challenges in order to improve your protagonist’s XP and they require you to kill a certain number of enemies with a specific weapon. Other aspects of the replay value include the game’s DLCs such as Enter The Dominatrix and How The Saints Save Christmas. These DLCs are separate from the game, but their short stories add more fun and humor to the Saints Row franchise.
I had a problem with occasional crashes on my Windows 10 (64 bit) that occurred, particularly when battles became intense. During the intense battles the game would freeze and then I had to start over from my save file. This problem occurred even with my GTX 980 Ti video card. I got over the problem by recovering my save file. This was my biggest gripe about this game.
The setting of the simulation looks monotonous because of the lack of a day-night cycle. After a while the game looks a little bit more boring than the game’s predecessor. However, the game still retains its great gameplay and sense of humor.
I would recommend Saints Row IV to anyone despite some occasional crashes and its monotonous setting. The main story missions are a blast to play because of the combination of fun combat and lots of buffoonery. There is plenty of replay value in this open-world simulation and it is still funny enough. The opportunities to find collectibles, complete challenges, complete activities, and side quests are well worth the rewards your protagonist will enjoy and the entertainment you will get from playing this game.
My Score: 9/10

This game has a LOT going for it, and I'd really like to recommend it -- but I can't. The first-person platforming works well at the start, but 1/3 of the way through the game, it becomes overwhelmed by its own clunkiness.
Take one look at one of the NPCs and you'll know what I mean: The developers have some good ideas, but (for whatever reason) they just don't execute them well enough. Beaming to rocks is neat, and the sensation of flying through such tremendous space is exhilirating. But you'll fall to your death over and over as you realize how tricky the mechanic really is.
I came really close to rage-quitting 3/4 of the way through, because the stalactite-jumping scene is simply TERRIBLE. Beam, beam, recharge, all while falling, all while trying to maneuver around falling rocks -- who needs it?
Worst of all, this tedious flinging of oneself (and it does get tedious toward the end) is rewarded with almost zero payoff. I'm sorry, devs, but the story here is just paper-thin. I felt no sense of accomplishment or awe when I was done.
This could have been the next MYST, and I really wanted it to be so. But it's not.
I enjoyed parts of it, and in general the mechanisms are okay. But the lack of satisfying story (or really any story) nudges it over the line into a thumbs-down.

'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' can aptly be described as a horror-puzzle game.  However, this label is slightly deceptive.  The game does not contain the B-movie scares of a 'Resident Evil' or the psychological terror of a 'Silent Hill'.  Instead it possesses a heavy atmosphere and a thick sense of dread.
You play as Paul Prospero, a noir detective investigating the disappearance of Ethan Carter.  This investigation takes you to the seemingly abandoned woodland environs where the Carter family once lived.  As you retrace Ethan's steps, you use your skills to reconstruct murder scenes that slowly link together to form a greater story, one that begins with Ethan's accidental awakening of a creature known only as the 'sleeper', and which continues into greater violence and madness.
Although the world seems quite big, it is actually quite linear.  There are ten puzzles total.  Half involve investigating the aforementioned crimes by recreating murder scenes in order to understand the chronology of the death.  The other half relate to Ethan's short fictions, which he writes with a lonely heart.  These puzzles seemingly have no connection to the main game, but...
From an empirical point of view, 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' does not contain much content; I played through it in three hours.  But having bought it during a Steam sale, I will say that it feels well worth the money I spent.  It is a heartbreaking story that filled me with uneasiness and mystery, and left me oddly pensive in the end.

Rainbow Six Meets Ghost in the Shell! A Tough but Rewarding Online PVP Experience.
Neotokyo plays a bit like a tactical shooter turned on its head. If you have ever played Spies VS Mercs in the Splintercell series, you have a very general idea of what you're getting yourself into here. Only main seperation being that you are playing both the 'Spy' and 'Merc' at once. There is an genuine game of cat and mouse being played at all times in Neotokyo, and knowing how to properly maneuver through each map is key in the same way that Counter Strike is. Death is quick and sudden, and often times occurs without your prior realization much like many other tactical shooters on the market.
This could be off-putting to some, and no one is to blame for that. If you're coming into Neotokyo expecting fast action, there is some to be found here, but it will be at the cost of much time learning the game mechanics. Like any good and compelling online shooter, the mechanical nature of the gameplay is rich and deep. For basics, you have 3 classes, each with their own edge, but none that will outright beat another (like rock,papaer,scissors). One is the very fast, lightly armoured, and stealth proficient Recon class. The Assault class focuses on moderate armour, great rifles, and grenades. Finally the Support is all about Heavy Armor and cannot sprint, but make up for this with lmgs, smoke grenades, and powerful vision modes to see enemy players through the smoke.
The art direction and music for this Half-life 2 modification are stellar! Ed Harrison NAILED the OST for Neotokyo, with a telling passion for the setting for which the music was to accompany. There is a blend of techno as well as other stringed instruments and ambient sounds. If you never play the game, just sit down and listen to the music! The art direction was clearly focused on bringing the world of Ghost in the Shell to the source engine. Evident enough by the spider tanks suspiciously close to resembling Tachikomas from Ghost in the Shell to the posters and sprawling urban architecture featured in every map.
There a only a few complaints I have to wage against this title. One of which being the hit detection. I'm not sure if this is due to the server I was playing on (likely it was as there are not many options to choose from currently). Most of the time, weapons fire and hit about where you would expect them to assuming you take into account that the game seems to barrow the CounterStrike style of weapon spray. But many times I found myself not landing aimed shots (could be my skills being flakey). Another small issue is the animations on leaning. Leaning was not an original Source Engine mechanic, and had to be hard coded in. Seeing as this mod was made back in 2009, there is much to be desired from the precision of leaning, but it will get the job done for you in most instances.
Overall, I have a special place for this game in my Steam library now. I found out about Neotokyo several years too late, and the player population is very small now. However, every weekend many of the regulars hop onto the game, and when the community returns to Neotokyo, many hours of enjoyable gameplay can be obtained. Do yourself a favor and give this game a shot one weekend. If you are a fan of tactical shooters, and need a breath of fresh air from the norm, give Neotokyo a visit. Plus, the community needs as many memebers as it can get! Welcome to Neotokyo!

tl;dr
Here is my full thought:
Nothing extraordinary to see here, though, they have done a good job making it fits nicely with the gameplay. There are some improvements over its console part, and clearly, it runs with decent performance on my medium-tier rig.
Surprisingly, there are more to the in-game audio than it seems (for this kind of game anyway). There is a little difference when shooting in different locations / areas, which give the sound a little more dynamic touch than hearing the same sound fx over and over again.
The Helldivers' responses are plenty, can be funny, can be annoying, and at times, it suits very well in the heat of the fight for survival. You can actually play the game without having to talk on the mic, as most of the time your avatar will says what you are doing out loud.
The basic command radio is there (Yes, No, Stop, Move) to help coordinating with your team too, which is more than welcomed for this kind of game, and it is quick and simple, no going through clumsy UI during gameplay.
I won't be going into detailed gameplay since you can find them easily already, though, I will be mentioned on certain aspects.
The tethered-screen gameplay, shared screen, locked screen, or whatever you may call it. It is NOT a bug (there are people asking the dev to fix this), but a design choice to encourage teamplay. It fits the gameplay nicely, though it can be VERY annoying when you have those deaf, blind, and selfish trigger-happy player(s) on the team. (not that many since those kind will get frustrated, and stopped playing, then start complaining)
The game is OBJECTIVE-BASED, not KILL-EVERY-ENEMIES, kind of game, so most of the time, your goals are to complete them (or fail them on purpose) and extract. You won't get anything out from keep on shooting enemies, unless the objective says so. (apart from steam archievement)
Here is the interesting part, the game feels a little bit likes sandbox-type game, where you are given things to play with, how you play is yours to be decided. Your loadouts play a huge part in how you play.
You can make it simple, or challenging at your own pace. The base game offers a number of equipments, support items, and etc., which offer different playstyles without having to rely on DLCs.
The DLCs are more of what they already offered in the base game, thus, they give you more of the flexibility than owning only the base game. however, most of them can be used by others, who do not own the dlc, which is a nice touch. At first sight, they may seems to be OP, but really, no, it is not. Just because you unlocked it right from the start that it feels OP when you start playing, not that it over-shadowed loadouts from base game.
The control needs a little practices to get used to, but overall the game do a good job for KB+M, while giving the game a unique control.
You can actually kb-input chat on PC for this game, that's a positive for me (and in my local language too, though it is not perfect but more than enough)
It is a nice game for coop play, it can be soloed too. Recommended getting the deluxe version for more gameplay flexibilities.

Essentially the same as "The Room" so I will copy my review of that game below.
The main difference is that now, not only have you got a different coloured lens to look through (that importantly is substantially more comfortable to look through), but you also have actual rooms instead of a box on a table in a room. Therefore you have a number of boxes within a room, sometimes there are puzzles which interact with each other across the room. It essentially means that you need to keep more in your head in case something you obtain in Box A works with cabinet C etc. The downside to this is that there is a lot of zooming out and zooming in to different things which means a lot of clicking - it can get a little annoying. What would have worked better in the port here are little buttons at the top of the screen for each 'Box' in the room so that you can quickly jump to and fro.
Personally I think therefore the first game is better as it is more focused and stream-lined.

Sure, the graphics, the design of puzzle mechanics, the audio, ... it all work very smoothly, but there are so many frustrating things (though not as bad as in the first game) where you are fighting the UI and order of operations in order to unlock things.
Basically the problem is that the puzzles resolution involves magic: Pushing or pulling something will work only if something else is one in a particular order, or when a particular condition is met. That you can't move something because it's physically blocked by something else, sure. But that you can't drag a book because you are not looking at it with the special colored glasses? Table flip.
Or things like rotating objects fast using the mouse, losing focus on the way, and having to redo it again.
So freakingly annoying.
Really.
Also, don't look for a story, there's none. There's just a pseudo babble steampunk scientist letters to kind of explain the mess where you are in, but that's about it.
Ultimately I'm clicking the "Yes" because there's some decent work involved, and the puzzles are intricate, but if you are not patient or if thins kind of problem drives you crazy, by all means avoid it.

Sure, the game may look decent but it's far from it. When I first started the game there were crates and other things floating in the air and I thought it's some graphic glitches which aren't uncommon in EAG (Early Access Games) but after I started walking around I got stuck on invisible things and all of a sudden a house was loading in on me and I got stuck in the floor and couldn't move. I restarted the game and waited a couple minutes to let the game load the buildings and the rest of the things and then set out to explore since I was now able to see what was there and in my way.
I was only able to enter one of the buildings in the area I started in and there's no explanation whatsoever on what you can do, other than walking around that is. A look into the control settings reveals that you use E to pick things up so I tried to pick up various things but nothing worked until I finally got a response after pressing the E button multiple times when standing in front of a bag which had a couple of things in it like cans of food and bottles of water. I put them in my inventory, the game lagged for a moment and suddenly the bag that was empty a moment ago was now filled with more cans and bottles. I guess the game comes with its own duping mechanism. ;)
I tried to open the door by also pressing E but nothing happened so my first thought was, damn I guess that's it until I figured out that you just have to walk right into the doors to get them to open. Guys, this is not how doors work, okay?
Great, now that I'm finally outside I walk around some more, pick up a knife and an axe and then decided to leave the small town, if you can call it that, after stocking up on food and water and explore the wilderness. Found a shrine of some sorts, a building on top of a hill, a castle you can't get into, a camp in the middle of nowhere and then I found the temple and that's where my story ends because I went down into it but I guess someone forgot the stairs because once you jump down, you're stuck and can't get back out.
All in all, in the state this game is currently in, it's nothing but a walking simulator. Just pack all the food and water you can and don't worry about anything else because you won't need it. The game has been released almost a year ago and considering that it feels a little like the developers have given up and abandoned the game.

First, I do have some credentials to mention, perhaps to add some validity to the review.  I served 6 years in the Air Force and while stationed in Italy in 1976, I joined a group of Italian hang glider pilots I found while driving in nearby mountains.  I bought a hang glider, flew 5 times from a 2500 foot peak, and then crashed and broke my arm. The military took care of me, and I'm okay.  Years later, I discovered flight simulators on an Apple II computer (SubLogic FS2). I've used simulators ever since then to an exhaustive degree.  In 2004 I had the means to start flight lessons, and obtained a Private Pilot license in 2006.  I put about 80 hours in command of rental planes (Cessna 150, 152, 170, 172M, 172P) and then got training in a Weight-Shift Control sport aircraft.(commonly called a trike) and then I bought one, N502PW.  I flew 100 hours in the trike over the next 5 years, then sold the aircraft in 2014. I have a Phantom 3 Standard quadcopter, a Spedix 275 FPV racing drone, a Vortex 250 FPV racing drone, a Blade NanoQX FPV mini, a Blade InductrixFPV, and an FPV Tiny Whoop I made from an Inductrix.  My FPV videos are on YouTube at patjoyce7323.
Liftoff is one of the most remarkable simulator products I have ever used.  It has the closest feel to the actual experience of controlling an FPV drone.  There are no "anomolies" or odd glitches when you use the controls aggressively.  The most remarkable thing about LIFTOFF is the support from Steam and the Steam Community.  I bought the software for only $20 (compare to MS flight simulator $60+ ) and was able to use my really old "Real Flight" USB controller from 20 years ago!  That controller is not always compatible with other simulators, but works great in Liftoff.
But again, the greatest thing, is how LIFTOFF has been IMPROVED since I installed and started using it.  LIFTOFF has amazing graphics.  Other simulators cut back a bit on the realism and the details, so that they can build a more expansive landscape filled with all of the actual structures that are there in the real world.  Liftoff is so designed to get the best balance of landscape detail (3d objects) and computer performance.  You can customize the complexity of the graphics displayed so that you can increase the frame rate of the simulation.  The physics are completely accurate.  You can build a new quad completely from scratch and save it.  You can select parts such as frames, motors, props, batteries, antennas, etc.  You can adjust the FPV camera angle, add a Mobius or GoPro on top, then go fly your customized quadcopter.
Back to the landscapes.  There are many environments provided for you to fly.  Each one is very different from the others.  The first "Straw Bale Field" is wide open space with no trees (except for a few outside the fence).  The bales of hay provide a clear ground reference.  The next environment has tall pine trees so you can learn obstacle avoidance and more advanced maneuvers.  The next is flying inside one level of a parking garage to teach you to manage your altitude carefully.  There were several more beautiful environments (a pro football stadium, for example) but here is the beauty of all this... they keep giving you more environments as they are developed.  And the latest one, called Hannover, is like the bando heaven we all seek.  No people, just awesome open places to fly and hone your skills.  The windows have reflections, and the level of detail is as good as it gets. There are lots of areas filled with trees, different sizes, types and colors, with gaps both big and small, and not always predictable, to challenge your flying skills.
I have not ever used the Multiplayer feature, or competed in races, all of which I am sure are worlds in and of themselves, with a huge number of tracks available for download.  LIFTOFF has a builder feature which allows you to build your own track in any of the environments.  Tracks can be saved and shared.  I've build a few tracks, and honestly, it takes a while to learn how to move and place the flags, gates, and markers, but in the end, you have a really nice race track that is exactly what you need.  Then you go fly your own track, and since you can edit tracks, you can always come back later to make improvements and adjustments.
In short, this simulator will make you a better pilot.  And it accurately portrays the experience of performing FPV quadcopter flying.  If you like the DRL product, you will enjoy LIFTOFF even more.  Worth it at twice the price.

The Good:
-- The art is very, very beautiful. The game is lovely, and provides a lot of things to see in a relatively compact area.
-- The minimal intrusion of HUD or other in-game reminders of the fact that you're playing a game were an excellent choice on the part of the developers.
-- The music is haunting, delicate, and never intrudes onto game play. Instead, it functions to reinforce tension, isolation, loneliness and other in-game themes.
-- The game is packed with in game references to a variety of interesting literary works, making it fun to play and try to spot all the references.
The Bad:
-- The game stutters, freezes, hangs, or otherwise has issues transitioning between game areas. This is likely due to the demands the game makes on your video card, but even with a brand new, top ten card, the game still hangs and freezes.
-- The game is very short, lasting me no longer than 3.5 hours.
The Ugly:
-- Story direction in the game is a mess. Game elements, while beautifully executed, are poorly incorporated into the game. As a result, when the ending comes around, it is frustrating, even aggravating. It's hard not to be angry when you finish the game.
-- Many of the story elements and references are poorly conceptualized, and seem added for no particular reason. While the easter eggs and story elements can be fantastic, they seem like the developers shoved a handfull of ideas into the game because they liked them, rather than because they were a part of the story.
I would love to whole-heartedly recommend the game due to the hundreds of hours the artists spent on design and music, but just cannot. Instead, I can only marginally recommend it.
Don't go in expecting the masterpiece that the trailer would lead you to expect.
Instead, you should expect something that is pretty, but oh so very flawed.

I have mixed feelings about this game.  I had been looking forward to playing it for some time, and while I enjoyed it, I didn't find it as good as I'd expected.  I'll give it a "recommend", but it's borderline for me.
+ Excellent graphics/visuals and sound effects - I took multiple screenshots of the environment just because it was so impressive
+ Easy Controls
+ Story is fairly interesting and doesn't drag on
+ Most of the puzzles are simple and don't distract from the story
- Game optimization - the game lags in several places, and there are strange "blinking light" artifacts that seem to occur on Radeon cards.
- A little more instruction at the beginning would be nice - while free roaming is a positive, I missed one part of the first puzzle and didn't realize it until I was already in the third "area".  Having to run all the way back to the start was somewhat annoying.
- One of the puzzles towards the middle of the game was rather frustrating, not in the "hard to figure out" way, but in that for some reason after completing it correctly, it didn't register, and I had to start all over from the beginning.
1. The game is fairly short.  I finished it in about 4 hours.
2.  This is the first game I've ever played that gave me a "vertigo/nausea" feeling while playing. There's a thread about it in the forums, so it wasn't isolated to only me.  There are some suggestions in the forum thread for settings changes to reduce this, but I didn't find them until after I'd finished the game, so I don't know how well they'd work.  I 'm not going to penalize the game for this, but just wanted to mention it, and the developer might consider defaulting to the recommended settings for that if it's a widespread issue.

An excellent space themed rogue like that has you exploring a randomly generated galaxy in an attempt to get some secret plans home. You will encounter all kinds of random ecounters and events as you journey along. Combat is real time with pause and you must assign your crew to different stations such as weapons and shields to maximize your combat effectiveness. Your ship can be equipped with various weapons and support systems and timing your shots and managing your energy is critical to survival for some of the tougher combats. Hulls will be breached costing you oxygen, systems will be damaged or disabled required on the spot repairs, fires will start and need to be contained, enemy boarders will teleport on board....things can get pretty tense. The graphics are simple but effective and the music really helps build the atmosphere of isolation and tension. They even released a free expansion a while back that adds further variety. Recommended.

We've learned from excellent games like X-Com that it's entirely possible to combine random elements and permanent death with a save game system without ruining the enjoyment for those people who want the full rogue-like experience, so why the developers chose to leave out this standard feature is beyond me.
The fact that battles are real-time while movements are not, and the ability to pause the game at any time, allows for a combination of thoughtful and tactical gameplay that is just as enjoyable here as in Transistor. While you can get away with leaving everything on auto in the beginning, eventually you will find yourself intensively micromanaging your weapons, systems and crew, which can get overwhelming fast if things turn sour.
All this having been said, I find FTL strangely addictive and keep coming back for more punishment. Because a full playthrough rarely takes more than an hour or two, it's well-suited for the occasional break. All in all, it's a very well-designed game that is unfortunately brought down by some very specific issues, hopefully to be resolved in a sequel.

If you liked Ys: Oath in Felghana, you'll almost certainly like Ys: Origin. It uses the same game engine, but with gameplay improvements. There are three characters to play as, with different fighting styles - while Yunica plays much like Adol, Hugo is an entirely different style with a very simple basic attack but more interesting skills, requiring better and more frequent use of them with a more defensive play style.
All the usual highlights of an Ys game come back too - polished art, rockin' music, metroidvania-type exploration, and interesting bosses. Definitely worth it, but if you're still unsure, there's a demo you can try.

Falcom decided to revisit the Darm Tower from the first Ys game (and you even visit it again in Ys IV: Dawn of Ys), so while it's a barebones concept on paper, they actually reinvented the mazelike floors of the Tower wonderfully. For the first time in the series, you can play with different characters (Adol is still in the game, don't worry) and the music proves once again how this series can brag with having one of the finest scores in video game history.
Sadly, in order to understand the full story, you have to go through the game with all three characters, which doesn't sound bad at all, but you still go through the same places three times and that can get boring.

It's a pretty decent hack'n'slash ARPG, if that's all you're looking for, but it doesn't particularly stand out unless you're there for the Ys part of it. The combat is solid but doesn't have a ton of depth. The characters are likable but don't have a ton of depth. The story is your standard "bad guys did something bad; now the good guys better do something about it" fare, so it won't carry anything on its own (not to mention it only shows up for a few minutes of exposition every hour or so). It would be a fairly satisfying little timekiller that doesn't really stand out in any way except for one thing: a lot of the unlocks feel like they're on a free-to-play schedule in a non-free-to-play game.
The higher tier upgrades in the story mode take an absurd amount of grinding to pay for. Can't beat a boss? Grind some levels, because a single level's worth of stats will make an enormous difference in the damage you deal/take. Two levels will change a fight from brutally hard to a pushover (although that's more "return of the 90s" than "when free-to-play games attack"). There are a bunch of bonus game modes you can unlock and extra characters and alternate character versions with different attacks and all sorts of stuff like that, but they require beating the entire story mode so many times (and weirdly, most of the achievement requirements are also "beat the game multiple times") that I'm guessing at least 90% of people will never even see things like arena mode. I know I certainly won't, even though I'd try it out if it were available immediately after having beaten the game the first time. It makes Korean MMOs look like they're concerned that you don't get outside enough.
Aside from that, it's fun enough, but I'd mostly only recommend it to people who want more backstory to the Ys games.

So just getting used to it isn't easy even when you fly in level/stability mode, it does get better in acro but the same issue with the punch power is still there. Like I've said I have several of these sims and the two I have found closest to real life are FPV Event and Velocidrone and it's because they both seem to be setup with real world physics. I fly a Robocat 270 racing drone and it has plenty of power and is capable of around 60/70 mph, and it feels nothing like the drones in Liftoff because they just shoot upwards like their on steroids. First off let me just say I got this game for free indirectly by the devs. I think they were just lurking in a popular stream of the game and handed out some keys to a mod who then started private messaging people who asked genuine questions about the game or seemed interested. I guess I just happened to be a lucky one and got a key.
After about 12 hours of play I seem to have 'finished' the game almost completely. I guess I'm sort of done with the game now at level 12 of something like 21 levels [last unlock is at level 21 I think]. You gain leveling EXP, called 'Insight', by clearing a zone/world. Further leveling would reward me with new playable races, weapons, and abilities/spells being added to the pool. Missing the 2 hardest [?] achievements which require a bit of focus [clear hard mode 5 times in a row, get 40 favour with Furere]. I've beat all the gods at least once and looped the world once just to try it.
Anyway I'll try to give my half cent on the game:
-Visually the game isn't too appealing at first sight and many people seem to compare it to flash games which honestly doesn't seem too far off. Just going by the screenshots on the steam store page I honestly wouldn't give this game too much thought, but after playing ~12 hours the visuals have somewhat grown on me and I now find them appealing. Enemy types are easily identifiable just by looking at them. The fields are randomly generated and have obstructions placed in them which can't be walked over but can still be attacked over. Some of these, especially on the snow levels, can be a bit hard to see during combat. All hitboxes and AoE's seem very clear, for the ones you aren't too sure about the game let's you see their AoE by mousing over the skill icon at any time. A small iffy I got with the fields, the forest one in particular, is that if you push an enemy to the edge of the arena then they can get completely covered up and hidden by the tree's that decorate the edge of the screen and it has gotten me hit a few times because I can't see their animations.
-Audio is pretty chill. I was quite content just listening to the BGM instead of putting on my own music, which is my usual opposite for games. Sound doesn't seem to play a big part in the game at all except for some hazard zones and knowing when things will appear from outside the screen [boulders mainly]. SFX is enjoyable except for when you have heaps of summons/helpers on the field helping you, then the sound of them bashing at things is quite overwhelming and unpleasant.
-Gameplay is the main appeal of this game for me. All races, weapons, and skills that I have unlocked so far seem to be viable for a successful run in some way and seem to be quite balanced. On each run the world also selects 5 sets of items from ~10 you can buy in shops which have stat boosts and special effects which usually carry your run. Every one of them has a use, although some are definitely more useful than others. Enemies, hazards, fields, bosses, shops, gold gains, etc, all seem fair and balanced in their own way. Even though the game is tagged as a rogue-lite, it is quite forgiving with being hit by giving you plenty of HP, it's possible to do an entire run without being hit. Every time you finish combat without being hit it says 'Flawless!' which stacks up with every flawless clear. Although this doesn't seem to add any direct benefit to the game it does feel good knowing you've fought X amount of battles without being damaged. I've gotten to the point where I can clear just about everything [except for arcane traps god I hate them, they're not even deadly it's like they're just made to break your combo] without being hit.
There are multiple game modes you can select which vary the difficulty of the game in some way. In normal mode you have a choice of 3 characters which are randomly generated. If you don't feel like doing a randomly generated character you can just choose custom mode and make your own from scratch, but receive less insight during the run in exchange. Hard mode just hands you a randomly generated character and you take 50% more damage, but double your insight gains. Then there is nightmare mode which is the same as hard mode, but forces you to loop the world in exchange for triple insight gains. There are also daily options for all of these which give everyone the exact same character loadout, world seed, etc, for you to compete on a leader board.
Not sure what else I can say about the game. I found it quite enjoyable. The challenge was definitely there. I guess I was pleasantly surprised by the game and stuck around longer than I initially thought I would. I would definitely recommend this game, but I personally probably wouldn't buy it even after watching other people play it and even if $10 USD isn't much. I might buy it if it was on sale but it wouldn't be high on my priorities. The game was good sure, but it didn't really feel memorable or anything like that. The most memorable thing for me was the little rhyming intro and outro screens that appear before every zone and after every boss. It just didn't feel very different from many other rogue-lite experiences for me.
I'll just say it again. It's enjoyable and not too brutal in difficulty, but it really doesn't feel like anything new. Even though I say that, I still recommend this game.

The Ys (prounounced Ees) series has long ben one of the finer series in Japanese action RPGs. It has been known for being one of the first game series to emphasize story, its brutal bosses,   fantastic rock soundtrack.....and barely ever being imported into the U.S. My own only experience with the series was Ys III, released in 1991, on the Sega Genesis
Ys Origins is a surprisingly polished game, considering its original release in 2006. With a focus on combat and dungeon exploration, the game feels familiar, but is polished enough to stay entertained enough through its campaign.
And what a campaign. Though a single character's story line is no longer than 8 to 9 hours, Ys Origins provides 3 different characters, each with a completely different fighting style, viewpoint in the story, and even differences in area accessability and boss battles. Combined with bonus time attack and boss rush modes, where devoted players can earn special costumes, battles, and even a bonus character, Ys Origin can easily be enjoyed for over 30 hours.
Ys Origin is not without flaws. The story is serviceable, but fairly predictable. Some later boss battles can be an exercise in frustration, and you'll wish that they mixed up the dungeons a bit more between characters. However, for anyone looking for a classic, rewarding, challenging action RPG with all of the Japanese trappings, you can do a lot worse than this artifact of the previous decade.

Ys Origin from Nihon Falcom is a Japanese take on the ARPG genre, so it's a JARPG I guess. I didn't really know what to expect when I started playing it but I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. The combat is solid and the graphics are charming.  Although you aren't given free reign to upgrade your character like a Western ARPG you level up as you kill monsters which strengthens your stats and you also gain SP by killing monsters which you can use to purchase upgrades for your character to increase passive stats such as Mana Cost for spells. Grinding is also well done in this game, if you kill the monsters as you advance through the game your character will be strong enough to defeat the bosses; however, if you're having trouble with a particular enemy you can grind up to increase your stats if you wish. Speaking of bosses, it was the best part about the game. The boss fights are well designed, challenging, but also fair. It's kind of a "find the pattern" type of deal, but there's a lot of skill involved in defeating the many bosses in the game. It had a Demon's Souls type of feel for the boss battles but the rest of the game had a Zelda-esque feel to it. The bosses were so fun I thought to myself while playing, "it would be awesome if this game had a boss rush mode." Little did I know, it does! It unlocks after you beat the game.
While I enjoyed the game a lot, it did have a few problems. The game is linear, with you having to find a key or item to get to the next area and there isn't an open world as you're just going up a tower. That's not to say the environments aren't varied, as they are, it just means there isn't much exploring to do. There's also a bit too much backtracking for my taste, but it wasn't too excessive. The music is pretty low quality and repetative and the control settings aren't adjustable in-game (you have to use a separately loaded launcher) so if you don't have your controller settings set properly you have to exit the entire game to get it right; other than that the controller support in the game is quite good.
There are three playable characters (one of which is unlockable), each of which gives you a different point of view on the narrative. The unlockable character is actually a demon as well, so you get the antagonist's point of view on the story which I found quite cool. The story itself is rather tropey, but still was a little more adult than other JRPGs I have played (it has swear words and death) which I enjoyed. The game loads and exits in a snap, which is also a plus.
Pros:
Gameplay
Storyline (multiple perspectives)
3 Characters that play quite differently
"Grinding" done well for a JRPG
Boss Fights
Unlockables and Bonus Modes (with leaderboard support!)
Excellent Replayability
Cons:
Music/Audio
Backtracking
Linearity
I really enjoyed this Japanese take on the ARPG genre. If you enjoy killer boss fights I'd recommend it for you. The three available characters all play differently and show you a different perspective on the events of the story and I'm really looking forward to coming back and playing this game again once I've finished the other games in my collection. There are a few negative aspects of Ys Origin (I really disliked the audio engineering) but they don't overbearingly detract from the fun I had with this game. A-
NOTE: I did play Ys Oath in Felghana and I have to say I wasn't as impressed with that game as I was with this one.  The boss battles weren't as epic, grinding felt more necessary, the music was better (but still repetetive), and basically everything that was good about that game is in Origin, but there's a lot missing.  The protagonist is also silent (which hasn't been cool since Freeman did it), and there's only one playable character.  I would NOT recommend Oath, but Origin is great.  If you want more of the same gameplay, play the other characters on Origin - skip Oath unless you REALLY love the series.

Let me start off by saying I really enjoyed playing this title, and definitely recommend it to any gamer who enjoys puzzle based games. The puzzles were very satisfying to solve, and there weren't really any points where I felt frustrated that I couldn't figure things out, the clues were pretty much all in plain view, or else not extremely tricky to find, and the puzzles followed a very logical and well thought out series of rules and mechanics. My only complaint is that there weren't more puzzles to solve. I really hope that Fireproof releases more titles like this, and I'll definitely check to see if they already have (there's The Room One at the very least). It is a little short, as puzzle type games tend to be, and I finished it in just a few sessions. Even though I bought it on sale, I'd say it's worth the full price of $4.99 (I think?). I look forward to rediscovering this title a year or more down the road with 'fresh' eyes.

Early Access Launch Day...  My YouTube Hour long Early Access Launch Day Review Video:
I bought the game less then an hour after it launched in early access on Steam..
Four fatal errors of which one hard locked up my PC requiring a hard reboot.
Then the game, even set at minimum graphics quality settings for everything was stuttering and running awful.  ..The good thing is the devs who are two 18 year old kids quickly put out a texture patch to make the game process the textures better on lower then high end gaming rigs and the game was actually playable!  YAY!
So then I deleted my first video on my youtube channel and was able to replace it with a full hour long first impressions and early access review video!
The bad news is that while the game was very playable now, I walked around for that full hour.. and I walked some more.. and I walked some more.  And still yet.. I walked some more!  There are NO creatures, friendly or hostile in this game at early access launch.  Resource gathering requires you explore the world enough to find the tools required to gather different types of resources.  So you will spend a LOT of time walking around the map.  Alone.  With weird glitches and oddities plentiful.  I found two pickaxes in a barrel sitting in the most bizarre spot off the trail.  Trying to simply equip the pickaxe, I magically turned it into 6 pickaxes!  Trails that you should be able to follow sometimes present invisible walls that can't be passed unless you jiggle and finess your character at exactly the right angle and spot in order to move on.  Shadows from trees seem to have epileptic seizures all around you making you get excited and think you saw some other creature off in the tall grass, but then realize that its just another weird graphical phenominon of this game.
While the world they have created shows promise and like a place I would someday like to have epic battles for my life in, this world now is just as blah and heartless as a skeletal corpse void of any life at all.  There is nothing here that makes you want to play.. or stay.  Atleast today on early access launch day anyhow.
Sadly, this is just another game that was released in early access way way way too early by a couple of teenages way way way too eager to see their baby out on Steam.  I'm sure they both had and still have high dreams for this game, and I hope that they don't lose their passion and vision of what they plan for it.  My mission however is to score this game the same way I do every game I review on Steam and protect potential disappointed customers.
At the time of this review on its launch day of its early access, I don't see the game being even close to what it "should" be for a very long time... at least a year away, and that's if the developers continue to work very hard on it and keep their faith.  I hope that I am wrong, but I forsee this game being yet another abandoned early access survival game that once had developers with incredible visions and even more promises to any customers who would support them.
At the time of this review:
This game scores an F
"While it shows some hope, it just feels like it was released at least a year too early."
Watch my video link above for a much more in depth review and all the reasons for why I scored it that way that I did.  Not recommended until this game is closer to 70% complete rather then the 15% complete it feels like it's at right now... and that's problably a long ways off, if it ever gets there and doesn't get abandoned first.

Are the developers giving copies to friends, family, and/or alt Steam accounts to hop in and add these mysterious positive scores?  - I wouldn't be surprised.  I could be wrong, but be wary!
