When you first open up FTL, the first thing that will hit you is the music.  From the main menu to the final boss fight, the dreamy space synth soundtrack blends throughout the game's entirety wonderfully.  The gameplay at first glance appears deceptively simple.  However, upon closer inspection FTL's skillful mix of real-time space ship battle strategy and rogue-like RPG shine through and show FTL's quality and charm quite clearly.
While the game's difficulty is adjustable, FTL is a rogue-like, meaning randomized game experiences.  As a result, you may be caught unaware by battle in moments of the game where you are least prepared, this can make the game quite frustrating at times, as defeat means starting all the way back at the beginning of the game.  One bit of advice: think your decisions through.  Your crew is expendable, and the game will take away your crew members for acting rashly in either a combat situation, or a text interaction situation.
And on two final notes I'll end this review: the boss fight and the value and quality of the game.
Some games are criticized for making their boss fights either too hard, where it punishes you for the slightest mistake and beats you bloody for it, or where the boss feels like every other enemy and fighting it is like running over cotton candy with a steam roller.  This is where FTL strikes something of a bittersweet chord, The Flagship is difficult beyond a doubt, I still haven't beaten it yet but that's not to say it isn't doable.  While the Flagship is difficult and can tear you apart quickly, given that you are skillful and have your ship put togther you can beat it and it feels like a fair boss fight.  Up to that point though, fighting the Flagship feels like taking fifteen hits to the kidney and getting your head slammed in a door, overall the Flagship is a tough but fair fight nonetheless.
Finally the overarching quality and value of FTL.  Being of the rogue-like genre, FTL inherintly has a lot of gameplay, when comboed with eight different unlockable ships, each with an unlockable alternate layout and a surprising amount of quests, your getting quite a bit.  As far as quality, FTL is a very sleek, very polished game that employs a top-down retro camera style to add a bit a nostalgia to your gameplay experience.  In addition to easy to pickup gameplay and a system of play that makes it easy to play for a few minutes, save and quit and have made progress, FTL is a very high quality game and a great value.
Overall, I highly recommend this game and hope you enjoy it as much as I do.

Had a blast playing this game. I have not played a good story driven FPS in a long while. This game does not disappoint. I wish I had picked it up when it first launched but with the graphical improvements of redux I am more than satisfied with my purchase. Only con I have is that I didn't pick up the bundle.

One thing I love, is shooting games. FPS in particular. I like shooters even if it isn't very plot heavy. I just love to shoot things. However, this FPS action-adventure-survival taught me how to truly love and respect those people who can make shooters that, despite their many counterparts, can bring something new to the party. As of the date of this review, those people who brought this thing to the party of gaming, have officialy earned themeselves the title of making what is now my favorite game.
Developer and Developer History:
You can read who the developer and publisher was on the steam page. So I will not bore you with something that can easily be looked up. However, it needs to be known that this game was originally adapted from a book series also called Metro by Dmitri Glukovsky. Not only that, but he actually took part in the development of the Metro game series which is cool because the man. the maker, the magnificent, has given the game version his stamp of approval unlike some other games and their authors (I'm looking at you, Witcher). Also, during development, 4A has never made any other games and this game was not incredibly known at the time of its release and did not receive much hype at the time. SO for a studio's first game to be a big hit and spark a huge cult following, is pretty impressive.
Plot:
One thing that I sometimes hate about games, is their attempt to add too much depth to the plot to where it becomes too confusing (eg. finding out you were fighting for the bad guys, deux ex machina moments with rediculous explanations, etc). However, this game kept it simple. You are fighting for the good guys, and trying to defeat the bad and restore order and peace despite your calm life before your involvment with the different Metros. Also, I love how explicit important parts of the story were made. In many games, any piece of information is usually implicitly stated and "represents" something. That is not a bad thing, but making details so ambiguous can cause hard-headed and naive people like me to have important details slip over their heads. So when this game reiterates an important piece of information via mission intro or diary entry in an obvious manner, it refreshes me on what has happened and what our goal is without confusing me. (As a side note, I personally love the addition of supernatural entities to add horror and supernatural elements to the mix as I have an interest in the Paranormal).
Characters:
The variety of characters in this game, whew. You do not just fight mutants. You fight humans, your inner demons, ghosts. You do not just get along with humans, you get along with mutants and any mutant or person can become your worst enemy or your best friend in the blink of an eye. SO do, not, fully, trust, ANYONE. Eat or be eaten, kill or be killed.
Playability:
I will admit, this was one of the downsides of the game. You cannot change computer volume in game so you have to use the volume slider built in the game. Also, if you're like me and change your controls often, you might want to leave defaults because certain combinations can make some aspects of the game unplayable (eg. Reloading BB gun air wont work without defaults). However, these aspects of the game can easily get used to within the first hour of playing.
Difficulty:
One think I love about this game is it can satisfy those who love horror and survival games and who scavenge often, while also allowing the option to satisfy those who like to go all out Call of Duty style. These options are given in the Spartan and Survival options provided at the beginning of the game to make ammo more plentiful, equipment more abundant, etc. Also, after selecting your play style, you are then given the option to choose your difficulty which I see to be pretty balanced.
Mechanics:
For the time that the game was made, these mechanics were not seen often amongst shooters. The gas masks, the guns, the movement, the agility, the endurance, the health systen, the guns' mechanisms, and how they performed were very new for its time and very unique which made me enjoy it even more when I shot somebody...or something. But you are also allowed to spare people's and mutants' lives from time to time aswell so there is that. However, one aspect I didn't like too much was the moral points system. Now I'm not saying that since on both games I was apparently a huge enough ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to not be given the opportunity to pick any good ending but because I do not think your actions early on in the game should justify what actions you take in the ending of both games because to me, what ending I choose or want at the end of the game, does not and, imo, should not coincide with my actions earlier in the game.
Graphics:
To put it simply, the graphics were quite stunning for being made in 2010 when compared to other games like Left 4 Dead 2 and CS GO and other FPS shooters. However, choosing your graphics settings are quite difficult to get used to in Metro because I have a Nvidia GTX 980 with a 144hz G-Sync monitor and I had to have SS off and graphics on medium for it to even run at 60fps. I don't know about you but I never had to do that with any other game.
Immersiveness:
This is, without a doubt, the most immersive first person shooter I have ever played. I usually play campaigns in intervals. After about 30 minutes I get bored and have to take a break. However, I found myself playing Metro for 3 hours and not even 1/4 way through the campaign. This is by far the most immersive FPS i have played and I never felt more significant than I have in this game and never have I hated or loved a bunch of people made of binary code or notepad more than I have in this game.
Entertainment:
Immersiveness is differnet to entertainment. Immersivness deeply involves and appeals to one's senses. Entertainment refers to how amusing something is when observed. This game, at first can be hard to get into as you are not quite sure what you are supposed to be doing in this game. However, the longer you play, the more the pieces to the puzzle start to come together and the more entertaining it becomes. So, this game is as entertaining as can be to me. Not in the sense of stimulating, but in the sense of appealing to your emotions and by the game almost asking you "how would you deal with this situation, how would you react?, how much do you want to live?" I found the atmosphere, the missions, the people you fight with and alongside, and just the moments looking back on what happened to your homeland more entertaining sometimes than the actual shooting of mutants and people. I found this game more entertaining in a movie sense more than a game sense as I loved just looking around and thinking about all that has happened to my character and what made me want to fight for the people of the Metro, and why this, in the matter of two days playing this game, made it my favorite game as of today!

I've already forgotten, how many times I've beaten this gem of a game. Including the original "Metro 2033" it has to be at least 5-6 times. Why? Because the atmosphere and the universe of "Metro 2033" is amazing, it's quite literally "dripping" with atmosphere. Game is fairly linear with minimal exploration, however it adds a lot of gameplay elements, like the possibility of avoiding confrontations with human enemies, incapacitating them without killing them and so on. Also, there's sometimes alternate pathways you can choose, especially when going the stealthy route.
Voice acting in English is very cringe-worthy, I'd recommend trying to play this game with Russian audio and English subtitles. It just feels way more authentic this way, and the VO actors actually do a good job in it's native tongue. If you are a completionist, then it's VERY likely that you'll play this game more than once, so I do recommend playing the game at least once with Russian VA - it's worth it.
Gunplay is very well polished and the "Redux" in this case feels welcome, because the gunplay in the first game didn't feel so great. Gasmask system was very poorly done, and you really had trouble recognizing how much air you really had.   Battery charging was extremely obnoxious and stealth was broken - however not in your favor, since if you got detected only
the enemies in the WHOLE FREAKING LEVEL will always know your position, and getting detected was very easy. It felt like the stealth was an afterthought, while with "Redux" they fix the stealth so that it works now like it did in Last Light. Enemies have a very low field of view and darkness = invisibility - hilarious, I know, but at least stealth is viable.
On higher difficulties you die very easily, and game does not have a regenerating health system. You need to use the medkit to make the "bloody screen so real" go away. Guns have recoil and the sound effects are awesome. Highly recommend playing this with a good pair of headphones for maximum paranoia. Ambient music is also phenominal, which has undertones of despair, hope and eerie beauty, especially when walking on the surfice in Moscow.
The story is simple, but it's just enough to keep you going. Highly recommend reading the actual source material for the game, because it covers more about other character relations with Artyom. Lots of phylosophy about life and such. A good read. Still have to get myself Metro 2034 and 2035.
There's also a somewhat hidden morality system (you can't really know how much you have) and it's tied to the ending of the game, or at least it gives you an opportunity to choose an ending, rather than an automatic one. Still, it's disappointing, due to the fact that the next game: Metro Last Light already has a set story, based on one of the endings, so it doesn't really matter if you pick the "good" one. My guess is that the studio lacked the manpower to actually make Last Light into a two-part game, where endings mattered and had to scrap the idea, due to limited time, money and inability to make a branching story actually work, which in the end I think is reasonable, considering the crappy environment the developers had to make the game in.
Would recommend this to any FPS game enthusiast and even more, to people who enjoy fleshed out worlds with tons of lore and interesting, albeit a little lacking in personalisation, characters. I do hope that more Metro games will be released in the future, because I can easily place this game together with other FPS legends like BioShock, Half-Life and the early days of Call of Duty.

Flamebreak takes the Binding of Isaac formula to the next level by combining it with the rogue-like/lite elements of FTL. This combination creates a game that not only requires mechanical skill but also good strategic planning as well. Each time you play the abilities of your character will be randomized in addition to the map being randomized resulting in each playthrough being a completely different experience. It is impossible to overstate how much replayability this game has, even the main game mode will take you quite a while to beat (still working on it myself) and even after that there are challenges and more difficulty modes to keep you interested well into 100+ hours.  If you enjoy the twin-stick genre and are looking for a challenge then Flamebreak is definitely worth a buy.

Imagine if Mirror's Edge, Dear Esther, and Myst fused together into one game.  Sounds amazing right?  Well this game exists, and it's called A Story About My Uncle.
With your adventure suit, you are allowed to fly and grapple across enormous and gorgeous chasms at break neck speeds.  It has the thoughtful internal dialogue you'd find in Dear Esther that will immediately resonate with you, the player.
The grappling puzzles are not punishing, in that you don't get angry if you fail.  In fact, you only feel encouraged to try again, and when you land it, it feels so good.  This game comes highly recommended.

A great and fun adventure. Only took me 6 hours, but if you're looking for a good adventure, then this bedtime story will take you thru a fantasy land as you search for your uncle. Using a grappling hook device, you will swing your way through 3 imaginative levels in caves and through a sky of airships and villages on floating mountains. Some parts can be a little difficult, but when it's all over you'll wish there was more.
Great story, great graphics, great atmosphere 11/10

This game was well worth the money, in my opinion. Controls were great, graphics were fantastic (minus the characters, but it wasn't about them at all). I guarantee if you buy this game you'll finish and still want more. Really addictive gameplay.
If I had one beef, the story telling. It was such a cool idea, to narrate something like this, yet I didn't feel like it added to the scope of the game. The accent was heavy, which lead to a bunch of grammar mistakes.
BUUUUT I'm rambling. I really enjoyed this game and have recommended it to everyone I know. If you like first person adventures at all (think portal mixed with bioshock's grappling mixed with dead space zero g) I'd try it out.
SUPER excited to see a sequel to this, I would buy it instantly.

One of the most believable environment I've been thrown in ever.
Now the game is short, extremely short but it's a quality over quantity kind of game. On sale, it's worth every single last penny of it. Review of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter
Rating: 8.8/10
Aside from the story and gameplay, lets start off by saying this game holds quite possibly the most beautiful graphics I have seen to date. If you look at the developers website, you can read that all the scenery and buildings are actually real objects photographed, and made into models for the game. Some of the sights make amazing screenshots, and well, possible desktop backgrounds. It's really breathtaking. Ethan's stories that he writes in his game are all imagined, some taking you to space, and others bringing giant monsters above from caves. It's pretty awesome.
The story is very captivating and mysterious. It's somewhat confusing but chilling once it is all puzzled together. However, this game even tells you that it does not "hold your hand," and whoever added that to the game is spot on. You'll need some serious brain power to pass some of these puzzles, and there is hardly any indication that what you are doing is right. As for the gameplay, it really isn't scary, just mysterious, in case you were worried.
In conclusion, this is definitely a game you should have in your library, try to pick it up in a sale, as it is a pretty short game. Beautiful graphics + Great Story = The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.

I bought this game with the desire to explore an interesting world. To say this game is beautiful may imply that the graphics are good. But it's much more than that. The detail in this game is astounding. Everywhere you look is gorgeous. I want to live in this world (sans all the drama that the story is based around.) The geography is completely convincing and draws you further into the map. Every place you're at makes you want to explore further if it wasn't for that thing you can see off in the distance that calls you to it.
I took my time through the game and got 4 hours of play out of it. So it's definitely short, but it's priced for that too.
The story is interesting and the discovery/solving mechanic is unique and fits in well with the environment.
I tend to be a wuss wth scary games, and there is one portion that has jump scares in it, but I managed to pull myself together and avoid that.
Overall, great game. I really enjoyed it. If you want to explore an intriguing environment, this is a sure bet.
I do have one gripe. The save system is obviously from a console. If you explore around for a long time (VERY easy to do) but don't solve a mystery, then none of that activity is saved. It's almost as if this game was designed to be played in one or two play sessions and nothing more. I don't really see why this couldn't have a full quick save feature in it. The game itself is not that complicated.

Neotokyo came a bit after the golden period of massive free to play FPS games, like Combat Arms, Blackshot, Sudden Attack, Alliance of Valiant Arms among many others. However, it gave a bit of breath into what I would say was the fall of the F2P FPS model. Being a mod, it offered a plethora of modified variants to the standard FPS game modes all without the overarching micro-transaction schemes that plagued other F2P FPS games. To me, this was a gem of a game.
It offered a bit of hype on its release with a stellar trailer:
It also introduced its new populace to a great universe, namely, Ghost in the Shell. A bit topical now considering the impending release of the live action movie; I digress, this was a great introduction to interesting character archetypes. Some of which are even utilized somewhat in the F2P FPS Ghost in the Shell: First Assault (not to say that they copied, but to show it's ability to carry over the common character themes.)
In addition to it's legacy, Neotokyo had or I should say, still has one of the best soundtracks in modern gaming. Made by Ed Harrison:
(Seriously, give it a listen :)).
Although I have given this game a recommendation it is quite reserved. As it stands, the game is with-out-a-doubt: dead. If possible, gather some buddies and have an in-house together, or just explore the maps by yourself. You'll give yourself a treat viewing what I believe to be some of the best put together community maps pre-workshop alongside a fantastic soundtrack.

Okay, so let's start with the negatives and get them out of the way:
-Very few people are playing the game (I have sometimes been online when only 12 others are on)
-There is DEFINITELY a steep learning curve, you will not immediately be good at this game just because you're good at CS
-The map design (although it's brilliant) can be quite difficult to comprehend when first starting to play the game
-The graphics are old, but not particularly bad by any means
-The community who typically play on the game have been playing for a very long time, therefore you will be killed A LOT when you first start
-Some of the maps are horribly optimised
Now for the positives, and there are many:
-It's free, you literally have nothing to lose if it's free
-The community of the game is still somewhat active; I've found that even when there is nobody online, simply joining a server will attract others to play with you in a matter of minutes
-The community is one of the nicest of any game that I have ever played, they are all very helpful and kind to newcomers
-Tournaments are still regularly held
-You can tell that the developers genuinely cared about the finished product due to the immense amount of detail put into the game
-The game is very satisfying when you get the hang of it
-The game will run on almost ANY computer regardless of the specs, so any of your friends will be able to play it too

Great FPV sim, specially when I hook up my fatsharks as well as the trans. Theres some issues with some of the inbuilt races at the moment though, where the quad gets damaged (on some tracks quite severely) before the countdown has even finished - making the races on these tracks almost useless since the quad is shaking badly before even starting the race.

Before I ever got a real quad, I bought a Taranis to practice in simulators. This was easily the best decision I made. I initially started with this simulator, but it was too laggy to be any good, so I spent a solid 30 hours on Hotprops. Now that I have 6 months of real life FPV under my belt, I've found myself coming back to this sim.
First of all, the physics are great. Being able to tweak so much in the flight controller settings has allowed me to set up my virtual quad pretty darn close to my Xhover Element. The only big problem I've noticed is that the sim can feel a bit too floaty, like any bit of throttle you give will keep you in the air much better than in the real world. Adjusting the throttle curve fixes this.
The graphics aren't terrible, and I feel like the sim has gotten much smoother over time. I'm running it on my iMac and find that 720p graphics work the best. I also like the ability to play with FPV noise. It's not exactly like experiencing real breakup in your video feed, but it does the job pretty well. My biggest grip with the graphics is the way the trees appear. If you're flying fast at all, you'll find that they sort of just materialize right in front of you, making it hard to avoid wrecking on branches or shredding your props on leaves.
With the more recent updates, you now have a whole bunch of frames to choose from. I'm really excited about this, although I can't say I feel a huge difference in the way the frames fly. As long as your motors, battery, and props are the same, the frames fly pretty much exactly alike, with the obvious exception of the much smaller frames that can only run 4" or smaller props.
So, what would I change? First of all, the crash physics are pretty bad. This isn't a huge deal, but there's something amusing about crashes with real life quads. One minute you're flying along fine, the next you're tumbling and bouncing across the ground. In the sim, you sort of hit the ground and slide, which isn't realistic at all.
Next up, I would love to see some 5x4x3 props. The "Propfan" 5030x3 do a decent job of simulating the HQ 5x4x3's that I fly in real life, but they're definitely not the same. A proper 5" tri blade with a little more bite in the air would be awesome.
Next up, some larger areas to fly in would be fun. I'm not much of a racer, instead I do primarily freestyle flying. Levels like the Hangar are so much fun because of the vertical structures, so I would like to see more stuff like that. Maybe even a more urban environment like an abandoned factory or office park?
The biggest thing I would change is the FPV camera lens option. First, I would move it to the workbench screen instead of in the settings screen. Next, I would add a 2.5mm option. I, like a lot of people, fly in real life with a GoPro lens on my HS1177 camera, which provides a superior field of view without the annoying fisheye effect that a 2.1mm lens has.
All that being said, I highly recommend this simulator. It's a great way to knock the rust off if you haven't flown in a while, or to teach somebody new to fly. Despite its flaws, Liftoff is my favorite simulator and I find myself coming back to it time and time again.

I love this game.
A friend started flying quadcopters and quickly pulled me into the hobby.  I had flown a toy grade Quad two or three times and realized quickly that it wasn't as intuitive as I thought and it was going to take a lot of crashing, buying parts, repairing and crashing again just to begin to grasp the fundamentals. Afterwards my friend introduced me to Liftoff. I was intrigued because it was radically different from actually flying the toy grade drone.  After spending a few days figuring out what radio controller was right for me I ordered one and immediately got Liftoff.
I played with an XBOX 360 controller untill the RC controller arrived. Playing with the XBOX controller is definately not going to allow you to experience the full greatness of the game but I was thrilled to have the option since I was waiting for the RC controller. When it arrived it made playing the game WAY more enjoyable but, the first few hours were miserable. I kept trying and finally I was able to complete a lap, then a race and then things fell together and the game became incredibly rewarding. Not only is the game tremendous fun to play but I eventually realized that awful learning curve was really Liftoff teaching me how to use a radio transmitter. About a month later (about 20 hrs of playing Liftoff) I built my first FPV racing drone and although I've had more than my share of crashes, I can honesty say that Liftoff may have saved me hundreds of dollars and hours of tedious repairs. It gave me a big head start on actual FPV racing.
If you're interested in learning to fly quads then you should do yourself a huge favor and hold off on the expensive quad, get Liftoff and a controller first. Learn to fly in Liftoff, then go fly the drone, you'll be glad you did. I also tried FPV Freerider and while it was fun to play it just didn't seem to replicate the actual flying experience as realistically. The drones in Liftoff feel real, plus, with the update there's new quads and propellers and a plethora of other new parts to play with in the Workbench. I love mixing and matching components and seeing how it effects flight characteristics. The workshop has a number of really great tracks available too.  The various drone options in conjunction with all the maps available really extend the game immeasurably. (Side note: the track creator seems a little cumbersome to use)
Knowing now how much fun the game is,  I would fork over the cash for a RC transmitter and this game even If i had no intention of ever actually controlling a real drone. (Kinda like buying a wheel and/or pedals for a car racing game.)

The puzzles especially were polished to a degree where they feel quite challenging, but not overly cryptic or difficult. I believe most common folk could figure them out even if they didn't used the hints that are given to them if it takes longer for them to figure said puzzle out.
Now Fireproof Games comes with it's sequel ''The Room Two'' and it is definitely a step up in terms of graphical design. Environments look much more detailed and the sound design is chilling at best. There is a bit of a horror theme going on but it's more disturbing rather than it is scary, really. The new puzzles do have a small similarity to the first game in terms of structure and progression but ultimately feel new and fresh on the way of how you solve it.
It takes roughly 1,5-2 hours to complete but for the price of admission, that is a wonderful little bargain. (even moreso when on sale which is quite frequently) Even if you're not a puzzle fanatic, I think you'll find this quite enjoyable.

Let me start by addressing some of the complaints about this games such as it being all based on luck and how it lacks content. There is a huge amount, I would even go as far as saying an equal amount of strategy to this game as there is luck. From what you buy, to if you decide to buy anything at all and instead choose to upgrade your ship giving it that extra fire power or hiding behind your many layers of shields. There are so many different ways of playing this game and a large amount of content if you bother to use it. You are able to unlock new ships and new set ups from completing runs and unlocking achievements along the way giving you an insentive to beat the unbeatable. This game is for the people who are prepared to get frustrated, pull out their hair, quit the game and then come back to it the next day with a fresh mindset and with the hunger to get further each time, learning more and more with every click of the start button. I have heard many times that the game is unfair and too one sided, let me just say "You is mad, cus You is bad".
I think its more than fair to say a large proportion of the game will come down to luck and finding either exactly what you need at a shop/encounter or you finding useless items not worth the jump taken to get there. For me this adds to the challenge and gives the game more depth, without it there would be less need for exploration of a star system and a lack of increasing intensity that you might not find a shop before you run out of fuel or needed items. If you were able to jump to a shop and have the full range of items from the game to choose from then this game would be a breeze. If you land at a shop and find the useless crap we all dread to stumble upon after jumping strategicly to the only shop visible then move on! Discover another shop. There are multiple shops per star system it just takes planning and insightful purchases to easily discover most of the map before moving on. However this game is not all based on random blind luck and any one that tells you so well...... I question their inteligence and so should you. This game has been built for replayability and the challenge that comes with it. Of course if you decide to send you crew down to a planet to help survivors there is a good chance they will not come back..... so dont!. If you rescue a crazy man from a pod or planet DONT take him on board. "If you avoid risky encounters then you survive risky encounters". That is a phrase that should be forced upon people when they start up the game.
As for the lack of content....... well I have to say that I haven't encountered this as a problem. I understand the feeling of getting to the final boss with an almost perfect ship, defeating him and not being able to help but want to carry on. Surely this in its self proves that the game has been entertaining though. In my eyes if I come to the end of a movie and I am left wanting more then surely that movie was a success and made me feel exactly how it should have. Going back to pure content, I have played this game and have gone through so many runs of it. Obviously I have my favourite set up that I tend to repeat and replicate from time to time to beat the boss or at least see if I can get that far, but there are so many different ways you can play the game. There are so many different set ups to choose from and the thing is.... its all up to you. There was FREE DLC content that added even more if you thought there wasnt enough in the game, but beware it makes it more of a challenge.
p.s. Avoid the nebula!

I've already forgotten, how many times I've beaten this gem of a game. Including the original "Metro 2033" it has to be at least 5-6 times. Why? Because the atmosphere and the universe of "Metro 2033" is amazing, it's quite literally "dripping" with atmosphere. Game is fairly linear with minimal exploration, however it adds a lot of gameplay elements, like the possibility of avoiding confrontations with human enemies, incapacitating them without killing them and so on. Also, there's sometimes alternate pathways you can choose, especially when going the stealthy route.
Voice acting in English is very cringe-worthy, I'd recommend trying to play this game with Russian audio and English subtitles. It just feels way more authentic this way, and the VO actors actually do a good job in it's native tongue. If you are a completionist, then it's VERY likely that you'll play this game more than once, so I do recommend playing the game at least once with Russian VA - it's worth it.
Gunplay is very well polished and the "Redux" in this case feels welcome, because the gunplay in the first game didn't feel so great. Gasmask system was very poorly done, and you really had trouble recognizing how much air you really had.   Battery charging was extremely obnoxious and stealth was broken - however not in your favor, since if you got detected only
the enemies in the WHOLE FREAKING LEVEL will always know your position, and getting detected was very easy. It felt like the stealth was an afterthought, while with "Redux" they fix the stealth so that it works now like it did in Last Light. Enemies have a very low field of view and darkness = invisibility - hilarious, I know, but at least stealth is viable.
On higher difficulties you die very easily, and game does not have a regenerating health system. You need to use the medkit to make the "bloody screen so real" go away. Guns have recoil and the sound effects are awesome. Highly recommend playing this with a good pair of headphones for maximum paranoia. Ambient music is also phenominal, which has undertones of despair, hope and eerie beauty, especially when walking on the surfice in Moscow.
The story is simple, but it's just enough to keep you going. Highly recommend reading the actual source material for the game, because it covers more about other character relations with Artyom. Lots of phylosophy about life and such. A good read. Still have to get myself Metro 2034 and 2035.
There's also a somewhat hidden morality system (you can't really know how much you have) and it's tied to the ending of the game, or at least it gives you an opportunity to choose an ending, rather than an automatic one. Still, it's disappointing, due to the fact that the next game: Metro Last Light already has a set story, based on one of the endings, so it doesn't really matter if you pick the "good" one. My guess is that the studio lacked the manpower to actually make Last Light into a two-part game, where endings mattered and had to scrap the idea, due to limited time, money and inability to make a branching story actually work, which in the end I think is reasonable, considering the crappy environment the developers had to make the game in.
Would recommend this to any FPS game enthusiast and even more, to people who enjoy fleshed out worlds with tons of lore and interesting, albeit a little lacking in personalisation, characters. I do hope that more Metro games will be released in the future, because I can easily place this game together with other FPS legends like BioShock, Half-Life and the early days of Call of Duty.

Metro 2033 Redux is a mostly linear shooter with a dark and gritty atmosphere in post-apocalyptic Moscow. Sometimes, especially during the stealth parts of the game, the game let's you choose from different paths. This game is inspired by a book written by Dmitri Alexejewitsch Gluchowski. It gets a lot of praise in the gaming community so it was a no-brainer for me to try it out sometime. They weren't wrong. It's clearly a classic.
+ Nice gameplay
+ Immersive atmosphere
+ Many weapons to choose from and you can upgrade them as well.
+ It runs well and looks very nice on high settings.
+ Stealth mechanics could be better, but do their job in the end.
+ Memorable enemies and scenes
- I wanted to hear Russian voices, but it's not fully subbed.
- I hoped to see more interaction with people that could have deepened the atmosphere even more. Also, there could be missions inside of the human colonies, too. I felt a bit disappointed by the human colonies and found myself craving for more.
- I don't want to spoil anything, but there is a hidden moral point system I don't agree with because some parts of it don't make sense.
- The FOV is rather small. Although there is no FOV slider in the settings, I have heard it's possible to change it manually in the ini file. You might want to check this out.
If you like singeplayer games with dark atmospere and some survival elements then this game is for you. I recommend buying the bundle with the sequel Metro: Last Light redux.

This is a game that will stick with you long after you finish it. This is a beautiful game both visually and emotionally, a truly immersive and atmospheric experience that will have you enthralled on the edge of your seat for the entire game. The way the plot unfolds is done expertly, and you will need to pay close attention to accurately interpret the story and it's ending. Inspired by Weird Horror Fiction like the work of H.P. Lovecraft, it truly is a great callback to his work with a twist that suddenly brings the story crashing back to reality. The ending is truly tragic and emotional once all the plot points come together, provided you read all of the notes along the way. The game is truthful in saying it will not "hold your hand", however the really difficult puzzles are at the beginning, while the later puzzles unfortunatley become formulaic and rather repetitive once you understand the mechanics. That being said, however, the story is what keeps you going for the rest of this rather short game. While this isn't your typical horror game, I would say there are some spots that are genuinely frightening, one sequence in particular catches you off guard because it plays very much like Amnesia, which is an unexpected and pleasent change of pace which results in the game becoming a bit jumpy. If you're a fan of mystery, horror, puzzles, and emotional plotlines it would be criminal not to pick this gem up.
Pros:
+Beautiful, near-photorealistic graphics
+Emotional and enthralling plot
+Genuinely spooky atmosphere
+Fantastic soundtrack only adds to the creep factor
+New, innovative gameplay in the first half
Cons:
- Gameplay becomes repetitive "point and click" after the mine sequence
- Short, I beat it in roughly 4-5 hours
- The "side quests", while contributing to the emotional impact of the plot, often take away from the atmosphere of the main game because they're tonally quite different from the main murder mystery/H.P. Lovecraft-inspired plot

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an absolute beauty of a game, from its stunning environmental landscapes to the fantastic atmospheric sound effects that you hear while walking around. I feel that this game has a mix of L.A. Noire with Dear Esther and a bit of Amnesia: The Dark Descent thrown in.
The story is very good and the ending is very good too. Although the game is pretty short, with only a 3-4 hour length in gameplay, it is still worth getting! Also, The Astronauts made a prequel comic which you can read to find out what happened before the events that take place in the game.
The voice acting, although not the greatest I've heard, it is pretty good but don't expect to hear AAA voice actors in this game
The environment as mentioned before is stellar and beautiful in many ways, I would recommend buying/playing this game on a computer that can actually handle it, although I was able to play it on the High settings, I did experience some sticking in areas where there is a lot of objects. And the FPS did choke down to even 10 FPS!
Although I never saw one single loading screen, I did notice some bugs in the game, in one part I had to put a certain scene in chronological order and two of the player models were missing even though I could still arrange them how I wanted them to be, plus the game did crash once (but that was probably my PC chocking itself with the amount of stuff it had to handle)
Even though the game is great, I wish they could of improved on some stuff. The place where you visit which is Red Creek Valley, is pretty big! I know that the developers wanted to immerse you into the game, but I wish there was a few maps placed into the environment like in the Mine (players who played this bit, you know which bit!) had. Plus some of the items you have to search you don't even realize until you almost reach the end,
Another thing which also annoyed me was where you are in the scene that took place, you would either have to find something or rearrange something, some of the items took me over 30 minutes to complete because I didn't know what on earth I was supposed to do! Also, the puzzles are a bit tricky until you get the hang of it!
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a great game to play and a job well done to the developers as this was there first game by the company The Astronauts, although the game may be a bit short and it may be a bit frustrating at times, this is a great first person mystery game!

The game is graphically beautiful. The levels look very colourful and vibrant, and fits well into the narrative as one can be quickly immersed by the landscape of the imaginary world. The lighting and atmospheric feeling of the environment blends in well with the narrative, making the narrative come alive and more interesting. The settings and the encounters in the narrative, such as the boss in the middle of the game, was very well done as it spices up the gameplay occasionally.
However, the level design is a big problem. Sometimes it is not clear where you are supposed to go because the path is not obvious.  I also managed to break the game on the second level when I accidentally skipped the third crystal core in the cave and went ahead to the next jumping pair (since I wanted to explore around first before entering the cave, not knowing that the cave is a dead end), which supposingly have to be solved with three crystals but could be beaten by using just two. I had to restart the level when I couldn’t go back the way I came in order to collect the crystal core that I skipped, when the puzzles further down the level required it.
Swinging from place to place really gives you a sense of freedom, and navigating the levels could have been fun. Unfortunately the grappling hook itself is frustrating to use, and it always feel like you are trying to beat the physics system rather than trying to beat the puzzle, since the solution is clear and easy but the execution becomes highly tedious due to the somewhat funky physics system. Occasionally you can get stuck in places and you slip off areas you think you should have a firm grip on. It is hard to get a sense of satisfaction for solving these puzzles when you constantly bang your head and smack your body on the floating stones, which causes you to lose momentum and sometimes narrowly misses the ledges of the platforms as a result.
The checkpoint system is also extremely stingy. When you travel for a long distance and have to grappling hook through multiple platforms (around 5 or 6), sometimes missing one of these platforms means you have to start right back at the beginning, and redo the swings again, which is rather punishing and torturing. Therefore I feel that the game should have a way for players to tweak the checkpoint system such that players who have difficulty in playing could have access to more checkpoints, rather than expecting everyone to be a pro and manage multiple swings without restarting.
The gameplay becomes too distracting due to these problems above and therefore spoils the flow of the narrative. I rather the game being a walking simulator, instead of experiencing a gameplay that sometimes doesn’t work well and frustrates you too much to continue.
The collectives are well hidden, but I felt that these collectives could have been modified to include additional lore or info. Collecting them now feels pointless as the place that you find them is actually not very interesting to be explored or looked at to warrant the trouble of searching and collecting them.
While the narrative and art style is fantastic, the gameplay leaves much to be desired, thus it is hard to recommend this game at the full cost of 12.99 USD.

But most importantly, this is a game that rewards risk. That faster and more efficiently you defeat foes, the faster you level, going up to 2x speed. Oh, and the bosses? Classic gaming style oozes from them as you learn patterns and find the weakspots. I bought this blind and couldn't be happier. I haven't had this much fun with a game in a long, long time. BUY IT ALREADY.

Let me start by addressing some of the complaints about this games such as it being all based on luck and how it lacks content. There is a huge amount, I would even go as far as saying an equal amount of strategy to this game as there is luck. From what you buy, to if you decide to buy anything at all and instead choose to upgrade your ship giving it that extra fire power or hiding behind your many layers of shields. There are so many different ways of playing this game and a large amount of content if you bother to use it. You are able to unlock new ships and new set ups from completing runs and unlocking achievements along the way giving you an insentive to beat the unbeatable. This game is for the people who are prepared to get frustrated, pull out their hair, quit the game and then come back to it the next day with a fresh mindset and with the hunger to get further each time, learning more and more with every click of the start button. I have heard many times that the game is unfair and too one sided, let me just say "You is mad, cus You is bad".
I think its more than fair to say a large proportion of the game will come down to luck and finding either exactly what you need at a shop/encounter or you finding useless items not worth the jump taken to get there. For me this adds to the challenge and gives the game more depth, without it there would be less need for exploration of a star system and a lack of increasing intensity that you might not find a shop before you run out of fuel or needed items. If you were able to jump to a shop and have the full range of items from the game to choose from then this game would be a breeze. If you land at a shop and find the useless crap we all dread to stumble upon after jumping strategicly to the only shop visible then move on! Discover another shop. There are multiple shops per star system it just takes planning and insightful purchases to easily discover most of the map before moving on. However this game is not all based on random blind luck and any one that tells you so well...... I question their inteligence and so should you. This game has been built for replayability and the challenge that comes with it. Of course if you decide to send you crew down to a planet to help survivors there is a good chance they will not come back..... so dont!. If you rescue a crazy man from a pod or planet DONT take him on board. "If you avoid risky encounters then you survive risky encounters". That is a phrase that should be forced upon people when they start up the game.
As for the lack of content....... well I have to say that I haven't encountered this as a problem. I understand the feeling of getting to the final boss with an almost perfect ship, defeating him and not being able to help but want to carry on. Surely this in its self proves that the game has been entertaining though. In my eyes if I come to the end of a movie and I am left wanting more then surely that movie was a success and made me feel exactly how it should have. Going back to pure content, I have played this game and have gone through so many runs of it. Obviously I have my favourite set up that I tend to repeat and replicate from time to time to beat the boss or at least see if I can get that far, but there are so many different ways you can play the game. There are so many different set ups to choose from and the thing is.... its all up to you. There was FREE DLC content that added even more if you thought there wasnt enough in the game, but beware it makes it more of a challenge.
p.s. Avoid the nebula!

Flamebreak is an absolutely gorgeous, well-polished game filled to the brim with RNG and awesome fights. Minotaurs with hammers, Halfling ninjas with throwing stars, lichs that ressurect fallen allies so you have to fight them again, the entire game is awesome in and of itself. It has features lent from DOTA in terms of item pickups as well, but the feature feels extremely good.
Gameplay:
Gameplay consists of you, the hero, fighting against denizens of the world in an attempt to reach the Godsplane and kill a god. It is... not a "twin stick shooter" but more of a top down shooter/meleer in my opinion, but whatever it is, it does it SO WELL.
Sound: Music is done excellently in the game as well as the fighting noises, skill ability noises and everything else.
Story: The story isn't really important in the game, but it does lend itself to the game at least instead of detracting from it. The little cutscenes are beautifully drawn and rendered in-game and are really very nice to look at.
Unlocks/Gameplay: So when you begin the game you only have a few races available to you to use: The Human, Minotaur, Dwarf, and Elf. There are an additional 7 races to unlock as well, and there are also multiple skills and weapons to unlock as well. There is also ONE unlockable race that you just unlock in the options menu by just checking a box labeled "bonus content" lol. But the unlocks just feel really great when you unlock them and get them added to the random pool to use in the game. Unfortunately, there are certain synergies with skills you'll find out that work extremely well together, but you'll barely be able to get them in the random pool, and I can't figure out how to make a custom character so whatever. Still 10/10 features lol.
Items: The items in the game are extremely well balanced in my opinion and it's DEFINITELY ALL RNG. And it's really nice to go into a shop and see a great attack damage dagger or anything like that, or going into a blacksmith and seeing that LAST SET PIECE. Great, great stuff. And also how each shop has cheese in it to regen your HP when you come across one, and there's no better feeling than getting a shop when you're super low on HP so you can continue your run and have MORE FUN. :D
Overall, the game is 10/10. I don't normally like these kinds of games, like Binding of Isaac and such, but Flamebreak just... pulls it off SO WELL. I actually am Let's Playing the daily runs every day, check out the playlist for them here:

This game controls as you expect it to when you move or use a power. The auto lock on system for gamepad control works great to target your attacks and powers, and it's easy to switch to the target you want usually. This game is also based on player skill and not luck. Every death so far has felt like it was my fault of skill, or a power/weapon selection that wasn't ideal in combo with my play style.
For this type of game that's high praise.
Your character has 4 powers and is made up of the following:
Race. Each race/species has slightly different stats and a unique power. For instance Humans have an ability which summons a 1 hit to kill ally that can distract and attack enemies, while the Dwarf has an ability to slam the ground and stun all nearby enemies.
Weapon. Each weapon mostly just attacks (which is another power) but at least one, the spear, you will throw if you wait a few second between attacks. There's a fair variety between melee and ranged weapons.
Abilities. There's a set of powers that you get two of. These have a range of effects. One throws a flame wave out, another throws out a stun that passes through enemies, and there's one that summons tiny skeletons holding bombs that seek out and explode on enemies. Of course there's more than just those 3 powers.
You start with 3 randomly selected characters with the above to choose from normally, though I just unlocked the ability to choose a combination myself at the price of only recieving half "Spirit" rewards which builds up and levels over games to unlock more races, weapons, and abilities.
There's a map screen and you shoose a spot next to you to move to and fight or shop at the location. There's some kind of evil darkness that comes from the bottom of the screen so you can't take forever and clear every spot. At the top of the map there's a boss you must defeat to move on to the next map area. There's a few different bosses you might fight at different maps.
At the shops you might pick up items that increase attack damage, attack speed, move speed, or certain shops have pieces of gear sets that when complete give you extra passive abilities. I believe there may also be items and gear sets that give active-use abilities.
Over-all a fun game.

Flamebreak is a roguelite action-RpG blending twin-stick and MOBA combat gameplay, whilst accompanied by a terrific story, brilliantly told in lyrical prose and voiced quite nicely. I felt as though I'd been playing for only half an hour when, in actuality, over 3 hours had disappeared! In fact, it was only because my index finger was seizing up - and not the fact that it was nearing 3:30 in the morning - that made me stop playing.
The in-battle gameplay is fairly reminiscent of TBoI, but it's far more enjoyable: rather than punishing you for even thinking you could play it, Flamebreak offers a real and rewarding chance at developing your skills and getting to know a bit about the game before dying a bajillion times. It's action-packed and fast-paced, and paying attention to how your enemies deploy attacks is required to overcome and go far. However, this game is not bullet-hell-silly like others similar and I really think that gamers who are usually hesitant to try such games will actually love Flamebreak.
Levels are randomly generated with approximately 25 possible waypoints that keep you moving forward to the boss' lair where success propels you on to the next level. Each waypoint can be a shop of sorts for upgrades, equipment and skills, or a battle. While on the waypoint screen, there are skill abilities you can use that give you a buyer's edge or just to stay ahead of the creeping Shadow that will overtake you if you dally around too long (like FTL's Galactic Federation fleet). In-battle is total arcade gameplay where you may encounter skirmishes, skirmishes with environmental or supernatural hazards bombarding all, gold nabbing and guarding challenges, shrines and temples, even mini-bosses. With numerous races, weapons, skills, battles and bosses randomised every level, not to mention unlockables you get as you become better and better, Flamebreak offers huge replayability and countless hours of white-knuckle fun.
I cannot comment on the use of keyboard+mouse, but I couldn't imagine playing this game with anything other than a controller. With slick, responsive gameplay; clean, bright graphics and pleasing artwork; great story narrated by an attention-grabbing voice; good music and sharp sound effects, I cannot recommend Flamebreak enough, and I feel the regular price is reasonable.

Plain and simple, I loved it. The game is a fantastic first person platformer.
Now, I know what you're thinking: "But first person platformers are usually awful! They're hard to control and land, and in general don't feel as good as sidescrollers!"
This game blows that assumption out of the water. The controls feel great, the atmosphere feels great, and the ability to move around freely feels great!
Overall, the game starts out with a bit of a Portal-meets-Dear-Esther vibe, in that it starts out with a paced narrative in a beautiful world, which follows through seamlessly into the actual puzzle game where you use some out-of-this-world technology to think quickly in ways you hadn't thought to before, allowing
The game does have a few issues here and there. First of all, there is a small problem with depth perception. Granted, that's going to happen in a first person platformer, but sometimes all it does is net frustration. Then again, that does tend to happen more often than not in a puzzle game designed to legitimately challenge you. In the end, that frustration can lead to some wonderful moments of, "Oh thank god I finally got that."
However, one MAJOR issue I have with this game was one point where I had just barely almost made it to the next platform before falling off. The game shoved a hint in my face, then cheated me onto the ledge. I understand why they might do that, but I felt cheated in that the game basically took the controller from me and said, "Okay, we'll just spawn you there." I didn't feel that I earned it.
Another issue ends up being character design. Some of the characters feel... awkward. While this is reasonable seeing as what they are (you'll understand), they didn't feel like living characters in a real world; they felt like VIDEO GAME NPC #37. Especially the few ended up talking to you, whose heads would spin around in order to keep their eyes on you, their necks snapping back and forth should you walk behind them. Granted, you could have it a number of other ways, all with their own flaws, but it takes you out of the experience of the game when that happens. Of course, the exception to this is the character Maddie; it felt like the developers spent time and effort in animating her every expression and motion, and she felt much more alive than any other character.
The attitude the game takes towards you wavers as well. In the beginning the game is chocked with wonderful experiences and delightful gameplay, but about halfway through, I felt the game calling back to my early childhood games, where, if you were lost, the game would whistle at you and point you in the right direction. Simply put, I felt like I was stuck in a game intended for children 8-12. I would have been fine with that, had the game decided to stick with that emotion; the challenge of the game seems higher than that needed for an 8-12 year-old child. Maybe I'm just overestimating the skill required to play this game, or underestimating the skill of a kid, but the two just don't feel like they match up. (Or maybe I'm just bad at vidya gaemz.)
Despite all of this, the game does do what's most important for a game to do: Introduce a skill/challenge, teach you how to use/overcome that skill/challenge, then apply that skill/ability/challenge to future situations in combination with the previous skills/challenges.
*SPOILERS AHEAD*
--This section touches a bit more on what I found wrong with the game, but requires describing aspects of the game that would be considered spoilers. You have been warned.--
When I had mentioned depth perception being a problem, I also had issues with the grappling hook. Sometimes, something would seem close enough to grapple, but the crosshair wouldn't light, meaning that you have to restart and try again, because maybe you just weren't close enough, or maybe you're going for the wrong rock entirely. A perfect example is the area just after  you leave the village: you head out, and jump across to some huge rock. You attempt to grapple it over and over, and for whatever reason, your crosshair won't like up, and won't hit it. You figure, "Oh, that must just be the problem with the distance." However, later on, you come across a rock which is undeniably further than the aforementioned one, and yet the crosshair lights up when aimed over it. It could have just been a matter of perspective, but over all, it tended to confuse me.
Again, the characters seem awkward. I understand, they're frog-people, but... if you're going to do that, do it right. Maddie was perfect, in that she appeared significantly inhuman, but still behaved in very human ways. At no point did I think, "Oh, she's just an NPC integral to the plot." Every moment I was with her, she felt alive and existant. She felt like a person! In contrast, almost every one of the villagers felt... dead. Sure, they were whistling, they were dancing around, they were lounging, but all in all, they didn't feel alive.
Despite all of this, the game still feels fantastic. When you're swinging flawlessly from rock to rock, when you take a huge leap and get a resounding "THUD!" on landing, when you climb your way around the map with every tool you have, you feel... free.

If you like Portal, and you like Spider-man, you'll love this game. Once you get the swinging mechanic down, there's nothing more satisfying than hitting your mark on the first try. Indie feel and terrible voice acting, but regardless I can't wait to find out more about this story, too. Recommended, especially for the price.

A Story About My Uncle is a first-person adventure platformer. The main gameplay involes using your grapple hook, power jump and rocket boots to advance through the level. The gameplay feels very fluid and smooth, and sometimes even challenging. The grapple hook is my favorite game mechanic in ASAMU because it feels amazing to zip through the air grappling from rock to rock, but it only has up to three uses before landing on the ground. The limited amout of uses creates another challenge for the player, where you must strategize how you will get to the other floating island before running out of charges. Most of the time this is easy to see where your grapple makes a mark on everything you hook on to, so you're able to see how your uncle made it across because of his marks on floating rocks. The power jump is exactly what it says, it gives you a very powerful jump. Combined with the sprint key, you're able to shoot out very far. The rocket boots don't feel very powerful to me, but they're useful nevertheless.
The story revoles around you, a father, telling your daughter a bedtime story. You tell a story of your uncle Fred and his adventures and how you always wanted to be just like him. You stumble into his house hoping he is home when you find an adventure suit, custom made for you but your uncle never told you about it. It seems that he wanted you to find out yourself. You strap it on and it's equipted with a grapple hook and power boots. You enter his gigantic 'garbage disposal' and you're shot into the sky, leading you to an unknown world. Naturally, you feel ready for the adventure, and continue moving through this strange world with one misson: find Uncle Fred. The story seems a little cliche, where you need to go out on this big adventure to find someone, but it's not horrible, it's quite alright.
The game includes no violence and no action, but it is better that way. The game focuses on the gameplay and narrative. As your progress through the world, you narrate what you saw and what happened. The game is very beautiful, with the textures very high resolution and the enviroments are mind blowing. Overall, the graphics are amazing, besides the people. The characters looks outdated the their animations are a bit strange. The audio is fantastic as well. The music always fits the athmosphere, ambient noises are soft and charming, and the landing sound is great. Another thing though, the voice acting isn't the greatest. You can tell the VA's first language wasn't English, but it's all right. The father and daughters voice acting is the best of the bunch. Maddie's is strange.
While the graphics and gameplay are great, the story and voice acting falls behind just a little bit, but what are you going to expect from a company's first game?

A Story About My Uncle is a narrative driven first person platformer from gone north games and coffee stain studios. Those scared of hieghts need not apply.
The story is presented as a tale from the unnamed player character after the events of the game. It starts off as a you begin searching for your uncle Fred in his house but instead find one of his "adventure suits" tailor made for you, and after you find a secret launch pad you get flung into space to follow the trail of crumbs he laid out for you. That's about as much of the story I feel ok with revealing as it is the games main focus and what I would guess something many people want to experience for themselves. Even though it was an aspect that I found thoroughly underwhelming.
From a story perspective I just flat out didn't care what happened. The game pushes you towards a few characters the it presents, but due to a lack of investment it just comes off as a hollow experience. It didn't ever really feel like the gameplay moved the story along and instead felt like the story was there to take you to the next amazing vista or cavern. Which is a bit odd since the big marketing point for this game was its story. Heck, it's the title, but I would be more upset over this issue if the movement mechanics weren't so dang fun.
And holy crap do I love the movement system. Seeing what next awesome view the game took me to, along with getting into more and more crazy platforming situations was easily the best part of ASAMU. The levels seem pretty linear at first but each one has a some room for exploration and each of the five brings something new to the table that allow you to explore them in different ways.
Yep, five levels. It's a short game, no way around that. I played the entire story in just about two hours and I imagine, for many will be the biggest issue when looking into buying it. At thirteen U.S. dollars the game probably sits a little outside the value range for most. It does try to add some replayability with a time trial and a few unlocks here and there, but even in these area's it feels like more missed potential. The time trial is nice but the imprecise nature of the grapple, something that isn't an issue in the story as you can quickly reset, just isn't as fun when put under a time requirement. And the unlocks from what I can see are just small cosmetics that may add a few giggles, but don't add much real value.
I enjoyed my time playing A Story as short as it was, and even if the game just didn't follow through with some of the things it set out to do. The simply joyous nature of flying around the beautiful landscapes overcame those pitfalls. I would love to see the developers to more with this system even if it was a couple levels disconnected from the story entirely.
If what you've seen interests you then I would absolutely recommend it, but you may want to wait for a sale first.

While short, as a debut from Gone North Games, this is a fantastic indie game. I hope that the success of A Story About My Uncle brings more titles from Gone North Games, which I await with anticipation!

Basically a SciFi B-movie take on the Magicka system. Get 2 to 4 players on the same screen, have no friendly fire protection, then have practically every action capable of killing your own team-mates.
The enemy types are different enough from each over to make things interesting, and there's a novel take on the campaign map screen that does hammer home the feeling of being in an "elite" army "fighting against hostile invaders" that "threaten" Super Earth.
And yes, the Starship Troopers style mockery of the action is funny, if it does get a little grating after a while. There's only so many times you can snicker at deploying a "Truth Trainsmitter" and knowing full well it's a mind control device.
As for the weapons, there's a fairly good spread of the standard fair. The DLCs does add to the pool with some intriging takes on the base loudout, but certainly not as "game-changing" as the forums are currently alight with. But I digress.
Multplayer runs fairly well. There's a tech in game that can bump you up the matchmaking list if you badly need another Helldiver to deploy to the squad, but finding the time to do this mid-mission when you're better off focusing on actually staying alive is a tad tricky. Aside from that, Arrowhead's love of not allowing players to hide behind turning off friendly fire brings it's usual bundle of backstabbing, accidental or otherwise, as well as all the wonderful ways to troll the party. Helldivers is a topdown shooter focusing on teamwork and spreading democracy to the oppressed, backwards planets across the galaxy. As one of the elite Helldivers of Super Earth's military, you deploy alone or with up to three friends to liberate planets from alien rule by killing them in droves and completing random objectives. The game encourages teamwork and, without it, you will find most of your time being spent ventilating your buddies.
The gameplay is solid and translates surprisingly well to Kb+M controls, even to the point of being more precise thanks to the added control of a mouse. There's a very large variety of weapons, strategems (radio support), enemies, and missions to keep the game interesting as the War progresses. I personally very much enjoy how the campaign is a community effort with every player contributing to the progress of the War until it is lost or won, another starting right after.
Graphically, you can tell the limitations it faced from its original console release. The game is smooth and anti-aliased, but you can see where the render distance for weather and world effects are cut at the edge of your camera. While the models are low-poly, the game has a definite charm to its artstyle and it's very well optimized. Not even a stutter when the screen is filled with fire, blood, bullets, and more alien bugs than you can shake a stick at. When it comes to sound design, everything is solid and you get to hear some pretty heavy English accents putting on their best American impression.
It's a definite recommendation from me.

4/22/2017

I have tested it with 3 different cables now and the issues are still present, but they only happen once every two hours or so worth of use which I consider acceptable. A splendid Action-Roguelike.
This game is my favorite game of the new year. It really captures that plug-and-play procedural action I've been looking for after hundreds of hours of The Binding of Isaac. It offers an immaculate blend of challenge and strategic options that keeps me engaged at the edge of my seat for the whole ~22-40 minute play session. I'm just starting to have hard-mode win-streaks. And even during a -29 lose streak I was having fun discovering character combinations and honing my exploration and gold-spending techniques.
My other favorite thing is the controls. I play mostly with a gamepad and the game offers seamless transition between playing with a controller and playing with keyboard and mouse. Simply move the mouse or joystick and the game snaps to the new control layout. Both options offer very different approaches and are both satisfying to play.
**There are a few issues with balance and (**seemingly) underpowered combos. I couldn't for the life of me get a Human-Sword-Arcane Blast- Meteor character to victory on normal. But in most cases in combination with good item and deity choices you could find the path to victory.
**EDIT** The Devs totally answered my implicit challenge and beat my run on HARD
Overall this game is a real gem and absolutely should be in your roguelike library.

By far one of the best experiences you can have playing a game.
There is not much more that can really be said about this game. This game really defies being labeled.
Is it a strategy game? Yes and no
Is it a RPG game? Yes and no
Is it an action game? Well again yes and no
It’s hard to pin this game under any kind of label because there are so many different factors that make up this game.
The weapon variety is pretty extensive , and with only 3-4 slots for weapons it makes your choices all the more important. Choosing between clearing the enemy ships of crew or just obliterating them its all in the way to play.
The boss difficulty borders on near insane. Even on -what can only be called a cake level lie - "easy." But that in no way means it is impossible, you will die...... A LOT....... and then some......and again. You will want to punch your brand new computer screen, take a sledgehammer to your mouse and scream profanity.
Now why should you play such a game that promises so much aggravation?
Because that promise of victory is ever so close you can almost feel it but just out of reach, and that pull of each new ship you earn through properly finished quests or achievements. But nothing compares to that first time you defeat the Overpowered Flagship..... The supreme elation that comes from crushing your enemies, seeing them driven before you, and hearing the lamentations of their women... and then the horror that comes when you realize that it's still not over.
You need to experience the sorrow, anger, and elation for yourself
It's worth the $10 easy but if you see it on sale
DON'T HESITATE!

I think this game has alot going for it. Strong original gameplay, varied factions and units, lots of different commanders for unique gameplay styles and brilliant workshop content.
If you like other RTS games like command and conquer (as I do) this may take a bit of getting used to. It works on alot smaller scale, so instead of legions of troops and whole tank batallions you would be more likely to field 6 squads of infantry, some infantry crewed weapons and a few tanks. Once I got used to the smaller scale and *shock* protecting/conserving my units (instead of just setting my spawn point in the enemy base and spamming units) I gre to like it alot. You have to play alot more tactically, but I enjoyed the challenge of this and the game engine itself helps you by being able to place your units in cover (or build your own), strategically block areas using tank traps/mines and lots more options available to employ.
Overall I would highly recommend getting this and the Western Front Armies if you have the spare cash, as it add 2 more factions who are different again, and add whole new dimensions to gameplay such as having mobile field hospital/retreat points, mobile artillery and more. There is an In-Game Store available which has vehicle skins and commanders available to purchase that are not available in the workshop or steam store, while these can be expensive (£3 for one commander!) they are occasionally on deal for 20-50p so it is worth keeping an eye out if you want more content.
The only bad thing I would say are Relic/Sega's price of the Ardennes Assault expansion. This adds no new factions or units (as far as I can tell) and is just a different type of campaign than we are used to with this game... for £30! So I would just pick up the base game plus the Western Front Armies as that's all the content you'll need if you like playing skirmishes with friends online or against the AI.

Dying Light for me at first i hated when i first played the demo. I thought it was not for me but replaying it a few times makes me enjoy it far more than i expected. The reason why I'm telling you this becuase that the theme here with this game, it looks average and perdictable at first, but BAM!! the game suprrisied attack you with fun gameplay and addictive gameplay loop.
Story: Well this is one of the weaker aspect of Dying light. What i'm saying is that the story at times is pretty average and predictable at times but there are certain scenes and plot points that is so bad. It is set in the fictional city of Haran where a zombie virus is spread there and it is qaurantined by the militery, leaving everyone to fend for themsleves. You play as Crane an agent to a mysterious orginisation set to Haran to find a man called Rais and got himself into helping surviours while surving agianist the hordes as well as Rais himself. It your typical zombie story plot that has potiental to be good but the writting sqauntered it. The problem is that there very little reason to care about these characters as they are two-dementional archtypes. There is the token indepedent female who has handle herself in battle but get captured by the villian to be saved by the hero. While the voice acting for Crane by veteren Roger-Craig Smith is alright but the rest is either decent ro pretty bad. The teenager that wants to be treated like an adult that the game so depesteratly wants to  care but he's too annoying for me to do.  And surprisingly a lot of similarites of Farcry 3 as Rais is pretty much a rip-off of Vass with his motivations and actions and the last level being in a drug-like filled with strange things happening. JUST LIKE FARCRY3. Also by the way the game ends with a qucik-time event "boss-fight".
Gameplay: The game sound quite bad now, but why did i gave a recommedation then? Well it's because of the gameplay that made-up all the faults of the story. The game is a first-person shooter with parkour elements similar to Mirror's Edge with looting and melle combat straight of dead Island . But let me warn you, the begining to the game is difficult and you will feel pretty underpower but trust me keep going as you will be rewarded and become death on two legs at the end. The parkour is very smooth and fluid just like Mirror's Edge but what make's it impressive that's is all from a single button. The melee combat is satafiying on zombies with the crunching sound effects and the gore on display. But the game like before is challenging with fast moving zombies always chasing you and spitters and those giant tanks that hit hard. But my problems with the combat is that that there are somtimes hitbox issues when using melee and remember that the redicule doesn't aim where the melee weapons is landing on rather aim the direction where it is going. Also the boss fights, are very sponge-bullet or melee-sponge and when you die the boss dosen't gain health so you can throw yourself at the boss multiple until you die.
Conculsion: The game, once you look past the story, the issues with combat and bosses, the game is utter fun in it's own way no other open-world game can rival at. Those i recommened you buy it on sale for those who are unsure and there's also a demo avialable to try out. Also the game is full of content to have as this version has all the dlcs as well as the following expanion that can also last 20 hours of content on it's own.
