I REAAAAAAAALY wanted to get into this. What was meant as an epic space RTS in the WH40K universe... It is not what I was hoping for in the end. I guess I was just expecting too much.
I really wanted good cpu ships that would do something other than simply rush in and get shot to♥♥♥♥♥♥ or my personal favorite - fly through an asteroid field and just explode.
On the up side I have to say the way the story was being told to the point I made it felt very well done. It captured the essence of the imperium and for the matter universe very well from what I saw. Still needed a bit more warp hijinks to get the real feel - IE your astropaths heads exploding or psykers going batshit insane.
The game play was too much micromanagement to make it fun for me. And escort missions for ether side were pretty stupid at the point I made it in the game - If it was you, the CPU just rushes your transports and tries to kill them which quickly turns into something akin to the benny hill show and you start just leading them around rocks and such as the enemy tries to shoot or ram them. If it is the CPU - you just rush the AI transports and become very confused/disappointed when they simply proceed to run right though an asteroid field and get torn to shreds before you even get a chance to fire a shot.
It may be my own fault for getting excited for it. I was looking for Epic several mile long ships and weapons that could crack planets in half, what I got was what felt like toy ships in a bath tub with a todler.
Now that I think about it, this is the only way I could see it happening as well, but the scale of it just feels soo very wrong. - It was like when you were a kid and you got that one huge fire cracker that everyone was eluding to being like a 50kt hydrogen bomb, and it looks the part (to a 7 year old). You wait with baited breath for the 4th of July to Light it up and just hoped that your little legs can get you just far enough away before it goes off. The day of judgement arives and you (with some generous help from the non-believers) Kick it off and head for cover, all this time in waiting for your master stroke, and it is at hand. Soon they all shall quake at it the fury and hellfire you have set upon them. The fuze quickly aproaches its destination. Finally it reaches what you lovingly dubbed "the big one" and sizzles for a few moments - You brace, but instead of a earth shattering kaboom - All you hear is a steady stream of sparks flying. You look and soon some fire appears to shoot a bit from the top and a black snake like thing begins to ooze out. This continues for about 60 seconds or so, and finally all is quiet. You walk up and everyone around you looks like nothing was amiss, like this was the expected result, but how could that be, they sold this so big, as if it was a Illudium PU-36 Explosive Space Modulator. All that is left now is disappointment and a snake of black soot. No bang. No hell fire storm and the end of days. Just some mildly impressive sparks and a beter than average black snake.
Oh well. Might be for you, was not for me. Personally I just don't think you could really capture the scale or feel of something like this outside of maybe VR thinking about it, the ability to look out the window and not be able to even see the far end of your own ship it is soo huge. To take a stroll to the other end of the ship and it take 3-5 hours at a brisk pace.

The single player missions are rough too. Rarely is there a standup fight, always the much maligned guard and escort missions. I just finished a guard mission, which I lost, because my own ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ships kept running into the stationary one I was meant to guard while they were manouevring. Turns out impact damage is really powerful. I like the ideas of this game - upgrade your persistent ships between fights, broadside combat and ramming, a bit of freedom to choose your fights in a 4x structure, but at the end of the day, those are just ideas, and they're wrecked by janky mechanics and a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥interface. Go dust off homeworld 2 or Galciv instead.

Half Life 2: Episode One (SPOILER WARNING)
(Story)
Half Life 2: Epsiode One (HL:EP1) picks up where Half Life 2 left off: with a bang.  Upon recovering from the influence of the vortigaunts, Alyx and Gordon find themselves at the base of the Citadel.  The reactor core, the Citadel's power source, is going critical and it's up to Alyx and Gordon to slow down the meltdown.  What follows is a series of events that put Alyx and Gordon at the top of the Combine's list of priorities.  As a result, the two must escape the city with their bought time, all the while helping Barney with resistance related business.
(Gameplay)
The game is first person with shooting and puzzle solving dominating.  There are no vehicular segments in this Episode.  For the first half of HL:EP1, pacing is a little slower to allow you to soak in the atmosphere.  The dark, underground segments will get your pulse going, especially with the new suicide zombies that run at you with live grenades.  The second Half of Episode 1 is more combat focused as you push through the last of City 17's defenders and fight gunships.
(Design)
There are several new textures to look at and things all around look a bit sharper coming from Half Life 2.  Sound and visual fidelity remain stellar.  Lighting is still excellent.  Story is well written and paced appropriately.  Alyx has several new animations depending on what enemy she is fighting or what weapons she has equipped.
(Final Comments)
As the sequel to Half Life 2, HL:EP1 continues the story of Half Life 2, giving us a better understanding of what is happening in City 17.  Gordon and Alyx become a dangerous team and the stage is set for Episode 2 very well.  Just remember to keep your flashlight charged.

Roguelikes can be very fun: The immense challenge can make you feel amazing when you persevere or it can inspire you to come back for revenge if you fail, and then there is the sheer scale of adventure in a world that is always different with each new game. This is not one of those roguelikes... At all.
See, the big issue with FTL is that the developers believe that random level and encounter generation is the very definition of what makes a roguelike a roguelike, but this is only one aspect. All of the other reviews touch on this over reliance on randomness so I will expose what I feel is the other critical failures: No backtracking and no picking when to engage an encounter.
In Nethack it isn't exactly impossible to go backwards to visit a store you passed but couldn't afford anything. Sometimes you have no choice but to leave behind a valuable and useful loot item. Big deal: Wait until you get better and go back for it. In FTL you only get ONE chance to buy that uber awesome missile launcher that you desperately need to beat the boss. If you cannot afford it (and you rarely can afford anything) then it might as well have never existed at all (which is also a very common problem because of the randomness). In my most recent attempt at the game I had to do an entire run using only the default weapons because I had zero capability to ever purchase anything other than fuel, repairs, and defensive upgrades.
Most of the time the game will straight up refuse to let you avoid an encounter in the first place, which is often something that must be done in literally every other Roguelike ever. Knowing when to fight and when to run and when it is time to go back is a big thing in the genre. In FTL you CANNOT afford to avoid an encounter and come back latter (not that it would ever let you anyway) because encounters are the only method to acquire the resources you need to buy that missile launcher you so desperately need and resources are always in short supply. Technically there is the ability to run away or not get involved, but in practice you will simply never do this; You have no choice but to engage in battle with that beast of a warship so that you can hopefully earn enough scrap to afford repairs and ammunition with a little bit left over for your next gun or upgrade.
When all is said and done, FTL plays itself because it makes all the decisions and railroads you into moving forwards. The player is only there to push the "jump" button. If the game was capable of pushing the "jump" button then it would be a fully functional fishtank and virtual fishtanks don't sell.
Pretty fun, although your finishing ship formula is always the same, so it loses a bit of replayability due to this. Worth buying if its on sale.

A Story About My Uncle is a narrative focused, first person platforming adventure developed by Gone North Games and published by Coffee Stain Studios. The game has great sound and music design, surreal environments, jaw-dropping visuals, and much, much more.
The story not only puts emphasis on the main plot and characters, but also on the side plot and side characters. You play as a dad telling his daughter a story about how his uncle, Fred, goes missing and how the dad goes after him. The father comes across his uncles' invention, a suit which has a grappling hook and lets you take no fall damage, to help the dad find his uncle. On your journey you will traverse through a multitude of different environments, while meeting numerous side characters that will help you on your way. The narrative is the soul of the game, but it's done in a simple and subtle manner that you, the player, have to explore and ultimately piece it all together.
The game focuses on movement, speed, freedom, and light puzzle solving instead of violence. Movement is the core element of the game. With the help of your grappling hook, you feel so free and fast; flying without restrictions and at uncontrollable speeds. It feels so genuine and fluid that it immerses you into this unique world. WASD moves your character, shift to sprint, LMB to use your grappling hook, Space to jump, hold RMB to power jump, and Shift and hold RMB for powerleap. Almost every new platform is a checkpoint where it gives you a certain amount of charges for your grappling hook. And then you have to use your charges and your skills wisely to get to the next checkpoint. Also, Later in the game you get rocket boots to help you through the harder parts of the game.
Like I said before, the graphics are very stunning. ASAMU runs on the Unreal Engine 3 and by god this game looks fantastic. It has gorgeous lighting effects, great world design, phenomenal texture work, and a fantastic attention to detail. Also the art style is very vibrant and dark at the same time; using greens, blues, and browns to convey the mood of the game. Sadly, character models are pretty outdated.
The sound and music design is absolutely brilliant. The sound is very immersive and completely engages the player into the game itself. The "Whoosh" that you hear when you soar through the massive levels is incredible and gives the player a huge adrenaline rush. The game exhibits an emotional, heart-felt, and melancholy symphonic, fantasy soundtrack. Voice acting is somewhat good and somewhat bad. The protagonist, the daughter, and the town elder are voiced well, while everyone else is poorly voiced.
This game has an FOV slider that can be adjusted from 60-120 FOV. There are 15 Steam achievements and the game is about 5-7 hrs. (depending on playstyle) and has a time trial mode. The game also features gorgeous water effects, best looking vegetation I've ever seen, beautiful architecture/ cityscapes, and stunning rock designs and textures. The devs are SO nice and are on the forums to answer questions and complaints!
A Story About My Uncle is Gone North Games' very first game and it is a masterpiece with phenomenal sound, music, atmosphere, immersion, graphics, gameplay, and a gorgeous world to explore. However, the game does suffer from character models that are not up-to-date, ok voice acting, and a poorly translated script. Overall, I can recommend this game to anyone looking for an immersive first person adventure with an unique world and tale to tell. And is most definitely worth $12.99.

This is a hard one. This game has both many upsides and many downsides.
-Its a great RTS, being able to plan ahead and play strategically is important here.
-It can be fun, winning battles is satisfying and even when loosing you can enjoy yourself.
-Winter mechanics are very interesting and unique thing, blizzards, snow and ice add more depth to gameplay on maps where they occur.
-Workshop and modding support is good.
Single player:
-Its pretty historically accurate, which is nice and should be mentioned.
-Can be challenging on higher difficulties
-Level desgin and such are though out well, same with mission objectives.
-Theatre of War missions can be fun to play with friends
Multiplayer:
-Rather satisfying to play.
-Community is nice enough, especially compared to other games.
-The game is poorly optimised, it does not run on minimal settings. It really dosent like certain hardware.
-The AI is too dumb to defeat a thinking player so it cheats, badly, on higher difficulties. Unfortunately Relic didnt bother puttig more work into it. It is also rather predictable.
-Somewhat steep learning curve.
-Relic dosent seem to do much with this game anymore, patches are released every 6 months or so, even though they promised what they called a "5 year plan"
-DLC practices are very annoying. There are tonnes of hidden DLC that dont show up on the main page on steam but are on the in game store or the discussion page (Commanders, Bulletins etc.) While those can indeed drop randomly from each match, it happens somewhat rarely and the chances of you getting what you want are low to say the least. Other things like additional ToW missions or the AA campaign are very overpriced for what they include (AA costs 40 euro which is more than the original game, yet all it brings is 5-6h campaign. ToW missions are the same, Case Blue which is 5 medicore scenarios is around 6 euro)
Single Player:
-The story line is downright average, there arent really any memorable characters, and unlike CoH 1 you go all over the place as opposed to playing with one company troughout the campaign.
-Very unbalanced Theatre of War missions, the Soviet missions can be beaten easily on the highest difficulty using the KV-1 tank with which you can roll in to the enemy base in 4-5 th minute and win. The German Missions are on the other hand way more difficult, in the 1941 scenarios you get no good armour (Only Stug and Pz IV with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 37mm guns that cannot take on any tanks) missing units and in general no acces to good AT weapons making it very painfull to deal with Soviet armour, especially the KV-1s which the AI will always start spamming in the later stages.
-The AI cheats on higher difficulties in many ridiculus ways. I cannot overstate this enough.
-AA campaign is way overpriced at 40 Euro.
Multiplayer:
-The Nations are somewhat imbalanced, If the game lasts into the lategame stage (around 40th minute) Germany will dominate with its heavy armour (Tigers, Ferdinands, Tiger IIs and jagdtigers). The Soviet Union has only two late game units (IS-2 and ISU 152) but those are rather medicore in offensive while the US get no late game units at all, (No Pershing for some reason, even though its kinda needed.) TLDR Germany will usually start to tip the scales towards them every minute past around the 40th min while the US and USSR have the best chance of winning around mid- or even early game. A good player can still however force a victiory in either stage.
-The servers have a tendency to cause some issues from time to time.
-People with slower computers (even if their specs are above minimum) can cause the game to load for up to 5 minutes for everyone else in the lobby and upon which will disconnect everybody one it finishes loading.
-DLC commanders somewhat separate less experienced players from those who are experienced and have those more powerful commanders.
TLDR i would recommend buying this if you have a decent computer and you like RTS games, otherwise you should think twice before doing so.

Right from the onset, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter pulls you into its simple yet intriguing and sometimes spooky story. The controls are extremely basic: you can walk, run, crouch, and interact with certain objects - that's it. The game doesn't tell you how to solve its mysteries or even how to do anything at all.
You can walk around at your leisure (you'll find yourself doing that quite a lot thanks to how beautiful this game looks) and figure things out as you go. But you'll never truly be puzzled, as investigating Ethan's vanishing is helped along by your seemingly supernatural detective abilities.
The actual content itself is somewhat bare, but that seems almost unimportant because where the game really stands out is in how it presents that content. There are beautiful sights and sounds to drink in at all times, and the entire thing feels like a surreal journey more than an adventure or a puzzle.
The atmosphere is truly exceptional, partly thanks to excellent graphics that bring out the best of the beautiful locale and photorealistic art assetts. I don't feel I'm exaggerating one bit when I say The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the prettiest games I've ever played. In fact, when I was done for the first time, it was not the lack of content I regretted but rather the lack of an excuse to keep strolling around the beautiful valley where the story takes place.
This means that although the game is very short (about 3-4 hours) and technically offers you no reasons to play through it again, you may find yourself doing so anyway, if only to further appreciate the gorgeous environments as well as the clues you can find throughout the journey, some of which make even more sense after you've already completed the game.

VR | Oculus Rift | GTX 1060 Gameplay:
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a first-person story-driven mystery game focused on exploration and discovery.
As occult-minded private detective Paul Prospero communicate with the dead to discover the fate of a missing boy and the mystery behind a dark ancient force lurking in Red Creek Valley. - Highly Recommended!

Roguelikes can be very fun: The immense challenge can make you feel amazing when you persevere or it can inspire you to come back for revenge if you fail, and then there is the sheer scale of adventure in a world that is always different with each new game. This is not one of those roguelikes... At all.
See, the big issue with FTL is that the developers believe that random level and encounter generation is the very definition of what makes a roguelike a roguelike, but this is only one aspect. All of the other reviews touch on this over reliance on randomness so I will expose what I feel is the other critical failures: No backtracking and no picking when to engage an encounter.
In Nethack it isn't exactly impossible to go backwards to visit a store you passed but couldn't afford anything. Sometimes you have no choice but to leave behind a valuable and useful loot item. Big deal: Wait until you get better and go back for it. In FTL you only get ONE chance to buy that uber awesome missile launcher that you desperately need to beat the boss. If you cannot afford it (and you rarely can afford anything) then it might as well have never existed at all (which is also a very common problem because of the randomness). In my most recent attempt at the game I had to do an entire run using only the default weapons because I had zero capability to ever purchase anything other than fuel, repairs, and defensive upgrades.
Most of the time the game will straight up refuse to let you avoid an encounter in the first place, which is often something that must be done in literally every other Roguelike ever. Knowing when to fight and when to run and when it is time to go back is a big thing in the genre. In FTL you CANNOT afford to avoid an encounter and come back latter (not that it would ever let you anyway) because encounters are the only method to acquire the resources you need to buy that missile launcher you so desperately need and resources are always in short supply. Technically there is the ability to run away or not get involved, but in practice you will simply never do this; You have no choice but to engage in battle with that beast of a warship so that you can hopefully earn enough scrap to afford repairs and ammunition with a little bit left over for your next gun or upgrade.
When all is said and done, FTL plays itself because it makes all the decisions and railroads you into moving forwards. The player is only there to push the "jump" button. If the game was capable of pushing the "jump" button then it would be a fully functional fishtank and virtual fishtanks don't sell.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is another example of the "murder mystery" trend more and more games of this sort seem to follow nowadays.
This title is a particular one. The story is simple yet complex, and while following the popular trend, it presents many new features to the actual gameplay experience.
The visuals are amazing, nothing more to mention, and the story itself provides more than enough details to keep you hooked.
There are a few shortcomings however...
The voice acting could've used more work, and I really wish there could've been some sort of DLC or add-on to expand on the storyline... unfortunately, the game lacks a sense of lasting appeal, which is disappointing...
But the soundtrack, visuals, and storyline all tied together provide more than enough support to compensate for that.
I'd like to state that this review is in no particular form professional in any way, nor is it based on an extensive analysis of "pros" and "cons", it is entirely based on my personal experience of the game as well as expectations of certain games.
Overall:
8.5/10

Now this, I enjoyed immensely.   Fantastic scenery, subtle storytelling, and a intuitive way to interact with the environment.  I've always been a fan of adventure games - games that fall into the old school genre of adventure - and it's great to do away with a little hand cursor and pixel hunting. Vanishing is a true adventure game, you begin the story, pick a direction, and you adventure!
There are no puzzles, per se, but rather you use logic and reasoning to fit the pieces of the story toghether.   The soundtrack is perfect and I spent a great deal of time staring at scenery and lost in the beautiful music.
That being said, I wanted not only to really enjoy it, but love it.   The only reason I can't quite bring myself to score it higher, is lack of content.   Such a lovingly crafted area deserves more story... I've poked into every nook and cranny and don't ever rush games, so after finishing with a mere 9 hours I was left wanting to play more Vanishing.  (Which in itself says something very positive about the game).
The story itself might not be everyone's cup of tea - you are not "saving the world" that seems to be the in thing nowadays - and again, it is very subtly told - but for myself, I had a great time roaming around trying to figure out just what was going on.
Score: 8/10
With more content, it could easily have been 9.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an amazing story-driven game, in which you travel through Red Creek Valley, solving mysterious killings along the way. You take the role of Paul Prospero, a supernatural detective set out to find the titular Ethan Carter.

. This is very true. You are put right into the world with no real introduction whatsoever, and you just have to figure out what's going on. The graphics is absolutely gorgeous. the sound and the voice acting is also very well done. The game took me about 3½ hours to complete.
I can not recommend this game to anyone, though. You will spend most of the time just walking from a to b, and and someone who requires some action to keep them entertained, this might be a bit boring. But if you, like me, enjoy just experiencing the world, and the story, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is certainly the game for you.

A very nice entry into Warhammer 40k's ever growing library of games in recent years. It does a rather good job in capturing the essence of the tabletop game (R.I.P.) in real time.
The game lacks polish in some aspects, but for such a rare sub-genre as Fleet-centric RTS that should really come as no surprise it won't be up to golden standards. Furthermore it is not an easy game, it is not a kind game, it will kick you when you're down in ways that will make X-Com feel like a hike through the woods. Sadly too, the battles all tend to feel very small scale, more skirmishes than outright naval warfare.
Having said all that it is still good. It is very good. The level of detail on the ships and stations is outstanding, and if you're at all familiar with the baroque battle barges and cloistered cathedralic cruisers you'll know just how many small details make such a difference. If not - imagine yourself standing in front of Notre Dame Cathedral. Now the large circular stained glass window at the front is a giant plasma spewing engine, it's bristling with guns, cannons on the side that you could walk through. That's a frigate of the Imperium of Man, and they only get bigger.
Gameplaywise it faithfully takes the tabletop's rules and slams them into real time making your judgement of turning and firing arcs run twenty seconds ahead of each engagement, which even with only four ships in your flotilla becomes micro-management heaven (or hell), this is made a little simpler and newbie friendly though thanks to the "cogiatator" system which slows everything down to a crawl for your convenience for a short while.
All in all, it's a very worthy try and if you enjoyed the likes of Empire at War's space battles or FTL you will find something to challenge and entice you in this game.

This action RPG drips "old-school" from its pores. While the series never caught on big in the US during its original releases, these remakes and rereleases are worth a look.
There isn't any variation or customization in your character progression, other than the order in which you buy some passive upgrades, so the game will succeed or fail by the gameplay itself. It mostly succeeds here, if you liked Secret of Mana and similar games. There's a great soundtrack to keep you going as well.
So what's old-school about it? Two things stand out: the punishing bosses and the level grind. You'll NEED to pick out the boss patterns to beat them. If you're not stopping to spill some extra blood as you play through the game, you'll be underleveled and you will die quickly. This can even happen on normal monsters - if you find yourself dealing weaksauce damage to new monsters, when you used to be cleaving through armies, go back and grind a few levels. Comparative level matters a lot.

While XCOM 1 may not have all the bells and Whistles as XCOM 2, I keep coming back to it here and there. It may not have procedurally generated maps like XCOM 2, the classes may be different, and once you've played it you kind of develop a definite strategy for how to win most games (Well unless you play XCOM 1 Long War, then you've got the "Dark Souls of Strategy games there), but when you add the expansion, Enemy Within, to the comparison, there is one thing XCOM 1 has that XCOM 2 failed at doing. proper robotic units (and if you count the expansion, Mech Soldiers and Genetic Warriors), all 3 of which, XCOM 2 lacks. Plus the atmosphere is better IMO. In XCOM 2 you're fighting the aliens as a resistance, whereas in XCOM Enemy Unknown, you are on the defense against them, using the majority of Earth's Resources to repel an invasion where you are the underdog.
In short, despite XCOM 2 having improvements, fancy graphics, etc., XCOM Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within still holds up as it provides some means of differing gameplay and atmosphere compared to 2. To put it simply, if you like fighting as a resistance against Aliens or already have XCOM EU (in which case why are you reading this?), then get XCOM 2, if you have not tried XCOM EU yet, and prefer the atmosphere that this provides (being in charge of a "UN" style paramilitary organization that is completely secret from the public as you wage a secret war to protect Humanity), then this is your game.
Also if I may add one last tidbit, once you've beaten Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within a few times, try the Long War mod, it 's basically a fan made expansion to this game that ups the difficulty, reworks the classes, adds new classes, changes how air combat works, et cetera. But be warned, Long War makes XCOM SUUUPER difficult.

I'm not sure about the Deluxe Edition, but I'll probabbly pick up the upgrade soon, if I don't unlock other weapons/items in the mean time.
One thing I will advise: rebind your keys, especially the strategem key.  I have mine bound to Mouse 3, so I can quickly click it and start entering the "codes" (like magicka's spell casting system) to call down my assets.  If you have to reach over for left control, and then move back to WASD to enter the code, it's possible to make mistakes, especially in the heat of battle.  I also rebound sprint to Mouse 4, again to reduce how much I have to move off of WASD.  Lastly, look at the control toggles for things like airm, sprint, strategem deploy, prone, and map.  You don't want to have to hold those buttons down the whole time you're using them. Toggle it on, toggle it off.

Saints Row IV has put a huge spin on the series, introducing new mechanics and story, while still maintaining the frantic, fast paced action that the rest of the series delivers. This game mostly impressed me, so let's get into this review.
Saints Row IV is, I'd say the easiest Saints Row game to pick up and play. While most sandbox games behave like this, Saints Row IV pulls this off very well, with a plot that doesn't require knowledge of the past games and characters, but still manages to keep your attention all the way through. The game has taken some big steps from the previous game, Saints Row the Third, and they are mostly good. New weapons, new cars, a new villian. Most of these things are things that you can only expect in a sequel, though.
The biggest innovation in Saints Row IV was the powers. They completely change the gameplay. Running on walls, doing super jumps, and shooting fireballs at people are only a few of the many powers you can get in this game. The powers made the game what it is, and if they weren't present in the game, it would be almost an exact copy game mechanic-wise, to Saints Row the Third.
Yes, that's right. Ignoring the innovation that was the powers, Saints Row IV has almost NOTHING to offer gameplay-wise that Saints Row the Third had already brought to the table. The game takes place in the same city, with only the difference of a few new cars, and new weapons. Graphics are nearly, if not completely identical to Saints Row III. The enemy gang operations that were featured in Saints Row the Third are back as well, only they have been changed to Alien hotspots, which are essentially the same exact thing. "Shoot all the bad guys, you win." For this reason, the added powers were a saving grace for Saints Row IV.
We have talked about weapons here and there, but we haven't actually stopped to say that much about them. I will say that the weapons in Saints Row IV are AMAZING. So much fun to use. Gun stores now have a mechanic where you can change the paint job on your gun, and even change the body of the weapon completely. By far the best weapon in the game is the Dubstep gun, using waves of epic bass-drop madness to slay your foes is entertaining and awesome.
Overall, I enjoyed Saints Row IV. It does present improvements over Saints Row the Third, but lacks in some aspects that could have been improved over the last game. Because of the addition of the super fun powers though, and the new story, and the DUBSTEP GUN, I'll have to rate Saints Row IV:
7.0/10

Seems like it could have been an interesting/fun game. But it was not.
Campaign missions are mostly just multiplayer/skirmish missions with a bit of plot/exposition in front of them. The problem with this is the MP missions are built or weighted with the idea that you are making a fleet out of scratch with full ships/abilities. You don't have access to these in the campaign making some early missions trial/error or which can result in restarting the campaign if you've built your fleet in ways that won't let you bypass certain mission chokepoints.
Many of the game modes rely on objectives other than simply killing the enemy fleet such as securing transports or playing 'tag' (data stealing missions). The problem with these mission types is that the gameplay relies on surprise. In single player the computer has full awareness of where all your ships are on the map, even when hidding or 'running in stealth mode'. You can see this as they beeline right for your location.
This renders the campaign play-able, but boring and frustrating especially as there are only small numbers of strategies that work for each mission type. Leading to a good deal of repetion.
The multiplayer is for the most part, dead.

Even before I first played the game I had wanted a game of this nature to come out in the 40K universe.  As lame as this sounds (and believe me it does) I wanted the game to be a little slower, more strategic and not so action oriented.  I wanted to take time to marvel at the detail that had been put into animating the space craft of the 40K universive unlike any game had ever done before.  Instead I was greeted with a game that requires quick and fast button clicking in order to gain victory over an opponent much like an RTS.
Naval warfare is strategic, it is slow and albeit most would say, boring, in a video game format.  I can appreciate that the developers tried to make it more fun to play by speeding it up but I think they went a little too far.  I was picturing something more akin to the Total War series take on Naval Warfare which is definetly a slower paced and strategic style.  Instead I got the Starcraft of Naval Warfare games which just left me feeling robbed.
Patches, expansions, or even....user created content via the Steam Workshop could adapt the game.  I agree with some of the comments below that some of the missions were just ridiculously unwinnable.  If I am playing on Easy difficulty it shouldnt be that way.  If I am playing on Hard difficulty it should be.  When you play a mission on Easy and still struggle to complete it in time something is just off.  Maybe thats what the developers wanted to instill?  That the nature of the 40K universe is unfair, punishing, hopeless and anything but easy.  All I know is that if I want a challege I play a game on Hard difficulty; if I want to veg out after a long day at work and just blast some Xenos I play on Easy, its therapeutic in a way.  This game didnt allow me to do that which let me down when I expected so much more.

One of my favorite games to play... and one that's really hard to recommend.
I dunno, this game feels right, it always has. Back before the Steam release, when there were only two servers with damn near no one on them 'scept at the right times. It's got bugs, there's some questionable design decisions, but all in all there's nothing REALLY like it on the market. Blacklight: Retribution and the new GitS game get the aesthetic right, but not really the gameplay. This feels like a game where you use your supersoldiery to its maximum capacity. Jumping around, cloaking, using your class's special vision all work wonderfully. The guns are cool designs too, very future but very grounded in current weapons development. These are believable firearms, and they all pack a good punch and feel good to use.
That being said, this game has a pretty high difficulty curve. Not a lot of bones are thrown to new players, and the scoring system really encourages good gameplay and punishes babes in the woods too much, not giving them the tools they need to do well, and giving people who don't really need them all the fun stuff. That being said, you can EASILY kill the entire team with the weakest gun in the game if you just do it properly, and there's nothing stopping you from killing a foe wielding a more powerful weapon and taking it. Most of the difficulty comes down to knowing the maps, knowing where the ambush spots are, knowing where to look, and knowing where to go. This comes with time, but it can be frustrating to learn. The community of crazies who stick with this game too are a pretty helpful and chill bunch for the most part; you have to be to stick with a dead project this long. But it can still be intimidating to start. I'd say give it a try, and if it's not your thing, it's not your fault!

Really great game. It's ok without the DLC. Not incredible but just ok. Really should get Brave New World, kind of needed imo. Check out some mods in the workshop, lots of great ones. Very steep learning curve, but there's 8 difficulties so anyone can play and start low. There's 5 different victory types. Science, Domination, Cultural, Diplomatic, and Time. It's a turn based strategy game meaning you have a turn to make some moves and decisions then you end your turn and the AI does the same thing. You don't control your guys in combat, instead you tell them where to go. You expand your empire by either using settlers to form cities or taking a different civ's cities over through war. You can do both. Though expansion isn't required to win. You choose technologies to research as the game progresses, each turn getting you 1 step closer to the new technology. Each technology gives some new stuff to your civ. Knowing what to research is key in getting the victory type you desire.
I haven't played Civ 6 becuase honestly, I don't have any need or really any want to. I am still to this day perfectly satisfied with Civ 5. It does exactly what I want from this type of game. A lot of what I don't like is fixed by mods as well. I have seen a lot of gameplay of Civ 6 and none of it makes me want the game. I'm fine with Civ 5 so I'd say just get Civ 5, preferably with Brave New World.
The AI can be goofy sometimes. Whether it be them making really unfair decisions that totally screw you over for no reason, or making really stupid decisions that doom their civilization. They can be really greedy in trade deals too. It's almost always gonna be a bit of an unfair trade for you. Best not to let your anger take over your decisions, and wait for the right times to declare war and denounce. If you go to war constantly just becuase someone's being a jerk to you things could go badly. Overall the AI isn't totally awful but it's far from incredible. I'd say it's good though. Generally does ok.
It depends on what time setting you have it on. There are a few options. Note you can save then exit and return to your game at anytime. Keep in mind these are rough estimates.
The game progresses quickly through the years. Everything takes less time. For a brand new player, I'd estimate an average quick game lasting around 6-7+ hours.
The most common setup. Things progress at an ok rate. Still a bit quick for my taste but for a brand new player, a standard game would take probably like 10+ hours.
My favorite. For a brand new player, probably 2 days.
Marathon is hilariously long. Could take a week or even longer.
Once you learn how to finish quicker, games will be much short. I play almost strictly on Epic speed and I'd say my average game on Immortal (7) difficulty is around 7-8 1/2 hours. It may take you much, much longer than these estimates, and that's ok. These are just guesses. I have read some people saying it takes them 15 hours to win a quick  paced game. Though I don't really see that being too likely.
There are 5 victory types. Basing these off Brave New World. things are a little different in Vanilla. Check the Wiki for victory types if you choose not to get DLC.
You must research almost the entire tech tree and get the technologies required to build the Apollo Program, then the ones to allow construction of spaceship parts. Once you have built all the spaceship parts and launched them into space, you will win a Science Victory.
You have to capture everyone else's original Capital and hold onto them. Once you aquire every other player's capital you will win a Domination Victory. This typically takes awhile, but is the most fun in my opinion.
. You gotta raise your Culture and Tourism to gain influence over the other Civilizations. Once you have 100% influence over every Civ in your game, you'll win a Cultural Victory. If you like to play passively and focus on building onto your cities, you'll enjoy this.
You need to win the World Leader vote in the late game. This can be done by buying off City States just before the vote, then using your newly aquired delegates from the city states to vote for yourself. You can also get other civs to vote for you.
A time victory occurs when you reach the end game. The Civ with the highest score wins. You get score from lots of different things, so just play well.
Also note you can disable any and even all victory types before you start your game.
It's not a graphics heavy game. I used to play it fine on a Dell Inspiron 15 a long time ago. It can run your computer hot becuase typical game sessions are long, so I suggest just turning some simple stuff down like shadows and what not. Here is where you'll set up what your game is gonna be like. What you want the map to be like, the difficulty, the game pace, starting era, the map size.. There's a lot of great options here so I'm just gonna go over the kind of obscure ones.
A younger world will have a rougher terrain. More hills and mountains. The hill will give you some more production but it also means it'll take longer for your units to navigate due to the roughness. An older world will be more flatened out, and faster to walk around on.
This effects how often you'll run into deserts and also plains I believe. Obviously the warmer the planet the more deserts.
The more rainfall, the more jungles and marshes.
This will set up the amount of resources spawned into the world. There's a lot of options in this one. Typically if I feel I want a lot of resources I choose Abundant. it spawns lots of good stuff all over the world.
There are a lot of Civs. Especially after you get all the DLC civs, there's a ton. Each one is unique in their own way. Some a bit more so than others. Personally, my favorite is Egypt. They are great at building wonders, and I love having a ton of cool wonders in the start. I always try to be the first to construct the Great Library, which grants a free technology. Really usefull. For Domination, I love the Mongols. They have a fantastic unit called the Keshik. It's a horse archer that allows you to move after firing. Which is insanely strong when using hit and run tactics. My favorite game ever was as the Greeks though, eventually winning a Late Science victory against 12 other civs on Deity. A very memorable game.

I got this game for something like $2.50 in the redux bundle.
I wanted to like this game so very badly but in the end, low production value and poor design just killed it for me. This game is almost exclusively a corridor shooter. That's not entirely unexpected seeing as this game is supposed to take place almost 100% in tunnels except this remains even when you go above ground on occasion. Now, I could forgive that if it were at least fun but as I said before, production value is low. Movement is slower than every game I've ever played except one, Front lines: Fuel of war, and gunplay is clumsy at best.
What prompted me to come here and write a bad review is a section in which you have to clear a nazi surface outpost. The outpost itself is so absolutely impossible to navigate that I could not take the game anymore. I don't mean that it's complex or that the enemies are tough, I just mean that there are jagged edges on the floor that kept catching my character and keeping me from moving. This happens nonstop in the more urban, non tunnel areas.
Besides this, there is also the problem that every weapon in this game fires nerf darts on a good day. Enemies and and yourself alike can eat entire magazines from the game's more powerful weapons, which again I would forgive if the game's lackluster weapon upgrade system allowed for damage buffs but of course, no it does not.
There is also the utterly useless inclusion of a stealth system to complain about. This game's level design does not allow for flanking or stealthy routes generally speaking. This means that you WILL have to gun down most of your enemies in a head-on fight, even when you start in stealth. Maybe you'll get an enemy or two without alerting the rest, but that's basically all you're going to get.
Overall, FPS games have been doing better than this game for longer than most of the people reading this review have been alive and your money would be much better spent on nearly any other FPS.

Ys Origin is an Japanese-style action RPG, set as a prequel to the Ys series. This is the first Ys game I've played, and I've definitely been enjoying it.
The game's combat system is the best part of it: normal enemies don't give you much of a challenge because they're easily stun-locked (as Yunica, at least), but the boss battles are intense. The bosses are difficult and they take a while to bring down even if you know what you're doing, but their attacks are easily predicted. It does take some skill to get through it, though (on Normal). The game's story and world are also interesting; it has one of the better game stories I've seen recently.
This game is definitely worth considering for any RPG fan, and I would recommend it even at full price to fans of the genre.

Whilst being a confusing and wordy title, It's fortunate that Valve decided to name their sequel 'Episode One' because its obvious that HL2Ep1 isn't a full-blown sequel the same way Half Life 2 was.
Half Life 2 was a gamechanger the same way Half Life 1 was. It further pushed the almagamation of gameplay and storytelling whilst expanding even more on the open-ended, dynamic gameplay system HL1 introduced. The Source Engine was unlike anything ever seen before, and to this day no game has toyed with physics like HL2.
Obviously HL2Ep1 couldn't do this all again after just one year. But, whilst the game is still very much worth your time, it's lacking and could have been so much better.
Alarm bells ring from the start as you find yourself back in the Citadel with an overcharged Gravity Gun throwing Combine around. Didn't we do this in the last game? Then we lead a group of resistance fighters around City 17 as war breaks out, then we battle a single gunship, and for an encore we fight a solitary Strider as the final boss. (Remember in HL2 when we battled over three Striders at once?)
There are some notable stabs of inspiration, however. Whilst the third chapter in the abandoned subway is a glorified sewer level, the last section where Alyx and Gordon must fight a large wave of zombies in the pitch black is sufficiently claustrophobic and tense. The part in the hospital is also fun for the same reasons.
Where the game really shines is with Alyx. There's a reason why she's on the cover of this game, and that's because its really her game. We see her go through a variety of emotions throughout, all of which builds her as a likeable and necessary character. Along with Elizabeth from 'Bioshock Infinite', she's one of the most useful and unobtrusive companions in gaming. I think the reason why I like the part in the hospital is because of the strange thrill I got pumping shotgun shells into zombies whilst Alyx stood beside me doing the same.
Also, I highly reccomend going for the 'One Free Bullet' achievement. Valve originally didn't want to give the player weapons until the third act of the game, hence the amount of throwable objects lying around levels (free tip: Radiators are the best weapon in the game. Always have a radiator to hand). They decided this was too limiting for the player, so after the first hour you immediately trip over a gun and cannot proceed until you've shot the lock off a door. But, of course, this doesn't stop the player from using the Gravity gun all the time anyway - and this self-imposed restriction is emergent gaming heaven. Fights turn from fast-paced if repetitive skirmishes into frantic, tactical puzzle solving....except the puzzle is always 'should I throw the computer monitor or the radiator?' This is also when Alyx shines, because often you need to rely on her to pick away at enemies whilst you distract them by tossing furniture. As you can imagine, this method of gameplay also creates many unintentional moments of comedy as you stack all the radiators and computer monitors in a pile ready for the next wave of enemies whilst Alyx looks on, quietly judging.
Of course, you still need to use your rocket launcher....I found out the hard way that radiators don't work on Striders...
Unlike Episode 2, which despite a slow start morphed into an excellent game that felt like the sequel we'd been waiting for (remember that final battle? And the moment right after?) this game feels much more like an expansion pack. Not in an 'Opposing Force' way, but in a 'Blue Shift' way. It's fun, but only because its more of the same.

This is a beautiful and interesting game which, with a few nudges and tweaks could have been even better. Initially there is no plot - you just have to find Ethan. Unfortunately, there is also no guidance or advice about how to use the tricks at your disposal. I respect the designers' intention to not hold your hand, but a couple of pointers would have helped. For example, there is nothing to prevent you from wandering into another area before completing the puzzles in the first. I would guess it's possible to complete the game while missing most of the puzzles due to over-eager exploration. There's also no clue about how to use the psychic powers to locate clues, which can leave you searching for a tiny object in a large map. Finally, the game's puzzles could really do with a few more elements: one sequence is unlocked by simply returning an object to its original location.
The psychic detective thing works nicely, though, and the idea of Ethan creating fantastical stories from modest family dramas is a compelling device which keeps the game moving forward. Graphically, this is about as good as Unreal 3 gets: high-res textures and masses of foliage show this was written for the PC but, as usual with U3, shaders are a bit sparse and there is no use of POM or tessellation. Most importantly, the world looks and feels real, and this is enhanced by the moody music. Given how few names are mentioned in the credits, the whole game is a pretty impressive experience. It's Dear Esther with a few more things to do, and there's nothing wrong with that.

(SPOILER FREE) Dying Light does achieve what it sets out to do, it has good parkour elements and a good variety of enemies to fight and interesting enough challenges to encourage doing side quests and trails even after you've completed the main story + all DLC.
Pros:
-Parkour feels smooth and you feel like through your 2nd playthrough you embrace the parkour alot more. You go from rarely making huge jumps to suddenly knowing which places you can and can't jump too. Which will save you dying alot.
- The enemies have variety and all have encourage different ways of encountering. Although the big brutes which will require you to either avoid or waste alot of your good weapons can be a huge pain at the beginning of the game. I always carry a gun and shoot them in the head once or twice and they die. It's a cheap way but it's exploiting the game's design. If you want challenge you can just try and take them on with a hammer or something. But personal myself and others just used a gun which don't take long to find.
- The map is beautiful, it feels like it was lived in but still feels like it was made for the parkour elements. Running across roof tops and climbing through buildings can be super fun. I've rarely had issues where my character should of grabbed the edge when they didn't but these were so rare I forgave it.
- The game is very visually amazing, I've rarely seen models or textures look bad and everything seems very well made. Everything from the enemies, weapons, buildings and cars/set pieces
Cons:
- The story is very lacking which is kind of dissappointing as the game does spend alot of time on this. Alot of the things happen in the game because of the story so seeing it lack any character depth or proper conflict. It wasn't that great, it was far better than Dead Island. But that's not saying much
- You start off very weak and even 20 hours in you still feel powerless. This might just be an issue I have but it's something to note. In Dead Island you can get your first hammer within 20 minutes and kill a decent amount of zombies. Dying Light almost encourages you to never kill them and just avoid them. Even later in the game where you're told to kill zombies. You basically abuse the insta-kill traps scattered all around the level.
That's all the pros and cons. Honestly I'll recommend this game to anyone who likes free-running/zombie games. If you think this game looks fun in trailers then you'll not be disappointed. Just don't expect a good story and don't expect to be a badass as soon as you play.

I got this game for something like $2.50 in the redux bundle.
I wanted to like this game so very badly but in the end, low production value and poor design just killed it for me. This game is almost exclusively a corridor shooter. That's not entirely unexpected seeing as this game is supposed to take place almost 100% in tunnels except this remains even when you go above ground on occasion. Now, I could forgive that if it were at least fun but as I said before, production value is low. Movement is slower than every game I've ever played except one, Front lines: Fuel of war, and gunplay is clumsy at best.
What prompted me to come here and write a bad review is a section in which you have to clear a nazi surface outpost. The outpost itself is so absolutely impossible to navigate that I could not take the game anymore. I don't mean that it's complex or that the enemies are tough, I just mean that there are jagged edges on the floor that kept catching my character and keeping me from moving. This happens nonstop in the more urban, non tunnel areas.
Besides this, there is also the problem that every weapon in this game fires nerf darts on a good day. Enemies and and yourself alike can eat entire magazines from the game's more powerful weapons, which again I would forgive if the game's lackluster weapon upgrade system allowed for damage buffs but of course, no it does not.
There is also the utterly useless inclusion of a stealth system to complain about. This game's level design does not allow for flanking or stealthy routes generally speaking. This means that you WILL have to gun down most of your enemies in a head-on fight, even when you start in stealth. Maybe you'll get an enemy or two without alerting the rest, but that's basically all you're going to get.
Overall, FPS games have been doing better than this game for longer than most of the people reading this review have been alive and your money would be much better spent on nearly any other FPS.

It's so good that when my original CDs broke, I bought it again on DVD.  Then, when I bought the Humble Star Wars Bundle, I redeemed the key on Steam anyway so I could always have access to a copy.
There are a few relatively minor issues with the game, most notably a ton of bugs with the Remote Rocket Launcher award weapon.  Sometimes your faction simply can't win on a particular map without an incredible performance by you.  Two examples would be the Republic or Empire on Polis Massa Conquest and the Republic on Naboo Conquest.  The last notable bug is that Han Solo can't switch back to his DL-44 after using his repair tool.
TL;DR: 10/10 must buy

This is coming from a hardcore gamer, looking to get into FPV drones because they look like fun,
I am enjoying the sim, it seems like a great way to learn how to fly before destroying an actual drone, and I could see it being a fantastic skill improving tool even when flying actual drones regularly.
I just have a few things that need mentioning if this game is to be the "gateway drug" for gamers becoming FPV pilots, and surely that thought has crossed the devs minds.
Firstly, that tutorial is brutal. Maybe coming from a RC background it would be easier, but having never flown a quad-copter before, being put in a box with one window to exit from is the equivalent of learning to pick locks by handcuffing yourself underwater. A typical gamer will need at least half hour in a large open space, preferably with a guide and controller indications explaining how the drone works by performing simple maneuvers ie "Take off, hover  at same altitude for 10 seconds" "Now fly forwards and backwards maintaining altitude" etc until the basics are natural.
Next up, there really needs to be some sort of pre-made drones that handle differently for different levels of skill. Begin with a slow and sluggish drone that is forgiving and easy to fly, then work your way up as your skills improve. I know there is a workshop where I can edit my drone, and options to set motor speeds etc. but these should really be options I fiddle with after I have learned what is what, not while I am struggling to stay horizontal as I smash into another hay bale.
Speaking of hay bales. The maps. Seriously, I could be flying anywhere in the world, but here I am in some unbelievably dull locations. I am sure more maps are on the way, but even for RC enthusiasts this can't make much sense. Here are a few map ideas I would be excited to see in the final release:
Boat (sinking titanic?)
Music festival (maybe Woodstock?)
Theme Park
Hot Air balloon Show. (Take off from one balloon, and there are 30 others just floating about)
Construction tower.
Literally ANYWHERE! I understand that this is trying to be realistic, but a game like this also gives you the ability to do things you wouldn't usually be able to do, like fly in public areas full of people, or dangerous locations, and the lines required the fly for racing could be a lot more interesting than markers on the ground, like ducking behind a waterfall to emerge near a roller coaster track, which you must follow for while before shooting into a ghost train tunnel. Gimmicky? Yes, but if just a couple of unrealistic tracks were included, it would be a lot of fun.
TL;DR I am enjoying the game, and hope to see it become more approachable, without losing it's realistic simulation edge. I recommend for anyone interested in FPV drone racing.

This is me:
I've never flown a quad copter or any airborn RC vehicle in my life but recently took a strong interest in FPV quads. So after a bit of research I discovered this simulator and bought it to help me get used to the controls while I begin buying/putting-together my first quad.
As of 03/05/16:
(using Xbox 360 controller)
Summary:
I'm really enjoying this early-access simulator. It seems to be very well put together and is a realistic (within reason) FPV simulator.
The physics seem to be near spot-on compared to footage I've seen of FPV'ers, though I have to agree with some of the reviewers here, they do seem slightly floaty. The collision and prop damage models are good, but I found myself wishing for a less forgiving collision model when it came to tree branches. Perhaps there might be a 'difficulty setting' regarding the damage model in future?
The visuals are fantastic for a performance-oriented simulator. The models are well-made, and the film grain and distortion prove to be highly immersive and make me feel like I'm actually controlling (and crashing) the quad.
Sound design is passable, as is par in most realistic simulators in my experience. It would be nice to hear some improvements here but definitely not neccessary.
The UI is well laid out, though not free of small issues. I suspect they will be remedied swiftly and easily.
Conclusion:
I'm looking forward to multiplayer and any of the other features/improvements to come. I definitely plan on continuing to practice using this simulator for many days to come. Also, I'll update this review once I have a transmitter and have flown an actual quad so as to compare the physics.

This is a beautiful and interesting game which, with a few nudges and tweaks could have been even better. Initially there is no plot - you just have to find Ethan. Unfortunately, there is also no guidance or advice about how to use the tricks at your disposal. I respect the designers' intention to not hold your hand, but a couple of pointers would have helped. For example, there is nothing to prevent you from wandering into another area before completing the puzzles in the first. I would guess it's possible to complete the game while missing most of the puzzles due to over-eager exploration. There's also no clue about how to use the psychic powers to locate clues, which can leave you searching for a tiny object in a large map. Finally, the game's puzzles could really do with a few more elements: one sequence is unlocked by simply returning an object to its original location.
The psychic detective thing works nicely, though, and the idea of Ethan creating fantastical stories from modest family dramas is a compelling device which keeps the game moving forward. Graphically, this is about as good as Unreal 3 gets: high-res textures and masses of foliage show this was written for the PC but, as usual with U3, shaders are a bit sparse and there is no use of POM or tessellation. Most importantly, the world looks and feels real, and this is enhanced by the moody music. Given how few names are mentioned in the credits, the whole game is a pretty impressive experience. It's Dear Esther with a few more things to do, and there's nothing wrong with that.

So, I started playing this game knowing absolutely nothing about it, other than it had been well reviewed. If you're contemplating buying this game, go in knowing as little about it as you can, because it enhances the experience something fierce. Half the fun of the game is the creeping disorientation early on, and having to feel your way through the game's most basic tasks. Conversely, if you jump in already knowing what's expected, having an idea of the basic mechanics, I can totally see you breezing through this, all the while wondering what the fuss is about.
It probably doesn't spoil things overly to say that the experience of this game thus far (I've only played a bit) has been something along the lines of Myst, and evokes feelings I haven't really gotten from a game since Riven. Gameplay wise it's interesting without being groundbreaking, and is much more about experience than mechanics. I have to say, though, it's an experience well worth having. Utterly gorgeous for an indie game (puts plenty of AAA titles to shame, thanks Unreal Engine!), and I love the amount of really cool stuff coming out of Poland atm.

5 hours, 88 screenshots and 14 achievements later, I think I can safely say it's time to review.
Now you're probably thinking; "4 hours to 100% a game? is that it?" Bluntly, yes - But it's a 4 hours you'd be happy you gave up when you finish the game.
It's hard to explain this game without giving much away, but I'll try. You play as Paul Pospero, a detective who traveled to Red Creek Valley to find Ethan Carter. On the journey, you'll see that a lot more has gone on than the fact that Ethan has gone. The twist is that you can see in to the past when core objects related to the mystery are found and put in their correct places.
When you get dropped in to the game, it's all down to you, the whole "This game does not hold your hand" screen at the beginning really means it. There is no order in the way you solve things either - "go do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ you want" has never been so literal in a game before.
Oh, and this game is ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous.
10/10 - I would recommend this game to everyone, it's an experience any gamer needs to have.

There is no hand-holding in this game, enter exploration. I often found myself wondering where to go next. That is part of the beauty of this game. The player is free to explore. Overall the game is short, the puzzles are fun, the story is thought provoking, and the graphics are stunning. I reccomend this title for a dreary afternoon.

Dying Light is one of the best zombie/coop games I have ever played.  If you are having any doubts about giving it a try please come to your senses and buy it, I promise you will not be disappointed.

Dying Light is ... ok ... I guess. It's a decent hack and slash zombie game with some light crafting elements that I would recommend if you can get it on sale. Especially if you have a few buddies to coop with. However the game has a variety of flaws:
- The story is serviceable but fairly predictable in places.
- The first person parkour/platforming is passable at best, frustrating at worst. It's a wanna be Mirrors Edge.
- The day/night mechanics are interesting but there's not enough to incentive going outside at night, especially late game.
- Shooting mechanics are pretty bad but given that it's primarily a melee game that's somewhat forgivable.
- Lock picking is a serious chore with no way to make it easier with skills or equipment. It also takes your character way way too long to open crates, doors, etc.
- Final boss battle is a MAJOR let down. Really soured the ending for me. The primary antagonist in general is underwhelming and more irritating than intimidating.
So if you don't mind any of these things I'd say go for it, if only because this is probably the best example of a melee combat zombie game on the market, just don't expect a master piece. This is a no joke 7/10 game.

This is the epilogue to Half-Life 2, and it plays well.  You can see the Portal-like thinking in the design, especially at the beginning areas, which are a bit puzzle-based rather than combat heavy.  The difference is rather than using a portal device, you are using the gravity gun.  You don't even start with a crowbar.
Of course, this is just while the game prepares to return to form.  By the time it's over, you'll be back with crowbar in hand and a full array of weapons.  As well as the return of Gordon's followers.
The game emphasizes the follower/NPC mechanics, as not only will Gordon have NPC followers helping him through parts of the game, but Alyx follows him for most of the game.  Rather than being a burden to be protected like too many escorts, however, Alyx is an active combatant, and more than holds her own.  You'll be glad she's there to draw fire and take down enemies at your side, and you'll notice the few times when she's pulled away to perform a background task and you have to go it solo.
It is a little abrupt, but it is worthy appendix to Half-Life 2's gameplay and storyline.

HELLDIVERS™ is an amazing experience. Essentially Starship Troopers: The Game, this is a well polished, balanced, and ultimately just plain satisfying experience. Twin stick shooters have been popular since, like forever. There's something elegant and pleasant about the simplicity of the controls, and everyone loves mowing down tons of bad guys while moving through an environment at a leisurely, god like viewpoint in the sky. However, the simplicity of the gameplay belies a really deep experience within HELLDIVERS™. You play as a faceless Orbital Drop Shock Trooper fighting a bloody war against many extraterristrial foes for an ultra nationalist, almost fascist like government of SUPER EARTH. For Liberty, Freedom, and Democracy! The world building is delightfully light-hearted and comical, despite the somewhat desperate backdrop. It creates a setting that anyone who enjoyed Starship Troopers will feel right at home in.
Originally a PS3/PS4/PS Vita title, the port runs fantastic, however this isn't really surprising considering the somewhat pedestrian graphics. The game looks good, but nothing amazingly beautiful pops out. The firing/ weapon effects are something to be commended; the landscape lights up with pretty volleys of bright, fiery torrents of bullets while you shoot various weapons. There are plenty of cosmetic customization options for your soldier, unlockable through gameplay. The deep gameplay I previously mentioned comes through the nonstandard interpretation of what most twin stick shooters are composed of. Ammunition is relatively rare, and you can't religiously reload after only firing a few shots because your soldier will discard the entire magazine, forever losing the rest of the ammo. Friendly Fire is ALWAYS on, and it doesn't only pertain to gunshots and grenades either. Calling in helpful equipment slams crates falling from space into the ground, but if you happen to be under the landing zone you will get squished immediately. The sweet dreadnaught-like mechs that you can drive will crush your teamates if they run underneath your robot feet. Your own gatling turret will also riddle you with bullets if you happen to be in the way of their view to an enemy. I can't overstate how great the Friendly Fire aspect is. In other twin stick shooters, even cooperative ones, I could easily hold down the fire button while spinning in a circle like a madman, with not a care in the world for running out of ammunition or hurting my teamates. HELLDIVERS™, with all of its dangers and challenges creates a more tactical, slow paced experience. Positioning and aiming are so important in this game, I honestly have never had so much restraint in firing in a twin stick shooter before, but due to the Friendly Fire in this game I'm constantly trying to avoid hitting my teamates. It's great stuff, I get a really Magicka-like vibe from it, which makes sense because I believe the series shares the same developer.
In addition to all of this, there is a huge selection of weapons and strategems (equipment/ support) to unlock, and you can choose which kinds of weaponry/ tactics to upgrade and specialize in. There are some neat team-work elements, such as being able to help a teamate reload a recoiless rifle or cruising around in an APC together. Calling down a strategem isn't as simple as pressing a button either, there is a nifty little DDR/Guitar-Hero like minigame to call in support. I actually loved this, it's a lot more challenging than just mindlessly pressing a button. It's pretty difficult to keep calm and collected as the hordes start to breach your position while trying to call down a life saving weapon/ artillery strike. There is a fantastic meta-game going on in the background as well: the Galactic Campaign. Every mission you complete, you add influence to a community pool which helps turn the overall greater battle towards a certain direction. Areas of the galaxy become unlocked over time and eventually we will be able to engage the enemies on their homeworld. There are also defense missions where one of the enemy factions will attack an area where you can join in on the defense, and I haven't played these yet, but I hear they are pretty difficult. Speaking of factions, I was under the impression that there was only a single faction, the steretypical Starship Troopers "Bugs", but there are actually three distinct factions! The technologically advanced Illuminate, which uses shields and weird zappy laser things, the rebellious human Cyborgs, which are heavily armored and have weird ♥♥♥♥ed up robotic attachments and♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the ravenous Bugs, which are essentially the Zerg/ Tyrannids. These factions all require different tactics to deal with and lend an extra layer of strategy to an already brilliant package.
This is one of the best twin stick shooters I've ever played and has surprisingly made it into one of my top 10 games of the year. You should definitely pick this game up if it sounds like something you would be into, it's worth every penny.

Spectacular. A very beautiful (literally) example of noir detective mystery story telling with enough horror elements to drag you in without the usual frustration or repulsion or terror that usually comes with it (I stopped playing Dead Space 2 times before I finally picked up the courage to finish it. I still haven't finished Amnesia!)
If you've liked Gone Home, you'll love this. This game places story & atmosphere at the forefront so that's a big hint to you on whether you want to pick it up. There's very little action, no health or time limit or such stress factors...just you and a story that you can peel apart at your own pace and from your own angles. And it's a very touching, emotional story indeed that I feel ended in a pretty satisfying way, contrary to what many reviews say. Take your time with it; explore. There's lots to admire just by strolling through the sprawling forest landscape.
Still, there're definitely game elements that draw you in and keep you engaged, besides the jaw-dropping scenery. Puzzles lie sprawled across the map waiting for you to discover and solve. They're not too hard - each puzzle was just enough of a challenge without too much frustration involved, and it's satisfying when you reach each answer, while at the same time, more of the story unfolds from there.
Which brings me to perhaps the only sore point: the save system is quite vague at first: the game only saves after each solved puzzle, which means you shouldn't explore too much and then quit the game without solving something first, and once - only once - did I encounter a bug that made me lose about 20 minutes of progress. It's not really serious, but it's there.
Overall, I'd heavily recommend the game. It's a little pricey normally (I bought it in the autumn sale), but it's definitely an unforgettable experience you have to try.

Dying Light is one of the best zombie/coop games I have ever played.  If you are having any doubts about giving it a try please come to your senses and buy it, I promise you will not be disappointed.

Dying Light is ... ok ... I guess. It's a decent hack and slash zombie game with some light crafting elements that I would recommend if you can get it on sale. Especially if you have a few buddies to coop with. However the game has a variety of flaws:
- The story is serviceable but fairly predictable in places.
- The first person parkour/platforming is passable at best, frustrating at worst. It's a wanna be Mirrors Edge.
- The day/night mechanics are interesting but there's not enough to incentive going outside at night, especially late game.
- Shooting mechanics are pretty bad but given that it's primarily a melee game that's somewhat forgivable.
- Lock picking is a serious chore with no way to make it easier with skills or equipment. It also takes your character way way too long to open crates, doors, etc.
- Final boss battle is a MAJOR let down. Really soured the ending for me. The primary antagonist in general is underwhelming and more irritating than intimidating.
So if you don't mind any of these things I'd say go for it, if only because this is probably the best example of a melee combat zombie game on the market, just don't expect a master piece. This is a no joke 7/10 game.

The game is horrible. why you might ask? Well let me explain:
- Relic ( alsno known as Reich Entertainment or Soon™) doesn't support it with full effort. They patch it every 6 months, with minimal effort, and add some little changes here and there. They claim the player base can't handle a radical change, the player base disagrees. This results in a game that gets very small updates once every half year(!!!), which means you will have balance issues, exploits, horrible faction and game design that might get fixed once every six months or not at all.
- The balance is horrible, the factions aren't made with the others in mind, they are simply build, with 'cool' stuff and thrown in there. You have a call in system that requires no teching of base structures to get very powerfull tanks. One faction can literally dominate the battlefield without teching and just solely rely upon call ins.
- RNG is the utter definition of this game. RNG (random number generation) uses a system that randomly generates changes of penetration, damage, citrical damage etc etc. For example you can throw a grenade and see it do no damage. You can have a tank at the brink of death, shoot at its rear with two powerfull tanks and see all of your shots bounce off and see your tanks get killed instead. You can get a recon plane shot down on your units, annihilating entire armies and even king tigers. You can have mortar shells wiping entire squads in one blow (german weapon teams consist of 4 men, they have this a lot), you can see flamethrowers do no damage, or wipe a unit in one burst. A tank can have 10% health left, it suddenly gets main gun critical, engine critical, gunner critical etc etc, every time cheating death.
This game is horrible with rng, they can't get rid of it since it is in the primary design.
- Map desing adds to the imbalances, if you have a horrible map as Germans, one that is way to open, the Allied early game will steamroll you and you can never win. If You have a map with chokepoints (few in the game), you will lose as allies because the German weapon crews can shut it down long enough for them to get their strong artillery and late game tanks.
- The game modes are horribly imbalanced as well. 4v4 will see Germans win 90% of the time due to their late game armor. 1v1 sees Soviets win all the time due to their strong call ins. 2v2 is pretty good, and that is the only game type that seems a bit balanced
-DLC. Relic keeps pumping out new factions($), new DLC ($), anything they can get money from, yet they don't fix the game. For example, the commanders have some standard ones you get with the game, the most powerfull ones that can literally give you wins, cost money. Skins for vehicles cost money, a single player expansion costs 40 dollars. Some singleplayer campaings cost 15-20 dollars.
-Alpha tests. You will have some alpha tests, you can test all their new ideas and potential fixes. Once you tested them and have given your feedback with good faith, they will simply throw away 4/5 of the potential changes (the good ones that is) and throw in some lousy changes (the other 1/5) after another six months. They stab you in the back over and over again. They are a horrible company, one that deserves no money let alone your money!
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME, safe yourself from wasted money, painfull experiences with horrible frustration

I just crossed the 300 hour mark with Liftoff. I started flying quads mid summer 2015 and only flew in level mode. Even though I used that mode I still had crashes. I spent some of the winter flying Liftoff in acro mode and improved to a great degree in that time.
