I have made many Liftoff videos to demonstrate it's power as a learning tool.
I can attest, after spending so much time in the sim, that anyone having a problem with this simulator is falling victim to either their own ignorance or outdated hardware. To speak to the later I feel that hardware non-upgraders are the bain of all gamers. If you are on an old laptop or a weak one for that matter you should naturally expect to have issues with games not working correctly. Upgrade or die! Seriously if you are one of these people realize you are holding us all beack. Please stop crying about games not working on your decrepit outdated machines. To the former; Why review a game poorly before you exhaust all efforts to learn the customizations? Sims always throw arcaders off. Just because you can't fly easily right off the bat doesn't mean it's broken. It means you currently lack the skill required to keep it in the air. This is remedied one of two ways. 1. Spend time learning to tune the aircraft by a. watching videos from people that have put in the work to help people such as yourself. b. experimenting a while reserving judgment until you figure things out. 2. Un-install the sim and go find something arcadish and easier made for people just like you.
Also why is it that some people forget the simple fact that this is an EARLY RELEASE title? Common sense dictates that it won't be perfect and that it is still under development. Updates for this and all other early access titles can sometimes have negitive affects. Be prepared for that. New resources for liftoff are added at a more than acceptable rate IMO. Further more the developers respond to questions in quick fasion. This sim/game is living up to it's potential in all areas, improving all the time.
To any prospective buyer please note that you will need some sort of a game controller to fly Liftoff. A keyboard will not work. Seems obvious but...
To get the best experience a interlink radio that comes with realflight or a game commander that comes with aerofly can be used and the buttons and switches can be used to switch modes or reset the aircraft. The gimbals aren't the best but this will provide the most in-game support of functions. The Sim supports field radios (remote controllers for real world aircraft) The easiest and best of these is the Taranis X9D/plus. This radio has a mini usb port on the back that makes it a perfect option for this and other sims like it. Liftoff has a preset for this controller as well. Even though it is perfect for the sim you will need to program the radio to work correctly. There is a guide for this and many other radios. That said not all radios play nice and there is nothing the developer can really do about that.
I own all the other quad racing sims out there and this hands down is the best and the other sims are complete products not under development. If you are thinking about buying Liftoff and especially if you want to use it to improve your real world flying I say buy it. You will not be disappointed as long as you are not under any misconceptions and are willing to spend time with it.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is predominantly a point and click game, reminiscent of Myst and similar titles. It is a captivating, if brief experience that immerses you in a gorgeous world as you attempt to uncover its dark secrets.
First off, the game’s strengths:
This game holds some of the best environment visuals I have ever seen. On my journey from plot point to plot point, I would often explore around for no other reason than to take in the views and enjoy the love and care the developers put into every detail. However, the game was very demanding on my computer's resources. On my quad-core i5 with 16GB RAM and Nvidia GTX 680, the game was all but unplayable on high settings due to framerate stutters. With some tweaking, I was able to reasonable smoothness but the framerate still chugged from time to time.
While most point-and-click game puzzles are simply a matter of finding an item X and combining it with location Y to proceed, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter introduces a refreshing take on these mechanics. Most puzzles consist stumbling across a potential crime scene, restoring the scene to its original state, and then deducing the chain of events that led to that outcome. The game offers only a bare minimum amount of hints and does not give the player any instruction on the mechanics of a puzzle or the expected outcome. While this may be a negative for some players, I found I enjoyed solving the puzzles more, as I had to rely only on my reasoning and observations.
I would not label this game as being a horror title per-se - there is only one jump scare to be found in the game (which is legitimately terrifying!) - but throughout my playthrough, I was surrounded by a constant feeling of dread and suspense. Walking through the game's seemingly abandoned rural setting evoked a great feeling of loneliness and mystery which, when combined with the game's superb score and dark supernatural themes, left me constantly expecting something terrifying to jump out at me or attack me.
And now, some things you might not like:
The game provides you with no guidance on what you are supposed to do or where you are supposed to go and places you in a fairly large open world where it can be easy to miss certain puzzles entirely. Indeed, I missed two or three of the first puzzles entirely and had to backtrack to complete them later. This can be frustrating and time consuming, especially considering the game's minimalistic HUD does not include a map. Fortunately, the game features a sprint option and does include a map/fast-travel system in one section of the game that allows you to jump to any puzzles you might have missed. The game's beautiful environment also helps make this trekking more bearable/enjoyable.
I found the majority of the game to be very intriguing. The fact that the player knows nothing about the events they are uncovering or even who they are or why they are there really drives the story and draws the player in. However, I found the game's ending to be rather predictable (I saw it coming about halfway through the game) and felt that the twist it tries to pull somewhat falls flat.
The few characters you see in The Vanishing of Ethan carter appear to be slightly stylized or are, at least, less-detailed/realistic than the rest of the game. This causes their visual appearance to jar with the heavily detailed environment. However, this is a pretty minor nitpick and is easily overlooked.
If you are looking for an atmospheric, narrative experience you can complete in an afternoon or are a fan of mystery, puzzle, or point-and-click adventure games, this title is definitely worth your attention. I enjoyed my playthrough a lot and wouldn't hesitate to recommend it. If you are looking for a longer title with more of a focus on dialog or action or are a gamer with a less-powerful rig, this may not be the game for you.

HELLDIVERS™ is an amazing experience. Essentially Starship Troopers: The Game, this is a well polished, balanced, and ultimately just plain satisfying experience. Twin stick shooters have been popular since, like forever. There's something elegant and pleasant about the simplicity of the controls, and everyone loves mowing down tons of bad guys while moving through an environment at a leisurely, god like viewpoint in the sky. However, the simplicity of the gameplay belies a really deep experience within HELLDIVERS™. You play as a faceless Orbital Drop Shock Trooper fighting a bloody war against many extraterristrial foes for an ultra nationalist, almost fascist like government of SUPER EARTH. For Liberty, Freedom, and Democracy! The world building is delightfully light-hearted and comical, despite the somewhat desperate backdrop. It creates a setting that anyone who enjoyed Starship Troopers will feel right at home in.
Originally a PS3/PS4/PS Vita title, the port runs fantastic, however this isn't really surprising considering the somewhat pedestrian graphics. The game looks good, but nothing amazingly beautiful pops out. The firing/ weapon effects are something to be commended; the landscape lights up with pretty volleys of bright, fiery torrents of bullets while you shoot various weapons. There are plenty of cosmetic customization options for your soldier, unlockable through gameplay. The deep gameplay I previously mentioned comes through the nonstandard interpretation of what most twin stick shooters are composed of. Ammunition is relatively rare, and you can't religiously reload after only firing a few shots because your soldier will discard the entire magazine, forever losing the rest of the ammo. Friendly Fire is ALWAYS on, and it doesn't only pertain to gunshots and grenades either. Calling in helpful equipment slams crates falling from space into the ground, but if you happen to be under the landing zone you will get squished immediately. The sweet dreadnaught-like mechs that you can drive will crush your teamates if they run underneath your robot feet. Your own gatling turret will also riddle you with bullets if you happen to be in the way of their view to an enemy. I can't overstate how great the Friendly Fire aspect is. In other twin stick shooters, even cooperative ones, I could easily hold down the fire button while spinning in a circle like a madman, with not a care in the world for running out of ammunition or hurting my teamates. HELLDIVERS™, with all of its dangers and challenges creates a more tactical, slow paced experience. Positioning and aiming are so important in this game, I honestly have never had so much restraint in firing in a twin stick shooter before, but due to the Friendly Fire in this game I'm constantly trying to avoid hitting my teamates. It's great stuff, I get a really Magicka-like vibe from it, which makes sense because I believe the series shares the same developer.
In addition to all of this, there is a huge selection of weapons and strategems (equipment/ support) to unlock, and you can choose which kinds of weaponry/ tactics to upgrade and specialize in. There are some neat team-work elements, such as being able to help a teamate reload a recoiless rifle or cruising around in an APC together. Calling down a strategem isn't as simple as pressing a button either, there is a nifty little DDR/Guitar-Hero like minigame to call in support. I actually loved this, it's a lot more challenging than just mindlessly pressing a button. It's pretty difficult to keep calm and collected as the hordes start to breach your position while trying to call down a life saving weapon/ artillery strike. There is a fantastic meta-game going on in the background as well: the Galactic Campaign. Every mission you complete, you add influence to a community pool which helps turn the overall greater battle towards a certain direction. Areas of the galaxy become unlocked over time and eventually we will be able to engage the enemies on their homeworld. There are also defense missions where one of the enemy factions will attack an area where you can join in on the defense, and I haven't played these yet, but I hear they are pretty difficult. Speaking of factions, I was under the impression that there was only a single faction, the steretypical Starship Troopers "Bugs", but there are actually three distinct factions! The technologically advanced Illuminate, which uses shields and weird zappy laser things, the rebellious human Cyborgs, which are heavily armored and have weird ♥♥♥♥ed up robotic attachments and♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the ravenous Bugs, which are essentially the Zerg/ Tyrannids. These factions all require different tactics to deal with and lend an extra layer of strategy to an already brilliant package.
This is one of the best twin stick shooters I've ever played and has surprisingly made it into one of my top 10 games of the year. You should definitely pick this game up if it sounds like something you would be into, it's worth every penny.

This is the quintessential Sci-Fi shooter.  Whether you're a fan of story-driven FPS/TPS or a fan of Star Wars, this is the game for you.
The campaign has a great story, following the 501st Legion (Vader's Fist) from Episode II all the way through Episode V.
After you've finished the campaign, instant action will keep you playing for years.  This is the most fun I've ever had in a FPS.
It's so good that when my original CDs broke, I bought it again on DVD.  Then, when I bought the Humble Star Wars Bundle, I redeemed the key on Steam anyway so I could always have access to a copy.
There are a few relatively minor issues with the game, most notably a ton of bugs with the Remote Rocket Launcher award weapon.  Sometimes your faction simply can't win on a particular map without an incredible performance by you.  Two examples would be the Republic or Empire on Polis Massa Conquest and the Republic on Naboo Conquest.  The last notable bug is that Han Solo can't switch back to his DL-44 after using his repair tool.
TL;DR: 10/10 must buy

This is an underrated but also sadly under-developed game. The base mechanics for what could be an outstanding simulation and/or suvival experience.
I've on/off played this since it was first available and to be fair, its come a long way since it first set foot on mars, moving along nicely from unlimited, creative-mode style play to "proper" survival levels.
However- the learning curve is pretty steep at first and until you become familiar with it, it's menu system, mechanics and control style it can be a challenge.
Thankfully you get enough resources and time to easily be able to get self-sufficient, but I can almost guarantee your average person will come at least passingly close to courting disaster before learning what's what.
Once that's done though? It's glorious. It's beautiful and has enough complexity in it to start to engage the more depth-seeking players out there that feel there isn't enough to keep them interested in other games. Heck, it's almost a mini-factorio to a certain degree, but just falls short.
Sadly development moves at sub-glacial speeds and there are long, long waits between any real milestones and performance is still pretty poor considering how long the game has been released.

The game is horrible. why you might ask? Well let me explain:
- Relic ( alsno known as Reich Entertainment or Soon™) doesn't support it with full effort. They patch it every 6 months, with minimal effort, and add some little changes here and there. They claim the player base can't handle a radical change, the player base disagrees. This results in a game that gets very small updates once every half year(!!!), which means you will have balance issues, exploits, horrible faction and game design that might get fixed once every six months or not at all.
- The balance is horrible, the factions aren't made with the others in mind, they are simply build, with 'cool' stuff and thrown in there. You have a call in system that requires no teching of base structures to get very powerfull tanks. One faction can literally dominate the battlefield without teching and just solely rely upon call ins.
- RNG is the utter definition of this game. RNG (random number generation) uses a system that randomly generates changes of penetration, damage, citrical damage etc etc. For example you can throw a grenade and see it do no damage. You can have a tank at the brink of death, shoot at its rear with two powerfull tanks and see all of your shots bounce off and see your tanks get killed instead. You can get a recon plane shot down on your units, annihilating entire armies and even king tigers. You can have mortar shells wiping entire squads in one blow (german weapon teams consist of 4 men, they have this a lot), you can see flamethrowers do no damage, or wipe a unit in one burst. A tank can have 10% health left, it suddenly gets main gun critical, engine critical, gunner critical etc etc, every time cheating death.
This game is horrible with rng, they can't get rid of it since it is in the primary design.
- Map desing adds to the imbalances, if you have a horrible map as Germans, one that is way to open, the Allied early game will steamroll you and you can never win. If You have a map with chokepoints (few in the game), you will lose as allies because the German weapon crews can shut it down long enough for them to get their strong artillery and late game tanks.
- The game modes are horribly imbalanced as well. 4v4 will see Germans win 90% of the time due to their late game armor. 1v1 sees Soviets win all the time due to their strong call ins. 2v2 is pretty good, and that is the only game type that seems a bit balanced
-DLC. Relic keeps pumping out new factions($), new DLC ($), anything they can get money from, yet they don't fix the game. For example, the commanders have some standard ones you get with the game, the most powerfull ones that can literally give you wins, cost money. Skins for vehicles cost money, a single player expansion costs 40 dollars. Some singleplayer campaings cost 15-20 dollars.
-Alpha tests. You will have some alpha tests, you can test all their new ideas and potential fixes. Once you tested them and have given your feedback with good faith, they will simply throw away 4/5 of the potential changes (the good ones that is) and throw in some lousy changes (the other 1/5) after another six months. They stab you in the back over and over again. They are a horrible company, one that deserves no money let alone your money!
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME, safe yourself from wasted money, painfull experiences with horrible frustration

Saints Row 4 was the first game out of the Saints Row Franchise that I ever played. The way I see it, it appears as a super-powered sandbox game with a higher grade of technology. The game follows a somewhat strong storyline and has some interesting side missions, unlike Saints Row: The Third, where there were no more missions after the story was complete.
Focusing more on the weapons, it seems that Deep Silver Volition went a little bit overboard with the humor of some of the weapons, mainly centering the Dubstep Gun, the Inflato-Ray, and the Plunger Gun. I disliked the Inflato-Ray and the Plunger Gun, but the Dubstep Gun was interesting. To be honest, I kind of wished that DSV (Deep Silver Volition) named the remaining weapons (SMGs, Rifles, Shotguns, etc.) like Saints Row: The Third. I felt I was playing at a more realistic level in those games, and when it came to Saints Row 4, you get names like the "Quickshot Pistol" or the "Pump-Action Shotgun". Not saying that's bad, just a little vague.
One of my favorite features of the game was using former villains as my sidekicks in intense battles like taking out flashpoints or taking down wardens. I loved making rival combinations like Benjamin King and Tanya, Fun Shaundi and DJ Veteran Child, Cyrus Temple and Kinzie (my FAVORITE xDD), but you get what I mean. I also loved the homie conversations that ensued between them as well, but to be honest, I was upset about one thing: I learned on YouTube that unused content included Phillipe Loren of the Syndicate as a homie. If you "spend quality time with Gat", you and Gat encounter a super powered Phillipe Loren to battle. Unlike other enemies like Tanya, Cyrus Temple, and DJ Veteran Child, Loren was not added as a homie. I was disappointed about this because the video I watched also included unused conversations. Which brings me to my final thought on homies. It would have been cool to earn Zinyak himself as a homie, but it would also be unusual for Zinyak to be battling his own army.
Looking at the super power aspect, I thought it wass okay, but what DSV was missing was a way to turn it off. Don't get me wrong, I love blazing across the streets, sending cars into the sky, but sometimes I just wanted to walk around and surprise attack someone by casually running past them.
Overall, I thought the game was pretty well made. In my opinion, the game deserves a 8.5/10

At first I thought this was an amazing game but then I relaised how short it was. It's pretty much over within two or three plays through - which might mean 5 attempts at the very-very-VERY short 'storyline'. It's not really a story - more a single quest.
Great game mechanics and beatifull game prodution, but why it ends just as it feels like it's getting started I have no idea!?
Just as I had my ship and crew more-or-less 70% of the way I wanted it, to play the way I wanted to play, the game ends - and I have to start again - with a bad ship, no crew and at the mercy of blind chance.
I don't mind the struggle, but my ship finaly became an expression of my choices, my play stye and my preferences and then it's taken away - that's not good game design in my opinion.
You can't play slower because you are forced along by a built in game mechanism that pretty much kills you if you want to slow down and explore.
And when you get to the end (win or loose) it's game over, there is litterally no reward for your efforts. You get the options of different ships (not better, just different) to do the same thing again.
I can see why people like it, but if you like to choose how you play a game, and if you like to explore a game then this will probably be too 'one dimensional' for you.
Perhaps if I think a little deper about it, I could say this is a game for people that like structure, rules, institutions and formats - if you get my menaing. This is not a game for creative thinkers, leaders and explorers. That's the way I see it anyway.
I'm only dissapointed because it has so much potential to be better....

I have played both the first game and this sequel; both I have found to be very enjoyable. They games are perfect for times when you just don't feel like getting really involved with complex stories and intense gameplay. The challenges are just hard enough to be intriguing while not being so hard that you have to use search engines to solve the puzzles. It is a very relaxed game that is perfect for passing the time.
A con to this game is there isn't much replay value; once you have completed the games, you are done. While you could go back, you will know how to solve the puzzles. However, I think the game's price is suitable for the game experience that is given; I wouldn't pay anything more than the price is marked. If you like puzzle games or games to pass the time, this is a good one. I recommend putting it on a wishlist and buying it when you really are just not feeling any other type of game.

It's a mix of MYST and those stupid "Escape the room" type games. Where those games failed, The Room blasts them all away and succeeds by miles. The PC versions of these wonderful games are absolutely stunning both in detail and atmosphere. The creepy sounds and music (box) are befitting the mysterious vibe. I love relaxing puzzle games like this and what a value; I picked it up for only 5 bucks. These games (both The Room and The Room 2) could easily fetch 10 to 15 bucks if they were just a bit longer. Some puzzles can be difficult to figure out, but the hint system is the best I have ever seen, nudging you at first and never just blurting out the answer. Hints like "There was something interesting on the workbench" - nudges you in the right direction whereupon you can click and prod your way around and figure out most puzzles here. The story is a bit "out there" and can be hard to understand but it definitely draws you in. I highly recommend this series of games. Do yourself a favor, especially if you were a fan of MYST and the like... get this game. It is much better. I just hope they create another that is much longer.

I dont leave reviews for games very often. But when a series deserves recognition... I give it! The Room and The Room 2 are AMAZING! A simple, yet clever and aesthetically gorgeous game, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a short narrative-driven game that won't take you by the hand and explain you the basics (or the story's background, for that matter). There isn't much action in this game but still, the dramatic story (a rather eerie and somewhat grim plot that is somewhere in-between Stephen King's finest works and Lynch's Twin Peaks) is unfolded slowly but carefully with fairly simple puzzles that require mere observation and logic. The story about Ethan's disappearance is told elegantly in the form of dialogs and small notes and documents that are aquired after solving varied puzzles (that mostly revolve about trying to figure out what actually happened in each location) and, although the path is fixed, these tiny pieces of the story are generally rewarding. The dam, lake and forest landscapes are incredibly detailed and feel pretty close to actual mountain scenery. To summarize, despite its simple mechanics and slow pace, this is a fine game that is well worth a try if you fancy an engaging mystery story, breathtaking visuals and don't mind learning things on your own.

When I first stumbled upon this game and watched the trailers, I thought this game was worth a try. Now that I have played it, I'm convinced that this is a masterpiece. It isn't action-packed, nor it is trying to challenge your abilities, it's simply trying to tell a story. And that it does well.
Once in the game, the first thing you'll definitely notice is the graphics. It's simply beautiful. Combine it with the atmospheric soundtrack, and you get yourself an experience you'll remember, feeling like you're actually a part of the world.
Now, about starting the game... You'll have to figure out how to play. There's no tutorial of any kind. The game starts, and you'll be standing on the (rail)road without any hints or quest markers. In fact, I'd say there are no quests at all. But don't blame the developers for being lazy. All of these things are intentional. The game is not about solving quest or beating a boss. It's about exploring and puzzle solving. It's about discovering the secrets of Red Creek Valley. And there
a few of those.
If you still don't fancy starting the game without some explanation about the game's mechanics, there's a commented gameplay video (with some light spoilers) on the game's Steam Store page that should have more than enough details to get started.
In general, the game is pretty simple. The interactions, the puzzles, the crime scenes - Nothing is too complicated. The reason behind is that the main focus is neither of these things. Instead, the emphasis is on the world and the story. This results in the game being surprisingly immersive and everything just feeling alive, despite the main character being the only living person in the vast majority of the game.
Though the amount of content, combined with the overall simplicity, has another side effect: short playtime. You can get from the intro sequence to the end credits in a few hours. Don't let that discourage you, though. Sometimes, ignoring the story and aimlessly wandering the forests of the valley can give you an experience that feels strangely satisfying. And if you want to rush through the game... Don't. It's okay for your second playthrough, but the first time is unique. Do it in a rash, and disappointment is pretty much guaranteed. Instead, take your time. Nothing's chasing you. Go in a pace that's comfortable for you. And live the game yourself.

This has been a ton of fun over the last couple of days. Purchased on the pre-release weekend and then played for hours. It's funny and brutal and hard. Watching the shuttle coming down as the last guy left tries to call you back to the field only to have the shuttle land on them before they finish is the funniest thing ever. Of course we lost but what a loss!
There is so much detail packed into the graphics. From the shadows and lighting (which I think are very well done) to being able to count the number of missles left in a support pack or your walker mech. The details are just everywhere and I think they help make the game just that much better. You can see what's going on. You know when you make a mistake and just how close a thing it was.
Everything can kill you, especially your teammates. The gameplay is brutal but fair. The game is about achieving objectives, not killing enemies. The rewards are quick to come in the early levels but you absolutely have to work for it in harder levels. Voice over comms tend to work good and the chat does well by color coding the messages according to who is in which position.
There have been a couple minor bugs, once I couldn't get back in a walker I had exited to help a comrade. Once it was only an audio glitch that kept occuring till the end of the match. Neither has happened more than once. This game has been running like a champ. I have nothing to say about it being a PS4 port. You can only barely feel the controller based UI. Mouse and keyboard controls work great. And while I have a controller I prefer the M+KB. Bonus points for anyone being able to grab that controller and join me playing right there in the room. It's like an arcade game that anyone can just join in on.
This has been so much fun for me. Helldivers scratches those itches that FPS wargames never do. I always prefer coop over pvp and Helldivers is coop at its best. 10/10

Saints Row 4 was the first game out of the Saints Row Franchise that I ever played. The way I see it, it appears as a super-powered sandbox game with a higher grade of technology. The game follows a somewhat strong storyline and has some interesting side missions, unlike Saints Row: The Third, where there were no more missions after the story was complete.
Focusing more on the weapons, it seems that Deep Silver Volition went a little bit overboard with the humor of some of the weapons, mainly centering the Dubstep Gun, the Inflato-Ray, and the Plunger Gun. I disliked the Inflato-Ray and the Plunger Gun, but the Dubstep Gun was interesting. To be honest, I kind of wished that DSV (Deep Silver Volition) named the remaining weapons (SMGs, Rifles, Shotguns, etc.) like Saints Row: The Third. I felt I was playing at a more realistic level in those games, and when it came to Saints Row 4, you get names like the "Quickshot Pistol" or the "Pump-Action Shotgun". Not saying that's bad, just a little vague.
One of my favorite features of the game was using former villains as my sidekicks in intense battles like taking out flashpoints or taking down wardens. I loved making rival combinations like Benjamin King and Tanya, Fun Shaundi and DJ Veteran Child, Cyrus Temple and Kinzie (my FAVORITE xDD), but you get what I mean. I also loved the homie conversations that ensued between them as well, but to be honest, I was upset about one thing: I learned on YouTube that unused content included Phillipe Loren of the Syndicate as a homie. If you "spend quality time with Gat", you and Gat encounter a super powered Phillipe Loren to battle. Unlike other enemies like Tanya, Cyrus Temple, and DJ Veteran Child, Loren was not added as a homie. I was disappointed about this because the video I watched also included unused conversations. Which brings me to my final thought on homies. It would have been cool to earn Zinyak himself as a homie, but it would also be unusual for Zinyak to be battling his own army.
Looking at the super power aspect, I thought it wass okay, but what DSV was missing was a way to turn it off. Don't get me wrong, I love blazing across the streets, sending cars into the sky, but sometimes I just wanted to walk around and surprise attack someone by casually running past them.
Overall, I thought the game was pretty well made. In my opinion, the game deserves a 8.5/10

My opinion of this game is generally positive, but I definitely have some issues with it. So... This 'review' is fairly mixed. Also, this is based on my experience of the campaign ONLY. I've not touched multiplayer at all, nor the Elite Mode, though I look forward to giving them a try.
On the plus side, it's nice to finally play a WH40K game that takes place in space, and the game itself plays fairly well. The campaign is fairly lengthy, but it doesn't overstay its welcome. There's also minor potential for replayability due to some choices you can make along the way. It definitely captures the grimdark of the setting as you play as the Imperial navy beset on all sides by Orks, Eldar, and Chaos, and having to choose which world you're going to defend [rarely having the resources to aid all of them]. I enjoyed myself pretty consistently throughout the campaign.
Now on to the cons... Every mission you run is of a certain type, Cruiser Clash, Assassination, Breakthrough, Convoy, Data Retrieval, etc... A lot of my decisions about where to deploy were based entirely on what type of mission it was. Some of the mission types just aren't fun, imo. If I had to defend a convoy, I wouldn't run it. I'd do Assassination missions but I didn't like doing them if I was the attacker. Likewise for Data Retrieval [though I don't recall being the defender on that ever].
The reason for this is, partly because the enemy AI cheats, and partly because of how those missions are handled. I'll get back to the enemy AI cheating in a moment, but for the Assassination and Data Retrieval missions, you have to destroy a vessel, or run a boarding action on it to get the data before it warps out. You have about 3-ish minutes to do this before the warping out ability is off of cooldown. The enemy ships will spend the entire time running from you, which, okay, fair enough. You can also force an enemy's warp out to be aborted by performing a boarding action, which IF IT SUCCEEDS, will cancel their warp and put it on a brief cooldown. These missions are doable, but they're frustrating because you end up spending the whole mission rushing towards the enemy ship just so that you can get there in time to be in range to MAYBE succeed in cancelling their warp out.
As for the enemy AI cheating? Aside from them always knowing where you are, even though they shouldn't, there's fleet limits. Each mission you can field a fleet of 300-700 points-worth of ships. So for a 300 point mission you could bring 2 Light Cruisers, and 2 escort vessels. Or a Light Cruiser, and 5-6 escort vessels. There's other various combinations you could bring, but the cheapest non-escort vessel you can bring is the Dauntless Light Cruiser at 105 points each. Ships get more expensive as you move up the tiers. The point is, because the cheapest non-escort vessel you can bring is 105 points, on a 300-point mission you can only bring 2. But the enemy - who should be on the same points-limit as you - will bring 3 Light Cruisers, and some escort ships. Or some other combination of ships whose points exceed the limit. I'm not referring to missions where it's stated you're fighting a superior force, or you're aiding an ally. I'm referring to missions where it's explicitly stated that you should be on equal footing with the enemy's forces.
And finally, the cost of the DLC factions seems a bit high to me. It's not as bad as the DLC factions for say... Blood Bowl 2 [whose faction DLCs are technically cheaper, but there's more of them], but I dunno. They seem a little pricey. My opinion here might be coloured somewhat by there being Space Marines ships already in the base game, though of course you can't play them. This point is, more than the other points I've made here, pretty subjective.
I know this 'review' seems overly negative, but really, it's easy to focus on the negatives, since they'll stick out at you more than a good thing. I'm still clicking the "recommend" button, because I *did* enjoy this game. Quite a bit, actually. And I'm looking forward to playing around with Elite Mode whatever that is, and the other factions, and maybe even replaying the campaign.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a nice little exploration-mystery game. It is beautiful, has a great setting and atmosphere, and have puzzles and detective bits that may stump you for a bit, but they're ultimately fairly doable.
You walk around the location searching for clues to solve the deaths of Ethan's family members. Backtracking is not a requirement, but if you somehow miss out on solving a murder or a puzzle, you can just backtrack. It seems vast, but on the overall the location is not that big. It may get a bit off-putting if you end up having to backtrack many times.
I would say it should take the average gamer 4-5 hours to complete the game. If you manage to "go with the flow" and solve everything fairly straightforwardly, you could finish the game in around 3 hours.
The game mechanics are fine. First, you need to find all items at the murder scene, then tag them in the order in which they happened. Some trial and error may be required for certain scenes.
I think it's a fairly decent game. There could have been more things to do, since the map does seem a bit large for what there is in the game. Another thing is that the mouse feels very floaty. It seems like there is a lot of weight attached to it.
My biggest complaint though is that the game stutters like nobody's business. You can confirm this by just looking into the forums. Whatever settings I choose, I get stutters every 5-10 seconds or so. For a game that primes itself on the atmosphere and setting, this is a real deal breaker.
Another thing is that this game is extremely graphically intensive. Even on the lowest possible settings, I get mid 40fps when I am in the middle of trees. And basically every other part of the game has trees. Basides, many graphics settings like Ambient Occlusion and FXAA do not seem to work.
I would recommend this game for those who don't mind something slower paced, or just want to take in the breathtaking visuals. Perhaps not at the full price though (I got it at 40% off).

You know how if you’re on a ship for a few days, you can still feel the rocking of the ocean when you lie in your bed? Ironically, that’s how it feels to play Battlefleet Gothic: Armada. The controls are so fluid for naval combat that you can feel the ship rotations in your walk and the rumble of engines in your sleep. For that, the game gets a massive recommendation. 40k games often work like that. They have this wonderful quality where the scene setting is always perfect. The voices are on point, the UI is appropriately gothic, and the music makes you feel like you’re charging into the final battle of the 13th Black Crusade.
Unfortunately, that’s where the exceptional for this game, at least for the campaign, ends. The AI for this game does not have the same rules as the player. As in most RTS, the AI is not effected by fog of war. That’s a massive hit as a fair number of skills, upgrades and rules revolve around stealth. Plus since the game is set in space, there's not a lot of terrain, it's all a flat, open expanse with a few navigational hazards here and there. At the start of the match, each ship appears as a red blip. There are also a few ways to enhance stealth. Every ship has an ability that causes the blip to disappear for 45 seconds. Additionally, clouds of space gas will make red blips disappear. So why is having the entirety of the stealth mechanic and the associated thrown out the window for campaign and skirmish a problem?
One of the game types revolves around either driving three weak transport ships across the map OR killing all of the enemy ships while protecting the transport ships. The problem is that from the moment enemy AI spawns, it makes a b-line for the transport ships. This means your only real chance of succeeding in this scenario is to annihilate the enemy or create a wall of ships and hope you don’t get rammed or shot at from behind.
Stealth is just one horrific aspect of the enemy AI. Most games increase difficulty with better AI or more damage and more health. In Battlefleet Gothic, the game just cheats and it cheats badly. Lets say you’re playing on Heroic (hardest) difficulty. In your first mission, you have 300 points to distribute between (2) level 1 light cruisers with 6,000 unit range and escort ships. The enemy might show up with a level 5 battle cruiser with 12,000 unit range, a level 4 light cruiser, and an envoy of escort ships. Not only that, but the enemy has a FAR greater critical hit chance on Heroic, to the point where nearly every hit causes a fire or a weapon, engine, shield, etc to temporarily or permanently become disabled. Even a master of naval strategy can only do so much against such overwhelming odds.  Worse, “Breakthrough” missions give the enemy AI (4) 12,000 unit range stationary guns with perfect accuracy spread evenly in a straight line across the map. After destroying all 4 turrets, you then have to get your line ships all the way across the map. Or... you would, if the game worked. Breakthrough is bugged so that when you destroy all the turrets, the objective doesn't update. You can only win by killing the entire enemy fleet. So it's cruiser clash, but with only half the map in use, and you STILL can't use stealth. The game explains how you can make sneak attacks and ambushes, then gives you no tools to actually accomplish such feats. There’s difficulty and then there’s madness. Battlefleet Gothic: Armada pits level 1 admirals against an armada of level 5 ships with extensive upgrades.
In addition to breakthrough, there's another mission where you have 180 seconds to destroy an enemy flagship before they warp out. The problem is that Battlefleet Gothic is meant to have a slower pace to it. Killing ships isn't easy and it takes 90 seconds just to cross from the middle of the map to the edge (which doesn't make sense since we're in space, but whateves. You need to destroy a flag ship in 2 minutes or you lose. The tutorial explains how you can stop a ship from warping out, but it's not 100% effective. So its perfectly possible to use the "stop warp skill" on an enemy 3 times and still fail to stop them. This was an incredibly poorly thoughout game mode with very little balance. It's only an insult to injury that another game mode did it right. In data collection, you use boarding actions to get onto the enemy's ship, steal their harddrives, and then be the first one to warp out. That level DOES work because the only action needed to steal the plans is some kind of boarding, either teleportation, boarding pods, or assault boats. You have lots of options and just landing the boarding action is an instant objective switch.
The point of this lengthy exercise is that the game has glimmers of brilliance, followed by long hauls of boredom and poor balancing.
The problem with all the game modes that aren't crusier clash is that you wish you were playing crusier clash. Why do any of the objectives when you could just kill everyone instead?
So let’s talk about those previously mentioned stealth upgrades. One skill causes ships to completely disappear until they fire their guns. So long as they’re far enough away, ships can make a clean breakaway in this manner, repositioning or escaping off the map. Another skill dramatically reduces the detection range of enemy ships. You’ll see AI abuse this skill and another that causes your ships to freeze for 15 seconds. Enemy AI will close in on you, board your ship, then use the sensor disruptor skill to disappear for a few seconds. They will continue to fire, but you are unable to target them as they have the hidden status. Since player stealth is completely ineffective against AI, you can’t pull this same trick. I tried it numerous times. At a range of 6000 units, the enemy AI still fired on my ship after I used the sensor disruptor.
Speaking of firing on ships, its very clear Battlefleet Gothic should NOT have been an RTS. Why? Well your ships don’t fire indefinitely. Every single weapon has a reload time between 4-17 seconds. Why is that a problem? Because you don’t know when your macro-weapons and lance weapons will fire. There’s no charge timer for your standard weapons, which severely limits your tactical input, which is all the more crippling when you can’t use stealth skills. Take for example, the lances. Lances have a perfect accuracy, reduce armor to 25 on hit, can cause either temporary or permanent critical damage, can be upgraded to cut through shields, but have a 12+ second reload time. A small unintrusive timer, even a refill bar on the weapon’s profile itself would let you save a shot until you're in the enemy's weak spot. As it stands, your captains are flying blind while the enemy has 20/20 vision.
To score a single hit in Battlefleet Gothic, you first have to penetrate the shields of the enemy ship (about 100-200 HP). To do this, your ship automatically fires its guns.  Each shot from those guns now rolls for accuracy. If they hit, they also have to roll against a possible shield upgrade that has a 25% chance to nullify accuracy rolls. Alternatively, there’s a class of weapon with a 12-18 second charge time that can be upgraded to be 50% more volatile against shields and has 100% accuracy, but must still roll against that 25% chance of nullification.  So you lower the shield and now you have to roll for accuracy against the ship you’re attacking.  Imperial Ships have 75 front armor and 50% side and back armor. This means every bullet that passes an accuracy check only has a 50% chance to damage an Imperial ship on the side. Most macro weapons do between 12-24 damage. The lightest class of non-escort ships have 800 HP. So in order to kill one ship, you need to pass an accuracy check, disable the shields, pass an accuracy check, pass an armor check (minimum armor has a 25% chance to avoid damage), and then continue doing this until the ship is dead. You need to do this for every single ship in the game.

One of the most fun FPS games I've played in a long time.
The only gamemode that's played is CTG which stands for Catch the Ghost, it's pretty much capture the flag but with some interesting changes. The player holding the "flag" (Ghost) gets the ability to see the locations of the enemy players through the walls, but at the same time all players can see the location of the player holding the ghost.
The player holding the ghost is pretty much incapable of taking out the enemies solo since it can't hold a main gun or run when holding the ghost so the player has to rely on communcating the enemy location to his/her teammates.
It has quite a high learning curve but well worth putting time into, feels very rewarding when playing good.
If I were to compare it to another game it's a bit like CS:GO and Quake had a kid.
Pros
+ Advanced movement techniques and strategic gameplay
+ High average skill and skill ceiling (if you're into that)
+ Extremely dedicated and nice community
+ Nice A E S T H E T I C S
+ Balanced weapons and classes (there's 3 of them)
Cons
- Gun mechanics are pretty much non-existent, after the first shot the gun just sprays in a cone.
- Map layouts are quite hard to memorize (imo)
- Outdated graphics (the aesthetics makes up for it)
- Very small player base (average somewhere around 15 players online)
This game is definitely not for everyone (see the bad reviews), but you should give it a chance!

What made The Room so good in it's great formula of mystery and puzzle solving is back yet again for an outstanding sequel! If you're unfamiliar with the series, The Room firstly came out on mobile platforms, and was then fully remastered for PC. The original Room was released back in 2014 and The Room 2 released in 2016. The game's quite simplistic in it's concept. You have a safe, a box, or just a lock, and the player is supposed to open it. To do so you're gonna have to solve all of the sub-puzzles before cracking the big one.
While I do get frustrated a lot of times in puzzle games, I feel the difficulty for The Room games isn't too hard but also not too easy, it's perfectly balanced and is able to be satisfactory throughout the entirety of the game. It lasts about 3.5 hours total if you don't rush through it, just like the first one. While some people may not like the short length, I think a short game fits the genre better than a longer one. There are 6 chapters in this sequel, one of them lasts a minute and another one is a tutorial, so in the end we have 4 chapters with challenging rooms to crack.
I was quite surprised by the creepy atmosphere in The Room Two, it certainly felt darker than the first game while the main objective is pretty much the same between the two. However, there's a slight difference in this installment, instead of being focused on just one safe or table, now there are multiple places in the room to explore, so moving around with the mouse is possible now.
The port is really well made but I did have some slight annoyances. Sometimes I wanted to move a drawer and the game decided to move the camera instead. Also, it should be possible to type on the typewriter with the keyboard. It's nothing game breaking or too frustrating, just little details I'd like to point out.
The Room Three is already out on mobile, but I do hope it is ported to the PC just like the first two games have been. This is two of my favorite mystery/puzzle games of all time and having to pick between which one is the best is a tough call, they stand on equal ground in terms of quality, challenge and entertainment, two phenomenal games I'd recommend anyone to check them out, even if you're not into point & click / puzzle games. 9/10

The overall plot is a bit generic but the dialogue itself is absolutely fantastic. The exchanges between the characters feels very natural and interesting. It is also free of the unintentional awkward moments that JRPGs tend to have due to sloppy translations.
The game is of about medium length for an action game, about 10-15 hours on hard mode. However  you are able to play through multiple times as different characters to get a different perspective on the story and each has a unique style of fighting.
The graphics are a little dated and look like they belong on the Playstation 2 but that's a minor fault.
Lastly, the game is clearly designed to be played on a gamepad. You can play with the keyboard and mouse but it's sort of clumsy.
For the price point, its pretty well put together. It reminds me of all the older jrpgs I used to play. Cant decide if I like this one or Oath better

Few games have ever had me wondering, in quite the same way as this game, what it was really like to be in one of those old Second World War films taken at the time on the front line. Few games have me starting to imagine myself going down a snowy street in Bastogne and actually starting to feel the cold ! It's usually a novel that does that kind of thing for me. Jump over all the nit picking (yes, there is a jump walls and sand bags command). Ignore the whining and notice how vehicle crews can get out of their vehicles and rapair them, as well as take sectors. Units in vehicles can fire from within the vehicle. There are many other little details, like Russian troops having to huddle around, rather enderaingly I might add, fires so they can keep warm in blizzards. This all goes to make something that is another impressive achievement for Relic if you ask me. There are some lovely model designs in there, soldier designs are very good as well with the Thompson looking good pulled in tight against the shoulder. There are a few problems. There is the "DX11 effect" as I'm calling it. I won't go into conspiracies about marketting here (but notice the "plays best on Alienware"). Suffice to say  the player is going to have to spend some serious time taking a methodical approach to tuning the game for their system. Look for guides about "configuration_system.lua" and remember IT WILL BE WORTH IT to get this game running as best as you can. Find a balance between framerate and visual quality. For example I turned off physics completely as well as snow (footprints), textures high, world to medium. Anyway there are plenty of guides out there. Just don't get sucked in by the DX11 hype and you'll be OK.
So the final verdict ? Basically I've never seen such unusually involving action in any video game except CoH1, apart from possibly when I first encountered arcade games in the 1980's for the first time. There's that true sense of excitement and somthing special going on. Well done Relic !

This game is great!! If you are looking for a fast pace fun easy to learn World War 2 game; this is that game.
Visuals- Like most PC games, your visual expierence is entirely based on your PC video compacity. I have played this on both a laptop on low settings and on my Homemade rig running a XFX R7. On the laptop, the game is playable but you will not really see the beauty of the game and in a game were the terrian is ever changing (ie the cover for your troops is changing) this will lead to problems. But if u have a good enough rig, this game is stunning to play. The physics in the game just make this game look amazing. You really do feel like you are watching the war.
Audio- Sound is key to this game. Tanks, aircraft, machine guns, rifles and arty make this game sound really awesome. Just sounds amazing.
Gameplay- 10/10 Easy to learn and impossible to master, COH2 really does have it all. Playing this game time and time again you pick up new tricks and you think they will work in the next game, but not really. Every game is different. Granted you will be playing on the same maps and the same objectives, the game is always different in the sense, you will never really be fighting the same units in the same way. The game does use the health bar system ( basically your guys will get shot x amount of times before they die ) and at times it does feel unfair. You might have 3 T-34s and the enemy has 1 Panther, you will fight and you will most likely lose 2 tanks to their 1. However, all and all the game is wonderful. Cover is key and every unit counts.
Cons- At times and that is a lot of the time, the Germans have a very unfair advantage. I play as the Germans and the Allies and I can tell you that the Germans are far far better. The German tanks cost a little more but are far far better. German Inf. cost at times the same amount and other times less than Allied Inf and come far better equiped and harder to kill. German MGs have 3 times the traversing distance of the Russian mg. German Anti Tank weapons are far more effective than all but 1 Allied AT capablity. All in all the Germans are better. Not trying to say that you should only play as them, but when you play as the allies, you have to be very good in order to win.
Overall- Wonderful game. Play it as much as possible.

I have honestly tried to love this game as much as I could, but after playing it for a bit I can say that yea, its a pretty good game. There are a few technical bugs in the game such as a rare chance to phase through the floor or roof, and the online multiplayer (which at the time I'm typing this review is still in beta, and hopefully by the time you are reading this it isn't) I have had some issues with, such as me and my fellow hive jumpers being "desynched", which causes everyone in the online party to be seperated from the same events and experiences taking place.  The enemy variety is kind of lacking too, and the bosses aren't too plentiful, both of these factors make the game feel too repetitive, but honestly most of my harsh expressions towards this game could be easily fixed in the future with a free update. On the bright side, the game's playing mechanics are pretty cool, the customization is also pretty cool (but could be expanded on), and the gameplay is just a delight, murdering a crowd of alien insects never felt so good.
Oh yea, and if people look at this and think, "Oh hey that looks like Metroid", you need to understand that this is like Metroid if all of the game puts most of it's emphasis on the combat and basically nothing else (not to be rude, and I know the developers tried, but the story is trash and is continuosly being shoved your way), but it should be noted that exploring does reward you... sometimes.
So yea, in short, the online capabilities, enemy variety, and boss variety are kinda meh, but could be fixed with an update, but the combat, progression and pixel graphics of this game are pretty nifty.

The leveling system is split up into 3 different categories. Survivor, agility and power (also driving if you buy the DLC). This is an amazing mechanic in the game and really helps progress the power of the player as the game progresses. For example, at the start of the game you need to hit zombies many times to kill but towards the end regular zombies can be killed in 1-2 hits.
Another thing im very glad the developers added are custom maps. Although there are some preformance issues with large maps, these custom playgrounds allow for even more replayability after a player has finished the game.
The multiplayer in dying light is a little unpolished, but that doesnt mean its not fun. Besides the bad character animations the multiplayer gamemodes are pretty well made.
Finally, the following DLC is my last critique, although the driving mechanic was a welcome addition to the game, the large fields and forests really destroy one of the biggest aspecs of dying light. THE PARKOUR, why would you make a map in a game strongly based around parkour in a f#!cking field. The story is also just as mediocre as the main story.
Besides the story, and the map choices for the DLC, Dying Light is almost flawless, and is definitely worth a buy. Easily one of my favourite video games. (Hopefully they come out with a second game soon )

They have irregular shooting patterns and will decrease in accuracy the more you 'spray' so correct aiming is essential although most enemies will be close enough that this won't always come into play.
Aiming is a little odd but i'm sure it's just a matter of getting used to it. What threw me off was that your cursor isn't permanently on the screen, and it changes position depending on what direction you are walking.
This means that if you're running and you want to shoot behind yourself, then you have to stop, turn around, aim, and then shoot.
Turn speed is not very fast but I think once in game and in a group, this mechanic will actually become part of the difficulty and that pals will essentially have to 'cover' each other as you cant just spin 360' and shoot everything like you can on some 1-MAN-ARMY style arcade games.
The coolest thing by FAR (and what already has me quite excited) is the STRATA-GEMS.
THESE, ARE, GOING, TO, BE, SICK!
They are summoned from your radio. You have to hold CTRL and then input a series of codes on your W.A.S.D. keys. This can be a more powerful gun, a turret orrr- a TACTICAL NUKE.
And this is what i'm guessing your loadouts and customization will be composed of. Some will bring great team fight potential whilst others will help you keep your buddies alive etc.
Having only done the tutorial, I'd already give this game a 7/10 with quick expectation to raise to 9/10 with potential wombo combo's and co-op teamplay.
TL:DR - GUN GO BANG, STRATA GO BOOM!

Written/Updated as of 11/26/15 Update
WARNING: To play this game, you MUST have a game controller with the analog stick that supports range detection (Like a PS2/XBox controller) or a quad copter transmitter that can be connected to your computer.
Liftoff early-access is a simulator for flying a drone, or quad copter in one of the most fun ways, FPV (first person view).  Imagine being a little bird able to fly and swoop in and out of trees, buildings, underneath bridges, etc.  That is what this simulator and what FPV flying is all about.
Liftoff is early-access and is already worlds above every other simulator out there, and it's just barely getting started.  I get the feeling that this game will build a huge passionate community around it, taking all of our passion for the sport, and allowing us a digital medium to share the art of flying and to practice our skills when we can't fly (when our copters are broken or it's night time).  When it is finally release, if this dream is fully imagined, it will allow us to challenge one another to unique challenges unable to be done in reality such as fly in areas that are generally off-limits for FPVers (like in a big city, or an airport, or around an ancient mosque).
If you're interested in getting into flying a drone in first-person-view (FPV), definitely get this.  When you can comfortably fly through the gates in the easy level, then go buy a copter and you won't be (immediately) breaking it so badly as most people do when first trying to get into the sport.  If you're ALREADY a FPV'er, and need to practice up on your skills, definitely get this.  Just flying it a couple hours already has significantly improved my IRL abilities, since IRL it's difficult to get that much consecutive time to fly (because of changing batteries/fixing parts/etc).

As a space trader you'll hop between planets and trade goods to try and make as much profit as possible in a given number of turns.
Astro Emporia describes itself as a "casual" game but in truth its gameplay would be best described as barebones and simply uninteresting.
-the soundtrack isn't too bad
-there's a decent amount of commodities to trade
-shabby graphics
-extremely basic, dull gameplay
-trade goods prices seem way too random
There's not much to do in Astro Emporia, load up on a few goods, travel to a planet that'd have a need for them in the next turn, hopefully sell for profit, rinse and repeat: there's nothing else apart from a slightly upgradeable spaceship...no random events, quests, achievements, leaderboards, nothing. This isn't casual, it's simply so shallow that it lacks any kind of staying power after a couple of games.
The actual resource generation and prices are also very weird. For example a "mineral" planet would often have iron, gold or gems for a price much higher than one not producing them...while I understand having a fixed system would make the game even duller this randomness makes trying to plot trade routes an exercise in frustration. The planets in need of a certain commodity would also often just accept a single type from that category, and sometimes at a somewhat poor selling price.
All things considered Astro Emporia is simply lacking, there's not enough to do to keep you interested for more than 15 minutes and what's there is not good enough.

I'm unsure exactly what I expected from Dying Light, but this title takes ideas from many other games, reuses them and executes them really well. Mirrors Edge style parkour, that's fun and (mostly) believable. Condemned style melee combat that offers satisfying feedback. Crafting that's extremely simplistic and not too grindy. Gunfights, but melee still playing a large and key part of any combat situation, and the DLC even has driving and rallying around in a buggy. Oh and you get a grappling hook so you can feel like Rico Rodriguez from Just Cause as well.
Openworld-sandboxy world to romp around in. Break into houses, looting various items to enable crafting recipes, main quests, side quests, pop up quests. Drop in and out coop play. There is loads going for it.
The name Dying Light I'm guessing refers to the day / night cycle... and at night as they say "danger is double, pleasures are few" - but the rewards are great. The day night cycle play a part throughout the game and usually not scripted either, it was a mechanic I often enjoyed, night time will creep up on you.
The story, its layer upon layer of blue cheese, but somehow it all works. The game initially looks as though it takes itself too seriously but it becomes apparent after the opening sequence that this is not the case... the story is merely a loose framework that provides a sort of structure to the whole playthrough - You are really free to do whatever mostly, exploration is encouraged and very often rewarded, but the story progresses the whole thing.
In summary; I would highly recommend this game for groups of 4 or single players alike.

Having played through and finished the original Metro 2033 on Ranger Hardcore, I was interested to find out that 4A games were creating a Redux of BOTH games, although Metro 2033 was the obvious focus.  They fixed a few of the original game's bugs, optimised it for PC, and changed some of the gameplay to be more similar to the sequel, Metro Last Light.  And now, having finished this game too on both Hardcore and Ranger Hardcore, does it hold up to the original?
90% HELL YES
10% No.
Metro 2033 Redux is the main game and focus of the Metro Redux series. Based on the book by Dmitry Glukovsky, where Russia has been destroyed in Nuclear war, and the survivors live in Moscow's Metro tunnels. If you've read the book, you'll have an understanding of the main plot, but if you don't: basically you are Artyom: a kid who has just turned 23, whose shone station is under attack by mutant creatures called "Dark Ones", and is told by a ranger to go to the Metro station of Polis and seek help, with Artyom having to survive and fight against Mutants, Communists, Neo-Nazis, Capitalists, and Bandits.
The guys at Ukrainian 4A games had previously worked on the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game series, and in the original Metro 2033 game it showed a lot with the visuals being similar to Shadow of Chernobyl's.
But with a new bigger budget, and a new publisher (Deep Silver) taking care of them after THQ's tragic demise, they had the freedom to expand and improve both 2033 and their own Metro game Last Light significantly.  Let me tell you what's changed:
Some gameplay elements from Metro Last Light have been added, such as adding the option to wipe your mask clean as well as combat improvements - like stealth takedowns and weapon customization instead of having to buy new weapons. This is a little bit sad though, as certain weapons (like the Ubonik (Shambler) with the Bayonet) which were unique to the base Metro 2033 are now gone, & that's a bummer. The gameplay is overall more fluid and smooth like Last Lights, but not as brutal and mechanical as the original 2033.
With an all-new lighting engine, the visuals have been overdone, and they look PHOTOREALISTIC. This is the best looking game I've played ever.
Period.
The cinematics have been redone and are now presented in first-person perspective, which removes the cinematic aspect of the original whilst making them look more realistic.
It now has day and night cycles, that change the way original levels play out as levels originally set in the day can now happen at night. It doesn't work in the metro tunnels though.
Some levels have been expanded such as the Dead City section, which is now a single level, meaning there are less losing screens.
Certain characters and items have new locations, like the Red Army prisoners have been moved in the Frontline level.
All character models have been changed to the Last Light versions, and some main characters now have their own custom models.
Artyom's dialogue is re-done by his voice actor from Last Light (though all other characters retain the original 2033 voice actors), meaning in Russian Artyom doesn't sound like an old man, and more like a 23 year old man.
All loading screens are changed to the Last Light format, with new music. I don't like this as much as the old ones because the original loading screen music was great for most of them.
Diary entries, such as to the ones in Last Light, can be found on each level, and now contain various references to the 2033 novel.
Some weapons from Last Light (and its DLCs) have been added, although I was only able to find a AKS-74, so try to look harder than me to find them.
But the biggest change is the two gameplay modes: Spartan and Survival
This means you can play through the game in the mode that fits your play style and choice. It also changes which watch Artyom uses.
Spartan is more in line with Last Light and is much more action focused and easier to play. Uses the Last Light watch.
Survival is more in line with the original Metro 2033 game, and is much harder and better to play as. You move slower, Reload slower, can carry more ammo, take more damage, and is much more horrific and tense than Spartan mode. Uses a revised Metro 2033 watch.
Last thing to note is that the Ranger difficulty  modes have been changed a little:
You still have no HUD, can take little damage, can kill enemies quickly, and find less ammo, that's all unchanged.
What they changed is that on Ranger modes you can only hold 2 weapons.
This sucks so much, because in the original Metro 2033 you could hold all three weapons without compromise.
So you have to play differently, and make both your weapons count.
Overall, Metro 2033 Redux is an improvement over the original Metro 2033, but not for everyone.
If you are a modern videogamer, or  someone who has never played a Metro game before, then buy this one.
If you are someone who has played videogames for more than 10 years, or have played 2033 before, I would still recommend this, as they have changed it a lot so it's its own game.

Quake Live is another case of a good FPS being dragged down by its playerbase.
The game itself uses Quake 3 as a foundation and builds upon it with new maps, new modes and retooled gameplay. It plays fast and good as it should, it looks and sound gorgeous for its time and has a good learning curve.
However, in multiplayer you won't see anything you haven't seen in Q3, at least if you're european.
It's hardly populated and those who are in it want to always play the same modes and maps. Most of the time, you'll only be able to choose Clan Arena, Duel, Team Death Match, Freeze Tag, Capture The Flag or Free For All (or a minor variation of them), even if the number of total modes is double of that . Despite some recent changes to make it more "newbie friendly" the game is anything but, so if you're new the playable modes fall down to CTF or FT. Entering any other will just send you in a respawning loop. This warning concerns also some "veterans" who enjoyed the old Quakes back in the day but have been out of the scene since Quake 3: the average skill level is much higher and the game plays a bit too much differently, so you might as well consider yourself completely new to it.
Even if you aren't new or unskilled at it, I hope you enjoy Campgrounds, Overkill and BloodRun, because you'll hardly see anything else. Always ready with the Railgun, always hunting for Red Armor or Mega Health, like a socially maladjusted version of Groundhog Day.
To make things worse the playerbase nowadays is made exactly of who you'd think still plays Quake in this day and age: neckbeards on Quad Autism. If they lose they'll blame it on someone else, if they win expect dumb bragging, in any case good luck coming out of a match and being glad to have played with other people. They'll try to hide their attitude behind the shield of ELO points, despite the fact it's not an official ELO system and that not all servers even have it. CA especially is a meeting ground for them.
Play it only if you enjoy shooting against bots, otherwise you're better off with Quake 3.

I greatly enjoyed the first game in this series, and was really eager to pick up the second. Unfortunately, I found myself disappointed. The Room Two wasn't *bad,* it was a perfectly solid room escape game with some lovely visuals, but that's about it. The original Room was gorgeous, smooth, intuitive, satisfying, and just challenging enough to feel rewarding without feeling so difficult it was frustrating. This one felt clunky and unsatisfying. It held my hand through extremely linear puzzles, removing more or less any sense of accomplishment from solving them myself. The final level felt less like assembling ikea furniture (place crystal A into slot B, then turn lever C...) but only because there was no real direction. The puzzle was just as straightforward, but I wasn't sure where in the room I should be looking. Compared to the original game, where every detail in the environment is meaningful and important, the level design was cluttered and confusing. Possibly worst of all; my favourite aspect of the first game was the deeply satisfying element of manipulating objects and devices, figuring out how they worked and how to solve them. Almost none of that was present here, and what there was was so simplistic that I often accidentally solved a puzzle while fiddling with a component, with no idea of what the actual challenge was supposed to be.
It's still worth a play if you like room escape games, I'd say, but if you're expecting something as good as The Room, don't get your hopes up.

Astro Emporia might well be the most bare bones and basic trading simulator out there. While it doesn't fail in what it sets out to do, it sets the bar so low and does so little that it's difficult to recommend. You travel between a random smattering of planets, purchasing goods on one so that you can sell them on another in purley menu-driven travel and barter. Once you get a feel for the price ranges of the very limited number of goods up for trade, you buy low, sell high, and repeat ad infinitum. That is rather literally the extent of the game. No unpredictable events to throw a wrench in your plans, no combat, nothing to add even the barest amount of variation, excitement, or entertainment to the experience. You have debt that grows with each turn, but it's easily paid off within a few turns, bringing the only challenging aspect of the game to heel in short order. There's a mode that allows you to also buy the planets, but having completed that as well, I can assure you that it's a very unrewarding experience. There are early Flash games on Newgrounds with more depth and content than Astro Emporia, making it a poor purchase at any price.

A basic turn based sci-fi themed trading game - think playing the classic Elite but with all the flying between planets and fighting off pirates cut out and it is fairly close. Fairly easy to play, a little bit of depth of how the prices work that you will probably pick up over time, but nothing too strenuous. Can be a bit frustrating at times due to not always being able to sell your cargo on some planets, but generally cheap casual fun if you like this sort of thing, but with nothing for anyone that doesn't enjoy the core gameplay mechanic, wants a very deep or complex economy, or gets too annoyed when a game is "unfair"/random.
Far too simplistic to keep my interest for longer. A game like this is probably fun on a tablet, but I can't see myself ever starting this up again.

Recently picked this up in the Summer sale. What a gem of a game.
I played this exclusively with 4 friends in coop. The campaign and DLC is 99% coop, with only the 'end boss fights' forcing you to play on single player. I must say that playing with friends totally made this game one of the best zombie apocalypse experiences I've played through.
I'm unsure exactly what I expected from Dying Light, but this title takes ideas from many other games, reuses them and executes them really well. Mirrors Edge style parkour, that's fun and (mostly) believable. Condemned style melee combat that offers satisfying feedback. Crafting that's extremely simplistic and not too grindy. Gunfights, but melee still playing a large and key part of any combat situation, and the DLC even has driving and rallying around in a buggy. Oh and you get a grappling hook so you can feel like Rico Rodriguez from Just Cause as well.
Openworld-sandboxy world to romp around in. Break into houses, looting various items to enable crafting recipes, main quests, side quests, pop up quests. Drop in and out coop play. There is loads going for it.
The name Dying Light I'm guessing refers to the day / night cycle... and at night as they say "danger is double, pleasures are few" - but the rewards are great. The day night cycle play a part throughout the game and usually not scripted either, it was a mechanic I often enjoyed, night time will creep up on you.
The story, its layer upon layer of blue cheese, but somehow it all works. The game initially looks as though it takes itself too seriously but it becomes apparent after the opening sequence that this is not the case... the story is merely a loose framework that provides a sort of structure to the whole playthrough - You are really free to do whatever mostly, exploration is encouraged and very often rewarded, but the story progresses the whole thing.
In summary; I would highly recommend this game for groups of 4 or single players alike.
