Company of Heroes 1 was a (mostly) great game that covered the early months of the Allied war effort against Germany on D-Day and beyond. As far as RTS games go, it was superb in just about every way with my only issue coming from the "Tales of Valor"campaigns being of a far lesser quality than the original one or the two from Opposing Fronts. Also I never really played the multiplayer. I got to the game a bit late for that, and i've not been keen on RTS multiplayer since the early 2000's (Warcraft III).
CoH2 had some big shoes to fill, and first impressions seemed a little mixed because of the DLC spam and the historical narrative. As a long-time player of the Total War games, I am very much aware that SEGA is among the worst offenders when it comes to having too much and too highly priced DLC. I got this game and some of it's DLC as part of a humble bundle, so I sit with most of the complete game with still some bits missing.
Truthfully, all I have done in this game is the single-player campaign, so that's all I can talk about. I'd heard before playing this that Russians hate this game's campaign story with a passion, and after having played it I understand why (even if I don't entirely agree).
To try to keep this short, the Soviet Union's "Great Patriotic War" was and remains a highly politicized conflict where the official narrative is one of a hard but glorious struggle to extinguish Nazi Germany. The uglier side of the Soviet War effort is basically ignored or shouted down as lies by the uninformed and the nationalists. This game does not shy away from bringing up things that Russians would prefer to pretend didn't happen. While the whole "sending men into battle without weapons" bit was mostly BS (The USSR's war production vastly exceeded the Germans), and Order 227 "Not a step back" was a feature of the early months of the battle of Stalingrad (not the entire war after it as the game depicts), the rest is largely true. "Penal Battalions" consisting of "enemies of the state" to be thrown at the Germans (or even used as human minefield sweepers), the outright murder of Polish partisans and the USSR leaving the Warsaw Uprising to die, massive press censorship and executions, and the Soviet tendency for butchery when it finally entered Germany are all things that actually happened. I suppose Russians and Pro-Russian sympathizers should be glad that the Soviets horrific treatment of its own liberated POW's (most were considered traitors because they gave up instead of dying or becoming partisans) and the mass♥♥♥♥♥♥of German women are not found in this game.
I'm not here to have a debate over these things. These are unpleasant
about Soviet conduct during WW2. The US is also fond of portraying WW2 as a noble struggle against evil, but their record is hardly clean either (see Operation Keelhaul, racial segregation, the tendency towards "Terror bombing" of enemy cities, and, of course, the nukes). CoH2 might have won more friends if it didn't include things that are so politically sensitive in Russia and the former Soviet nations, but it would have been a bit disingenous as well.
Though it might have helped if the game had also made more of a point of featuring the Germans own behavior on the
that rallied the Soviet people to fight back and ultimately cost Germany the war. The War in the East was a terrible example of the truth of that old saying: "You reap what you sow." A bit more focus on the fact that much of the Soviet war effort focused on revenge for German crimes might have been better.
I probably shouldn't have typed all that. Sorry. History nerd who had a focus on the war between the Germans and Soviets for many years. XD

Everything about the packaging is great. The art is beautiful, the voice acting is good(a rarity), the music is perfect, the sound effects are impactful and meaty, the UI is functional and straight to the point.
So it's just a shame the contents don't quite measure up. The issue can be summed up in three points:
Firstly, a lack of feedback. In the interests of a slick UI, the game gives you very little feedback on your actions, in terms of, for instance, damage done. Sometimes attacks will do tons more damage than others, and it's hard to tell if it's down to how you executed them or a random roll of some sort.
Secondly, speaking of the random rolls, the game is PAINFULLY random. Most missions are down to your deployment vs the enemy's deployment. Whether you can gobble them up piecemeal or end up in a painful face-to-face slog. Whether you can corner the assassination target, or whether it has a chance to run... and you deploy without being able to have any idea where the enemy is deploying. So success in missions is often down to deploying, seeing where the enemy ends up, and restarting if their deployment is completely unmanageable.
(Oddly enough, while you can restart a mission as many times as you want while it's still going... if the loss conditions actually roll up, you're barred from trying again. Strange design decision.)
Lastly, the AI is boneheaded. Well-designed for a couple of factions(Orks, mostly), mediocre for some(Traitors and Chaos) and terrible for a few(for instance, the poor, poor Eldar. Ramming and knife-fighting range does not work as well with Eldar ships as it does with Ork ships!). This is mostly an issue when some missions split half your deployment points with, for instance, Eldar, who waste all of their points on suicidal rushes in the first thirty seconds of the game, leaving you outnumbered two to one(points-wise) against the enemy.
Eventually it just rolls up pretty unfun to play.
I wouldn't recommend getting this unless it's REALLY on sale and you've got a LOT of patience.

Hive Jump is an awesome mix of Contra and Hell Divers, with a Starship Troopers (the movie) atmosphere constantly surrounding you.
Some rogue-lite elements have been included, such as a sort of pseudo-permadeath, randomized levels, and collectible powerups ("relics") which last for the duration of each mission.  There is also an overworld game between missions, where you progress through each planet via a series of offensive & defensive choices.  The overworld is also where most of the narrative dialogue takes place; the banter can be pretty funny at times.
The soundtrack and audio are excellent.  Most of the controls are tight.  There is a great variety of guns, grenades, and utility equipment which can be passive or active w/ cooldowns.
Online play is currently in beta (as of late April 2017), but is really fun.  Aside from occasional desyncs and movement glitches, it is shaping up nicely.
As an FYI: I may be wrong, but I believe single player runs at 60 FPS, while online coop runs at 30 FPS.  This doesn't seem to affect the gameplay significantly, at any rate.
If you want a fun action platformer, Hive Jump is a solid contender above a sea of mediocrity.

Xcom lets you take the command of Earth last line of defense against an alien invasion (yeah, I know, I mean what would be our odds against a race who master space travel...).
The game offers an interesting gameplay, composed of a base management phase, where you purchase new installation, develop research projects, produce equipment, etc, and a battle management phase, when your troops have to operate somewhere on the planet.
Now should you buy Xcom? Totally if you like turn-based tactical games. The game has plenty to offer, and with the Long War mod, you are up for dozens of hours of gameplay to finish the campaign. And the graphics are still nice, despite its age.
However, there are some negative points:
1/ The maps are quite repetitive. Whether you operate in Europe, America or Africa, the maps look the same. Only the missions in Asia have dedicated maps. The rest are based the american template.
2/ The difficulty settings can be quite unforgiving / unfair, especially with the Long war mod. So I advise to play with the ini settings to change some aspects of the gameplay.
3/ After many hours in the campaign, it can become a bit boring as it's always the same missions in-between the scripted ones (the ones that move forward the plot).
But overall, it's a must-have for any tactical game fan.

NeoTokyo started as a source mod way back in the day.  I couldn't tell you exactly when I started playing but it was near the time that steam came out along with the orange box. That said, it had always been a great game I occasionally dipped my toes into over the years.
During those years, a small, tight-knit community has formed (ANP) and it has only been recently that I have dug deeper into the game and it's culture.   Like the community, Neotokyo is meant to be accepted wholly with it's flaws intact, they only serve to make the game a richer, character building experience.
Indeed NT would not be the game I and many others have come to love if it didn't crash every few map changes (redlight!).   I have come to embrace these NT-isms as part of the entire experience, as have many others.
The game has not changed much since 2006 but it does not need to.  If you are looking to play this free source mod, just know a few things:
-Know when to play, certain times of the day will bring more players to servers if it is afternoon/evening/night in their respective timezone.  This has been my tactic to work around the small amount of active players.
-Friendly Fire is always on, so be mindful of teammates when lobbing dat nade into that crowded hallway.  While it is mostly forgiven, consistant teamkilling will bring the ire of the admins upon you.
-Use a mic, beyond the tactical implications, getting to f--- around with the rest of the NT community is always a laugh.
-Have fun, this is not CoD, Battlefield or even CS:GO, it is a free mod that people really enjoy for the fun of the game with competition being second to that.
Keep those in mind and join up today!

This mobile port is an exercise in randomness and not worth your time.
Lately I've been feeling nostalgic for games like Sundog: Frozen Legacy and Escape Velocity Nova. With space trading games I generally dislike the combat systems and would prefer to travel around and explore, perform missions, upgrade my ship, etc. But most of the space trading games I've found force combat upon you. Astro Emporia has no combat, it is purely a trading game, but it is too random and simplistic to be enjoyable. The game was designed for getting the highest score you can in a set number of turns. You have a choice of 15, 30, or 60 turns or a Buyout mode where you attempt to buy all the planets in the solar system. Every game starts you with $4000 credits and a loan payment of $4000 credits. The loan just seems like an artificial difficulty to soak up some of your early profits. Assuming you can find decent trades you can pay the loan off quite quickly. After that there are no costs outside of buying goods. Your ship apparently has infinite fuel and all routes between planets are open from the beginning of the game.
After my first couple plays, feeling the game was very random, I began tracking high and low prices for goods in a spreadsheet. Across three games I found the highs and lows quite similar. At that point it was easy to determine which prices were the best at a planet and buy accordingly. Each planet has two icons, one that indicates the type of goods the planet produces and the other to indicate the type of goods the planet wants on the next turn. For the most part you can ignore these. There are 4 main groups of goods: natural, mineral, gemstone, and technology. Each of those groups has 3 possible goods. For example, natural is comprised of wood, food, and oxygen. Each of the groups has a low-end good, a medium good, and a high-end good. For example, technology has scrap at the low-end, nano bots at the medium level, and ship engines at the high-end. As the game progresses you'll need to focus on higher level goods to maximize profit from your limited cargo area. What I've found on numerous occassions is that planets which indicate they specialize in a good will have terrible prices for those goods. And the indicator about what goods the planet wants on the next turn as often as not ends up with you bringing a good they just don't want at all. You will have turns where you are unable to sell and just need to go to a different planet. Once you complete the number of turns in the game you will be insulted for your score, even if it is quite good.
The buyout mode doesn't change the game in a major way. Your goal is to buy every planet in the system. The starting price is a bit over 39k and it doubles each time you buy a planet meaning the final planet will cost around 50 million. You score is basically the number of turns it takes for you to buy all the planets. I found the prices did not line up as well with the timed modes in my spreadsheet in that prices were often lower than I'd seen in previous games.
The port is fine. It is built on the Unity engine and you can select your resolution and graphics quality as well as fullscreen or windowed mode. The game looks nice, though it definitely has a mobile game feel to it. The artwork is fairly generic but there is no confusion between the various goods. Although the solar system is randomly generated it doesn't matter. You can get to all planets from turn one and each planet's goods change from turn to turn.
I picked this up for $0.89 on a Steam sale and I've gotten my money's worth out of it, but it wasn't due to enjoyment. It was much more because I stubbornly wanted to see what the economic system was like. In a word: random.

The goal is simple: make as much money as you can by buying low and selling high within so many turns.  The problem: the tutorial will leave you with some unanswered questions and the market simply doesn't make sense, at least to me.  For one, the pictures above the planets don't always match the goods in the market...take the tree symbol, for example.  Does this represent oxygen, lumber, or both in the market?  If the atom icon is a category (it's not sold in the market), then what goods fall under it?  Why can't the symbols above the planets match the pictures in the market exactly so that there is no confusion?  Very little about this game makes sense (lack of tool-tips don't help either) and has the potential to frustrate first-time players as it did me. I personally can't recommend this game until it becomes a bit more-user friendly and less unnecessarily difficult to figure out.  If the above issues don't deter you, then please feel free to pick it up as the idea of a quick buy/sell romp does have value for when you're in a pinch and need a quick fix.

UPDATE 2/16/15:
The developer dropped me a line and was nice enough to provide me with intel as to what the different icons represent:
The Atom  = Technology Type. (Scrap,Nano Bots, Ship Engines)
The Tree = Organic Type. (Wood , Food, Oxygen)
Pink Diamond  = Gems (Crystal, Siliumantite, Amandamite)
Gold Bar = Metal (Iron, Gold, Palatium )
Brown Box = Normal (Not seeking or selling any specific type)
Hope this helps anyone else who may also be experiencing the same frustrations I had.

Console port with meat, yet bugs and limited options detract from gameplay.
$9.99
Just as I said in my review for Rainbow Six: Vegas, you should come to expect some meat when "Tom Clancy" is slapped on a title. There aren't really any issues with the branding, but it's the expectation that isn't quite lived up to.
What I mean by "isn't quite live up to" is simple. If I came in expecting a tactical title that works, and really pushes the edge of what tactical titles offer, well it's kind of a disappointment.
For sure though, it is many times better than the joke of Takedown: Red Sabre, which was hyped up and demanded by many. If you played Red Sabre, you will find that the game should have been something like Vegas 2, but without the whole cover system.
Speaking of which, the cover system is one of the key aspects of the game. Just like Mass Effect 1/2/3 it's engrained into the game mechanics. You can't play the game without using it. You will find however that unlike Vegas 1, it has been improved and feels smoother.
Being a console port, the Field of View (FoV) is like having a snake constricting your neck. The game would have improved by allowing you to at least have 90 degrees, not the 60 some odd degrees. Half of the challenge when in cover comes from having to wave your narrow camera angle around to look for enemies. For sure though, it is an improvement from Vegas 1, being that you can select an aspect ratio, and at least have some third-party fixes to attempt to resolve the horrible monster of FoV.
Unlike Vegas 1, the multiplayer is alive and rightly so. The title still has a single player campaign, but the blend between it and the multiplayer environment isn't night and day. By performing certain kills, you gain points in certain areas. Say, when you make a "blind" kill while in cover, that would grant some assault class points. By gaining points, you level up each class, and unlock new items. As you will see in multiplayer, kills give you general XP, which is for ranking up. These two systems (the classes and rank) are related, but are distinct. Coming from Vegas 1, I was disappointed that the shield was at the end of the list for a certain class, and could not use it until I had unlocked it.
On the case of multiplayer – it's alive but there are hitches with it. The most common and well known is the gun sound bug. It seems when someone kills an enemy, it has a chance to bug the sound of the gun, and thus making it sound like it's continuously firing. The only ways to resolve this are to host the game (and not hear the looping sounds), or to mute your sound in the case it does happen. I have played a few coop "Tango Hunt" games without this issue happening, but it still happens from time to time. Ubisoft being Ubisoft knows the problem exists, but hasn't addressed it and probably won't ever. All you can hope for is for the round to end, or a mute button is close at hand.

Edited 12/16/2015:
We've had pretty great communication with the DEVS and community members using the Discussions forums as well as the in-game error reporting features. Several users have expressed issues with Transmitters not calibrating correctly or at all with the software.  If you have an RC Transmitter, there are a few guides already posted and several discussions with topics discussing how we've worked through some of those matters - but there are ultimately a LOT of cables and variances in how they're produces, and even more Transmitters that users have. If you're  having errors connected, post it and let's get you flying!  I personally have a Spektrum DX6, DX6i, Taranis Plus, and Turnigy 9x and all work well using a USB cable. The Spektrum devices took several calibration attempts, and then additional Sub-Trim manipulation, but work well after.
* * * * * * * *
All around - I am really excited to see how they progress with this game. The 3 current levels are already beautiful and the multiplayer is going to be very exciting. Two thumbs up! (Then back to the joysticks!)
Note: While this game does work decently with 360 or similar gaming controller, I do not recommend spending time to get used to it. Gaming joysticks are meant to center themselves when you release pressure. This is ideal for most game situations, but not with throttle. While I did use the 360 controller for the tutorial and first test level, and it was decent enough, once got my Spektrum transmitter connected to the game and calibrated - it was a night and day difference. Much easier flight, it was much more fun and it was much smoother feedback from the camera also as you won't be bobbing up and down.
This will be a must have for pilots that want the FPV experience without ruining their setups or going through tons of props in the early learning stages. Would also be great for teaching purposes.

My old review was too long, so let's clean it up.  Overall, 6 or 7 out of 10.  Not a definite recommendation.  Only play it if you don't mind slogging through the middle of the game where it's absolutely no fun at all.
This game was decent.  It's a linear shooter.  It's the low point of the Half-Life series, but it still was fun until you got to the "Low Lifes" chapter.  Then, we get to fight the real enemies, not this underground-low light crap with antlion spam.  We get combines and more zombies, with Alyx usually either sniping or in the middle of a battle with you, which means no more cheesy lines from her that irritate the hell out of you.  The hospital level was perfect for getting you out of the underground crap, taking you right into where the game belongs... something reflected in Episode 2, where we didn't have that downtime where antlions are everywhere and we can't see anything.
As for storyline, maybe it felt different as what "re-opened the HL series and made something out of that unresolved ending from HL2," but for me, it felt like that explanation between HL2 and Episode 2.  It would be fine as a 3-minute recap (which is in there for Episode 2, if you just want to skip over this).  It's okay.  The storyline itself is just continuing HL2 straight from the ending, where (NOT SPOILING IT) and you wake up in a junkyard where D0G uncovers you.  You go back to (NOT SPOILING IT) via junkyard car now powered by D0G's incredible hulk powers and (NOT SPOILING IT).  You end up... look, I can't tell you, it's all just spoilers.  It was okay for storyline, while adding more space for time-consuming lore that I'll never even bother to google because of my social life conflicting with spending all my time pondering the mysteries of the Half-Life franchise.
Either get this game and force yourself through the middle part where the game sucks, or just skip to Episode 2, a game without any sort of "crappy section," and watch the 3 minute recap of Episode 1 complete with post processing as soon as you click new game.  The choice is yours.

Cons:
* Only one type of Suit, an EVA suit so your charactor is very slow and it takes a long time to do the simplests of tasks.
* Storage containers hold much less than real containers today requiring you to have a large number of them and change them often.
* Radiation Levels spike to lethal levels for about 5 min forcing you inside every 15 min (give or take).
* No other Atmospheric dangers other than radiation and a non-breathable atmosphere.
* No way to depressurize the inside of a base forcing you to have to wait in the airlock evertime you come in and out while moving supplies inside or out.
* Mods are required to allow the player to have a more realistic power supply, storage ect.
* Limited world size, you can not travel all over mars you are limited to one area.
* Random bugs that force you to start over, Like dieing when you lay down or sometimes when you eat, tripping and your charactor can't get up without falling right away again. ect.

Pros:
* It's a Challange.
* Requires the player to prioritise each action by Benifit and need over cost and time.
* Sandbox Style Gameplay allowing the player to build how they want for the most part.
* A decent sized modding community supporting the game with mods that make gameplay better.
* A helpful community willing to take time to help you figure out any problem you are having.
Over all:

Greetings all, I'll preface this review by saying I kickstarted this game and played it both in Early Access and once released - so feel free to note any bias as you wish. This review is being written in regards to the current state of the game as it is today when this review is written; not to what it might be or will be down the road.
Hive Jump is a simple but fun game, where you and up to three other friends can shoot some bugs! While you can play this game in singleplayer, it is the multiplayer component of Hive Jump where this game shines. The game can be played locally if you have controllers and online support is available. Notably, challenges aren't available at this time for multiplayer - though the developers have suggested that they may make Endless mode available for multiplayer play.
The base gameplay sees you entering a hive of bugs, starting at the top of the hive and making your way down to its lower depths level by level. Along the way you'll blast bugs that will spawn to take you down, bug spawners that spawn bugs, bug eggs which will explode into goo, and bug bosses for you to overcome. Their are four environment layouts to encounter including ice, lava, crystal, and mushrooms; all giving you a variety of hazards to watch out for and avoid.
To help out your jumper, you are entering with a multi-purpose rifle that can be modded to fire various type of weapons and effects. You also have access to multi-purpose grenades and powerful utilities to help you out too. You can only equip one type of rifle mod, grenade, and utility for use, but if you have the transponder backpack with your jumpers then in-between level changes you can swap out your equipment for different setups.
As you go around in your adventure, you or one of your fellow Jumper friends will be carrying a special transponder backpack. Notably, this backpack is vital to your journey, as it allows players to respawn. Of course, when the Jumper carrying the backpack dies, it is vulnerable to attack, and if destroyed means you can no longer respawn. As you reach deeper depths, respawning will take longer, so one must be careful the deeper into the hive they take that backpack. To help overcome the fact that in singleplayer there is only one person carrying the backpack, you have the luxury of being able to move the backpack around to help avoid enemies and their attacks until you respawn.
From what I've seen, the developers are also quite receptive to player input and comments as well. They are also working hard to eliminate any remaining bugs (the game code kind) and fix any remaining issues that have yet to be addressed from the release of their game.
And now we get into why this review is being given a thumbs down rating.....
Hive Jump overall is a fantastic game, but it still has a way to go in order to be one worth recommending for purchase. Namely, there are a few game bugs and issues that the game needs to improve in - balancing bosses for multiple people, balancing for weapon usage, and problems with online multiplayer. I also have a bit to say about a couple of the bosses too that come off as being a bit lacklustre to fight against.
In general, the run of the mill gameplay for Hive Jump is well suited for playing in singleplayer or multiplayer, but the bosses aren't. Comparing the game from a single players perspective to that of someone playing with his friends though, you'll find that when you encounter any of the bosses that their health doesn't properly scale for the additional jumpers with you. With a competent four man team, you can fight the Queen for example and kill her BEFORE the Nuke goes off; upon starting the fight activating said Nuke. Typical bosses like Charger or Caretaker might melt in less then 20 seconds - and that is being EXTREMELY conservative.
Then there is balance between weapons. While the developers did a pretty good job with helping to shore up balance for grenades by altering the base number you receive and altering some of the rifle mods so that nothing was truly overpowered; they still have some work to do in shoring up weaker rifle mods, grenades, and utilities. For example, some rifle mods like Mag Slugs and Cryobeam don't offer enough in terms of damage capability or unique features to warrant their use in comparison to others; the Hover Jets utility comes off lacking use with limited situations for it to shine; and then Cluster Casings.... Don't start me on those.
However, most damning of all for this game has to be for online multiplayer. This is a game that was developed with multiplayer gameplay in mind, but unfortunately the games multiplayer scene is non-existent as people are having dysync issues when playing with other people; thus they are discouraged to play the game with other people currently. The developers have stated that they are trying to locate the problem, but they still have yet to fix it. While playing in singleplayer or locally won't have these problems, this is likely a major selling point for people purchasing the game.
Without that online multiplayer component properly working, the game is definitely NOT WORTH the price the developers are asking for the game. Many of the other shortcomings above also dampen the overall worth of the game.
Likely for some players it might also not still be worth the price they are asking if online multiplayer was working as well; as while there isn't a lot of alternatives for playing with four people cooperatively, those other options are much cheaper - plus apparently Valve is trying to cut back on developers offering 4 packs of four player cooperative games while still allowing older titles to offer 4 packs, which unfortunately hurts Hive Jump further (though that one isn't on the developers, that ones on Valve).
As a last note, I'll also throw in something in regards to the bosses. In total there are 5 main bosses you can fight in the game - Harvester, Scorcher, Caretaker, Charger, and Queen. Of these bosses, I don't have much of the ways in complaints to levy against Harvester, Scorcher, or the Queen; regarding Caretaker and Charger though, these bosses generally don't come off as very fun and could have been better.
In Caretakers case, the fight has the potential to be fun as it has you jumping on appearing and disappearing platforms or in small nooks in the wall, while chasing Caretaker up and down the level. However, Caretaker only has one attack and summons enemies - and that's it. Outside of its attack and summoning, it can change its weakpoints (which are also where it attacks players from) but Caretaker comes off as being an extremely dull boss to fight.
Charger could perhaps also be quite fun to play with. In his case he has a sort of arena, where he stands in the middle of the instance and the rest of the instance has harmful crystals that harm the player if they stay near them too long. However, his AI is easily baited, allowing an experienced player to lock him into a simple charging attack over and over again (a little harder to do in multiplayer, unless you know he's targeting your character specifically). While he has a few attacks, in comparison to Caretaker with just one, he is a ground based boss without any real anti-air ability; with jump jets and some initial breakable rock platforms, you shouldn't have too much trouble staying out of his reach and pouring on some damage...
Overall with the following said, I have enjoyed the game - when it isn't dysyncing in multiplayer or exhibiting any really annoying issues. I can't recommend purchasing this game as it is now as it isn't living up to its potential as of yet -
but, I do recommend keeping an eye on its development to see if it might be worth checking out in the future when the developers get at least the dysync issue sorted out.

8 years passed since QL's existence. Through time, the game was demoted from the Intel Extreme Masters, then the game didn't get the attention to be treated as an equal eSport by the public... and the reason (my best bet) is the graphics, because duh, the game still looks like a 1999-2000 game.
Things went better and worse at the same time. We had to wait 6 years for them to make up their minds and finally release it fully into Steam, with the capacity to create online and LAN servers, the mods people would gladly upload through Steam Workshop, the demo player... all of these were asked as suggestions in their forums to be included. They did all of this too late. Quake Live's dead now because the only active players that remain, are the ones playing only Clan Arena.
Also they added some totally unnecesary things, like the total replacement of one of the QL voices, and boring gamemods such as Domination. It's not even like UT: you have to stay inside the point to capture it, just as if you were playing Battlefield. *yawns*
The most curious thing, they never intend to create new models besides keeping the originals from Quake 3 and Team Arena. They're all the same, but with the sport and bright variants.
The game always kicked♥♥♥♥♥ but the people behind it handled Quake Live very poorly. And thus the reason why many people I cared never actually came back. With nobody to play with and the long-term hipocrisy period the company had before, I left.

Recently picked this up in the Summer sale. What a gem of a game.
I played this exclusively with 4 friends in coop. The campaign and DLC is 99% coop, with only the 'end boss fights' forcing you to play on single player. I must say that playing with friends totally made this game one of the best zombie apocalypse experiences I've played through.
I'm unsure exactly what I expected from Dying Light, but this title takes ideas from many other games, reuses them and executes them really well. Mirrors Edge style parkour, that's fun and (mostly) believable. Condemned style melee combat that offers satisfying feedback. Crafting that's extremely simplistic and not too grindy. Gunfights, but melee still playing a large and key part of any combat situation, and the DLC even has driving and rallying around in a buggy. Oh and you get a grappling hook so you can feel like Rico Rodriguez from Just Cause as well.
Openworld-sandboxy world to romp around in. Break into houses, looting various items to enable crafting recipes, main quests, side quests, pop up quests. Drop in and out coop play. There is loads going for it.
The name Dying Light I'm guessing refers to the day / night cycle... and at night as they say "danger is double, pleasures are few" - but the rewards are great. The day night cycle play a part throughout the game and usually not scripted either, it was a mechanic I often enjoyed, night time will creep up on you.
The story, its layer upon layer of blue cheese, but somehow it all works. The game initially looks as though it takes itself too seriously but it becomes apparent after the opening sequence that this is not the case... the story is merely a loose framework that provides a sort of structure to the whole playthrough - You are really free to do whatever mostly, exploration is encouraged and very often rewarded, but the story progresses the whole thing.
In summary; I would highly recommend this game for groups of 4 or single players alike.

Oh well ... what fun I had for once playing essentially the Questgiver for the hero of the Story. That basically sums up my feelings towards X-COM: Enemy Unkown, after I finished the campaign for the first time. I like this game quite a bit with it's Turn-Based Strategy element paired with base building and Economic simulation.
The biggest seller is probably for me the base building element, where you have to juggle quite a bunch of tasks. First there's your budget to consider, for which there are only 3 ways to get money. The first one is the monthly income you gain from participating countries, that pay you for your protection when you give them Satellite coverage. Somewhat like the Mafia, only that there's the Alien threat looming over every country instead of you telling Brazil that you let the German's football team loose on them, if they don't pay up.
The second option are Quest Rewards, for interfering with Alien Activity and from time to time the Councils special missions. Though it's a rather unstable source of income, as you can also gain engineers and researchers from that instead of just a bunch of money and for the Alien intervention the panic level is the more prevalent thing to consider, on where to send your soldiers so you don't risk countries opting out of the X-Com Program.
The third Option would be sell the Alien stuff you recovered while in the field on the Grey Market, which is a rather double edged sword, as you need it for Research and Engineering at times, but sometimes cold hard cash is more important, as you sometimes just can't even do anything without the money.
From the base you also send out your interceptors when your Satellites have found a UFO scouting the country side. You can unlock one other type of Interceptor and equip basically just differing weapons, to shoot down UFO's that become even bigger with the time. And while they're engaged you can offer some support with targeting help, evasive maneuvers and one thing I never used, when you told your guys in engineering to build it. Otherwise you can only Abort the mission if it looks like your interceptor is on the short end of the straw.
The turn based combat on the other hand during fights with your squad is a lot of fun, although it can be quite agitating when your guy misses a 95% hitchance shot. On the other hand it happened quite frequently they would hit at 40% chances, so I shouldn't complain as much. The tactical Options you have are quite a few. Luring enemies into traps set with setting all your guys to Overwatch, blasting off a wall with your heavy to let the Snipers take care of the enemies from the distance or simply using cover to your advantage as you advance against the enemy.
Having four types of Specializations for your soldiers and a lot of different options on how to equip them, also impacts how you can play the game, giving you a myriad of options of how to go about killing your enemies. Although I mostly used my Snipers to cover for the advancement of my team, using Heavies to take out Mechanical enemies, while the Assault bumrushed unsuspecting enemies and Support was stacked so hard with Med-Kits that I rarely ever lost someone in the field.
Well ... having said so much about the game mechanics it's kinda odd I never got to say something about the Story ... it's fine I guess? The story took more or less a backseat, as I simply wanted to have my fun building my base. So after I finished with the last mission I was somewhat left unsatisfied as I really wanted to continue endlessly to fight Aliens ... but at least the Ending gave me the feel of the most important Quest Giver of all time! So I can only recommend this game, for anyone that likes Sci-Fi and Turn Based Combat. It's just a blast to play X-Com.

This game takes the concept of the first The Room further by expanding the puzzle boxes into puzzle rooms. Now you interact with several puzzles spread out in each room, seeing what happens when you flip this lever, rotate this device, and so on. It sounds deceptively simple, but there's a pure enjoyment found in seeing what each puzzle device will do as you solve its stages. A subtle hints system ensures you won't get stuck on any one puzzle for long.
Like the first game, the experience is beautifully rendered and animated. And this time as well, the story isn't very deep, but the game nonetheless draws you into its dark and occult world. The puzzles didn't feel as ornate or intricate as those of the first game, and this is definitely the weaker of the two titles. That said, if you enjoyed the first game, you'll find more of the same to enjoy here. And if you like this game, go get the first The Room!

Hive Jump is a rogue-like shooter that does a pretty good job of speaking for itself. Between the crazy weapons and cheesy soldier mojo, you're here to bust up some bugs and bust them up good. Frankly, things don't get much more complicated than that. But if unloading ridiculous amounts of firepower on thousands upon thousands of insect grunts sounds like a good time, you have no shortage of ways to do it in this game.
In Hive Jump, you are tasked with "jumping" alien bug hives that have taken up residence a bit too close to human civilization. This can be done solo or with friends, local or online. The online portion is supposedly still beta-ish, and I can confirm that I ran into a few hiccups. The developers appear active in fixing up launch issues though, and if I was able to get into a match without an immediate lag spike, things went pretty smoothly.
Hives (or levels) in the game are procedurally generated; the strength or difficulty of the hive typically determines how many floors you'll have to best to consider it cleared. There are four different environments to explore and mid-hive bosses to conquer, as well as player-boosting "relics" to find. A form of permadeath is present here but its implemented in a unique way: the team must hold onto and protect a backpack that acts as a mobile spawn point for reinforcements. Its one of the more interesting wrinkles in this game: instead of being cast as a single soldier, you're actually a legion of soldiers who one-by-one fill the shoes of their fallen comrades. Not only does this make for a rather intuitive death mechanic, but the game injects a little extra character via an end-mission memorial for your recently fallen soldiers.
Beyond little touches like that though, the game's wit and humor will probably be a love-hate thing for most people. Loading screens have corny one-liners that range from pure silliness to meme references. The brief interactions with NPC's are largely forgettable and often feature fairly random dialogue. There's a bit of charm to it if you don't take it too seriously, but you won't be missing much if you ignore it altogether.
Fortunately, you can skim past the goofiness pretty quickly and get straight to what matters most: the running and gunning. The armory in this game is very robust and most everything feels not only usable, but unique. The heavy hitting guns in your arsenal feel plenty powerful, but the more nuanced weapons usually manage to give you nice perks while not sacrificing too much damage output. Grenade and utility equipment types are also used and do a great job of rounding out your loadout. The tactical depth in all three categories of equipment--rifles, grenades and utilities--is pretty impressive.
Player customization is easily one of Hive Jump's strongest points. Not only is building a loadout straightforward, but you can swap equipment in between floors if your handy-dandy backpack is still in one piece. As you get used to the basic level structure, you can begin trying to foresee what's coming next and tweak your loadout accordingly. Hive Jump, perhaps in true rogue-like fashion, is a game that gets better the more you put into it. Its a great feeling when a good plan and an optimized loadout come together in a particular run. When taken into account with the numerous game and challenge modes available, such as daily and speed-run challenges, there is a lot of room for trigger-happy players to self-improve and compete on leaderboards.
But if you're more into the discovery elements of rogue-likes, Hive Jump's general lack of depth could be a deal breaker. You are going to see a lot of the same type enemies even as you get deeper into a hive, and this repetitiveness generally carries over between runs. Unlocking player equipment does provide some longevity, but not much considering how easy it is to unlock most things. There is a campaign mode (which is also available online,) but it only adds a light tactical layer that is loosely-connected to the actual hive levels themselves. At the end of the day, you should be in this game for the in-level shooting action, because if you can get past the lack of variety the floor-to-floor bullet grind feels surprisingly engaging.
So in short, the strong run-and-gun action is clearly the star of the show here. Procedural level generation does just enough to keep a bit of freshness and allow the bullet storm antics to shine. If gun-slinging prowess and a never-ending supply of targets is all you need to have a good time, make no mistake that this game delivers in spades.
Quick Summary
[+] Strong Run-and-Gun Action
[+] Flexible, Fluid Customization
[-] Repetitive In-Level Content

In a corrosive, primal, psychedelically toxic world of spores and insects. One not too different from how one would imagine the Sea of Corruption told of in
's classic
, a group of hardened yet gaudily colored space marines are tasked with ridding the badlands of deep and twisting Hives of an oppressive insect species. Kinda sound like something you've seen? Well.. the story isn't too important here anyway, because
Jump will have you incapacitated with flashing lights, intense action, and plenty of bug guts, anyway.
is a sci-fi roguelike with an emphasis on volatile and intense multiplayer action. It also has an emphasis on big, satisfying to use guns. And lots of them. The variety of weaponry in
,  the customization they come with in the form of upgrades, and the satisfaction caused by their force of impact and the crunchy explosions which send the currency flying across the screen play center role in keeping you engaged and hunting for satisfying to collect bug Goo.
It's also absolutely gorgeous.
creates visualizations that I've probably never seen achieved with such a distinct pixel-art style particularly through its incredible usage of lighting. Every bullet flying down a frozen hallway, and every fire-y explosion of a grenade lights up the surrounding surfaces and backgrounds with sense-assaulting lights, colors and sounds.The bosses are impressive, majestic and grotesque behemoths that cover a good portion of the screen. With complex and dazzling bullet patterns, fighting these gigantic insect beasts reminded me of the sacred Ohmu species from the aforementioned
and makes me wonder if it was an influence.
The forward-pushing, cave clearing, dungeon crawling nature of the formula here was spot-on, exactly what I expected from a beautiful pixel-art roguelike at first. That was propelled into in absolute addictive phenomena the moment I thrust myself into the chaos of online co-op.
supports online and local multiplayer for up to four players, which was an inticing premise to me for a roguelike and probably one of the central and integral features here. Once I found a nice, quiet overseas friend with the matchmaking we dove into the Hive over and over to collect that sweet Goo and upgrade our weapons. Then we'd take our upgraded weapons and do it again just to see the carnage. This repeated several times until I realized my entire night had gone by and I was actually happy for it.
Even after all this, I still had so many weapons and gadgets to unlock and try, so many more upgrades to unlock, so much more goo to collect. Each consecutive night was spent hunting for new comrades to drag into the depths with me.
has a seriously effective way of dragging you back in and making you think about it when you're not playing, especially with a good partner or team to stick with.
The challenge rooms take a much needed turn away from the monotonous randomness of the standard roguelike fair, pitting you against challenging and well-designed platforming sections that feel more akin to addictive classics of the SNES era in exchange for new upgrades and extra loot. These were a very nice distraction from the randomized dungeon delving, and a great opportunity to score much needed upgrades.
A campaign mode is now available after a long road to the final release of
which adds a layer of strategy and progression to the game that offers even more incentive to jump into increasingly difficult Hives. It features a tactical, turn-based overworld map that gives you control of building bunkers, setting traps, and using your hard-earned Goo to reinforce them all with more troops. This mode can be tackled with as many players as you wish, but it's especially nice to have around for solo sessions when you want more motivation than just incredibly paced action.

The music is as infectious as the venomous insectoid lifeforms your team will be mowing down. The visuals are a wild and neon ballet of bright bullets and colorful insect plasma. The weapons all feel heavy, bad♥♥♥♥♥ and ultimately satisfying to use and the action is as addictive as it gets.
isn't just another roguelite, it's an evolution of the genre.

The mitochondrion (plural mitochondria) is a double membrane-bound organelle found in all eukaryotic organisms, although some cells in some organisms may lack them (e.g. red blood cells). A number of organisms have reduced or transformed their mitochondria into other structures. To date, only one eukaryote, Monocercomonoides, is known to have completely lost its mitochondria. The word mitochondrion comes from the Greek μίτος, mitos, i.e. "thread", and χονδρίον—, chondrion, i.e. "granule"[3] or "grain-like". Mitochondria have been described as "the powerhouse of the cell" because they generate most of the cell's supply of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), used as a source of chemical energy.

Star Wars Battlefront II is probably one of my favorite games from my childhood.

The Good: Space battles, land battles, Jedi, and everything in between! While some say that this Battlefront game should have been a separate game, I disagree. While Battlefront II did fix many of the performance, textural, and overall glitchyness, the developers brought in new mechanics that effectively made the game special. I probably had thousands of hours in the game before I found it on Steam.

Battlefront II is definitely outdated, but that might not be a bad thing. I will go into the bad parts of this statement in the next section of my review. Level design, a useful class system, harder multiplayer rounds, and single player that does not suck. What I have noticed in FPS games for the past few years, is that they completely miss on level design. For instance, EA's new Battlefront has absolutely terrible level design. They tried, though not very hard, to imitate the level design of the old games. The classes actually have a purpose, not just, scout, plain infantry, and heavy. If the enemy team is being a bunch of lazy campers, assemble an even mix of regular infantry, engineers, and throw in a few snipers, and you have yourself a camper-killer-squad. The multiplayer rounds aren't todays, shoot-shoot, die, respawn, shoot-shoot, die, etc... There is an actual strategy to the game, not today's spammy stupidity. Singleplayer, THIS GAME ACTUALLY HAS SINGLEPLAYER. Look back EA, you screwed up. Battlefront II actually has multiple singleplayer modes.

The Bad: While I do love this game to death, it is definitely outdated. The graphics are old and buggy, but they get the job done. Just remember that this game is old and should be held to the standards of that time. There are compatibility issues with anything past XP. With that, there are multiple fixes and guides on how to fix most issues. I am still running on Windows 7, because I screw Microsoft's spyware, and Battlefront II runs very well with only a few minor bug issues.


Verdict: Definitely worth a buy, even at full price. A blast from the past, that I will continue to play for years to come.

When I first heard about
I thought it would be some sort of murder mystery/action game a la L.A. Noire. I was of course wrong. It's far closer to
, but with more interaction with the world/puzzles. In some sense I guess you could consider it a lite version of an old point and click. In first person.
I paid about $10 for this game, and, really, that's what it all comes down to for me. When I'm done with a game, I ask myself if the money I paid for it was worth it. Normally I try to quantify this by comparing the amount of hours I played a game to the amount I paid for it. The more hours per dollar, the better. There are exceptions, though, and
is one of them.
It's short. I didn't even get the 7 hours Steam says I got; I was idling my computer for a couple of them. It should take about five hours or so for you to complete in full. It's a worthwhile experience that's interesting throughout, with a solid soundtrack, stunning visuals, and a pretty damn good story that wraps itself up nicely and even delivers a feel or two.
As the game will tell you the moment you start playing, it does not hold your hand. I was excited to hear that; in fact, it was probably the reason I said "Oh what the hell?" and picked it up.
But.
The game won't exactly be intuitive at first. My advice to you would be to take your time and try to get a feel for things before resorting to moving on. Exhaust your options. Once you understand how the game flows, you'll enjoy it a lot more. I bring this up because I failed to complete one area, realized it later on, and had to make tracks back to a prior area to make things right. Don't make my mistake: avoid unnecessary backtracking with prudence.
I wouldn't call the puzzles challenging, but most of them are creative and engaging.
suffers the same curse as all point and click/mystery games, though, and it can get annoying. To "solve" an area you'll need to interact with certain objects, all of those objects, in a specific way. And if you don't you can't move on. In a point and click you'll end up clicking on random spaces on the screen hoping to find something useful. The
equivalent of this is slamming down the shift key and running all around the area desperately hoping to find something you overlooked. Be creative and keep a sharp eye out and this won't bother you too much.
If I can spend $13 to see a bad movie, I think I can spend $10 to play a pretty good game. Tonight,
is that game, and I recommend you make it yours too.

When I look for an immersive game, I look for atmosphere, I look for story and the pace of that story, how everything flushes out and how connections between characters break or reconnect.
This game has almost all of it, the atmosphere is amazing as it changes day to night, background of amazing scenery, if you see it then you can go to it. It doesn't hold back on the horror aspect either, it has lots of scare moments and takes every opportunity to build you up to be scared.
The gameplay is fluid, one of the things that drew me in so much is how fluid the parkouring in this game is. The ability to aim your weapon and feel like you're actually slicing through the neck of a zombie, it feels very satisfying.
As for the story, it's okay, but it fails to pull you in to connect to any of the characters as the ones you want to know are barely in the game, I've constantly found myself asking "where these important characters that were shown in cutscenes are??" because that's just it, once they are out of the cutscene they are gone. Don't expect to have some emotional attachment to any of the characters that you interract with somewhat through the game.
As far as just a generic story goes, it's okay and understandable why it's like this, as the game mostly focus's on the gameplay aspect more than the story which is what makes this game worthy of being 60$ still for the Dying Light Enhanced Edition, which includes everything and more to come!

I was mixed about the original Half-Life 2, so what can I say about Episode One?  Well, it's merely more of the same...just shorter.  I bet some of you are rolling your eyes and going, "Well, DUH, that's why it's called Half-Life 2: Episode ONE!"  Well, it certainly feels as if I played the game already...which I did...and Episode One is merely the equivalent of a DLC add-on...which, given the title, it certainly is.  The game doesn't really add anything new apart from a new area to trudge through, continuing from the previous game obviously, and about one to three new enemies to shoot at for the entire game.  This is the same FPS-platforming-puzzle story I've played already, only this time it felt as if the whole thing was going in reverse.  An example would be how in the original game, the gravity gun got upgraded at the end, whereas in Episode One, it gets upgraded at the very beginning...and then it's suddenly downgraded to its usual status during the rest of the game.  I was hoping I would be able to lift and throw enemy bosses with the thing had the upgrade stayed on, but the game said no, which is still a very major flaw with this game.  Getting through Episode One literally got me through half the time it took to get through the orignal game, and that's including getting almost every Achievement.  All in all, what can I really say that hasn't been said before?

Take on Mars is more simulation than game, and clearly showing that the goal was a simulation first, and a game second. That said, it remains very interesting and works quite well as a game, when you can figure out how to do things and get it to work.
And that is one of the problems. The biggest problem however is the complete lack of time acceleration and slow speeds. I understand wanting realistic speeds in your simulation game, but this is not an experience that any but the most patient people are willing to go through. For reference, to complete the unmanned campaign you will need to travel ~50,000m at speeds between 1.5m/s and 2m/s, or in more understandable terms, your rovers go at the speed of an old man with a walking aid and you need to travel roughly a small country's length. The game does helpfully offer you a realistic wheel speeds option, which will bring your speed down to around 0.6m/s, or roughly the speed of that old man if he had to stop to take a breather after every step. I firmly believe that I am one of the most patient people in the world and submit this game as proof for that.
With the biggest problem out of the way, the smaller problems are still noticable. It essentially does not tell you how to do or use most things. When starting a campaign, the first thing I had to do was push every button on my keyboard in the hopes that it would move along the interactive first landing of an historical Russian lander. It worked eventually, and I could play the game after that. After that, you are never told how to use specific instruments, and you aren't told what technologies actually do for you as a player. But that is something you can figure out as well with a lot of looking for things, so eventually it will work out.
There also still appear to be a fair amount of bugs in the game, including random missions asking you to take microscope pictures of the atmosphere, and one that makes it so missions do not spawn when they should so the game literally becomes unfinishable. With the last one in mind, I had to stop my playthrough before I could get to the manned stage, as the missions I needed to complete did not ever show up. The physics at times become a large problem in that your science instruments need to be held still to do science, but the physics tries to make your rovers almost dance, which makes it nearly impossible to use your instruments unless you forcibly jam them against the rock or sand you are trying to perform experiments on.
Even then, Mars is a nice and often varied place, with a lot of interesting terrain and good looking locations, with missions placed so that they show you to all the good places with almost scenic tours. The economic part of the game- Getting your funding, is very rough early on and practically doesn't exist in the later stages. This may be to save up money for the manned missions, but I never actually reached that part, so I wouldn't know.
All things said, Take on Mars needs work. It is not an unpleasant experience for one with a lot of patience, but I struggle to see what would draw in anyone other than the most scientific minded people who at the same time don't mind gameplay. For anyone else, it is a nice novelty, but very repetitive and slow. There does not seem to be that much here, at least not in the unmanned campaign.
There is also a multiplayer mode, but I've yet to be able to motivate anyone into playing it with me. I will update this review whenever I get people into a server with it.

Despite my play time saying four and a half hours, in reality it's only two, as I left my game running for about two while dealing with other things. This game is in some ways better than the first, but it has all the same weaknesses as the first. Either the game's puzzles are laughably easy, ending up being "here is a thing now use the thing" or it becomes a matter of sitting around looking about cluelessly because the game provides you no actual idea as to what you're supposed to do. It is, simply put, a 3D game of eye spy at that point, and there is very little 'puzzle' and a lot more looking about. This game, however, is slighty better than the first, in that it did contain a few puzzles, which were at least interesting, and it uses the themes of its rooms well.
There is just one, majorly glaring flaw with this game over the first, and it's that it attempts to tell a story, and for what it is, it's a mighty confusing one at that. The only real 'puzzle' element is that this game makes no logical sense, by which I mean there seems to be a gulf of a disconnect between the puzzles and the supposed narraitive that we are trying to tell. For reasons never explained, we are solving puzzles in rooms while following someone else for... reasons. This is all caused by something called the 'null element' because reasons. The guy who was preceeding us somehow found the time to turn a ship at sea, a mayan temple, and a seance parlor into a puzzle filled room because... reasons? There's no clear reason why you're doing anything in this game. And then the ending gets all metaphysical, talking about souls and trading the guy who's leaving notes everywhere for some woman's, and then hers for yours, and then you come out of a room and an explosion and... that's it? I said of the first game that it made no sense, and it seems this game is essentially more of that, more nonsensical than anything else. I thought, perhaps, that they were going for a bit of a Lovecraft vibe, given the final chapter revolving around the reanimation of corpses, and the ship level mentioning a crazy man grasping onto something. But aside from that, there is no real story to tie everything together. You're just sort of walking from room to room, solving puzzles for seemingly no reason, which leaves the whole thing feeling rather empty.
If the game wants to be a story-driven game with light puzzles, it fails because the story is incomprehensible. If it's meant to be a hard puzzle game with story elements, it fails because the puzzles are too simple. It tries to be both, and succeeds at neither as a result.
Of course, if you're just looking for a quick two hour puzzle game in some interesting locals, it might be worth it for you. But for me, I expected a bit more than more of the same for a sequel.

I really wanted to like this game, but I'm disappointed.
Movement lacks interesting physics or techniques. See Super Metroid, Smash Melee, Duck Game, various 2D Mario games, etc. for good examples. Google search "The guide to implementing 2D platformers".
Most weapons lack depth; the main exception is Brass Blessing, which has interesting risk/reward mechanics. Rockets are also good in that they work differently depending on the distance to the target, but they should have a faster fire rate. It would introduce the risk of overheating as well as allow a little more choice in use.
The utilities seem poorly balanced; Quantum Blink is obviously optimal for speed running normal hive stages, while Overshield is obviously optimal for boss fights and ambushes. Even in multiplayer, everyone using Overshields and healing grenades is almost certainly better than other options; it's significantly lower risk while still offering high effectiveness. Also, all utilities should have a sound cue on recharge.
All in all, loadouts feel flat. Two weapons and two utilities would give player characters more depth and feel much better to play. If you don't want to overwhelm new players with options, make the extra slots unlock as you hit higher difficulties.
The Queen is great, but the other bosses aren't interesting, as patterns are not varied enough. Players can generally stick with one strategy or position for the entirety of the fight with minimal risk. The standout example is the Crusher, which you have to repeatedly jump over and shoot in the back. The boss lacks an anti-air pattern, so players always know to just jump over it when it gets ready to do anything. This is known as degenerate gameplay, and it's boring. Look to bosses from 2D Mario, Castlevania, Metroid, Contra, etc., for a spectrum on pacing, difficulty, and complexity.
There's an apparent lack of AI-based enemy and item spawns. See Resident Evil 4, Pac Man: Championship Edition, Geometry Wars, etc. for good examples.
Lack of overall polish across the board; less an issue for player characters. See "Juice it or lose it" and "The art of screenshake" talks on YouTube.
I can run Witcher 3 on high settings at 60fps, but this game chugs and skips at times.
Lack of originality in the writing. Look at HELLDIVERS for an example of using popular works as inspiration rather than resorting to lazy plagiarism.
All in all the game isn't bad, but it rarely rises above mediocrity. It's just not fun most of the time.

I bought this and then I played it solo for 14 hours straight, completely screwing up my sleep schedule. If I had one complaint, it would be that I wish there were more cosmetic options; there's only four skins (five if you're a kickstarter backer) and I can't tell the difference between the starting skin and the last one you can unlock. I would love some armor designs that reference great classic sci-fi games, like OldCom or Doom, though I understand they can't do perfect representations for legal reasons.
My extremely minor nitpick aside, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. Most of the weapons are fun to use and of the two that aren't, one states in the codex it's meant for co-op play (the cryo beam) and the other is probably fun if you have other Jumpers to cover you (the Mag rounds; it just fires too slow for solo play. It's the only weapon I died on the first floor of a hive with.) The grenade types are varied and the utilities are all useful. My current build is E.U.V. Beam, Healing Grenades, and Overshield, and I can usually clear Arcade mode on Medium; I've even solo'd a Queen difficulty run with this set-up.
The graphics are great; they remind me of a good DS title, and there's usually very little visual confusion. There are a few different types of enviroments with their own brand of hazards and their own unique stage boss every three or so floors of a hive, with the possibility of a floor being an ambush floor or a dark floor which has a variant itself - a rather dangerous one. As for power-ups, you can collect yellow goo to power up your guns and unlock new grenades and utilities, as well as find relics in boxes and challenge rooms that give a few bonuses such as increased max health or faster movement.
Speaking of movement, this twin-stick-shooter controls very well. You have a jump with a limited flight extra jump to navigate, as well as a standard walk that's fast enough that I didn't mind a lack of sprinting. I didn't have a problem with aiming exactly where I wanted with the analog sticks, but if you do, you can use the laser sight utility to get a clear line on where your shots are going to go.
In my time playing I only encountered one bug: in the ice levels, sometimes when you're running along the ice and you hit slightly raised solid ground such as a ramp, you will glitch into the enviroment. It's easy enough to get out - you just have to move around a bit - but I can see how this would be annoying and could potentially get you killed.
Overall, I highly recommend.

After many hours of play, I find that there are quite a few balance issues in FTL that can highly frustrate the player.  This stems mainly from the fact that FTL is far too short of a game and does not give the player enough rolls to allow the randomness to even out.  This leads to runs of the game where you win because you were thrown free items all game long or lose because you had no time/resources to prepare for tough times.
This flaw could have been resolved by either making the game longer or by giving the player an fairer early game then ramping up the randomness as the game progressed.
However, this does not detract from the fact that FTL is a highly replayable game with many enjoyable game mechanics and is worth recommending simply because it is a fun game to play.

The basic premise of FTL is micromanaging your crew as they "jump" between nodes through various sectors, trying to stay ahead of the all powerful Rebel Fleet (why Rebels got so powerful, who knows?!). Some planning is required to optimise maximum exploration & resource collection against the advance of the rebel fleet, versus hull damage and upgrade aquisition from merchants, etc. This is the unfortunate limitation to an otherwise fantatic game, as the single mode available forces linear progress through the story line and sectors without being able to upgrade to the ship of your dreams (the fact you can get quite despondent when a random encounter wipes out your ship, or miss out on getting 'that last part' is testament to how well it its structured).
Crew management is simple enough, with click/move allocation to rooms where they will automatically work/repair/fight as required. Ensuring that your strategy for defense and attack matches your allocation of work is the amazing element of this game that just works.
Choosing how you attack is very important - you can opt to board enemy ships, damage the hull, damage the enemy personel, use drones remotely or use a combination of weapon techniques. A handful of enemy ship configurations mean that you need some range in your capabilities (for example remote rebel scouts have no people, therefore cannot be boarded). Keeping the same crew is set locations helps them level their abilities (making them faster/better at each action) and adds a minor story type element to the game.
After the work that goes into  getting to the final boss encounter  - one can get rather tense - it is a decent boss fight however it would be nice to have more of these scripted into the game. Replayability comes from choosing different strategies and ship configurations; believe me when I say a different ship can completely screw your highly refined strategy completely!
If you enjoy space sim/ turn-based fights/tactical/ resource management games then you are likely to find something with FTL and end up spending many hours getting frustrated and enjoying the satisfaction of upgrading yoru ship.
PROs:
*Frustratingly random
*Replay incentive, various different strategies enactable
*Good balance for resource mangement
CONs:
*Frustratingly random
*Linear progress through the story is enforced - no sandbox type mode to complete how you want to build your ship

I tried to like this game, but it really makes it way too much of a chore.
That's how I'd describe it best. A chore.
Yes, the atmosphere is perfect, yes they got post-apocalyptic moscow just right. The russian voice acting is awesome, and the soviet placards everywhere fit right in.
The weapon system is much better than anything in most games I've played. All the weapons are pretty much available from the start, and most of your enemies have the same weapons you have so you never have to worry about switching and picking up something else.
But then: some of the enemies are annoying. I'm not a grand master of FPS, but I've never had a problem killing enemies. I know what horror is supposed to feel like, enemies in Dead Space jump out at you and attack you out of nowhere, but they don't stay so close to you you litterally cannot aim at them and have to run away or hope they move 2 inches away from your face.
The level design is awful. You never know if that hallway/tunnel over there is the way you're supposed to go or just a bonus room for ammo. Maybe I'm just a moron, but 9 times out of 10 I would find a staircase or tunnel after killing all the enemies "ah, that's the path they wanted me to take to get around everyone!"
But its worse than that. You will be stuck multiple times with your oxygen running out not knowing where you're supposed to go or what you're supposed to do. The game is very vague with its mission objectives, and there's no map, which would be fine IF the levels weren't so samey looking and bland after seeing them for a while. I said before they did post-apocalyptic moscow well. Well, they did. Its all very gray and everything looks the same, so you forget which corridor is which and where you've been already.
The game does a terrible job of explaining how things work. Even on normal with all "tips" enabled it won't explain to you how to stealth kill enemies.
The stealth is completely random. Sometimes the enemies see you and sometimes they don't. I'm not a fan of MGS's system where enemies can't see you unless you're 6 feet in front of them, but this "realism" is just annoying because I eventually gave up on stealth and just shot everyone in the face.
This game has a lot of good in it. It does immersion well, combat is good, weapons are done right, and the story is there. But its so damn annoying to play if I had the choice I'd just watch it on youtube instead.

I've heard SR described as “GTA that doesn't take itself seriously”. I haven't played the previous installments, but if the 4th is any indication, the description is pretty accurate: it's an open world game where you run, drive and fly to participate in various activities that more often than not end up with you being chased by the police – or the setting's local equivalent of it.
In SR4 we assume the role of the president of the United States, who is a superhero at the same time. The game shows exactly how serious it's going to be with an opening sequence where the player character kills a bunch of terrorists, jumps on top of a nuclear warhead, detonates it mid-flight to end up jumping down to the ground and landing right on the presidental chair in the Oval Office. Soon after that the alien invasion begins, and we end up trapped in a computer simulation with all the other humans while our real bodies are locked in red containers full of life supporting fluids. We're soon taught how to bend the rules of the simulation which effectively gives us superpowers, allowing us to fight the oppressors. Sounds familiar?
While the Matrix is easily the most prevalent inspiration for the game, it draws ideas from tons of other works of popular culture, to the point where I'm not sure whether it's meant as a parody or a tribute. One mission will have you crawl through a level disguised as a cardboard box (with the appropiate Metal Gear Solid sound effects), in the other you are put in a 2d side-scrolling beat-em-up, with mechanics about as sophisticated as Franko had (anyone still remember it?). About every other story quest mocks or refers to something, but I haven't found it annoying or obnoxious at any point. The main storyline is quite fun, funny and enjoyable; the only thing that I can pick on in this game is... everything else.
It seems to me that Saints Row IV would be a much better game if it was a bit smaller and more focused. It gives you a massive amount of options to upgrade and customize your cars, which seems like a good thing, except that with your superpowers you run much faster than any vehicle drives, making them pretty much useless. You get a pretty impressive arsenal of weapons, ranging from typical pistols, shotguns and rifles to goofy, (and actually quite hilarious) stuff like a rectal probe, dubstep gun, a black hole generator or a strangely familiar Laser Sword. Almost all of them can be upgraded in weapon stores, but the game is easy enough to beat it entirely with a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat (I didn't actually try, but I did beat a few combat-focused side missions equipped with nothing else but the aforementioned sex toy). The game features a Homies system, where you can either recruit your gangmembers from the street or call them from your phone to join you in battle, but it never seemed necessary, with the superpowers giving you so powerful AoE attacks that 3 NPC shooting their guns look mildly amusing at best. The game gives you a lot of mechanics to use and play with, but it doesn't really capitalize on any of them. It even allows customizable skins on your weapons (presumably to have a potential to crank up some DLC money), which I enabled at the beginning of the game but never even noticed them in my 21 hours of playing it.
The game has a lot of features that see little to no use in it, yet it fills your time with dozens of similar, repetitive minigames, ranging from quite enjoyable (like hacking stores in form of a classic “plumber” game) to straight up annoying (like ragdolling through the streets trying to hurt yourself as much as possible, that being a lot less fun than it possibly sounds like). It seems like for the amount of content and mechanics that the game has, the side missions could be a bit more elaborate and original, rather than being a combination of 10 or so minigames over and over again – to the point where the reasoning of your questgivers literally becomes “I don't want to waste my breath, just go blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, okay?” at some point.
Apart from missions we get the expected open world goodies like collectibles scattered all across the city, a chance to (re)play the minigames that the side quests require you to do, extremely high structures to climb, and of course countless excuses for mayhem and havoc that we all know and love. All that acompanied by 8-ish radio stations, which we can thankfully listen to also when on foot, which is quite useful in a game where cars are mostly decorative. I found the music quite okay, ranging from rock, reggae to some heavier techno. There was nothing like the absurd talk show station you may have liked in GTA, the only ersatz being a clearly stoned announcer in the dubstep-y station. Still, nothing to complain about.
All in all, I quite enjoyed my time with Saints Row IV. While I do think that the huge part of the game is mediocre at best and it'll be better off without it, the main story is pretty solid and quite fun. Being the completionist that I am I couldn't ignore all the sidequests, even after I decided that they're bad and I don't like them, but I can easily recommend picking the game up just to play the story quests. It's nothing special, ambitious or worth replaying, but it does have its memorable moments that still make me giggle inside when I think about them. I'd advise to not bother with sidequests to much, since the rewards for them are negligible at best and their gameplay isn't very fun itself, but the main storyline should give you about 8 hours of fun. A pretty fun game for those evenings when you don't feel like doing anything constructive and want to lay back and relax with something that'll make you smile and rapidly exhale through your nose every now and again.
