Rebus Forever here with another 1minute-ish (very ish) review for a strategy game, with spaceships,  set in the 40k universe.
As a bit of a goth who likes spaceships, strategy and Games Workshop, I felt ethically and morally  compelled to review Battlefleet Gothic, my massive throbbing bias aside, here goes.
Do you like gothic cathedrals but wish they were better at flying?
Has your love of spaceships been impeded by their lacking crenellations and stained glass windows?
Do you like your games so grim that the best available outcome is maintaining an interstellar fascist theocracy  that glorifies in the elimination of any trace of freedom of thought or expression?
Then this might be the game for you.
Battlefleet Mock Tudor has two major components, the main campaign and 'online'  consisting of two modes.
I'm not gonna lie, the multiplayer does seem to be pretty much dead.
While online was active it was good fun, with one mode based on a persistent fleet you built up over time, identical to the skirmish mode you can play vs AI and the other based on teams buying a large fleet and then fighting 3 rounds.
As online is less active- unless you and a buddy or a small group agree to buy the game and play against one another- don't buy Battlefleet Baroque for its online features.
Let me instead spend some time talking about how awesome the campaign is and why you should buy this game if you have any interest in 40k games, lore, Sci-Fi in general, well written long linear campaigns where every battle matters or just a healthy appreciation for kilometer- long space cathedrals.
This game's main campaign can be played at various levels of difficulty including an ironman mode preventing save scumming.
Regardless of difficulty, after completing or skipping the tutorial phase you will be presented with a turn based persistent galactic map.
The galactic map provides a macro view of the regions you are responsible for, how well you are doing and as a hub for other actions.
From this view you select your potential battles or gain access to port facilities where you can upgrade and purchase ships with your spoils and sector's resources.
As you play, your fleet also grows and gains XP in a persistent fashion.
Each turn you get a number of deployments, allowing you to choose which threat or front to reply to with different planets providing different perks to the overall war effort. Tough choices will need to be made as a consequence of losing too many random battles with the scripted battles causing the most hurt;  try not to lose at all but if you do lose don't lose the scripted battles otherwise you are gonna have a bad time! The engagements take place on a 2D plane making gameplay more straightforward and providing a nod to Battlefleet Postmodernism's tabletop roots.
Folks expecting a Games Workshop game to be a realistic simulation of Newtonian Physics with fully realised 3D space battles might need keep their fingers firmly crossed in hope the Kerbal Space Program devs buy the Homeworld license.
Anyone comfortable watching improbable, impractical, space castles destroy each other with future magic and skyscraper sized space cannons have found the game for them, but I digress.
Each battle consists of picking your fleet from available ships, deployment/setup, and then the actual battle itself with battle objectives ranging from a straight up cruiser clash to having to defend stations or escort transports- all this combined with key scripted battles often containing unique objectives- provides diversity that helps keep long campaigns interesting and increases replayablity, no two runs of the campaign need be exactly the same.
The battles themselves play like naval warfare in the age of sail on account of the 2D plane and are a tight affair, encouraging the player to play to the strength of the ships they choose.
Success in battles will see you earn extra deployments a turn or extra resources, defeat will leave you having to make tough choices about which systems you can afford to lose and limit your ability to react to the events of the following turns.
Pulling a campaign win from the jaws of defeat is possible, as is the opposite.
Battlefleet Art Deco is perhaps an overpriced  game at 30 quid with nobody online during the times I tried, but the research and effort put into the campaign elevate it above some of the cheaply made 40k licenses. If the game itself wasn't fun (which it is), the lore and overall presentation of the campaign alone make it an easy recommend during a sale for anyone into the 40k universe or space themed RTS games.
Thanks for your time and marking this review as helpfull here or letting me know you came from here if you watch on youtube is super helpful for me.

Acquired this in a giveaway on twitch, and it's quite the rough little gem. I do recommend it, if you watch some gameplay of it and think it may be your thing, I think it's worth the purchase. I find that even when I get tired of it, I also want to play it again within the next few hours. But I do have some things to nitpick, though it may be because I'm probably in the minority in how I play this game.
That minority being, I use the KB+M and generally prefer to play solo.
The overall control of the character feels a bit sluggish, it's definitely not snappy like a precision platformer. Probably a design choice, which is fine, but I do feel like I encounter control issues. Control via keys that I am not able to remap to an ESDF format (compared to WSAD, which I used until about 6 years ago).
Strong kit selections for a solo player feels pretty limited. Understandable with the coop-centric design. Weapons seem to vary from "always good", to "situationally good", to flavor choice. Not necessarily a bad thing, but you definitely feel it most when playing solo.
I've had a lot of issues with the teleporter, with it's short charge time and the seemingly unforgiving amount of precision and attention that it requires (in the heat of battle) in order to actually teleport to where you want, in a quick fashion (within the high speed nature of a solo jump, which a lot of gear already doesn't suit well). Especially if said area is full of eggs or a narrow space. It's not a snappy "blink" style teleport that is always capable of getting you away instantly. Bit janky to use. Could also be intended, though.
Lastly, I think I was secretly hoping for something like classes, possibly with skills or class specific traits to add more individuality and range to kits. Something to be that "next Risk of Rain" in a way. I think this could certainly become a competitor, atleast for me.
Overall though, solid game with a promising foundation. Hope it goes places.

The gameplay is pretty simple. Turn based strategy combat. If you've ever played Fire Emblem, or really just any strategy game, you probably know the jist. You click to move people places and there's cover and high cover. When you go to shoot people, it's percentage to hit changes based on how close you are, whether you're flanking, y'know, the obvious stuff. Pretty much anything can be destroyed, and most of the environment can be used as cover. Yes, even that teeny, tiny mailbox.. Maybe mailboxes aren't the best cover... Oh well, let's just move this guy behind the trashcan, what could go wrong? And this guy behind the gas station, TOTALLY won't explode. It'll be fine, trust me. Also, explosives can destroy cover. For example, you throw a grenade at a brick wall, it'll damage anything near that wall, and most likely break the wall. This allows for people to get higher hit percentages against whatever was hiding behind that cover.
As much as I enjoy the strategy combat, that's not all this game has to offer. It also has a base building side to it. Basically, you get "X" amount of money per month. This amount goes up as you get later in the game. The XCOM base is underground, so you'll need to excavate areas to build new things. Building new facilities can grant you new abilities, sometimes it's more scientists, sometimes it's new "research", and sometimes it progresses the story.
Next up, lets talk about the time progression. In XCOM, time has to pass for new things to happen. For example, research will take 10 days. So, you need to scan for 10 days in order for it to finish. This is, in my opinion, one of the biggest issues with the game. A lot of your time, if not most of it, will be spent sitting in the command room, waiting for time to pass. Then some research would finish, and I'd assign new research. Then a few days later, an excavation finishes. Then I realize I can't do anything with it because I don't have enough funding, so I have to wait until the next payday.
It's very possible, of course, this was just me not being great at planning. But I still think that it's partially an issue with the game. Let's say you research new weapons. The thing is, to equip your squad with these new weapons, it's gonna cost you you're entire salary. Sometimes, even one weapon is so damn expensive it drains you completely. Then you gotta scan until next payday, and the same cycle repeats until you slowly upgrade. This basically doesn't let you do any base building at all because weapons are really important and should probably on top of your priority list.
Sometimes the aduction missions felt like a serious bother, because I knew this research or facility was almost done building and I really wanted to get it done, but then a new mission comes up and I have to do it. The missions were fun sure, but it still felt somewhat repetitive. Go into the spooky area, go kill the spooky aliens, rinse repeat. But at least there is enough map variety to make it feel somewhat fresh.
Something I need to bring up before I finish this review is this. This game is BRUTAL. It is unrelenting. It is hard. Yes, even on easy. If you don't like hard games.. Maybe stay away from this one.
Now, lets talk about what I call, "the jank." Now what is the jank you may ask? Well good sir, allow me to inform you. Have you ever played Sonic Adventure? If you have, you would know about how buggy and derpy those games can get. XCOM has a similar problem. Not as bad, but still pretty bad. First, the camera. In XCOM, you can scroll up and down elevation levels to choose how high you want a soldier to be or, how low. The thing is, sometimes this doesn't work. You see, the problem is that the alien ships can sometimes be really strangely shaped, so the game can't quite wrap it's head around exactly where it is that you are pointing your mouse. Sometimes it's very hard to get a unit to move up to a specific elevation, because the game get's confused. You end up having to mangle with the camera, or just give up and place the unit elsewhere.
The camera issues sadly don't end here. Sometimes, it feels like if a unit is too close to what it's attacking, the camera doesn't know what to do. It'll get stuck on an object or be on the wrong side of a wall. Also, the animations can be janky too. Sometimes a sniper won't even be looking at the target he/she is shooting at. They'll buggily turn to the wrong side but the shot almost warps to whatever it is they are hitting.
I think these are somewhat nitpicky, but they still really give off that unpolished vibe, and that's not a good vibe. Maybe I'm spoiled from being a mostly Nintendo gamer, but I think some extra polish time on this game would've been nice. If you like strategy turn based games, you'll probably like this game. The base building is shallow but it's not like it needs to be super complicated, it's not the main focus of the game, though I still wish it could've been expanded upon.
Anyway, that's it. If you actually read this all the way through, thanks! Lemme know what you think. I know it it's a huge wall of text but I had a lot to say about this game. Imnapr out.

Company of Heroes 2 is intense tactical RTS game revolving around explosive WW2 Action.
Bear in mind i will not reviewing any aspect of the Singleplayer portions of the game.
If you were interested in a realistic WW2 Simulator Game, warning this game may not be your cup of tea, as the gameplay is  exaggerated at best with much shorter combat ranges and tanks with health bars. However there is a deep tactical emphasis on combat, with unit suppresion, Frontal/rear armour on vehicles, units with true lines of sight and the usage of combined arms to accomplish objectives.
The base games revolves around the Eastern front, themed especially about the plight of the Soviet Red army against the overwhelming Oberkommando Der Wermacht which equals to 2 Unique Factions each with their owns Techs and historically accurate units. These 2 factions can be expanded upon with various DLC obtainable in-game as well through a unique Item drop system which includes various Commanders to use different tactics or various Skins for vehicles.
There is also the Western front armies expansion which can be bought in which 2 new factions come to play which are the U.S. Forces and the Oberkommando West, each again with their own playstyles and unique units.
PROS:
- Easy to Learn, Hard to Master with a fairly friendly gaming community willing to help give help and advice
- Games are always Intense, with action happening constantly
- Spectacular Graphics, from fiery explosions to Dusty Smokeclouds all the way to the small details on the Soldiers themselves
- Risky and rewarding gameplay, sure to get your mind thinking
- Soundtrack is stunning, with amazing orchestral music bellowing at you during battles
- Unique Resource system in which to obtain resources, one must capture control points to obtain bolster your income which includes Munitions and Fuel
- A Challenging Unit conservation mechanic in which Infantry can retreat from the frontline back to the HQ and reinforce their numbers and retaining the veterancy.
- Large pool of multiplayer maps in which the game supports community made maps
CONS
- Game is demanding in resources on Older computers
- DLC is really extensive and the In-game Item drop system is rather unrewarding
- Certain elements of the game such certain unrealistic aspects of short combat ranges or vehicle HP bars may deter certain WW2 Simulator fans
- Base Game only comes with 2 factions, Further factions must be bought through DLC
- Somewhat Steep price on Base game and DLC
All in all a real good game in which i have invested several hundred hours into.

I'm not quite sure why this game is getting all these good reviews. I can not really recommend it. There is way too litte gameplay here. All you do is play as a camera moving through the world and doing very simple interactions. That is
you can actually find the interactive pieces. This can be quite unfun, in fact, when you are looking for the proverbial needle in the haystack. Many things are obvious but there are also several annoyingly hidden things that are quite easy to miss and it is simply not fun to pixel hunt in a world of this size when you don't even know whether to look close by or far away.
The game definitely should have had a short example murder case separate from the story as a tutorial to explain some of the basics. It is easy to miss the forest for the trees and get confused about how to progress in the beginning (the "no handholding" thing is not a good excuse to not explain at least the fundamental gameplay stuff).
Exploration is a massive waste of time as most of the world is empty. The lack of any real save feature is also irritating to say the least.
On the plus side we'd have to acknowledge that the visuals are beautiful. Very nice and atmospheric. The only problems I noticed were that my MSI Afterburner showed thousands of FPS in DirectX 9 mode, even though the game was actually stuttering quite a bit at the highest details with 8x MSAA turned on @ 2560x1440.
The story is interesting and was the only thing that motivated me to keep playing. Unfortunately, it was also fairly confusing at times and pretty weird with that sleeper and some of the supernatural stuff that did not really match with the whole setting very well. It did come together OK in the end, however, and it was fun reading about others' interpretations of the events and the ending on the forums.
On a whole I just can't recommend this game. Maybe when it's on sale for €/$ 4.99 but anything above that and you risk severe disappointment. You can spend probably between 5 and 10+ hours playing the game if you don't know what to do and have to search, pixel hunt and trial&error a lot but if you know what to do then the actual content is only about an hour or two MAX and that's just because -even when sprinting- it will take lots of time to cover the long distances in the game world. Some people might consider the pixel hunting and trial&error fun but to me it was just a waste of time at some point so I admit I used a guide every time when I couldn't figure something out after a few minutes.
A possible sequel needs:
- A proper tutorial (separate from the main game, maybe even just in text form accessible from the main menu)
- Way more gameplay and interaction with the world, NPCs and objects
- A less empty game world where exploration is more rewarding
- Maybe a journal with optional basic hints on how to proceed and maybe with a map, too
- More risk (for the MC to die)
- A save feature - ideally save anytime/anywhere quick saves for people with RL obligations

I think that the atmosphere itself is brilliantly crafted and I would recommend playing it simply to have the experience. Just be prepared... We don't get to escape our experiences in the video game world just because they are not "real" life.

So I picked up HELLDIVERS Deluxe Edition
This game is a twin stick shooter, that focuses on Cooperative gameplay (amazing squad based tactics) but also offers a variety of weapons and perks you can customize your character loadout with. Also the maps are all randomly generated so if it doesnt feel like your doing the same thing over and over. Theres 5 different types of planets. Ice, Snow, Forest, Volcano, and Mega Cities. All of which feel even more unique with the three different alien factions you can encounter. Cyborgs (Think Orks from Warhammer. The like Explosions and Machine guns) Illuminate? (Cant remember their name but their like a Protoss/Eldar hybrid. Emphasis on shields and Beam Weapons) and the Bugs (Zerg/Starship troopers vibe. Scary strong at close quarters and have a rediculous amount of health.)
Despite all the positives the game has a few issues. For one, sometimes you cant control spawning in and will accidentally kill a teammate. In a team you have infinite respawns, but the enemy is aware of you when you drop it can be a bit of a headache. Spawns sometimes fall on important emplacements to complete a mission (the falling objects will kill the mission objective on the ground and you fail that objective.)
The BIG features of this game were the customization characters. The incredible variety. And the heavily advertised friendly fire. I didnt count the friendly fire as an issue because it makes the team work together to prevent team killing. But guaranteed you will die. Random Drop pod, bad airstrike position, or backing up off a cliff, this game will get you. All these things including the friendly fire work SO WELL in unison. Its a fantastic team based shooter. Also this game allows you to connect a controller and offers up to four person coop support.
The most exciting parts of this game, after a long mission, your low on resources and your in the last thirty seconds waiting for the dropship to evacuate your team and pull you out. Depending on the difficulty it can actually be pretty amazing in those final seconds.
The only game this reminds me of is Alien Swarm. And truly this game is everything Alien Swarm wished it could have become. I hope this game gets a massive following and the developers grow this game even more on pc.
HELLDIVERS – yell various patriotic things and woohoo america things. Theres not too many different sayings and it does get a little old after a while. Theres voice commands for those without a mic that allow for easier squad communication.
Combat sounds amazing, miniguns, airstrikes, and alien noises however help you get lost in the games atmosphere.
The graphics are well done. Nothing groundbreaking, but combat looks pleasing and customization is very satisfying. Also the gameworld despite being randomly generated fits together well and almost borrows its look from Diablo 3.
The games story is almost defined by the player, you have to do missions and take sectors of space until you wipe out and alien homeworld or the aliens can launch and offensive on the humans space and if you fail to defend them the aliens retake that part of space.
This game has amazing replay value with the random content and keeps you busy with trying to earn new perks, upgrades, and cosmetics. At least keeps you fairly busy until you hit the games max level of 50.
Overall im VERY pleased with this game. I havent been this excited about a game in a while, and looking forward to DLC and future additional content.

I first played this game at night with the sound turned up. My black cat sitting on my desk, watched as I crawled through black tunnels and stealthily made my way around enemy's. The story griped me as the hours ticked by and the plot became more then what I set out for. As the evening became early morning and my cat long since stalked off to sleep, I prowled the metro in search for the answers I needed to save my people.
I was afraid of every turn I took and jumped at every flickering shadow. The music played a haunting melody that only served to heighten the tension as I sat there in the dark, struggling to go on. I shivered in fear as I moved from tunnel to tunnel, alone with only my thoughts to ward off the terrors the lurked always just out of sight. The few times that I was blessed to have companionship, didn't last long as the evil of the metro always saw fit to take these brave souls away. Leaving me alone, weary, and sad for the loss of such good men.
I knew that my journey would be a lonely one filled with fear as well as terrified excitement. The metro is never a safe place and much of what dwells in its dark places wish only to see you dead. Only your wits, courage, and gun will serve to see you through this hellish landscape of a long forgotten time.
I sit alone in the dark now, trying not to shiver. I listen to the howls as they echo from deeper in the tunnels. I know I have to move but I am so tired..., So cold. They're getting closer, the howling. I ready my rifle and take a firm grip as I was taught so long ago. Is this where my journey ends, after I came so far, is this my time? The flame from my light starts to flicker and die as I prepare myself for the same. After all, it's what they've been waiting for....

Lets start the hate:
The entry cutscene where your ships move to battle should look epic but since the first relaese there was terrible screentearing that completly ruined it and it hasnt been fixed since then.
Your settings dont save, so everytime you enter the game, you have to personalise them again.
The AI allies in the campaign are totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.. and I mean completely, totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. they ram spacerocks and keep it going until they explode, they charge into groups of enemies to pointlessly die and leave you outnumbered and they dont use their faction advantages correctly. (ex: Eldar prince charging into closequarters with an Orc horde)
Balance is almost totally absent at this point with the DLC's (alias pay to win content) even if factions seem specialised and balanced at first you will find the opposite after playing a while.
reason beeing:
- Imperial Navy and other tanky factions are slow, but there are tons of battles (even in the campaing) where you have to destroy enemy flagships or capture data by boarding during the timelimit. Your main Opponent, Chaos, has the second fastest ships in the game so you will find them fleeing into one corner of the map and warping out before you can even get into shooting range. -Bots disrespect the game rules for whatever reason. In skirmish battles, where each player has the same amount of deployement points, bots will sometimes choose the same ships as you while beeing able to bring a few escortships more than possible in addition to their actual troop value.
- Eldar are rediculously underpowered when you try to play them. They are supposed to be the "hit and run" faction, they have no shields but a miss chance based on their speed instead and they can only shoot in front of them. The problem with this is that almost every escort ship in the game is faster than Eldar line ships and will end up chasing them down by simply flying behind them. Eldar in this game have no HP, no shields, no armor, not enoug speed and are overall useless.
- with the introduction of TAO empire trough DLC's the game has changed again. Now orcs aren't the most Op faction anymore. Tao can, similar to the Eldar ony shoot in front of them, with the difference that they are absurdly heavy armored in the front, they have incredible high turning speed so you cant surround them to shoot their weak back, they have incredible high range aswell as the strongest guns and Torpedos that can crossmap you and are the only chasing torpedos in the game plus the most damaging ones. oh and I forgot to mention that they share the longest vision range with chaos, who where originally the sniping faction, only that they had weakspots. Its just abnormal how powerful the Tao faction is, they are basically the paywall solution for people who want to win fights without much stragtegy, diversity or effort.
In general, dont try something interesting like Eldar or any other tactical faction in this game, just play cheesy or pick tanky guys and send them in, the game will do the rest. You could as well be watching a bad action film where the end is predictable from the bginning on.
I highly recommend you buy something else with your money, if you dont know what to do with it then send it to charity organisations for kids with cancer.. cause this game gave some people cancer for sure.

A prime example of what happens when developers are pressured into releasing a game too early!
Easily the most frustrating game I have ever encountered, not because it is difficult to play or not an enjoyable game, but because it is so glaringly obvious that it simply isn't finished!  It should be in beta, ironing out the glitches and responding to testers observations, like "Why do I have a bed if I cannot sleep at night?" (A Mod is available, but shouldn't be needed)
While some on social media and in video reviews slate the game as 'just a "The Martian" game' (Which could be helped by adding a bit of variety to the diet! ( also avaiable in a Mod)) it is close to being a diamond in the coal seam of current games.  The atmosphere is spot on, for the most part it plays very well and it's easy to pick up.  It's also very easy to die.
Multiplayer is another story unfortunately.  The single player "Human missions" pit you against the elements with little equipment and requires you to harvest resources to create items in a small 3D printer.  Use the small 3D printer to make bigger versions and you can craft anything, if you have the resources.
Competetive Multiplayer (which states you are landing on a part of the planet where resources are scarce!) consists of landing on the planet, finding the nearest supply drop which all have a "Creative" printer that requires absolutely no resources at all, so you can make whatever you want unless it's massive, what exactly is the point?  Why fight over resources you don't need anyway?
Co-Op Multiplayer hits the mark better, although the option to begin a game with minimal gear ( Tent, Small Fabricator and enough resources to get the basics made) without the MAV would have been a nice touch for "hardcore" explorers.
I sincerely hope the developers have the will to finish this game and add some polish to some of the mechanics that aren't perfect as yet.  If they do this game will, for some, be one of the best survival games to date.
As it is though there is a lot of pain for the gain.  Please finish this properly Bohemia!!!
Still recommend although with a lot of caveats.

I can't believe that I forgot to write a review about NT° up until now.
That said... Changing this now! This game stuck to me for pretty much 4-5 years, so I might aswell add my few cents to this.
First things first. We're looking at a Source-mod based on the SDK from 2006, so I warn you in advance that it's of course not free from any flaws. Those flaws, so we say, are called the "Authentic NEOTOKYO° Experience" - Last through those, and you are battle-hardened to enjoy this game.
Now, going down to the core. The game itself offers a pretty straight-forward style of gameplay, you boot it up, join a server and play, just like it was with HL 2 Deathmatch back in the day. You join a team, either NSF or Jinrai, which both function the same way, no different weapons or skills, just different skins.
The objective of the game is either to eliminate the enemy team or capture an item called the "Ghost", which functions as a kind of flag to deliver to the enemy's spawn which is also known as your cap-zone. The Ghost allows the holder to see enemies on a range of 45 meters, which means that he can give his team a great advantage by calling out location and range.
Both teams have three classes: Recon, Assault and Support, which obviously have different attributes to them.
Recon - Unlimited sprint, longest cloaking duration, fastest moving speed, Nightvision mode, a remote detpack at 4 points, a low-dmg silenced pistol, a super-jump (Uses "Aux-Power", makes you leap a greater distance), low HP as a trade-off, comes with mostly SMGs early on. Usually recommended to more experienced players.
Assault - Limited sprint, medium cloaking duration, medium moving speed, Motionvision mode, a grenade by default, a semi- or full-auto pistol (can alternate), medium HP, comes with SMGs and ARs early on. It basically is the all-rounder to start with.
Support - No sprint, no cloak, slow moving speed, Thermalvision mode, two smokegrenades by default, a heavy-cal. revolver, high HP + no headshot dmg modifier when hit, comes with medium to heavy weaponary early on. It's beginner-friendly, yet sometimes impractical when you try to retreat.
Having that explained, there's one or two dozen of maps to try out these classes on. Some are community made, some are not - that said, we always encourage mappers to create some of their own battlefields to spice things up, every admin would be open to give it a test run.
As for the gameplay, it feels a little slower than other games, yet is quite fast-paced. There's no iron sights, bunnyhopping is encouraged, you can use E and Q to lean around corners to gain an advantage and like mentioned in the class descriptions, there's also cloaking to gain an advantage over the enemy. To top this off a bit more: When a team is also willing to actively communicate, you can get very good coordinated and tactical play going aswell. This can be enforced by locking down areas, defending the ghost, or using it to gain valuable intel that can win the round.
... That said, don't expect much on a Friday, because that's where the bizzarre side of the game comes out... I speak of experience here, I am part of the problem.
With all the good out of the way, there obviously are flaws, which I hinted at as the first thing in my review. Time to get to those aswell!
The engine: Yes, it's dated. Knowing this, the game won't perform in a way it should at times, also making the game crash on map-change or when joining a server. My advice would be to set the textures to medium, that fixed crashing for me. Besides that, it may also make maps run a bit less fluid than they should. My rig for example should run source-games just fine, but there's two maps that still cause my FPS to slide down by a fair amount. It's overseeable, but not optimal of course.
The gameplay: The game is a rough diamond, so the gameplay is far from perfect. There's things such as the "sprint-bug/no-shooting bug". It's a bug that appears when you reload and then follow up with sprinting right after, causing the weapon to still remain empty until the sprinting has been ended. It doesn't happen often, but it is there. Then there's other bugs like your camera spazzing sometimes when throwing a nade, or your vision tweaking out when scoping in with a sniper. Tabbing out can also be a murderous thing for the game, so beware. And the last bit is that the movement and certain other aspects just are not fully-optimized, so I advise you to go into the game with that mindset.
Team-attacking: It's on. Permanently. There's anti-TK measures in form of plugins, but people yet always try to abuse the idea of being able to kill mates. Though, to cure that warning a little, we have a lot of admins that spread across all current servers, making it an easy problem to deal with. Just.... keep in mind that it might happen, even when it's not unintentional.
That said, I think that sums up the general idea, I personally can say that I love the game to bits ever since I picked it up. Not only that, I also do think that it's the only community that I ever dedicated so much time to. It's a great community to be in, wonderful people and memories to be had. If you want more info on what shenanigans can be discovered behind this game, check out this video, which also comes with a stat-rundown with a few things!
That said... Enjoy the game if you decide to pick it up, I am also open for any sort of questions related to it! Thanks RADI-8 for this rough, yet wonderful gem.

Unlike my other reviews, this one is not going to be a detailed one because just about
and their dog knows how amazing this game is, so instead?
Instead, I'm gonna tell a story.
Once upon a time, a nerdy, white, bespectacled kid with Autism had his parents divorce. The father was a former alcoholic who would (sadly) get a year in jail. Even so, despite his flaws, the son loved his father, and the father was a loving parent when he was around, which was rare as he moved to Boston, Massachusets. But one day, when he was 18-years old, he finally got the opportunity to stay with him in Boston for a week, much to his mother's regret.
So he brought with him his gaming laptop to play his recently-purchased Civilization V, which everybody was gushing over how amazing it was. The boy was playing as Denmark (he loves axes) and he just wrapped up his invasion against India, when his father told the boy to go to bed at 9:00 - yes, even when an adult, he still doesn't mind going to bed early.
But at 2:00 AM, the boy couldn't sleep, so he snuck downstairs and smuggled his gaming laptop upstairs to play more Civilization V. Everything was fine, until suddenly, the boy's father snuck upstairs, clearly hearing everything.
"What are you doing up at
time? It's the middle of the night."
Clearly seeing his disappointment, the boy blushed. "Um... Civilization V?"
Instead of being utterly disappointed, the boy's father laughed - not out of condenscendation, but out of joy.
"Wh-What's so funny?"
"Nothing," The father laughed. "You're exactly like your old man, you know that?"
He took the boy downstairs to his work place, and booted up the computer.
He smiled mischievously at the boy. The computer had Civilization V on it.
"Wanna have some good times with your old man?"
The boy smiled ear-to-ear. "Would I."
For one whole week - and fortuitous timing, since the father was on break - the father and the son played hours upon hours of Civilization V all the way until late in the night for a whole week. Even when the mother had to pick up the son eventually, the week-long fun and 81 hours of gameplay time was far more than enough for the memories to last forever. He knew he wouldn't be able to see his father for a while, but he knew that - despite his flaws, despite his former-alcoholism and arrest - the father would still love the son, and the feeling would always be mutual.

Oh, a note about multiplayer.
The game lets you set an input delay on the online multiplayer lobbey.  When setting this, be sure to set it above the highest ping of your group.  My friend has pretty poor internet and when we kept the input delay low, we would desync a lot.  However, when we set the input delay to 100ms, we had no further problems with desyncing without any noticable delay in the gameplay.
Your milage may vary, but I think a general rule of thumb would be to set the input delay to just over the highest ping of your players.

I've heard SR described as “GTA that doesn't take itself seriously”. I haven't played the previous installments, but if the 4th is any indication, the description is pretty accurate: it's an open world game where you run, drive and fly to participate in various activities that more often than not end up with you being chased by the police – or the setting's local equivalent of it.
In SR4 we assume the role of the president of the United States, who is a superhero at the same time. The game shows exactly how serious it's going to be with an opening sequence where the player character kills a bunch of terrorists, jumps on top of a nuclear warhead, detonates it mid-flight to end up jumping down to the ground and landing right on the presidental chair in the Oval Office. Soon after that the alien invasion begins, and we end up trapped in a computer simulation with all the other humans while our real bodies are locked in red containers full of life supporting fluids. We're soon taught how to bend the rules of the simulation which effectively gives us superpowers, allowing us to fight the oppressors. Sounds familiar?
While the Matrix is easily the most prevalent inspiration for the game, it draws ideas from tons of other works of popular culture, to the point where I'm not sure whether it's meant as a parody or a tribute. One mission will have you crawl through a level disguised as a cardboard box (with the appropiate Metal Gear Solid sound effects), in the other you are put in a 2d side-scrolling beat-em-up, with mechanics about as sophisticated as Franko had (anyone still remember it?). About every other story quest mocks or refers to something, but I haven't found it annoying or obnoxious at any point. The main storyline is quite fun, funny and enjoyable; the only thing that I can pick on in this game is... everything else.
It seems to me that Saints Row IV would be a much better game if it was a bit smaller and more focused. It gives you a massive amount of options to upgrade and customize your cars, which seems like a good thing, except that with your superpowers you run much faster than any vehicle drives, making them pretty much useless. You get a pretty impressive arsenal of weapons, ranging from typical pistols, shotguns and rifles to goofy, (and actually quite hilarious) stuff like a rectal probe, dubstep gun, a black hole generator or a strangely familiar Laser Sword. Almost all of them can be upgraded in weapon stores, but the game is easy enough to beat it entirely with a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat (I didn't actually try, but I did beat a few combat-focused side missions equipped with nothing else but the aforementioned sex toy). The game features a Homies system, where you can either recruit your gangmembers from the street or call them from your phone to join you in battle, but it never seemed necessary, with the superpowers giving you so powerful AoE attacks that 3 NPC shooting their guns look mildly amusing at best. The game gives you a lot of mechanics to use and play with, but it doesn't really capitalize on any of them. It even allows customizable skins on your weapons (presumably to have a potential to crank up some DLC money), which I enabled at the beginning of the game but never even noticed them in my 21 hours of playing it.
The game has a lot of features that see little to no use in it, yet it fills your time with dozens of similar, repetitive minigames, ranging from quite enjoyable (like hacking stores in form of a classic “plumber” game) to straight up annoying (like ragdolling through the streets trying to hurt yourself as much as possible, that being a lot less fun than it possibly sounds like). It seems like for the amount of content and mechanics that the game has, the side missions could be a bit more elaborate and original, rather than being a combination of 10 or so minigames over and over again – to the point where the reasoning of your questgivers literally becomes “I don't want to waste my breath, just go blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, okay?” at some point.
Apart from missions we get the expected open world goodies like collectibles scattered all across the city, a chance to (re)play the minigames that the side quests require you to do, extremely high structures to climb, and of course countless excuses for mayhem and havoc that we all know and love. All that acompanied by 8-ish radio stations, which we can thankfully listen to also when on foot, which is quite useful in a game where cars are mostly decorative. I found the music quite okay, ranging from rock, reggae to some heavier techno. There was nothing like the absurd talk show station you may have liked in GTA, the only ersatz being a clearly stoned announcer in the dubstep-y station. Still, nothing to complain about.
All in all, I quite enjoyed my time with Saints Row IV. While I do think that the huge part of the game is mediocre at best and it'll be better off without it, the main story is pretty solid and quite fun. Being the completionist that I am I couldn't ignore all the sidequests, even after I decided that they're bad and I don't like them, but I can easily recommend picking the game up just to play the story quests. It's nothing special, ambitious or worth replaying, but it does have its memorable moments that still make me giggle inside when I think about them. I'd advise to not bother with sidequests to much, since the rewards for them are negligible at best and their gameplay isn't very fun itself, but the main storyline should give you about 8 hours of fun. A pretty fun game for those evenings when you don't feel like doing anything constructive and want to lay back and relax with something that'll make you smile and rapidly exhale through your nose every now and again.

Despite all of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and the glitches, this game is one of the few games that has this level of character customization. As you play through the game, no matter what you're doing, you're ranking up what the game calls "A.C.E.S.", which unlocks new weapons and equipment, and ranking up your overall level unlocks new clothing and armor items for your character, and even a bunch of real-world accurate camouflage patterns. Eventually you'll even unlock the ability to create your own custom camouflage patterns, so that you can look like a pink and purple tanktop wearing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or spiderman! And that's not all! Not only that, but this game has a campaign that you can play fully co-operatively with a friend, and terrorist hunt mode, a returning mode from previous Rainbow Six games, which allows you and up to three buddies to take on multiplayer maps that are swarming with terrorists, the goal obviously being to eliminate them all. TL;DR: Though it was not as thought provoking or emotionally moving as Gone Home, it is still a rollercoaster ride and kept me glued to my seat until I finished. Grab it when it's on sale.
I have a soft spot for story games such as Dear Esther or Gone Home. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, though very good, has a little more thrill than both of those. The game actually startled me at a few points, but not enough to make me stop playing like Amnesia would. It has a very strong focus on Music and visuals, which are both fantastic. If someone told me the game was a graphical mod of skyrim, I wouldn't have been surprised.
Be prepared to get dropped in with little-to-no handholding, which is intended by the developers. At first I was annoyed as I felt like I had to comb every inch of the sprawling landscape or risk missing an interesting part of the story. I ended up backtracking a huge amount when I realized I missed a large chunk of content. Fear not though, the game will tell you to go back before the end if you have missed content and where to find it.
I eventually enjoyed the lack of handholding. It made the game feel more sincere and left the ending to have a lot of interpretations. Some would call the ending cliched but it still left a lot to think about. There are also a few subtle hints regarding the ending that you can find if you keep your eyes peeled (take a close look around the abandoned train station).

1) No dedicated server option

I'm a huge Mars and space fan.
I've been really happy with Take on Mars, although I did have to push through a few clunky UI challenges and google a few things early on.  But once I got them figured out it has been rewarding, and I do feel like I've accomplished something by surviving from day to day (playing the manned story mission so far).
The graphics are good, although the engine is similar to ARMA and it can therefore be a bit of a beast to run at high frame rates.  Be warned (nVidia 1070, but I can tell it's CPU-bound on my i5-6500).
Some reviewers commented about dying while going up stairs, rocks, etc.  This sometimes happens if you rush up them, and in a bulky spacesuit is probably very realistic!  You will need patience to play this game, as one would need exploring a planet in real life.
Take on Mars is a simulator, and it is the best Mars "experience" I've ever tried.  Very few truly goofy paradigms for the sake of gameplay (although there are a few, but are easy to overlook).  There's also a great ISS scene that is apparently pretty accurate in its layout, and a few lunar missions too.

Take on Mars is a serious simulation of what it would be like to explore mars in real life. And since mars has no magnetic field, you'll need to find shelter from the solar events that saturate the planet in extreme radiation. And you'll need to make your own oxygen and water before your current supplies run out.

Between the hostile environment and equally hostile physics, you'l have a challange in every play session.

Instead, I'm gonna tell a story.
Once upon a time, a nerdy, white, bespectacled kid with Autism had his parents divorce. The father was a former alcoholic who would (sadly) get a year in jail. Even so, despite his flaws, the son loved his father, and the father was a loving parent when he was around, which was rare as he moved to Boston, Massachusets. But one day, when he was 18-years old, he finally got the opportunity to stay with him in Boston for a week, much to his mother's regret.
So he brought with him his gaming laptop to play his recently-purchased Civilization V, which everybody was gushing over how amazing it was. The boy was playing as Denmark (he loves axes) and he just wrapped up his invasion against India, when his father told the boy to go to bed at 9:00 - yes, even when an adult, he still doesn't mind going to bed early.
But at 2:00 AM, the boy couldn't sleep, so he snuck downstairs and smuggled his gaming laptop upstairs to play more Civilization V. Everything was fine, until suddenly, the boy's father snuck upstairs, clearly hearing everything.
"What are you doing up at
time? It's the middle of the night."
Clearly seeing his disappointment, the boy blushed. "Um... Civilization V?"
Instead of being utterly disappointed, the boy's father laughed - not out of condenscendation, but out of joy.
"Wh-What's so funny?"
"Nothing," The father laughed. "You're exactly like your old man, you know that?"
He took the boy downstairs to his work place, and booted up the computer.
He smiled mischievously at the boy. The computer had Civilization V on it.
"Wanna have some good times with your old man?"
The boy smiled ear-to-ear. "Would I."
For one whole week - and fortuitous timing, since the father was on break - the father and the son played hours upon hours of Civilization V all the way until late in the night for a whole week. Even when the mother had to pick up the son eventually, the week-long fun and 81 hours of gameplay time was far more than enough for the memories to last forever. He knew he wouldn't be able to see his father for a while, but he knew that - despite his flaws, despite his former-alcoholism and arrest - the father would still love the son, and the feeling would always be mutual.

I've finally played this now and would perhaps say that I think The Room Two is better in a few ways than the first game! That was a pleasant surprise as while I loved opening catches and manipulating secret compartments on boxes in order to reveal their hidden secrets, the very final block shifting and moving a ball around a maze puzzles of the first game worried me a little in that they felt more like standard puzzles than those that came beforehand. They were not particularly bad, just placed that nagging feeling that the game designers were starting to run dry of novel puzzles at that extremely late stage of the game. So I would not have been too upset if the sequel had continued that trend, but ended up very pleasantly surprised!
It was also nice to find out that the sequel is a direct continuation from the first game as after opening the portal to another dimension Hellraiser-style, we play as the same character exploring strange realms by following in his master's footsteps. Even more than the first game this literalises the spooky and Lovecraftian aspects to all of the box openings (it feels as if this game knows it is working in a darker register than the more enchanted with scientific wonder first game had. Which is appropriate for the second game involving someone now trapped inside a different dimension!) , as now instead of one box opening to reveal another smaller one Russian-dolled inside it, or a single table revealing hidden secrets (which the first game still does the best) the second game has a single room contain multiple different areas that all inter-relate to each other. The backgrounds open up to reveal new elements (particularly in the Egyptian tomb level), or new boxes or treasure chests magically appear once a particular piece of the puzzle is unlocked (the pirate galleon level). There's a great ghost photography automatic typewriting, writing desk with secret compartments, tarot card seance level. And then the final level is a kind of archetypal mad scientist's lab that contains the most elaborate set of workstations and puzzles of them all (including a very Jan Svankmayer-esque segue into collecting various types of insects to replace on a pinboard!), and an amusing ending that literalises the Lovecraftian aspects!
Perhaps the aspect I most liked about The Room Two is that all of the puzzles still felt naturally arising and flowing from one into the other. Both the first game and this one have a wonderful, almost tactile sense of flicking switches, opening cupboards and exploring the wooden surfaces of various pieces of equipment in seach of a hidden catch or rotatable element that will lead onto the next puzzle (yes, there is a moment when you pull a particular book on a bookshelf to open a secret compartment!). And there is never a moment in this second game where I worried that the game designers had run out of ideas that felt as if they were arising from the evocative environments and then had to throw in a standard-issue puzzle instead. There is one extremely short level trying to pulley a boat to shore whilst surrounded by an aquatic tentacle creature that is more of an evocative location approaching the final laboratory level than anything particularly taxing, but I'd rather they did that than trying to pad the level out with shoehorned in puzzles! (And on checking the playtime on Steam, I played for about three and a half hours, the exact time that it took to play the first game, so the sequel does not seem to be cutting corners either)
I think the best compliment I could give this series is that, although I keep going back to The Witness to complete a puzzle or two, I think these games are more evocative, mysterious and entertaining! Now I just have to wait for The Room Three to get ported across from mobile, which should be around 2018! (Apparently the length of time it takes for these games to reach PC is due to the way that they are getting completely re-made for the platform, rather than just being the original mobile game version transferred across)

I'm giving this game a non recommendation.  If you like to play solo, then this game might be fine for you.

Add onto that the fact that each time you desync (once every 10 seconds or even more frequently), a large message pops up and gets in the way of the game.  The desync got so bad that soon we realized we were nowhere near each other.  Yet on our own computers, we were all relatively close.  My friend tossed a grenade that killed another friend.  He said he was alone in a pack of mobs where the guy who died said he was right beside him with no mobs nearby.  Very pooly optimized with 30 fps the max you can get.
Could be a fun time for a couple of dollars but $15.00 is way too scammy.  Got my refund immediately.

This is probably the most interesting game I've picked up on Steam in ages.  I really enjoyed it.  It's very short and I'd have a hard time justifying it's full retail price.  That said, I LOVED it.  Reminds me of a mixture between Myst and a murder mystery.  Very little explanation or hand holding, but the puzzles are not too horribly difficult.
Graphically it's insanely gorgeous.  I LOVED it.  Like a virtual hike through a gorgeous Autumn forest.  Reminds me of the Pacific Northwest.  Just sort of a haunting location and some of the most realistic foliage I've seen.  Seriously hats off to the devs on what they pulled of.  It's magical.
Story wise I was sort of a little disappointed but still more thought provoking than most stuff out there.
I heartily recommend it to anyone that likes thoughtful single player experiences, beautiful nature scenery and murder mysteries.

This game was a surprise.  I hadn't actually heard of it until the day I bought it, and the gameplay trailer hooked me.  The atmosphere is engrossing.   The graphics in tandem with the music are a strong combination, invoking a feeling that I don't really want to leave.  I find myself just idly wandering the terrain, taking in the surroundings.  Vanishing reminds me, after it's fashion, of Shadow of the Colossus.  It has a story to tell, and it does this well, without unnecessary asides, distractions, side quests, or whatever.

The outdoor visuals by the lake are absolutely breathtaking, so much so that I feel a aching to see that kind of landscape for myself. That was the best part of the game for me.
Other than that, I can't say it was really my kind of game. It's certainly different, I'll give it that, and I'm sure lots of people will enjoy it a great deal. But I was expecting a certain kind of story/game, and it ended up being something quite different which turned out not to be something I was after. Vague I know, but I can't really say it properly without giving spoilers. I liked the investigation mechanic but {spoiler}.
Having finished the game, I feel somewhat cheated, which was built up throughout the game by certain recurrances that I can't say here (again due to spoilers).
It's a shame that Steam doesn't allow you to give a review based on a percentage or number of stars, because I'd like to give the game props for its beautiful graphics and bravery in being different. But I think, in terms of it being a game that I did not ultimately enjoy, I am going to have to give it a thumbs down. For me, it was not worth the purchase price, even discounted. And for those that like to know about these things, I finished it in 4 hours of solid play.

Metro 2033 is an awesome game. It has great looking, well optimized graphics, an interesting story, and fun, addicting gameplay. The game can be completed in a short time, but with two different playstyle options, it has replay value too.

This game is a must-buy if you like story driven (the story is from a wonderful novel) post-apocalyptic games (with an added element of mild horror). Plus theres added bonus of the crazy fourth reich (Nazi's) in the tunnels and many other hostilities.
The Library Level is also very iconic - you will never forget it if you play it.
Pros:
*Guns are decent (you can't shoot long range accurately with shotgun for ex + you can modify them with things such as silencer or laser sight which have negative and positive consequences)
*Ammo conservation is important - you can't just blind spray.
*Story is truly immersing.
*Environment and music/ambient sounds are great.
*Stealth system is arguably decent.
Cons:
*Wish it was longer than about 11-12 hours that it takes to finish it.
*Compass is very clumsy takes hours to look at, plus you can by accident light your lighter which is frustrating if you were trying to stealth around.
*Trying to change a gas-mask filter in the middle of an extended combat is annoying as you can't shoot for about 5 seconds as you change it - and if you don't change it you die.
*Not having a manual save is slightly annoying if you urgently have to go somewhere, or as in the librarian level if you want to save every tiny second of progress so as to not repeat it :)
Overall: 9/10 and a must play.

Get the game if you are a Warhammer 40k fan.  If you are not then the game may not be up to your level of understanding.  Those expecting 3d space combat will be disappointed.  But those expecting to fight for the Golden Throne will be happy.
Lore: 10/10 There are lots of tiny details that are well incorporated into the cut scenes and voice-overs.  Right away we are treated to a scene of the main character going through a re-education session from an Inquisitor.  Bombastic speeches filled with hyperbole and religious fanatacism, large pointy hats that would make a North Korean general jealous, ridiculously over the top ship names, and casualty figures (we are told) in the billions the game captures the feel that you are doing something epic.
Game play: At first I was inclined to give it a 6/10 but over time i got to know the individual ships and now rank it a 8/10. Dont just click and expect to go charging in.  Approach from cloud cover, try to cross the naval T, and do not hesitate to send hordes of sacrificial escort vessels to soak up enemy fire.  It is the Imperial way!

An absolute shame as its predecessor was one of the best RTS games ever concieved for the PC.

XCOM is demanding, tedious, and doesn't forgive your mistakes, that goes without saying.
But it's not only about enemies with high stats and HP, no, it's about enemies being equals to you: can be one shot, can make mistakes, can launch grenades....
And I thought, before playing, that this game was only about being on the field with your soldiers (what it's advertised for), but it's so much deeper. You actually need to protect the main countries of your council (or you might loose funds), research alien technologies (to get stronger), spy on corrupted humans (EXALT), etc...
You feel rewarded any mission you finish with all your soldiers alive, and the different levels of difficulty, second waves, and Ironman mode makes that game so much worth it...
Create a squad of all your friends! Chop off their limbs turning them into robotic monstrosities. Just pray that RNGesus allows that 99% shot to connect.

I'm a bit late to the party, but XCOM is still a really good turn-based strategy game. It really makes you stop for a second and weigh up the risk/reward of each play.
At the beginning you're trigger happy and will take any 70% shot that comes your way but in the later stages of the game you can end up losing one of your most valuable soldiers by being impatient and taking unnecessary risks. Sometimes it's better to roll the dice and burst an alien if they pose a very strong immediate threat but against larger groups of enemies you really have to play your cards right to gain the most ground and lose the least amount of assets. And you can tell the entire game is built around punishing reckless decision making. Even if you don't lose anyone, you can have a soldier in the hospital for the next big mission. XCOM is a game that doesn't let up, it can have some insane difficulty spikes but not in a way that feels unfair, moreso as a result of poor decisions previously. Sure you can get RNG crit to death, or you can miss a 92% roll but hey, if it ain't 100% it ain't guaranteed.
It's a really well designed game and Enemy Within is easily one of the most essential DLC packs for any game I've played. I think Firaxis/2K are aware of this because on sale it tends to be the same cost as the complete version of XCOM. If you haven't got XCOM: Enemy Unknown yet then I definitely suggest getting it with Enemy Within. I do find the levels/scenarios to be a bit repetitive but maybe because I'm not bothering with the main quests as much as I should be. Either way it's a great game that I've enjoyed more often than I've found myself frustrated, and I sure have found myself frustrated with it. Oh, if you're wondering - the story is SUPER cliche and the writing is equally corny. If that's a big deal to you then prepare to be disappointed in that regard. You're in it for the gameplay or you're in it for the wrong reasons.

I don't generally write reviews, but the developers deserve all the feedback they can. Jumping into this game, you won't expect much. This game is a roguelike, so death is final. However, there is a twist. Your main HP is linked to your backpack. Once your respawns are up...you will be seeing the ever familiar "Mission Failed!" Fear not though! You get to keep your earnings(Most of them) and upgrade to try again with a better aresenal. Like I said, I normally don't write reviews and this was more of an explanation of what kind of game this is, rather than what I feel about it.

Hive Jump is an interesting mix of some light XCOM base and resource management and co-op platforming that feels like if Metroid hooked up with Risk of Rain.
You're in a universe very reminiscent of Starship Troopers, where alien bugs are invading and you've got to murder them all because as we all know, the only good bug is a dead bug. In the campaign, you are trying to head off the invading wave by fortifying bases and pushing your battle lines forward, until you've completely taken control of a given planet.
The base management portion of Hive Jump is unfortunately super thin. You have a few basic options to spend in-game resources to fortify your lines, then you end your turn and watch some automated firefights take place. You either hold the enemy back or they take your front lines. That's kind of it. This portion of things is pretty boring and uninteresting to me.
The real meat of things is in the combat, where you're invading the randomly generated, multi-level alien hives. These can be played either solo or with a group of up to 3 others. You have a variety of weapons and utility items you can equip, purchase and upgrade and they all play very differently. I had an easier time with some weapons compared to others but that was probably down to my personal taste, rather than balance. The combat is unending and you're going to have to do a lot of crowd control while constantly moving forward. Staying static is not your friend here. The controls are snappy and responsive and combat flows wonderfully.
One of the unique mechanics is how death and respawns are handled. You carry around a backpack with you and when your character dies, the backpack counts down for a few seconds before a new trooper is beamed in. In this time, the backpack can take damage but you have some measure of control over it and as long as it survives, you can respawn troops indefinitely. If it gets destroyed, it's game over. It's an interesting middle ground between an old school lives system and regenerating health and always keeps things tense, even in between lives. One real bummer is that there's no way to quit out of a mission midway and have it save your progress for later. Some of the later campaign levels require a real time commitment and having to set aside that much time in advance is tough for many. Even the ability to back out and return after every mid-boss would be very welcome.
Different hives have different numbers of levels and every 3 or so, you'll have to fight a boss. The bosses are all very different from each other and have totally different strategies to taking them out. The variety is great, though they do get easier once you learn their patterns. There are also challenge rooms peppered throughout the levels that can get you extra bonuses if you complete them but you only get one shot at them and if you die, you don't get to try again.
Outside of the campaign, every mode centres around the side-scrolling combat. There's an arcade mode and Daily, Monthly, Speedrun, Hardcore and Endless challenge modes that can keep you coming back. Every campaign and arcade mission can be played online as well. There's certainly no shortage of replay value here and even the easy campaign difficulty gets challenging later.
Hive Jump looks and sounds great. The pixel art style is sublime and looks great in motion. The chiptune soundtrack can get a bit repetitive at times but also fits the aesthetic well. One major problem is that while solo play is at 60fps, playing online cuts the frame rate down to 30fps. I don't know why this is but for a pixel art game in 2017, this is inexcusable. I'm not a frame rate snob and play lots of games at 30 but being forced to that to play online is not cool. The developers say a patch is coming later that will allow the host to toggle the frame rate but at time of writing, that's not here yet. It's absolutely playable at 30 but if that's a concern to you and you plan to play online, wait for the patch.
Overall, I've enjoyed Hive Jump and plan to keep playing it. I really wish the base management was either deeper or could just be automated and the time commitments that are sometimes needed are difficult for people with busy lives but the core action is great and though I couldn't find anyone online to play with when I had the press build, I'm hoping to get some people at work to buy this so I can play it with them. I can see this being a great co-op experience. If you like shooting a ton of bugs with wacky weapons, definitely give this a shot.

It's great, but it would need some things to be perfect:
1. The ability of repairing vehicles
2. Set more vehicle, like mars planes, shuttles and things like that
3. A manned campign, but sending some vehicles with crew and supplies

So far it's the only game that gives you that
/ Mars-survival-feeling over a whole and complete campaign.
(For this review I played the manned program a second time, half of it in
, and played multiplayer scenarios).
During the campaign you have to fix leaking suits, find/collect supply drops with the truck, set up devices/machines, extract resources, refine chemicals, travel to the MAV, analyze soil samples, build/puzzle 3D-printers,  to – eventually – produce fuel for your ship back to earth. You get to experience the ISS and in flashbacks the Moon too.
The graphics and the atmospheric background music are really nice. The controls could be better/smoother, but you get used to it. The game is a simulation: pitch black night; correct sound (no atmosphere - no sound: well done in the air lock!); or low gravity: no crazy sprinting or driving possible!; not to mention the laborious machinery-based grinding process: electricity, chemistry, potato-horticulture... cool!
Do not expect an action-packed game, or a huge ecosystem of dinosaurs to tame, or hundreds of enemies to kill. You WILL feel cast away and very lonely. It's just you against the odds on a beautiful but hostile and empty planet (similar to "The long dark").
And every now and then, unfortunately, it's you against the physics/collision engine, that can kill you by accident (catapult you/things in the air, or smash your helmet – followed by a quick death). But with wise save-games and experience this can be overcome (single player allows reloading). Btw it adds to the survival setting – catastrophe is just around the corner.
A top-up is VR: you can play TKOM with the Vive and Vorpx. It works nicely, but you need to know the menu/control system, because the inventory-font-size is too small in some cases).
Read some tips and tricks to have an easier stay on Mars (see below).
The game has a bigger potential (multiplayer, mods, and user made scenarios) that is sadly not being exploited much due to slow bug fixing, which disappointed the community, and made it shrink, and the reviews drop. Which is a pity because self sustaining bases are best build with other players.
Similar games are in development / early access. So far TKOM is the most developed and offers the  biggest variety of features and scenarios (editor, user made content). I wish it had a modern engine and a bigger community. This way it could compete easily with the upcoming similar games and could carry itself quite some time into the future, especially with VR.
Some tips and tricks (no spoilers):
* always use multiple savepoints
* do not jump crazy (bunny hoping)  - eventually you will fall on your visor and crack it
* do not be slow: you can run out of food quickly
* nights are fairly long and very dark - use your vehicle lights (there is no time lapse during sleep yet, but announced)
* always stow truck ramps and stair cases before driving (can be ribbed off at rocks)
* even a flat and empty water bag can block your way inside the truck cabin – keep everything tidy and crouch when it happens
* its hard to move inside vehicles while having it parked on a slope
* activate the mission parts to see the waypoints of the supply drops or be a very good navigator instead
* the building system is not as fast as in Ark Survival due to smaller parts and real 3D printing – be patient
* the object snapping works fine and is more accurate but slower in speed – be precise
* resource grinding is much more challenging: think carefully about chemistry and ALL your resources at hand
* never forget your helmet or do not take it off to early inside an airlock/pop tent (yes, it happens to everyone at some point in time)
* plan ahead
* do not forget to play some disco music ;-)
Have fun - be save!

So I've played around with this game alot. While I enjoy, mostly, what exists..I have too many concerns with it.
This game is so far from finished it isn't even funny. Like.. imagine the worst game you can remember playing.. then delete half the code. It's almost *literally* a perfect analogy.
That being said, here is my list:
Pros:
Mars Survival: (If you liked the movie "The Martian" you might like playing this.)
Diverse building/construction capability. There is a lot you can do in the game.
The graphics are not too shabby at all.
It's a game.
It's one *heck* of a way to waste time.
Cons:
- It's 90%+ a rip off of "The Martian". In both, you are named Mark. A Botanist. And you grow potatoes for food. Just for starters.
- In order to grow potatoes.. you need potato seeds... Think about that for a second. Potato seeds. *Hint* Potatoes *are* the seed! So when you are farming.. in this game.. you plant the "Potato Seeds" and grow a potato plant.. Which you can harvest for potato seeds and potatoes. (NOTE: As Vas pointed out.. the potato *isn't* actually the seed. Learn something new every day! Unfortunately however.. that *really* doesn't change anything now does it? This game is still "The Martian" v.01)
- The physics are completely broken. There are things that happen when running wires, or even just laying down in your emergency poptent that can not physically happen, will kill you, and potentially waste hours of your time if you haven't recently saved.
- The graphics engine is one of the worst I have seen in years. The coding of the game causes even my 1080 SLI setup to get so bogged down while I am playing.. That even it can't keep up. How this "developer" managed that.. I don't even know.
- The UI is so painful to use.. you will constantly find yourself yelling at the screen.. after you tried, unsuccessfully, to put something in your inventory several times.. but instead dropped it on the floor... several times. You have to have the pointer in *just* the right spot, or the item in *just* the right position.. or it is either going to go where you don't want it to... Or the item is going to *literally* shoot off like a rocket to parts of Mars yet unknown. Possibly Pluto.
- As you build up your base.. the game becomes so bogged down that the screen has a persistant "shake" when you turn your camera. Build too much (which is something like 20-30 items--impossibly easy to do) and it happens, and only gets worse.
-Build too much (40-50+ items) and the game starts to slow down.. Allowing you to do slow motion Moon-Jumping... because the game is now running at a fraction of it's normal speed.
-The Narration is garbage. The voice actor will eventually make you want to deck the crap out of him--Because he is an idiot. You can tell they watched the movie "The Martian" too much, and tried to think of good dialog to replace it and do the exact same thing... And could not have done a worse job.
-You build in this game using a 3d printer to build everything. Clothing. Glass. Computers. Wires. Complex Refineries. The developer apparently doesn't understand 3d printers.
-Electrical cables are alive. They do not just lay down. They squirm and/or float up into the air like earthworms in pain. It is a *painful* eyesore when trying to build a cool base.. and the wires float up, around, and other insanity.. making your base look like cancer.
-So very much more.. I can't even begin to remember it all. You have to just learn to ignore everything about this game.. in order to just play it, let alone like it.
-ET for the NES was better. This alone speaks volumes.
I will update this if I think of anything I've forgotten. Do yourself a favor. Don't buy it. Take an intro to C/C++ college class.. and I guarentee you that within a year.. You can program something better.
Yeah.. that's not true. But the sad part is... it *almost* is.

Battlefleet Gothic Armada offers a fun singleplayer experience with a decent amount of replayability. Multiplayer's depopulated, and split between two gamemodes, but there's still some gameplay there if you're patient and play at the right times. Best recommendation I can give is to say: Buy if you're happy with single-player, pass if you're looking to all multiplayer all the time.
It's essentially a finished game, imperfect but still fun. The ships are pretty, and the sound effects meaty. UI/UX and controls are actually really solid. There's a well-built core in this game, even if the content around it has some bumps.
The campaign only has the Imperial Navy as a playable faction, and is told through cutscenes and unique storyline-specific battles. you're given a kind of sector map and can pick which battles you want to fight, which may or may not advance the story. Losing a story mission doesn't necessarily lose the campaign, the story can continue- but it often has consequences later on.
Skirmish (and to an extent campaign) don't let you choose what match type you're going into, but offer persistent fleets that you level up and build out over time. I know that bothered some people, but I liked it, it felt a little bit like a randomly generated campaign and creating different builds gave a lot of replayability. There's also a custom option that lets you choose the hostile faction and game mode, for those that are interested, but I can't speak to it as it never really used it. Once you fully level a fleet in skirmish, you can turn on elite mode, which gives you special battles of escalating difficulties and occasionally unique enemy ship types.
This is certainly the sort of game we don't get very often. The simplest thing I can say is that it's an experience that had me playing 'just one more match' quite a lot.

If I have to categorize this game I'd say this is a lovecraftian game, it's a detective story with paranormal and horror features all perfectly encased in the most beautiful and realistic environment ever seen in a videogame, not to mention the absolutely perfect music that will give you goose bumps.
***GAMEPLAY 8/10: Investigative, slow paced. You won't be running around guns blazing in this game, you have to look for hints or you'll be missing something for sure. You can complete everything or nothing in any order. You won't see any kind of log book, map or quest marker. I really liked it, but unfortunately the game is a bit too short to enjoy the investigative experience. Another great thing about the gameplay is that you will never experience any interruption because the game needs to load areas, you start from the beginning and reach the end in one single walk. This is probably the reason why this game is so short, a longer and a bigger game environment might have required a loading screen or two.
***STORY 8/10: That's all this game is about, story. As you are told at the beginning of the game "This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand". Step by step you'll discover the truth about the mysterious events that happened in Red Creek Valley until you reach the end where the ultimate truth will be revealed. I can't tell anything without spoiling something, so I'll just say it's really enjoyable.
***GRAPHICS 10/10: I have never, NEVER, seen such beautiful environment. I grew up near the Alps and I can see that exact scenery in this game; rocks, trees, bushes, and even the undergrowth look absolutely real. The textures are high quality photos of actual, real life environment. I suggest you read this to learn more about this spectacular creation.

***SOUND 9/10: Beautiful music completes the game, it goes hand in hand with the environment. I could stay hours looking at the landscape listening to the music... and maybe i did.
Overall score 9/10
Grab it when it's around 10€, you won't regret it.

The Astronauts have built a gorgeous, unsettling world to explore.  The atmosphere, aided by the sound and music design and the minimal interface, is engrossing and lingers with you (with the possible exception of the voice acting, which is - perhaps intentionally - less than completely convincing).
The underlying plot is nothing ground-breaking, but it unfolds in sublime ways with twist(s) that never feel insulting to the player.  There is always a feeling of more stories, more mysteries, more history shimmering at the periphery.  All in all, I would gladly have spent two or three times as long in that world if there had been the content to support it -- one or two more puzzles (or perhaps just more depth to the existing ones) might have better rounded out the already wonderful experience.
