Overall a great game that I would reccomend to any puzzle loving explorer.
Pros:
Absolutly beautiful - I never got bored with running around aimlessly when I got stuck because there was so much to look at.
Interesting puzzle mechanics - The main puzzles were fun since you not only had to find/move objects but then decide the order of events. The game also mixes in other puzzles like having to remember the layout of house as you pass through portals, figuring out the correct letters of a name to unlock a door by running around and inspecting dead bodies while avoiding a creepy zombie guy.
Engaging story - You get to see things from the view point of Ethans stories as well as the reality of what inspired the boy to write the stories to begin with. It has a very dark undertone but fits with the vast open world. The ending was sad but very touching.
Music - very soothing at times but creepy at others. All the tracks fit their respective events/areas.
Acheivements - From what I've read the developers were against putting in acheievments before? Not sure why considering I found them helpful. I don't really like the idea of getting all the way to the end just to find out you missed a ton of events that you needed to trigger. So they helped motivate me to explore more and look more carefully. Plus there were a few that made me explore and try doing random things that I wouldn't have normally done - like The Tunnel
Cons:
Buggy - very very buggy. The game froze on me twice when I accidently double clicked while inspecting an item/body. I had to quit and go back into the game after door to the building with the dam pumps wouldn't open (with me stuck inside.) Speaking of quitting to restart - because there is not save option you loose any progress if the game doesn't auto save. This wouldn't be so much of an issue if when you quit the game didn't actually reset. I ended up back near the beginning a couple of times after dealing with the game freezing or bugging out and was very confused when everything I had done in previous puzzles was reset. Also, if you didn't ride the elevator up from the lower area then you'll have to run through the mines all over again to get back down.
A slow-paced, exploration adventure game, with great graphics and a beautiful story.

Beautifully written adventure, with plenty of intrigue, a great atmosphere, and stunning visuals. The pacing feels just right, and it's a real pleasure to play. Genuinely one of the best games I've played in a long time.

Full Review:
Personally I really enjoyed this game. The story is rather bland, with mostly forgetable characters. But, the gameplay is truly this game's strongest aspect. The combat is great. You can really feel every hit as you are smashing about zombie brains. The human enemies use better tactics, such and dodging and actually trying to survive. My favorite part of the gameplay is actually the parkour. It is simply incredible. You will feel very slow and sluggish in the beginning. barely being able to swing a hammer a couple of times before becoming exhausted and maybe running 100 feet. But as the game goes on you will become a freaking ninja god zooming around the map with a grappling hook, jumping off of buildings and drop kicking everything.
The exspansion has a much better story than the main game, but I didn't like the buggy part of it. My favorite part of the game is the parkour and it is greatly limited while in the countryside, the location of The Following exspansion. I prefer the main game's maps.
All in all this game is great, with good and varied enemy types, amazing gameplay and a excellent co-op and pvp mode.
8/10, a good buy even without a sale.

I'm posting the same review for The Room and The Room Two, since I feel the same way about both...
I was expecting a 'room escape' game, and although I suppose it does fall into that category, it feels much more like a puzzle game with escape tropes mixed in - but it actually makes for a better game than most room escapes!
I think I purchased them for something like £3.99 each. They're well worth that and if they come up in a sale then you'd be missing out if you didn't grab them. Highly recommended!
Pros:
- Several rooms, lots of puzzles in each.
- Brilliant interaction mechanisms (pulling, turning, etc. - all new to me in this type of game!)
- Clever feature that adds an additional dimension to puzzle seeking and solving (I'm being deliberately vague - it arises very early on, but I don't want to spoil it for you!)
- Although it's linear in progression from room to room, there is a lot of back-and-forth with the puzzles themselves, which makes it more challenging and fun.
- Tiered and non-intrusive hint system.
- Non-puzzle story elements that are intriguing.
- Much longer than some 'short' puzzle games such as Tiny Bang Story, but see corresponding Con.
- Great visuals and scene changes.
- Beautiful but non-distracting background music.
Cons:
- The story is hard to follow, but this didn't matter too much to me (and I love story).
- There are the odd frustrating moments where you have no idea what to do, which is annoying in itself, and there are some puzzles which seem very easy - this leaves it feeling a little imbalanced.
- Top-level hints are vague, which is sometimes good but in this case gets annoying, since you're most likely to use them in the aforementioned moments of bafflement.
- Sometimes it feels that the hints take too long to trigger.
- Not immensely long - I completed it in 3.7 hours and I'm not a fast player. But perhaps I would have become bored if they were longer, who knows.

Hive Jump is a retro-styled run-and-gun, crowd-slaughter game. Humanity is at war with the Ordovician bug menace, an interstellar, extraterrastrial menace that is threatening humanity's existence by destroying their colonies amongst the stars. The only way to effectively deal with concentrations of enemy troops, hives, is by the JUMP (Justified Use of Military Power) Corps dropping directly into a hive, fighting their way to the quees, and nuking the place. JUMPers are not expected to survive, and neither are you.
You WILL die in this game. Again and again. But that's part of the gameplay - when a JUMPer dies, it's not game over - the person merely has to wait a few seconds before reinforcements beam in. The game only results in a game over when the Transponder Backpack, the thing that allows reinforcements to beam in, is destroyed - it can be knocked off and made vulnerable when the carrier dies, or from a few environmental/enemy effects.
All in all, the game is a great time. There's plenty of weapons to choose from (from your standard assault rifle and shotgun, to a plasma ball launcher, rocket launcher, poison gas, flamethrower, and a random effects gun), grenades to use, and utilities (shields, turrets, and lasers, oh my!) to master. Each run is randomly generated, so you almost never get the same level layout.
Bosses are nicely varied in both mechanics and designed, and all are very deadly, being able to murder you in under a second if you're not careful.
PROS:
-Game looks great
-Sounds are very well-done
-Gunplay is fun and exciting - you can aim in all directions, shoot in all of them, and enemies explode into goop when they die, which you can collect and use to upgrade / purchase weaponry.
-Bosses! Challenging even in a group, and always a sight to behold.
-Weaponry is varied with each one providing something for a team or solo.
-Utilities are pretty useful - as such, the name. No forgetting about your gear in this game.
-Grenades, while limited, are a big help. Makes you consider what you're doing with these (friendly-fire enabled) weapons rather than just chucking them everywhere.
CONS:
-Gun sounds are lackluster for the bullet guns. The assault rifle sounds like I'm shooting wet farts.
-Certain things can get very annoying - the enemies hiding under the ground, that are extremely hard to see unless you're scanning every section of the ground, are invincible to everything except explosives, and will instantly kill anyone who walks over them with a short cooldown after they do so (Overshield will protect against instant death when it's charged).
-Bosses are endemic to certain environments - you always know what boss you'll get depending on the "biome" of the hive you're currently in. Understandable lore-wise and even planning-wise, but always knowing what you're going to fight can reduce the impact a lot.
OVERALL
If you're looking for a fun game to play with friends, this game is it. It's an absolute blast. Not as good solo (things like ambushes and bosses are quite clearly balanced for multiple players), but still excellent.
I give this game a 9/10.

That said, I've noticed a trend of these strategy games that use a full RNG instead of the native dice probabilities at work in their original versions.  X-Com, for instance, had a great reboot because the probability system was always a percentile curve.  Going back to battlefleet gothic, damage is unnecessarily inflated from single digits into triple digits- WHY.  Taking 3 points and turning it into 75 is inflating the granularity by a factor of 25 for absolutely no reason, are we going to have things that do single-digit damage values under the new system? for what reason is that even desirable outside of low-key trickle damage toxin effects?  BFG isn't about trickle-effects, it's about hammer-blows and massed barrages regardless of the race.
Torpedoes spread too much, I miss the classic wall of warheads you got in the tabletop incarnation and, worse, there's no firing mode for squadrons, micro-managing a cobra squadron to launch a massed wave of torpedoes is all but impossible anywhere outside the opening phase of a skirmish and since the torpedoes are all launched independantly, there's little use to all that effort.  Nova Cannons are, however spot-on in feel, they got that bit right.  Commands are... I understand sharing the timers on them, but good lord, they're almost useless for the length of that timer- I just keep my ships locked into 'Lock-On' or, if a carrier, 'Reload' and forget about microing them.  Speaking of carriers, useless, useless, boarding actions are more valuable and easier to manage and have faster results- another departure from the tabletop I don't like, the timers prevent getting all your ordnanace on the field as rapidly as you could orgininally, instead you have piecemeal deployment having to be managed between role and target alongside timing issues.
Back to arbitrarily skewed values, Armor Soak is a 25/50/75 scale against the d6 system which would work out to 50/67/84 under a percentile RNG- that's right, despite damage scaling up numerically and ordnance scaling back damage, the DPS on a macrocannon is king because armor was scaled down simplistically- defeating the charm of lances being your anti-armor option
When I play for fun, my battlegroups run themselves for the most part, monotasking MC broadsides with nova cannons dropping potshots in support, nothing else is worthwhile for the amount of effort required compared to "Imperial Easy Mode".  The core mechanic was fiddled with and broken causing everything that isn't the lazy answer to be too much work to be fun.
Lastly, Eldar are a joke, the level of micro they require combined with their fragility, while making them an 'expert race' that's nigh impossible to enjoy casually- actually, everything but Imperial Fleets feel like expert races and none of them fun- not even Ork "Kustomisation"
I recommend this game only to fans of the woefully undersupported boardgame who want some nostalgia and Imperium Stronk, God is a Man feels- everyone else has many other options for space combat sims that are so much better.

This game is on the fast track to being a classic.  It's starting to show it's age a bit now as it is several years old.  However, in spite of the aging graphics, this is one of the best tactical shooters on the market, and can go toe to toe with any of todays tactical shooters.  Character customization? Check. Loadout customization? Check. Weapon customization? Check.  Reasonably smart AI squadmates? Check. Co-op? Check. I could go on, but the long and short of it is, that there's just not much to dislike here.  The controls are decent, the handling is still exquisite, the character movement feels a little old (to be expected), and the graphics don't hinder things, but definitely show their age.  There is a decently lengthy campaign playable in solo or co-op format.  In the campaign the host (or solo player) gets control of two AI squadmates.  They aren't as smart as you might want but they're far from stupid.  You can stack them against doors (for breaching), have them hold position, follow, regroup, go quiet (stealth), or weapons hot.  You can have them rez each other, and they're usually pretty good about rezing you in co-op (in solo you can't be rezzed).
There's also a terrorist hunt mode that features randomly spawned terrorists and generally functions as a hoard/survival mode.
If you "must" have top tier modern graphics you may want to looks elsewhere. No 4k or fancy lighting here.  The models aren't terrible but as I mentioned above, it's clear that the game is several years old.

XCOM is the reimagining of a classic, adapted to the modern times both graphically and on design/mechanics.
I remember playing UFO back in the nineties and the tense music still haunts me to this day. Despite this, I still fondly remember playing it and spending countless nights trying to outsmart the aliens and eventually repel their invasion of Earth. XCOM brings that same formula to the 21st century, updating graphics and streamlining the gameplay, allowing for faster, less onerous, gametime. This isn't necessarily saying the game has been dumbed down, although it might seem easier to veterans of UFO or the TB games of 15 years ago. The game is still punishing enough to be a challenge without being annoyingly difficult to the point you just give up.
Highly recommended, even 5 years after its release.
P.S. The game has also a strong modding community, which allows for longer a longer lifetime and a good way to change the gameplay to your tastes.

If I had a dollar for every night I've stayed up way too late trying to get a mission *just* right...  I'd have enough to buy XCOM 2 at full price, in which case I'll probably have to add this review to that game as well.
In all seriousness - this is an amazingly fun game to play, for a short time (*snort*) or for a multi-hour marathon of alien-slaying, research-funding, base-building goodness.  The story is whacky, the graphics are pretty good, the voice acting is top-notch (despite some of the cheesy dialogue they wrote).

The game is well designed and provides a wonderful top down squad based strategy experience. You will become attached to your soldiers as they complete missions and rise through the ranks of the increasingly powerful XCOM project. You can research new armors and weapons for your soldiers to keep them alive in the late game as your enemies will not wait for you to be ready to face their most elite soldiers. The game creates feelings of tension and dread as your soldiers become wounded or even die, never to return to the battlefield as each death is permanent. The story is fun as well as engaging and will drive you forward as you attempt to deal with the alien threat to Earth. If you are a fan of the Sci-Fi genre of video games and you do not yet own this one, then I recommend it heartily. If you have no inclination towards squad based tactics or strategy games in general, then don't worry about it, as this game will not suit you. Overall I believe XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a wonderful strategy game and an excellent Sci-Fi title that really provides a great example of the best the genre can offer.

Turn-based tactical game where you control and orginization responsible for defending Earth from seemingly never-ending alien attacks. The game has little-to-no room for error resulting in a very stressful experience, especially for the completionist who wants to play flawlessly and save the world with 100% efficiency—it is not going to happen. I can definitely see the appeal here, but it is sadly not for me.
For me it is a great game: plenty of fun and a good difficulty. If you like of the genre (as stated in the tags), play it.

The TL;DR version: Buy with Enemy Within DLC which fixes all the bugs and glitches, plus adds more variety and addresses many of my complaints.
-It offers something for a wide range of players. Like RPGs? This has RPG qualities. Like tabletop wargames? This game has that type of a feel to it. Like strategy and tactics? Like micromanaging without getting too overwhelmed by the details? This game has it.
-The Combat system is fairly refined. There is both simplification (take only two actions) and variety (each class has its abilities).
-Many of the maps are well done in terms of mechanics (elevation, cover, size, etc.)
-Some of the missions offer variety (escort VIP, rescue civilians, capture alien, bug hunt, etc.)
-The graphics on the maps are pretty good with sometimes small details like birds that spook on your approach, some leaves occasionally blowing in the wind, water running along the street.
-The maps sometimes have a sameness to them and aren't always representative of their locations. If I'm on a mission to Japan then where are the cherry blossoms, the Buddhist temples, and the Japanese arches? Europe has a lot of old city squares with Medieval, Gothic or Renaissance architecture. It maybe cliché, but I was in Russia and there was no snow. The whiteness would have broken up the constant nighttime fog of war gloom. There is a lack of distinctiveness which is not a negative by itself, but neither is it a positive.
-For a game with RPG elements it’s lacking in story. Researching tech, building facilities, recovering alien tech, fighting the enemy is not a story. They are just missions and goals. At the very least there could be some drama. Have NPCs like lead Scientist and Engineer bicker a little. Its not a negative, but something of a missed opportunity.
There was way too many glitches and bugs. I have a fairly big list, but I wont mention them all just a few.
-There’s something screwed up with the line of sight in the game. Sometimes both PCs and enemies seem to be able to see around corners they shouldn’t be able to. Other times it seems that if the PC “saw” the alien before they moved out of sight and behind full cover they will register as being able to be hit. I got fooled a few times by having 80-90% to hit chances at what seemed like shooting thru a wall. I thought maybe the wall was destructible and that’s why, but no the wall did not break and no hit on the alien.
-Sometimes the issue is that the cover continues to count even after its gone. In one memorable encounter I blew away all the shrubbery and trees that had been providing the aliens “cover”. However none of the characters could see them or shoot them even with the arc tool telling them the aliens were there nor after PCs moving closer. The arc tool knew aliens were there but still wouldn’t fire. Oh, joy.
-Had aliens go invisible in front of my unit a few times. Only after PCs moved did the aliens become visible, but still couldn't shoot them (even when standing in front of them). It was only on the aliens next turn did everything go back to normal.

First off let me state that I'm not the type of person to say "I told you so".
But during this game's time in EA I kept stressing the fact that Bohemia Interactive missed several deadlines that they themselves assigned; even making a
on the Discussions board and leaving a
to warn people about what to expect. The responses I'd receive were in the field of, "It's Alpha just wait it'll be great!"
Well now after several delays we're here and out of EA and while this game is an interesting concept it handles like hot garbage. Bugs bugs and more bugs. The controls are awful and getting anything built of worth is a slog through sticky muck.
I enjoyed the concept of the single player campaign/story they added (ignoring that it mirrored the Martian almost completely, cause original story design is hard), but my enjoyment was hard fought after dying when I tried to lay down in the Poptent my first night, dying when I sat down in the Cargo Truck, dying when a canister I dropped into a cargo box ricocheted and slammed into my head (that was pretty funny despite the auto save being almost an hour old), and the worst of them all, me eating one of the ration packs erasing the progress I had on a previously completed objective making it impossible for me to actually finish the story. On the subject of Multiplayer, why in the world does this game lack the ability to host Dedicated Servers? The Peer-2-Peer that they have in place now is god awful. I guess I can hope that eventually they’ll address this issue and release dedicated server files, but I’m not expecting much.
So to wrap this up after all the delays and all the “It’ll be great” fan service what we’re left with is a game that feels unfinished and an overall sense that BI didn’t have the time to sit down and actually test their game from a playability standpoint. I’d say avoid at all costs unless it’s on sale for $5 and you really enjoy the concept of space games, even if this one explicitly does a bad job at most everything.

When I originally played Metro 2033 I lasted for a solid 3-4 hours of pure gameplay before I put it down. I have never been a fan of survival horror games and have tried my best to avoid them. However I grabbed the Metro Redux pack in hope of finishing what I put down ages ago, and honestly I have no regrets.
Metro 2033 is more than just a FPS Game, It’s horror survival experience that does an amazing job of immersing you within the world created. The most memorable thing of Metro 2033 Redux is the upgrade of atmosphere and environments you come across compared to the original game itself. Every place in this game has an outstanding amount of detail, the water drops that run down your mask or even the fog/mist that covers the air when you turn your flash light on. This game prides itself on It’s presentation, and it’s this aspect of the game that made me enjoy it so much.
You play as Artyom, a citizen in a ruined world that by chance is tasked with delivering a message to another station. The Metro 2033 Redux world is unique, after a nuclear incident people are forced into the Metro tunnels as their only way of survival. Each station within the underground city of Moscow serves as a different city/community. Getting from one station to another can become a lot more complicated than expected. This is your standard linear first-person shooter, but the mechanics behind some of the gameplay is intriguing and memorable. There are pressurized guns which you have to reload and pump in order for it to work, there are radiation zones in which you are required to wear a gas mask which means you also have to change the filters within these masks quite regularly and also the actual currency for the game is bullets. These are small things within Metro 2033 Redux but they play such a huge role in making the gameplay all the more fitting within the environment.
From the supernatural beings, to the creatures that lie within the tunnels, each place is more dangerous than the previous, not even man is your friend in this game. Metro 2033 Redux is an unforgiving experience that looks to immerse you in the post-apocalyptic ruins of a Metro system, and the story of a man with no purpose but an opportunity to reclaim the world there once was. There can be times where this game can feel quite linear, and the character development isn’t the greatest but the atmosphere and soundtrack makes up for everything by giving us an intense and cruel world where not even a fully loaded gun can save you.

Hi everyone,
I just finished my first playthrough. After all I have some mixed feelings. Dev's asked for a comment so here you'll get. A possible buyer might skip most parts, as they're long and boring ;)
result:
A very nice game. Some flaws in gameplay, which are settled by atmosphere. When on sale you shouldn't consider twice! Buying at fullprice wouldn't probably be your worst mistake in life.
Contra:
-Greatest flaw in my opinion is the control. I played with pc-mouse.
I got stuck in a few hotspot notivications, because I used right klick out of reflex to quit, countless times I steped back to a previous perspektive because of reflexive use of right klick, and so on. I like the mechanic to manually switch every lever, crank, etc. BUT: circular movements are very painfull. Worst moment was the safe at the seance. I'd loved to see a "use right-klick for look around" button in the options menu would be worth 1 to 2 stars ;)
-Difficulty:
At the beginning the puzzles are possible a bit too easy. But that would be fine. Later on the puzzles mostly don't get much harder, but more abstract. Way too often I felt tempted just to click and see what might happen, than to think of a next step. Too many solutions were hidden hotspots without a clue leading towards it. Maybe just 2-3 times I actually thought "OK, I knew about this lock, mechanic, key, but I forgott." The question if and where to change the tables left  mostly unanswered.
Pro:
- Grafics:
It's not a Bottlefield 1, but looks perfectly nice for a puzzle-adventure. I saw what I had to see (buttons, switches, etc.) I didn't saw what I shouldn't (secrects, bugs, too much pixels). I got pretty fast deep in the atmosphere of the game. Maybe a bit adjusting of the flashing symbol would be nice. The first time it was quite perfekt, but I was either missing a link to my looking around, nor was it shown long enough to actually tell my what I was searching for. But it flashed often enough to interrupt my search a bit.
-Puzzles:
Maybe I'm totaly wrong, but the fact that I'm thinking about it now, tells me to add this point on my list. Even if you have to do some same puzzles (like rotating your view to get 3d lines to a picture), there is a good variation. I never felt like repeating the same puzzle over and over again, and when I got an equal feeling it was more like "Oh, I know the way to fix this, but I have to adapt" or there was a chain of events which justifices a repeating puzzle (like the mirrors in the lab).
- Atmosphere:
Nice and dense. Everything done right from my point of view.
I felt close to playing a shortstory of H.P. Lovecraft. Lot's of parallels of charakter-knowlege, story / background advises, locations, presentation of the monster and overall mystic worldview.
Constant reminder:

He knows where the Old Ones broke through of old, and where They shall break through again. I previously enjoyed The Room, so I picked up The Room 2 on the Steam Halloween sale. It is what you want from a sequel: more of the same but better. In this case, we are less confined to a puzzle box and instead get to see a variety of puzzle rooms (or is it the same room across several dimensions?). More puzzles, more steampunkish mechanical boxes that whirl, better graphics and art, creepy settings for Halloween. Recommended.
The biggest improvement from the original is the expanded scope. You get puzzle boxes, but you get a seance room, a laboratory, a fallen temple, and more. It’s good. The puzzles are mostly fun, and there is joy in watching it all come together, watching the completed device whir. The use of the eyepiece is significantly improved, with visual indicators that you might want to try it out rather than randomly needing to double-check everything, and the places where you need the eyepiece are more intuitive. The shifting camera does a good job of directing your attention towards the next step.
The flaws of the game remain the same, more or less the flaws of this type of game. Sometimes that shifting attention feels like a trail of breadcrumbs you are following, a very visual non-novel, particularly at the beginning when there are fewer moving pieces (less so by the final room). Sometimes the game operates on old school adventure game logic, i.e. arbitrariness that might have made sense to the designer. Why does putting X in Y make Z open? Why is there a fuse in there? Just keep playing the game, and the illogic is less severe and less common than in the previous game, although some of that might be having learned how the developers think after playing through the first game. The settings of the various rooms lack a unifying theme other than “A.S. was here,” but they are rather nice rooms with variations on “creepy.”
The puzzles are better, the settings are better, the graphics are better. If you liked The Room, you will like The Room 2. If you almost liked The Room, you will probably actually like The Room 2. The game is short, but it is longer than a movie, more interactive, and far cheaper, even before the Halloween sale.

Hive Jump is like Contra had a baby with Metroid, but the Dad was actually Usain Bolt.
The gameplay is fun, fast, and frenetic, but some nicely implemented mechanics keep it from being overwhelming. The current mode available, Arcade, plays like a rogue-like, with death ending your run, but any goo (money) earned can be spent toward various unlocks for your next run. The action is further tempermented by the ability to use a jetpack after you initial jump, so you can maintain some distance from the bugs before being overwhelmed.
I think the best mechanic for this game is that you can die as much as you want. Each death simply results in a new clone being teleported to your location via a backpack that you carry around. When you die, that backpack is open to attacks from the bugs though, and when it's gone that's game over.
Overall, what's here is great, and I'm really looking forward to seeing what they do with the full campaign mode. I highly, highly recommend it with some buddies. It's one of the few good games with honest to god couch co op, and it works really well.

The Asskickers is a beat em up. I love beat em ups. Um, this one has a few problems.
1.) You often clip through the environment, or your character and the enemy characters teleport
2.) Dreadfully short, lacks the replay value of other games like it
3.) One of the most important things in a beat em up is being able to quickly turn and deliver a blow to an enemy behind you. Instead of turning instantly, the character has a drawn out animation to turn, and if you press punch before he's turned fully, he performs a back attack. This might not be so bad, if the back attacks actually hit the enemies.
One and two may not sound so bad, depending on how starved you are for another beat em up to play.  Number 3 is the big killer, but if you can work past that, there are some positives. Namely, the design. Like a lot of older side-scrolling beat em ups, Asskickers likes to introduce new enemies and gimmicks each stage. In one stage you're on top of a train dodging signs and bars, on another you're hiding from searchlights, and so on. The bosses are also very gimmick focused, probably because the actual combat is not robust enough to support much more.
The enemy design is decent. The most basic goons walk into your punches, but later enemies require precise timing and frequent use of your special attacks. There's really nothing particularly special here, and beat em ups made over a decade prior have done much better.
The humor, which was probably a big draw, is just generic "hurr durr corporations are evil", to the point where one of the enemies is a teleporting yuppie. The game has a few positives going for it, but no, please don't.

I can't, in good conscience, recommend this game. I know that the time on record reflects a very short period of time with the game play, but given the mechanics and what I did endure, I honestly couldn't tolerate any more. I was hoping it would be a fun side-scrolling beat 'em up game similar to Streets of Rage which, in all fairness, "looks" to be that way. The premise is the same, the style and design all seem to mirror similar titles, but the game mechanics are just off. The combat isn't fluid, combos are somewhat frustrating to pull off, and if you're not doing combos or jump attacks, your character's attack combos are non-existent. Basic attacks are limited to a single punch, there's no basic strike fluidity.
Enemies are significantly faster than you too, so it's always a matter of chasing them around on screen while they stay just out of range and then resolving to just wait for their attack animation before you can hope to get a strike in.
All-in-all, it seems like a very hastily put-together flash game. I'm quite disappointed with the purchase.

XCOM is a franchise I hadn't thought about picking up. I didn't even know what it was up until I saw it on sale for around £5 with all of the DLC. I feel stupid for not picking this series up earlier.
First of all. This game feels great to play. The choices that matter, which research you do and what you build, but especially in the heat of battle. The base game has 4 classes. These classes being Assault, Sniper, Heavy and Support. Each of these roles play an important part in your team build, with you relying on your Sniper for most shots due to the high accuracy and your Heavy being the one who can take a FEW hits. I emphasise few because even in situations where some aliens wouldn't normally kill a heavy, a random critical can happen or a well worked flank. It really adds an extra layer of surprise and tactics. The feeling of fear when you realise you've put one of your soldiers in a bad situation is immense, and when a character dies, let's just say you'll feel a little empty for the next couple of missions.
The character customization in this game is limited but still good. You can choose from 4 different races, around 10 different voices, over 30 hairstyles/helmets, 32 colours of armour etc. So it may not be on par with XCOM 2, but you can still create some interesting and enjoyable characters.
The Enemies in XCOM Enemy Within are tough to begin with but do feel a lot weaker once you have experienced soldiers. I have lost many a Sergeant and even Majors to an enemy I took lightly.
The game to me is very worth it, if you can't run XCOM 2, or want to try a cheaper version first (especially with this Autumn/Fall Sale :)!!!). So don't miss the oppurtunity to get this game. The World Needs You, Commander!

XCOM: Enemy Unknown was a game that I never knew I was craving for until I found it. It is one of the best strategy games I have ever experienced. It mixes fast-paced turn-based combat segments with slow-paced planning-focused strategy segments so that at every moment you are making decisions and either increasing or decreasing your odds of success. Even without expansions and mods it's a stellar experience and those additional features make it even better.
The only downside that I can think of is that the multiplayer feature has always been and probably always will be dead. But if a shoehorned feature for marketing doesn't work being the biggest gripe then there's not much else wrong with a game, is there?

Half-Life 2: Episode One
Story (8/10):
The story of Half-Life 2: Episode One plays on from the original Half-Life 2.
Therefore, in order to fully understand the logic of the story, the original Half-Life 2 should be played.
Half-Life 2: Episode One's story spans over five chapters, immersing the player with original characters and enemies.
As explained in the Developer's Commentary, there are admittedly some sequences where dialogue is too long and ruins some crucial parts of the story.
Although, the story does run well with the five chapters and the ending will possibly leave you wanting the next Episode in the series.
Overall, Half-Life 2: Episode One has a good storyline and a few boring non-interactive dialogue moments here and there.
Game play (8/10):
The game play of Half-Life 2: Episode One is fluent and rewarding.
Whilst progressing through the storyline, there are pieces of equipment acquired after reaching specific points.
These rewards are motivating and is enough to push the player towards the conclusion of the game.
Within this game the player will encounter many weapons from the original games, like the iconic crowbar.
The combat system in conjunction with weapons is a fluent mix and certain game play mechanics like the flashlight capacity, intensifies certain levels.
Also included within the levels is a variety of environmental objects that are interactive and combat effective.
These environmental objects are used to create smart solutions to simple problems.
In this case, Half-Life 2: Episode One's game play is constructive and destructive, making an enjoyable experience.
Graphics (10/10):
The graphics of Half-Life 2: Episode One is outstanding for it's time.
This game has perfect settings for graphic options, from Shader Detail to High Dynamic Range.
The lighting and detail of the sprites within the game looks realistic and it immerses the player into the environment.
Guns, environmental objects, enemies and everything included looks like real design was incorporated when producing.
Explained within the Developer's Commentary, many environment objects were based off real creations and it is reconstructed effectively.
In other words, the game developers made the environment look realistic and it is a true accomplishment for the time period for when it was development.
Audio (7/10):
The audio of Half-Life 2: Episode One is realistic but the soundtrack doesn't immerse the player.
Whilst playing through the story, combat and exploring situations included music that wasn't exciting enough.
Although, the environmental, character, enemy and gun tracks included did give a sense of presence.
The sounds when an enemy has acquired a target, a mine has exploded or if a zombie is nearby was executed well.
If the player listens closely they can recognise footsteps and the direction of any sound.
In conclusion, the games soundtrack is mildly boring but the environmental sounds are good.

Additional Features (8/10):
In Half-Life 2: Episode One there is an additional feature that many previous players of Valve games could recognise, the Developer's Commentary.
This feature of the game becomes unlocked once the completion of a desired chapter is registered.
The Developer's Commentary provides an inside look on the previous and/or designs, ideas and game play mechanics considered throughout the development of the game.
This is encoded using floating speech bubble sprites spread across the five chapters in their appropriate positions.
Also, once a commentary is being played, the player becomes invincible to enemy damage and can sometimes freeze the enemies themselves to state an idea.
This additional feature is a productive way of expressing the developer's ideas and explaining the nature of the game.
After completing the game, it is recommended to try the Developer's Commentary for an in-depth explanation on the games features and aesthetics.
Overall (8.2/10)

THIS REVIEW WILL CONTAIN SOME SPOILERS FOR BOTH THIS GAME AND THE ROOM. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.
The Room 2 follows the style of the first one very closely while adding new elements and a much more exploratory puzzle system. Each room leads to the next, giving a sense of an adventure! With every room I finished, I was excited to keep going and to finish the next, and the next, and the next...
One thing that I found surprising was the more complex story that was able to string a seemingly unrelated group of locations and situations together. Sure, sometimes you had to piece details together for yourself by observing several scraps of papers, notes of medical experiments, letters and notes to various people, and so on, but it left you to decide whether this game will leave you an experience in puzzles or an experience in story-telling AND puzzles.
The puzzles also had a few fresh twists. In the first, most puzzles could be completely solved with various parts and mechanisms of the box, and very rarely involved things around the room. The Room 2 widens the spectrum and does just that. Instead of focusing on a singular box, each puzzle may involve multiple puzzle boxes to lead to the penultimate door to the next room. It made for a more complex and time consuming experience, as you constantly zoom in and out of different points of view to solve one portion of a box, get a key, go to another box, open it, solve a puzzle, which then gives you a tool to solve the next box, etc.
Overall great game 9/10 can't wait for The Room 3 for PC

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter sets a new precedent for storytelling in videogames. There's no question that this game's narrative is miles ahead of anything we've seen recently from the game industry as a whole. It's terrifically paced, the voice acting is superb, and the visuals...oh my goodness. You will be floored.
When I initially set out to play this game, I planned  to record my playthrough and upload it to Youtube (with commentary).
The thing is...once everything came together (the story, the atmosphere, sound design, visuals), I could barely form a sentence anymore.
I was HUMBLED into SILENCE.
How many games can claim to have had that effect on anyone?
There's something infinitely special about The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and it might not be evident in the first 30 minutes, or even the first hour of gameplay, depending on how soon you clue in to how the game works.
Don't get me wrong, the game isn't difficult, but it's definitely cryptic.
There's no tutorial or "hand-holding" at all. It's entirely up to the player to figure out the different ways that the 'sensing' ability works. I guess it adds to the sense of discovery, but I would've appreciated a little guidance from the start, since I ended up missing some not-so-obvious puzzles that I had to backtrack to later.
Once everything clicks though, you're in for one hell of an experience. The game does a fantastic job of keeping you guessing. There will be moments when you think you've got the story figured out, but all of a sudden, the game throws you a curveball, and flips your perception of the narrative on its head. It never feels cheap though, and everything that didn't make sense to you at first, is eventually cleared up in the game's jaw-dropping conclusion.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is undoubtedly one of the finest stories that's ever been told in a videogame, and it's got great pacing, striking visuals, and an excellent soundtrack to boot.
If you're at all interested in story-driven adventure games, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an essential play. The game is undeniably short, but those few hours you spend with it will leave a lasting impression. All in all, it's a journey that's WELL worth your time.
9.5/10

After cramming hours upon hours of time in to this game every day since purchase, I feel pressure mounting on myself to say thanks to Techland for giving me such an outstanding gaming experience, and giving me something extra to look forward to every day.
I'm not sure what I'm more grateful for though, because there's so much to be thankful for. The map(s) are absolutely rammed with interesting things to do that completely submerge you in replayability, and anticipation for 'what you might come across next' even after completion. The atmosphere and landscape is tangibly realistic yet it maintains a firm grasp of what games are supposed to be primarily, and thats unadulterated FUN! What makes all of this even better is indulging in all of this as part of an online COOP with other likeminded people who either want to set about any of the many challenges, or just want to play within the amazing engine and just get up to crazy stuff.
Maybe what I love most is that thanks to the game, I'm now a qualified orthopaedic surgeon who can carry out complex surgery within seconds with tools such as 'Dark sickle' etc! It brings a tear to my eye when i think back to when I stepped out onto the brilling slums and performed my first septorhinoplasty with a hunters knife and a cricket bat.
The storyline is gripping with excellent flow and like many good stories, leaves you wondering way beyond the finale, for which the very good acting adds punch.

This game is awful in so many ways - and yet, I highly recommend it!
The basic premise is to run a space program, explore Mars and other parts of our solar system, and if you play the campaign from start to finish, you start with Rovers and progress to manned missions. As the player you can very much scale the challenge to what you want to do - some missions require you to just move a camera, others need you to pilot a spacecraft in zero-g - and that is both as boring and as challenging as it sounds.
The game tries to give you that Space Program feel, and there begins the problems. The interface is clunky, it's not explained at all, and there are any number of cutscens that just bore the crap out of you. Some of the challenges require a mindnumbing rover-drive for 1 km across mars - that gets really boring too, and feels like you're investing offline time for in-game progress.
The game is just as unforgiving and buggy as all of Bohemia's products are. I've had two crafts fall through the ground on insertion, and since you're always kind of strapped for cash, that can cripple your program and force you to do some of those long drives or reload. The game - for some inexplicably bad design reason - doesn't autosave when you start a mission, so reloads can cost you if you forgot to constantly save.
And yet, it is so much fun! The feeling of building a space program is very real and the challenges with bugs and the penalties for failure make you feel exposed to the elements like in a survival game. I've played a ton of Kerbal and I love the heck out of this experience, bugs aside.
So really: give it a go if you love space exploration and strategy games.

A fun, challenging, four-player-coop rogue-lite run-and-gun game, with a surprising amount of backstory that reminds one of the best parts of classic space-marines-vs-bugs stories. Humanity, previously alone in the universe, has encountered a bug race known as the Ordovicians, and is now fighting a losing war against them. Outer colony worlds have been abandoned, forcing refugees onto the core worlds, creating overpopulation and resource shortages. Given the bugs' preference for digging and ambushes, conventional war tactics do not work well, but we've hit upon an alternative: Justified Use of Military Power, or "JUMP", a corps of elite troopers who can be dropped directly into bug hives via tunneling pods. Their objective is simple: find and eliminate the bug queens, ending their assaults at the source. There's some other interesting bits: a centuries-old AI, sentient robots who can have their killswitches removed in exchange for JUMP service, and a psychic who represents the necessary suspension of genetic modification laws in light of the bug threat.
Gameplay is not unlike Contra, but the movement feels a bit heavier and a tad janky by comparison, though this can be due to lag compensation. You can aim in eight directions and double-jumping triggers a short-use jetpack. The levels consist of electric, poison, lava or ice-themed biomes with corresponding enemies and bosses. It has an excellent chiptune soundtrack and pixelly graphics, tons of weapons, grenades and items, procedural levels and support for online coop, which was intitally glitchy and prone to desyncs, but the netcode has been patched several times since it entered Early Access and as of release, it functions significantly better. EA had arcade and challenge modes, but he release brings a campaign mode with a tactical world map that allows you to build up your forts' defenses before launching attacks on individual bug hives, and you can invite your friends to any strike. Goo found in levels can be used to upgrade your weapons and equipment as before, but can also be used to build up your forts with additional troops, traps and defense mechs. You have the option prior to attacking a hive to bomb it to reduce its overall strength (which decreases the number of levels you would need to complete it) or to scan it for a queen once the psychic, Delphi, joins your team.

As long as you understand which of the 2-3 commanders in your faction are ever worth using (hint: the ones who summon a heavy all-purpose strong vs. everything tank at the end of their chain), the game is good. Play other commanders if you want an obvious handicap. Some of these other commanders have only one or no worthwhile abilities, while others are interesting but only situationally useful.
Or, better yet, play with an in-game mod that lets you build any unit (of which there are many) and forget about the base game's creaky balance as much as you can. It's worth mentioning that the workshop mods for this game are pretty good--or at least, the ones most frequently used by players are.
The game's early release days of having almost every commander behind a paywall are long over, so that's nice, but the system for unlocking commanders and various upgrades is an insane grind, especially considering how little most of these commanders and upgrades matter. What you're really trying to get from the loot RNG are the rare (blue) commanders and
some tank upgrades, which even then aren't too important. Everything else is inconsequential or trash.
Be prepared for every other faction to be straight-up better than the Russians, who are weaker at every phase of the game (early, mid, and end) because their heavy tanks are not as good and unlike the other factions cannot really make antitank murdersquads that are strong vs. everything. This latter problem was addressed in a recent balance patch and yet is still a problem. Russians are just not good at the things a faction needs to have in order to be seriously viable. The game is a Wehraboo's dream come true. In a game that was supposed to showcase the Russians (for once), most players play German or American.
If you want a historically accurate game you will also be disappointed. Germans are depicted as a technologically-advanced, super-competent army. Historical Wehrmacht armaments that were a tactical disaster/almost never used (the Elefant, for example) are depicted as amazing super units. The game keeps up the myth that Russians had only one gun for every 3-5 soldiers, and is unable to explain why the Russian army routed the Germans and largely won the war in Europe themselves, so that we Americans can continue to mythologize D-Day as the great hammerstroke on Hitler.
So why do I play this game? Because conducting a multi-bridge war against the CPU, shaping the battlefield to my needs, relentlessly bombing and hammering the enemy with artillery, and finally sending forth a horde of armor to crush the enemy scratches an itch. One important thing carried over from COH 1 is that the physics are hilarious. COH 2 is often compared unfavorably to COH 1, but COH 1's interface and lack of modern multiplayer features is getting long in the tooth.
I recommend this game at $5, which is about the price it's coming down to during sale season/bundle weeks. Relic is a developer that is about presentation and flavor. They have never been very reliable on gameplay or polish in any of their games and have never made a game that has any potential to make an impact in e-sports because of their mechanics problems.

I bought this game hoping for an old-school beat-em-up in the vein of Double Dragon, Battletoad, Streets of Rage and all the rest of their ilk. What I got instead was a SHODDY beat-em-up in the vein of... well, incompetently-made, poorly-thought-out games of any era you might care to name.
The controls are stiff and wooden, the fighting is booring - basically no combo variation - and the main 'special move' (forward, forward, attack) is simultaneously hard to pull off in the heat of battle, and easy to fire off accidentally... at least if you're using a controller, which would seem to be the obvious choice. The actual fighting boils down to 'stunlock them before they stunlock you', aided by enemies walking in random circles around you most of the time.
Said enemies are generally annoying and often use hit-and-run tactics which you are poorly-equipped to counter, since you can't move faster than a laid-back saunter - there's no run, dash or dodge-roll option. They also enjoy attacking from beyond the edges of the screen, where you can't see or reach them, or just positioning themselves INSIDE you to attack, taking advantage of the poorly-made hitboxes. Several of them also have far greater reach than their animations would suggest.
The bosses are, perhaps, the worst of the lot - they're invariably invulnerable, except for during a specific interval, for abso-bloody-lutely no apparent reason. Your punches just pass through them without doing anything, not because they're hiding behind a shield or using some kind of force-field, but because the game arbitrarily decided that they aren't vulnerable at that point.
Sure, it's funny - sort of, if you're into anarchic, rebellious humor - but the translation is as shoddy as the rest and the text is rife with poor spelling, messed-up grammar, and just plain old errors.
But hey - the GRAPHICS are very nice. Love the style. Looks great. Maybe they should've made a cartoon or a comic-book instead...

These days tactical shooters (as opposed to the modern military run-and-guns of certain yearly franchises), are few and far between. A good tactical shooter is almost unheard of. Luckily there's Vegas 2 which is the latest (2008!) in the venerable Rainbow Six family, which has stood the test of time.
While the graphics certainly aren't up to current gen specs, it runs smooth and doesn't look so dated as to be distracting. There is one big bug still in the game which leads to a continuous sound of an enemy machine gun firing. It doesn't happen to everyone or every time you play but it can be annoying when it does. Besides this, and a control scheme that's different than every other game, it's very solid mechanically, one of the best really, and delivers a gameplay style that's hard to find anywhere else. It's also pretty packed with content.
Besides a campaign that's plenty long, and that can be played all the way through in co-op, you get the terrific Terrorist Hunt 4-player co-op missions, which involve clearing various levels of enemies, and various vs. modes. The Hunt missions with 4 players are the real show stealers here and really get to the essence of the tactical shooter genre. The AI, a large part of making a tactical shooter work, is mostly strong. Occasionally they will rush a choke point one at a time or fail to spot you in an obvious location but most of the time they use cover effectively and are quick to break off and flank you.
If you're longing for an old-school style game where you move slow and die fast then this is what you're looking for. If you've got some friends looking for a challenging co-op experience you'd be hard pressed to do better than this. Overall really just a great, great game.

Rainbow Six: Vegas 2 is a game I'm very passionate about, from wonderful memories playing with my dearest of  friends, to the excitement I feel whenever I rank up and unlock more equipment. Speaking of equipment, this game offers a fairly complex  loadout customization system, probably one of the most indepth systems I've ever seen in a videogame to date, though the actual avatar creator leaves much to be desired from. (Only allowing you to chose a pre-made set of skins, gender, and war paint) Gear isn't the only thing to unlock either, weapons are another aspect to look forward to, the game offers a selection from light support guns, sniper rifles, assault/battle rifles, handguns, and sub-machine guns, not to mention grenades as well as other explosive devices of varying type, making replayability quite fun, getting to create a new gear set, and try out a new weapon. The campaign can be seen as quite straightforward, though my nostalgia blinded eyes believe it's something quite special, I'll leave the decision up to you whether it's one of a kind, or generic. Besides the main story campaign, there's a fairly run of the mill multiplayer, though with the benefit of you getting to use your custom geared loadout, and a mode called 'terrorist hunt' which is a blast to play with your buddies or even just solo, as you select a map, and clear out a set number of enemy combatants, this mode is great for grinding! The soundtrack is enjoyable to listen to, the enemy A.I is somewhat competent, the guns (dependant on which you use) sound meaty and powerful, there's also fairly realistic gameplay, even if you chose the beefiest of armour, a few well placed shots from really any weapon is going to send to you to the grave, creating adrenaline filled tense moments, which could end up with a single bullet to your head, or the enemy's. All in all, I strongly recommend this game, it's a lot of fun, and should keep you busy for a while!
I hope my review can help you decide whether or not this is the game for you! ^-^

Once again, we have the annoying situation where by a developer (this time Tindalos Interactive) have taken a great IP and somewhat fumbled the ball on the game. Not by being inept, but more frustratingly, by releasing something that is both bugged and annoyingly flawed yet shows a great deal of promise.
In this instance the issues are detrimental to the game to the point where I almost wish I never bought it. And very nearly shelved the game.
1) Save games dissapear for no reason and are totally irrecoverable. Game breaking if you are later on in the game. Make sure you set up AT LEAST two saves.
2) The Orks are over powered in the game - at least if you are playing the Imperial Navy.
3) The "tutorial" is woefully inadequate and the only way to really learn about the UI and game mechanics is either to spend hours sifting through the FAQ and game advice files, spend ages watching youtube videos or by hours of painful trial and error.
4)  The game difficulty is too high. I am a hardened Homeworld player and my grasp of space combat in both 2 and 3D is above average and this game (mainly due to it not elucidating on it's myriad combat systems and how they work) is too hard even on normal difficulty. Eventually, through lots of punishing trial and error, you will get the hang of it and then it is a good (and can be a great) game. It's just that most people will have walked away in frustration ages before.
I'm not saying I want the game to be dumbed down. Simply that it should have a FAR more comprehensive tutorial and the balancing between races needs some work.
I have changed my mind about recommending this game but only after over 11 hours of figuring out it's intricacies. This problem could be avoided by simply easing the player into the experience. Which ultimately, if you can get past the ridiculously steep learning curve, is very good.

It does feel like a post-nuclear war world where humans have to suffer from radiation, lack of resources, and, most importantly and terribly, mutants born from the disaster.
Every kind of weapons can be used throughout the game, and there's no "best" weapon which can be used for all battles. You have to pick the right gun to fight against different kinds of enemies and different situation.
Just as good as the novel. There are some changes and cuts here and there, but the awesome main story and background remains there.
Human combat is generally average, fighting mutants is a horrible experience. The AI is horrible that sometimes you have no idea what the hell are your enemies doing with the walls and floors. And for most of the mutant combats you should have some Ai teammates with you, who have unlimited ammo, will never die (unless plot), high dmg output and some sort of taunt ability. You can't damage them (neither can the enemies), so you can happily hide behind him and throw grenade under his feet, kill all the enemies around and he won't take a scratch,
I understand that this game is kind of a horror game if we consider its background story... but all the jumpscares in the game are basically just for the sake of scaring you. They'd put a shadow man in a daytime building when you're looting the place and have no idea why there appears this ghost for like 5 frames. Yes I'm scared but like why the heck do I have to deal with these things during looting or intense gun fighting?
As I mentioned your teammates take no dmg from your source at all. So you can throw knife, grenades, lightbangs, firebombs under their feet to clear out a huge wave of mutants (usually 4-5 which is really a lot). And, especially incendiary, is way too powerful in mutant combat. 3 incendiaries can just block the path and secure the position for some 20 seconds. "Survival Game" seriously?
I play in Ranger mode, and I've expected to be always out of ammo and other resources. Well the fact is, you hardly lack of anything unless you pour them like water in every fight. Almost all enemies can be dealt with within 2-3 shots by any gun (to the head I mean), and combat against humans usually means you can loot something after each kill. Yes you may not have enough ammo to literally pour on your enemies, but it’s always enough to secure a walkthrough. Well this may be newbie-friendly but I really don’t feel the pressure that it should give me in high difficulty.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a wonderful game with a well written story and a suprising end, however once you have played it through there's nothing that makes you want to play it again. It's a one time game and it's a rather short experience. You can finish the game in about 5 hours with no need to stress it through. So you should think about if it's worth paying a full price for such a game, I waited until there was a Steam sale for it.
One small irritating thing was the autosave. There is no manual save and it autosaves once you've completed a "task", or story. All the other stories that you haven't completed to 100% will be reseted. When you reload you start where you last autosaved which was at the last story, not where you stood when exiting the game.
The graphic is really awesome realistic made. Rarely have I seen such beautful made graphic, really an eye-candy! That togheter with a good ambient sound enviroment made it feel like I was really there. The performance was great, almost no stuttering or fps dips. With an Intel i5 cpu, Geforce GTX 660 and 8 gb ram I could play on almost max settings at 1920x1080 resolution.
So to summarize it then.
Positive:
+ Great well written story in abit spooky enviroment.
+ Awesome graphic and ambient sound. Runs well without problems.
+ Fitting soundtrack.
+ No bugs, no ctd. Stable.
Negative:
+ Very short story and there's no meaning to replay it really.
+ Not worth to pay full price considering above statement. Wait for a Steam sale to get it.
+ No manual savegame mode availible.

A new discovery could take corn farming to perhaps the last place you'd expect to see it: in underground mines and caves. Perhaps, eventually, even to other planets. It sounds like science fiction, but it's real, and it could drastically change the future of food production as we know it.
It all started when researchers at Purdue University tried growing corn in an abandoned limestone mine. Despite the seemingly non-ideal conditions of the mine (specifically, higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and artificial light), the crops actually thrived. "We coddled the plants with such luxurious conditions that the corn was touching the lamps before it had even tasseled," then-postdoctoral student Yang Yang said.
So the team tried a technique used to keep holiday poinsettias from growing too large: a blast of cold air. The control group grew at 80 degrees Fahrenheit in light and 65 degrees in darkness (simulating day and night); the test group's conditions were identical except for a two-hour blast of "day" spent at 60 degrees.
The group that experienced the temperature dip produced the same grain yield, but the stalks were 10 percent shorter and weighed less than the control group. In other words, same amount of corn in less space.
That means that corn—a species that normally requires bright light, lots of heat, and infinite headroom—could grow in cool, cramped areas—you know, like caves. Cary Mitchell, professor of horticulture at Purdue, explains:
"This is a technique you could easily do in a mine or cave. It is an affordable, non-chemical means of taking genetically modified crops to harvest maturity without getting any kind of pollen or seed into the ecosystem."
In other words, GMO crops for those who want them, without opponents having to worry about modified cross-pollination tainting their heirloom crops.
Okay, so corn can grow in caves, and with the right temperature control, it'll put out normal yield without bumping its head. But there's another important implication straight out of science fiction: if we can grow corn in caves and mines, without having to worry about the unintended effects of cross-pollination, we could use genetically-modified crops to produce medicinal products, like antibodies or components for vaccines.
And as Michael Byrne points out, if we can reliably grow corn in closed environments hidden from the sun, maybe we could eventually grow crops in caves on other planets. "In this way, underground farms could one day become terraforming machines, converting high levels of underground carbon dioxide into oxygen, to be released on the surface," he theorizes.

Played this game back in the day tons of times. Good memories.
The good:
Graphics are a later Unreal Engine so they aren't bad.
Highly customizable loadout that is made available to you as you progress through the levels with experience.
A very detailed upgrade model based on experience and types of shots made. You gain experience points based on the shot you make, be it close quarter, long-range, assault mode, etc. Each shot gains you XP points for a specific type of ladder and each ladder (CQB, assaulter, marksman) has its own rewards and perks.
Very good cover, concealment, shoot and peek controls. You can crouch or stand by a corner or behind cover, peek out and shoot, or peek out with zoom in function already selected, shoot, peek and go back to your zoomed view on your weapon without having to zoom in simply because you went into cover. Very useful when shooting multiple enemies from one location.
You can choose an array of weapons, armour and equipment.
When you have the gameplay mechanics downpat, it becomes super fun breaching and using different tactics when clearing rooms.
The Bad:
The AI is at times inept. They take forever sometimes to follow through with commands once you give them.
The AI cannot throw a grenade competently. Frequently I've given the command for my squad to throw a grenade at a precise location, only to watch it bounce off a wall and land back at my squad and wipe everyone out. At certain times they will refuse to even throw one when requested.
AI does not auto-heal itself. I have to backtrack and tell one AI squad member to heal another. Duh.
Very fun as you're able to plan your approach differently - either going in assault-mode or silent.
Overall it's a fun game well-intentioned hampered by some AI problems.
Worth the download if it's on sale.

HELLDIVERS is a co-op two stick shooter with a galactic military strategy theme. This game was very well received by the Playstation community and has finally come to the PC. The game has several elements that make it really shine including planetary domination and eventual galactic conquest. The instanced feel of each encounter makes it easy to pick up and play for any period of time. The controls for the PC are just not workable so having a controller for this is the one major hiccup if you don't already own one.
What I enjoyed:
Dropping in – I liked that you sort of set your own fate in multiple aspects. You choose where to fly and begin your conquest. Once in a system you choose which planet and mission to take. You get to place your drop pod anywhere on the map for the instance you enter on the planet, which can be a blessing or a curse as you see in my video. The feeling that you are in control of your own fate with so many facets is certainly a unique and fun mechanic incorporated into the entire experience.
Environmental planets – Each planet I dropped into had different themes, all which fit the entire art style and “space travel” story line  exceptionally well. The environments are also dynamic and certain ones have lava explosions or other hazards that can kill your Helldiver. I ran into some lava on a bug infested planet and it wasn't pleasant. The variation in planet type and environmental atmospheres is done well enough that the feeling of travel and exploration is felt strongly.
Shoot up some aliens – Shooting aliens and taking over planets is fun. I really enjoy a game that has a simple style like this, incorporated into a bigger overall picture. The combat is dual stick and these are the same designers of “Magicka” so be prepared for a frustrating situation here or there, but mostly it comes down to managing your mobs, and if in co-op, managing your team well.
What I disliked:
Controller Required – If a game comes to the PC, it should have a workable control scheme right out of the box. I found the default to be just awful, and honestly for a two stick shooter you need a controller. I have one so it was not that big of a roadblock, but for someone without a PC stick, this could be very annoying.
Missed shots – I felt like at times my bullets sort of passed through certain mobs rather than killed them, which caused a death here and there. It may be that there is a miss percentage, or that you've got to line right up to their center. I think this was the only major area of combat that felt like it could use some work.

For those of us who enjoyed the original Metro 2033, the new Redux version is a real pleasure. The original game looked amazing, even in comparison to today's newest titles, but it was poorly optimized. Upgraded to Last Light's newer engine, Metro 2033 Redux plays much better than the original. However, some inherent problems from the original game still persist and they can still make some aspects of playing the Redux version just as frustrating as the original.
Metro 2033 is about as linear of an experience as would expect from a modern FPS. Exploration is certainly encouraged, especially if playing Survival mode, but not really a necessity. However, the linear experience of the game is most infuriating during the generic rail car shooter levels and the, not-forced-but-very-heavily-suggested, stealth sequences of the game. The stealth gameplay of the original was by far the worst part of the game. Enemies were hyper aware at all times, there was no means of knowing Artyom's exposure to light, Artyom's movement was sluggish in tight areas, etc. Thankfully, the Redux version of the game certainly has much  better stealth gameplay (not to suggest that it takes much to be better than the original). Also, sadly, QTEs, which, on their own, are awful, but can be turned up a notch to rage-inducing for a reason to be explained next shortly.
Personally, I believe the best Metro experience can be had by playing Survival mode with Ranger Hardcore difficulty. Survival mode limits the amount of resources in the game, thus leading to a more tense game with resource management being a priority. Additionally, exploration becomes much more important and justified during the game. Ranger Hardcore difficulty removes the HUD completely and provides the most immersive experience. However, going back to the buzzkill QTEs, with no HUD, there is actually no way of knowing what to press or when QTEs are even initiated in Ranger Hardcore. This leads to several frustrating deaths where you might think you are watching a scripted event when really you have to be spamming a button for the sake of muh QTE. Also, there is no display for your current ammo or what secondary you have equipped without pulling up your journal. Hopefully that sneaky stealth kill with a throwing knife you were planning does not end up with you throwing a grenade at someone's head.
TL;DR: Metro 2033 Redux is a considerable upgrade to the original. The most obvious difference will be graphically, but the gameplay sees improvements as well. I was skeptical towards whether or not Metro 2033 Redux would be worth a purchase considering it is a remaster of a game that is not even that old. I am glad to say it definitely a wholesome experience with plenty of new content to justify its new Redux title. I suggest playing on Survival mode with Ranger Hardcore difficulty for the best experience. However, expect plenty of deaths due to no HUD that will have you contemplating an uninstall.

A good sequel to The Room, The Room Two was an enjoyable experience to play. The original took place around one puzzle per level, while The Room Two has a larger room with a few small sections to each one. I prefered the style of the first game, but this one plays quite well. If you want to follow the story definitely play through the first one, but the game is certainly playable without background knowledge.
The graphical improvements over the mobile versions are quite beautiful. The shadows are done well, and are used quite nicely in-game to draw or detract focus to/from various areas. For a game built in the Unity engine it is fantastic looking.
The game does rely heavily on observation; if something looks different from others, it's likely important. This was probably my biggest gripe with the game, was that in some cases it wasn't very intuitive as to what to do next. Most of the time you have an idea of what you need to open, but you don't have the requried item at the moment. The hint system is there for these situations, but any time I used it I felt the resulting piece I needed to find etc wasn't particularly well placed. In particular there is a jar at one point with a particular importance to it, while it only looks slightly different from the others... While I feel this is an area the game could improve, I did still quite enjoy the time I spent playing it.
Overall this game is an enjoyable puzzler with good graphics and gameplay, and quite a good price point. This is easily one of the only games on Steam that I paid full price for. I eagerly await the arrival of The Room Three, although as it was just recently released on mobile it will likely be a while.

Once again, we have the annoying situation where by a developer (this time Tindalos Interactive) have taken a great IP and somewhat fumbled the ball on the game. Not by being inept, but more frustratingly, by releasing something that is both bugged and annoyingly flawed yet shows a great deal of promise.
In this instance the issues are detrimental to the game to the point where I almost wish I never bought it. And very nearly shelved the game.
1) Save games dissapear for no reason and are totally irrecoverable. Game breaking if you are later on in the game. Make sure you set up AT LEAST two saves.
2) The Orks are over powered in the game - at least if you are playing the Imperial Navy.
3) The "tutorial" is woefully inadequate and the only way to really learn about the UI and game mechanics is either to spend hours sifting through the FAQ and game advice files, spend ages watching youtube videos or by hours of painful trial and error.
4)  The game difficulty is too high. I am a hardened Homeworld player and my grasp of space combat in both 2 and 3D is above average and this game (mainly due to it not elucidating on it's myriad combat systems and how they work) is too hard even on normal difficulty. Eventually, through lots of punishing trial and error, you will get the hang of it and then it is a good (and can be a great) game. It's just that most people will have walked away in frustration ages before.
I'm not saying I want the game to be dumbed down. Simply that it should have a FAR more comprehensive tutorial and the balancing between races needs some work.
I have changed my mind about recommending this game but only after over 11 hours of figuring out it's intricacies. This problem could be avoided by simply easing the player into the experience. Which ultimately, if you can get past the ridiculously steep learning curve, is very good.

It is a game very much about not so much choosing the actions of your ships on the map screen, but also setting their underlying engagements attitudes/parameters from the HUD and best aligning them with the developments on the map and how you see the enemy strengths/weaknesses/strategy playing out.
Here's a simple scenario:
Enemy Chaos is cutting sick space donuts around one of your orbitals platforms as it pummels it from range, now depending on how you set your ships to engage from their HUD engagement profile orders many different things are going to happen. You could have them set to engage from their prow weapons hoping to snipe them with your big torpedo hits and a circling chicken chase is exactly what they will do (bad), or you could think for a moment, see the enemy is moving in a large clockwise circle, order your ship to engage from it's port side weaponry only which means it will be on the inside eventually because it's cutting smaller space donuts. Which is ESSENTIAL because the Chaos ship will be faster than your Imperial Navy ships. There's the learning curve, but once u got it, u got it.
It seems that a great deal of the negative reviews come from overlooking that this game emphasizes positioning and timing for a great deal of success. But that is just my assumption. Luck does play a noticeable role, but hey, there's no such thing as a sure thing anywhere. That'd be boring!
Some of the mission objectives are however ridiculously stacked in favour of defense or offense. This is incredibly frustrating. For example the escort defense missions, sometimes it is almost worth just throwing the damn thing from the start. Your escort objectives are going to get annihilated.
Basic mechanics of some mission types are invariably stacked very much in favour of one side or the other (Escort, Data recovery). It would be moot to choose any of the above mission types for multiplayer, the outcome would probably be decided in 90% of cases after deployment aside from for a very shrewd (and lucky) captain.
TL;DR: A very unique RTS unlike anything else I, at least, am aware of. It's an unforgiving but gratifying game once the mechanics have been understood. I hope the developer support remains with more fleets being added down the track.
