I'm very disappointed - so much potential wasted in half-baked beta sold as actual game. I wonder whether people at Bohemia Interactive know that ideas like testing (SQA) and user experience (UX) have been conceived long time ago. I heard that TKOM was in development since 2013. Seriously? What were developers doing for four years? Designing new bugs? Here is the list (incomplete) of 'features' I have found out while playing the game:
- when I load saved campaign I have to 'press any key' twice - why?
- the graphics is blurry! I guess it was meant to simulate depth of field, but it resembles severe case of tunnel vision instead
- there is no user manual
- rover missions are designed in absolutely pathetic way - on several occasions I have sent a rover with black and white
camera, only to find out later that color photos are required to complete the mission - description of required equipment of the vehicle clearly indicated 'BW camera'.
- Terra Imager, the camera capable of taking color photos, is considered black and white when it comes to completion of missions where color photos are required.
- on several occasions I was stuck in a mission because there were photos to be taken, but one of markers was not turning green (in open terrain, pretty close to the rover), or a marker was inside a boulder
- when I drive a rover, something really strange is going on with solar panel (there are no other power sources on board). For instance: during the ride charge is 20W and drain is 30W, but when I stop the rover, the drain drops to 0 (it's not realistic, but I can live with it), but charge drops to 10W! Why??? Of course it's 20W again when the rover starts to move
- animation displayed during time skip is simply awful
- just after start of a campaign, several locations are described as 'all missions in this location have been completed' - by whom?
- from time to time whole mission control room turns black and I have to restart the game.
- level of detail in mission control room was probably designed with ZX Spectrum in mind
This is not to say that the game is worthless, there are several aspects that are pretty good:
- technology tree is rather short, but organized in sensible way
- Mars shown as far, lifeless, desolate place.
Long story short, currently the game is piece of you-know-what, but in few months it may become something worthwhile. Meanwhile, I'm getting back to absolutely fantastic Kerbal Space Program!

This game is hard for me to place, here's why:
The game still ahs that wonderful feeling that the first one going to the table. The soldiers move at realistic speeds and use cover very efficiently (assuming you tell them to get in cover), the tanks feel bulky, heavy, but destructive (as they should), and artillery is very effective and a viable combat strategy (please don't spam artillery, though, no one likes those guys, not even their team mates). Battles are addictive and long, even though it feels so short because of everything that's happening. Not only that, but the Line Of Sight system allows for great ambush scenes.
All the factions feel unique and distant from each other, changing up your gameplay slightly depending on who you choose. The Axis forces rely heavily upon their armored vehicles, and use smaller, but more effective infantry to support them. Meanwhile, the Allies are more infantry-based, but things like light AT guns and efficently placed mines are able to counter the Axis advances.
Not only that, but there's something here for everyone's taste. For example, if you love cooperative games, then the Theatre of War scenarios contain challenges against AI that you can take on with a friend. It's also fun just joining in a team for a skirmish. If you're a defensive horde lover, than the victory point game mode is for you, where you must capture and hold points on the map from the enemy, or assault them. If you love destroying the world, (hello, Planetary Annihilation players) then the Annihilation skirmish mode will have you delighted as you watch the enemy's bases crumble underneath you Sherman tank's and airplane's bombardments. If you like playing alone, the AI is decent enough to keep you entertained and feeling fresh, you can even direct AI on your side using in-game commands.
Now, you've heard me rave about this game, so why is it hard for me to place? Well, the game isn't without flaws.
The singleplayer campaign is a bit... lacking. I felt like there wasn't much of a variety in missions, like the first COH's campaign (or Starcraft 2). The first COH had so many memorable missions that I remember years later, such as storming Normandy, commanding paratroopers the night before, defending a town from Axis advances, controlling the all powerful King Tiger, landing british gliders, I have so many memories of it. With this campaign, I don't really feel like I'm taking any of it with me. I think there was one mission with a castle I enjoyed? There was also a mission with snipers in winter that was alright. In fact, I don't even remember if you storm Berlin or not in this game. I remember doing it with the Eastern Fronts mod in COH 1.
Another gripe I have is the sheer amount of DLC. You have to pay in order to be the Americans or OKW, which I really feel should've just been included with the Ardenne's Assault expansion for the $40 price. Such as when we got the British and Panzer Elite factions in Opposing Fronts. I also feel that the paid Theatre of War scenarios could have been included with the game. I do believe that the Stalingrad mission pack would be great paid DLC, but at least give us Case Blue or Southern Fronts with it. I also am not a fan of the new commander system. The variety of commanders sacrificed the depth and game changers that the first commanders had to offer.
One last thing I have to say for the negative is that the multiplayer maps aren't very memorable. There were no impressive maps like the best map in RTS history, The Scheldt. Though, you can get some maps from COH 1 from the Western Front Armies, I actually enjoy most of the user created maps more than the vanilla. THE STALINGRAD MAP IS ONLY 2-4 PLAYERS!!!! I also feel like they added more urban maps than COH 1, which I like, but there still could've been more. Also, for anyone planning on getting this, do get the user-created map "The Oder," while it is not the scheldt, it really has something for everyone. Bridges to explode, urban areas for ambushes, rural areas for strategic unit placement...
Anyways, I recommend with a 7.5/10

HELLDIVERS is a co-op two stick shooter with a galactic military strategy theme. This game was very well received by the Playstation community and has finally come to the PC. The game has several elements that make it really shine including planetary domination and eventual galactic conquest. The instanced feel of each encounter makes it easy to pick up and play for any period of time. The controls for the PC are just not workable so having a controller for this is the one major hiccup if you don't already own one.
What I enjoyed:
Dropping in – I liked that you sort of set your own fate in multiple aspects. You choose where to fly and begin your conquest. Once in a system you choose which planet and mission to take. You get to place your drop pod anywhere on the map for the instance you enter on the planet, which can be a blessing or a curse as you see in my video. The feeling that you are in control of your own fate with so many facets is certainly a unique and fun mechanic incorporated into the entire experience.
Environmental planets – Each planet I dropped into had different themes, all which fit the entire art style and “space travel” story line  exceptionally well. The environments are also dynamic and certain ones have lava explosions or other hazards that can kill your Helldiver. I ran into some lava on a bug infested planet and it wasn't pleasant. The variation in planet type and environmental atmospheres is done well enough that the feeling of travel and exploration is felt strongly.
Shoot up some aliens – Shooting aliens and taking over planets is fun. I really enjoy a game that has a simple style like this, incorporated into a bigger overall picture. The combat is dual stick and these are the same designers of “Magicka” so be prepared for a frustrating situation here or there, but mostly it comes down to managing your mobs, and if in co-op, managing your team well.
What I disliked:
Controller Required – If a game comes to the PC, it should have a workable control scheme right out of the box. I found the default to be just awful, and honestly for a two stick shooter you need a controller. I have one so it was not that big of a roadblock, but for someone without a PC stick, this could be very annoying.
Missed shots – I felt like at times my bullets sort of passed through certain mobs rather than killed them, which caused a death here and there. It may be that there is a miss percentage, or that you've got to line right up to their center. I think this was the only major area of combat that felt like it could use some work.
A two stick shooter like this with co-op for a few friends is certainly something worth looking at. I enjoyed playing it and can't wait for release to spend some time with the co-op. It's already been highly reviewed by the Playstation crowd, so I'm affirming that it's a fun game and if you didn;t get to play it on the PS3 or PS4, you should pick it up for the PC.
Score: Buy it now

I got into this one for my wife, who likes low-difficulty level (coordination-wise) games.  I tag these games with "No Combat".  Anyway, Ethan Carter is definitely a no-combat game.  And, honestly, I usually find these types of less-hands-on, less-player-interactive games quite boring, like, oh, the granddaddy of all snoozefests, Myst.  This qualification, I think, is important here.  It tells you a) that this IS one of those (basically) minimalist point and click adventures and b) despite disliking these games, I found enough intriguing about Ethan Carter to invest in it for myself.  There's no denying it's lush, and not just graphically.  The storytelling is right up there in the lush department as well, although not in terms of minute detail, but more in terms of coherent, well thought out, and above all good and interesting and intriguing story.  The only complaint I have with the story is in sputtering pacing.  It almost seems as if there are a few puzzles missing.  The, well, I guess you'd call them side quests, help to flesh out the backstory of Red Creek Valley and enhance the main story, but are not required as far as I can tell.  If I had to compare Ethan Carter to other works, I don't think it would be to another game at all.  I'd compare it more to an earlier Stephen King novel set in Castle Rock, perhaps Salem's Lot or Pet Cemetery.  It has that Stephen King brand of casual creepiness to it that makes it more of a hybrid media, not-quite-game, interactive storytelling experience.  While not necessarily linear, per se, I can't see anything that allows for changes in the story (i.e. player choice doesn't effect the world).  But that's not a bad thing any more than a novel not rewriting itself the second time you read it is a bad thing.  All in all, if you understand what you're getting into, I can highly recommend The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, even at full price, which is still a third of current A-list titles.

Fast-paced team shooter set in near future Japan, where players either take control of Government security forces or a rogue special forces unit within the military. With
distinct cyberpunk style and accompanied by a two album OST by
While often compared with Counter-Strike, the only things these two games share is an engine and round format for its primary game mode (Capture the Ghost). NEOTOKYO's complexity and depth derives from its in-game features (invisibility, vision modes, etc...) and engine functionality, and less from its weapon handling (which is basic at best). Old Source rules here, 6 years past its initial release players have adopted playstyles that make the most of how Source engine used to deal with movement; bunnyhopping, wall-strafing, air-strafing, wiggle-walking are commonly deployed situationally alongside the game's core features. Positioning and movement is key and a heightened situational awareness is required (which can be greatly helped by a little teamwork). The game can be played at a blistering pace between as little as 6 players on many of its deeply dynamic maps.
Unfortunately to some, the majority of NEOTOKYO's depth and learning curve comes from the aforementioned points. While it may have never been the original developers intention for these "exploits" to manifest themselves in common meta, the game would have very little depth without it. The gun mechanics are next to non-existant, working simply as a random cone of dispersion effective immediately after a first shot. Pace would be dictated solely by the limitations put upon each class in terms of sprint speed, duration and map accessibility. Essentially leaving the skill cieling to peak as far as map knowledge and basic situational awareness, with little room for individual player ability to flourish without these "exploits".
However, if what you're looking for is a fast-paced, cerebral game where raw-input finesse is as important as it would be within an Arena Shooter, but with added scenarios for team work. Neotokyo just about manages that, even amongst its many flaws.

I like this game, specifically the manned portion of it. You really get to experience what it would be like on Mars.
But I can't really recommend it.
1. The manned portion is short, and rather disappointing. Storywise it was ok, but not great. Most of the manned portion mechanics are completely unused. You can build bases, but it's not at all needed. You can mine, but it's also not needed. It almost feels like they ran out of ideas or got sick of developing it..
2. The game is buggy. Really buggy. You can accidently kill yourself at times by jumping and somehow getting launched into the air. You can stand on items and pick them up to find yourself surfing through the air. The atmosphere in your base can suddenly vanish, for no apparent reason, leaving you to asphyxiate because your suit ran out of air.
3. It's poorly documented, making it very difficult to know how to do some things, ie pressurizing a base.
4. The UI is not great. It's very easy to accidentally use the wrong refinery recipe. It's sometimes hard to see the displays on machines because you just view them as in game scenery rather than getting a display interface. It's sometimes hard to connect barrels to slots and the key needed changes depending on scenarios.
The robotic portion of the game is ok, but it again is hard to work out what to do at times, and can be hard to meet objectives because it's either unclear how or buggy, though it's not clear which.
If you are only interested in the manned portion, then you most likely will need to be playing multiplayer, because the campaign is brief.
If you can tolerate all these issues, and the idea interests you, then you'll probably love the game, as I do, but as it is, it should not have left early access.

The levels start out pretty easy, and get more difficult as you proceed down through the hive.  The first few times playing I didn't make it very far (which surprised me), but as I continued to play and collect the goo, I started unlocking new weapons and perks that allowed me to start forming a playstyle and I gradually got farther and farther.

This is my favorite kind of retro game.  It's great in all the ways that WOULD have made it an awesome classic game if it had actually came out decades ago, but at the same time it incorporates all the modern features and conveniences we grown accustomed to.  In that sense it reminds me a lot of Shovel Knight.  It captures the right look, feel, and sound for the era but doesn't have some of the more annoying or tedious issues that older games so often have.  For example I love how respawning works.  You are suitably punished for dying but you are still able to quickly jump back to exactly where you left off.  Had this been made back in the early 90s you'd have to start at the very beginning of a level and after 3 deaths you'd have the restart the entire game.
Great graphics--I'm a total sucker for really gorgeous pixel art.  Gameplay is awesome.  And the music--sweet mercy!   Like chocolate coated beef jerky for my ears!

I started up the game to try it out and found myself playing for over an hour. This game is a blast; I can't wait to play the full version with friends!
Side Note: Thank you, Hive Jump team - I originally picked Wii U version in my backer survey and you were nice enough to let me switch over to a Steam key after just one email!

There's a lot of charm all throughout it, I especially liked the respawn system where your respawing backpack has its own health bar and you have to control it after you die. Feels like the team put a lot of effort into making everything makes sense in the game world while still being fun to play and you can tell that lead to some creative game design.
Controls are good for the most part, though the camera tends to lag behind your characters movements which can lead to some annoying deaths because you can't see what's ahead. This is more noticable when dropping down shafts where you can land on a hazard without seeing it at all and take a lot of damage. Other than that the aiming felt a little stiff, like it was locked to how your characters weapons are rotated. Hard to explain, not a big problem just something to get used to.
Overall very fun game, though the single player felt a little repetitive it feels like a fun couch co=op game. I'd wait until online multiplayer is added before purchasing unless you've got someone to play locally with.

Hive Jump is a fairly simple idea: Jump into a hive, shoot some bugs, use their goo to get new stuff, and jump into another hive, shoot more bugs. I'm sure you already know that. As simple as it is, it has a great array of weapons and gadgets to help you out with killing bugs, and its simple-yet-randomized gameplay gives it a lot of replayability, even with just the Arcade mode available, as I'm writing this in Early Access.
If I had to say anything bad about the gameplay as-is, it would be that once you find your preffered loadout combination, there isn't really any reason to switch it up, especially if you do really well with a set. I've jumped five or six times, and all three times I've completed a mission, I got an "S" rank by simply going through with the Spread Shot, Sticky Grenades, and Overshield.
That isn't to say it isn't worth playing - far from it. There's a certain satisfaction to going around, exploring, being ambushed by a random cluster of bugs, and conquering them, and I look forward to playing with new gear and new game modes in the future.
Oh, and Graphite Lab: if you need any ideas for anything in the game or someone for voices, I'm your man. ;)

I have played Quake Live since 2010, back when it was a free plug-in for major browsers. I have also played Quake III Arena for longer, casually.
Of course, nothing will beat the original Quake III Arena (Q3A) game, but this is a direct replacement for me. Instead of running a game from 1999 and using hacky methods to get it up to modern standards (native 16:9/16:10 resolution, HUD, etc), I just play this from now on. It includes many community fixes and has been supported for many years (and still is?) so that it looks the best it can be on modern systems. Plenty of bug fixes, too. The games only
difference is the addition of a new weapon: the Heavy Machine Gun. It does not replace anything that I know of, but should be known.
It still has that "boot up and frag 'em" mindset in that if you have a few minutes to kill, you can just get straight into a match with no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but is also flexible in the way that you can spend hours on it playing FFA, Clan Arena, Duel, CTF, FreezeTag and more! My personal favourite is Clan Arena :-) (There's a massive map pool, too!)
HOWEVER... This game can be plagued with ♥♥♥♥ing veterans. Some people on this have played since the dawn of Quake. They know all of the tricks in the book. Strafe jumping, rocket jumping, all that tomfoolery... So my recommendation to new players is: just stick to Free For All and Capture the Flag until you git gud. Clan Arena and Duels are the most likely to be riddled with these aforementioned skilled veterans. Best to stray away from that frustration. You will only end up abandoning the game like some of my friends have.
It used to be completely free with no subscriptions and extra stuff. It simply ran off advertisements. Apparently this was not enough for id software and decided to chuck in subscriptions. Then it was migrated to Steam as NPAPI plugins were no longer being supported on major browsers. Then you had to pay for the whole thing to phase out subscriptions and gain a more sure way of profit. No biggy, you essentially get the most definitive shooter of all time for £6.99. Bargain!
The players themselves are usually quite friendly, certainly not as bad as what can be found on CS:GO or any other modern shooter. Players from all over the world play it and you meet some of the best people.
... The closest thing you will get to mods are custom maps and some server side scripts. Type certain things into text chat and a sound plays. Class. You can get stuff from the Steam Workshop too, but nothing amazing. Maybe some "HD" models, and new extra player models which you cannot use in an online game, so pretty useless otherwise.
If you plan to buy this game, and you are new, I would recommend heading straight into the training arena bit (subject to change, name has changed throughout the years) and get yourself acquainted with the basics. Watch some videos on it. Give yourself the best headstart before you dive in head first. Also, bear in mind it is STILL based off the graphics from Q3A, which was released in 1999. The graphics were ahead of its time in those days and most people only play it now for the gameplay.
All in all, it does not stand up to its original counterpart for obvious reasons, but it gets a solid 9/10. Sticks true to its roots, plays well on modern machines, pleases eSports fans, fun with friends, and includes original game modes. If you are a seasoned Q3A player, you might find some things that annoy you but all in all it is the same old same old, and if you are new to the series or have not played Q3A, you will find the experience difficult to start, but is still fun in its own right!
EDIT: I should also mention the "liveliness" of the game. Is it popular? No. Will you find the same player(s) in a server in the same week? Probably. It should be mentioned that whatever game mode you want to play, there will be a server or two that have enough players in. Do not let this hinder your initial thoughts though (however positive or negative) because there is
a bunch of servers to play on that have a good amount of players on. Tip: When on the server browser, filter out the empty and full servers and you will pretty much always find a decent server to go into every time you log in!

Pros -

-Nice blood & gore aspects

You know, I never got around to reviewing this game.
But I absolutely love it. It captures war on the Eastern Front perfectly, allowing you to see how terrible and terrifying the war was by watching soldiers get blown into infamous 'red mist', gunned down by officers for retreating, mass-charges into well-defended positions, begging to fail, and tanks slipping through ice. But at the same time, you can also bring a little bit of kindness into the war by saving civilians in the line of fire, rescuing soldiers, etc. There is even an intense mission where you have to take out a TIGER! With only infantry! Not hard but fun and intense. This would be in the campaign. The story is also very interesting, btw.
But your journey won't end there. You can take the fight online in awesome, yet brutal mutliplayer matches or against the AI in co-op missions or 'Comp-Stomp' matches, which are basically normal multiplayer matches but with AI instead of human opponents. Mapmakers also make epic maps for this game that blend very well with either the theme of the Western Front pack, such as the endless D-Day maps, or remakes of the large-scale fighting in both cityscape and countryside on the Eastern Front. There are so many maps to choose from, I wouldn't be surprised one bit to find that nearly every single engagement of the war in Europe is covered by some map.
And finally, the editor. The editor for this game is extremely simple. I have zero coding or mapmaking knowledge and I actually managed to make a couple ok maps. Not the best, mind you, but I'm sure you could find somebody else who is worse than me. Anyway, the editor has a few great guides on Youtube and in the guides section of the community, allowing for an even easier time using the editor. I'll admit, it wasn't the easiest for me to learn how to use, but I don't have alot of experience using editors for games, so I'm not really familiar with alot of the different formats of interface.
What about cons, you ask?
Well, one con of this game is, for whatever reason, my game would occassionally reset campaign save data. I could be on like mission 10 and after not playing for about 5 days, I'd not have any save data at all, and it was very frustrating having to play the same missions like 20 times. This could be fixed though, I don't know, I haven't really checked.
Another con would be that, well, sometimes teams in multiplayer would be so stalemated it just killed the game. It happened rarely but often enough that it was really annoying. I can't count the amount of games where nobody ever captured a single victory point the entire game, all the way up to the end.
Ok, so next up is unpredictable AI. There are plenty of times where the AI will be a complete idiot one game, and completely ignore repairing extremely important bridges needed to cross a map, but other times where, nomatter how hard you tried, the AI would completely wreck your Tiger I that hasn't even been spotted on the map even once yet, with an ambush of about 5 panzerfausts out of literally nowhere. It's so obvious the AI always knows exactly where all of your units are, regardless of FoW. Also, AI would sometimes ignore bridges that were vital to crossing the map, and other times they'd repair completely useless bridges put in the game for purely aesthetic reasons. I mean, it's mostly probably due to custom map design, but still. Very annoying to see AI go for useless bridge instead of Ace Tiger II with like 30 tank kills, hundreds of inf kills, and in need of vital repairs ASAP.
Sometimes, if battles prolonged for too long, FPS would tend to drop a bit. Not alot but definitely noticable. This is probably due to alot of detail on maps alongside alot of new 'features' added like firing hundreds of artillery shells at one spot causing an FPS tank as you marched your little horde of infantry and tanks across it.
But all that said, these cons are really mostly just annoyances, and the vast majority of gameplay was fun and engaging. Even a little bit immersive at some points, playing alongside good friends in a co-op game. And those cons are really just things you should expect, though a little bit more prevalent due to the massive amounts of custom maps.

Granted I've only played an hour of the Steam version. I've played over 20 hours in the Playstation 4 version. This is a great game if you're into twin stick shooters and Starship Troopers. It becomes an amazing game when you're playing with a group of friends though.
A buttload of wepaons and stratagems keep the game fresh and allows you to come up with so many different types of strategies. Want to be completely defensive and rely on turrets, mines and airstrikes? You can do it. Want to be completely offensive and rely on mechs, heavy armor and heavy weaponry. Go for it. You can even loadout your character to be completely support driven. Healing your allies, providing ammo and weapon pickups. Half of the fun of this game is coming up with these strategies with your group. But implementing them can be a challenge.
This game is very difficult. Everything can kill you very easily. All stratagem drops are able to squash you. Reviving enemies can squash you. New players joining the game can squash you. Even the dropship that is rescuing you can squash you. Allies and your own weapons hurt you. Meaning that if you walk into someones/somethings fire, you will be killed. You have to make sure to dive to the ground and crawl out of the way. You also have to manually reload your weapons and ammo is pretty sparce. So this is a game that should be taken pretty slowly. Which is kinda different than most twin stick shooters.
You fight three different factions in the game. Bugs, Cyborgs and Illum. Each faction is completely different than the others and this provides a lot of playability to the game. Getting tired of fighting one faction? Well, switch it up and go fight some Cyborgs for a bit. Each planet has a few battles that you have to complete to liberate the planet. Each battle has randomized objectives like setting up air support, radio beacons or capturing points. Every planet conquered gives influence to a completely community driven War. The entire Helldivers community fights over different sectors of the Galaxy with "Super Earth" in the center. The goal of the community is to fight each faction back and destroy their homeworlds while also protecting Super Earth. The more difficult planets you take over, the more influence is added to the War effort. Random events also happen which can completely turn the tide of the war. The community doesn't always succeed.
So get out there and defend Super Earth! Bring democracy to those disgusting aliens!

WHAT IS THAT? NO, NOOO!!!
WE NEED EMERGENCY EVAC!
ARGHHH
This a typical work day in XCom, Enemy Unknown. Not such a good advertisement isn't it? Yes the game is hard but it's also so rewarding...
Tactical part is really... er... tactical: each move has to be balanced, bad luck can ruined a good plan. So you have to build even better plans that are bad-luck-proof. But if you only hide, you die; if you rush, you die (even if, sometimes you have to rush to get out a desperate situation... but if you are in such a situation, it's perhaps that you did not so well before...).
Strategy part (base and research handling) is also well balanced and it's critical to think ahead (in-game help is perhaps a bit light, don't hesitate to go on the web for more info).
The campaign keeps you under constant pressure and, for a long time, you cannot explore different strategies in parallel: you have to make choices, with limited ressources, and assume your mistakes.
Besides, your choices in each part influences the other (do I kill aliens or do I take risks to capture them alive? (seeing what the chief scientist inflicts them, I almost pity them); do I develop better armor or better firepower?).
And, eventually, you have a progression system for your soldier (again, a matter of choices).
Anyway, even if some choices are more difficult to assume than others, there is not only one way to play the game...
IMHO: all game mechanisms are well articulated with each others and logically introduced during the campaign.
Besides, I merely love the atmosphere (there is a real effort in storytelling).
The only negative point is perhaps that the endgame becomes a bit repetitive (especially if you have discovered enough technologies). But it still probably one of the better game I have ever played and I'm eager to test Enemy Within and XCom 2.
Now it's time to go back to Mission Control!

I've been playing Battlefleet Gothic: Armada for a good 18 months or so now, on and off, and I must say I find it jolly good fun. I only play the campaign or skirmishes against the computer so I cannot comment on it's apparent balance problems as a PVP RTS - I can only give you my opinion of it as a solo experience. And that is, quite simply, that I keep coming back to it. I'm currently only playing Imperial Guard and Space Marines as I'm enjoying the vaguely RP idea of being the goodies versus the various nasties that exist in the Warhammer 40k world. My Guard are a pretty advanced fleet that spider-tanks shield between each other whilst my Space Marines are investing heavilly in deploying boarding parties. Both fleets have a lot of micro-jumping going on, which they use to either do double broadsides (fire everything off your port side and then microjump to the other side before firing all your starboard guns) or ramming.
Mmmm, ramming. A well-timed ram where you shove the target vessel for what seems like miles whilst toggling your boost off and on so you reapply the impact damage is deeply satisfying. Yes, Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is pretty damn micro, but this is mitigated by developing a fleet that automates successfully and (most importanly of all) bunging it into slow-motion whenever you feel you need to. Yes, it can be a bit repetitive. But, like I said, I don't play it very often so whenever I return to it it feels fresh and exciting.
To be quite frank, BG:A is scratching an itch that nothing else I play seems to quite reach. I deploy 2-6 capital ships, each of which can be preset regarding how it engages the enemy if left to it's own devices (attack range and preferred angle of attack i.e. broadsiding or strafing) and each of which has a number of abilities which I activate as I see fit. Some of these are standard across all ships, some of these are standard across my race, some are particular to my class of ship and some are the upgrades I have personally chosen with my xp to augment the vessel as I deem appropriate. Creating functional synergies across your fleet and seeing them work in theatre remains very pleasing.
Is it the perfect game? No. Do I kinda love it a little bit? Yeah, yeah I do. I'm never unhappy after a game of Battlefleet Gothic: Armada - I either feel like a badboy 40k fleet admiral or I'm cursing the xenos scum with my fist held high whilst figuring out a strategy that might work next time. Pretty cool, huh?

I will start out by saying that the mixed rating for this game is well deserved.  The multiplayer is completely dead and even when people were playing this game you would always run into an eldar or chaos player that would run some strategy that you couldn't really compete with as any of the other races.  The balance on the eldar is just ridiculous. I am not going to go into that because this review would be too long and I would like to keep it relatively short.
On top of the multiplayer being dead, there is pretty much no word from the developers on what's going on with this game so it could really be dead.
HOWEVER... Visually, this is possibly the best representation of warhammer 40k out there.  The attention to detail is astounding, coming down to the individual characters for each chapter of space marines there are in the game.  The game is challenging enough to keep you entertained.  Watching as your ships ram, blast and board their way to victory makes you feel extremely satisfied.
You DO have to micro. Alot. Like alot. If you aren't able to give commands to several ships at the same time, you are probably going to have a hard time with this game, but on the other hand there are many different playstyles that could allow you to outweigh the micro.  You could go with several large battleships for close range macro-cannon barrages and boarding actions, or you could go for a long range approach and shred your enemies with lance fire.  With several strategies spread out over 6 races (imperial navy, space marines, chaos, orks, eldar and tau) there is plenty for you to try out and experiment with.
My biggest problem with this game besides balance is the number of points you are given to use ships in skirmish modes.  800 points is just not enough. It's a joke.  I get two battleships and a battle cruiser? Sorry, but I want more.  I don't care if it's harder on my machine or if it breaks balance in the game (what little balance there is).  I don't need to play against humans who are going to cheeze my a** with their broken eldar.  I want to destroy the xeno and the heretic as the crushing fist of the Imperium!!
To do list for devs:
Campaign expansions - You need more from the campaign, even if it is the gothic war.  I love that you paid attention to detail and kept to the true events of the gothic war.  You are held in high regards with the community for your respect for the lore, but you could add different campaigns for different races that could go outside the gothic war.  You need to tie in the variety of all six races you have into that story.
More ships! - These battles just need to get bigger. They don't need to be ridiculous, but the game is called Battlefleet Gothic! Five ships is not a battlefleet.
More races - keep good on your promises and you will be rewarded.  Even with your silence I wait eagerly for a tyranids expansion and possibly more.
Balance - This is the big one.  I am really not exaggerating.  The eldar are broken, plain and simple.  You have to balance the speed of the eldar with the damage they can dish out and take.  They can't have it all.  Figuring out what to balance comes from playing the game against everything and seeing what is and is not fun to play against.  The eldar are not fun to play against, and everyone played eldar.  Hence the death of multiplayer.

is a hectic 2D shooting platformer with procedurally generated levels. You play as a
, fighting a war for the very survival of Humankind against an hostile alien race (kind of reminded me of playing Infested Planet, only this time in the role of a single marine). The game offers both single and local co-op, with online co-op coming “soon”.
There are 3 different modes in the game right now. Youv’e got the Arcade mode which lets you play through a series of levels, defeat a few bosses and then, if you manage to survive, your mission is complete. The other 2 modes you’ve got are the daily and weekly challenges which, at this moment, still don’t have a leaderboard system in place but I feel like they are harder than the Arcade mode. The thing that really makes me excited about this game is the Campaign mode which will come at a later date which is a mix of the current combat gameplay with turn-based base management. Right now, you’ll be moving around through different hazardous materials, dodging projectiles with your jetpack while blasting your way through piles of alien filth. Shooting itself is pretty satisfying but I feel like there needs to be more visual feedback as to how destructive your weapons actually are.
At its core the game has some features which are reminiscent of rogue-likes/lites that might appeal to fans of the genre. The game has permadeath but it does so in a rather unique way. You carry around a backpack and once you die a countdown timer will begin for you to respawn at the backpack location and this can go on forever. If, however, your backpack gets destroyed you’ll have no more respawns. The game also features some sort of permanent progression in the sense that as you complete missions you’ll unlock more cosmetic items. As you clean up hives and kill aliens you’ll also pick up goo which acts as a form of currency. At the end of each stage you’ll be able to upgrade your weapon, purchase a new special ability such as a auto-turret or a shield, and you’ll also be able to get a new type of grenade such as poison or remote detonated explosives. In terms of weapon variety the game already offers a nice range of weapons and mods but it would be nice to see more added down the road, and the same goes for enemy types. Stages are divided into different biomes (e.g. lava and ice) and they can have special hand crafted challenge rooms in them which, upon completing will grant you a passive bonus. At the end of each one you’ll face a boss, overall they’re pretty easy once you figure out their patterns so maybe having a bump in difficulty would be nice, as well as more boss variants.
One thing I can’t stress enough is how good the soundtrack is and how it has a very retro feel to it (the composer has worked on Mass Effect 2). The controls also have a very retro feel and remind of something in the veins of Contra, Gunstar Heroes or Metroid. In terms of visuals, the pixel art is on point and the combination of different colors helps distinguish things on the background. The game also features some pretty neat lighting, which plays a huge role on dark levels, forcing you to shoot in order to light your path and make sure you don’t fall into your death.

To say this game is great is like saying that America is the best country in the world; It goes without saying. Taking cues from Risk of Rain, Spelunky, Bro Force, and Soldat, it takes the best parts of each, and improves on them, while also staying very unique. Overall good RTS game, comrade, should try.
Pros -
-Nice representation of life on Eastern Front
-Interesting story

-Nice blood & gore aspects
Cons -
-Low FPS at times (Sometimes games last so long the map is literally a bunch of craters. Not often, though.)

You know, I never got around to reviewing this game.
But I absolutely love it. It captures war on the Eastern Front perfectly, allowing you to see how terrible and terrifying the war was by watching soldiers get blown into infamous 'red mist', gunned down by officers for retreating, mass-charges into well-defended positions, begging to fail, and tanks slipping through ice. But at the same time, you can also bring a little bit of kindness into the war by saving civilians in the line of fire, rescuing soldiers, etc. There is even an intense mission where you have to take out a TIGER! With only infantry! Not hard but fun and intense. This would be in the campaign. The story is also very interesting, btw.
But your journey won't end there. You can take the fight online in awesome, yet brutal mutliplayer matches or against the AI in co-op missions or 'Comp-Stomp' matches, which are basically normal multiplayer matches but with AI instead of human opponents. Mapmakers also make epic maps for this game that blend very well with either the theme of the Western Front pack, such as the endless D-Day maps, or remakes of the large-scale fighting in both cityscape and countryside on the Eastern Front. There are so many maps to choose from, I wouldn't be surprised one bit to find that nearly every single engagement of the war in Europe is covered by some map.
And finally, the editor. The editor for this game is extremely simple. I have zero coding or mapmaking knowledge and I actually managed to make a couple ok maps. Not the best, mind you, but I'm sure you could find somebody else who is worse than me. Anyway, the editor has a few great guides on Youtube and in the guides section of the community, allowing for an even easier time using the editor. I'll admit, it wasn't the easiest for me to learn how to use, but I don't have alot of experience using editors for games, so I'm not really familiar with alot of the different formats of interface.
What about cons, you ask?
Well, one con of this game is, for whatever reason, my game would occassionally reset campaign save data. I could be on like mission 10 and after not playing for about 5 days, I'd not have any save data at all, and it was very frustrating having to play the same missions like 20 times. This could be fixed though, I don't know, I haven't really checked.
Another con would be that, well, sometimes teams in multiplayer would be so stalemated it just killed the game. It happened rarely but often enough that it was really annoying. I can't count the amount of games where nobody ever captured a single victory point the entire game, all the way up to the end.
Ok, so next up is unpredictable AI. There are plenty of times where the AI will be a complete idiot one game, and completely ignore repairing extremely important bridges needed to cross a map, but other times where, nomatter how hard you tried, the AI would completely wreck your Tiger I that hasn't even been spotted on the map even once yet, with an ambush of about 5 panzerfausts out of literally nowhere. It's so obvious the AI always knows exactly where all of your units are, regardless of FoW. Also, AI would sometimes ignore bridges that were vital to crossing the map, and other times they'd repair completely useless bridges put in the game for purely aesthetic reasons. I mean, it's mostly probably due to custom map design, but still. Very annoying to see AI go for useless bridge instead of Ace Tiger II with like 30 tank kills, hundreds of inf kills, and in need of vital repairs ASAP.
Sometimes, if battles prolonged for too long, FPS would tend to drop a bit. Not alot but definitely noticable. This is probably due to alot of detail on maps alongside alot of new 'features' added like firing hundreds of artillery shells at one spot causing an FPS tank as you marched your little horde of infantry and tanks across it.
But all that said, these cons are really mostly just annoyances, and the vast majority of gameplay was fun and engaging. Even a little bit immersive at some points, playing alongside good friends in a co-op game. And those cons are really just things you should expect, though a little bit more prevalent due to the massive amounts of custom maps.

Games a keeper, and for $20 the value is definitely there.   I've been excited for the game since it was first announced for the PS and man was I excited to see the announcement that it was coming to PC.
The Pros:
I'm still very new to the game, but I love the linear progression, higher levels just gives you access to more gear and customizations, so new players and vets can play together and still have fun.  The shared Galactic progress is a pretty cool idea, so even if you play solo every contributes to an online collective, which unlocks additional missions as you clear out sectors.
Weapons and equipment all feel fun, the game doesn’t hold your hand so you have to manually reload, friendly fire is always on, and you can fall off ledges. (I totally learned that by...my friend falling off yeah!)  Since progress is linear, unlocks just give you side grades, mag increase, less recoil, faster tracking on turrets, etc.
Missions so far it all feels fun, tasks have been varied so far so it’s not just “go here and kill that”.  Each of the different environments have their challenges which is fun, snow makes you move slower, lava planets have small chutes that can spit out lava.  It’s set up so each planet has 2-3 (so far) missions, the missions take 10-15 minutes each, and when you clear the planet you get a bonus reward.
Cons:
Shared Screen - This is rather popular with Coop Top down games like Gauntlet, and it’s nice for forcing players to work together, but I still have to put it in the con side as I find it more annoying than helpful.  Especially with pugs, I’ve had times where I was out of ammo and there is an ammo box just off screen that I can’t reach.
Keyboard and Mouse controls - It works well for the way it’s designed, I just don’t like the design.  Essentially you move with the WSAD not with the mouse.  And your aim follows the way your character points, so it’s nearly impossible to hipfire.  To shoot you have to Right click so your character Aims down sights which gives you the mouse cursor and can aim where you want.  What’ worse is the cursor always appears a few feet in front of where the character is pointing, instead of where you left it so it can be very disorienting as my brain is telling me the cursor should be somewhere else.
I’m starting to get the hang of it now after a few hours, but the I really wish the game followed the standard controls of mouse controlling aim, and W/S controlling moving forward and back and A/D controlling strafing.

The game has plenty of weapons and loadouts to choose from (even without the DLC's) to give it a good variety. Even though the game is still good in single player (at least for the easy missions), it is a game meant to be played with friends, or online, to really fulfill how the game was meant to be played.

I may not have much time in this game, but I spent MANY MANY hours in Q1-Q3A games.  I spent a lot of time mapping for Q2 (CTF) and was part of the Quake community for many years.  This game brings it all back.  Back in the mid to late 90's QuakeWorld became (one of) the first online multiplayer games FPS games.  The games were insanely fast and intense.  After spending many years playing Quake, it became a treasured memory, until I discovered Quake Live.....
After buying this I fired it up and found some matches online.  Just because I played a lot of Quake in the past doesn't mean I'm great - I am a 'geezer' after all.  After getting completely owned in a few matches I decided to start my own match with bots.   After a few matches I realized that the free-for-all Quake game is still one of the most intense FPS multiplayer games ever.  The only downtime you get is when you die - as soon as you spawn it is non-stop action until you die again.
Bots have been a party of Quake for many years.  When Quake III Arena launched over 16 years ago, id was smart and made this part of the core game.  The "single player" portion of Q3A was really multiplayer against bots.  Quake Live is the same thing, though the bots have improved.
From what I've seen the bots in Quake Live can be very challenging (if you set their level correctly).  If you have never played Quake before you can easily start a match with low level bots and learn the ropes.  As you progress you can easily ramp up their level to match yours.   They may not be a match for the Quake masters, but they I can see how they will provide hours and hours of entertainment.  FYI - this is the best way to learn the maps!
I would recommend this game to any fan of classic multiplayer/FPS games, but also to those who never experienced the thrill of the game that started it all.

This game is as old as it looks, but for an ancient hidden object game, the only thing that can be held against it is the overabundance of unnecessarily dark scenes. Still, if you don’t mind a half-finished story and you like old-school HOGs, it’s not a terrible pick.
The Secret of Hildegards was released in early 2011 as the first project of Komar Games, and while it was somewhat late on the scene with its mechanics, I cannot say they did a bad job.
Gameplay-wise, it is a classic hidden object game, meaning it consists of hidden object scenes and nothing else. (There are a few simple puzzles, but they don’t really stir up much.) As far as 2011 standards go, the scenes are above average, although the later ones tend to be annoyingly dark.
Unlike most old pure HOGs, Secret of Hildegards tries to have something we may call an actual plot. It involves the controlled character’s missing father and their family estate, where she eventually learns about a sinister plot against her entire family. To be honest, the story isn’t bad at all, but it lacks an ending; this is why I can only recommend this game with a great deal of reluctance.

Only play this if you are a hardcore fan of hidden-object games, and even then only if you're run out of what to play.
It's pretty much a pure, old, low resolution hidden-object game. There are plenty of good hidden-object scenes, the puzzles are very nice, but there's little else: the story is thin and there's no real point-and-click adventuring.
The graphics are OK, but the music is painfully repetitive.
Unfortunately, several small bugs force me to give this a thumbs down. There are instances where you are asked to find an item and there are several items on screen that would logically match but only one is "correct." Worst, the objects might be wrong: in one scene I was told to find a "hammer" but through trial and error I found out that the required object was actually a chalice. YOU HAD ONE JOB.
Also, when there is some point-and-click to do, there is no indication of where you're supposed to click on screen. For example, at one point you're supposed to use a paperclip to unlock a door, but the cursor doesn't change or otherwise indicate that the door is not part of the scenery.
Still, I'm giving this a thumbs up for hardcore fans only: there are so many hidden-object scenes that it's still fun to play despite the problems.

2.5/5 stars
tl;dr: If it's more than a dollar, give it a pass.
Pros:
- If you only wanted to do the HOG parts, you can skip the puzzles after a 45 second delay.
- Unlimited "Find" button with a 45 second cooldown if you get stuck.
- You get 5 clicks before the standard "oops" screen pops up, and there is no penalty for the 5 erroneous clicks.
- Room graphics are not repeated.
Cons:
- Objects aren't truly "hidden" by being embedded into the scene. Rather, the object search relies almost exclusively on visual clutter. The simplicity of this searchstyle is reinforced by the use of perspective: if the shoes you must find are on a shelf in the rear of the room, then the graphic of the shoes will be relative to the visual distance of the shelf.
- The background objects (non-clickable items) in several rooms are softened while the clickable objects have a sharp edge, making some of the searches far too easy.
- The story is uninspiring and almost non-existent.
- Some nouns are not Canadian/N. American or are spelt incorrectly. For example, a "case" would be better described as a box, a "mallet" as a pickaxe, a "watch" as a clock, a "trident" as a gardening fork, and "mandeline" should be spelt mandolin.
The game cost me $1 and took me 2 hours to play through. The screens were pretty much non-stop hidden object events which was pleasant and what I wanted; no long dialogue screens. The movement from screen to screen was laid out for me in a direct path. The game, to it's credit, is linear so you don't wind up going back to previous screens wondering if you completed the requirements. It displays/removes directional arrows on the screen to let the player know that they are done in one room and are now required to move to another location. As with many HOGs, this one has zero replayability. Get it uber-cheap and gift it to someone who is learning how to play HOGs, and you've got a decent game on your hands. Otherwise, pass on this one.

Vegas 2 is a hard game to judge, as it's not just a game, but part of a rather prolific series. So I'll touch on Vegas 2 first for fans of the series/genre, then as its own game.
So first, for other fans: you're best off looking elsewhere, Vegas is no better a tactical shooter than Modern Warfare 2, "featuring" such inconveniences as mobs of enemies, regenerating health, and a crosshair that can't be dismissed. The planning aspect is gone entirely, and the only real strategy you'll see is queueing up endless "stack up" orders on the occasional larger-than-average corridor. It's a game that pays only lip service to its forebears and altogether a bitter coda for a once great series. One is best off looking elsewhere for a proper tactical shooter.
But, assuming for a moment that the game were to exist in a vacuum, with no relation to the series, then the prognosis is a whole lot more optimistic. Vegas 2 is a rather robust title with a tremendous offering of content for fans of arcade FPS. While nothing particular about the game really jumps out, it's far greater than the sum of its parts. The shooting is punchy, the weapons feel real, the locales are sufficiently varied to never feel repetitive, and your enemies are truly a force to be reckoned with. And it's the AI that really shines. Each enemy feels individual, intelligent, and dangerous; they suppress, they flank, they aggress when they have the numerical advantage, and defend when they lack it. They're not perfect, and actually seem to be artificially gimped to make them easier, but you won't find many PVE shooters with the same caliber of opponent. The actual gameplay is largely preferential, but can be roughly generalized as a slower-paced Call of Duty with fewer enemies.
However, unlike Call of Duty it's a pretty robust offering of content, featuring a rather lengthy campaign (with co-op!), numerous bonus missions (co-op again!), and a lengthy--if very grindy--levelling and unlock system to keep you grinding that treadmill forever. So, a note on each. The campaign features those wacky terrorists making another attack on the biggest casinos in Vegas, and Team Rainbow is called in to clean up the mess. It's full of cheese and stupidity, being just about the campiest thing since the 50-Cent games. The plot is further hamstrung by the occasional attempts at seriousness, notably as a few VERY contrived "tearjerkers". But! It's only mildly distracting, and serves as a fine vehicle to take the player to a variety of wonderful casinos full of wonderfully dangerous prey. As for the bonus missions, they take the form of numerous big non-linear maps full of bad terrorists with guns for you to hunt down. They call it "Terrorist Hunt", why, I'll never know. The maps have a high degree of replayability, and are just good mindless fun all around, especially with a buddy. Finally is the unlock system. It's all remarkably fleshed out, allowing you to create a new operative, customize their guns, armor, clothing, camouflage, gender, face, and turn-ons/turn-offs. It's a very novel system, combining the best elements of GI Joe and Barbie Dream House so much so that customizing your vanity avatar is something of a game in-and-of-itself. By locking everything behind an XP wall, it gives you a great incentive to keep playing and something to look forward to as you progress. A lot of the weapons are locked behind that wall however, so if you're not a fan of Skinner Boxes you're gonna have a bad time.
So in summary, Vegas 2 is a terrible Rainbow Six, but a pretty good and very content-rich FPS. But make no mistake, it's no more a tactical shooter than Unreal Tournament so don't expect the second coming of Rogue Spear.
P.S. Play on Realistic difficulty and if you're obsessive about firearms get
.

SpaceCorn is a text game that might have been cutting edge technology in the 1950s, except that computer programmers in the 1950s probably wouldn't have made so many spelling mistakes, or used the humour of 12-year-old for a publicly-released game.
Be warned that this is a text-based game based upon you choosing from multiple choices being offered.
You would be forgiven for assuming that picking an option would be as simple as clicking with a mouse - but, no, your mouse can't be used with this game. Or you might think that you could, at least, make a choice by typing in a number - but, no, when you are offered a choice, you have to type in the entire answer - again, and again, and again, ad nauseum.
It should be mentioned that the way that the game has been designed means that a lot of anti-malware programmes treat it is as malware.
When I first got the game I couldn't even play it, as my anti-virus programme deleted the exe file - because it was deemed to be a threat (the game had an update at some stage, which temporarily seemed to allow it to by-pass my anti-virus software; either that, or my anti-virus programme had gone on holiday).
My account shows a few hours played on this game, but that's because I had left it running whilst I went to do something else, and had forgotten about it - but, hey, at least I got some Steam cards from doing so.
Here's my experience from the game:
"Level 1
You wake up in a strange planet, your journey was a success.
Your horn is damaged, you encounter yourself surrounded by barbed wire, guarding a house.
What will you do?
<enter/suicide>"
After making some choices about where to go, I went into an upstairs office . . .
(In the following paragraph, I censored two words for the purposes of this review, otherwise they get censored automatically by Steam.)
"What a weird office. There are 2 pink dil**s on a desk
Theres [sic] is a laptop on the floor, you turn it on
The screen is somewhat blurry, it reads something craft
Meh, the game probably sucks, sh*tty graphics"
Talk about the pot calling the kettle black.
It appears that the programmer is having a go at Minecraft for its graphics - but his own game is so backward that it has no graphics at all!
At that point, the game kept repeating the same choice which led to the office in the first place.
"You climb the stairs and find an office
What will you do <enter/go back>"
I tried typing "enter" a few times (and even tried the "enter" key), but no go.
You only have one choice, i.e. to type "go back".
"Where should I go?
<climb stairs/left hall/right hall/sit>"
By the way, there are a lot of spelling mistakes in this so-called game.
For example, in the left hall, the narrative  text tells us that there is writing (presumably on the wall) which says "I like gaems1!1".
As you journey down the left hall, the game gets rather bizarre:
"A key drops for no reason, what to do, what to do?
<put it up your♥♥♥♥♥ignore>"
Well, guess what? Just as with the office, you only have one choice.

I will start out by saying that the mixed rating for this game is well deserved.  The multiplayer is completely dead and even when people were playing this game you would always run into an eldar or chaos player that would run some strategy that you couldn't really compete with as any of the other races.  The balance on the eldar is just ridiculous. I am not going to go into that because this review would be too long and I would like to keep it relatively short.
On top of the multiplayer being dead, there is pretty much no word from the developers on what's going on with this game so it could really be dead.
HOWEVER... Visually, this is possibly the best representation of warhammer 40k out there.  The attention to detail is astounding, coming down to the individual characters for each chapter of space marines there are in the game.  The game is challenging enough to keep you entertained.  Watching as your ships ram, blast and board their way to victory makes you feel extremely satisfied.
You DO have to micro. Alot. Like alot. If you aren't able to give commands to several ships at the same time, you are probably going to have a hard time with this game, but on the other hand there are many different playstyles that could allow you to outweigh the micro.  You could go with several large battleships for close range macro-cannon barrages and boarding actions, or you could go for a long range approach and shred your enemies with lance fire.  With several strategies spread out over 6 races (imperial navy, space marines, chaos, orks, eldar and tau) there is plenty for you to try out and experiment with.
My biggest problem with this game besides balance is the number of points you are given to use ships in skirmish modes.  800 points is just not enough. It's a joke.  I get two battleships and a battle cruiser? Sorry, but I want more.  I don't care if it's harder on my machine or if it breaks balance in the game (what little balance there is).  I don't need to play against humans who are going to cheeze my a** with their broken eldar.  I want to destroy the xeno and the heretic as the crushing fist of the Imperium!!
To do list for devs:
Campaign expansions - You need more from the campaign, even if it is the gothic war.  I love that you paid attention to detail and kept to the true events of the gothic war.  You are held in high regards with the community for your respect for the lore, but you could add different campaigns for different races that could go outside the gothic war.  You need to tie in the variety of all six races you have into that story.
More ships! - These battles just need to get bigger. They don't need to be ridiculous, but the game is called Battlefleet Gothic! Five ships is not a battlefleet.
More races - keep good on your promises and you will be rewarded.  Even with your silence I wait eagerly for a tyranids expansion and possibly more.
Balance - This is the big one.  I am really not exaggerating.  The eldar are broken, plain and simple.  You have to balance the speed of the eldar with the damage they can dish out and take.  They can't have it all.  Figuring out what to balance comes from playing the game against everything and seeing what is and is not fun to play against.  The eldar are not fun to play against, and everyone played eldar.  Hence the death of multiplayer.

The character art is gorgeous (on the rare occasions you actually see it) and the music isn't bad.
That said, "I do not think that word means what you think it means" seems to fit far more often than it should, especially for a hidden object game; a few objects seem to have their names switched, and others are just... off. For example, if it says you need to find a watch, you're probably looking for a wall or table clock.
Many backgrounds have very dark edges where you have to be perfectly lined up and rather close to your monitor to find that last item or two. The other items? Well, if you go around and click anything that looks out of place, you'll probably find most of them within a minute.
Minigames seem to switch between ridiculously easy and time consuming enough that you might as well wait for the skip button, with a couple that could really use an explanation tossed in the mix.
The story seems more like an outline to work with than something that should have been released - absolutely no character development means the few snippets we see make very little sense as a whole, the "ending" in particular. Speaking of the ending, it's... not really an ending; I'm assuming there is or will be another game that picks up where it left off.
If you want item hunt after item hunt and very little else, this might be worth looking into. Otherwise, it wasn't even worth it as part of a bundle.

100 minutes into the game and the scant satisfaction I'm getting from it is from the fact I didn't pay 7€ for it, but got it in a bundle with other games I wanted to try... It's just a generic "hidden object" game with more than a fair share of its problems. The graphics? Hit and miss - and those few "hits" that show some trace of style or care aren't making much of an impact. And yes, as someone has stated already, blurry graphics in some scenes are one of the rare things that put some tiny grain of difficulty into the game.  They tire the eyes - I can go on for tens on tens of hours staring at a computer screen if needed, but I can't play more than a few of these scenes in the row. Varying degrees of blurriness between different objects don't help.
And neither does the game's shoddy English. I was left stumped looking for a "watch", until I clicked at a "clock" in desperation. And "won". Next screen got me a "clock" that was actually a watch. Great. And that's hardly the only mistake. Oh, and the game will sometimes put multiple instances of the same object and ask you to find only one - so yeah, that key you see there might not be the key the game wants you to click, but some other key. Because why not. There's no timer, no lives to be lost - the game warns you if you "overclick" and that's it. Only you vs. crappy text & graphics...
While what seems to be the single music track in the game (though I didn't pay that much attention) loops incessantly, the transition between the beginning and the start of the track being painfully obvious.
The puzzles tacked onto the hidden object scenes? Simple, seen before, and the game doesn't give a damn about you actually solving them, you can just skip them (so far) if you wanna. I didn't, but I don't see why you would care if the game doesn't. They will hardly challenge or intrigue you.
Oh, I'll finish it since I got it and update this if I notice something that redeems the game in my eyes, though now that I read that the game stretches the story into a sequel, I feel quite confident in saying that this one is to be avoided. Shame.

The game on its own? VERY negative. This is not even a complete game compared to what Civ 4 was.
The game with expansions? yes, that is the typical Civ game experience: A game you'd play to ruin your social life, make you sleepy at work, help you fail your courses, kill your marriage (unless you get your wife/husband addicted too, in which case you'll happily die of hunger together ever after), increase your tollerance to filth around you, teach you how to squeeze seconds out of every other aspect of your life like looking at yourself in the mirror before heading out (if you ever do that again) and... In brief, it is THE game that you'd want to play One . More . Turn before 5 more hours are gone.
As for specifics of this particular version of the game, the hexagons are an improvement. Non-stacking units are a nice touch though they don't go well with all gameplay styles. City defense is a shallow concept but ah, well. There are plenty of bugs that 7 years on are not fixed and will likely never be. AI is a bit dumb like before and only wins because of the advantages it is given (Let's be fair, if your AI can solve this kind of problem at runtime, governments are more likely employers than game companies). The technology tree is more homogenous, less in dept and makes less sense than before. And finally, it is a game which is slow as hell: Towards the end of the game there is so much waiting for the computer players to play their turn, even on a state-of-the-art machine.
Turn based strategy is more in dept than real time strategy. I know a lot of people hate me for saying this but they do know well that a lot of RTS is just about pressing the buttons and using shortcuts to produce units faster and attack sooner. Patient sneeky late bloomer is king of this game. That's a joke in a typical RTS.
So, if you are considering this as your first Civ game: Pick it up with its expansions, be ready for a lot of learning, and be patient. And I am not responsible for loss of the other aspects of your life.

If you like Counter Strike (CS) you'll like Neotokyo (NT) for a variety of reasons.
To start off, NT is mechanically similar to CS but tactically, it's a different game entirely.
You have 3 classes each with separate vision modes, armor, and movement capabilities.
In a unique version of Capture the Flag, NT’s Capture the Ghost gives the player carrying the Ghost vision off all opposing players within 50 meters. However, all opposing players can also see where the Ghost is at all times at all distances. The vulnerable objective carrying player must now lead his/her team to victory by calling out enemies as their team heads toward the capture zone. Veteran players refer to this phenomenon as “Ghosting.”
The level design is intrinsically paired with the dynamism of each class' strength and weaknesses, as well as encouraging teamwork to provide a distinct tactical experience that isn’t available in CS.
It's a free game and well worth your time to give it a try.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Hive Jump is currently in Early Access. This review covers versions 0.036.1211 and 0.039.1461.
Hive Jump is a two-dimensional side-scrolling science-fiction platformer / shooter with a retro theme, complete with pixel graphics and chiptunes. It includes some rogue-like elements, such as procedural level generation and perma-death.
You play a member of the J.U.M.P. Corps, humanity's last chance against an aggressive alien race. Your mission is to infiltrate the alien hives and destroy them, one by one.
Graphics - Hive Jump incorporates 2D pixel graphics that are very reminiscent of an 80s game. They move well and presumably achieve the desired effect, but I do find the colours a bit garish in places, and the colour scheme makes a lot of enemy types look very similar.
Animations on the player characters are good, and the different skins and insignias available are a nice touch.
Graphics options are limited to resolution and screen mode, as well as toggle switches for lighting and particles.
Sound - Weapon sounds are good and solid, and other sound effects are acceptable. Music fits in well with the retro feel of the game. I found it a bit annoying to begin with, but it's grown on me. There are no voices.
Gameplay - Hive Jump is a side-scrolling platform game with a focus on action and shooting rather than puzzles. It's designed to be played in either single-player or cooperative multiplayer mode, the latter with up to four players at once.
At the beginning of each game, each player chooses a Hive Jumper to control, with appearance defined by skin, colour, and insignia: symbols that appear over the characters' heads to help differentiate them. The only other differences between players are the equipment choices, which come in the form of a weapon type, an explosive type, and a utility item.
The game proper involves relatively simple 2D platforming coupled with shooter action as your team of Jumpers attempts to eradicate all of the aliens in each procedurally generated hive level, moving to the next by reaching the cave opening somewhere in the hive. Most defeated enemies drop yellow 'goo', which acts as a currency of sorts, and can be used to purchase weapons, upgrades, grenades, and utilities, but only after a completed hive level.
Hives can include doors into special rooms, which involve passing a platforming or shooting challenge, and only give you one chance before kicking you out and back into the main hive. I've completed a few of these and been rewarded with 'relics': so far either cold or 'electric' resistance, or increased flight duration, none of which carried over after the end of the game.
Controls are via keyboard and mouse or controller and are easy enough to learn, but the game doesn't currently support control display or key/button remapping, so it will take you a few minutes using either to work them all out. Available actions are move left and right, jump (double jump and hold to use jetpack), shoot, throw grenade, use utility, and interact. I tried both an Xbox360 controller and keyboard and mouse, and found keyboard and mouse easier and more accurate in the end.
The rogue-like aspects of procedural generation and perma-death are relatively well integrated. The hive levels do look very similar and could use a few more base components and layouts to feed the level generator, but so far I haven't seen any unwinnable levels or became stuck anywhere. The perma-death is a unique implementation whereby player characters can die and are replaced by reinforcements with the same appearance and equipment layout, but the team has a tactical backpack that calls these reinforcements. If the backpack is dropped (such as when a character carrying it dies), it can be attacked by any aliens on screen, and cannot be healed using normal means. If the backpack is destroyed then death is permanent, and it's game over. But any upgrades or unlocks you purchased carry over to the next time you play, as does any goo that was collected in a completed hive level (goo collected on the level on which you die is lost).
The game also includes daily and weekly challenges that differ from the normal game mode and can only be attempted once in each time period, which are a nice idea to increase replayability beyond the standard game mode.
Hive Jump is in Early Access and has some issues, as one might expect. My observations and suggestions are below:
- There seems to be no way to play a multiplayer game ("Find match" is always greyed out)
- "Lore" on the main menu is also greyed out
- There's a game-breaking bug where control is lost when the controller batteries go flat, and cannot be regained
- There are only limited unlocks available: I already had only one weapon left to unlock and have upgraded two to full power after playing for just a couple of hours
- The game gives no feedback to the player how many levels there are; what is the end goal, or how far away it is; or any sort of idea of progression
- When using keyboard and mouse, the menus force the player to use the mouse to select things, and the keyboard to confirm them, which is annoying
- Grenades don't 'feel' like grenades; I think it's something to do with inertia or bouncing, or both.
- There's no visible jump jet fuel meter, but they do stop working sometimes, and I found a relic that 'increased flight time'. Can we have a meter for this, next to the weapon heat meter, perhaps?
- So far I've only seen a very limited number of enemy types, with a few variations, making every game feel the same as the last
- A minimap would be useful
Pros:
+ A fun homage to retro action platforming
+ Good integration of rogue-like gameplay elements, with an interesting twist to perma-death
+ Good chiptune music, if you're into that sort of thing
Cons:
- Graphics can be a bit hard on the old eyes, and lots of things look a bit too similar
- Enemies sometimes move through the edges of platforms and can attack from within the terrain sometimes
- No control layout information or reconfiguration
- No feedback on game progress
- Somewhat limited enemy types and procedural generation 'components' lead to many hives looking a bit too similar
- There's no way to pause, even in single player
With loud chiptune music and glary graphics that all looked similar, Hive Jump annoyed me at first. But after a while it all just clicked and I started having a good time. I think it will be a hoot with a group of friends.
According to the Steam page for the game at the time I first looked yesterday, Hive Jump included 'rougelike' elements. I'm really glad the developers decided to change it to 'roguelike' elements, because they're a lot of fun.
