I have 92 hours of play time in Take On Mars.
This is the only review I've done since joining steam 8 years ago. I can not in good conscience allow this game to be released without saying anything. This game was not and still is not ready for release. It is still full of bugs and crashes a lot. I've tried so many work arounds I've seen on the forum and elsewhere to stop this from happening but to no avail. Personally, I feel like I shouldn't have to do something like all that just to get the game to work at it's basic level.
The game crashes when you try to scroll with the mouse wheel. It also crashes when exiting to the main menu. The worst crash for me, is when you try to overwrite a save, the game crashes without saving and deletes your current save on top of that.
I think a fair amount of the issues could be temporarily remedied by incorperating an auto-save feature into the game. Or even a quick save button. Like just pressing F5 to save for example. As it stands, you have to go through a few menus just to save. It gets tedious to do this every five minutes in case the game decides to randomly crash. Then you wouldn't lose hours worth of work when it does.
The discussion forum is full of threads about crashing issues. A lot of people can't even get the game to start running. I've spent hours going back through the thread's and I've come to the conclusion that these developers put the game into release to make one last cash grab and then wash their hands of it.
And this game is certainly not worth the 26.99 they want for it. Discounting the problems this game has, I would say with how basic it is, it's worth maybe 10 to 15 dollars at most. I really regret the 30 dollars I spent on it a few years ago.
The thing that really bugs me the most about this game is the power production. I had to download a mod increasing the power production of the nuclear reactor just to be able to play. In the vanilla game, you have to build 11 nuclear reactors to power one simple device continuously. With resources as scarce as they are in the game, that is just rediculous. And solar panels are a joke because they produce even less power and obviously none at night. And the night lasts far longer than the day. And there are no batteries you can make to store power for use at night so wasting resources to build solar panels is pointless.
TL;DR
This game is an obvious bug/crash fest and cash grab. The devs obviously want to wash their hands of it. Please, protect your hard earned income and do not buy it.

Where do I start?  I've been eye balling this game for a long time and when Steam put it on sale I made the decision to buy it.  Little did I know that after 6 hours play that I would delete the game and refuse to load it again.  So what are the negative points that inspired so much distain?  Here they are lisited below...
Loading screen.  What is with all GW computer games that require such a long load time?  Battlefleet was no exception but in my eagerness to play I over looked it.
Normal play.  I started the game in solo, non campaign mode.  I started as the Imperium but after 5 battles I had won only a few games.  No matter I jumped over to Orcs.  After several battles there my win record with the Orcs was worse.   Hmmmm.  After the last defeat I saw that the best factions to start with were Imperium or Chaos.  So I started a third game but this time in Easy mode and with the Imperium.  I know...Easy mode.  As a long time computer gamer I felt dirty when I did it.
Easy Mode.  I used this setting to try to get a grasp of the game and for a while I felt like I had the hang of it.  But the next day the game had changed drastically.  My next 4 games were all losses.  My once sleek, victorious battle fleet suddenly turned into something different.  At one battle I was struggling to bring my fleet to together to focus fire when one of my light crusiers, barely damaged decided to teleport out.  That changed the battle completely and I lost.  I tried various combinations of ships but nothing seemed to work.
The Game Cheats.  One battle I loaded I had 4 ships but was shocked to see the enemy AI had 10 and no they weren't all escort ships.  Somewhere in the game my level 3-4 captains, pilots and gunners were suddenly struck blind as I watched the ships meander around the map and those in combat couldn't hit or damage the opposing ships.
The final straw came when I saw an enemy escort ship hold up my level 4 Imperial crusier.  I watched in shock as the rest of my fleet was ganked and this equipped crusier was held up by a single escort ship.  In my 25+ years of computer gaming I have only been this frustrated one other time and that game came on a 5.25 disk.  Forty five minutes afterwards I was still upset!  Do I recommend this game?  HELL NO!
As a side note, I thought about making this a funny review but afterwards I was still so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that was not possible.  Why didn't they have fleet formations but instead it felt like you were trying to herd cats.  I tried auto pilot but one escort wandered off never to be seen again while the rest flew right into the thick of the battle.  <sigh>  I wanted to like this game but like several others it to fell to the GW curse.

My mother gifted me this game, knowing I do so love hidden object games, and despite the negative reviews upon it, I decided to give it a shot. It is indeed as it was explained on the tin, a hidden object game. However, I sadly found it a bit lacking.
First off, gameplay. Scenes didn't have quite as many items in them as previous hidden object games I've played, which I guess made it overly easy for me. Save for a few points of which I must address. There are a few mispellings, as well as wrong labels for intended objects. In fact, once while playing a hammer was labeled as 'Goblet', and vice versa, making it a bit difficult if I was relying closely on the list. Other times, it was... Insanely easy to pick out the items due to how their texture quality clashed with the others around them. I would highly advise the makers with the next game, to make sure they don't enlarge items just to put them in the game. If you want it in so badly, add it in as it's current size to make it look further away.
Now, on to the puzzles between the games. Now, some of the puzzles sure were fun, and were a nice touch. However the sensitivity on some of the puzzles were off. I recall having to try and finish a puzzle three times, due to the fact it was not registering I finished it. And it took a little to figure out what I was supposed to do with some of them. It'd be a nice idea for the next installment to try and polish such things, and also let the player know what exactly is needing to be done.
And to the art. I must say, the art involving the characters was, actually quite to my liking. Characters looked quite lovely, and had plenty of differences between them. Which, given the small cast, is not all that surprising. Personally I would have loved to see more characters involved, especially with the talent of the person who drew them. A pity that there were not many scenes with the drawn characters though. Mainly dialogue snippits involving their base portraits.
And finally, the Story. I found myself disappointed, really. I was hoping the story would have more involvement with the gameplay. But there were very, very few intervals where storyline was inserted. It made the game... Grueling, almost. Having to deal with back to back searches and puzzles at times, just to try and progress the story some. I understand that they wanted to give the players more game to play, but that's not the direction to go with it. Now, nobody wants dialogue and story that drags on, but I'm sure no one likes speckles of storyline either. It's all about retaining a happy balance. Inserting plenty of interaction, without overdoing it, and plenty of story without dragging things out.
Either way, it was a decent game, perhaps okay for someone starting out with hidden object games. But for anyone who's looking for a immersive story to follow, or a challenging point and click game, I would not suggest it. Either way, it really depends on the kind of person who's checking it out.

I thought i had missed a trigger inorder to continue, but since there is zero backtracking in this game i would assume not. afterwards i was just left with unanswered questions. All in all this game made me feel lacking. There was so much more the devs could have done. it was if i asked for a ham sandwich and all i got was two pieces of bread. all filler and no flavor. In other words, this game is... well, a video game. And it makes sure you remember this by breaking all immersion with its very limited and irrational AI. You cannot reason with any of them. You cannot explain to them WHY you are at war with another civilation. Was it really that hard for the developers to have created certain lines of dialogue to choose in order to explain your actions and give the AI a select amount of ways to react to them? The game even includes quotes about how war is a terrible thing yet isn't afraid of making it seem like something that just happens every other day.
So if you're looking for a game about even semi-realistic relations between nations, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a p*$$ing contest with a historical twist on it, this is for you. SPOILER: I'm going to give this game a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ review. Keep on reading if you want to know why.
I dislike this game strongly not on account of being Russian and have some game writer who have seen one Hollywood movie take a dump on the history of my country. Nor for displaying the Soviet Red Army as a horde of ruthless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ animals who were killed casually by friend and foe ("Enemy At The Gates", anyone?), hinting at the assumption that the only reason Soviets were able to kick the Germans out of the Soviet Union was because the latter ran out of bullets. Also, Winter. Then again, if you want to learn history, play the Civ series.
I dislike this game because of the following: dumb and poorly written dialogues, with cliché lines and stories taken from thin air. I dislike this game because of the language, with a mix of Russian obscenities and ridiculous accents (like "Red Heat"); either you go all the way and do dialogues in Russian and with English narration, or do it like in Red Alert-series. This language/accent mixture makes me think of parodies on Soviet armed forces from various comedies, action movies from the 80's and 90's and games like "Red Alert", which negates this game's attempt at being a serious and challenging RTS about a serious and grave war. Unlike CoH, where dialgoues, speech and general use of spoken langauges were well executed, which gave CoH the perfect mood the creators intended for it, I don't feel passionate about anything or anyone in CoH2, mostly due to the fact that the characters make me think of cartoonish characters.
As for the gameplay aspect, well, the perfectly imbalanced forces on both sides are...imbalanced. On one hand you have the OP German forces, on the other - Soviet morons who die like flies from everything, including breathing, apparently. Heck, in CoH I often managed to keep at least one squad alive throughout an entire mission; here, you are lucky if your Soviet squad lives the first 5 minutes of a battle! Even 'elite' forces drop dead for no reason! Which sucks bum on missions where you have to rely on special tactics squads. With this in mind, the intense action and fast pace of the game are more of an annoyance, rather than a pleasant challenge. The Winter missions were an interesting aspect, but, again, with your forces' life expectancy equal to that of a banana in a family of monkeys, restarting these missions from last save time and time again became tedious very fast.
As for the performance, I don't get why this game needs more than 15GB of free space; the graphics haven't improved, the cinematics are crappy; what the heck does it use this space for?!
In conclusion, I only bought this game because it was on Relic sale on the weekly Humble Bundle, and I won't play it again. I don't care for the graphics, I wanted the story. What I got was crappy dialogues, badly written plot and story, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mission, irritating gameplay mechanics, and general annoyance every time someone said something (yes, I'm obsessed with language, but then, I'm also a linguist, so shovel it, OK?). This game takes a huge dump on CoH-series. Mods is this game's only hope. What the clucking bell were SEGA and Relic thinking when they released a sequel this bad? And I am not the only one to give the game a scolding review, far from it.
Buy it if you have too much empty space on your hard drive or want to revisit the Red Alert universe. Otherwise, you'd be better off with other Relic games.

So.. I played this game for about ten hours now... and I would say it has tremendous potential... but that is as far as I will go. Potential.
While the robotics programme starts fo kinda slow, the manned programme throws into the deep end and does so in a very immersive way. You are actually afraid of running out of oxygen...
Soo.. now for the other side of the medal. Bugs... everywhere... and the occasional probelm with the UI or generally how the  player interacts with the surroundings. Ramps are aparently a massive problem! You can not simply walk up a ramp. You'll get stuck and have to jump (and jumping is dangerous.. more on that later). Once I parked my vehicle on a slope so it was tipped slightly to one side. My character, always facing exactly 90 degrees from the ground would simply not fit through the now slanted (reliative to him) doorframe anymore.
Another thing is buttons... you can't reliably press them... and in an enviroment with a LOT of buttons a characters button pressing skills should be considered essential.
On the other hand when you are working with equipment that has a touchdisplay, simply stand in front of it and click on the screen... and that is really cool.
So... I stopped playing after about 9 hours... because some of the bugs just made it too frustrating... I was trying to get into a vehicle over a ramp... got stuck... tried to jump.. aand I asume i clipped into something, was propelled towards the vehicle and upon the impact tore my suit and died... it had been a while since I last saved.... (no autosaves and no quicksaves make it really hard to keep on top of that).
As for the robotics... I built my first rover launched it to a site somewhat close to the edge of the map... It missed its drop zone... by enough to entirely miss the map... and it just kept falling the distance numbers next to the site markes started growing bigger again after a while... and it just kept falling... and since I had spend my last few coins on that rover I was stuck...
So in its current state I cannot really recommend the game... but If the devs iron out the most annoying of these bugs and glitches I think it can be a very interesting game. Let's hope for the official release!

The developers took the best things of an interesting turn based tabletop game and turned it to the worst in a 2dimensional real time environment.
If you want to make it real time clickfest (because thats what this game is) so be it, but then add the third dimension to the combat.
The combat is meant to be broadside style? ok then keep it in 2 dimensions like the tabletop version but for goofs sake make it turn based.
Once you start playing is like watching ships floating on some invisible pudding.
The gameplay features are really nice, lots of customization, skirmish mode for those who want to play solo outside the campaign, an interesting campaign mode aswell (havent advanced much yet), the ships look amazing, but making this game a real time was a terrible mistake.
It has a slow motion mode that allows you to issue commands with some logic other than click-click-click-click, but that does not change the fact that a real time game in space should have that 3rd dimension available.
Its a nice looking game and all but at the end of the day and having purchased it for 14 dollars on a sale, I think I made a terrible mistake, should have listened to my common sense.
I dont recomend it but it is not necesarily a bad game if you like real time strategy.

You unlock guns as you advance in rank, and some fun perks like different types of grenades and weapon enhancements. There is also something of a perk spec system, RPG like, but not RPG. You end up spending research points on weapon upgrades, and upgrading your orbit drop abilities.

This game is just too much fun!
Remember that black dude at the beginning of the first Daniel Craig Bond movie that's jumping and climbing all over ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like a boss?  Do you want to be that guy, only head-bashing zombies, crafting weapons, and throwing molotov cocktails ate the same time?  Then, yeah, you need to buy this game immediately.
So, alot of the negative reviews...  Yeah, so parts of the main story (i.e., the main villain scenarios) are pretty cheesy and cliche.  And yeah, as far as the main story goes, the protagonist brings alot of unnecessary drama upon himself.  And yeah, if you rush through the main campaign you can beat the game in probably 10-20 hours (if you don't mind dying and hitting the continue button alot).  And yeah, the zombies are hard to kill.
However, what those reviews don't tell you, is...
- Aside from those main villain scenarios, the game is packed with side quests that are not only fun and engaging.  But that offer a ton of story-based play-time.
- The voice acting is actually very good.  Especially by the main character, not only in his interaction with other characters, but in his interaction with the world.  Very well done.
- The skill progression system is nice and easy, but offers plenty of needed upgrades and special abilities for your runner.  It also allows for a wide variety of play styles (especially in regards to combat).
- You want weapons?  We've got weapons!  Knives, hammers, clubs, wrenches, machetes, swords, police batons, pipes, axes, sledgehammers, baseball bats, cricket bats, sickles, picks, hand axes, two-handed axes... not to mention expendable throwing weapons (although the best thrown weapons are your standard melee weapons), pistols, shotguns, rifles (and SMGs in The Following), grenades, molotovs, bows... Plenty of variety in the weaponry.
- The melee system is difficult at first (weapons are weak, zombies are tough), because in the early game you're not meant to mow through hordes of undead, you're meant to mostly evade them.  Once you start progressing, you learn how to mod your weapons to make them much more effective, and by end-game you are rocking weapons that not only slice multiple zombies in half with one swing, but simultaneously electrocute them and set them on fire, too.  (How can you not love that?)
- Lots of ways to kill zombies, and it takes time to figure them out.  On my second playthrough I was using environmental tricks that hadn't even occurred to me in the first game.
- Yeah, humans are hard to kill.  But they need to be, because the offer the best experience progression.  Rolling up on some bandits to claim an airdrop is and should be dangerous.  (P.S. if you're smart and conditions are right, zombies can do a lot of the work for you :D  )
- And yeah, when you chop body parts off, you chop body parts off.  You even get to slice things right in half... at the waist, or right down the middle of the head :D
- It's really easy to get lost in looting.  Often times you'll get side-tracked scavenging for supplies, or rushing head-long to claim air-drops, or stopping to help other (NPC) survivors, and night will hit before you know it.   Thus delaying your story progression and extending your game time.  (I mean, you COULD play through the night, if you were a total masochist).
- "Survival" is very well integrated into the game, so to make each play session fun and worry-free.  You don't get hungry, you don't get thirsty.  Scrounging for supplies is scrounging for mats to make weapons, defensive items, (and buggy parts if you have The Following).
- Night offers a whole new challenge, one that I haven't even come close to mastering yet.
- Despite there being no branching quests, replayability on Normal is excellent.    Replayability on Hard is even better, as not only do the zombies get tougher, but loot becomes rarer.  Healing changes from instant to gradual, and the need for performance enhancing cocktails becomes more apparent.
- For any reviews that say the parkour is ♥♥♥♥♥♥... lies.  It's all lies.  Take a little time to learn the controls, and you can jump and climb on almost anything.  What's especially nice is your parkour skill progression, which (even with replays) makes you feel like a total noob in the early game, and a parkour master in the late game.
- I have a very capable system, and with the graphics setting maxed out, the game is absolutely stunning.  Your milage may vary based on your system specs.
- The second act of the story takes you to a new portion of the city that, by virtue of the different architecture, offers new challenges.
- The Following takes you out of the city and into fairly open countryside.  Although that detracts from the parkour elements, it opens up the driving mechanic which is fun.  However there is still plenty of parkour to be had (and frankly, it's nice to not have to jump and climb all over stuff for a change).
Have I gotten into TL;DR territory yet?
The game is just a joy to play.  I'm hoping that some of the upcoming DLC will open up new portions of the city for us to explore, because this game is incredibly addicting.
I'm really really looking forward to co-op play with my friends.
One last thing, a "con"... the key missions in the main story arc can be frustrating.  It's clear that the devs didn't intend them to be "masterable" gameplay, but rather dramatic cinematic events that fuel the story.  You just have to suck it up and power through them.  It is totally doable, but can be stupidly frustrating at times.  That being said, once those 20-30 minute long scenarios are over and done with, you'll be back to skill-based, enjoyable gameplay.
Welp... back to my third playthrough :) Hard really does make you take the game at a slower, less aggressive pace.  When I get there, it will be fun to see how the next mode affects the gameplay (I can't remember what it's called, nightmare or extreme or something).
Oh, and last but not least - HEAD STOMP!!!!

Played this game on a friends computer and had to buy it for myself, so that's why my time played is low.
Summary:
While this game does have it's bugs, and the physics system can be downright frustrating, this game is addictive and should be looked at by all survival game enthusiasts.  So far I'm loving it and with the modding and multiplayer features, especially the custom scenarios, it has alot of replayability potential.
Long version:
The campaign mode is broken up into two parts. The first half involves you sending unmanned probes and rovers to the mars surface to complete missions for money.  That money gets spent on purchasing new equipment to carry out those missions as well as the research required to build new devices.  You can customize the equipment you send to mars as well, and its possible to use the rovers to complete multiple missions if it is equipped properly.  To be honest, this part of the game bored me, and I didn't get past the first hour of dropping probes to map out different parts of mars.
The second half of the campain mode is the manned storyline.  It includes voice acting (well done imho) and a cohesive storyline that parallels Andy Weir's "The Martian."  This part was fun and well paced.  It centered around a manned expedition to mars that goes completely wrong and you are left stranded.  You complete goals and gather supplies to survive and attempt to make it back home.  The final mission even gives you a 3d printer that you use to craft things with to complete some goals, and in my opinion, this is where the game was the most fun.  I encountered a few issues with the storyline getting stuck (cutscene transitions mostly), or goal completion not registering properly, but not often and nothing game breaking, and I'm sure those will get resolved by release.
However, this game doesn't come without it's problems, as any game does.  The biggest problem is with the physics engine's collision detection.  Object seperation due to collision does not always resolve gracefully, and many times results in a violent seperation.  Too many times you will die from an object (or you) spazzing out trying to resolve a collision detection event resulting in your death, or objects will be sent flying off at great speeds.  Because of this, SAVE OFTEN as this game has no autosave function, and you could potentially lose hours worth of work to a buggy physics death.  As a developer, I realize that physics are important for realism, but sometimes there is a need to disable physics or fuse objects together for the sake of game stability.  For instance, grabbed items (in your hand) should not clip with the avatar, creating a "surfing" effect causing you to fly off into space.  Some of this might be fixable before release, but I imagine some of it might require some extensive changes to the core physics engine, thus we might be stuck with it.  Movement is slow which makes accomplishing tasks take longer than in most games, but that's part of the realism and completely intended, so I don't have a problem with it.
The modding system seems pretty powerful and already there are some interesting mods in the steam workshop, including scenarios for you to play that have unique environments, goals, and starting supplies.  Fun survival vs environment mechanics that is a refreshing change from the constant stream of zombie survivals.
Multiplayer:
I've only played locally by myself on a LAN, so I can't really tell you much about net play.  From what I've read, it's buggy, but the devs are working on making it more stable.  It has two game modes, competitive and co-op, so that part is nice.
Survival aspects:
Resource gathering is done via powered machines that gather generic resources from the martian environment such as rock, dirt, and atmosphere.  These are then put into a refinery to be broken down into chemical compounds, as well as raw elements.  These resources are then used for crafting, vehicle fuel, and personal survival (oxygen and water).
Crafting in this game uses a unique modular 3d printer system.  The 3d printer is capable of building most game objects, but larger objects need larger printers.  Upgrade to bigger printers by building the parts from the previous one and assembling the new one.  Habitats can be custom built through a modular part snapping system.  Crafting and resource gathering is fun, but after a while you might get sick of hauling tons of resource barrels around from place to place.  That's where mods help out (resource cables/digitized resource transport)
Can't think of anything else, so if I missed something, feel free to comment.

This game is the truestest and one of the best transitions from tabletop turn based wargame to computer RTS.
The quick of it, if you love BFG, you'll probably like this game. If you've never heard of BFG, pick it up on a sale or watch you letsplay videos to get an idea of it.
Overall, I love this game. I love BFG, I love spaceships, I love giant space ships blowing each other up. The best features of this game are also some of the biggest complaints leveled against it, such as random mission type and a steep learning curve. In defense of the game, random mission type is there to stay, as the Devs litereally explained it is to force players to make different fleets and make a single build/spam fleet impossible to use. And it worked. However, people who like to spam and not change their tactics hate this mechanic for obvious reasons. So if you are that kind of gamer who cannot handle varables, you may wish to avoid the competitive scene (whatever is left of it) for mulitplayer and stick with skirmish or with friends vs AI. Steep learning curve is an understatment. I play alot of RTS games, but this one took me about 15 hours to get a really good grip on how the game mechanics work. From the purpose of small escorts to the massive battleships, and how the range, pen and lance weapons and their firing arch best support each other. If you never have played the tabletop or similar style games, you will need quite a bit of time to get accustomed to this. The good news is with all the advanced tatics and detail, you can really delve deep into fleet building, customizing and synerge of your feet. Playing with your buddies against AI is great fun. Till you learn how it works, eventually, onec you get past the hard difficulty mode, you'll start craving fights against humans, which is a good thing.
The campagin is good and is easily playable twice. It also is a great way to learn how to play and fleet build without holding your hand past the first mission.
The biggest problems with this game is the devs, they didn't quite finish the game and it is littered with bugs. At this point in time, there are still bugs which have plagued the game since Alpha and have never been addressed, such as, selecting a ship in the deployment phase, locks out your keyboard until you select another ship. Several features which were promised have not been implamented at all yet, or only slightly so, such as the fleet color cusomization. And sadly, due to this game having a rather small population still playing on mulitplayer, you'll be hard pressed to find strangers to play with, I recommend using the BFG discord or forums to meet and play with people, if you don't have any friends who own this game.
There is one game mode, which I truely hate, plantary assult: due to its completly randomized nature. The super breif version of it, is almost no skilled is required and its wholly luck based. Here is a quick example of the game mode: Move a ship to point A, point A is on the other side of the map behind the enemy fleet. Its literally impossible to get your ship there in the allotted amount of time. Move a Ship to point B, oh, you have a ship on point B already, here is a score for you, Move a ship to Point C. and so forth. Except each point you must take a ship to is literally complelty random. A random spot on the map will be selected, this can me in a minefield, on a spot you or your enemy already occupies and so forth.
Overall, this game is a love letter to the tabletop game and it shows, even through the problems and hurdles this game has, how much the Devs actually like the property they are working with they made a gem of a game. I love this game and encourage all those to give it a try, if you're into the genre.

This is an OK game. As far as a spiritual successor to C64 Red Storm Rising I would agree in that it has about the same level of complexity and realism. It is a very simplistic sub combat model suitable for the casual player. I'm a little disappointed in some of the interface mechanics. For example, there is no running time indicated for torpedos. The torpedos should have a countdown timer. There is also no way in game to get weapon statistics for either your own platform or the enemy. So unless you have them memorized or printed you cant look up ranges and speeds of weapons. The signature analysis is ridiculously simple. With so few platforms in the database, you can identify an acoustic contact in about 10 seconds. The signature analysis could have been so much more realistic with a few more tweaks like doppler shift and variable signature based on target speed. It is Red Storm Rising with a new skin, but with some extra work, it could have been much better. If you are interested in a casual experience, this is for you. If you are a sim fan and want some weapon and sensor platform realism try Command Modern Naval/Air Operations or the Silent Hunter games. I hope this game will be updated with some more flesh.

Ammunition and time management are as important as situational awareness and planning ahead. Solid controls, good gameplay, great tension.
Con's:
Graphics aren't great. Tutorials are bad, just go to YouTube and learn from others.
Cold Waters is a very different game (ok, probably not if you play a lot of sub sims), the pacing is varied, some missions feel very slow and all you do is wait for a telltale sound of another sub, some missions are breakneck torpedo spamming nightmares.
The dev's appear to be continually adding new content, new subs, campaigns and such. I initially stopped playing after about three weeks of playing every day. I was even dreaming about torpedo evasion. But now there's a new campaign, and the mod community is going mad, so maybe I'll be back to sea...

A wonderful pseudo-arcade submarine simulator game. Cold Waters may not have the same "simulation" feel as games from the Silent Hunter series, but it more than makes up for it in excitement and heart. Cold Waters feels like something out of a Tom Clancey novel. Tactics are important, and the action can be incredibly tense at times. Highly recommended for anyone intrigued by the idea of commanding a submarine during the Cold War (and other more recent campaigns, thanks to the awesome modding community!).

AWESOME game.  This is not another photo-collage, inventory-focused murder mystery!  Searching for clues feels natural and actually makes sense, the graphics are absolutely gorgeous...And most importantly, it has an extremely rich, original, rewarding storyline.
Typically I'm not a fan of murder mysteries, but this one is more like the earlier Myst titles in its powerful sense of atmosphere.  Realtime, full-3D that looks REAL is just crazy awesome.  I know there are plenty of titles out there with great graphics, but this one gets it all just exactly right.
There are actual easter eggs in the game, too.  I'll be replaying this one a time or two just to explore a little more.
The game doesn't hold your hand; it doesn't have a handy-dandy HUD to tell you what to do; and it doesn't have an interactive map and magical floating location markers in case you're not very bright.  However, you don't just drown either.  You're given a nudge or two to make sure you can actually find what you're looking for, but you still have to figure out WHAT you're looking for, and then you work out WHERE to look for it.  THEN you start scouring, after plenty of honing-in.  But you don't just go around peaking in every corner and then magically activate some event.  And the WHY of everything matters in this game - it is actually useful to stop and consider the environment, because The Astronauts were careful to tie things together in the game, not just throw in some pretty distractions as filler.
For a casual gamer, this game will probably require a walkthrough.  For someone who plays a lot of puzzle games, this game is probably pretty average in its difficulty, perhaps more on the easy side if you're hard-core about your puzzle-gaming.  Stop and consider, and you should figure it out - no tedious, methodical combing necessary.  Just explore and think.
That said, I think The Astronauts got it just right with difficulty level.  This isn't an action game or a time waster to appeal to casual gamers, but it doesn't throw itself all-out into the puzzler niche, either, instead pouring itself into storyline.
These guys might easily inspire the next Myst-type cult fanbase! 10/10

This is review is on point (I have played the game for 100 hours + on the PS3, I am a lvl 27 helldiver). THIS GAME IS AMAZING! A 9/10 easily. Lets start with graphics and sound. Both the graphics and sound are flawless. The aliens sound and look like aliens should for their particular race. The explosions/dust particles/weapons fire/environments/planets themselves and all other aspects involving graphics and sound are fantastic. I have ZERO complaints about that!
Now, lets talk about the gameplay. The gameplay mechanics are for, without a doubt, hardcore coop players. If you are not a team player, you will find it difficult to make it through the game alone (but it can be done). Friendly fire is 100% and can NOT be turned off, the game was designed this way for intense fights and epic battles where you and your team have nothing but coordination and cooperation to survive the mission. THIS GAME IS NOT EASY! Enemies are endless and will constantly spawn. You do not get xp for kills. You will find a large learning curve when you first start out. However, you will enjoy it as you can't help to admire the beauty as your entire team struggles to make it out of certain, impossible situations alive. My one complaint about the game is the strategems. Strategems are how helldivers call in equipment/bombing runs/defensive structures/ect from space. These take time to arrive (some are faster than others) and you WILL ABSOLUTELY USE THESE! ALL OF THE STRATEGEMS ARE AWESOME! However, my complaint rests with certain strategems eventually becoming useless or out of date. Do not let this discourage you though. That is just my opinion. EVERYONE will find a strategem they feel is pointless but other players will use quite often because everyone is different in how they play the game. It is important to know you need to pick your strategems based around the objectives and what your team is choosing to use. Another mechanic that is worth discussing is the weapon stats and description. THERE IS NO SUPERIOR WEAPON IN THIS GAME! WHICH IS AMAZING! Every weapon has its pros and its cons and the statistics on the each weapon are to the letter. If a gun has low stability but heavy power, it will perform as such. If the gun has high rate of fire but long reload time, it shows in the game. This mechanic is very well done and worth highlighting as other games have weapon statistics but sometimes the weapons all the feel the same (a good example is *cough* EA battlefront *cough*).
Now lets talk about story (my only real complaint): There is very little story.... AH WHO AM I FOOLING! THERE IS STORY!!! You are helldiver spreading democracy and FREEDOM! AND LIBERTEA!!! but thats about it. But in reality, that is all you need. The missions you go on with your best friends and how you survived a near death experience will create stories. Those are the best kind of stories in my opinion. I enjoyed discussing over chat on how we were completely surrounded without our backs to backs and we still made it out by the skin on our teeth.
In summary: this game is fantastic, buy it and get your friends to buy it. I RECOMMEND IT 100%!
Good luck recruits and to the veterans of PS3 transferring to PC, I"LL SEE YOU ON THE FIELD FOR FREEDOM!!

This is definitely one of my favorite shooters of all time. The gameplay feels very tactical, as well as balanced. The main game mode is capture the ghost, where you can win the game by either capturing a ghost, or eliminating the enemy team. This is a bare bones description of the game, because there are so many more intricate mechanics that keep the game interesting, like how each of the 3 classes (light armor, medium armor, and heavy armor) play, including movement speed, their type of sight, weapon selection, amount of cloak, and many more differences. And somehow, the game still feels very balanced, in how all of the classes just synergize together. The maps are very diverse and large as well, taking on a futuristic city vibe for the most part, and it works wonderously. Lastly, the soundtrack, by far, is one of my favorite soundtracks of all time, no question. it's a perfect mix of orchestrated and electronic, and a little bit of rock, and it melds so well with the game. You should definitely give this game a shot if you want a very nice tactical shooter, and bring some friends, this game definitely needs more of a community.

Battlefleet Gothic is probably my all time favourite Games Workshop miniature game. Sadly, while I still have my fleets in a box under my bed, the people I used to play with have long since moved on and away, so they will not see much use in the future.
Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is not exactly the same game, although it does do an excellent job of translating a turn based miniature wargame into a real time strategy game. It's a game of massive hulking ships clashing in deep space, unleashing broadsides of unimaginable power at each other until only one fleet remains. The game looks gorgeous, plays really well and has a good variety of content for both single player and multiplayer fans. The multiplayer community is decently healthly, although there could of course be more players to match up against. Still, it's not a ghost town.
The game also has some DLC out, which is not necessary by any means. The fleets you get with the basic game offer drastically different experiences as they have different strengths and weaknesses and require completely different approaches to be successful. Personally I prefer the Orks, because who doesn't like a bunch of space pirates ramming the latest technological wonders of more advanced races into bits with their ramshackle hulks?
Overall Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is a great game. If you liked the original miniature game, you'll probably love it as well, and it's definitely worth a try even if you've never head of Battlefleet Gothic or Warhammer 40K.

I bought this yesterday and binge played it for over 12 hours. I started with a Robotics career, I haven't touched the manned career that Manley showcased in his video that inspired me to purchase Take On Mars.
- It's very easy to go down a path that leaves you with no more viable missions, and not enough money to progress down the tech tree to a point where the game spawns more missions.
- the surface is littered with side missions, but you cannot just send a vehicle down to do them. You have to be seeing a big main mission to launch a vehicle at.

- I build my first rover after the third restart of a career (tech tree, and mentioned mission issue). Upon launch, the vehicle flipped radically and parts broke off as the chute deployed. (the player does not control maneuvering, it is scripted at this point). The rover free falls to the surface, crashing. This repeated six times with various builds to see if it was my fault.

- Expect to spend twelve hours of play in your second career, getting a little bit further, but hitting a similar block further on.
- Expect to spend... no forget it.
In summary, this game does not play like a "release candidate." I get the sense that Take On Mars is a money farming mission for the developer company to generate a new engine for their Armed Assault line, which desperately needs multi-core CPU and GPU support. Take On Mars could have been a fun title, but it's not a $22 experience. It is a frustrating series of dead ends, messed up careers, and buggy robot deployments. Avoid this title until is matures (it hasn't done so in three years). This title suffers from an obvious lack of QA work in terms of bug stomping and play "fun factor," something this company is notorious for. Even with their policy of de-centralizing testing, in other words, letting the community test it, this title has essentially been in community testing for over two years, and this resultant game is COMPLETELY UNSATISFACTORY.

I didn't finish the "game" but I've seen enough to strongly disagree with the gamedesign of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. Here, I'm going to try and understand what happened in the mind of whoever did that. How did we end up with this "game"?
Basically, this product is absolutly blinded by its own concept.
The author had an idea, a great idea. He had a story to tell, a world to show, he had a vision. Yet this vision wasn't (yet) playable, he figured he had to make a game to actually share it with gamers. So he went on and did it : he built a 3d world, he grabed some music, animated the thing, and voilà, he had... something. Not a game, but something really nice looking/feeling that he could pour a game into.
Then he wrote the story, whatever happened inside that world, whatever he had to tell. But the story was subtle, fragile, it was precious to him. So he only told the very bare minimum of it, by strange fear it would collapse, maybe, then cut what was left from 80% of its content, and then some. When he was left with only a handfull of texts, a couple of bookpages, some remaining dialogs which survived the sacrifices, he managed to get some of it into the world.
The product was shaping somewhat like the idea in its dreams but now it was real, not a dream anymore. Which was a problem because it wasn't like its dream. So he kept doing a lot of wrong moves and classic game design errors until he somehow figured that it was "ready to ship" (I know that because the game's binary is called "AstronautsGame-Win64-Shipping.exe", not because I played the damn thing). He either figured this out because nobody could work on "that" anymore or either because he ran out of things that he shouldn't have done in the first place.
Somehow he remembered he had to do the basics : start, options, exit. He forgot to get rid of some leftover "gaming elements" so he put in some keybindings to do other things than just moving around. Someone must have told him very loudly that his game was TOO SLOW, so he placed a Run button just for the sake of it, not that he seemed to care.
Whatever he had in mind stayed where it was. What he shipped to the world was a crude piece of nothingness. It really feels like there was something in the game, and then everything was removed before someone could enjoy it. That would have been far too... popular, vulgar. That would have been gross, ew! Someone enjoy himself! Thinking, reacting, choosing, playing! Yuk!
Let's dwelve into the tenderness of doing nothing at all, instead. Let's hear noises, read few words, and virtually walk for miles. Let's not instruct anything to anyone, let's not prevent any player from missing the only point we had to make, and then let's call it elegance or any similar ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to top it all.
What a sweet time wasted for everyone involved.

It is quite a feat for a game to completely and utterly absorb a player into its world. It is an entirely more impressive feat when the only gameplay consists of walking and simple puzzles.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is very short. It took me about 3 hours to play through it, taking plenty of screenshots on the way (as well as just gazing into the exquisitely rendered distance).
The core premise of the 'game' (similar vein to the Stanley Parable and Dear Esther, more interactive fiction than anything else) is that you are a detective that specialises in supernatural incidents, and that this will be your final case.
Paul Prospero (the player) provides retrospective commentary as you progress through the story, happen upon new zones and complete the puzzles (any order, I accidentally missed the first one in my playthrough until I came back later... lost in the scenery). This commentary serves the purpose of indicating story progression as you push through each scene and letting you know that you are not alone in this foreboding world.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter does several things very well:
- Generating atmosphere
- Communicating a troubling and unnerving story
- Making walking through a zone with very little to interact with engaging
Depending on how easily you scare (I scare extremely easily), The Vanishing of Ethan Carter will most likely unsettle you. The game world is stunning and vibrant, yet something seems so very, very wrong right from the get-go and this played on my mind every step of the way. Particularly the mines section...
Even if you aren't ruffled by the game's atmosphere, I can almost guarantee that you will still appreciate just how wrong the world feels which is of utmost importance to the game's communication with the player.
The story itself is quite good. Hardly groundbreaking, but the way it shifts from something that wouldn't be out of place in an X Files episode (minus the scepticism) to a disturbing family drama (albeit a Lovecraftian one) is admirable, though it does perhaps meander a mite too much in the later stages. Regardless, Ethan's plight is enthralling, and is communicated extremely well.
If I have one major complaint, it ties into a 'puzzle' (more of a chase sequence) in the early game (shortly after the initial puzzle). It corresponds with one of Ethan's stories, but the way it is delivered shattered my immersion. If/when you stumble across it, you'll know what I'm talking about. You may not feel the same way, but you'll definitely know what it is I am referring to.
Performance-wise, I was able to run it on my aging laptop (GT630M, 8 gigs DDR3 RAM, 2.4GHz Core i7 mobile processor) on max settings at 60 frames per second... while I was looking at the sky. Jokes aside, it ran at a cinematic 25 fps (on average) which was less than ideal, but the low framerate does not impact the experience as much as it would a twitch shooter or real time strategy game so I put up with it.
For the purposes of testing later on, I dropped settings to medium/low and came up with far superior framerates.
In summary:
+ Engrossing story
+ Extraordinarily atmospheric
+ Absolutely exquisite visual quality
- Quite short
*I* strongly recommend The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, though some folks might find the price of entry steep for the amount of time they will probably extract from the game. It was enough for me, however, and I fully plan on playing through once again after I have built my PC.

This game is just too much fun!
Remember that black dude at the beginning of the first Daniel Craig Bond movie that's jumping and climbing all over ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like a boss?  Do you want to be that guy, only head-bashing zombies, crafting weapons, and throwing molotov cocktails ate the same time?  Then, yeah, you need to buy this game immediately.
So, alot of the negative reviews...  Yeah, so parts of the main story (i.e., the main villain scenarios) are pretty cheesy and cliche.  And yeah, as far as the main story goes, the protagonist brings alot of unnecessary drama upon himself.  And yeah, if you rush through the main campaign you can beat the game in probably 10-20 hours (if you don't mind dying and hitting the continue button alot).  And yeah, the zombies are hard to kill.
However, what those reviews don't tell you, is...
- Aside from those main villain scenarios, the game is packed with side quests that are not only fun and engaging.  But that offer a ton of story-based play-time.
- The voice acting is actually very good.  Especially by the main character, not only in his interaction with other characters, but in his interaction with the world.  Very well done.
- The skill progression system is nice and easy, but offers plenty of needed upgrades and special abilities for your runner.  It also allows for a wide variety of play styles (especially in regards to combat).
- You want weapons?  We've got weapons!  Knives, hammers, clubs, wrenches, machetes, swords, police batons, pipes, axes, sledgehammers, baseball bats, cricket bats, sickles, picks, hand axes, two-handed axes... not to mention expendable throwing weapons (although the best thrown weapons are your standard melee weapons), pistols, shotguns, rifles (and SMGs in The Following), grenades, molotovs, bows... Plenty of variety in the weaponry.
- The melee system is difficult at first (weapons are weak, zombies are tough), because in the early game you're not meant to mow through hordes of undead, you're meant to mostly evade them.  Once you start progressing, you learn how to mod your weapons to make them much more effective, and by end-game you are rocking weapons that not only slice multiple zombies in half with one swing, but simultaneously electrocute them and set them on fire, too.  (How can you not love that?)
- Lots of ways to kill zombies, and it takes time to figure them out.  On my second playthrough I was using environmental tricks that hadn't even occurred to me in the first game.
- Yeah, humans are hard to kill.  But they need to be, because the offer the best experience progression.  Rolling up on some bandits to claim an airdrop is and should be dangerous.  (P.S. if you're smart and conditions are right, zombies can do a lot of the work for you :D  )
- And yeah, when you chop body parts off, you chop body parts off.  You even get to slice things right in half... at the waist, or right down the middle of the head :D
- It's really easy to get lost in looting.  Often times you'll get side-tracked scavenging for supplies, or rushing head-long to claim air-drops, or stopping to help other (NPC) survivors, and night will hit before you know it.   Thus delaying your story progression and extending your game time.  (I mean, you COULD play through the night, if you were a total masochist).
- "Survival" is very well integrated into the game, so to make each play session fun and worry-free.  You don't get hungry, you don't get thirsty.  Scrounging for supplies is scrounging for mats to make weapons, defensive items, (and buggy parts if you have The Following).
- Night offers a whole new challenge, one that I haven't even come close to mastering yet.
- Despite there being no branching quests, replayability on Normal is excellent.    Replayability on Hard is even better, as not only do the zombies get tougher, but loot becomes rarer.  Healing changes from instant to gradual, and the need for performance enhancing cocktails becomes more apparent.
- For any reviews that say the parkour is ♥♥♥♥♥♥... lies.  It's all lies.  Take a little time to learn the controls, and you can jump and climb on almost anything.  What's especially nice is your parkour skill progression, which (even with replays) makes you feel like a total noob in the early game, and a parkour master in the late game.
- I have a very capable system, and with the graphics setting maxed out, the game is absolutely stunning.  Your milage may vary based on your system specs.
- The second act of the story takes you to a new portion of the city that, by virtue of the different architecture, offers new challenges.
- The Following takes you out of the city and into fairly open countryside.  Although that detracts from the parkour elements, it opens up the driving mechanic which is fun.  However there is still plenty of parkour to be had (and frankly, it's nice to not have to jump and climb all over stuff for a change).
Have I gotten into TL;DR territory yet?
The game is just a joy to play.  I'm hoping that some of the upcoming DLC will open up new portions of the city for us to explore, because this game is incredibly addicting.
I'm really really looking forward to co-op play with my friends.
One last thing, a "con"... the key missions in the main story arc can be frustrating.  It's clear that the devs didn't intend them to be "masterable" gameplay, but rather dramatic cinematic events that fuel the story.  You just have to suck it up and power through them.  It is totally doable, but can be stupidly frustrating at times.  That being said, once those 20-30 minute long scenarios are over and done with, you'll be back to skill-based, enjoyable gameplay.
Welp... back to my third playthrough :) Hard really does make you take the game at a slower, less aggressive pace.  When I get there, it will be fun to see how the next mode affects the gameplay (I can't remember what it's called, nightmare or extreme or something).
Oh, and last but not least - HEAD STOMP!!!!

In Company of Heroes 2, you will experience the memories of a Soviet army officer who fought both the Germans and his commanders ambiguous decisions, before ending up in a Political prison camp. From the early days of Operation Barbarossa to the freezing winter of late-41, to Stalingrad and Leningrad, before fighting to encircle Halbe and fight through the streets of Berlin to the Reichstag itself, you will be given resources to produce infantry, support weapons and armour, whatever you need to accomplish your objectives, from holding out against a German onslaught to breaking the walls of Poznan.
For those looking to experience the Western Front like the good old CoH, Ardennes Assault lets you command 3 separate Companies against Oberkommando West strongpoints. But choose wisely, do you reinforce your companies at the cost of experience? Do you attack a small outpost, knowing that survivors from the attack will make later areas harder? Frankly the price of it is a bit high (around 30 pounds) for the content it provides, but it's there, so, if you want, give it a go.
Of course the 2 campaigins aren't the only single player modes. CoH 2 introduces the "Theatre of War", where a player will be given some units and an objective, or may have to strike at the enemy to gain more help. One can participate in the encirclement of Smolensk or the tank battle of Brody in "Operation Barbarossa", make a last ditch throw for the Caucasus oil fields in "Case Blue", make several supporting strikes before hitting hard in "Victory at Stalingrad" or wade through the spring rasputitsa in "Southern Fronts".
Multiplayer is functional, though I believe this is where the game falls short. Because players can pay for commanders (special abilities that can give access to new equipment and units), those willing to pay for commanders can get better units, such as a Veteran Tiger Tank.
Another area where the game falls a bit below the bar is balancing. Some maps are unbalanced because of starting positions. The US and USSR can simply spam Conscripts and Riflemen, which can be a bane for both armour and infantry, but if Allied forces can't maintain an advantage, then German Panzer's, Panthers, and Tiger's may just be capable of bringing down even the largest forces. Also, several times I've seen USSR and US players simply wait until they can use their IS-2's and M4A3E8's. This is merely an observation, however.
Overall, I would rate the game 7/10. A most splendid game indeed, those with some minor inperfections here and there.

Much like it's predecessor, The Room, The Room 2 follows a similar style of game-play; Therein, instead of focusing on one puzzle box after another within each other, you're guided into "rooms" that each contain a series of puzzles around the place.
Be it on a table, on the floor, in the back corner of a room. Each puzzle in a room may be independent from one another, or one puzzle will activate another one in sequence upon finishing, but all puzzles come together to activate a doorway that allows you to progress to the next room!
Being quite the fan of puzzle games and using the grey matter to solve these puzzles, I found myself rushing right through the entire game as everything is sort of “given” to you, of what to do. There wasn't much involvement for thinking or problem solving as the game loosely guides you through the puzzles, and found myself finishing this game in 2 hours. Compared to the 4-6 hours of The Room I did a review for previously.
My overall score for this game, would be a 5 / 10.  It's got very nice graphics, a lovely style, a game with working mechanics, nothing glitches or breaks. Some puzzles may be hardy, but are quickly solved with little thought in it.
If you want a casual puzzle game without racking your brains out in stress trying to solve impossible puzzles, this game is for you!
I found myself enjoying it though regardless of it's shortfalls and easy difficulty, which is what matters, having fun with games! :)

I can't understand, why people are so angry about a Early Access Game with some bugs and glitches. Yes, they are in the Game and maybe a long time, but I repeat: It's Early Access!!! The other thing is the way you play the Game. Myself, I had the patience to drive around a Rover for HOURS and I MEAN HOURS!!! You can adjust the speed to "realistic" but that is too slow, even for my kind of patience. For a "realistic" player, i must mention, that you can also give orders in form of timed console inputs, instead of driving a rover (or other craft) with the keys. I am bit over 40 Years old and can remember the steps of Mars Exploration from my Childhood until now, so for me, a dream came true, when I saw the Game in the Sale and decided to buy it now, even in EA-State, because I watched the Game for a long Time.
I still enjoy it very, very much! I have a 4 year old PC and a 2 Year old Graphic Card, not the best, not the worst. The only lag i had was, when physics and graphics, for example in a sandstorm, came together. Then i noticed, the game becoming "clunky". Simple Trick: Save the Game, back to Game and it vanished and you can play another hour without disturbance. And I'm playing on max Graphic settings, so can't understand the problems of the other people here, having massive lags and graphic problems.
As you watch my gametime, be advised, I'm still in the Robot-Exploration Phase, because I want to play the Campaign "My way" with discovering ALL Missions and earn lots of money. You may play the Game another way and that's also, what pleased me much: Do what you want, when you want, where you want and follow the path of Exploration, but: LOOK FOR HAZARDS!!! The sandstorms can kill your Rovers in short time, so seek shelter behind rocks or dunes, before the lenses of your cameras are so scratched, that you only can drive in 3rd person Mode. I love this realism! I love the way my Rover makes a "Salto" when i underestimated a small cliff. I love it, when Energy runs out, because i forgot, that the polar region is MUCH colder than the deserts and driving AND heating the Instruments need too much energy together.
That leads me to another point: You always can save and load, WHEN you decided right at start, where the Game asks you, if you want to play realistic (no fast forward in Mission Control) or not. A crash? Ok, loading Game, once again. What  are the people expecting, when they play the "realistic" way??? Donuts and Coffee? Self steering, magic, landers, avoding obstacles and rocks for themselves? Red Carpet for your machines and a flat road leading to your exploration targets on the surface? Man, THIS IS A SIMULATION!!! Maybe realistic, maybe not, that depends of the player, but you have to LEARN, that Mars Exploration is a series of failures and crashes. Mr. Google can help you find out, what REAL Exploration is like. I am German and watched with great interest the actual Mars Probe of the ESA. What happened? Another unsuccessful Mission and a bit of very expensive hardware rotting in a Mars Desert! That's LIfe!
Hey, i bought this Game, i can exploring the Mars myself and don't have to wait until ESA has success!

Love this game and totally recommend it! First - don't get fooled by the bad reviews. They complain about bugs, slow performence, etc.
First off, this game isn't released. You need to accept that.. some of the bugs are actually really, really fun and cool. Though, the game is in early access. I would seriously hate for the game to go down, but I don't think it will. :)
Take on Mars is very realistic and a REALLY, REALLY good Sandbox game. The campaign so far is really good. There's an awesome editor mode for making your own scenarios (and just for awesome role play), kind of like Arma III. I love that!
The space and planet mechanics work great. Not in an equally pressurized place with no oxygen? Your oxygen in your lunges gets forced out of your mouth and you eventually die, unless you are smart and have a space suit on.
There's an awesome damage system, meaning you can crack your helmet and break a big component of your suit, and it takes lots of your oxygen away and lowers the duration and time you got left till you run out of oxygen.
The gravity in the game is also very realistic. If you are in an edit mode and go on the moon, you'd always want to jump around and see how high you can get in the air. Though, if you're in space, such as in the International Space Station or a little rocket ship, and you jump out, you probably won't be able to control where you are going due to gravity. This means that you're probably going to float away. You can avoid it by exiting your station/vehicle in space, but stay very, very close to it. For extra security, I hold down "E" to grab it. Then if you want, you can learn how to use a thruster pack thingy to thrust yourself back.
There's a variety of space suits and vehicles to choose from, in which is a BIG bonus to the developers. Example, heavy space suits have more oxygen due to longer EVA sessions.
In the editor mode, you may feel bored.. but then you just need to try things, such as placing a manned landing rocket thingy in the air, and watch as it falls and land on Mars, then step out and do whatever you want. I usually make up my story as I go in the editor mode.. that is what is fun about it.
Then there are also robotic stuff, like landers and rovers that you can actually be in the campaign/edit mode. It's fun to mess around with that. Anyways, there are some bugs in the game. If you come across one, don't just quit and refund the game. Enjoy that it is a really cool game and in early access. Some bugs are fun to mess with! That's something to do if you're bored. Just.. don't get too crazy with them.
Overall, great realistic sandbox space game! So far, the best space game I've ever played yet. I hope to see this game thrive and release in the future.

TL;DR I've had this game for a good long while now, and every now and then I start it up again to see what's changed, but this last time had me really disappointed as I finally realized that in four years they've only made the game less fun.
Let's start with the normal, singleplayer campaign. The beginning is going to be about 15 missions of dropping an unmanned, unguided probe and watching it land for about five minutes, then returning to the menu. Over and over. This could've VERY easily been skipped and the game would have lost absolutely no value. But I did it anyway. And then I started dropping actual probes, and even a couple rovers. I eventually had a decent amount of money which I spent on one really nice rover that I planned to drop in one location and then once it was finished drive it all the way to another, because it would save money which the game does not give generously. Let me clarify, the game gives money generously, but I found out why that's a bad thing when that special rover with all my money on board's automated landing system that you cannot control crashed into the surface and destroyed it. This is "realistic," however this is not fun, nor a consequence of my actions. It should not be in the game. It only detracts from it, and it cost me roughly six hours of gameplay. I have not played this game mode since.
Now let's go to the "special" singleplayer mode, the manned missions. Back when the martian was first hitting the shelves the first iteration of the gamemode came to players, and although the two were unrelated it was a somewhat similar scenario (not a bad thing). It's entire gameplay was about 5 minutes of a scavenger hunt in the wreckage of your ship followed by a Coming soonTM style screen, though. So I left it. I came back to it today and found the following. The mode now starts with a short video in which the audio and video desync rapidly, to the point that they call liftoff on the rocket about 40 seconds before the video shows liftoff, which is sad as not only do you miss the joy of a rocket leaving earth, the video cuts out over a minute early from where it should, so a good portion of the intro is never seen. You dock with ISS (though I only know this through the audio cues) and gameplay starts. And by gameplay, I mean a micro-scavenger hunt through the station to find a console, and then a repeat of that exact task, and then a flash forward. Do the same thing as before where you commit to a scavenger hunt on your downed ship on mars, but now with the worst voice acting I've seen in a long time. After it ends with literally no content added, you get a flash back to the moon, because apparently your character was on the moon in the past. To clarify, the actual stranded on mars part has not changed in about 2 or so years. The moon mission is a scavenger hunt of the worst kind, as there are no HUD cues and the objective is to find three supply drops that nearly blend into the ground, are far apart, and take a while to get to. After about 30 minutes of driving the moon buggy and finding two I stopped and wondered why I just wasted all this time doing literally nothing that I want from a game like this. So far the ENTIRE manned portion of the game is just various prescripted scavenger hunts accompanied by horrible acting and poor design.
Now let's move onto the multiplayer. There is none. To clarify, there is multiplayer, but there are no players. I logged today and say exactly four people across four servers. It's dead. The reason being that it takes literal hours to build even the smallest of outposts with the game's mechanics and griefing is exceptionally easy as even the smallest bump can kill you.
Overall, given the ample amount of development time and the substantial lack of progress that is good or promising in any way, I have to say this game is absolutely not worth $22. Go buy astroneer instead, the only thing this game has on it is the BI label that implies realism, but in reality the airlocks don't vent or pressurize and oxygen is handled very poorly indoors in general, and the whole game just feels like a strange pipe dream that wanted to go many directions and never picked one.
3/10, without the awful random chance of losing everything the singeplayer would not be bad, but due to how slow and simplistic it is, I cannot say it's worth the buy on its own. Buy it on sale and avoid the manned stuff like the plague.

This is pure magic.
Firstly, I've never seen a game so beautiful when it comes to photorealistic landscapes. It even tops Skyrim in my opinion. What is more, being able to discover so many in-game sights that I have already seen with my own eyes during mountain hikes (e.g. the astounding Vang stave church in the Polish town of Karpacz) was truly a one-of-a-kind experience. Generally, while roaming the forests of Red Creek Valley one can feel as if he or she was really strolling in picturesque mountainous surroundings.
Secondly, the story is interesting enough to keep you motivated to find out what it is really about. We are introduced to it somewhere in the middle and have to figure out everything on our own by solving consecutive crimes and reading burned newspaper articles or discarded notes with strange stories. The more you explore, the more it all starts to fall into place and it becomes apparent that every slip of crumbled paper contributes to the plot. There's nothing random about this game and I take it for a big upside, especially when you don't feel you're being guided as you can wander through the land freely, discovering different parts of the story in any order.
Finally, there are some little factors which make me like this game even more. For instance, the music is perfect to set a cryptic mood, voice-acting is really well executed, the land we cover is desolate and deserted what contributes to the overall feeling of yet unfathomable mystery. and importantly, the puzzles we encounter are challenging enough to give you the sense of satisfaction after solving them, but they're not that difficult to discourage any casual players.
Summing up, "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" is like a good book or to be more precise a good short story, it is well-thought-over, cohesive, gripping and entertaining, while all the landscapes are so beautiful you are going to often find yourself exploring off-track just to admire the views. Last but not least, it's been a long time since the ending of a game left me this bewildered and amazed at the same time.
Dear Astronauts, thank you for the ride and I'd gladly appreciate you making more games like this!
Btw. the copy I've purchased came with a nice artbook full of great images comparing real photos taken by the crew to what their graphic designers were able to achieve. Plus there were some postcards and lots of "making of" footage.

“This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand.” Well that’s an ominous start to a game. You’re in a tunnel walking into the light, maybe you’re dead. Apparently not as you emerge from the tunnel into the glory of the atmospheric eyeful that is The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. You’ve just exited a train tunnel. The sunlight filters through the swaying trees. You can hear the wind as it rustles the grass. The occasional crow or songbird can  be heard from an unknown direction. I assume you have to follow the train tracks, but instead I go off the tracks to see just how intricate the rock textures are. I hear a slight whooshing sound as a ball of sticks, logs and rusty nails swings past my face and hits the rocks nearby. The.♥♥♥♥♥♥
They weren’t kidding when they said the game “does not hold your hand.” This game took me 4 hours to finish (so not a huge game), but I could have done it in 2 if I knew where I was going or what I meant to do from the beginning. Though this wasn’t necessarily a bad thing. It’s a game of atmosphere and the best way to absorb the atmosphere is to wander aimlessly. I enjoyed  discovering new areas, even if there was nothing there. What I didn’t enjoy was retracing my steps several times to discover the puzzles I missed at the start because I didn’t realise it was a puzzle. But not a huge deal. Fortunately the world isn’t too big and there is a run button which helps you traverse it faster.
The only real fault of this game is the hideous save system. There is only auto-saving. It could be because of the nature of the puzzles, but I don’t see why they couldn’t have saving in the in-between parts. This wouldn’t be a huge factor if the auto-saving system wasn’t absolutely terrible. It only auto-saves after you finish a puzzle, or when you use an certain old elevator. That’s it. If you spend half an hour looking for a puzzle, then 10 minutes working out that puzzle. Then unless you solve it, that 40 minutes was for nothing. It almost put me off the game, especially when the above happened to me. Later, I found out that one of the autosaves occurs before your entirely complete one of the puzzles, and I din’t realise it was unfinished until the end of the game.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the most visually impressive games I’ve ever played. It’s incredibly photo-realistic with amazing textures. I won’t deny that I’m a bit of a sap for great graphics.  It is well worth the $20 I paid for it, despite the short play time. I do recommend it playing it all one playthrough, if not only to avoid the save system.

I bought Take on Mars (TKOM) a couple of years ago, following an article in PCG, while it was early in it's early access phase.  It was at the time monstrously, hideously, gloriously broken.  How broken you ask?  Well, most of the main game didn’t work and while there was a game engine for clamouring around on Mars, trying to build anything usually resulted in catapulting fragments of base hundreds of meters away.  Your character on Mars also lumbered about like an arthritic pensioner in the final stages of terminal collapse, and it crashed at the merest hint of a physics-object conflict.
And yet…I kept playing it.  Slowly, glacially slowly, updates came out.  Months went by at one point where a build made it impossible to play at all.  Most games like this, I’d have shrugged, written off the purchase price as an object lesson in looking before I lept and moved on.  But I’ve never uninstalled it, and periodically, between games of GTA, Kerbal and Metal Gear, I’d pop back to Mars to see how things were going.
As a result of my continued curiosity, I’ve somehow managed to sink over 60 hours into this game now, and rising.  It is still, safe to say, far from polished.  Movement is still a challenge.  Building anything before starving to death or running out of essential minerals, certainly in the core ‘manned exploration’ missions is a Sisyphean struggle.  But it DOES payback in spades in giving you that feeling of being the first person on Mars, exploring in a hostile environment.  Survival SHOULD be challenging, and every minor victory feels like a grand slam.  Didn’t starve to death before getting the mobile lab down?  VICTORY!  Managed to work out how to build a working, modular 3D printer? VICTORY!  Damn…out of resources to build anything else though…
Don’t buy this game if you’re lucking for something easy to play, honestly hours can be sucked in and you’ll only make teeny, tiny progress.  But what progress you, and the developers, make in TKOM, will really feel satisfying!  See you on the dawn side…

I've played this game for over a decade and a half, and I still return to it from time to time. In contrast with the Kalypso releases of this game (Patrician IV) this game has a far more detailed background system that controls the market, and the way to get a promotion isn't as restricted as in Patrician IV (No requirements for boats, businesses etc. Instead, it's about reputation, service people, bribe councilmen and you'll quickly rise the ranks to Lord Mayor). Also, there is almost no handholding, like you see in Patrician IV (but enough to help you get around and start your adventure). Another massive difference is that you can build your empire through a variety of means. Want to become a pirate hunter? You can do that. Or try to get a monopoly on iron goods? You can do that too. Want to be a jack of all trades? You guessed it, you can do that as well. The choice is yours.
Some minor points:
- Graphics are a bit dated, but that doesn't spoil the game-play in my opinion.
- No standard full HD, but there are modded files you can use which give you 1080p
- Mouse input is a bit strange for some reason (but not frustratingly so, because it isn't an FPS)

Being one who played the original tabletop Gothic back when it was launched in the 90's, I was curious about how the game would be. Sadly, my economy did not allow me to buy the game at first, so I waited patiently for a deal, read reviews, and decided to buy it, taking into account that I seldom play multiplayer, so the unbalance issues would not affect me that much.
The graphics and general atmosphere are brilliant, and the gameplay is relatively straightforward, with a not-so-steep learning curve as it would seem in the beginning, I am not a hardcore gamer, and in a couple of evenings I could confidently and consistently win most battles, it is only a matter of getting used to the interface, and of withholding those boarding actions on the dreaded Data Recovery missions everyone complains of. Skirmish mode is a delight to play, even if the Tau simply railroad most other navies, but you can play it casually and try new tactics for the campaign mode, or simply play other races, while at the same time see progress. Campaign mode is very good too, with an interesting story, even if the side missions become somewhat repetitive after a while.
In my opinion, if you like playing solo, get this game at a sale and you will not regret it, i think I paid about 20 euro for the game and the DLC and for the moment is money well spent. But it is a shame development appears abandoned, this game has so much untapped potential...
