Alright I just finished watching this movie as I love mindbending films and games about quantum physics and I decided to write a proper review about it.
This movies plot is about a man who lost his wife in a car accident and as he falls into depression, he decides to bet his life on a theory called the multiverse theory (A theory that means that there are millions of different parallell universes apart from our own). This results in that he builds the Quantum Suicide Machine which allows him to jump between these different universes in order to find an universe where his wife is still alive.
Plot: 6/10
The plot is to me pretty much the only thing that makes this movie decent. The plot is everything in this movie. Everything else looks like the result of a teenager creating a movie for a school project. It doesn't look one bit professional. The characters are literally 6 people and 6 people only. You don't see even one human being except for these 6, even when the main character is in the middle of a city. This makes the movie really unrealistic. The actors are also not very good at acting in general. Honestly, I don't even think these guys are actors at all, just some random people that the directors thought looked like the characters they imagined while writing the script. The best actor in PARADOX according to me is the main characters wife as she is the only one with an actual realistic personality.
Characters: 2/10
About the camera, you know when you were young and wanted to create a random movie or simply had school and the teacher forced you to film a 5 min long movie with your group as the actors and you are the camera man who never have filmed a movie in your entire life so you literally run after the actors with the camera, this is the very definition of the cameraman in this movie. Sometimes he just stand still and films the actors while the camera shakes, or he walks after them while they walk and so on. In very few cases, the camera is actually still for once.
Camera: 2/10
The one who edited the movie looks like an amateur as well. The editing looks like the ones behind the movie went to some freelancer site and hired some amateur guy for 5 bucks to edit this film in Windows Live Movie Maker.
Editing: 1/10
The music is actually pretty good according to me. Its mysterious and quiet enough for you to be able to focus on the movie without even noticing that it's even there while still being noticeable if you try to listen.
Music: 6/10
As a quantum physics based movie, I found it incredibly dull. There is nothing special that stands out except for the negative aspects. And it has the one thing that a quantum physics movie or game never ever should be: OBVIOUS plottwists. Plottwists are a must in these kinds of movies or games but they should never be obvious. In the first 5 minutes watching the movie, I figured out the thing that was supposed to be the major plottwist blowing your mind the last 10 minutes of the movie.
Lastly, I just want to say that this movie is definitely worth the money if this is one of the first time travel movies you've ever seen as the plottwists probably aren't gonna be that obvious to somebody who doesn't really know what multiverse and paradoxes really are. However, if you're a time travel/quantum physics fan like me, don't even bother rent or buy this movie. It's simply not worth it. Go play the Zero Escape trilogy instead or find another movie with better quality than this one.
Overall movie score: 3/10
I like this movie alot, it reminds me of Inception and Interstellar but stands on it's own.  Very very good sci-fi thriller, worth the watch in my opinion.

When I first saw the trailer for VEC I was pretty excited. The world was beautiful, the mechanics were clean, and the play style was new and refreshing. The creator made it seem like open world gaming was finally beeing taken seriously and I just HAD to play it. When I did I found that the world WAS beautiful, the mechanics WERE clean, and the play style WAS new and refreshing. HOWEVER, It is definitely not an open world game. Running around I wanted to explore the vibrant world, in the beginning I felt like I was getting off the beaten path. But I soon found out that that wasn't the case. The world is not open and the game play is actually very linear. You can't stray too far on this "theme park" game. Each section of the map has a specific reason for being there, you can complete each section in any order you want, but other than that, there really isn't much exploring. There are only a handful of buildings, fewer that you can actually enter in to. The natural environment is fenced in by a bunch of rock slides, and the locale is just very empty feeling. I explored the entire "open" world, and it only took me around 3 hours. 3 hours is on the shorter side of games (I usually enjoy playing games that are 4-6 hours long). The game was fun and entertaining FOR SURE, but it has no replay value, no explorable value. The story is ok at the end. They build it up to be something great and the ending is just mediocre.
World - 7/10 (10/10 for looks, -3 pts for not being able to fully explore it like advertised)
Story - 5/10 (Did M. Knight Shamalan write this story? absolute let down)
Mechanics/Style - 10/10 (would love to play another full game or some DLC of the same style)
Overall - 7.5/10
It is an ok game to play, I guess I would recommend it.

This was recommended to me by a coursemate not long ago.  The description was rather simple, straightforward and the screenshots he posted were spectacular and sparked my curiosity. I have to say it was worth every penny.
Immediately after being submerged into the game I was overwhelmed by the environment and its atmosphere. I was constantly spamming F12 as I explored the regions; I wanted to document the whole journey. The level of detail on every aspect of the game was incredible; terrain, vehicles and interactive objects, you name it.
I've always been accustomed to standard games where you have numerous commands, so it was a change for me to play a game where the gameplay was limited to so few controls. But don't get me wrong this was no issue at all. The murder scenes and reconstructing the events were a lot of fun, I do wish there were a several more of them. When investigating objects related to these events and your thoughts visualise themselves as words around you it reminded me of Sherlock (Benedict Cumberbatch) and his mind palace. Since open exploration is what the developers probably wanted it was good of them to make it so that you had to search for these said objects rather than having all of them there at the scene waiting for you.
From the title alone one might assume this is a simple investigation; that you're trying to find Ethan and discover what happened to his family. However as you pick up the pieces it's becomes clear that there is an unseen darkness at work; a mystery that serves as the subplot as you progress. Be sure to read everything and interact with any object you can you find!
The one frustration I found with this game is the auto save system, there are a total of 10 chapters in this game and it only saves after you had completed each chapter, which in most cases is solving and recreating a murder. Because of this I found myself having to replay large chunks of gameplay to get around to the next saving point, which in some cases involves covering a lot of ground. In addition I do wish there was some form of journal or log book which kept all of Ethan's stories and the notes that you find along the way.
Despite this I stand by my opening statement that this was well worth the money. Another personal highlight-no loading screens. It was a delight to play, albeit the odd sinister moment (spoilers!).

Take On Mars is one of my personal favorite games. It looks great, plays well, and the experience is always different. All of the modes are really fun to play, and you have a lot of freedom in either scenario. You 3D-print pieces to make and personalize your base in human mode, and you can choose what equipment gets loaded onto your landers or rovers, like extra batteries, higher-powered antennae, or even nicer cameras. The game is still in development, with the release just on the Horizon (is that a Mars rover joke? I don't know. I don't keep up with that♥♥♥♥♥♥.
While I do love this game, I have to talk about performance. I said it "looks great." That's sort of a half-truth. I run a modest GTX 660 in combination with a Core2Quad that's always on its period and is more irritable than you would believe. Due to my budget-level setup, I get okay performance on okay settings. Luckily for me, the engine the game is built in has the most ridiculous graphic settings menu I've ever seen. On top of being able to change regular settings like anti-aliasing or SSAO, you can set the actual render resolution, which basically just renders everything at a level proportional (or equal, if you choose) to your screen resolution. I play in 1080p, but if I need to, I render at .9 times the resolution, or 1728x972, to get those extra frames. The most recent update added adaptive physics, because those can really kill your performance, especially when you build a big♥♥♥♥♥base for no reason. Hey, I can't blame you.
TKOM, even in its current state, is very playable and highly enjoyable for space-y types. It has a vibe similar to that of The Martian (starring Matt Damon, fantastic film, watch it if you haven't already) and plays however you want it to. If you like KSP, you might like the space program management gamemode, except you may be disappointed in the fact that you don't hand-craft your ships, hand-pick your crew, and personally control the flight. Otherwise, TKOM is a fantastic game well-worth the price, and it comes from a reputable dev that knows how to deliver a damn good game.

You start out with a ship and some money. Buy some goods, transport them to another town, avoiding pirates, and sell the goods for a profit. Rinse and repeat until you have a trading fleet, then some them on auto-trade to do the work for you. When you have enough cash, you can start building businesses and houses for additional income. You have to really pay attention to trade routes once you have businesses, because they can sink you fast if goods sit in warehouses for too long.
Supply a town with enough goods for long enough, and you can become the Lord Mayor of the town. Do missions for the Hanse, and you can become Alderman, the top position in the game.
Overall Patrician 3 is a great game, especially for the price. Late game is pretty much devoid, once you become Lord Mayor and then Alderman there is nothing to do with those positions. You just call meetings as an Alderman or defend your town from sieges as a Lord Mayor. Cash is only useful for buying ships/goods/buildings, so stockpilling cash at late game is rather pointless. Still, the fun lies in building your trade empire from nothing.
NOTE: This game is currently in a bundle with two other games. I haven't played the other two games, but the bundle is only $3 more and the other game goes for $10, so I would buy that bundle instead of just this game.

I have been a fan of the series for a long time, and to see the original game remade, in my opinion, to be better than the original is a nice addition to the series.
The game plays smoothly and looks good graphicly, even at low visual settings. There are barely any bugs or glitches (only one that I have noticed in my first playthrough). You can get immersed real easy, especially in the ranger modes. The game gives you a choice of either stealth, full on attack, or both, which are satisfying to the player if done successfully. The weapon customization is easy and intriguing, with the modifications suiting one's preferred playstyle. The linear story is still the grand satire of the original with a lot of replayability. With all this I really can not find or see anything about this game that is negative.
While some may think it is the same game as the original but with better graphics, they would be wrong. The game is not entirely different, but there are new experience. There are new or barely changed areas. The voice (in the english version) and model of the male child changed, and the models of Khan, Ulman, and Miller to the Last Light models. There are many more that I have noticed but do not want to spoil or did not notice at all.
The story is exactly the same as the original game, but some chapters are a little longer or have no seperate loading screens like some did in the original. The installation of the journal entries adds a whole lot of lore and satire into the game. Also, some mutants from Last Light are added in, such as the spiders.
A seasoned Metro fan and players new to the series who are into the FPS genre will appriciate this game, especially ones who like a good politcial satire and are into philosophy in general.

I played this one immediately after finishing the first. The scale of the puzzles expands beyond the table to include the entire space around you, which can occasionally lead you astray. When you find the solutions, though, you'll either facepalm because it took you so long, or you'll feel like a champion wizard. Fantastic, creepy atmosphere in every space. I especially loved the area resembling a temple, very creepy and elaborate.
If you like puzzle boxes or point-and-click games in the style of Myst/Riven, this will be well worth your time and money.

The Room Two:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Confined in a room without visible ways to escape, all you can see are a couple of tables with several items lying on them. A letter from someone who was in the same predicament you find yourself in. All you know is that the way out of this particular room has something to do with these objects. Resolve these intriguing puzzles to get to . . . The Room Two!
The Room Two is an adventure game where you have to find your way out of six rooms through very interesting puzzles. The first room will be the crypt, which is a very good and easy tutorial to follow. It will give you the feel of how the game mechanism works. You will also be given an eye piece which will be extremely useful to see additional clues that you can’t see with the naked eye.
From the start, I really enjoyed the intense atmosphere (horror), the feeling of being alone in these rooms where your only friend is your sense of deduction in solving puzzles. In total, you will have six rooms to escape, including the tutorial and the crossing, which is really a cut scene to the last room.

Each room is well-designed and provides good puzzles. I really enjoyed the entire game, especially “The Ship” and “The Séance” Rooms which both were quite long to get through, with challenging puzzles. Make sure to check thoroughly each item you pick up; they might conceal additional clues. If you get stuck in a puzzle, you can ask for some help by using the hint button.
Graphically, The Room Two is very well polished, which make this game a pleasure to play. In terms of controls and interactions, they are easy to use and master.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~~

-	Great graphics
-	Well-designed rooms with good puzzles
-	Intense atmosphere
-	Good price point
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~~

-	Game can be beaten in under four hours
If you like puzzle games, The Room two should find its way to your game library.
8/10

This game is well worth your time and money.
I've played both The Room and The Room Two and enjoyed both immensely.  The closest equivalent I can think of is the Myst series, but with better logic and no tedious backtracking.  (And no obnoixous NPCs that I wanted to murder instead of helping.)  The graphics are gorgeous and the controls are smooth.  While a few puzzles require you to position something, there's a fair amount of leeway allowed - no hunting for that one exact pixel.
As with a lot of puzzle games, the game is light on plot, but that's not a bad thing in this case.  There is a story, but it's subtle and sprinkled through the game, leaving you with questions as well as answers at the end.  You're searching for a powerful artifact that can only be uncovered by solving intricate puzzles.  Amongst the puzzles are letters and journal entries from someone who came before you, searching for the very same item.  As you progress, the game becomes darker and creepier, adding an emotional atmosphere that's lacking in a lot of games.
The game offer solutions for different puzzles, starting at hints and getting more detailed if you ask for more info.  You can't immediately click through the hints to the solutions, though.  You have to wait a bit after each hint before you can get the next one.  It makes sense - it allows a person to revisit the clue before getting the solution.
I finished the game in 4 - 5 hours, which is more than fair given the price of the game.  I did need a few hints, mostly because I was getting a little tired at the end.  There was one puzzle that I probably could not have solved without a hint, but that wasn't the game's fault.  I misunderstood what I was seeing at one point and overlooked the obvious solution.  I can't think of a single puzzle in the game that didn't make sense once solved.
I hope there will be more Rooms to explore in the future.

I wanted to like this game so much.  But I am already fed up with it after about an hour of just doing the training tutorials.
I can't get past the basic game movement controls, inventory, etc.  Walking is hideously slow, sprinting makes you exhausted, and you get caught on items/objects/people/etc.  In your inventory, you have to "examine" items to see details about them.  (For example, I can quickly double-click to add water packs to my inventory, but to see whether they are full or empty? Right click on the individual ones, click "examine," and THEN it tells you if it's full.  Uh... no.)
I had to do the first part of the tutorial 3 times because it had so many bugs.  The first time, I interacted with a tutorial "quest marker" before I had actually put a tool in my inventory.  The only way to exit that section of the tutorial was to put the tool in my hand... but I had no tool yet... so there was no way to exit the screen.  Had to restart.
Then, the next time, I was putting water packs in my inventory.  I accidentally dumped one water pack on the ground.  But, again, in order to exit that specific part of the tutorial, I had to put THAT water pack from THAT slot in my inventory into a water machine.  Couldn't exit my inventory to pick up the water pack.  Had to restart again.
Then, it took me 5 full minutes to get into a goddamn helicopter.  The tutorial said to use spacebar to jump in at a specific point (highlighted by a tutorial "quest marker").  Well, no manner of jumping, running and jumping, jumping while close, jumping while far away, etc. would get me in the damn helicopter.  The only way I could get in was to go around to the other side and enter in a different entrance, and even then I think it was a miracle, since I hovered in the air unexplicably for several seconds while trying to get in that doorway.
Then, in the next part of the tutorial, half of my time was spent trying to make sure my cursor was within the 5 pixels necessary to open the airlock button on multiple sets of doors (but not the "cycle airlock" button, which was right next to it).  Then, I was supposed to switch out fuel cells in a buggy, but taking them out and putting the new ones in apparently requires some kind of god-like precision using the rotate button... or something....
Not to mention that, when you move your mouse to look around, your view moves hella-fast, but when you move your mouse in an inventory screen, the cursor lags slowly behind your movements.  There were no settings to change your mouse sensitivity, so you're stuck with it.
Honestly, maybe this game is awesome.  But I have played a lot of 1st person games, and the mechanics of this one are so ponderous that it isn't even worth it to me to learn more and keep trying.  Maybe if I could get through the creeping walk, getting stuck on corners/container lids/etc., having to spend forever centering your cursor on little buttons, or spending minutes rotating fuel cells so that I can get them at the right angle to switch them out (so that I have enough fuel to take another 90 second jaunt in a buggy), I could get to the good stuff.  But it's too maddening, so I'm gonna go play something else.

This was recommended to me by a coursemate not long ago.  The description was rather simple, straightforward and the screenshots he posted were spectacular and sparked my curiosity. I have to say it was worth every penny.
Immediately after being submerged into the game I was overwhelmed by the environment and its atmosphere. I was constantly spamming F12 as I explored the regions; I wanted to document the whole journey. The level of detail on every aspect of the game was incredible; terrain, vehicles and interactive objects, you name it.
I've always been accustomed to standard games where you have numerous commands, so it was a change for me to play a game where the gameplay was limited to so few controls. But don't get me wrong this was no issue at all. The murder scenes and reconstructing the events were a lot of fun, I do wish there were a several more of them. When investigating objects related to these events and your thoughts visualise themselves as words around you it reminded me of Sherlock (Benedict Cumberbatch) and his mind palace. Since open exploration is what the developers probably wanted it was good of them to make it so that you had to search for these said objects rather than having all of them there at the scene waiting for you.
From the title alone one might assume this is a simple investigation; that you're trying to find Ethan and discover what happened to his family. However as you pick up the pieces it's becomes clear that there is an unseen darkness at work; a mystery that serves as the subplot as you progress. Be sure to read everything and interact with any object you can you find!
The one frustration I found with this game is the auto save system, there are a total of 10 chapters in this game and it only saves after you had completed each chapter, which in most cases is solving and recreating a murder. Because of this I found myself having to replay large chunks of gameplay to get around to the next saving point, which in some cases involves covering a lot of ground. In addition I do wish there was some form of journal or log book which kept all of Ethan's stories and the notes that you find along the way.
Despite this I stand by my opening statement that this was well worth the money. Another personal highlight-no loading screens. It was a delight to play, albeit the odd sinister moment (spoilers!).

Only two games in and this is already easily becoming one of my favourite series to play on Steam. Little under a year ago, I posted my
where I sang its praises as a puzzle game about discovery and atmosphere more so than about testing one's knowledge or skill. Everything I said about the previous title largely stands true for this outing as well, but this time they've taken off the kid gloves and upped the scale, along with the challenge.
The biggest change this time around is we are no longer confined to studying a single, increasingly sprawling contraption in each chapter. Now, each one consists of an entire room with multiple points of interest for you to live out your Sherlock Holmes role-playing fantasies to. You're still kind of rooted to the spot, but you can zoom in and out on objects and view them in detail from most angles. Tap on suspicious looking panels or mechanisms, uncover an object or key, find the next device to use it on, then rinse and repeat until you open up an exit and move on to the next room.
It's the rooms themselves that I like so much more than that last time around. We seem to be taken on something of a history lesson of the origins of the discovery of the mystical world we're trying to escape from and the people involved in acquiring that knowledge and the dark paths it took them down. One moment we might find ourselves below the deck of a ship, the next might be in a parlour as the setting for a séance, or in a laboratory experimenting with reanimating the dead. And, thankfully, it still maintains the high production values as the first game throughout.
The increased challenge doesn't necessarily come from the puzzles (though they have been ramped up), but more from how much more deviously things are hidden. It may test your patience a little bit more, but everything still seems pretty fair and more often than not your next step will be signposted, albeit subtly.
There are six chapters to complete (well, it's really more like five real ones and a short build up sequence to the final chapter) and little real replay value beyond that. But even clocking in at around three hours, I think the price is fair and I was left more than satisfied with my final experience.
I can pretty much only echo my verdict of my review of the previous game for this one - a great puzzle game that could easily be recommended for just about everyone, "casual" and "hardcore" alike, and I'm really looking forward to future titles hopefully coming to Steam, too.

This game truly is amazing and detailed.
It heavily focused on putting the player into the right mood and make it feel as if you were actually there. It is based on a book, where they took all the most exciting parts and made it as scenematic as possible. Think of games that feels like a AAA movie and puts you right there as the main protagonist (Crysis 2-3). Nothing stays the same and the gameplay is constantly evolving and presenting you with new things. Every time there is a possibility to shock you, they've utilized it the best way possible. They pull this off without the boring "Tap E 100 times to get through the cenematic" and really gets you to feel scared and vulnerable to this extremely hostile environment.
The environment is very very well done, with plenty of things to do each time you are in a safe area. The level layout is made so you kind of start in a safe and cosy Metro station, which is your home. You will really feel safe here and you will want to stay in the warm little cabin, instead of going out into the cold and hostile new Russia. You then proceed to venture out to dangerous and hostile places both inside the metro tunnels and up on the frozen and dead streets of Russia, to reach a nice and safe Metro station, only to venture on into the scary places again. This is somewhat how you will go on in this game, and each time you reach a Metro station you will feel the relieve of safety and almost cry of happiness. Each and every single level is massively thought trough and very detailed. There are numerous ways to complete each level, even with multiple ways of doing the same style (Stealth or Head-on action). There will be many inactive things, such as personal stuff, cups and cans bags and all that stuff, to give life to each room and level. Enemies or NPC will not only be there as a filler, but will actually be there for story-related reasons. There is a reason this guard is patrolling here, a reason this enemy is hiding here and so on. Almost every single human enemy will have very deep and lore-related dialogs that you can eavesdrop in on, or just ambush kill them before they finish talking. Most of the dialogs are taken from the original books and really gets your attention, as it is actually interesting to hear what they say. Then you can always kill them afterwards ^^
The combat is IMO very good and just my taste. Some who wants more difficulty might not agree, as it is really easy to get headshots on humans. They almost always use headlamps... Yet no one can say the mutants are easy to kill, if so they lie. They are ruthless, strong and a fast way to die brutally. They take alot of shots to kill and deal insane damage, which makes you want to just cramble under a car and hide forever. When amongst the mutants you are constantly aware and have the finger on the trigger always, and when you hear them come running from deep down the metro tunnel.. You better get prepared.
Just a sidenote - All the mutants are very detailed, and somehow 'realistic'. Take that lightly. I mean if you look at their corpses, inspect them and watch their behavior, then you can really see how they resemble animals very much. They look good and well designed, and I personally think they look very dang cool. Nothing too mutant or too fantasy tentacle laser beam hype here. No here you get very realistic and natural looking mutant animal beast (No stupid human zombies). They are hard to kill, but almost every one has their ways of living, like the ones that calls for help like the raptors from Jurassic Park III. So just try not to get spotted ^^
I much more prefer the combat with humans, which I won't spoil the factions, but they fit in very well in this enviroment and reality. I see such parties rise realistic and sadly it probably would happen. Yet it is so much fun to sneak around throwing knives, shooting silent arrows or just doing melee takedowns to get through the level unseen. Or just pack the heaviest weapon and blast your way to the end.
The leves are linear, which I love as open-world is often useless in the end. Yet it is as open-world as a linear game gets. The levels are big and has plenty of secrets stashes away everywhere. Most are of course useful loot, but sometimes you will come by this deep and impactful little secret, that makes you see things differently. That is of course only if you dare to explore in this scary and hostile world. I mean.. There are one level with 47 secrets... They are small and such, but hey...
The story is absolutely amazing and drags you along. I never got bored and was kept suprised all the time, which is something I rarely do. I almost alway guess the big twist before the movie ends. This however kept me distracted and hook on all the lore and stories the inhabitants of the Metro stations had to tell. When you reach the safe stations, you really dont want to ever leave again, but... You have to. If you listen at what people say to you, especially the characters who is briefly with you (no they don't all die, they just don't follow all the way to the end. They have stuff to do themselves you know), they really have interesting stories and you really get to feel connected to them. Each person has so much character, that you easily know exactly who is who. You really get attached to them and your fingers are constantly crossed to see them survive.
I could keep talking forever, so I'll try to make it short now. The game is really good, well made and IMO easily sits amongst the best games out there. There has been very few masterpieces such as this, and it is one of those games you'll remember longer than you own mom's name. It is really a game of it's own. It has some replay value, as you want to beat it at least 2-3 times to get all the lore, or achievements. Yet it is for sure a game you will return to in the future, just to experience this epic story.
I easily give it 10/10
I'll get the sequel and review that too, yet I've already completed it some times before. Yet I really got excited while playing this and almost couldn't wait to play the sequel again, yet I have to wait a few days to buy it ^^  This game is very much focused on the enviroment, humans surviving, the hostile mutants and the aftermath itself, where the sequel is more focused on action and amazing human conflict. Both games are equally good in their own ways and they are very much the same (same world, same stations and stuff), which is nice as you see how things has evolved.
Well that's it. Now I have to wait until the 1st to get the sequel. If only get all achievements if I like the games and the achievements are fun and not stupid (Get all classes to lvl 99.... wut?). I did with this game, and surely will with the sequel, which shows how good these games are.

This review may be a bit outdated but I hope it helps some people: Neotokyo was my first steam game ever -- It's not a hardware intensive game and It was (and still is) free, which was a great plus back in the day. You are an Exile, struggling to survive on the dark continent of Wraeclast, as you fight to earn power that will allow you to exact your revenge against those who wronged you. Created by hardcore gamers, Path of Exile is an online Action RPG set in a dark fantasy world. With a focus on visceral action combat, powerful items and deep character customization, Path of Exile is completely free and will never be pay-to-win.
Key Features
Freedom. Power. Revenge.
Banished for your misdeeds to the dark, brutal world of Wraeclast, you play as the Duelist, Witch, Ranger, Templar, Marauder, Shadow or the Scion class. From forsaken shores through to the ruined city of Sarn, explore Wraeclast and uncover the ancient secrets waiting for you
Unlimited Character Customization
Create and customize hundreds of unique skill combinations from tradable itemized gems and our gigantic passive skill tree. Combine skill gems, support gems and trigger gems to create your own unique combination of power, defense and destruction.
Deadly Missions
The Forsaken Masters each have their own style of mission and each of these missions has many variations. As you explore deeper into Wraeclast, the pool of available variations increases to challenge you in new ways. All of the Missions and their variations can occur anywhere in the game, including within end-game Maps.
Dressed to Kill
Path of Exile is all about items. Find, collect and trade magic, rare and unique items with arcane properties, then customize your character build around the deadliest combinations you possess.
Brutal Competitive Play
Battle in PvP tournaments seasons and Capture the Flag events for worldwide recognition. Compete in Daily Leagues and Race Events that run as separate game worlds with their own ladders and economies to win valuable prizes.
Customise Your Hideout
​In their extensive travels throughout Wraeclast, the Forsaken Masters have discovered ideal locations for an Exile to use as their own secret Hideout. Once you've earned a Master's trust, you may be taken to a Hideout, where you can create your own personalised town. Masters residing in your Hideout offer you daily Missions and train you in advanced crafting options. Use your Hideout as a quiet place to craft after battle, or expand it and use it as a personalised Guild Hall with hundreds of decorations.
Fair-To-Play. Never Pay-To-Win.
We're committed to creating a fair playing field for all players. You cannot gain gameplay advantage by spending real money in Path of Exile.

After several failed attempts at docking with International Space Station (ISS), decided to just relax and let my ship auto dock. I sip my coffee, and watch the ports line up on my display. I raise an eyebrow. "Seems rather quick for an auto- JESUS CHRIST!" I swat at the manual override button, but it's useless. A loud bang and explosion of gas as my hull depressurizes. The cockpit canopy above me shears away, revealing a dizzying spectacle of swirling stars. On instinct alone, and in what could have only been a second or two, I release my harness and dive out through the gaping hole. A section of the craft snags my suit, tearing one of the legs. Still spinning. I see the solar panels of the station. Stars. Panels. Stars. I'm getting closer. I might just- Miss it completely. I close my eyes. I ponder how far I'll drift in 45 minutes before my oxygen runs out. Do I even have that long? I only know one thing... I'm dead. Twirling amidst the vacuum. Glancing at the blue sphere I occasionally catch from the corner of my eye. The ISS growing further away... did it mean anything? Any of it? No. Not now. Not for me. F--- it. I sigh as I begin disconnecting my helmet and fade further into the black.

A Virtual Mk48 Torpedo: $3.8 million, A Virtual Blue Whale: $??!, Cold Waters: Priceless!
I digress - whilst shooting whales is undoubtedly ammusing the main aim of the game is to get to grips with the submarines of the Cold War. At first the interface seems a bit busy, but considering the controls for a fairly accurate rendition of a US nuclear attack sub have been streamlined into four simple interface tabs/ screens, i was impressed. The game offers Campaign and Single Missions, but is split between two primary era's 1968, 1984, depending which era sub you pick alters your enemies and tactics needed for victory. 68' is all about close range duels and knife fights in relatively untested technology using mediocre weapons. 84' is definately more of a stand off approach relying on sophisticated torpedo and anti ship missles and ultra quiet sub designs on both sides. Yes you will eat your own stray torps, some crusty soviet diesel sub will come out of nowhere and kill you, you will get disabled and slowly slide beneath crush depth (ugly), the soviet airforce decides to send in the anti submarine torpedo spam, etc etc. But once you do the tutorial to explain the interface, and then have a couple of goes in single missions the basics come quite quick, a solid arcadey/ sub sim lite with a lot of realism and plausability.

Conan the mighty pig’s sheer freedom and sense of adventure is a remarkable achievement. Right from the start, the vast landscape of the Heart of the Forest is thrown completely open to you, and it constantly finds ways to pique your curiosity with mysterious plants, complex hidden truffles, and enemy camps to raid for truffles and plants. The fact that you can tackle any one of these things at your own pace and almost never get pulled to the main path is liberating, but the way all of Conan the mighty pig’s systems fit elegantly into complex light survival game is even more impressive. I’ve been running around for over 50 hours and I still have plenty of mysteries left to track down and lots of wonderfully crafted puzzles to solve. I’m in awe of the scope and scale of this adventure, and I often find myself counting the hours until I can get back in.

This game is great. Let's be honest, for a puzzle game, it's not that challenging but every resolution made me feel great regardless and here's why:
1. The game is nothing like the adventure games of yore. It sets its ground rules clearly. You'll never suddenly discover that wax plus stick equals win. At times I found myself trying to make impossible things work but as I remembered how the first game played, I remembered that there's no fooling around here. There's clear progression. Have the thing? There's a thing that thing does and it's pretty much never nonsenical.
2. The atmosphere is great! While the first game was decent in terms of setting the story out through letters and atmospheric hints, The Room 2 took that to a bit of higher level and I felt compelled to solve the mystery.
3. I love that The Room 2 never grows so arrogant as to tell you its story. You have to figure it out and piece everything together. While the letters are a nice touch of exposition that eventually piece everything together, they really don't hand it to you on a platter and I like that.
4. It's just really pretty to look at!

Clan arena is a team gametype where you spawn with everything and the team with better positioning, aim, and coordination will win. Why is this the first part of the review? Well if you only like clan arena, Quake Live is great. Everything is clan arena; every freeze tag, every free for all, uh wait that's it. Clan arena, freeze tag, and free for all are the only servers anyone plays. There are no machinegun starts, everyone spawns with all weapons. The last update three years ago added a class system which offered to allow players to spawn with one good weapon and one more basic. This was universally♥♥♥♥♥♥on, no servers utilized it, but now I don't understand why because it seems preferable. There is little item control in even gametypes originally based around the concept, there are ammo boxes but even that is only a maybe, some servers use universal ammo boxes in place of the old ammo boxes to refill all your weapons at once. Remembering item spawns? Unnecessary, there is now a popup above the item which tells you when it spawns. Every server feels like a completely mindless spam fest. All the clan arena servers elo cap at 1700 which is about average skilled, better players seem to have left the game because they aren't wanted so it is very hard to improve. Adding onto that, there are hardly any players left, most of which stick to a very small subset of servers with a high playercap, again a spam fest. There are good servers and you can try playing around in them, but don't expect players to join, especially not duels. In fact you could probably get a duel up faster in Quakeworld, people really dislike dueling in Quake Live, maybe because they are coddled by clan arena and don't know how to play any gametypes that actually came with Quake. If you are interested in this game, I have two separate recommendations. Either play Quake Champions, or play Quake 3 singleplayer, you will have a better time.

Right from the start the Vanishing of Ethan Carter manages to draw you in with its gorgeous atmospheric graphics and wonderful music score. It truly is a joy to walk through the rich and mysterious forest environments. It needs to be joyful, as that is 90% of what you will be doing in this game.
Just like Dear Esther before it, there is not much gameplay to be had and the main goal of the developer(s) is to immerse you into their world and have you experience a relatively short story. The fact that it is a short game is not by definition a bad thing. I personally loved Dear Esther and it was a few hours shorter even than the 5 hours I spent on Ethan Carter.
The reason that I cannot recommend this game then, is for a few, obviously personal, reasons.
Dear Esther was extremely linear and to me this helped with the story telling. You were guaranteed not to miss anything, get all the elements of information that the developers wanted you to take in, before arriving at a satisfying conclusion to your story. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter gives you more freedom. There is sort of a path the game guides you on, but it allows you to deviate from that path into various nooks and crannies and later on you even have some freedom to explore your surroundings as you see fit.
The problem with this is that the story is told through solving some puzzles that are scattered here and there. You solve a puzzle, you get more information. These puzzles themselves all use the same mechanic in which you reconstruct various bits of the story and thus it is told to you. They are not hard to solve, but you do have to find them. By the middle part of the game, I no longer felt as if I was experiencing a story, so much as I was looking everywhere for the same puzzle to solve again. It detracted me from the experience. I missed a puzzle all the way in the start of the game and had to back-track, which did not help much.
While the story itself was certainly decently written, I never felt immersed the way I was in Dear Esther, which made me think and reflect upon what I had just experienced. Rather I felt disconnected from it as if looking in from the outside.
So to me personally, as a story experience it was not immersive enough, as a puzzle game it was not complex and interesting enough, as a horror game it was just not scary enough.

Short version -
Take On Mars is a AAA game being made by an indi publisher. As such it's still in Beta and probably will be for some time - if that's an issue for you, favorite it and be patient. It is however being crafted with more realism and simulation and depth than any other space game you've played since KSP. You're going to kick yourself if you're a fan of real space sim stuff and don't play this game.
Longer version -
It started focused on sending probes to Mars and the inherent complications and experiences you'd find in that. That's already a very rich, very complex experience and worth the money. There's a tech tree you need to unlock, upgrades, scaling missions and tech and challenges that are a fun game already. Pick a location (created from actual surface scan data from Mars. No♥♥♥♥♥♥ it legit mapped from photos and heightmap data of the surface of Mars) and start figuring out what missions you can do with a single probe. Much like current space exploration you have to gauge the money and tools available to you to maximize your productivity on the surface. You'll find challenges of opportunity that provide additional income and so you need to plan for the unexpected while keeping in a manageable budget and resources. It's challenging in similar ways to Kerbal Space Program only focused on a far more realisitic experience rather than a somewhat fantastical one.
The probe missions and content is a fun and challenging game and, again, worth the money.
However the devs have recognized the demand for something more personal and have started laying the groundwork for manned missions to Mars. It's still simple and in a development state and has a long way to go. However the devs have shown with the content already created that they're dedicated and focused on making a deep, complex and challenging environment. That's going to take time and as the scope of the game has changed so has the development timeline.
If you like what you see so far, pick it up. If you're concerned, then wishlist it and wait. If you're reading this review though then you're probably the sort of person intrigued by a realistic, challenging view of what exploring and even visiting Mars would be like, using actual mapping and images of the Martian surface and science we theoretically have today. If that's the case you're going to want this game sooner rather than later.
If that's something you want then why settle for later rather than sooner?
Game In Beta Note:
Some people are concerned with the development pace of the game. Always a concern with indie titles and it's a legit concern. You don't want a game that's been abandoned. That's not this game though. Devs have been working steadily so far, it's just a lot to make for an indie studio and there's no way you can look at the content that's already in the game and not realize that when it is released it's going to be the best, most realistic sim you could really hope for. It is a sim by the way - simulation is the name of the game. From different weights, uses and limitations to different sorts of suits to limited uses in the tests you can run on your probes to deadly radiation bursts from the Sun that Mars' whisper thin atmosphere and lack of magnetic field don't protect you from. You want a quick and dirty survival shooter they're already out. You want a realistic sim that tracks your oxygen usage based on your physical exertion, you need to have some patience.....
and if you want to survive on the Red Planet you're going to need to be patient.
It's been in early access for an unholy amount of time, which is ridiculous since these aren't indie devs, theyre a full professional team. Game's broken, buggy, and never updated.

Neotokyo is one of the few FPS games I have actually enjoyed. It has a blend of realistic tactical gameplay and stylized cyberpunk environments, abilities and characters.
Now be forewarned: This is NOT a run and gun game like COD or CSGO. The close quarters and multiple flanking routes mean you have to rely on close knit teamwork and communication to gain a tactical advantage.  The three playable classes offer well rounded playstyles giving players the ability to augment the squad in different ways and with different weapons. This  as well as various types of  class abilities such as active camoflauge, thermal vision, night vision, and motion detection, all add to the overall tactical gameplay experience.
This is a great addition for people who are looking for a well-paced tactical shooter that provides fairly realistic CQB scenarios, all while putting a very subtle but refreshing sci-fi spin on things.

There was a slight learning curve in the beginning but after a few hours, it got much easier. The game is fun but my only gripe is that it feels short and repetitive. The missions are just a mix of a few things that repeat over and over. So while fun, it gets old very quickly.

Cold waters had a bit of a bumpy start, but it is a game that has progressed well over time with several updates changing the game and adding things that I felt was missing, such as crew voices and ordering the crew to steer for you by setting depth, speed and heading. Making you feel more like the captain of your own sub as compared to playing all roles on your own. And while the game is by no means a simulator it is still a very hard and challenging game especcially when you are new. But once you get more experienced and know when to be quiet and when to be loud then you will be rewarded by sinking entire groups of ships and submarines with ease without them even getting a chance to fight back.
Graphics are alright, but the sound design is great for a smaller game like this with sonar pings that can be very satisfying as your torpedoes lock onto a submarine or terrifying when you are the one suddenly being targeted. The soundtrack is pretty nice too with more suspenseful tracks fitting a stealth game like this as you search for Soviet subs.
My only complaints are that there are very few quick missions to select from and scenario editor to generate your own missions. And also that the campaign feels a bit short sometimes at around 10 or so missions. Though your actions do have an effect on the war so this could partially be because of me as I win most of my engagements, nudging the war in favour of NATO with each successful mission. So therefore the campaign might be longer if you fail a few missions.
Overall it is not a game for the impatient or those who prefer more simple games, but if you enjoy the complexity of controlling your own submarine and stalking your prey for a while before unleashing a planned out attack then this might be the game for you. Good hunting!

Okay, let me start by saying I think this is a game with a good intent.  It's aiming to revive the old submarine sim genre.  A lot of hardcore simmers have complained that this game isn't realistic enough (along the lines of the Silent Hunter series).  It's true that you can't physically walk between stations and manually engage operations.  However, on a modern nuclear sub, that would be a bit overwhelming to do.  I think this game strikes a perfect balance between simulation and gameplay.  On the tactical battlefield map, you can in fact give various navigation, weapons and emergency control orders via an intuitive hud system or using hotkeys.  And most orders will result in your AI crew giving a readback and confirmation of orders, which greatly enhances the realism in my opinion.  This game very much reminds me of the old Tom Clancy game SSN, except that you have somewhat better graphics, a much more developed battlefield HUD and orders system and  much more realistic gameplay (the Tom Clancy game did feel somewhat arcadey compared to Cold Waters).  This game is very enjoyable, especially if you're looking for a sim-like experience for submarines.
Now some critical feedback that needs to be mentioned:
1) The gameplay is very hard and the learning curve is extremely steep.  Even on the less difficult levels, you will get detected and killed quite frequently if you're not paying attention.  This is a sub game, so a covert, strike-and-run style is the name of the game.  The game does provide decent tutorial missions (and a manual) to help you understand the basic fundamental mechanics of submarine warfare (detecting and classifying targets, weapons employment, navigation, sound detection in various temperature gradients, ect.).  However, the problem is that these tutorials do a poor job of preparing you for actual combat with AI ships, subs and aircraft.  There is no room for error when playing this game; early on you'll find yourself dying a lot because you don't know how to deal with the enemy AI's tactics (and they do cheat somewhat at the higher difficulty levels).  The game manual and tutorial missions DO NOT HELP YOU with overcoming these challenges.  There are some youtube videos that can provide decent advice, but I do wish the game had spent more time teahing the player the nuances of submarine warfare.
2) The game still has some issues to work out.  Upon starting one of the single player missions, the game freezes for me.  The campaign map has clunky user interface and doesn't seem well designed.  You have to drag your cursor around to move your sub's icon to various areas on the map and hope that you get into contact with the appropriate enemy icon or location.  The mission objectives aren't always clearly laid out and sometimes you can fail them simply because the enemy force wasn't visible on the campaign map.  There is a fog of war on the campaign map, so you don't see everything; still if the game assigns you an objective and you don't know where to go for the objective, it's kind of pointless.  Some of the missions (both single missions and campaign missions) start you out in very stupid positions (ie very close to enemy vessels, or in very shallow water).  There is one single player mission (Strike from the sea) where you're supposed to do a TLAM strike on a nearby land objective, but you are in 250ft deep water and there are enemy ships and aircraft patrolling all around you...I've yet to find a way to launch those TLAM's without getting detected, and because the water is so shallow, you're dead upon detection.  Just stupid stuff like that that makes some of these missions really frustrating.  Also, the developers need to add some indicator or shading system to the tactical 2d and campaign maps to depict water depth; as it stands, there is no obvious way to gauge the depth of the water either on the tactical battlefield or the campaign map (other than actually driving into and testing the waters).
3) The early period (1960's) campaign gameplay is especially difficult because the sonar detection wasn't very developed and you only have access to unguided torpedo's (which are useless in most situations) or very slow guided torpedo's (slow to the point where everything except a few merchant vessels can outrun them).  There are some good youtube videos explaining how to work around these disadvantages, but again, the game itself should be instructing the player on how to be effective with these early sub and weapon variants.
4) The gameplay options are quite limited.  There are 7-8 missions in single mission mode; as mentioned before some of them are very difficult and one freezes upon startup.  There are also 2 campign modes (a 1980's mode and a 1960's mode) both of which take place in the same area of the North Atlantic.  The campaign map mechanics are klunky and it's hard to control which battles you want to engage in on the campaign map.  You are pretty much limited to playing a few different American sub types for any of those modes.  There are mods which allow for more playable sub types, but I would like to see the game enable that with future updates.  As well, it would be nice to see more single missions and campaign eras and locations (a 90's Spratley island campaign, a Cold War Mediterranean campaign, ect.).
Despite all of this critical feedback, I do like the game a lot.  When you are running silent, trying to position yourself for a surface strike or trying to locate enemy subs, the gameplay is immersive and very fun.  The music, the sounds, the crew's AI voice responses to your commands (which sound fairly authentic), the different weapon loadouts you can choose, and the combat itself (when you can figure out the right tactics) all make for engaging gameplay.  The graphics are nothing special, but they work well enough, allow the game to run smoothly on most systems, and honestly you spend a lot of your time on the tactical 2d map (which uses military sumbols to depict vessles, weapons, and movement, similar to Jane's Fleet Command).  I think this game has a solid foundation, though there are some bugs which need to be addressed.  It also needs to refine the campaign map UI and allow for more user selection on how certain battles are started.  For example, doing TLAM strikes in very shallow water, literally right next to enemy vessels is not very realisitic or very fun.  Again, I will warn any buyers who are casual gamers that the learning curve is extremely steep.  You will need to do research and watch youtube videos to get a better grasp on the tactics required for the different submarines and weapons.  The tutorials and manual provide you with a basic understanding of submarine warfare, but that won't be enough to allow you to complete most of the missions (especially on the harder difficulty levels).  It may come across as a slap in the face, that after spending an hour or so doing the tutorial and reading the manual, you're still getting killed by the enemy even in basic missions.  This game requires a lot of patience of the player and a very nuanced understanding of naval warfare.  If you're the type who wants to jump quickly into the game, see some action, and get a quick and easy victory, this game may not be for you.
I bought this game knowing that it wasn't entirely fleshed out.  But I'm glad I did, and I hope my money supports KillerFish in contuing to refine and update this game; it has a lot of potential going forward.

WARNING: Do not play this game while sitting on an exercise ball. You may fall off. 2Spooky4me.
Anyways, game is basically an on the rails shooter depicting life in and around the Russian metro stations after some kind of nuclear war.
The game is dark, gritty, and at times quite frustrating. Oh yeah some how there are nazis too. Monster tries to kill man, and man tries to kill man. War, war never changes.
Even on the easiest difficulty I was constantly dying. Despite being "on the rails" there are quite a few parts where you have to wander around small areas to complete objectives, and you will mess up a lot.
The game does a great job of making you uneasy. Later in the game I felt constant pressure, either enemies you can't really kill, or low ammo, or low air filters. I almost couldn't finish the game because I was about 10 seconds (or less) away very late in the game from dying from not having any air filter time left. The struggle is real.
The ending was rather satisfactory. I really felt like part of some kind of spec ops group during the final push of the game. Just you and crew vs the world.
Game is paced good, challenging even on easiest difficulty, interesting story, good visuals, and good ambiance. Not a long game (about 10 hours for 1st play through), but worth the time. Look forward to the sequel.

I must say I bought this game without knowing much about it, I've vaguely heard about it before but that was all, so I didn't really knew what I had to expect from it. And in the end, it's been a very pleasant surprise that I've discovered!
One cannot say that there is a very developped story and character as it mostly kept its role as a strategy game. But on the other hand, on the contrary of games like Sudden Strike or Company of Heroes, just to quote some, the men and women you controls aren't just soldiers, an amount of pixels with the same faces, instead, you've got an ammount of pixels with names and different faces from each others which is allowed by the management of a team that can hold at least 3 dozens of soldiers and of a single commando that can be composed to 6 soldiers maximum. The gameplay is well made and easy to understand with 6 classes of soldiers to use effectively. I personnally just loved it and I spend few entire days playing it.
Now, for the (little) negative points. If the gameplay is really great, it still doesn't mean that it's flawless and sometimes the management of the 3D environnement can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥as you may misclick on the wrong case, sending your soldier on an upper or lower position, exposing them to a direct enemy fire. But that's not very serious neither as it's just a question of paying attention and being used to the game machanics.
Another little negative point, on my opinion, is that even if you've got characters with names, their own faces and nationalities, they don't seem to have their own story or personnality. After, I'm maybe asking a bit too much for a strategy game as Xcom, even more by the fact that there aren't predefined characters. But, if you're like me and have a good imagination, you will quickly make abstraction of this point as you may get their own strories in your head!
So to resume, this game hasn't a very developped story; aliens attack Earth, defend earth, but it's more than pleasant to play it, so it totally worth to spend money and time in it!

I'm not sure why this game has mixed reviews.  It's still in beta, people.  Does it crash?  Yes, but you can STILL progress and have a meaningful experience if you're patient and save often.  I can't speak for multiplayer at this point, but in the last week I've built a fully functional base by myself (I'm a fan of the manned missions) and was into full-fledged methane production (a very time-consuming compound to make in the game).
It's worth your time if you're a space/science buff and are looking for an immersive space exploration experience.  With the way that development is going now, it seems like when the kinks are worked out of this game it could be a real-life simulation of survival on the red planet...if NASA ever develops space suits that can be put on/removed by one person. That's how immersive it is.
It doesn't just stop at Mars, either.  You can send rovers or conduct manned missions to asteroids, the moon of earth and the moons of Mars (Phobos and Deimos).  The devs have thought of everything and the attention to detail is fantastic.  I'm eager to see what will come in future updates and the anticipated v. 1.0 release.
I highly recommend this game as long as the devs keep up the good work.

Nominated for an award. This game was gifted to me.
I enjoy the realism, even at the lower difficulty levels, of this game. If your tactics are not correct, torpedoes will find you. I experience genuine accomplishment when enemy vessels are sunk. I experience genuine sorrow when my submarine is sunk. As a Disabled Veteran, (U.S. Air Force), I can honestly say that I do not fully understand the experiences of those who served, and are currently serving, on submarines. I personally salute those extraordinary servicemembers, and their families, for their dedication and sacrifice. o7
With that being said, this game offers exceptional capabilities that its predecessors could not. The cutscenes for weapon launch sequences are amazing. The underwater scenes and details are breathtaking. Have you ever chased a Blue Whale? I have...in this game! Did I mention this game is amazing? I have screenshots of the encounter.
If you have never played a submarine simulation game, this is the one with which to begin your journey. I am currently playing the "Single Mission" scenarios, and each one is different from the last. I can play "The Duel", and easily find, attack, and sink the enemy; exit and play it again, and the enemy will be almost impossible to find and sink; exit and play it yet again, and the enemy will lauch three or four torpedoes from its Vertical Launch System, (amazing cutscene to watch, but do not watch for too long), and completely annihilate me. This happened to me tonight. The enemy killed me first, but I was able to launch two torpedoes during my evasion maneuvers, and was able to kill him, too.
That is how "Cold Waters" will treat you. I love this game and highly recommend it to anyone interested in trying something different. You will not be disappointed. You will be frustrated, but you will enjoy that learning experience, as well.

Hello people,
in the end Battlefleet Gothic is a good game and I would give it 7/10 points.
Atmosphere is very well done and you can find yourself in this vast universe. The music and the speakers are good and in the end you can follow it. The design of the ships is exactly as portrayed and gives the game the edge.
I finished the game with no big deal but with some redoings of missions to adjust myself accordingly. Was not too challenging but I also didnt play it beyond normal and actually I didnt want a heartbreaking challenge since I wanted a nice relaxing singleplayer with a story and the possibility to load my ships and play with my setup. So I finished the game in turn 33. Also I dont judge the multiplayer since I dont want to play it.
Therefore the problems are starting right there. The game is obviously made for multiplayer, the different mission types are Cruiser Clash, Assasination, Breakthrough, Data Recovery, Planetary Assault, Convoy - all missions can be done in 3 - 5 minutes, which is perfect timing for some fast pace multiplayer matches and your trying of new strats and tactics and loadouts. You may accustomize your ships for gained renew points for crushing ships faster, for disabling them, for sensorrange and so on, so in a multiplayer you can try that out and enjoy the fast paced fights. But in a singleplayer all these missions are pretty fast repetetive and even though there are story missions those are rarely in comparison to the normal typical missions. The repetetive character makes it a bit boring and sadly there you lose the grip in the atmosphere. You may inflluence the game a bit but it doesnt feel that way. Your battlegroup is limited to 1 Battleship, 2 Battlecruisers, 3 Cruisers and 4 Light Cruisers - while this maybe a good setup for multiplayer in singleplayer it isnt too decisively. You dont really feel the touch and while you are losing points in the multiplayer and you need them to repair and therefore any loss is crucial the same can not be applied to the singleplayer. Sure losing a ship is bad but it is more an inconvenience.
My biggest issue is that we are in one of the biggest universes of sci-fi and actually even though you are fighting in many systems it is always a sqare map, some obstacles (whyever sometimes there are some), some background graphics and thats it. You cannot really influence some politics, some researches, you are playing 5 years of war but it is more like weeks and you dont feel the distances, that your ships maybe late and so on. The story follows the black crusade and that is ok - problematic is you cannot change the outcome. You cannot play other races or fleets and this could have been a nice story addition to play Eldar for instance or the Chaos Fleet in some occasions. So the story is a bit lame, you are bound to the happenings, your have one fleet and your battles - even the end one is limited to max of 700 points.
The game is not bad, it shall be a good implementation of the battefleet gothic rules even though I dont know them. But the missions are very repetetive, the maps not very inspired and even though the different loadouts of the ships - seriously I cannot complain about it since you can adjust the factions (which kind of fervor you want from for instance Mechanicum or the  Astartes), you can make your ship to a evil brawler or a very awesome supporter and also train the crew (with a very basic point system) - can be cool it is sadly just small. Small fleets, small maps, small mission variety.
I give therefore 7 points of 10 since it has a good grasp of the Warhammer universe, the ideas are good, the ships are cool, the game looks cool and is played casually. The missing points come from the repetetive missions, the lack of bigger fleets, the average singleplayer and well to be a game I was really looking forward to play my first month resulted in a wanted refund but because I already played too much I couldnt and in the end the game was ok. Not bad, not very good, just ok to good.
A good game when it is on sale - and a challenging game when you play multiplayer and then you may try out the Orks, the Eldar, the Tau, the Space Marines, the Imperial Navy and the Chaos with all their destinctive ideas. Surely all have light cruisers, cruisers, battlecruisers and -ships but all races are different and you can give them your loadout. So I heard and read the multiplayer shall be good and challenging.
I've thoroughly enjoyed this game regardless of the bumps in the road and feel it deserves a positive review. I hope they release more factions soon i'd happily buy.

I must say I bought this game without knowing much about it, I've vaguely heard about it before but that was all, so I didn't really knew what I had to expect from it. And in the end, it's been a very pleasant surprise that I've discovered!
One cannot say that there is a very developped story and character as it mostly kept its role as a strategy game. But on the other hand, on the contrary of games like Sudden Strike or Company of Heroes, just to quote some, the men and women you controls aren't just soldiers, an amount of pixels with the same faces, instead, you've got an ammount of pixels with names and different faces from each others which is allowed by the management of a team that can hold at least 3 dozens of soldiers and of a single commando that can be composed to 6 soldiers maximum. The gameplay is well made and easy to understand with 6 classes of soldiers to use effectively. I personnally just loved it and I spend few entire days playing it.
Now, for the (little) negative points. If the gameplay is really great, it still doesn't mean that it's flawless and sometimes the management of the 3D environnement can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥as you may misclick on the wrong case, sending your soldier on an upper or lower position, exposing them to a direct enemy fire. But that's not very serious neither as it's just a question of paying attention and being used to the game machanics.
Another little negative point, on my opinion, is that even if you've got characters with names, their own faces and nationalities, they don't seem to have their own story or personnality. After, I'm maybe asking a bit too much for a strategy game as Xcom, even more by the fact that there aren't predefined characters. But, if you're like me and have a good imagination, you will quickly make abstraction of this point as you may get their own strories in your head!
So to resume, this game hasn't a very developped story; aliens attack Earth, defend earth, but it's more than pleasant to play it, so it totally worth to spend money and time in it!

This game has a really steep learning curve. 61 hours on record since I've written this, and only now can I say that I can play relatively competently. This game isn't for people who just want to pick up and play.
However, if you git gud, this game is fun as hell. Plus, it's a free stand-alone mod. So hell, there's really no downside to downloading it.
The comparison to CS is made a lot, but really only because it's the only thing close to it. Games of Neotokyo are extremely dynamic, and each round can go in any direction. The first round, you could spend the whole 2 minutes slowly picking off stragglers. The second, you could get your whole team wiped out by a recon det-rush. The maps were designed for easy flanking. Because of this, teams need to adapt to their enemy strategies, block off route (A) because their recons bunny hop through there. They know they're blocking off route (A) and coming around through route (G). etc.
What makes the game the most fun though is the ranking and class system. You gain experience for killing, capturing the flag (ghost), surviving the round. Unlike CS, you unlock weapons through what your rank is. This doesn't necesarrily give any player a distinct advantage. There are Assault players who swear by the ZR Silenced, a rank 1 gun, and for myself, whenever I play recon, I won't play by anything other than the SRM, another rank 1 gun.
Unless you're playing recon, and you're really confident in your bunnyhopping skills, you literally need to stay by your team mates. It's way too easy to die in this game, and believe me, sitting out for 15 minutes a game is not fun. If you want to stay alive, get a mic, and start talking. If the ghost is close to you, pick it up, and call out positions.
If you're a beginner and you want to learn the ropes of how to play neotokyo, then I suggest going to Agiel's Deathmatch Server. It's usually dead, but it lets you learn the ins and outs of how brutal combat can be, and how to move faster.
Overall: 8/10. It's not for everybody, but it definitely should have more players than it does now.

I am rewriting my review to this game due to the fact that I have gained a lot more experience since the day I wrote it in 2014.
Patrician III could be the best trading/management simulator I've ever played. Sure, I've played other games like The Guild 2, or Banished, but there's just something about having a fleet of ships simultaneously roaming the open seas trading from port to port that gives me that good feeling. Not to mention the graphics are simply beautiful. They may be old but they've aged beautifully, even the little animated parts aren't bad to this day. Now if you want to know how to the game works, read on.
The player starts off as a simple citizen in a town of their choosing, with one or two ships at their side. From here they must build their trading empire, or perhaps they would like to pursue a more cunning route and build up their relationship with the town, eventually becoming the Lord Mayor? Or perhaps they are a more brutal player who would like to pillage and plunder towns and board other ships on the seas.
There are many choices in this game, but I'd say it's best to do a mix. Generally once I have built up a sizable cache of money from trading, I start building trading offices (which let you build buildings in other cities than your starting town) in other cities, and start building production buildings in my starter town. It all depends on what you would like to trade, as there are many options. If I have a run of bad luck and I'm low on cash I usually pillage a town, some of them are very tough but early in the game you can usually find an easy town to loot. You generally get around 10,000 gold - 1,000,000 gold so it can be very worth it.
There are four ship types: the Snaikka, Crayer, Cog, and Hulk. The bigger they are the more powerful they are, and the more storage they have. The only issue is they go slower so they won't be able to catch smaller ships in combat if the smaller ship decides to run. It's good to have a mix due to this. Don't forget to arm your ships as well, or you might just get boarded. When pillaging cities I generally go for a ton of hulks, and a few cogs. It might not be the best strategy but it works for me. One issue is that Hulks and Cogs cannot navigate down river cities, which are sort of inland. So if you want to trade to the inland cities you'll need Snaikkas and Crayers.
Like I said before, I love this game for its charm and challenge. It's got plenty of both. Easy 10/10 in my book. Just watch out for random crashes. Luckily it has an autosave feature.

I want to defeat the Nazis myself. I want march up the steps of the Reichstag and plant a big flag on the balcony that says: You lose!
has got me covered.
Relic is a developer known for making high quality strategy games for PC. Their work includes the
series which I enjoyed very much. Turning the second World War into an RTS seems like a dead giveaway. It was the first major conflict that saw large scale use of mechanical divisions. Trench warfare was turned into mobility warfare and air superiority became a deciding factor in the war. Turning this into an RTS sounds cool, but it is a lot harder than it sounds.
Tradtional RTS games have these very well defined unit roles. One unit for shooting other units. One unit for shooting vehicles. One unit for shooting buildings, and one unit for support. Actual warfare isn't so clearcut. Which Relic managed to convey quite well. Tanks are quite useful against other tanks, but their presence alone provides cover for infantry. Infantry can be outfitted with advanced weapons to make them stronger, but only very specific units can specialised. You still need a balanced force to counter all sorts of threats, but the main kicker in this game is intel.
The fog of war mechanic in
is rather advanced. You can only see where your unit would see. So unlike other RTS games, where a unit has perfect radial sight, you can only see round walls if you actually go around them. This makes for a very tense system when fighting in urban areas, where enemies can hide in allyways and quickly put five panzerfausts in your grill when you drive by. Scouting is so extremely important in this game that knowing the location of your enemy quickly gives you the upper hand by a mile. Having a good sightline will give you the opportunity to unleash all sorts of hell in the form of artillery, once again making the need to a balanced attack force that much more important.
The game's main campaign has to command the Soviet red army as they counter attack the Germans all the way back to Berlin. The light story tries to present an ethical issue to the player, but it falls flat on its face as you quickly deem all conscripts expendable, regardless of the game wanting you to think otherwise. The stages are diverse and interesting, and you'll be acquainted with the game's core mechanics when you're done.
Besides the campaign the game is host to an extensive online versus component. You get to pick your own ability boosts before trying to outfox your opponent on a wide variety of maps. The persistent unlocks will keep you busy for a while, but with only two armies to chose from (barring DLC) you might get bored fast.
The two armies are still quite diverse. The Soviets play a swarm style. Sending in conscript after conscript with minimal arms against the beast, letting them scavenge for their own weapons. Their tanks are simple and light, nimble and cheap. The Wehrmacht is not so expendable. Their units are well armed and equipped with effective weapons and a further set of counter weapons so deal a variety of threats when armour support is not near. The Nazi tanks and mechanical units are fast and well armoured, in exchange for a higher pricetag. The forces are evenly matched, so it will take a capable commander to lead them to victory.
can be expanded through extensive DLC; adding the allies and western branch of the German army to the game. Unfortunately, the expansion so weird, you're not quite sure what you're buying. The game's DLC policy is unclear and extremely expensive to boot, so consider this before investing.
What stands out in the myriad of options and modes is the sound design. Relic has taken special care to make sure that every rifle ♥♥♥♥♥ with a recognisable sound. Every tank rolls with a distinct rumble and every shell hits with a reassuring clunk and boom. The intensive sound of war will suck you right in as you lay wast to all who stand in your way.
