I really liked this game. But I did love 40k before going into this.
Story is quite nice, I am fond of the 'moving picture' type of cutscenes such as the THIEF series had, and it's quite satisfying to hear Inquisitors and Admirals tell you how great you've been doing.
Not knowing any details about the Black Crusades helped make it a more 'new' experience than others might have.
One thing though, is that I would have really liked to have more scenes with some of the characters, of which a few make only 1-2 appearances (such as the Astartes and Mechanicus leaders).
Music was really good, but there seems to be about 4-6 tracks, which can get repetitive after a while.
The gameplay requires a lot of slowing down time and managing each ship, but I hold nothing against it, as that's what I want from a strategy or semi-strategy game.
However, I would say that I kind of want there to be MORE things you can do. Perhaps I missed some mechanics, but considering how long the cooldown timers are for each skill, a lot of times it feels like after using them, all I can do is slightly maneuver the ships for better offence/defence and wait while the abilities to come off cooldown.
I would love to have more things I could do in the meantime to better my chances against the enemy.
The sector-map and missions were nice, though as much as I liked the voice acting, I would have loved to have more of the texts and dialogues voiced.
In fact, the only thing I'd consider even slightly bad about the singleplayer campaign map, is that there are a lot of what seems to be randomly generated/generic missions, and I would have loved those (kind of optional) missions to have been replaced with (preferably) voice acted and hand-written scenarios, as that would greatly mitigate the feeling that in between critical story-missions you're doing the same activities over and over.
I'd say there are too few game-modes, but as I said a bit of flavor could fix that really well.
The ship limitations per battle are....acceptable. Though I really wish I could have had more chances to have bigger fights, and a few fights with waay more ships.
Customizing the ships is fun, as is naming the captain, all of that is a great addition. I love the idea of getting attached to my ships and crewmen, and these features contribute to such an end.
I like 40k but prior to this game was ambivalent towards the space fleets and such.
But the story, music, cutscenes, art and acting introduced me to this part of 40k in what I would say the best way I could imagine.
So in summary - I really like this game, and consider most of it's downsides to have been incidental to the intentions of the developers, and if a sequel was ever made - if all of the existing elements were simply taken to a greater level, (in quantity AND depth) that would fix most of my complaints.

TLDR - Worth $20.
I recommend this game but I also don't. See below. I think you should get this game but only if you don't mind the stuff in the bad section.
-EDIT- Added a couple of negatives below related to the graphics.
-EDIT 2- Changed do not recommend to recommend. Changed nothing else in review. New content coming for free is stuff I still would have paid for. Based on how much game time I have now and the dev's continued development, I believe the game is worth the $40 investment.
The good
1- It's fun. Plain and simple. The gameplay is enjoyable, especially when heavily buzzed off [drug of choice]
2- Very easy to learn. The learning curve in this game is easier than learning how to ride a bike with training wheels.
The bad
1- Graphics are laughable by modern standards. Models are EXTREMELY low poly. There are games released in 2001 that had better graphics and models. My biggest beef with the graphics is the fact that you can't see your sub through the water. That is to say, if you are at periscope depth and you look down at your sub, the surface of the water is a solid barrier. No occlusion whatsoever. Submarines that should be round are instead dotacohedral or whatever. Very basic graphics and engine.
2- Tomahawks don't follow terrain.
3- Terrain on ocean floor and land is flat, barren, devoid of any life or human activity. I realize it's a sub game but I feel that more attention could have been paid to this area.
4- Can't play Soviets without mods and even with the Subs and more mod the game is devoid of NATO surface vessels so we are left fighting against reskinned Soviet surface vessels.
5- Game is overpriced for what you get. 17 hours in and I'm averaging just over $2 per hour played so far and can see myself getting bored very quickly. Game would be a much better value at $20 price point but I'm used to paying much higher prices for military sims.
6- Campaign is pretty dumb and has constant useless popups. When you start a campaign you'll get 5 stupid news articles pop up and each one restarts the music. It's irritating. Worse still, periodically throughout the campaign the more dumb stuff will pop up. Soviets killed children in Norway. Ok cool, just let me play the game thanks.
7- Music. There is literally one music track you'll hear while playing.
8- Voices. Turn them off. You'll understand why if you play with them on. They're as abrasive as 1 grit sand paper.
9- HUGE chunks of the map, sea floor and land, don't even render. I'll often get a sub to 95% solution and then go look at it in 3d and there's nothing rendered below it. You can see large blocks where nothing simply renders, I assume because you are not by that area even if your camera is.
10- The second screenshot above with the heavy cruiser. Yeah the game looks nothing like that. The models and textures don't look that good.
11- The sea state never changes. Ever. It doesn't matter if it's calm or stormy. The water always looks the same calm. No big swells or anything.
12- No actual weather. It rains sometimes but there's no volumetric clouds, just a skybox. See my point below where games that are 10 years older than this look better.
I like this game a lot and I don't regret buying it. But I am also more tolerant of stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥when it comes to military sims from small companies. You may or may not be as tolerant as I am. The game is overpriced for what you get by a long shot and everything it does, Silent Hunter 5, Silent Hunter 4, and Silent Hunter 3 (all of which have better graphics) do better. I am eager to see if the company continues to support and develop the game in the future. It needs a lot more content for $40.
To be clear, I have enjoyed all 17 hours I have played. I am however starting to feel I have enjoyed all this game has to offer me, even with a mod that adds like 40 new submarines, and there are several issues ranging from irritating to outright BS.

At first, I had disdain for this game, something near disgust. ''What is this another clone of Fallout? Screw it.'' So I forgot it. To be honest, at this time, I was more interested by the Fallout franchise, it was when the dual Reduxes reboots weren't on the market, only the original games were there. When the Reduxes came out, I was curious to see what they changed,updated.upgraded,ect. I watched a couple of gameplays on YouTube, I wasn't impressed. So, I went on the review section on the game's store page. It all came to one thing: the story.At this moment, I dared this game to be better than the FPSes I played: the Bioshock franchise, the Half-life franchise, Deus-Ex: Human Revolution and Wolfenstein: The New Order. Suprisingly, A sale on the dual reduxes came out. I bought them both. Then I started playing Metro 2033. There is one thing that the Metros had but the other games didn't have: The urge to scavenge, keeping track of how many minutes you had left on your filters, looking for filters,ammo, new gaz masks,etc. It may seem like nothing, but this makes a big difference in how you play this specific game. It adds another dimension in immersion which makes the game spectacular. If you play on Ranger or Ranger Hardcore, you'll be immersed in the game in maximum 5 minutes. You won't pay attention to the hours passed on this game, you'll pay attention to the game. Apart from the immersion ther is alot more to the game. The story 10/10 : the mix of present and past adds alot to the experience. The music 11/10, it makes you feel like you are wandering throughout a wasteland but it makes you feel like you have nostalgia for the land that was before the War, which is exactly what this game needs. Characters: 9/10: it does not make you feel like these people are your friends but more like partners,comrades. The art style, 10/10 : the perfect balance of colours and ruined landscapes for this kind of game. The combat system, 7.5/10 Intuitive but lacks originality in using the environment around you and your enemies. Overall Gameplay: 9.5/10.
Final Verdict: 10/10, for standing out for this kind of game. Must play/own.

I have mixed feelings about Battlefront 2, and for every positive I can think of, there's a negative. I mean, for example the big, BIG positive is that it isn't the DICE reboot - nothing personal against DICE, since I'm a fan of some of their work - and that it isn't a pizza without the toppings (some of you might or might not have seen that image of comparing a game and paid content to a pizza where you have to pay extra money for the toppings since they aren't included by default)... but then you can also say that unlike the DICE reboot, its graphics are shameful and bland. But then from THERE I can point out how this game will give you an unbelievably high frame rate. 60 without question.
Battlefront 2's gameplay itself isn't too shabby, since, again, unlike the DICE reboot, or "Battlefront 3", for those of you who may try to call it something else; BF2 comes with everything advertised (presumably, since I was unaware of this game when it first released and thus never saw any trailers or anything of the sort): a decently satisfying campaign that sort of follows Republic Commando's vision of showing the Star Wars saga through the perspective of the troops; in this instance a member of the 501st Legion who fought from the Battle of Geonosis at the beginning of the Clone Wars, through Order 66, and then through several battles that we saw in the Original Trilogy plus a few extras added in just for diversity. As for other modes, there's also a "Galactic Conquest" that serves as the baby lovechild of this game and Empire at War, where you build and move fleets across the galaxy to conquer planets. It's decent, though nowhere near as potent as Empire at War's. You get both of these major modes, as well as the basic skirmish modes that can take place on the ground or out in space.
The gameplay itself, for ground combat, is basically class-based cannon-fodder combat that is stunningly uncoordinated, since I've yet to observe teamwork and coordination from AI or players on a smaller scale, so the "classes", where you'll have like an Engineer who can drop health and ammo and repair vehicles, which also makes him the most OP class in the game, but he seldom helps out the other soldiers on his team and just uses the health and ammunition to heal and rearm himself after a firefight. You can also get "Hero" units, which are 90% composed of Jedi and Sith users that, if utilized correctly, break the game. On the Kashyyyk map (that Dagobah-like planet that Yoda and Chewbacca were on in Revenge of the Sith), a random player on the Republic side can spawn in as Yoda, who is very small; very fast; and can hide in the long grass and spring out like a Bouncing Betty. And mirroring this, on the Coruscant map, when playing as the CIS/Separatists, the hero unit is Darth Maul, who, as in The Phantom Menace, carries a double-bladed saber, which he spins very quickly and will heal him with each kill. Combine that with the massive scores of clones you encounter in the confined quarters, and the game breaks itself. It is fun, however, playing as Maul and buckminstering all of the clone troopers when you're facing AI opponents.
Space combat is a little bit cooler, since you do have access to different types of fighters and bombers, however not all of them are properly explained (neither is much of the mode specifics itself) so it's kind of a DIY unless you're looking off of YouTube, and even then most of those videos are probably going to be coming from people who've played this game nonstop. Space combat is a bit more fun than ground combat, to me at least, and it's actually included in the game.
So Battlefront 2 is just kind of a tossup of if you want to play a Star Wars video game where you fly in space and fight on the ground without having to pay a king's ransom. If you can accept mediocre graphics (which again, make up for it by making the game run like the wind), a general sense of boredom, and a font of game-breakers, then by all means, buy this game; it's only 10 bucks as opposed to 60+ for an incomplete game and incomplete expansions.
Don't buy the new battlefront unless you want a water downed call of duty with a star wars skin.

I enjoyed this game a lot more than I expected to. It's FPS sandbox parkour zombie bashing with loot and guns.
The parkour was fairly easy to master and while there might be a few occasions where you swear that you should have grabbed the ledge rather than just plummiting to your death, it's solid.  The grappling hook skill, once unlocked, is interesting; while it's certainly a bit game-breaking as far as some of the parkour and jump puzzles go, I found myslef not caring because of how satisfying and fun it feels to zip around the world like Spiderman.  I was also happy the game included a co-op mode, if for no other reason than because it's sometimes fun to just have a friend or three to play alongside with. So let's cut to the chase:
Pros:
-Parkour is fun. Feels good to just jump/climb/explore the city.
-Lots of loot, good weapon variety
-The weapon degradation system encourages you to try different weapons frequently.
-Fun skills to unlock, and mastering them is satisfying
-Gunplay is solid, if not sometimes a bit OP. It still feels good to watch even the big zombies die after a couple headshots.
-Great sound design and soundtrack
-Great visual detail, world building, and level design. Just great atmosphere all around really.
-Grappling hook is a blast
-Co-op so you can play with a friend. Or two or three.
Cons:
-Writing is passable at best, downright silly on average, and cringe-worthy at worst
-The voice acting, with the exception of the Crane, is generally pretty bad
-Prepare yourself for a really mediocre final boss encounter
-I personally would have preferred some really big, tough, boss encounters. There aren't any. It's more like a couple mini-bosses that just become fairly regular encounters towards the end of the game.
In summary: I bought it at half price ($30) and it was easily worth that. Honestly I probably still would have felt satisfied if I'd paid $60 for it.  I'm looking forward to the DLC, the idea of driving a buggy around and pancaking zombies on the pavement seems fun.  If you like open-world/sandbox exploration games with lots of action and whacking things with a crowbar or machete, or maybe just sniping down from the rooftops, you'll probably dig this.  If you get motion-sick a lot and are just generally not into the whole zombie-thing, maybe give this one a pass I guess? But that should probably be obvious already.

Do I think Battlefleet Gothic is an okay game? Honestly it's 50/50 for me, but if pushed I'd have to say no, not in its current form. Besides which, if a game only scrapes into the okay catagory, then frankly it's not worth it anyway. Who wants to play something mediocre given the massive selection of games availible?
The game itself is pretty solid in my oppinion, of course it could be better in several small ways but the core mechanics are solid and promising. Ship movement/combat/skills are all relatively intuetive and the tactical cogitator is a nice touch to help you manage several things in a short space of time. They seem to be adding flavour with different races/fleets represented with their own quirks and playstyles, which again is commendable.
On the downside however are two big things that frankly spoil it:
1) Repetative modes - There is destinct lack of variety in game modes availible, and this make the single player campaign a downright grind for the most part (I'm on my 3rd attempt to get through it, but every time I try I just get bored of the same old same old and walk away to find something actually fun to play)
2) Crashes - To be blunt I wouldn't call this game stable, in my current playthrough I seem to be averaging a crash to desktop every hour or so.
Playing a game should be challenging sure, but it should be fun! A game stops being fun when barriers to enjoyment keep being placed in the player's way, and frankly the repetative modes and frequent crashes just spoil what otherwise would be a pretty good game.
TL;DR  -  Please fix the lack of variety in the modes, and please fix the crashes.

OVERALL
--------------
The game is very subtle.  Economies can be chaotic (where someone just floods a market and you have to wait for it to dry up before it's profitable again).  I'm always feeling like I'm on the verge of losing, and by some miracle it continues.
Some strategies do turn out to be a complete disaster and I have to revert to a previous save to continue.
The game mechanic feels "like German engineering" - meticulously detailed and almost overwhelming.
The game sort of reminds me of my first all-nighter game-plays of Civ II - where there is a grandiousity that can be achieved with many parallel elements in play.  I'm just beginning to get glimpses of that "big" feeling the game has to offer.
PROGRAMMING
-----------------------
You don't have to, but the game includes all the mechanisms needed to program ship routing (similar to programming resource shipping in Sid Meier's Colonization).  It's very satisfying to set up a stable system that allows going into fast forward and just rakes in the money.
YES/NO?
-------------
I highly recommend it - but only if you are in no hurry.  I get the feeling this game could take hundreds of hours just for one or two games after having mastered it.  It's mind-bogglingly slow, with a million things to keep track of.

Relic is a developer known for making high quality strategy games for PC. Their work includes the
series which I enjoyed very much. Turning the second World War into an RTS seems like a dead giveaway. It was the first major conflict that saw large scale use of mechanical divisions. Trench warfare was turned into mobility warfare and air superiority became a deciding factor in the war. Turning this into an RTS sounds cool, but it is a lot harder than it sounds.
Tradtional RTS games have these very well defined unit roles. One unit for shooting other units. One unit for shooting vehicles. One unit for shooting buildings, and one unit for support. Actual warfare isn't so clearcut. Which Relic managed to convey quite well. Tanks are quite useful against other tanks, but their presence alone provides cover for infantry. Infantry can be outfitted with advanced weapons to make them stronger, but only very specific units can specialised. You still need a balanced force to counter all sorts of threats, but the main kicker in this game is intel.
The fog of war mechanic in
is rather advanced. You can only see where your unit would see. So unlike other RTS games, where a unit has perfect radial sight, you can only see round walls if you actually go around them. This makes for a very tense system when fighting in urban areas, where enemies can hide in allyways and quickly put five panzerfausts in your grill when you drive by. Scouting is so extremely important in this game that knowing the location of your enemy quickly gives you the upper hand by a mile. Having a good sightline will give you the opportunity to unleash all sorts of hell in the form of artillery, once again making the need to a balanced attack force that much more important.
The game's main campaign has to command the Soviet red army as they counter attack the Germans all the way back to Berlin. The light story tries to present an ethical issue to the player, but it falls flat on its face as you quickly deem all conscripts expendable, regardless of the game wanting you to think otherwise. The stages are diverse and interesting, and you'll be acquainted with the game's core mechanics when you're done.
Besides the campaign the game is host to an extensive online versus component. You get to pick your own ability boosts before trying to outfox your opponent on a wide variety of maps. The persistent unlocks will keep you busy for a while, but with only two armies to chose from (barring DLC) you might get bored fast.
The two armies are still quite diverse. The Soviets play a swarm style. Sending in conscript after conscript with minimal arms against the beast, letting them scavenge for their own weapons. Their tanks are simple and light, nimble and cheap. The Wehrmacht is not so expendable. Their units are well armed and equipped with effective weapons and a further set of counter weapons so deal a variety of threats when armour support is not near. The Nazi tanks and mechanical units are fast and well armoured, in exchange for a higher pricetag. The forces are evenly matched, so it will take a capable commander to lead them to victory.
can be expanded through extensive DLC; adding the allies and western branch of the German army to the game. Unfortunately, the expansion so weird, you're not quite sure what you're buying. The game's DLC policy is unclear and extremely expensive to boot, so consider this before investing.
What stands out in the myriad of options and modes is the sound design. Relic has taken special care to make sure that every rifle ♥♥♥♥♥ with a recognisable sound. Every tank rolls with a distinct rumble and every shell hits with a reassuring clunk and boom. The intensive sound of war will suck you right in as you lay wast to all who stand in your way.

Pros:
Great replay value with many ship types, randomly generated sector maps and "challenging" difficulty.
Cons:
This game's hard mode isn't just hard, it's randomly hard, which limits the possibility of compensating with your own skill. You live and die by the will of RNG. One time you get to sector 8 by the skin of your teeth, without finding any decent weapon, another time you find a Chain Vulcan just floating in space in the first sector. Same goes for enemies you encounter. It's also regrettable that the game doesnt have steam achievements.
[edit]
After additional 50h of playing I've come to a conclusion that the game actually scales enemies' setups (shields, weapons, engine strength) according to how good weapons/drones you own (even if you can't yet use them), making the game easier for unlucky runs and harder for lucky runs. It diminishes the role of RNG a bit, making it possible for skilled players to make do with what little they find.

I bought this game because I had bought XCOM 2 and thought I should play the first, first.... and to support a Linux build!
My feelings about the game are somewhat mitigated:
The game ran very well on Mesa (radeonsi) and the performance looked fine (though I did not measure anything).
I really enjoyed some parts: the HQ, the story missions, the idea for EXALT, etc...
I also liked how we get a mix of weapons, psi-power, gene modification, skills, and mechs (the last ones I did not use), it's a cool variety.
But I really disliked how so many "missions" felt like filler: All the UFO crash/landing site, the terror ones, the abduction ones. I would have definitely skipped those if they had no implication on the rest of the game, and alas we mostly get those randomly generated, but fairly much the same, missions. I really wish we had more missions like the story missions, these were really nice! (and I don't mean more copies of these, but more different ones).
The game also felt slowed-down for no good reason: every time we see a new group of enemies we get a quick useless cinematic about them (it was fun at first but eventually it's just wasted time...), having to wait on shots when we already know they missed... I actually wish each bullet from a shot had its own chance of missing, that way it would make sense to wait on all of them, no ability to queue orders, we have to wait for the units to stop first, etc, having to wait for the alien turn, even if we don't see what they do nor get the noise thing....
And since I wanted to achieve all upgrades I care for it took me way too long to get the end story mission, which means way too many filler missions....
For the EXALT missions, I didn't get that we had to force the final one, I thought it would start on its own eventually, and so I also got a lot more filler ones there... I thought the idea of EXALT was really cool, but after the last mission there was no explanation... and it never got explained in game... a bit strange/lame.
This game is tagged as a strategy game, but I didn't really see much strategy... Bring strong units and hope to not get out of luck, that's about it I think. Sure there's the HQ's strategy, but that's not that involved in the fighting.
The end story was as expected, which is kind of sad I suppose, but the end cinematics was like 5 seconds... I thought more would come, or just people at the HQ talking but no... a bit lame again.
Difficulty wise, as many people wrote before the curve is pretty bad. It's quite difficult as first, and way too easy once you get to the middle and have enough good units with good gear. The end mission is way too easy.
I still had a pretty good time playing this game, so it definitely gets a thumb up from me, and I will probably play it again soon.

At first, I had disdain for this game, something near disgust. ''What is this another clone of Fallout? Screw it.'' So I forgot it. To be honest, at this time, I was more interested by the Fallout franchise, it was when the dual Reduxes reboots weren't on the market, only the original games were there. When the Reduxes came out, I was curious to see what they changed,updated.upgraded,ect. I watched a couple of gameplays on YouTube, I wasn't impressed. So, I went on the review section on the game's store page. It all came to one thing: the story.At this moment, I dared this game to be better than the FPSes I played: the Bioshock franchise, the Half-life franchise, Deus-Ex: Human Revolution and Wolfenstein: The New Order. Suprisingly, A sale on the dual reduxes came out. I bought them both. Then I started playing Metro 2033. There is one thing that the Metros had but the other games didn't have: The urge to scavenge, keeping track of how many minutes you had left on your filters, looking for filters,ammo, new gaz masks,etc. It may seem like nothing, but this makes a big difference in how you play this specific game. It adds another dimension in immersion which makes the game spectacular. If you play on Ranger or Ranger Hardcore, you'll be immersed in the game in maximum 5 minutes. You won't pay attention to the hours passed on this game, you'll pay attention to the game. Apart from the immersion ther is alot more to the game. The story 10/10 : the mix of present and past adds alot to the experience. The music 11/10, it makes you feel like you are wandering throughout a wasteland but it makes you feel like you have nostalgia for the land that was before the War, which is exactly what this game needs. Characters: 9/10: it does not make you feel like these people are your friends but more like partners,comrades. The art style, 10/10 : the perfect balance of colours and ruined landscapes for this kind of game. The combat system, 7.5/10 Intuitive but lacks originality in using the environment around you and your enemies. Overall Gameplay: 9.5/10.
Final Verdict: 10/10, for standing out for this kind of game. Must play/own.

Quake Live is ,simply put, a perfect competitive multiplayer experience. Few things feel quite as tight, exhilarating, mentally taxing, and because of all these things, quite as rewarding. I have thousands of hours logged on this game before it ever came to Steam and whether I was giving 100% of my focus to dueling friends and foes, or just throwing on some music and playing the roller coaster of a game mode that is clan arena, Quake has never let me down. Other newer games wear on me, or have some glaring flaw. Quake does not. It is hard. It is fast. It also makes absolute sense. What it lacks in gimmicks and complex ability interactions it makes up for in nuanced decision making capability and the potential to transform your mind into hyperaware machine. Whether it is as simple as a nasty air rocket or pixel rail, or the subtle complexity of lining up item respawns for several minutes just to make that one play that gives you back control of the game, Quake Live can be enjoyed by literally anyone who likes fast multiplayer gameplay. If you even consider yourself a fan of shooters, you owe it to yourself to have experienced Quake. Warning however once you do, every other game will likely leave you wanting. Long live the King.

I want to like this game. But it just doesn't let me. I tried to give it a chance, and it blew it. Let me start with the story.
The story is good, the art is fantastic, if not to my tastes, and the voice acting never comes close to dipping below good. The plotline is the classic 'baddie has world-obliterating macguffin,  go stop him' deal, but it's not bad, given that all the characters have some degree of life to them. The Warhammer 40K setting is a good one, as usual. But, then again...
...Everything else feels half-baked. Now, I don't know how involved Games Workshop is with this game, but they're likely the reason for all of this if they had any power. If they didn't, then I just don't know what to say. It's like the devs made a game that they would know how to play, and just decided to release it to the public. The UI is terrible, to start with, as is the tutorial. For example, there are two buttons to execute sharp turns. One of them is left, the other is right. However, it doesn't matter which one you press, since either one will let you make a turn in either direction. The tutorial and UI both imply that it's directional, when it isn't. Why even have two buttons if they both do the exact same thing?
Some missions are so easy that it's boring. Others are frustratingly hard for no good reason at all. A good example is a certain mission where you defend a planet from attack. Troops on the planet will request orbital bombardment, and you have to fulfill those requests. To do so, you simply travel to various sites and park a ship there. Done and done. Sounds insultingly easy, right? Well, what if I told you that your ships were under attack by vastly superior forces the entire time? That's a good mission, right? Well, those bombardment points appear totally at random. You have two minutes to get to each one, while avoiding enemies, while flying the slowest ships I have ever seen, and you may have to cross the entire map to get to a point. Two minutes may sound like a lot, but it's not nearly enough time to crawl across the map. Oh, and if you miss more than two, mission failed.
Okay... so what about the multiplayer? It's dead. Yeah, pretty much dead. Honestly, given the quality and balancing(Or lack thereof), are you surprised? The Eldar suck, the Tau are pretty much a pay-to-win button, the Orks are just boring, and the Imperium can win against pretty much anything if you bring enough ships. And, speaking of boring, that's what the space battles are. Even if you manage to get a good one going, they aren't terribly impressive. You get to hear the same sound effects over and over while you wait for boarders to recharge, and space just sound so... empty. I get that it is empty, but this is Warhammer 40K. Impressive, over-the-top, and realism-defying are pretty much the name of the game. This one, has none of that.
In short, worth around Ten Dollars. Skip it unless you want 40K, and even then, Space Marine is a much better game.

I tried this game early last year, and it was okay then.  A friend of mine picked it up recently and we have been playing it a lot.  Is it a perfect game?  No.  Is it a lot of fun single player and co-op multiplayer?  Yes.
The single player campaign lets you refight the Gothic War as an Imperial Admiral.  As someone who played a lot of the board game, I know the history and scenarios pretty well.  You can also pick any of the factions for a single player Skirmish (non-scripted) campaign.  It throws a series of battles against you, pretty much like you would expect if you showed up to play BFG at a game store with a group of random people.  When you hit level 8 for your admiral, you can play in Elite mode, which is significantly more challenging.
However, the real fun came when we discovered we could play multi-player co-op with our Skirmish Admirals.  This is a great way to play the game and have fun.  The scenarios go quickly and it is fun to level up the ships and play that way.  I have not enjoyed a GW game this much since DoW and DoW 2.
As I said, the game itself is not perfect, I'm not incredibly pleased with the design decisions behind the Eldar Pulsars and Holofields.  Plus there seems to be a rather annoying bug where if an Eldar ship even gets within close range of an enemy ship it counts as "ramming".  But overall, this one is well worth the money.  Way more than certain other Games Workshop products available on Steam.

I played Sid Meier's Red Storm Rising to death, first on my c-64, and later on my Amiga 500. This was back in the late 80's, just before the Berlin wall fell. I was a teenager during the last years of the cold war, and Tom Clancy and Larry Bond books, were prominantly featured in my bookshelf.
The game Red Storm Rising actually played a big part when I decided to join the submarine service.
So you can imagine my joy, and my fear when I found out that Killer Fish Games were working on the "spiritual successor" to a game very close to my heart. Can they possibly re-create this, for me, life changing game?
The final days before launch, I paced my living room, probably driving my family crazy. I must have seemed like a little kid on Christmas eve, eagerly awaiting Santa's presants.
Then it was released, and all my fears dissapeared. The game looked great, and I imideately fell in love with it. Sniking my first Alfa class submarine with a Mk 48 felt even better than I remembered from my Red Storm Rising days.
Sure, the game had it's obvious flaws, but the developers suddenly went in to overdrive, and fixes and updates were coming out left and right. I found my self in september with the 1.08 c update, thinking: Why can't all game developers be like this?
The game keeps getting better and better, and the developers listen to the community, and have implemented a lot of features based on player requests. It's great.
So, what makes this game so fantastic?
Well, first of all, they pulled of the "spiritual succsessor" part. For me, that was a big deal, because of what the original ment to me. At the same time they managed to merge just enough simulator feeling into the game, without ruinining the entertainment factor. Because make no mistake: This is not a simulator. Simulator entusiasts might still find them selves strangely attracted to this game,and rightfully so. It is a marvellous game.
I will end this review by saying that Iam amazed by the ammount of work the developers have put into this game after release. Iam looking forward to added campaigns, and more added content.

It's difficult to figure out where to start on NEOTOKYO, so I'll say this right up front: NEOTOKYO is--in my humble opinion--one of the single greatest achievements in videogames, and a true masterpiece right up there with the likes of Catacomb 3-D, Wasteland, Pathologic, etc. Now, I've been playing videogames 40 hours a week for the past decade and a half, so at the risk of hubris I'd say I'm well qualified to make such a claim. The hard part is substantiating it.
So why is that? In short, NEOTOKYO is a wonderful marriage of art and craft: it combines the disparate elements of Japanese cyberpunk with high-impact tactical shooters and does so with such flair and polish that I've never once seen before. Consequently, it maintains a duality between its inspirations and must be judged on both the quality of the gameplay, and the world that it inhabits. You'll often hear the term "Ghost in the Shell meets Counter-Strike" bandied about, and while such a phrase is no doubt accurate I think it sells the game short.
As a game, NEOTOKYO has many superficial similarities to Counter-Strike: it's a round-based, objective-oriented FPS without respawns and a heavy emphasis on teamwork wherein the player picks their loadout at the beginning of each round. That may sound like derivative-going-on-copyright-infringement, but just as there's more than one way to skin a cat there's more than one way to make a high-lethality team game. Unlike Counter-Strike and its clones where terrorists must plant and defend a bomb, the goal in NEOTOKYO is to recover a neutral item 'ghost' from the center of the map and escort it to the enemy spawn. This is further complicated by the fact that the 'ghost' will provide what's effectively wallhack to whoever has it equipped, at the cost of being unable to defend themselves and lit up on the enemy HUD. The effect is profound. Where Counter-Strike is strategic zone control in a very simple, small scale environment; NEOTOKYO is about successfully navigating a very large labyrinth and either escaping with the ghost or eradicating the enemy team before they can. The maps are suitably large and full of various nooks and crannies, which makes the CS style of covering all approaches and knowing exactly where the enemy is coming from impossible. Instead, it's about keeping close to your teammates, keeping alert and either outmaneuvering or ambushing your

. Situational awareness is the name of the game, and you must at all times be aware of every angle while being careful not to expose yourself to enemy fire. It's tense and immersive in a way that is difficult to put into words, but suffice to say I have no doubt that the games' best players are the sort that can catch flies with chopsticks.
But that's not all; there's also a class system. I won't get into the specifics, but here's the broad strokes: there are 3 classes, a light ('recon'), medium ('assault'), and heavy ('support'). Light classes move faster but have less HP/armor, and vice versa. Each class also has a vision mode (NVGs, motion-tracking, thermal), and the ability to cloak or otherwise conceal themselves. Lighter classes cloak for longer, vice versa. Each vision-mode makes tracking your foe easier when they're cloaked, uncloaked, moving, hiding, etc. but weak against the inverse. Thermal can't see cloaked people, night-vision can't see anyone in bright light, and motion-tracking should be self-explanatory. It's all very simple in the abstract, but when you put it into practice in real nuanced environments everything becomes infinitely more complex. It's a lot to take in, and that's only vision! Movement affects timings and map access, and max health (of course) tempers your aggression. Can't go in guns blazing when a stiff breeze is enough to put you in the ground, right? And this all works within the context of your team, necessitating you change your class and loadout whenever possible to maximize your and your team's effectiveness. There's an old tagline from the original Counter-Strike which I think fits better for this game than any other: "Your role affects your team's success. Your team's success affects your role."
So I've talked a lot about to everything leading up to the gunfights, but what about the gunfights themselves? Since I've used Counter-Strike as a reference so far, I'll continue the trend here. The shooting is suitably visceral, the guns have real punch, and you can see some pretty high octane ultra-violence on occasion. The single greatest change is the precision. Weapon accuracy has been uniformly reduced from the genre standard laser beam precision, and recoil is a simple random spread that increases with fire. There's no 1-AKs from across the map or recoil patterns to memorize here, there's so much focus on everything leading up the shot that shooting is almost an afterthought. It however, is by no means simplistic and you'll find it easily up to par with the various Call of Battlefield fare that's the current norm. The spray does introduce an element of randomness into firefights, and while death is never cheap, the imprecision will no doubt be frustrating to the sort of people with <100ms reflexes that railgun in Quake Pro duels. Everyone else won't notice after the first 10 min. Finally, instead of the complex economy and money system, loadouts are based on a simple ranking system. After scoring a certain number of points, the next tier is unlocked. It's not earth-shattering, but the choice of primary weapon is a significant consideration. So that's the gameplay, what of the
?
As for the world the gameplay inhabits...it's like nothing else. Not since Mirror's Edge have I seen such a pretty game. The world is fully-realized, the art style is powerful and unique, and I've yet to find a single asset that hasn't been made from scratch. The dev team says that the game was in production for 4 years, and it absolutely shows. This is the kind of quality that can only be seen from a team with the passion to work a second job for free, just for the love of creation. The world is so believable, so incredibly atmospheric just because of this dedication! It's abundantly clear the devs took the time to sit down and think through everything about the world: the logistics, function, architecture, style. It's not just convincing, it feels truly real! The devs say that the game was heavily inspired by the likes of Ghost in the Shell and Akira, and it certainly shows! But more than that, the world isn't just a tribute to the works of their inspirations, but different and its own. It's a world that can exist in tandem with Shirou's and Otomo's, but is neither a pale shadow of nor dependent on theirs.
If you want to see the love put into this product, this absolutely free retail-quality product, just listen to the
. Only once before have I heard a soundtrack that complements the game so well (Morrowind). In the end, I can count on two hands the number of truly great tactical shooters I've played. I can count on one hand the number of truly beautiful games I've played. I cannot think of another truly great game in such a picturesque setting. And that's why NEOTOKYO isn't just "Ghost in the Shell meets Counter-Strike". From there most games would stop, but that's only where NEOTOKYO starts.

I'm only reviewing this because this somehow has gotten "Mixed Reviews". Let me start off and say that it used to be "Very Positive" for very constructive reasons, and it needs to hit that mark again, because this game doesn't deserve it's brief negativity.
The reason people seem to be thumbing this game down is not because of the gameplay or anything. Almost every aspect of this game is amazing, and as I said, this game used to be "Very Positive". The reason why people are thumbing this game down is because of a moment where the community sort of died. There were hardly any players at all, maybe a couple of players in a single server, but that was it. The negative reviewers seemed to have installed this game at a low time for this community. If you want further proof, just check the front page reviews, and you'll see they're all positive and reasons why.
However, this was a brief moment and the community is alive again. Now I'm seeing two full servers at once, and maybe a couple of others player alone in another server. It's not particularly a Call Of Duty-level playerbase, but it's certainly just enough to get a game going any time. I started playing Neotokyo again and It has sucked a lot of hours out of my life.
Just remember: The community isn't the most living, but don't say a game sucks because of it. It's an excellent free game, without any microtransactions, so downloading it wouldn't hurt your wallet if you happened to find a day where the servers are empty. Thumbing it down because of small playerbase is just silly, because I don't see many people saying Team Fortress Classic or Battlefield 1942 sucks for the same reason. Considering those games are also something you pay for.
Oh, and people say it's Counter-Strike with Ghost In The Shell influences, but I prefer to say it's Japanese Cyberpunk Rainbow Six.

First, The Room is one of my favourite games and this is by no means a terrible game, I think this is just a terrible sequel. I will also confess that I personally just don't handle stress and fear well.
Apparently, what the makers took away from the praise of the first game is what people loved the most were the scary/scary-y parts and the scary noises. The first game already had an unnecessary amount of those and it was just distracting from the clever puzzleboxes. What kind of use could semi-jumpscares possibly have in these games? Making the game artificially longer by making me too nervous to pay attention and observe well? Not to mention the silly alchemy-like symbols which were, judging by the scary noises, also supposed to be scary. (Yes, I could turn off the sounds, but then I also have to miss the sounds of the drawers opening, handles turning, picking up objects and more good ambiance.)
This part has a scèance room. I have no idea how it feels for people who actually believe this stuff, but I suspect that people who actually go to these old-fashioned scèances would be used to the shenanigans at the last part of that chapter. As someone who doesn't, the only scary part is that I constantly fear loud noises when I solve puzzels and things thrown to the monitor for a semi-jumpscare. The people who believe but fear it... I hope they didn't have to close the game never to play it again out of fear for inviting bad things in their house. In other words, it was a beautifull room but who was supposed to be impressed?
This is actually my biggest problem with The Room Two: I don't like to solve puzzles in this sequel. Almost everytime I have to be ready to hear scary noises, or loud noises, combined with things suddenly opening. The first part had it's moments too, but there it felt good to peel away the layers of the puzzle box.
Aside from the very annoying sounds, there is also the shakey camera to underline how dangerous everything is supposed to be and flashing images at the end of most chapters.
And the puzzles aren't even good enough to make up for it. As others have said, the multiple spots in every room make that you regularly just zoom between tables and cabinets to find that one spot, a thing much less frustrating if you can focus on just one thing, like the first game. It's not that all puzzles are boring, but a lot felt just too short and easy like I was just finding stuff to use on other stuff to find more stuff. If I recall correctly, codes were just to be found and used in the right place, which is not that different from picking up object A and using it on object B. Part of what made the original game fun is that you had to figure out how to use things and what the goal was, which still happens in The Room Two, but less.
Oh, on the subject of A's and B's, a minor complaint: could the makers of this game really not do any better than formulas with nothing but placeholder letters? Was it really so hard just to insert 6.35 or (34/11) somewhere?
I do still have high hopes from this company and the idea of The Room, I just hope they drop the scary-alchemy-Null-powers plot somewhat and focus more on the puzzles.

The Room Two, if you missed the first game, is at atmospheric, somewhat creepy, 3d puzzle game with a light story and a heavy dose of silent narrative. For those into super hardcore puzzles, it's probably not as challenging as you might hope, but for the more casual audience, or one where you need to pay attention to the environment and the detailed objects you can interact with, it's very fulfilling.
The Room Two picks up where the first game left off - our protagonist venturing through time and space into increasingly creepy locales. Now instead of focusing on a single puzzlebox, you explore a little room and multiple puzzleboxes that interact with each other in different ways.
I do kind of wish the ambient sounds of the first game made a return, but the new areas in the second game are pretty good, with some rooms being a little too poorly lit in my opinion. I also think some effort could have been spent on further narration in little notes, like being able to select a random book and see a couple pages from the "life and times" of each room.
No matter the case though, The Room Two is a short, enjoyable casual puzzle game with excellent sound and graphics, and an appealingly chilling story that genuinely makes you curious what is further down the rabbit hole.
Fun puzzler oozing with ambience and character. Don't hesitate to support this developer so we can get more of The Room on PC.

--For those wanting to just get to a hands on review skip to the secondary section.--
I have been watching and following, and in the past had time to help with hunting bugs and harassing the devs with copy pasted reports since it first came out on early access. Over time I have gotten to see this game grow more and more, thus expanding it's own potential. Take On Mars not only is a simulator, but an educational platform (Hence the wiki data you unlock in the Robotics portion.). With games like this, and Kerbal Space Program, I see a lot of potential for games to bring new challenges and focus to many forms of education in simulation that can even be utilized in classrooms to get kids interested in space exploration, physics, astrobiology, and aeronautics through adaptive and hands on learning.
I know it's been a long time, and yes the due date has been pushed back, and yes there are still bugs that need to be smashed. But in the end, Take On Mars will be a perfect platform for both simulation lovers, and Mars Enthusiasts as the work put into this makes it one of the most unique games currently in beta. Long strides have been made in gaming technology that opens up more intuitive and complex forms of learning and adapting to in game demands through user comprehension and skill. This game needs as much notice and support as possible.
------------------------------------------------Section Two--------------------------------------
Take On Mars is a game based on the research of Mars in understanding what is to be expected for human crews to work with. In the first portion you are able to utilize probes, lander, rovers, and advanced equipment to study the martian surface and gather real world intel based on scientific findings. In chapter two you will take the role of a surviving astronaut who has to survive on the surface through building and maintaining equipment (Chapter2 is still in development.)
Also there are singleplayer and multiplayer scenarios, along with an editor so that you can build your own scenario and upload it to the workshop. Along with this is the ability to easily mod the game files via the developer toolset if you're into that. This gives grounds so a lot of malleability to the game and what players can do with it. Overall, despite it being unfinished I have to give it a 8/10 for both the improvements, the dev team, and the uniqueness of the game. There are others sure, like Mars: Challenger, which is fun but not one I can honestly recommend.
All in all, Take On Mars is a gem, and to those wondering if it is worth buying I will say this:
If you don't mind putting in the effort to submit bug reports, push the game mechanics, and test different aspects of the game then yes, buy it and help the developers expand and debug more of it.
If you want something polished off the bat and are not patient or willing to aid in development, then no, and nor should you buy any game on Early Access because that is what it is for.
I would recommend this game for fans of the film "The Martian", although this game could do a little bit more TLC, I would reccomend to all who want to be Mark Watney on Mars.

This game saved my life. There I was, sulking in my depression, eating nothing but microwaved Kids' Cuisine every day, wishing my miserable excuse for a life would end. But then. Then it happened.
Conan came to me.
A dear, sweet, beautiful friend gifted me this game. I had no idea what to expect. I assumed it was just some random game sent to me as a joke. Little did I know, I was about to embark on a nonstop 3 hour journey that would forever change me.
As soon as I saw that small animated pig, my soul felt renewed. His eyes. His breathtaking, gorgeous eyes hypnotized me. It was as if he was speaking to me, right from his heart to mine. I felt him say, "Bread, everything is going to be okay. You will never feel alone again. You will know no more pain or suffering. I'm here now." At this point, I only had the game open for about 5 minutes, and there were already tears of joy streaming viciously down my face. I lifted my hands into the air, as if I was attempting to reach up to God, and I screamed, "I am alive! I am well! I am whole once more!" I could not contain my overwhelming happiness.
Once I calmed down a bit, I began my journey with Conan. We hid from the wolves. We bypassed the bees. We bravely crossed the ghosts. We did it all together. After hours of searching and strategic gameplay, we found them all. Every. Single. Truffle.
We laughed, we cried, we lost some, and we gained some. Throughout it all, the highs and the lows, Conan was with me. And I was with him. He is the best friend I have ever had. It was an experience I will hold onto in my memory until the day I leave this earth and go onto the afterlife, where I hope to meet him face to face someday. As soon as I see him walk through those pearly gates, his snout sniffing the ground for more delicious truffles, I will run to him. I will call out to him, "Conan! Conan! Come to me, my best friend! We will spend eternity in paradise together, endlessly searching for more truffles. No more wolves. No more bees. No more ghosts. Only happiness. Only love. Only us.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who feels lost. Anyone who feels alone. Anyone looking for the light at the end of the road.
Conan will be there for you, the way he is here for me.
He will help you.
He will comfort you.
He will save you.
He is not the hero we deserve, but he is the hero we were blessed with.
Be good to him. He will be good to you.

The Quake series has a legendary legacy, but games have changed so much since it was at the top of the industry. Heck, I was too young and almost totally unaware of PC gaming when it was in its prime. In a way, it's not surprising that many don't really know about Quake anymore, or have just forgotten about it. Nevertheless, its age and decreased popularity hasn't stopped it being one of the most fun and skillful multiplayer first person shooters ever.
Quake Live is an updated version of Quake 3 Arena, origially released in 1999. Its hallmarks are fast movement, great array of game types, diverse-functioning weapony, huge collection of maps, deep customisation and that classic kleptomanic video game logic that drives you to pick up every big, shiny, spinning, colourful item you see. Those pickups are really important too because in most modes, everyone starts off with almost nothing, so get prepared for the fight ahead!
There's nothing to bog down its pure and simple design either. Quake doesn't obsess about its characters, distract you with in-game stores where you can dress up your player model like a doll, charge extra for content or flair, offer artificial rewards, give players advantages over each other or have any cheap, unfair, exploitable tricks. It's all about the people you meet and the stuff that happens in your games. Just pick a match from the server browser that has some players and you're ready to go! It's a pity so many games tie themselves up with that other junk.
I started playing Quake Live before I created my account on Steam, back when it was free and ran in your browser. My old account accumulated hundreds of hours over the years on top of what's recorded here. While this doesn't compare to those who've been playing Quake for about a decade before that, I quickly learnt why they never put it down.
Take that as glowing praise, but it has one unfortunate problem. Those players are masters; they have a level of skill that's ruthless to compete with. Don't get me wrong, I have a heap of respect for them, I just wish I was anywhere as good! This coupled with the low population means you'll probably have a tough time. Some people irreverently compare it to chess, but there's some seriously incredible strategy and expertise to back that up. (Professional games are actually reasonably easy to watch and understand, even if you don't have as much experience.)
Don't let that discourage you too much though. Quake Live has one of the most friendly communities across any game I've played. They're the old guard. They're passionate. They play for the love of the game. I remember one time I was in a race server on the strafe-jumping challenge map and someone helped me improve my circle-jumping technique (an advanced movement ability) so I could complete the last obstacle with greater consistancy.
Experiences like that stick with you. As do the ones where you play really well or meet great opponents. I have a lot of good memories from this game, and am still having awesome moments. Hopefully the upcoming Quake Champions revives interest in arena shooters like this. They're brilliant.
While I didn't pay for Quake Live because I downloaded it while it was still free-to-play, I've bought four gift copies for friends so far, and will probably keep buying it for more in the future. It's definitely worth the price, and a total ball with mates.
Give it a shot. I reckon you'll like it.

A game with "Cold War" as the setting? That got my intrest, a "Submarine Simulator" game? Sign me up. Mods supported? Shut the hell up and take my money! After this I played and found a game alike to the early Silent Hunters, and well, I can't help but say that if you like all that my opener says. Do yourself a favour. Buy Cold Waters.

I am pretty sure that i have played every version of Silent Hunter. All of them, versions 1 through 5 have always been challenging, rewarding and very interesting to play. So when Cold Waters was released earlier this year i was very excited and happy that a newer, more modern submarine simulation game had finally come along.
It had been seven years since the release of Silent Hunter 5. After a couple years of playing Silent Hunter 5 i grew weary of the game and let it fall by the wayside. I was honestly quite happy to once again go into the murky deep, explore the oceans and destroy enemy combatants. I just knew i was going to be enjoying many hours of game play with the modern submarine simulator offered in Cold Waters.
Well, after 90 hours of game play, i must say i truly appreciate Silent Hunter 5 once again. I reinstalled Silent Hunter 5 and got futher into the game and it's career mode than ever before. While Cold Waters does have some charectoristics and feature that you will not find in Silent Hunter, such as verticle launch systems for surface to land missiles and a wide selection of submarine classes, it deeply lacks in aspects of the game like careers, crew interactions, and torpedo sciences. By sciences i mean that Cold waters gives you a mostly fire and forget use of torpedos while Silent Hunter gives you more of a learning experience when it comes to torpedo usage.
Rather than spending the $40-$50 dollars cold Waters cost me, i would have been happier if it had only cost me say $14.95, because thats about all it was worth. There are some really great YouTube videos out there (primarily by Jive Turkey) that really make the game seem fun and enjoyable. But i mostly want to thank the developers of Cold Waters for reawakening my past enjoyment of the Silent Hunter series.
So, in closing, if you are paying more than $15.00(U.S. dollars) then wait a bit for the price to come down.

The game doesn't have much replay value. The campaign is around 7-12h long depending on the difficulty you choose.
There's no multiplayer, co-op or "survival" (1 room with waves of enemies) mode to play.
The only thing this game offers you is a very linear and quite short singleplayer campaign.
So why am i recommending this?
It's very well done.
You can tell that a lot of heart was put into making this game. Not only that but being linear actually helps this game.
The game, as the title suggests, takes place in a metro. An open world/sandbox metro wouldn't make much sense, right?
Being linear helps you to get immersed with the world and creates this claustrophobic feeling you're supposed to have. Being stuck in a long, tight, dark tunnel. Hard to see anything and the graphics and eery* music just helps to get into the mood.
Have to give credit where credit is due. The ammount of detail in this game...Amazing! I couldn't stop taking screenshots!
Artyom is very well voice acted and so are some other characters but there are some very cringeworthy moments. Some of the russian accents are sooo bad i just wanted to cover my ears.
However that is the only complaint i have.
I haven't done a "pros and cons review" in a while so why not list some of 'em now, right?
+ Good and very detailed graphics
+Very good and spot on music
+Well done sound effects that help you get immersed
+Intriguing story
+Amazingly atmospheric
-Voice acting can be VERY bad at times
-After finishing the game you end up wanting more (which is a pro not a con...)
*I do realise that some people spell it "eerie" but when we do a bit of Googling it turns out that both "eery" and "eerie" are correct...Or so it seems.

STORY
Conan the mighty pig has a story that is open to much speculation. It is implied by the title that the pig you play as is named Conan and was for some reason granted the epithet, "the mighty pig," most likely earning it for proving his strength during combat. Ironically, Conan does not display any strength and has to sneak around tougher opponents and has to use herbs to get past bees. After years of owning a farm and not making profit (speculation of the story told without dialogue) he decides to move on from the farm and look for truffles. Truffles can potentially be very expensive in a larger size and are found in the ground by animals like pigs and trained dogs in real life and are profitable if the time and effort are put in to the labor, so it is reasonable that Conan would make the choice to look for truffles. He sets off on his quest to find one hundred fifty truffles.
My honest opinion on the story is that it is too reliant on the silent, mysterious approach to telling the tale instead of giving concrete facts on what is happening through dialogue or text. It is very underwhelming and not is what you should purchase the game for if you are looking for a story.
GAMEPLAY
When I played this game it felt some mechanics of other games are being recycled. The pig sniffing for herbs and other articles of potential pig food is a mechanic that reminded me of witcher senses from The Witcher 3. I felt the sniffing mechanic was a good throwback and improved on the flawed witcher 3 version. The sneaking mechanic in Conan the mighty pig seems to borrow ideas from the Metal Gear Solid franchise like how you must sneak in grass to avoid your enemy, where in this game the enemy is a wolf instead of humans. My biggest gripe with any elements of gameplay that seem to borrow from other games is the double jumping mechanic. That is obviously a rip off of Titanfall and I am seriously upset how blatant it was they stole Titanfall's idea. My final verdict on the gameplay is they heavily improve the mechanics they are borrowing, however they are borrowing too many ideas from rivaling companies like Konami and CD Projekt Red.
PERFORMANCE/GRAPHICS
Much like Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition, Conan the mighty pig is locked at a depressing 30 FPS. This restricts you from competitive play and makes the overall quality of the game drop but I must admit it adds to the games atmosphere. The only way to get above 60 FPS is by modding the game, potentially opening yourself up to breaking the game if installed incorrectly. If you are willing to play at 30 FPS, this game may be for you. If you are a 60 FPS junky like myself, this game is off limits without going through hours of modifying its .ini files.
The graphics of the game are where it truly shines. The well sized map allows for multiple environments from lush green forests that make your head spin in awe to the untouched tundra in the Arctic. They are pretty to look at thanks to the game’s modern engine which has real time lighting. There are no poorly created textures or clipping that I could find in my time on the game. This game will be easy on yours eyes.
MUSIC
When you are playing a game, you should often be hearing music. Music is what will remember when you are finished playing the game. If the music from the game is good, it may give you a nostalgic experience and you will be craving more gameplay. The music in this game is up to par in the industry. It is extremely trippy and will calm your nerves to a near sedated state that will have you hypnotized. During gameplay, you will love chilling to the tunes and collecting truffles while you do it.
FINAL VERDICT
Pros
•	Graphics are pretty
•	Improved gameplay mechanics from other games
•	Reminiscent of classics like Domestic Dog Simulator and Turbo Pug
•	Truffles look tasty and are a joy to collect
•	Multiple endings that are open to interpretation, much like Dark Souls and Counter-Strike.
•	Trippy music
Cons
•	30 FPS Lock
•	Lack of originality
•	Story leaves much to be desired
•	Stole ideas like double jumping from Titanfall
•       The overall concept this game agrees with is offensive and untrue. It tries too hard to spread the idea of multiple genders like “demi sexual” and “pig,” both very inappropriate things to identify as. I am very upset with the political incorrectness found in this title.
•	Women are identified as objects in game.
This game is a must buy if it is on sale if you want a relaxing experience and jam out to some chill tracks. Hopefully the multiplayer update will allow for me to sink more minutes in to the franchise.

The Room Two sacrificed some of the ingenuity of the previous game’s mechanical puzzle design on the altar of visual presentation. It is both simpler and more complex than the Room was, and it is still a highly recommended puzzle game.
As its title suggests, The Room Two is the direct sequel of a clever little puzzle game called
, both released originally for mobile devices, before they were remade fully for PC.
This time around the title bears more meaning, as the mechanical boxes of the first game have been replaced with entire mystery rooms, where several small “stations” serve as pieces of the current puzzle—and usually only of them can be considered an enigma box.
Broadening the playing field like this adds a variety in gameplay, but it also means that all small segments are a lot simpler by themselves. The result is something that is more tedious, yet strangely not as challenging as the original, but even these drawbacks couldn’t take away all the excitement that makes The Room Two a highly recommended game for anyone.

If you like business management types of games of the likes of the old Koei games such as Uncharted Waters/New Horizons, this game might be right up your alley.  Action game fans... probably should look elsewhere.
Unlike Uncharted Waters, you control a whole company, safely ensconced in your corporate headquarters, while directing whole fleets of ships to run trade routes.  Once you build up a set routine route, you can even just automate the route, so that the ship sails between up to around a dozen ports buying and selling the same things over and over for a profit.
The best aspect of the game, however, is how much of a subtle, but ever-growing impact you have on the world with your actions.  The more you trade with a city, the more it prospers economically, the more its population rises, the more it has to trade, but the more it needs to trade to get products it doesn't manufacture, itself.  Then, you can outright build a branch office in a city, build up your own personal industries, and outright control the whole city.
It's dirt cheap at sale prices, and if you have any interest in the genre at all, it's worth looking into before going into more pricey, more modern versions of the same game.

If you're wondering why the game is so janky, has a bunch of dead ends and most anti-virus software flag it as potentially harmful, there's a very simple reason for that: the game is a Windows Command Prompt batch script wrapped into an executable file with a tool called batch2exe, then packaged inside a dropper that places the file in your temp folder and runs it, which is in turn packed with UPX. All of that together makes it seem like a very suspicious file for any anti-virus with a heuristic scanner.

I really want to like this game. I really do. But I just can't bring myself to.
NEOTOKYO is a free Source-based mod of the FPS genre. It takes place in futuristic Japan, where people have been infused with technology and where two groups - government-funded army and a group of terrorists - fight against each other to collect and hold the "Ghost".
First of all, let's talk about the graphics. While the graphics themselves look somewhat aged by today's standards, they still look okay, which is boosted quite significantly by the good map design, reminiscing either old Japanese shrines or futuristic technologically-advanced undergrounds. If someone likes this kind of stuff then he/she can appreciate it.
Aaand then we come to the gameplay. You can expect only a few servers to run this game, with maybe one or two decently populated, which means you're going to be playing among the regulars most of the time. The game lacks any kind of tutorial or bot practice, so you are forced to figure out everything on your own.
NEOTOKYO very closely resembles Counter-Strike, unfortunately mostly in the bad ways. It has round perma-death, meaning that if you die to the aforementioned regular players, you're forced to wait until the next round for another chance at actual combat. Which means that you'll get maybe a minute total of combat time out of a half-hour game unless you're good (which you aren't due to being brand new). The fact that you unlock more weapon options if you do well in the previous rounds only widens the gap. This is not a great place to learn, the only way I can imagine you getting somewhat better is if you train in Counter-Strike before since it's somewhat similar in execution.
The whole gameplay revolves around the mode called "Capture the Ghost". In the middle of the map there is a robotic torso called the Ghost, which you are supposed to capture before the other team does. Having the ghost on slows you down a lot and also disables your primary weapon, making you rely on your teammates for protection. Holding the Ghost out however allows you to see the enemy positions, so you can inform your teammates where they're going to strike from. It's a somewhat unique and pretty interesting idea, and the execution of the gamemode itself is very good.
There are three classes: highly mobile but weak Recon, balanced Assault, and powerful but slow Support. Each one has a different selection of unique weapons and abilities - for example, Recon has infinite sprint and dark visor, Support has smoke grenades and thermal visor, and both Recon and Assault can use a camo module which makes them harder to see for a limited amount of time.
...and then everything breaks due to glitches. Bunny-hopping, as well as other speed-increasing techniques completely destroy any sort of realism in this game. People will hug walls and wobble back and forth to move faster than intended by the developers, thanks to the buggy physics engine. It also puts yet another wall to overcome for newbies, since regulars will be moving through the map at insane speeds, killing them before they can get anywhere or position themselves well.
Overall, I highly recommend you don't play this game. Making a sightseeing tour of the maps is an option, but it's absurdly imbalanced when it comes to the actual gameplay. It's a newbie-unfriendly territory with physics glitches that could be very easily fixed but aren't. This game is a brilliant concept, a good execution, but it's all ruined due to the buggy physics engine. It's sad to see something like this.

First let me say, I'm really loving this series so far and really hope the developer keeps on track and makes more.
Now, that's not to say there aren't a few issues this time around, but let's start with the Pros.
PROS:
- Fun, thought provoking logic puzzles
- Interesting story that does a decent job of not forcing itself down your throat
- Great graphics
- Relatively diverse environments keep it feeling fresh
CONS:
- Way too dark by default and even with a maxed out brightness in both the game and my monitor settings there were many areas and details I struggled to make out
- While having more movement capabilities is nice, navigating to and from puzzles in a room slows down the fun especially when each move has a relatively slow transition animation
- In that same vein, once a table/cabinet/general puzzle box location is selected, not letting the player interact with objects so some degree can trick them into thinking they can't interact with a required object simply because they haven't double clicked the area enough to zoom in on it (Might just be me, but I had some issues with this)
MINOR PERSONAL ISSUES (Spoilers?):
- Interaction with the "typewriter" was a novel idea, but tedious in action.
- The "4 letter vault" in the same chapter was another example of an interesting idea that was more annoying to physically DO than it needed to be, though still clever.
- Obtaining the "Death card" was slightly counter intuitive to me, since most times you see half of something missing, you have to find a key or piece to fill that gap first, especially when the object is small and looks more like a button than anything else.
SUMMARY:
Overall, this game is great and the pros outweigh the cons easily. I highly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of puzzle game, especially if you like games like The Witness or other atmospheric games. For $5 this game is well worth your time and money, as is the original.

"The Room" games are so much fun.  I've played all of them on Android, and I willingly play them on Steam, too. They're just fun. There are no idiotic combination puzzles like a lot of point and click games have; there is no death; you don't have to take a wild guess of what to combine in a massive inventory. It's all logic. The answers are all there right in front of you and they are all common-sense solutions. If you still get stymied just wait for a little bit and the hint box will help you along.
There is nothing about this game to not like. There's no bizarre obscurity to the puzzles and the minimal story is intriguing even if it really doesn't go anywhere. What's also great is that the game is long enough to warrant $5 (for whose who stupidly equate "hours of gameplay" with "value") but short enough that it doesn't overstay its welcome.
If you like puzzle games, buy it. You won't be disappointed.

I had been following this game for a while and had decided to wait until it was on sale before I bought it.  The more I read, the more I wanted to try it out so finally I just said screw it and picked it up.
Gotta say, $20 well spent!
Sure, the game is only 4-5 hours long, depending on how much exploring and running around you do, but the whole package is so interesting that it feels much deeper than it really is.
Everyone talks about how pretty this game is.  Well, it's no lie.  I found myself taking constant screenshots like I was on some sort of nature hike.  You know, those shots that everyone takes when they go on outdoor trips.  Trees, rocks, water, old buildings. All of it looks great in this game and I was a real shutterbug.  I just left the settings alone, but with my system it was at max by default.  Smooth animations too!
The voice overs, the music, the ambient sound effects.  All very authentic.  Similar to the above comments on graphics, the sound can realy draw you in.  Just put on some headphones, go stand by the water and just listen.  Wind, water flow, bugs, birds.  Nature.  It is very peacful.
This is another part of this game I really enjoyed.  The whole discovery mechanic for finding objects and solving puzzles is refreshing.  I could do without time stamping events, but thankfully those are few and far between.  If anything, I wish there were MORE puzzles.  This game makes me want a full blown "Sherlock Holmes" style mystery adventure with similar mechanics in place.  Would be awesome!
This will be my only knock on the game.  Don't get me wrong, the story is really good, but it became a little obvious too soon (for me at least) what was going on.  So a few times in the game I found myself rushing a bit.  So when I say it's a negative, I mean like when an actor in a movie does a bad accent.  It doesn't make the movie bad, it just is someting that bugs you if you pay too much attention.
I just wanted to touch on this one more time.  Some might say $20 for such a short game is too much.  And maybe you are right, but the overall package is really what is worth every penny.
So in the end, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who just wants a refreshingly new adventure in a beautiful world.  Just dive in, and enjoy!

I have been with this game back when it didn't even have dlc. The good old days of that weirdly pale blue border... Anyways, I digress. This game has a niche for people who want to play as their own empire and rule the world through certain means, Its great fun!
