If you've come for an interesting zombie game with an enthralling single-player story, then you're looking for the wrong game. The story is cliched and predictable. The characters are forgettable, the dialog is dull, and the main villian is generic and boring.
However, the gameplay more than makes up for the lack of story. The parkour is fun, the levels are fun to explore and reward you for doing so. The combat system can feel a little clunky at times such as when you try to dropkick someone and you just awkwardly vault of their head. While on the combat system, I have to comment on how annoyingly tanky some of the enimies are in the game. Humans feel like they take forver to kill (until you get guns) and some of the special zombies can be downright frustrating to fight. Not to mention the game is a lot more fun when you play it co-op (which greatly lessens the frustration of fighting said annoying enemies). Playing co-op imo is a lot more enjoyable than playing it by yourself as it lessens the penalties of dying since a teammate can pick you back up. Which brings me to my next point.
Another gripe I have is dying. The agility and power skill trees are easy to level up as they improve by freerunning and fighting. The main skill tree, survivor, fills from completing missions, side-quests, and events. Survivor is the only skill tree where it's possible to lose points, when you die you lose your points. If it were a small amount, I wouldn't be complaining about it. Sometimes it just gives you a cheap death such as when an explosion randomly kills you or you fall to your death when your character just wouldn't grab the edge. It takes away so many points when you die, that the surivor skill tree ends up being way underleveled compared to the other trees.
Overall, I'd reccomend the game, especially if you plan on playing it with friends. The fun of exploring the open world and dropkicking zombies off of rooftops makes up for the gripes I had. Though I'd probably wait to pick this one up on sale. IMO it's not worth $60.

Amazingly assembled. Ship management at full detail. I'll tell you what this game is about so you know why this game is worth your money. Pros and cons aside, I'll start off saying that I purchased FTL to fight the starship/crew-management urges that came with StarCitizen endless development. You can have the feeling of it, like approaching to the idea of starship development, crew hiring, pieces improving, etc. This is definitely a proper game for those who seek building up potential and fighting tougher and tougher enemies.
Pros:
-Wonderful music. Plenty of themes that match your situation and follow the genre assets.
-Well written story-ridden theme. Developers paid attention to detail, and little sparks of context make the whole product shine.
-Challenging. Like, don't even think about playing on "normal" at first. I haven't been able to finish it yet. Damn rebel flagship. The player can't even save and keep playing. You save, then you force-quit. If you keep playing after that, you can save again and quit again, but if you happen to lose, die, run out of fuel, or whatever, your save is deleted. Willy Wonka approves. You gain nothing. You lose. Have a good day, sir.
That's why the full playtime of the story is short. You're not even supposed to complete it at first try. Even then, new and rarer ships will be unlocked that change the playstyle and allow for nearly infinite replayabilty.
-RTS management. But pausing is allowed and encouraged. There are plenty of elements to manage, from single crew individuals to pieces of armament and dozens of gadgets. And they have no IA, they do what you tell them to. If they are left in a room, they will operate its systems. If there are none, the crewmember will stay idle until, say, there is a breach on the hull that needs to be repaired or an enemy invader comes by. No looking for something to do; after all it's a crew management game. What's the point if the crew didn't need managing?
-Low price. A must-have.
Nor pros nor cons:
-Pixelart design. While I enjoy the style, it's restrictive and choice-limited to certain public.
-Many more places than you can travel to. It's just like that, it allows open choices but forces many environments to be left behind.
Cons:
-Steam achievements lacking. There are ingame achievements just in the same way Steam offers. But there is not a link into that that allows for those achievements to be shown on your profile. And this game's achievements are a rewarding feeling.
Final note: Like Dwarf Fortress fans say, Losing is Fun. And so is FTL, in that way. Every game teachs the player something new.
Overall score: 9/10

Metro 2033 Redux is basically a remastered and polished version of the original Metro 2033. You play as Artyom, a Russian soldier tasked with eliminating threats, delivering messages or just surviving as they travel through the metro and upon the surface of post-apocalyptic Mosow, Russia. The metro is littered with mutated abominations such as the Nosalis and the 'Dark Ones'. The stations of the metro are almost like different cities with completely different citizens, merchants and even beliefs. It's mainly a first person shooter but also has stealth and horror aspects.
This game does a great job of making you feel immersed as you traverse in the deep, dark crevices of the metro or the blisteringly cold and pale surface above. This also helps give the story a nice outline and makes the entire gaming experience more riveting.
Although the main focus of this game is the first person shooting, it has surprisingly nice hints of psychological horror. This fits with the theme of the 'dark ones' and how ominous and mysterious they are. You sometimes see flashbacks and shadows of events that occured in areas you discover, and they're honestly pretty spooky.
Being an FPS, you can expect good and fun shooting mechanics from this. You are also able to select up to 3 weapons of your choice either from merchants or the bodies of the deceased. You can customize them with attachements too, if you're willing to spend the money.
You can choose to either go guns-blazing and pumping your enemies with lead, or taking the more concise and stealthy route and take out your foes from within the shadows. The way you play also has an effect on the ending of the game, there's a good ending, and a better ending. The better ending requires you to play completely differently from the start of the game, I don't want to spoil how to do it so a quick google search should do the trick.
Although stealth is an option, I just don't feel like this game was meant for it. Map layouts can be weird sometimes as well as enemy spawns and pathing. You do have stealth weapons such as silenced guns and throwing knives, but I still think stealth is hard to pull off, even if you're skilled.
If you're new to this game, there isn't a lot of guidance or help. The games seems to not inform the player on basic mechanics such as using your lighter to burn cobwebs, or what your watch does. This isn't really a problem after you get used to the game, but it still is for newbies.
Unfortunately there isn't really a character you get to create a bond with, not even your own, Artyom. He doesn't speak at all during gameplay, the only time he does is between chapters and he only sums up what just happened in the form of a diary entry. You can find diaries lying around as you play the game which unravel Artyom's past and thoughts, but other than that there is not much.
8.3/10

When my best friend told me about this game he described it as an updated version of the 1986 Microprose game Red Storm Rising, which is exactly what it is. If a Commodore 64 could track play time like Steam you'd seen the teenager me with hundreds of hours split between that, Silent Service, Gunship and Project Stealth Fighter. (Those were they days, my friends...) So, I bought the game, largely sight-unseen, because of a handful of pre-release videos and the developer's state goal of exactly what I said above.
First what this game is NOT: It is not a station-simulator like Janes 688i, Sub Command or Dangerous Water. Don't buy this if you want to play out fantasies (or recall the good-old-days) of the minutea of operating a sonar set on a nuclear submarine. This isn't an underwater Falcon 4.0.
Nor is this Harpoon or Command: Modern Air-Naval Warfare. It is not a rigerous simulator of operational-level actions. You are not COMSUBLANT giving orders from on high to defeat the Soviets in the North Sea, you are more like Commander Daniel X. McCafferty of the USS Chicago hunting fleet oilers and Kirov task forces or firing Tomahawks at Soviet airstrips in the Kola Peninsula.
This game is what I stayed up late playing in my teen years with a closed door and towel under the crack so my parents wouldn’t suspect. It is the game that at my 20th high school reunion classmates I hadn’t seen since I was 17yo recalled me playing. This is the game that got me into reading Tom Clancy, Larry Bond, Michael DiMercurio and playing the GDW tabletop games Harpoon and Twilight 2000. This is the game that I consumed gallons of Mello Yello at $0.49 per 20oz bottle playing. All of the fun of those memories, but with reasonably modern graphics and a decidedly better interface (as of the 1.07 patch).
Like it's 1980s predecessor this game has non-player crewmen operate stations like sonar, torpedo control and ballast control while you concern yourself with tactics, weapon choice and employment and the decisions of command during combat. Like the older game the most useful screen is the map view and the 3d cinematic¬¬¬ is mostly for vanity’s sake. The updated UI allows more of a “giving orders” feel to the game and software like Voice Attack is compatible with many of the game commands if you want to play out your fantasies of standing on the bridge giving orders.
There are two campaigns – one set in 1968 and another in 1984. I’ve only played a small amount of the 1984 setting, but the scope is about the same as the older game, but no more than that. Essentially, it is your single American boat against the Soviet Navy. There’s no support from other NATO units. The available US boats are the Skipjack, Permit, Sturgeon and Flight I Los Angeles-classes and a handful of sui generis testbed boats like the USS Narwhal. Though there’s been no announcements yet the developers has openly stated their intent to add friendly units, more campaigns and allow play as other NATO (and even Pact) members.
Modding new ships and weapons and adjusting the values of existing units is trivially easy, they’re all plain text files, but the game engine’s middleware makes adding new 3D models virtually impossible. The developers have it on their long wishlist.
Gameplay: 8/10
This is essentially an improved remake of my second favorite games of all time. (My #1 favorite, the 1984 space sim Elite, already got its improved remake.) The game has a learning curve, but it’s not as bad as many of the pure-simulator games out there. It’s not quite an arcade game, but it’s a game first and simulator second. I’d compare its complexity and authenticity to Microprose and Janes simulators from the 1990s – complex enough to require reading the manual (and making real-world knowledge helpful), but simple enough to be approachable by interested laymen.
The knocks are partly because the interface still feels incomplete and partly because there’s still some balance issues that need to get worked out. I’ve not played a huge amount and with the updated interface the controls aren’t terrible difficult to learn if you’re used to similar games, but even with the recent (1.07) updates there’s still a bit of bugginess.
Graphics: 6/10
Serviceable is the best way to describe them. They’re not bad, per se, but nor are they top of the line. Of course, this is also a good thing because it means I can play it on my Surface Pro 3, but it also means it doesn’t look astoundingly better on my high-end gaming desktop. Each enemy boat has a single (or a small number of) 3d models showing damage and objects like crates on the deck don’t fall off when a boat capsizes. I’d compared the graphics to a top-of-the-line game in 2001 or so, and with vehicle-oriented games that means they look pretty good until they get damaged and then the flaws in the simplicity start showing.
Ignoring 3D, the game’s map and interface graphics are decent for getting the information required across. I could certain suggest improvements for information density and availability, but again, it’s serviceable.
Sounds: 7/10
I’ve never served on a nuclear sub, but the game at least gets the Hollywood version of it across with the hull creaking, pump noises, wooshing of torpedos firing and, more recently, the crew responding to orders. The only real downside to the recently implemented crew voices is I can’t figure out of there is a single voice actor doing them all, if a handful of actors provided voices for different words or if a given actor plays a specific position on the boat where helm, diving control, sonar, weapons, chief of the watch, etc. are different people. The sounds are good enough for what they need to be, but won’t be winning game awards.
Controls: 5/10
The controls in the game how it originally shipped were crap (or maybe I’m just spoiled by my mouse). The original game was 90% keyboard driven and unlike the 1980s version there was no custom-cut keyboard overlay in the box. The keyboard commands were also oddly organized with one command toward the top of the keyboard meaning “up with ballast” while another command toward the bottom meaning “up with planes.” Yes, it makes sense in context of how the stations actually work, but it’s confusing if you’re not well versed in it.
Since the 1.07 update the game is a lot more playable with a mouse-driven interface for dive control and engine room and the ability to click on the screen to steer the ship along with a panel for operating the masts and clicks for countermeasures. (I wish you could manually set the bearing with numbers instead of clicking, though and as of this writing there is no “up periscope” button I’m aware of.) The interface just gives me the feeling of needing lots of work, though it is decidedly better than many subgames from years ago.
Social/Community/Developer: 9/10
First off, there is no multiplayer and it’s a far-off goal for the developers.
Second, the community for the game on Steam and SubSim Forums is generally friendly, though I’ve had no direct interaction. (If I have an account it’s only to gain access to members-only downloads.) The Developers, however, are extremely active on those forums and listen to requests and respond as to why they will, won’t or can’t do it. For example, the interface changes and crew voices were due in large part to community requests and the voices are actually members of those forums.
The developers are willing to help with modding to the extent they’re able, but there are some technical issues as to why their assistance is somewhat limited. The Unity engine the developers used makes it difficult to modify 3D models without a recompile of the game assets. (Kerbal Space Program uses Unity as well and 3D modding is trivially easy in it, so the problem can be overcome but it is still a future goal.) Having said that, nearly every settings file are in plain text and the developers are friendly to modders changing them and adding new content.

A classic entry in the Seafaring Trading Game genre. It sets the stage for later, more developed, titles like Port Royale (which oddly is seen in the second preview screenshot above).
What do you do in the game? Quite a bit. Trade is only the beginning, and the player is only a small part of the greater game, where the local royalty, the chuch, pirates, the Hanseatic League, and other traders all play a role. Hunt down competitors on the high seas as a pirate, run goods around the North sea in a small trading ships, build and control towns and the Hanseatic league, lead huge convoys across the map and on expeditions.
Sea combat is conceptually interesting, if functionally uninteresting at times, such as when your ship going 6 knots chases another ship at 6 knots. Ships may be fast and quick to run, or heavily armed with cannon, or somewhere in-between with ballistae and catapults.
Blah blah, try it out if you're into trading sims. It's worth the $2.49 aand I'm out of review space

Even the situations where you're forced into combat has a certain physicallity to them that outshines many encounters in other games.
The soundtrack is also pretty great with a call back to 80's synths and horror movies, though it only seems to play during main-story missions.
The bit about the ost aside, my biggest and only gripe is that sometimes the HUD elements for where to go and what to do with certain quests, has a tendency to just not tell you, or it'll give you an overly broad area to search.  While annoying, a quick trip to google usually fixes it.

Amazingly assembled. Ship management at full detail. I'll tell you what this game is about so you know why this game is worth your money. Pros and cons aside, I'll start off saying that I purchased FTL to fight the starship/crew-management urges that came with StarCitizen endless development. You can have the feeling of it, like approaching to the idea of starship development, crew hiring, pieces improving, etc. This is definitely a proper game for those who seek building up potential and fighting tougher and tougher enemies.
Pros:
-Wonderful music. Plenty of themes that match your situation and follow the genre assets.
-Well written story-ridden theme. Developers paid attention to detail, and little sparks of context make the whole product shine.
-Challenging. Like, don't even think about playing on "normal" at first. I haven't been able to finish it yet. Damn rebel flagship. The player can't even save and keep playing. You save, then you force-quit. If you keep playing after that, you can save again and quit again, but if you happen to lose, die, run out of fuel, or whatever, your save is deleted. Willy Wonka approves. You gain nothing. You lose. Have a good day, sir.
That's why the full playtime of the story is short. You're not even supposed to complete it at first try. Even then, new and rarer ships will be unlocked that change the playstyle and allow for nearly infinite replayabilty.
-RTS management. But pausing is allowed and encouraged. There are plenty of elements to manage, from single crew individuals to pieces of armament and dozens of gadgets. And they have no IA, they do what you tell them to. If they are left in a room, they will operate its systems. If there are none, the crewmember will stay idle until, say, there is a breach on the hull that needs to be repaired or an enemy invader comes by. No looking for something to do; after all it's a crew management game. What's the point if the crew didn't need managing?
-Low price. A must-have.
Nor pros nor cons:
-Pixelart design. While I enjoy the style, it's restrictive and choice-limited to certain public.
-Many more places than you can travel to. It's just like that, it allows open choices but forces many environments to be left behind.
Cons:
-Steam achievements lacking. There are ingame achievements just in the same way Steam offers. But there is not a link into that that allows for those achievements to be shown on your profile. And this game's achievements are a rewarding feeling.
Final note: Like Dwarf Fortress fans say, Losing is Fun. And so is FTL, in that way. Every game teachs the player something new.
Overall score: 9/10

DISCLAIMER: This review is solely based on the singleplayer portion of the game.
This game is a hard one for me to review. On one hand, I really like it, but on the other, there are so many aspects of this game I wish were different or better.
The good stuff:
- Nice graphics and artstyle: The crazy spaceship designs from WH40K are in here, ranging from the Emperial Cathedral looking ships to the "garbage-pile-glued-together" Ork ships. It's amazing.
- Good story: The story is pretty interesting, albeit a bit dramatic (againt, classic WH40K)
- Micromanagement in spades: You get fine tunes controls over all your ships, and knowing how to position your different types of ships can often mean the difference between a win or loss. Firing non-guided torpedos and watching them hit enemy ships never gets old.
- Customization: You can customize each of your ships, from the small, fast frigates to the city-sized Battlecruisers.
- Bite-sized mission structure: Each match takes anywhere from 3-8 minutes, which makes it so it doesn't feel like a waste of time when you lose.
Although all of the above makes for a compelling argument, there are also some significant drawbacks that are important to know about:
- Slowly paced story: The story is waaay to poorly paced. Combined with the next criticism, I imagine that it's too much of an endurance test for most people.
- REPETITIVE AS HELL: You are introduced to a range of (not so) different mission objectives, which you have to do over. And over and over again. Sure, the occassional story mission mixes it up, but when I'm completed my 16th Data Recovery mission, or I've Assassinated someone 12 times, it get's real old. Also, certain mission types are easily broken by employing certain strategies (Escort missions, I'm eyeing you).
- Way too long: Although it might seem like a weird thing to complain about long games, this is just too repetetive to earn a completion time of 25+ hours. I feel like this game could have been 10-12 hours long, and actually be better for it.
- Small space battles: You never really get a sense of epic space battles, as at most of the time, you'll have an average of 4-5 ships on you side.
- Cheesy story: If you are not into the over dramatic type of story WH40K often brings, you'll roll you eyes all the time.
This is definitely a cautious recommendation. Do you like WH40K? Then probably get it. Do you like micromanagement heavy games? Then there's something for you in here for sure.
I just can't get over the repetetive gameplay and mission structure, so I would highly recommend getting this only if it's on sale, and only if you don't mind doing a lot of repetition. That being said, there are some awesome moments to be had in here for sure  (winning a fight with half of your ships on the verge of blowing up is so satisfying).
Some people like scores, and for them, I'd give this game a 7/10

Veterans of the original version of Metro 2033 will notice a change in how the game starts. Before you pick your difficulty, you pick the way you want to play the game. Will you pick Survival, which will require players to conserve ammo, utilize stealth, and pick and choose when to fight or flee? Or will you pick Spartan, which is more akin to the action style of Metro: Last Light? The ability to pick between Survival and Spartan is included in both of the Metro: Redux titles, and each play out very differently. Not wanting to risk compromising the dark thrill of the first time I played Metro 2033, I opted for Survival and though I was also tempted to go with the hardest difficulty available I passed it up for the normal difficulty instead.
So here I was, once more taking that first climb into the outside world. Or rather, first from the gameplay perspective. You see, Metro 2033 actually begins at a climactic moment in the story and then in a flash the main character Artyom retells the story, and as such you relive it from his perspective. That first scene really helps set the stage and the gut wrenching feeling of the troubles that wait ahead. The story remains as superb today as it was in 2010 as it successfully combines the horrors of war with the supernatural and paranormal sprinkled in just enough to add another layer of tension. However with Metro: Last Light showing us what the canon ending is, returning players may feel inclined not to make same the choices for what - at the time - seemed like the "good" ending.
The first thing I noticed other than the graphical enhancements, were the controls. I'm not sure if it is all in my head or if the controls are honestly much more polished than they once were, but I went from a game where I died more often to accidental falls or overextended movements to something that controlled as crisp and precise as other shooters. Firing from the hip was actually a viable option this time around, whereas in the past you'd be lucky to hit the broad side of a barn without aiming down your sights.
Another thing substantially improved is the friendly AI. I cannot express how many times in the original I died because of failures of the AI. In games like Call of Duty, the AI is intentionally made useless so that the player can feel like a hero, but that same thought process doesn't transfer over well if it is one of several parts where you have to fight tooth and nail for survival. In the original game, you'd be lucky if your comrades could even kill a single enemy. Now, they still let you do most of the work but they are actually helpful in situations that would otherwise be frustrating to the point of pulling your hair out.
Hopping back and forth between the games to compare the graphics across all settings, the game looks better across the board. Of course this means that if your current PC struggled with the original version of Metro 2033 you're going to have to sit this one out. Character models and environment textures have been majorly improved, offering an intense, almost real display of a downtrodden society that dwells beneath the surface. In the above-ground segments, however, the appearances of humans takes a slight hit. The beautiful display of life in the tunnels of the Moscow metro was already amazing just a few years ago, but now that beauty has increased tenfold.
While the visuals have been majorly updated and the gameplay itself feels more polished, it seems as if all of the original dialogue audio was left the same. Not that this is a bad thing mind you, but I have a pet peeve when I encounter enemies in the game that are supposed to be of an entirely different nationality using Russian accents as though it's just business as usual. Other than that, the voice work was great then and it's mostly a good decision to have kept it as is.
Metro 2033 Redux has taken the original title and increased the quality to such heights that it was like playing a completely different game. Amazing graphics, refined and tweaked gameplay... it all makes for a much smoother experience. There are no sacrifices of the good of the original but it does successfully eliminate the bad - this is how remakes should be. Whether you have played the original or not, this is a game for anyone seeking atmosphere, story, and FPS gameplay blended into something amazing. Do not miss this experience.

Metro 2033 Redux ist an incerdibly atmospheric first-person-shooter.
The story takes place mainly in the metro of moscow and occasionally in the ruins of moscow in the year 2033 about 20 years after an atomic apocalypse due to a third world war resulting in atomic winter. Along your journey to save your home station against a new kind of hazardous creatures you encounter various interesting characters and meet several groups of humans such as a newly formed Nazi Reich and a station of communistic fascists. I don't want to say anything further about the plot just a few words: It's not the best plot ever, the characterization could be better and hopefully is improved in the sequel I didn't play until now. However the story is still entertaining and you want to see what happens next.
Gameplaywise you get different playstiles, often, but not always, you can choose wether you want to kill oder knock your enemys out stealthy or just rush through the tunnels of the moscow metro like a gunslinger. Either way ist really fun. To further underline your playstile you may choose between survival or ranger mode which grant you more or less ammo and have effect on your enemys health and the damage they deal. Though the stealth gameplay is not as good as in other games that focus mainly on stealth, it is a worthy addition in combat.
For a remastered game of this age the graphics are really nice and the background music does a decent job in further taking you into the deep atmosphere of the tunnels and stations. The levels are well designed even though they are often pretty streamlined straight forward. Luckily it does not damage the overall expierience hence the tunnels and stations give you constantly a claustrophobic feeling. All the detail both in the more civilized inhabited and deserted stations is plain and simple awesome and often gave me the chills. Due to the atmosphere the game even tends to be a little scary from time to time, especially if you choose the survival mode and focus on stealthy enemy approach.
I strongly recommend this game if you like well crafted singleplayer shooters with fresh settings. If you liked the stalker series, you certainly will enjoy Metro 2033 Redux!

If you are reading this, I want you to not buy this game unless you are extremely UNPICKY about games in general.
-----SPOILER ALERT - MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS, BUT ONLY MINOR ONES
If you have night vision on when you are transitioned into a gunnery position, you cant turn night vision off. That function is not in the game's engine, so let's say you like Far Cry 2 and onwards at least, then Metro 2033 is nothing like it. They simply have no idea how to make this first person shooter feel real. You cant do two things at the same time basically. Its an either or throughout the game.
-----STEALTH:
When you stealth, if you get caught (levels are btw usually not put in place for it to be possible to pull off cool stealth things), so uh if you get caught, everyone will immediately know where you are. If one person saw you there, the others who are somewhere completely different, will know instantly. The mechanics of all AI in this game is quite dumb.
-----RAILS:
You are on rails in different carts in this game quite a lot. Do you remember sitting in the back of a lorry in Call of Duty (the first game, the good game that had actual content) and you used bazookas to kill trucks following you? How great that was. In THIS game, you see a bunch of dumb monsters jump around your cart underground and scream etc. Everything is predetermined at that point, and you're not able to shoot any of these, because to save money and programming skills, the engine in this game is so bad, that it can't produce anything but different stages and modes. Let me explain:
If a monster is running around your cart, it is in "Fixed animation mode" where it wont actually be a moving thing, it will just be an animated thing which cant interact with the world, and the world cant interact with it. It just looks the same as the things about to interact with you. What you'd think really, is when you see a monster running around like this is "OMG SHOOT IT!" but actually you cant, because it's not actually there yet. It will then make itself look like its jumping onto your cart, and then change its mode to "Stuck to your cart and you can interact with it-mode", where it will scream at you and attack you, which means you can actually shoot this thing which now has landed at a predetermined moment on your cart. It was not of its will, it was just programmed to do exactly as it was told, and that goes for every AI throughout the game. I hope my explanation was.. OK.
-----GASMASKS (and finding your way):
Oh lord -.-
The most advanced and lively aspect of this game, is the realism the gas mask brings you.
First of all: You need one now and then to breathe. It then gets a bunch of blood on it which you have to clean away, and while you're running around, your guy will start breathing heavier and heavier because the filter needs to be swapped quite often. This means you have to stock up on filters when you can, which means you have another thing to spend money on which in my money is just like.. "we didn't have any better ideas dude, so we put this in".
This also means you'll hear a heavy, annoying breathing noise. It will also cover with droplets, making your screen covered with this blood now and then and these droplets. Ugh...
Now to finding your way. You know when you see that area over there where there's basically nothing, so it's probably barred off with something so you're supposed to go somewhere else? That's quite often where you're supposed to go, and you'll be stuck running around wasting precious gas mask time which you previously stocked up on, to look for where to go. Then you may ask yourself: "Where should I move?" and the answer to that is: "On". That is all. "Move on! And then when you have reached a boring cutscene of fake russian accents, stop, stock up, and move on some more in this extremely dull and boring world."
There is no objective to follow, you can't ask the journal for help or anything. It just happens that whatever road is open to you, is EXACTLY where you're supposed to go, even though the story has a predetermined set point of where you're going. If you're lazy, you'll be googling quite a lot to find your way before your gas mask filters are all gone. This puts a stopper to the whole gameplay experience.
-----THE GAMEPLAY EXPERIENCE:
is quite sucky anyway. If you've ever seen videos of this game thinking "This game looks like another dull FPS with no real content but to move from A to B to C and kill people as you go" then you were completely spot on correct. I bought this game because everyone bragged their asses off at it, but I should seriously have trusted my instincts, and so should you!
-----THE STORY
It sucks so far. You meet people now and then, and then they die so that you can meet a new person somewhere else. Mostly you meet them when they come in at the last second to save you. So you are a survivor, saved by those you meet, but everyone you meet who had a really good first impression, will die.
-----MISC
They say it's a game based on a book, and the book I bet is great. The game is there to milk the book for money as cheaply as it possibly can. I'll add here that the graphics and other mechanics are also pretty bad. Voice acting is also bad.
You can save a little boy. I really wish I hadnt. He was just annoying. While carrying him, the mechanics of the movement and aiming has as slight delay because you are.. carrying a boy. Later, you will give this boy to his mother. A music will play, which means you now have 2 soundtracks playing at once. At this point, without the kid, the kid is still on your back on your shadow, and youre running with your hands as if holding a gun, without holding a gun.
Small mutant dogs or whatever come at you from wherever they want, holes here and there, which then attacks you once and runs away. While running around finding your way, this becomes extremely annoying.
The game is outdated in most aspects. For both its initial release, and the 2014 Redux update.
Weapons have mods, but these are few and boring.
You're usually doing the same thing over and over again in this game, not a lot of new stuff.
The weapons are very few btw, and only 2 weapons are actually stealthy. A melee knife which you stab at people or cut their throats which both look very weird, and throwing knives, which are clunky to throw, or even find. Google how to do it, and you'll have both Xbox players and PC players ask for this. The thing is to clunkily hold tab, drag with mouse to specific thrown item (no, you cant quickly swap, are you mad?) and then hit the throw key. Which reminds me: Throwing a grenade from darkness into unsuspecting enemies means they will see you the moment you throw it, scream "there he is" in fake russian, and everyone in the area will shoot at you immediately like that.
-----CONCLUSION---------> VERY disappointing game which I dont understand why people have been bragging about.

Metro 2033 is probably one of the most suprising games I have played recently.  This is one adventure that should be taken by all.  The graphics are shockingly good when played on a decent pc.  The atmosphere of post apocalyptic Moscow and its surrounding ruins is incredibly well done.  In fact, this is probably the second most atmospheric game I have ever played (first being Metroid Prime).  The sound design is also fantastic with the beasts sounding menacing and the dark tunnels sounding empty.  The lighting is also extremely impressive and really adds a lot to the atmosphere of the game.  I will say that gameplay wise, Metro 2033 is probably my favorite fps game gameplay wise of all time.  The shooting is extremely satisfying, weapons behave like they should.  There is decent customization to weapons and there are also many additional side mechanics such as pumping pneumatic weapons and charging capacitors for your torch.  However a few problems I had with the game was that it was definitely a bit buggy at times.  The AI can be buggy and there is clipping at times.  For one mission, enemies that were supposed to spawn failed to do so and therefore I had to restart the whole mission.  These issues should have been smoothed out as this is the redux version of the game.  I can only guess on how buggy the original game was...  Another issue I had with the game was that it had a rather limited soundtrack.  There was this one song that just kept being repeated over and over whenever you encountered portable radios in the settlements beneath Moscow.  The final issue I had with the game was that the narrative was simply not deep nor intresting enough to make me really care for the story.  I stuck around for the incredible atmosphere and the tight gameplay.  Metro 2033 Redux is about 12 hours in length and the game is very linear in structure (good amount of side paths to discover) and lacks any form of replay value.  However, it is such an incredible gameplay experience that I have to highly recommend this title to any fans of "real" gaming.  Go out and get the Redux bundle with Metro Last Light Redux today.  Rating: 8.3/10

The good:
-the cinematics and voice acting are excellent. They really capture the feel of the different species, and I found myself really enjoying the exploration of the Warhammer 40k universe.
-no bugs, I'm reporting this since other users reported issues with stability.
The bad:
-Some factions are incomplete. Eldar, I'm looking at you.
-Unwise UI element choices. I had to restart the game because I misspent resources. On one page a button is required to be pushed in order to commit a choice. On another the same button is a costly reset of your points, without a confirmation to the action. There are other small issues. You'll see.
-Steeply difficult game. It's definitely not a relaxing game, Your loss or victory is completely based on the RNG generator. It can be pretty brutal.
-Not fun. All of the gameplay is watching your ships turn like slugs in slow motion. Its entire mechanic is your own ship placement to best use their abilities, which doesn't play well. I found myself saying, "Come on! Come on!" over and over again. Small successes feel like enormous victories.
-Stingy with resources. It feels like the developers wanted the player to feel like they were up against losing odds. This can work sometimes, but when your principle game mechanics are annoying, the game boils down into frustration.
-Cheap AI. Even on easy, the AI will wait till the last possible moment of your success to steal it away from you. It breaks immersion, because I see the hand of a cackling developer, and not a challenge to overcome.
I've spent 3 afternoons playing the game, and honestly it's affected my peace of mind. It's the first game in a while I'll quit playing simply because I don't like it.

Another thing that should be mentioned about the story is that quite a few missions are just side activities, which was a cheap was of adding more digits on the playtime number. Overall, the story is pretty decent, but no mass effect 1
Characters: 9/10
They aced the characters in this game. The main character is very easy to like and funny. The lighthearted tone of this game truly does prevail through the characters. All of the characters in this game are different from one another and mostly not cliche. Overall, the characters in this game are nearly perfect.
Gameplay: 10/10 or 6/10
The gameplay is their biggest strength, yet the cause of their weakness. In the first hour of the game, you get super powers. The first two are super speed and super jump. It may sound good to you, but super speed is way faster than a car, which literally ruins the purpose of vehicles in this game. The other issue with this is that if you sprint towards someone and left click, you do a cutscence that one hit kills them. Although the super powers are really fun, they also completely destroy balance. It does not mean the game is unplayable, but the casual gamemode is designed for a guy who plays on his playstation 1 for ten minutes every sunday. Definitely turn up the difficulty if you want an enjoyable experince
Content: 9/10
This game defenitly has a good amount of content. I was able to beat the campaign in about 18 hours, but that also includes the loyality missions that you do if you want to get the best possible ending. Without them, it will be around 16. There are many side activities to do, along with the giant map. Overall, this game definitely has enough content to keep you satisfied.

I do feel that i was hard on the game, and I did bash the game for errors it did make. That being said, I still loved this game and thought it was definitely one of the best third person action games I have ever played. Aliens have attacked, the world is in ruins, and now the only thing that bars the aliens from completely annihilating the human race is you: the commander of the XCOM program. They murdered your people, brought your cities to the ground in flames, now you’re given the chance to form an army of special forces soldiers set with the single task of ending the alien invasion, as well as ending as many alien lives in the process. In XCOM: Enemy Unknown you not only command your men in the field of battle, but you’re tasked with keeping the XCOM headquarters up and running as well. You build engineering labs to ramp up your production, thermal generators to keep your buildings up and running, or science labs to give a hasty boost to your research. This isn’t even close to all of the constructs that you command as Commander of the XCOM Project, but just an example of the full range of control you exert over the HQ. You control a significant part of your soldiers as well, deciding on what they’ll bring into battle or who’ll be awarded with what medal, even deciding their cosmetic features like hair color and facial shape. This is pretty fantastic, and since the commander is a faceless entity you’re also able to easily fill the role yourself, making Enemy Unknown incredibly immersive. There’s simply such extensive detail in XCOM: Enemy Unknown that you really feel you’re the commander, and you really feel like the whole defense of earth has fallen into your hands.
Considering that there’s an alien invasion currently underway, you’re going to be doing a significant amount of fighting, boots on the ground. It’s important that you have some kind of mind for strategy as you’ll quickly find out that the aliens in XCOM:EU pull no punches, throwing just about every kind of monstrous extra-terrestrial in their arsenal at you. There’s such phenomenal variety among the alien units that I often found myself, to my slight dismay, excited to see a new type of enemy, temporarily forgetting that they were here to obliterate me. There’s alien mechanized units, mind-controlling commanders, and so much more that you’ll still be seeing new units even in the end game. Something that I really appreciate about XCOM is how enemies are introduced gradually as the game progresses, which always gives you something to look forward to outside of your activities in the HQ. Your foes are tough, but fair, requiring you to plan ahead and understand which foes you might encounter and how to properly counter them. Equipping your soldiers properly is critical to the success of the XCOM Project, your level of technology and gear possibly meaning the difference between life and death for your men in the field. In order to get new and better technologies you’re going to need to research them in your laboratories, one of the buildings you can construct throughout your HQ, and these projects consume your most valuable resource: time. There’s an abundance of projects to research and even though a story is present, I felt in a lot of ways that I was more looking forward to what new technology I could unlock more than what was going on there. Once you research these new technologies you then set your hulking foundries to the task of producing them. Remember that not only are you the manager of the XCOM HQ, but also the manager of the entire XCOM Project, and as such you need to ensure that the project doesn’t get axed. About a dozen countries back the XCOM Project, and each one has a rapidly rising panic meter, forcing you to become a bulwark against their terror, protecting them at all costs. If you fail to stop their rising panic however, countries will begin to pull out one by one, with the game ending after a certain number of countries leave the project. Their fear and panic are managed by sending men on missions with a reward of panic reduction, though you can deploy satellites above each country in order to give a one-time panic reduction as well. I don’t think that it’s possible to fully express just how frustrating this system is, losing the game because you weren’t able to satisfy these countries is infuriating as hours of progress could be lost simply because you weren’t able to meet some trivial request. There’s mods out there to turn this off, and, while I don’t think that it’s necessary, it’s heartening to know that this isn’t going to ruin the XCOM experience for those who desire the option.
When the heroic men and women of the XCOM Project aren’t preoccupied with training to miss 95% shots, they’re being deployed on perilous missions in the hope of ridding earth of this alien menace. Combat in XCOM is stressful, and I mean that in the best way possible. There’s a palpable tension as you make the decision to risk that 65% shot or open your flanks so you can get a kill. That kind of risk is what makes XCOM’s combat so special: you have to make decisive choices in the field that could mean either life or death for those under your command. Even just your basic attacks have a chance to miss, so performing actions as basic as firing on an enemy sectoid could go wrong, leaving your men vulnerable and possibly dead. XCOM’s combat feels just like a colossal gambling ring, where every choice you make has a percent chance attached to it, which I believe is what makes XCOM so extraordinary. XCOM as a series likes to punish you firmly and often for making mistakes and Enemy Unknown is no different. A single mistake can actually end a mission for you entirely or lead to a full squad of casualties, something that you’re going to learn as your first few squads are promptly butchered and returned to HQ in buckets. What’s interesting about XCOM is that punishment is actually an enjoyable part of the game and adds to the experience, you never feel you’ve been cheated and instead are left with a motivation to do better next time. I found myself analyzing what I had done wrong and then going back to HQ and researching technologies in order to better fix my mistakes. Few games can actively pull this off, making XCOM all the more unique in a market oversaturated with more and more of the same.

This is a great example of a fairly accessible submarine simulation. The game puts you in command of a US nuclear sub in a cold-war gone hot scenario. The game is not easy, althogh largely simplified to hardcore sims lie Dangerous Waters.
Controlling the sub is fairly easy and anyone who can bother to play the tutorial, should have no problem in starting to play. That said, if you are completely oblivious to the topic of submarine warfare, nothing will make much sense to you, since the game doesn't bother to explain how nuclear subs operate and fight. So a word of warning, if you have no idea about submarine stuff, go online, or just read a book on equipment and tactics. Despite interface accessibilty, there is a serious level of simulation underneath, so the game will expect you understand concepts like thermal layers, sonar arrays and weapon firign depths and ranges. However, if you have any interest in the subject at all, these things should be comprehensible and you should have no trouble employing them in combat.
A few things worth noting:
There are just two campaings, but they are both dynamic with various missions, so replay value is high.

A survival horror-rpg game. Pretty much in the first Resident Evil style. Visually is modest, but is not bad at all. You just need to get used to it. Found no bugs or crashes. Also the game got a free expansion and some stuff was changed for good. So old reviews might not reflect this.
Now, I had to play it the casual way, cause it is very hard otherwise, specially at first. The monsters are really though and you will not get any followers after several fights. In normal difficulty I was pretty much about to quit. Playing casual allowed me to finish the game, still not very easy, but the challenge was more fair. And you really need to fight, cause this is all about getting experience points and getting stronger, so you just shouldn't avoid fights. There are a few puzzles, not very hard ones. One or two are head-scratching. There are different endings too. So some replay value.
Overall, despite it is lacking some balance, once you get into the story and learn a few things is entertaining and provides plenty hours in return for the money you paid and there are also cards. Is a good little game and the Mythos theme is always welcomed.

I recommend The Walking Dead: Season 2, WITH some caveats.
GRAPHICS 8/10
Pleasingly pixelated. Final Fantasy style graphics are used in combat (eg. no animations, just effect overlay to show attacks).
SOUND/MUSIC 8/10
I liked the sound and music very much and found it quite evocative.
CONTROLS 10/10
The game was clearly made with RPG Maker or a similar clone so the controls are perfect.
PLOT 8/10
The locations are diverse and well illustrated. The story as written (ignoring combat, gameplay, etc.) is very Lovecraftian and well written. Lovers of Lovecraft, such as myself will be quite pleased :3.
GAMEPLAY 5/10
This game is the opposite of fun. Enemies in later areas are impossible to beat unless you "cheat" and only use the first save room to save your game.
Every time you enter a save room the cost of upgrades increases to the point where it becomes impossible to upgrade yourself enough to fight enemies.
If you do cheat then the game becomes ridiculously easy. A happy medium would have been nice (eg. make it possible to win without cheating ;p). I sense they were going for a Resident Evil style experience where you have to avoid enemies but it is impossible to avoid all of the enemies or use alternate solutions (bosses, etc.) making the game combat heavy yet ridiculously,,, avoidance based \0_o/. I was having quite the time passing the first boss until I figured out that I had to beat every single enemy in order to level up enough to stand a chance against more powerful enemies.
FINAL VERDICT = Pick a play style and stick with it }:|.
OVERALL 6/10 C-

This is an adventure "survival horror" game with a Lovecraft theme.   It's an extremely bad treatment of the genre, and it's an insult to fans everywhere.
Technical problems abound.  Mythos the Beginning plays a lot like a game from 1992.  When I first ran it, I thought I'd picked up some abandonware/retro game I hadn't previously heard about.  Unfortunately, after some research, the game really was published first in 2014.   It has pixel graphics and only supports 4:3 aspect ratio - you cannot change the resolution of the game, and the inputs are mostly controller based (despite the game having no console release!).   If the low effort technical implementation isn't enough to scare you away, the rest will.   You also need to enable your Windows Firewall to run this game, because bad game design is bad.
Graphics are really bad - they're pixel level, clunky, and of course the 4:3 technical limitation just makes things worse.  Animations are almost comically bad - you have about 3 different frames for walking (left arm forward, arms middle, right arm forward), which just looks terrible.  Extremely low effort and clunky.
Gameplay is fairly pedestrian but they also make your life hard by adding unskippable slow dialogue and intro text.  Considering all the other problems you have to go through to get into the game, being presented with a very average adventure game just doesn't make all the hassle worth it.
To add insult to injury, they actually want you to pay them money for this poor experience.  Impossible to recommend.  I hope the developers get eaten by a Shoggoth.

Metro 2033 is probably one of the most suprising games I have played recently.  This is one adventure that should be taken by all.  The graphics are shockingly good when played on a decent pc.  The atmosphere of post apocalyptic Moscow and its surrounding ruins is incredibly well done.  In fact, this is probably the second most atmospheric game I have ever played (first being Metroid Prime).  The sound design is also fantastic with the beasts sounding menacing and the dark tunnels sounding empty.  The lighting is also extremely impressive and really adds a lot to the atmosphere of the game.  I will say that gameplay wise, Metro 2033 is probably my favorite fps game gameplay wise of all time.  The shooting is extremely satisfying, weapons behave like they should.  There is decent customization to weapons and there are also many additional side mechanics such as pumping pneumatic weapons and charging capacitors for your torch.  However a few problems I had with the game was that it was definitely a bit buggy at times.  The AI can be buggy and there is clipping at times.  For one mission, enemies that were supposed to spawn failed to do so and therefore I had to restart the whole mission.  These issues should have been smoothed out as this is the redux version of the game.  I can only guess on how buggy the original game was...  Another issue I had with the game was that it had a rather limited soundtrack.  There was this one song that just kept being repeated over and over whenever you encountered portable radios in the settlements beneath Moscow.  The final issue I had with the game was that the narrative was simply not deep nor intresting enough to make me really care for the story.  I stuck around for the incredible atmosphere and the tight gameplay.  Metro 2033 Redux is about 12 hours in length and the game is very linear in structure (good amount of side paths to discover) and lacks any form of replay value.  However, it is such an incredible gameplay experience that I have to highly recommend this title to any fans of "real" gaming.  Go out and get the Redux bundle with Metro Last Light Redux today.  Rating: 8.3/10

Awesome Game!!! I played it on the slightly harder mode my first time through and it took me ~15H to beat. I can't wait to start Metro: Last Light (Redux) now!!! 9.4/10!
Pros
=====
-Good story
-Atmospheric
-Multiple Enemy types where some are not so wise to shoot (keeping it spoiler-free! :])
-Ammo conservation for realistic survivalism
-You're alway kept busy whether it's shooting mutants, watching your back, reloading your weapon, cycling through grenade types/knives or wiping blood and dirt off your gas mask (very cool in my opinion! I wish more developers would incorporate these effects!)
-P + NPC vs E (Mutant/Bandits) Teamplay
-Weapon Trading System was not too complex (Although if they incorporated armour that would be even better! :D)
Cons
=====
-You always get the feeling like you're coming back to where you started (Your lifeline is holding "M" which will give you a nav point. This game may have taken me ~2H less if I knew that...)
-Some parts are not so straight forward (Ex: You're in the tunnels and you need to burn the cobwebs to proceed - I had to YouTube the answer. The game will not always spoonfeed you the answer)
-The use of gas mask filters is both a positive and negative - It's cool that you need to replace your filters to mimic realistic filter replacement... However, when you're down to about a minute and the game autosaved then you're frantically running around either trying to find more or beat the level - There was one level that took me over 4 hours because I got lost in a building and had to be on the other side of it. The game had saved and I had to remember about 6-7 turns and drops then wedge myself in a crack in the floor in order to get to the near end of the level. Then I had to fight 12 guys with basically no filter. I barely beat the guys when my filter had run out and I had to make a mad dash to the exit, I could've sworn I had less than 3 seconds before I died :/)

Even though no one plays it, if you love Warhammer 40K and space ships, you need this game. The campaign is enough to recommend it, and it's certainly worth getting on sale.
There's lots of negative reviews, likely due to the fact that the multiplayer is pretty dead. While that is true, it's still an extremely fun co-op game to play with a partner in skirmish mode, and very occasionally, there are other players online to play against.
This is one of the best Warhammer 40K games out there, so if you load your Bolter immediately before oiling your chainsword when you wake up in the morning, this is your bread and butter. The voice acting is great, the story is fun (it's the Black Crusade), and the graphics are damn near perfect.
Buy if you can enjoy what it is, which is a great adaptation of a table-top game that I would probably have to take six mortgages on my house to get the same experience from, with a decent amount of replayability due to the skirmish mode and the different races, you will enjoy it a great deal.
FOR THE RUINOUS POWERS

Don't get me wrong, this is a good game. However, this is just not a game I would usually recommend to people. Firstly, the singleplayer is hard and quite interesting.  The story isn't short and the plot quite interesting. However, after one singleplayer story, there isn't much to this game anymore. The multiplayer is more like NotiPlayers now. The DLCs are all mutiplayer only so there isn't any reason to get them as multiplayer is dead.  I wish this game did more in the single player department. There is massive amounts of lore in the 40K universe but one main imperial storyline and that is it?? You can only fight with orcs chaos and eldar in the single player story. Furthurmore, the developers should know that this game will never be the next starcraft or anything so the emphasis on multiplayer is quite a bad decision. To make a multiplayer, the game has to be balanced. Balancing a games takes a lot of effort and data but I dont think the devs are capible of such a feat. Maybe some games are meant to heve a better singleplayer experience and the multiplayer is just some extra flavor. The tabletop didn't have so many players and the devs decided that a video game of a specialized tabletop would have a big fanbase for multiplayer?? I really hope the devs can look further into the 40K lore and give us more single player stories that involve more characters and races. Why can't we play as the SM helping the IN in their greatest time of need? Why can't I play as Chaos to bring destruction to human worlds? Maybe a better Coop would be helpful too. Like fighting more bosses and such.

Saints Row IV! I love this game. As of the time of this review, it is on sale for 4.50, and I definitely reccomend you play it. Like seriously, if you have five bucks sitting around, get this. Now on to the review
Story: 8/10
The story is that some evil alien named Zinyak is taking over the world and you have to stop him, which is sorta cliche. You start off as the president, which really was a wasted oppurtunity since you only press 2 arrows until the Zin come. It would've been cool if those decisions you made would alter the endgame. Another thing that should be mentioned about the story is that quite a few missions are just side activities, which was a cheap was of adding more digits on the playtime number. Overall, the story is pretty decent, but no mass effect 1
Characters: 9/10
They aced the characters in this game. The main character is very easy to like and funny. The lighthearted tone of this game truly does prevail through the characters. All of the characters in this game are different from one another and mostly not cliche. Overall, the characters in this game are nearly perfect.
Gameplay: 10/10 or 6/10
The gameplay is their biggest strength, yet the cause of their weakness. In the first hour of the game, you get super powers. The first two are super speed and super jump. It may sound good to you, but super speed is way faster than a car, which literally ruins the purpose of vehicles in this game. The other issue with this is that if you sprint towards someone and left click, you do a cutscence that one hit kills them. Although the super powers are really fun, they also completely destroy balance. It does not mean the game is unplayable, but the casual gamemode is designed for a guy who plays on his playstation 1 for ten minutes every sunday. Definitely turn up the difficulty if you want an enjoyable experince
Content: 9/10
This game defenitly has a good amount of content. I was able to beat the campaign in about 18 hours, but that also includes the loyality missions that you do if you want to get the best possible ending. Without them, it will be around 16. There are many side activities to do, along with the giant map. Overall, this game definitely has enough content to keep you satisfied.
Final Verdict:
I do feel that i was hard on the game, and I did bash the game for errors it did make. That being said, I still loved this game and thought it was definitely one of the best third person action games I have ever played. If you are looking for a fun, lighthearted experience, then I couldn't reccomend this game to you any more. My final verdict of this game is...

Saints Row 4 is an open world crime game that throws a load of over the top wackiness in to the mix and its actually quite an enjoyable game for that. In the first half hour of playing i had infiltrated an underground terrorist base, rode a nuclear missile while Aerosmiths "Dont wanna miss a thing" was playing in the background and defended against an alien invasion in the White House. Its like the guys making the game were told "♥♥♥♥ it, do what you want" but i dont mean that in a bad way as theres a lot of fun stuff to do i this game. You have the staple stuff from previous Saints Row games like the Insurance Fraud and Mayhem actvities, but this time around you gain super powers which is new and adds a new level of craziness to what has been already a pretty crazy series of games.
Good Points:
- the super powers are a lot of fun. You get stuff like super jump and sprint which let you tear about the city really quickly as well as offensive powers like blast and telekinises. Add the crazy weapons your given like the black hole gun and combat has a nice enjoyable variety
-because your character is in a simulation of Steelport this time round this gives allows for more imaginative story missions and theres quite a few that are really enjoyable. (A Streets of Rage tribute and entering a amateur stripper night  for example)
-you get to pick Nolan North playing himself as one of the voice options for your character
Bad points:
- the city is more or less a copy and paste of the city from the last game with a few bits of alien architecture thrown in. A new setting or greatly changed one would have been nice
- the games humour is a kind of love it or hate it type of humour and its not something that will appeal to everybody
tl:dr another step up in the wackiness for the fourth entry in this series. It may not appeal to everyone but if shooting guys in animal costumes with a dubstep gun sounds like fun to you, you may well enjoy it.

Few games define a genre as thoroughly as the way in which Sid Meier's 'Civilization V'.
RTS Games and 'God' Sims are a mixed bag at the best of times, though for almost two decades Sid Meier's 'Civilization' series has long been regarded the pinnacle of the genre. Not least of which because of the series' ethos of being a 'thinking man's video game' - a bold statement given the overall intellectual overtones of the RTS genre in general - which time and time again has been proven to be a true reflection.
More than just an update of the previous games, 'Civilization V' takes the traditional macro-cosmic look to the series and builds on it immensely. More than simply your typical strategy game that focused mainly on building armies and eradicating rivals, 'Civilization V' now features a far greater focus on culture. Players can now choose whether to fill their countries with wonders to attract foreign tourists or non-militantly conquer the world with their own custom-built religion. As in previous games, players are encouraged to think very carefully about their decisions and to balance the polarizing elements of domestic and foreign policy to the best of their ability if they are to succeed. Add to this greatly advanced graphical quality and there really isn't much else one could ask for.
In truth, it is difficult to really fault 'Civilization V'. Perhaps the only reason not to invest in it is that 'Civilization VI' is now also available, boasting an even more evolving experience again.  Still, 'Civilization V' is nonetheless a quintessential strategy and management experience. If you fancy yourself at trying a hand at politics and world leadership, then this is definitely the right choice.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is turn-based strategy game that has better graphics, and AI as compared to its predecessors.
Personally, this was my first game within the Civilization series. I used to play this on a friend's account until I managed to purchase one on a sale. The dynamic range of options that suits your playstyle and the completely random occurences within the game is what makes it unpredictable and exciting at the same time. It might look complex for newcomers even with tuorials coming from the advisors but as you play further, you'll manage to set your tactics and startegy to achieve victory. I will give out my review on each basic feature and some overview for the benefit of newcomers.
Civlizations, Leaders and their Bonuses/Perks:
There are only 18 civilizations to choose from when you only have the Vanilla version. However, you can have a total of 43 civilizations if you purchased the "Gods and Kings" and "Brave New World" and some "Civilization and Scenario pack" DLC's. Each civilization has a leader and contains unique units/buildings and perks by which you can choose depnding on what victory you would want to achieve and they come from what we all learned from history from early to later eras. Personally, my first civilization was Bismarck of Germany due to its early-game advantage of acquiring a military from clearing barbarians.
Victories:
There are different victory types for this game that will most likely fit according to your playstyle. These victories are: domination, cultural, time, science, and diplomatic each of which has goals to achieve. For instance, if you're the expansionist and aggresive type then you are most likely to be best for domination victory which requires controlling both your capital city and all the other civilization's capital cities. If you're the "I want to lead by science" type, then science victory is your choice and so on. Personally, I always go cultural or science as aggresion is not my preference or playstyle.
Diplomacy:
Basically, this is where you set agreements to other civilizations (AI or another player) or trade resources and gold. The World Congress or United Nations (late game name) can be founded once you or another civilization finds all the other civilizations within the game. However, I find the founding of this organization too simple to handle as all you can do is use your delegates (gained from support of city-state allies, wonders, or being the host) to vote for a proposal to be enacted or repealed. Additionally, international projects are available here that would give bonuses once completed.
Social Policies:
In order to prevent the game looking linear everytime, there a wide range of social policies available. They come in social policy trees, and each has social policy branches that will help boost your civilization as you progress further into the game. Moreover, once you completed/acquired all the branches then it will unlock a permanent bonus on your civilization. Once you reach the modern era or you have built your third factory (whichever comes first), you will have access to choosing an ideology the would permeate your civilization. Basically, there are three ideologies to choose from: Freedom, Order, Autocracy which will be explained through the game itself. Note, only a few social policy trees are available at ancient eras and others can be unlocked through later eras.
Buildings and Wonders:
Buildings are the atoms of your civilization by which are constructed by cities. Each building gives off bonuses such as production, science, gold, and so on. Keep in mind that they have maintenance costs so plan ahead on what you want to build. They can be sold too at any time and you can only sell one building per city, per turn. Some requires location of the city such as a hydroplant requiring a city adjacent to a river, while some require strategic resources such as the factory requiring coal. In my case, I prefer to build producton buildings then science buildings to so my production can catch up to whatever building I unlock as I progress. Wonders are buildings that can only be built once, they can be universal (can be built by any civ) or one-sided (cannot be built by others once its built by a civ).
Units and Resources:
In this game, there are two type of units: civilian and military units. Military units protect your civilization from unwanted visitors, either from barbarians or other civilizations at war with you. They fall in range and melee types each of which has specializations and corresponding strengths, thus the higher the strength, the better its performance. Some require strategic resources like Swordsmen, Battleships, and Nukes (*evil laugh and smile*). They also gain experience when fighting other units. Civilian units help improve your city or perhaps expand your empire further. They range from great people to settlers and workers. However they are vulnerable to capture either by barbarians or other civilizations at war with you so they must be protected by your military anytime. Resources, on the other hand, also fall into two categories: luxury and strategic by which both are tradable to other civs. Luxury resources provide happiness to you and gold when worked by a city, they can be used to trade for another luxury resource you don't have or for gold itself and they are more expensive than strategic resources when trading. Strategic resources are what powers some of your most powerful military units. They consist of: horses, iron, coal, oil, aluminum and uranium. Acquire any of these and you can train a military unit (e.g. Battleship requires oil) that can be of great support. Personally, I like battleships and modern armors, as they really have high strengths which are good in combat.
So if you have any other questions, there is always a civilopedia within the game to guide you. It contains a more detailed explanation of what I explained in this review. Personally, I find this game addicting. Just a caution, you might not be able to leave your computer/laptop once you started this game.

This game is simply amazing. Me and my best friend used to play the original for 360 all the time just for the all-mighty T-HUNT feature.
NOTE: My review is based off of my MULTIPLAYER experience, I only toyed around with the SP for a level or two on the 360 version and immediately left to go T-Hunt.
Now let's get to the real reason people buy R6V, Terrorist Hunt;
Terrorist Hunting is when a set group of terrorists (the amount is also changed by the difficulty along with their skill level) is scattered around a small map and your job is to neutralize all of them without dying. Rules can differ by how you choose to approach the set-up. If you play it offline, you can play with bot teammates, or as a lone-wolf. However, if you choose to play as a lonewolf, when you die, you die and you start back at the beginning. If you play with teammates, you can revive each other. On the online version, servers usually allowed 1 to 2 respawns with a 2-4 player team from normal to very hard settings (the amount of respawns depends on the difficulty settings). You get XP for neutralizing the enemy and winning the round. Other than playing the story co-operatively online, this is about as much teamwork as you can get on an online shooter besides playing a competitive match on CS:GO.
You can rank up your character and unlock new weapons, attachments, gear, and articles of clothing like the last edition. In my opinion not much has changed from the last R6V other than the storyline, and some of the maps (although the great Calypso Casino is still there).
If you choose to play the game strictly for the campaign, it has favorable ratings, but the game is definitely hinted at for it's T-Hunt feature. The usual DM, TDM, etc. are also availible but not often played as much as T-Hunt.
If you are able to pick this game up cheap, please do. The player base is great, but very small and shrinking heavily, and a lot of the times you are paired with someone from a country thousands of miles away. However, do not for you can T-Hunt offline as well although it might feel a little less rewarding as you're unable to show off.
All in all I would give the game a 8.9/10.

If you haven't heard about Quake 3 Arena, then you won't like this game.
It looks fast paced. A shooter in the demon world? Kick♥♥♥♥♥
A lot of weapons? Super cool!
Skill based gameplay? Great! Gotta pick it up as soon as possible! Right?
Don't get me wrong. I LOVE old school shooters. Team Fortress 2, the first two Half-Life games, more to count.
However the game itself is designed well. A port of a grand dad of arena shooters. The problem is not in the game. The problem is in how it was handled in this version.
Most of the players of Quake Live are veterans by now. They played the original Q3 multiplayer and they're amazing at the game. For newer players, that's going to be a problem. There is a system that tries to guess your skill level, but it seems like there are only 8 levels of skill. You determine your skill via bot fights, you're going to get bombed on your normal games. Bots are more intelligent than in the original, but they're still predictable and make the same mistakes. The skill measurement system is broken. This means that you'll always play with the pros. No matter the server, no matter the gamemode. There's no balanced gameplay. There are always the two guys that fight with each other, while dismembering everyone on their way. Others become invisible. Basically frag dispensers.

Mythos: The Beginning is an horror themed RPG where you'll be investigating the disappearance of some students at Harborough Asylum using a character of your choice.
While its story is interesting and it does have a few Lovecraftesque vibes the low production values and frustratingly difficult combat makes it hard to recommend.
-interesting story
-out of combat skills (investigation to find clues, occult lore to read texts etc) are fun to use and it's nice to see they provide you with exp
-good amount of choices in how to build your character (but read below to see how they're, imho, squandered)
-nice monster design
-interesting puzzles require you to think and keep notes
-atrocious voice acting
-barren graphics
-awkward UI and controls, why am I allowed to use WASD to move but have to use arrows in menus and combat?
-combat is frustratingly difficult even on the lowest difficulty level: I love a challenge but meeting monsters that can wipe my party in two turns after just 30 mins of play feels unbalanced. You can try to escape but even if it works the monster will still be near you once out of combat and probably attack you again right away
-the issues with combat means that if you build your character for, say, investigation or occult lore you'll be screwed since you'll be useless in combat and won't have npcs to back you up for quite a bit: the one npc I've met was also a pushover and could only withstand two hits. You'll have to try and come up with a cookie cutter combat oriented build if you want a chance in fights, especially with bosses , and this means you won't be really free to create a character as you see fit: also if you screw up your build I doubt you'll manage to advance much and might need to start over
I went into Mythos expecting a good mix of combat and investigation but was sadly quickly disappointed when I realized that, despite investing equally in combat and non-combat skills, it still seemed it wasn't enough and that I'd have to just try over and over again to win a fight with wandering monsters. I do not find this enjoyable and the fact you can only save in certain rooms, thus having to walk back to where you were each time, just made things boring and frustrating.
Apart from combat the game suffers from very poor production values, the graphics are dark, lack detail and are quite low res, the sounds and music are basic and the voice acting is so bad that it ruins the otherwise interesting dialogues.
If you are ok with extremely hard games and don't mind being shoehorned into combat builds then you might find it decent but I honestly can't recommend it after my experience.
