So, as I was writing this review, I switched my recommendation from yes to no and back about three times.
Consider this a very conflicted 'yes', with a lot of qualifiers.
For example: $1 is about what you want to spend on Mythos: the Beginning. Allow me to explain why.
Mythos is a survival horror rpg with heavy-handed Lovecraftian elements. It's a very short game (clocking in at about three hours, playing as a completionist, on the hardest difficulty) so long as you don't get stuck, but it's also got puzzles and lacks a walkthrough, so your mileage may vary.
In Mythos, you investigate a semi-condemned asylum/hospital/thing, skulking around in the dark and occasionally falling through the floor to your death. The game is class-based, and it lets you freely spend exp in safe rooms to progress your character's combat abilities and investigative chops. Raise your int stat high enough (60) and you can bypass every puzzle in the game. Raise your sense stat high enough, and hidden items start appearing on the floor around you. Stats are reasonably well balanced, and most character builds are viable. So long as you build high int and throw spells, or build high attack and hit rate. Some combats can be optionally sidestepped, but a lot of monsters on the map clip towards you at just barely sub-sonic speeds, making evasion unlikely. Monsters and investigation points are also your primary source of exp, so I found myself combing the asylum for every squamous horror I could locate in order to make my intestines stronger. Optionally, you can also spend items for exp, which was kind of a neat feature. I mulched my entire inventory into my statline and promptly discovered I did not need to be healed when my defense was so high that I could not be hurt.
Which brings me to game balance. Mythos is a little wonky in this regards. Played properly, it probably is a nail-biting exercise in inventory management. However, exp costs for stats progress based on how many save rooms you have discovered, not on how many points you have spent, so I just scooped every single point I could find in the first few areas  and made myself indestructible before even seeing a boss. If I hadn't decided to spend points to pad the survivability of my companions, I would have breezed through the final act of the game too.
Regarding raising any of the stats on your companions: don't. Them dying in combat has no actual repercussions whatsoever, so just use them as one-hit distractions for the monsters. Get your luck and guts high enough, and status effects and damage will not touch you.
Mythos' design also falters when it comes to its graphics and voice acting. The rest of the sound design on the game is utterly lovely, and evokes just the right atmosphere, but I've never seen worse (and buggier) voice-work. Everyone you meet sounds like they're trying to force a British accent through a sieve of rusting fish-hooks and razors, and that in turn is wrapped in some kind of low-fidelity distortion that made me take off my headphones every time someone spoke. I believe you can turn voiced dialog off, but you have to go into a menu in the game. Which means the intro voiceing is probably unskippable.
Graphics are not much better. This is an RPGmaker title. It shows. On top of that, all the character portraits and monsters look like they were whipped up using some sort of 1991 home edition 3D modeling software. It's garish at best, and comical at worst.
So, what's good about this game? Why did I eventually switch back to a 'yes' rating?
Unfortunately, it's fun.
I genuinely enjoyed most of my three hours playing it, and I even managed to get kind of immersed in the story and ambiance a few times. Mythos does not outstay its welcome (I'd say it understays it), and I found myself thinking about it after it was over - and not just in a "what did I put in my brain?" kind of way.
I don't think this was because of the writing, which was bog-standard Lovecraftiana. I don't think it was strictly the gameplay either. But somehow the whole of Mythos is greater than the sum of its jumbled-together parts. Dollar-for-dollar, I wouldn't take it over Alien or Amnesia, but if you want to support a pretty cool indie dev or slum it with a project-on-a-budget, you could do worse than this.

NeoTokyo is a free sourcemod FPS game similar to Counter-Strike that revolves around two teams using teamwork and tactics to defeat eachother. There is one main gamemode in NeoTokyo (Capture the Ghost) which is very similar to Capture the flag in which opposing teams must either eliminate the enemy team entirely, or return the "Ghost" to the allied team's score base. The weapons in the game unlock as you play the game and "rank up" over time from your performance. The game also has a slew of maps to choose from which is quite impressive for a mod with relatively humble beginnings. It has a meager but dedicated community of players from all over the world, and it's quite refreshing to play with people speaking multiple languages and cooperating together. If you can handle the occasional lag that is.
+ Is completely free
+ Plays very similarly to Counter-Strike
+ Promotes teamwork and skill to win
+ Most maps are very detailed and interesting
+ Dedicated servers
- Some weapons feel unbalanced
- Some maps are very confusing to navigate
- Relatively small but dedicated community
- As far as i know, updates are very rare
- Only has one serious game mode
NeoTokyo is a really fun experience that's free to play with a melting pot of players all working together. The gameplay feels solid and despite only having one mode, can be a lot of fun in small bursts at a time, especially on weekends.

Greetings as always!  Let me start by saying I love the Warhammer 40k Universe, the fiction, the setting and especially the games.  But some of the games are just bad.  Thankfully this is not one of them!  I really enjoy this game and will continue to play skirmish for some time going forward.  To be transparent I did not play any multiplayer as I don’t really play against others but enjoy co-op style games for multiplayer.  That may seem odd but I get my competition out of the way in other mediums like miniature wargaming.  But, back to the game, yes it is a solid real time tactical game that tells a simple story in a decent way.
Mechanically, the game shows you exactly why you want to play it.  The ship battles are done in real time with overall strategy and adjusting on the fly more important than how many clicks per second you manage.  Although micro management can be a thing for certain factions the overall game seems to self function on most of the more tedious components.  I didn’t feel I was cheated and although some mechanics are brutal they are fair.
Graphically, this game is exactly what you’d want from the Battlefleet Gothic setting in warhammer 40k, the weapons feel both tiny (due to scale) but impactful, the ships look and move in an awe inspiring manner.  No graphical bug and framerate seemed strong, though I did the occasional refresh lines during the cinematic beginning of some games.  The sound could use a bit more help though, the same small selection on (albeit epic) the music and the voices tend to all be very similar and lacking character…get used to hearing how your cogitator has been engaged…a lot.
This game isn’t going to break any barriers in narrative or story but what it does tell you is a good solid layout to help propel the campaign and immerse you in the world of the Imperium.  The way they tell the story is through an amazing use of still pictures and slightly animating various layers of the picture, this is easily done but doesn’t feel cheap or lacking (I’m looking at you Warmachine Tactics).  I would have liked to see more actual story but I think the game gave exactly how much it wanted.
Overall, if you are a 40k fan then get this game; if you are a strategy fan get this game.  If you like watching big space ships make pew pew, then get this game.  Only reason I could see you not getting this game is if you don’t like 40k or space ship games.  Sadly, no Tyranids though, one day maybe…the great devourer will rise again!
Remember, knowledge is power, guard it well.  Bleh, and no Blood Ravens…

Squaddie runs, but right before he takes his shot two Chryssalids appear. He destroys the disc with his last shell in the tube the turn before it was about to kill the two civilians, but one of the Chryssalids charges straight at him.
My sniper luckily was on point and managed to hit the charging chryssalid before it made it's way to my squaddie as well as land a shot on the other at the beginning of the next turn - not enough to kill the deman thing. There was no way that my squaddie was going to be able to make it to the squad medic before the poison ended his life.

The most notable thing about this game is its stunning graphics and the beautiful world that completely holds your attention for the four hours or so it takes to complete. Despite the short completion time the game has a fairly slow pace, giving you time to really soak in the environment as you walk from puzzle to puzzle. There's no real explanation given as to how to solve the puzzles but seeing as they are largely straight forward I never found myself frustrated (with the exception of the infamous mine puzzle). Although not hard, the lack of any hints really made finding a solution that much more rewarding. 
The story is fairly interesting and carries a sense of mystery all the way until the end. The story might not stick in your head in the way something like "Gone Home" might, but it holds your attention throughout. It's primarily going to be the environment that keeps you wanting to explore. That said, the ending I found particularly good, I want to stress though that the ending seems to generate polarizing opinions. 
Looking to the cons, there really weren't that many, The mine stands out though, it's fairly visually uninteresting, and also contains the most irritating puzzle in the game. Sometimes it could be argued that certain spaces were lit poorly and as a result you really missed out on seeing all there was to see. I did also encounter one bug in my play through, it lead to the game becoming unresponsive and I lost maybe 15 minutes of progress. It didn't repeat though and just seemed like on of those unlucky things that can randomly occur in most games. 
I think you'd probably enjoy this game if you liked "Ether One" or to a lesser extent "Dear Esther". Overall I was quite pleased with what I got for my £15. I have little doubt I'll be loading it up again soon, but not to play through the story again, just to wander through the map. It's solid game that managed to really do a lot with such a short run time. It doesn't run for any longer than it needs to nor does it cram every second with gameplay or exposition. The time between the puzzles really gives you a chance to reflect on the mystery and enjoy the beautiful game world. 
8.5/10

So, this a survival horror RPG game that's actually pretty good but it has a few flaws or issues.  You create your own character, so your character isn't voiced, and the story is mostly fixed, although you can effect parts of it.  You have enough control to feel that you are in control of the game.  The story is mostly good but it's based off a perversion of the bible....sorta.  It is based around the lore of the bible but twisted to fit their vision of the scope of the story, but it doesn't play as big of a role as you might think.  This honestly feels like a resident evil rpg style game except you don't have to worry about ammo, and you can save the game in save rooms (reminding me of the type writers) but you can save in those rooms any time and as many times as you like.
You do get a limited amount of save items to save anywhere, but there are no random battles. It's chrono trigger style battles, you see enemies on the map, and make contact with them to start battle.  Battles are quick, defending is a big broken though.  When you defend, you get a percentage of health and sp back, which is nice, but it seems like if the enemy goes before your action, you don't get reduced damage.  I need to test this a bit more, and there are a few small bugs here and there, such as a few places refering to my female created character being refered to as a male, and a few text bugs, but nothing major.
This is actually a fun game, once I started it, I kept playing, and there are moments in the game that are quite scary.  You can pick most locks instead of having to find a key, but a small issue with this is that when you do find the key, it serves no purpose, and the key items can get a bit cluttered.  The regular items though can be traded in at the save rooms for experience to level up which is actually quite nice, as the healing items were common but i rarely had any as they were more useful as exp instead of using them to heal.  This gave the game a great balance, but it might be possible to get to a no win situation, but so long as you save an item or two, or put the game in easy mode, this can be avoided.  My only issue with the diffculty though was that it only effected leveling up, you always got the same amount of xp from battles, the difficulty seemed constant regardless of difficulty.
I enjoyed this game and the ending wasn't bad but i got a D ranking at the end so i will play this again and see what i get when i get higher ratings.  Not sure how that will effect the game and what it's based on, and i haven't figured out what some items do, so it's worth a replay.
One other issue I found was though was that all bosses in the game can be beaten by exploration and finding items that insta kill the enemies.  I used persuade to prevent one boss, and the final boss i didn't fight because i found items that killed him.  The reward for xp is the same if you fight him or find the items, and I found that to be disappointing.  I felt like you should get bonus xp for actually fighting, as that was much harder then just quickly finding the item.
Over all, this is a cheap game and I got nearly 8 hours out of it on my first playthrough.  The graphics remind me of phantasy star but the atmosphere was excellent.  There is a part where you explore the catacombs and wondering the map, you hear grunts and groans and the occasional zombie crying out 'brainssssss.....'.  It got a good sense of dark humor.  Try it, if you like resident evil and rpgs, you'll enjoy this game.  It's not a killer ap, it's got a few scares, solid gameplay, an interesting story worth reading, and it's a solid and addictive 8 hours or so.

PROS:

CONS:

Mythos: the Beginning is a lovecraftian horror RPG adventure game, set in the early 1900’s and done in a retro 16 bit art and gameplay style.  The gameplay is standard tuned based RPG goodness; you can attack with psychic powers, physical attacks, guard, heal or use buffing powers.  There are several statistical categories that govern how powerful your characters are and also many skills to purchase, all of this is done with experience points you either earn in battle and also by trading in unwanted items.  The character building is quite deep, allows for some different playstyles, and absolutely necessary to master and maintain as this is not an easy game, even on casual difficulty.  Took me 6 in game hours to complete my play thru on casual difficulty, but 10 real world hours due to dying without getting to the next save room, and I have beaten many and old school RPG in my time and am no novice to this style of game.
The story itself is suitably creepy and mysterious, the writing is decent, the voice acting is poor but for a small project like this I was great full to have any voice acting at all.  The music adds to the atmosphere and never gets tiring.  The asylum you explore is filled with puzzles, monsters and mysteries to solve, and how you choose to do so is up to you.  Suck at the puzzles, spend some experience points on your intelligence levels and you can bypass them.  Want to unlock that door or decipher that secret evil looking book, purchase the appropriate skill powerups.  You have to pick and choose as XP points are limited, making Mythos a fun, deep and challenging adventure fit for any RPG gamer that likes lovecraftian horror and old school charm.   First part of a planned series, but Mythos: the beginning stands on its own two feet as a complete story, and plays great with a gamepad.

Neotokyo
Tl;dr (see bottom)
Neotokyo is a mod made from the Halflife engine. This game has no campaign or singleplayer. Only Mutiplayer, you basically join a server and complete objectives. There are two sides who fight one another, one of the sides are called the Jinrai and the other is the NSF both sides offer only cosmetical and external features differences. However if you would like to know the lore of the game, I suggest finding it yourself. The gameplay is very similar to CounterStrike or the Classic Halflife. In Neotokyo however the two teams try to recover a device called "Ghost" (a robotic dummy torso of a female humanoid) which each team tries to retrieve and bring back to either one of the two recovery sites whilst both teams try to fight it out until the last man and prevent the other team from capturing and bringing the device back to their own recovery site. A combination of Deathmatch and Capture the flag.
There are three classes;
Recon: The recon is the lightest and fastest of all the classes, ability to jump very far (those who can bunny hop can exploit this classes speciality), comes with a Remote bomb and detonator, has also a cloaking device.
Assualt; This Assualt class comes with a fragmentation grenade and cloaking device also wears a medium armour but has relatively normal human walking speed.
Support; The support class is the slowest of all the classes but wears heavy armour and has a thermal vision.
The Maps are themed basically of mix of Traditional and Modern/Futuristic style that blends together to create neotokyo.
This mod is for free, and no cost at all, I recommend anybody who enjoy First Person Shooters!
Conclusion; is it worth your time to play Neotokyo? I bought the original "The Room" myself back when it first became available on Steam. I was instantly in love with that one as well. The puzzles were tanalizing. And the atmosphere and visuals were both beautiful, and a just the right amount of spooky. I also enjoyed the subtle DaVinci-esque feel, blended with a dash of Steampunk elements (gears, sprockets, and cogs, etc). And to top it all off, toss in some dark elements of alchemy and arcane magic, and you have a puzzle game that is sure to please.
Now, Fireproof Games is back wit "The Room Two", an actual full-on story-sequel of the previous, with +1 chapter/puzzle added. The puzzles are, admittedly, much longer and more challenging in this edition. And certainly very different. And in some parts, yes, even more spooky (I won't spoil anything, but if you want to know more, you'll have to "pry it from my dead hands"... hint hint). Admittedly, at some points in this edition, the first time around, I became so quite literally stumped, I actually, and regrettably, (and cringing while I did), forced myself to look up small pieces of walkthrough (but only in the final two chapters, when things got really hard).
Pros:
- Storyline is literally a continuation of the previous game. Hurray for continuity!
- New chapters/puzzles that are different and unique from the previous, as well as longer and more challenging.
- Six chapters, in comparison to the previous game's five.
- Up to three savable profiles so you and three others can play separate game files, without overwriting each other's progress.
- A few new game mechanics, such as being able to move around an entire room to different spots (instead of just around one object), and even interact with physical objects (like aiming and firing a crossbow, or aiming light beams at mirrors)
Cons:
- Perhaps, maybe, it was just me, but I found a few areas in some puzzles' progress that didn't match up to the walkthroughs. Maybe I was just missing something entirely and being dumb (it was at an ungodly hour of the morning, as I finished the game across night to almost dawn in one sitting). I'll likely play through one more time and see if it was just my imagination.
- The graphics, while beautiful, were of course a little more detailed than the previous, so if you have a video card that has JUST entered legacy status, like mine (AMD Radeon HD 6670 2 GB), you might want to keep it on somewhere like "medium" settings, if you prefer better framerate over aesthetics.
Highly recommended for puzzle lovers (as well as the previous edition, too). Fireproof Games continues to amaze with mind-tantalizing puzzles with amazing atmopshere, aesthetics, and story.

The Game has the same level of difficulty and genious, well thought puzzles as the first, and that alone will make me recommend the game for all of you out there, but unlike the First, the puzzles aren't in a single element in the room, but now it is in the entire room. I find this, in particular, to be a really bad choice by the Devs. In the first game, everything you need to do and know is in a single box full of different mechanisms, and it makes it easier to do stuff without seeking tips and help from other sources other than your own brain, since you're focused in the same place all the time, each chapter. In The Room 2, there are many things to focus and remember in a room, this kinda ovewhelms the player and forces him to focus more on memory than on puzzlesolving, plus the incountable clicks you make to drag the camera across different spots in the room each time you think you know something.
With that being said, The Room Two is still an excellent game with mind blowing puzzles and excellent atmosphere, and cryptic story. The only thing that keeps it from being a better puzzle game than the 1st is the new "many objects" mechanic that adds many other things for the player to observe in the room. I can't wait for The Room 3, which, as far as I know, will be a prequel and a sequel to the story we've been seeing. And you better bet i will buy it as soon as it goes out on Steam.
TL;DR-  Buy the game, the puzzles and everything are just as good as before, just not as intuitive as the first is.

It might be a walking simulator, but it is a beautiful one. The story is a supernatural investigation into the disappearance of a boy named Ethan Carter. This mainly involves walking through great looking environments and solving simple puzzles. If you seek action and challenges you will not find either here, the puzzles are pretty simple and action is pretty much non-existant. If you enjoy walking through beautifully rendered locations and slowly watching as the story unfolds then it is worth a buy. I enjoyed it quite a lot and consider it money well spent.

First of all, this is an absolutely beautiful game in terms of visuals.  While this would normally be just window-dressing, in "Ethan Carter", it reflects the fact that you are meant to explore every inch of the world they've created.  It's not as overwhleming as it may first appear (it's certainly not Skyrim-scale), but it certain forces you to pay attention to your environment.  And given that there is only minimal guidance from the game about what to do at any given moment, making exploration visually appealing is a must.  The music also does a tremendous job--perhaps as much as the visuals---at bringing you completely into the world of the game.
As to the game itself, I found it very satisfying.  I played it in a single 4.5-hour marathon session, but one could certainly take a more leisurely pace.  Some will certainly balk at the relatively short playtime, but I personally found it extremely fulfilling and compelling to play.  The story keeps you thinking and wanting more information.  More importantly, each revelation makes you more invested in the fate of the titular character and in his relationship with the world you're exploring.  The lack of hand-holding makes the puzzles satisfying to solve, and the variety of puzzle types means you're always looking out for new clues and ways to interact with your environment.
In short:  If you liked "Gone Home", you'll love "Ethan Carter".  And I loved both.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is truly one of the absolute best games that I've played this year. It's also one of the best games that I've played in a long time.
It's not often that a game like this releases. A game in which you know nothing about, and how others don't want you to know what it's about. You just need to play it on your own and have your own experience with it. Like I said, these kinds of games rarely ever come out. Last year’s example of this kind of game would be 'Gone Home', or in 2012, 'Dear Esther'. I'd strongly recommend playing this game for yourself before reading this.
One of the things that got me the most excited about this game was its opening scene. When you start, you'll get a black screen with this simple line of text: "This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand." This line really is true, because the game just drops you in the middle of a gorgeous world to explore. You'll play as the protagonist Paul Prospero, a detective. Throughout the game he'll talk to himself about the surroundings and hints of what to do next. But honestly, I wish this was different.
The game has a story, yes. One where a series of crimes have centered around the Carter family, and you are sent to investigate. Where the game doesn't hold your hand, you are left to just wander until you find floating lines of text which are the "clues" to the investigation. Honestly, I didn't know what these were, and I continued to aimlessly collect them until I found the final act. I understand that this is the story of the game, but it just felt... odd. All I wanted to do was explore the environment. I'd still play this game if that's all it had to offer. The world in this game is pretty big (not as in like Skyrim big, though) and it's beyond beautiful. The lighting and textures are some, if not the most beautiful graphics I've ever seen in a video game before. It felt almost too lifelike. Most of my time with the game I wandered taking screenshots of the world (check out my screenshots library, I took way too much) and then taking part in the story.
The story, after you find these clues, shows how some supernatural being basically brainwashed the Carter family into killing each other. After you witness the ghostly reenactments of these deaths, you get one step closer to finding where Ethan Carter is. That is, until you reach the ending. I won't say what happens in the ending, that's for you to see. But where it wrapped up in the end, I started to appreciate more of what the story was trying to tell. It was almost touching in a way. The story wasn't nearly as good and drawn out as say, Gone home, but it was interesting to say the least.
As I mentioned, I sort of almost wished the story wasn't included in this game, but in the end I'm happy with the outcome. But just the aspect of wandering and exploring is enough for me to want to play it again and again. I wish that someday we could all get a game as beautiful as this on the scale of an Elder Scrolls game. For the price of $20, I feel it was well worth spent. It almost feels like a bargain for how good it was. Don't be surprised if you see this on my top 10 games of 2014 list, because it definitely deserves a spot in there.
Overall, I'd give this a solid 8/10.

Mythos the beginning offers well crafted locations with appropriate background music which adds depth to the environment. The difficulty of Mythos for every playing style is equal. Whether you are fighting every enemy or avoiding every enemy, this shows how Dark Gaia really thought about the execution of this game.
Mythos the beginning also has many puzzles in which some require a keen eye to detect and good logic reasoning. Mythos will wreck your brains on some puzzles which are yet fustrating but interesting.
I highly recommend this game for those who enjoy the classic survival horror game. Mythos is the quintessence of a survival horror game done right.

CONS:
The graphics are extremely rough (spites, text, AND animation).
The voice acting suffers from both poor audio quality and poor acting talent.
The controls are somehow oversensitive (selection) and undersensitive (movement) at the same time, and are non-customizable.
The item system uses up items if you cancel partway through.
Object interaction only works when standing in VERY specific spots, with no indicator of where you're supposed to stand to interact with any given object. You generally end up trying each side of the object one at a time, because there doesn't seem to be any pattern.
OVERALL:
As of this writing (11/10/14), this game is not fit for public release. I appreciate the amount of work that goes into making a game, but this game is simply not finished. I might give this game another shot a few months from now, but at its current stage, it is simply not playable.
Bear in mind that if the devs continue to patch the game, this review will become obsolete, so be sure to check how long it's been since I wrote this. A year from now, this will hopefully be completely wrong. If that happens, I'll update this review with a new date of reviewing and new analysis.

A fantastic game which captures the Warhammer 40K and Battlefield Gothic vibe very well.  The atmosphere of the excellent Graham McNeill novels and comics is also very well captured.   You really do feel like you are an admiral commanding a fleet of Imperial warships.  The voice acting, cut scenes and plot in the single-player campaign are really good - the best since Final Liberation (so far as PC games go).  The only quibble is you cannot skip some of the pre-combat animations and have to re-watch them even if you are retrying a mission.  The gameplay takes some getting used to since (true to the source material) you have limited control over the firing of guns on your ships since you rely on thousands of crew and ratings to do this.  Your job is more to position your ships in the right way so as to maximise the damage they can cause to enemy ships.  This can get quite tricky when you have command of a number of different ships at the same time and have to keep track of what each is doing (and to stop each of them getting into trouble).  You are helped by the "slow time" function which you can switch on with spacebar, but it is still quite challenging.  I found playing on Normal too hard, and found Easy a well-balanced setting.  The load times within the game are generally quite short, with the exception of the initial loading screen, but you only have to put up with this once per play session.  Overall, an excellent game and highly recommended.

Still fun, though! Lots of potential to be an awesome game!

Just got 100%, and i'm about to make a short pros/cons list trying to avoid spoilers
PROS
-Solid gameplay. Challenging but entertaining FPS game, where you fight both human and monster enemies, with survival elements and a little bit of stealth
-Atmosphere is awesome. By atmosphere i mean: Locations, soundtrack, dialogues, voice acting... it's really well done
-Plot is cool, maybe not the best i've seen but thrilling enough, with a bunch of cool characters to boost it
-The game has muuuuch more content than it seems. I don't wanna spoil it, but there is a very important thing about the game you probably will find out only checking guides
-You can really replay several times and actually have a different gameplay experience: 2 modes (more resources, everything does more damage/less resources everything does less damage), with/without HUD, 2 difficulty levels.
-Achievements are pretty challeging/interesting, and for a completionist like me pretty funny to get
-Realism: Russia after nuclear apocalyplse, lack of food, medicines, fresh water, monsters, radioactive spots, but GODDAMN they still have infinite provisions of vodka
CONS
-More could have been done towards enemy variety: human enemies are just regular enemies/armored enemies (instead of, dunno, snipers, shotgunners etc.) and also monsters look quite the same: they run of top of you and try to slap you. Also, several species of monsters appear ONLY IN ONE LEVEL. Come on, i like those guys, let me deal with them some more
-Stealth is cool, but actually pretty hard to figure out, since there is no tutorial at all and you need to understand how it works trying over and over. I learned to stealth properly only during 3rd (and last) playtrough
-The hidden thing i was talking about above. That's pretty important, if you want to keep it hidden maybe give me a couple hints? This really makes a person risk to give up the game while actually missing a lot of content
-It's pretty creepy in certain levels so maybe if you don't like creepy atmospheres this might not be your thing (i'm quite a ♥♥♥♥♥ about horror and i dealt with this just fine though)
-Can't skip cutscenes and speeches even when reloading a chapter. The plot is cool, but when i had to play the same levels over and over to get achievements it was pretty painful
So as you see cons are rather small, this is a good purchase if you are looking for a good fps with survival/creepy elements and a well done plot/setting

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is truly one of the absolute best games that I've played this year. It's also one of the best games that I've played in a long time.
It's not often that a game like this releases. A game in which you know nothing about, and how others don't want you to know what it's about. You just need to play it on your own and have your own experience with it. Like I said, these kinds of games rarely ever come out. Last year’s example of this kind of game would be 'Gone Home', or in 2012, 'Dear Esther'. I'd strongly recommend playing this game for yourself before reading this.
One of the things that got me the most excited about this game was its opening scene. When you start, you'll get a black screen with this simple line of text: "This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand." This line really is true, because the game just drops you in the middle of a gorgeous world to explore. You'll play as the protagonist Paul Prospero, a detective. Throughout the game he'll talk to himself about the surroundings and hints of what to do next. But honestly, I wish this was different.
The game has a story, yes. One where a series of crimes have centered around the Carter family, and you are sent to investigate. Where the game doesn't hold your hand, you are left to just wander until you find floating lines of text which are the "clues" to the investigation. Honestly, I didn't know what these were, and I continued to aimlessly collect them until I found the final act. I understand that this is the story of the game, but it just felt... odd. All I wanted to do was explore the environment. I'd still play this game if that's all it had to offer. The world in this game is pretty big (not as in like Skyrim big, though) and it's beyond beautiful. The lighting and textures are some, if not the most beautiful graphics I've ever seen in a video game before. It felt almost too lifelike. Most of my time with the game I wandered taking screenshots of the world (check out my screenshots library, I took way too much) and then taking part in the story.
The story, after you find these clues, shows how some supernatural being basically brainwashed the Carter family into killing each other. After you witness the ghostly reenactments of these deaths, you get one step closer to finding where Ethan Carter is. That is, until you reach the ending. I won't say what happens in the ending, that's for you to see. But where it wrapped up in the end, I started to appreciate more of what the story was trying to tell. It was almost touching in a way. The story wasn't nearly as good and drawn out as say, Gone home, but it was interesting to say the least.
As I mentioned, I sort of almost wished the story wasn't included in this game, but in the end I'm happy with the outcome. But just the aspect of wandering and exploring is enough for me to want to play it again and again. I wish that someday we could all get a game as beautiful as this on the scale of an Elder Scrolls game. For the price of $20, I feel it was well worth spent. It almost feels like a bargain for how good it was. Don't be surprised if you see this on my top 10 games of 2014 list, because it definitely deserves a spot in there.
Overall, I'd give this a solid 8/10.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a first-person adventure that harkens back to the days of Myst and Riven.
The same elements that made those games unforgettable reside in this atmospheric mystery adventure.
From the outset, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter lets you know you're on your own. There are no objectives flashing on screen, no reminders telling you where to go, no tutorial.
The game does a fantastic job of helping you feel utterly alone within its gorgeously detailed world. There are acres and acres of lovingly crafted contryside for you to explore.
In The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, ambience and environment are the stars of the show. Very few games have ever felt this immersive both visually and audibly.
You play the roll of Paul Prospero. A skilled investigator who has been summoned to Red Creek Valley by a young boy, Ethan Carter, to investigate strange events.
As you guide Prospero, you will have access to his thoughts and expertise.
You may even find that Mr. Prospero has a trick or two up his sleeve when it comes to connecting with world around him.
I remember feeling this in-awe of a game world the first time I played Bioshock: Infinite a few years ago.
That place was magical and powerful right up until the point where is shoved a gun in my hand and forced me to shoot hundreds of nameless bad guys.
Look, I'm not specifically against shooters, I like shooters, but in that case the game's mechanics detracted from the game's setting.
I love The Vanishing of Ethan Carter because it never allows the mechanics to ruin the experience. Where you are and what you're doing are the same thing.
The sound design is nearly flawless. In addition to enhancing immersion, music and audio cues are used to let the player know when they're on the right track.
Accomplishing this with nothing but sound effects keeps the interface clean and again, increases immersion.
When the interface requires text to lead the player it does so with subtle, simple visuals.
These text pop-ups are placed in the environment in such a way that they never feel like a heads-up-display.
Even the font used has a hand-written look that lets you almost feel these could be your own thoughts.
The music is eirie and drives a sense of mystery and the feeling that something is definitely not right in this place.
I strongly recommend playing with the lights off in a quite place with headphones or nice speakers if possible.
This isn't a game to play at a party or with your friends chatting in the background.
Don't confuse The Vanishing of Ethan Carter with an open world game.
Yes, you're technically allowed to roam freely but this isn't Skyrim and there aren't dozens of side quests with hundreds of hours of gameplay.
Instead, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter focuses on a single story.
It took me about 8 hours to complete the game and uncover exactly what happened in this mystery. Although, I probably spent more time sightseeing than others might.
Upon arrival, Paul Prospero discovers a gruesome scene. But is this a murder? An accident?
You'll need to search for clues and recreate the scene if you want to learn what's going on.
Scenes like this make up the core gameplay in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. The mechanics are mostly simple observe, click, observe some more.
I won't go into the details of these event but I will say that Paul Prospero definitely brings a unique skill set to these investigative moments.
The challenge is not in being quick enough or outsmarting an opponent, it's in understanding what you're seeing and what Paul Prospero brings to the table.
Paying close attention to his insights will allow you to understand how to proceed.
The game also features several puzzles that will require some critical thinking.
They're not unfairly complicated and they always provide you with the information you need to solve them.
The way this information is provided is what's impressive about these puzzles' designs. Most people can create a complicated puzzle with a difficult solution.
Good puzzles, like good gameplay, reward the player for doing what feels right and learning from mistakes by studying the details.
THESE puzzles offer subtle clues to let you know when you're on the right path and when you need to reevaluate your strategy.
So, is there anything I didn't like about the game? Well, I will say I was a little dissapointed in the other character models and animations.
They are not bad and certainly don't ruin the game, but they do stand in contrast with the lavshly detailed environments.
At times, these character models almost seem cartoonish next to the world around them.
Fortunately, the voice work is mostly strong with only a few lines where it seems the director and actor may not have been on the same page.
I also expereiced the occasional graphical hiccup. A few times the frame-rate would drop for a moment or two and every once in a while you might notice the seams of the environment.
But the fact that there are no loading screens during the entire game more than make up for these small issues.
If you allow yourself to be immersed in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter you will experience moments of surprise; moments that will shock, startle and maybe even scare you.
There were definitley a few times where I was so impressed by my experience that I had to stop and soak in what I had just witnessed. Do yourself a favor and download this game.

So, as many other reviews have said, this is a visually stunning game. Everything about the environment is just gorgeous and the opportunity to explore and just take it all in is a huge part of the reason I bought this game - and I wasn't disappointed.
On that note, though, I do think the game is marketed as a fairly casual walking-sim-style mystery game, which for the most part, it is, and that's exactly what I wanted and was expecting when I bought it. With that in mind, I personally could have really done without the one chapter of the game with jumpscares. I don't want to spoil anything for people who have yet to play the game and there are some who will probably enjoy that part, but in my opinion that's something people should be aware of beforehand. I don't handle jumpscares well so I avoid horror games like the plague and was more than a little put off by that bit once I realised what was going on. The general atmosphere of the game is very eerie as it is and I think that's effective enough not to need anything outright scary. That's just my preferences, though.
The only other negative is that it's very possible to miss things as you're walking around admiring the scenery, and if so then you'll do a lot of walking before you come across the next part of the story. The chapters don't necessarily need to be played in order but I did completely miss out certain things on my first walk around and then had to go back to look for them later which was a little inconvenient. Having said that though, the game does open by saying it won't hold your hand, which is a fair warning that you'll have to work these things out for yourself.
Overall, I did really enjoy the game minus the one jumpy part. I thought the story was actually very good; despite some people thinking the ending was predictable, I didn't really see it coming and I was satisfied with how everything tied up. Honestly though, the outstanding feature of the game is its visual impact and it's got to be worth the money for the work that must have gone into that alone.

My first experience with the XCOM franchise and boy have I been missing out. The early and mid game are satisfying difficult as you race against time to fight panic (through satellites), enemy UFO's (through your own aircraft), and on the ground (in the missions). The missions are a lot of fun and I never felt like the AI was cheating or that any soldier death was anyone's fault but my own. I especially liked the added options of Hidden Potential, Not Created Equally, Training Roulette. It really helped make each soldier feel and play differently depending on how they ranked up over time.
The only downside is how easy the final mission is once you're rolling with 6 fully upgraded colonels with plasma weapons. I'm not sure if it's because it was balanced for the pre-expansion XCOM, or what, but you're probably going to steam roll anything in your way fairly quickly. I was hoping that the aliens were going to hit me with a ton of the most powerful aliens but I had more trouble with random terror missions.

FTL is like the chess of space exploration. It is based on simple rules but allows a lot of variety, in the the gameplay and the 'story'. Therefore every game is different, with it's new challenges and surprises, only you get better with every each one of them.
It is a very deeply strategic game, with multiple ways to arrange your ship and your crew to win. For example you can buff up your ship with powerful weapons to deal with enemies faster than they deal with you (classic). Or you can play defensive and have a well crafted defense plan that no ship can go through, leaving you time to flee or even dish some damage overtime. Maybe you can specialize in boarding enemy ships with your crew of blood thirsty aliens, or even with drones. You can spy on the other ships to evaluate the best way to take them out. Hell, you can choose to make their oxygen supply room out-of-order, then breach the hull and let them die in the vacuum of space. You get it, the possibilities are numerous. But most importantly they are epic, making you feel like you are making your own science-fiction story.
FTL: deep and awesome strategies, exciting procedural narrative, great music and atmosphere. A+

Open Beta Review:
Please note: I am biased in this review as I'm a hard-core GW tabletop gamer, a lot of GW games have failed to hit the mark for good conversions to computer game.
This quite a good simulation/conversion of the BFG tabletop game to a RTS format, while staying true to feel and atmoshpere of the original tabletop game.
good graphics.
Most in game "on screen controls" are pretty self explanatory, but without a manual or tutorial system, some of the more advanced abilities or tactics remain either unknown to the player ot unusable (like formations for escort class ships).
Being still in Open Beta, there are still some bugs and not everything has been polished to final release standard yet, but the developers are listening to the players and implementing fixes.
Single player campaign looks interesting, but no being able to save games at the moment mean progression isn't saved to resumed later, a bit annoying, but makes me want the offical release date all the more.
Solo Skirmish and Multiplayer are reasonable good, although there is an issue with Multiplayer mismatching players at the moment (see "Known Issues" post in steam forum). still the ocassional crash to desktop but these are become less and less common now.
Overall, for an open beta, the game still needs polish before offical release, but its well on it way to hitting all the marks for a very good quality release.
Release Review:
Most of what I posted in my Beta review still apply to the the Release version, matchmaking for multiplayer issues have been somewhat fixed but are still far from perfect, some of the dlc fleets seem kind of overpowered but that mostly levels out as you level up your fleets (although Tau dlc fleet still need some rebalancing in my opinion).
Majority of bug and crash issue have been fixed, I haven't had a crash months.
Longer load screen then for most other games, but if you are a tabletop gamer a 20 to 30 second load screen is nothing compared to hours it used to take to play the tabletop versions of 40k, Epic, Necromunda, and BGF.
Lack of a manual or an accurate fleet glossary is somewhat annoying for the veteran 40k/BFG wargamer. Favours have no tooltip details until after you purchase them, and that a big waste of renown if its not the one you thought it was.
Overall a nice game, 7/10.

Hard core FPS for people who enjoy strategy and skill. It's an updated version of the Classic Quake3Arena. So if you enjoyed that, you'll probably enjoy this too.
While it it seems very simple on the surface, a new player quickly realizes that it's not as easy as it seems, and without mentoring by proficient players, some people can take years to developed an understanding of the strategies. Partly, people's difficulty with this is exacerbated by a lack of understanding of physics tricking. Early in the Developement of Quake3Arena, a bug was discovered in the physics engine that allowed some crazy effects to happen. The developer considered fixing it, but it was realized that it actually added an entire new dimension to the game, so they left it as it was. While the physics are slightly different in Quake Live, the same physics effects were intentionally incorporated into it.
If you are a new player, learn the physics tricking, practice it in the provided training levels. I've been playing since 2010, and I still do practice runs in the training levels. I also use them to set up my system if I get a new Graphics card or mouse.
Over time, features were added in response to community feedback in an effort to retain new players, but many longtime players saw this as a step backwards and did not make the move to Steam... Personally, these changes made no real difference for longtime players who stayed. While I also thought the changes were a bad idea, it did not affect my enjoyment of the game, I just thought there were better ways to increase the playerbase without alienating the existing players.
Every FPS player will enjoy this game. Unlike Counter-Strike: Global Offensive this game is really about skill. That's what everyone wants from an FPS game, right?

I am an old computer gamer.  I'm old enough to remember the Microprose sub sim called "Red Storm Rising", based upon the Tom Clancy book of the same game.  I loved that game, and although I've only played Cold Waters for a mere 9 hours, I think that it will become a close second to my favorite game, Skyrim (which I've player for over 1000 hours).
This is an incomplete game, at the present time.  I don't mean to attack Cold Waters, in any way.  I've enjoyed every hour that I've played, so far.  Indeed, I stopped playing the single mission scenarios quickly, in favor of a 1960's campaign,  But the pace of the game is much too fast.  Submarine warfare, in the modern era, is a slow-paced process of hiding, staying silent, building up a firing solution on the enemy, firing wire-guided torpedoes which can take a long time to get into position, torps going active, and hammering a Soviet sub.  This should not take 5-10 minutes, and it does is Cold Waters.  This harms the realism of the game.  In fact, I've built up 95% firing solutions in a minute, without a single transient from the enemy.  Not realistic.
In one action against two Soviet destroyers, it was a simple matter of reloading four tubes with Harpoons, going above the layer to get an accurate solution, firing the things, and dropping back below the thermal.  They fired their equivalent of ASROC at me, and shot down one of the Harpoons, but the whole action was over in 4-5 minutes.  Once again, realism suffered, and even their torpedoes were easy to evade.
But this game is in its infancy of devolopment, and will get better, as time goes by and the DEVs receive feedback from us, their customers.  And we all have one big advantage.  There is a dedicated "fleet" of mod developers at
who have already started making modifications for the game.  By the time they're done with this game, a player will swear that he had just been in combat, as he wipes the sweat from his brow.
With the game "Red Storm Rising", there was another anomaly.  I brought this game to a sheltered workshop for some of the clients to try out.  Once, the manager of the workshop called me and said, "You've got to come see this one kid play." I was excited for The Vanishing of Ethan Carter ever since the first teaser trailer came out.  I'm a big fan of psychological horror, especially the works of H.P. Lovecraft.  It was one of the very rare games that I actually pre-ordered on Steam.
Unfortunately, I was not able to play it on my gaming PC and instead was forced to play it on my non-gaming laptop (due to a faulty power supply switch).  I had to put EVERY setting on Low and drop the resolution to 1280x720, and the game still completely paused every 10-20 seconds to load data.  Still, the game was beautiful even at these settings; beautiful enough for me to take some screenshots during my playthrough.
I completed the entire game in one sitting, and it took me approximately 5 hours. One hour of that was me running around trying to find the entrance to a place that I just couldn't find for some reason.  Another hour was spent doing the required backtracking that the game makes you do at the end.  It won't let you finish the game until you go back and find 5 items that you very likely missed (I had only found 1 of them by the time I reached the end).
The gameplay is a mixed bag.  The investigations are neat and I really like piecing the clues together in chronological order.  However, that is pretty much the extent of the gameplay.  Invisible walls are EVERYWHERE, and prevent you from venturing too far off of the path that the developers made for you.  There are no people or even animals to interact with.  There are only 8-10 "puzzles" in the game, and one of which was simply annoying for me.  One, however, was quite intense and had quite an enjoyable payoff for me.
Regarding the story, I was disappointed to find out it was very predictable and cliché.  I had figured the entire story out about an hour or two into the game.  This made the mandatory fetch quest at the end even more painful, since it was just delaying the inevitable.  The multiple levels of metaphor were well done though.
Overall, I would recommend this game, especially to people who can play it at the High graphics setting.  I'm willing to play through it again once I get my gaming PC fixed just so I can see the world as the developers intended.  Now that I know what I'm doing, it should take less than 3 hours to complete.
UPDATE:  I replayed it on a new PC and was able to set everything to max.  It is the most beautiful game I have ever played.  It is a true "screenshot generator".

Not as much as an Ark port as a lot claim. Most who claim that don't understand this games mechanics I'm sure. Played Ark for 2 years before switching to this game. A much more difficult game all together, the system is more balanced for the player to be a part of the game play instead of having to entirely rely on tames to be able to survive and progress. The melee pvp is a lot more entertaining the arks as well. Game is still early access so there are some bugs and fixes, updates and changes, complete work arounds or do overs to certain areas. Although, recently the developers have been churning out fixes instead of just focusing on new content. Great change of pace from how ark behaved during early access. Not to say that the new content isn't coming out but has been obviously been placed on the back burner for them to work on the games optimization and general fixes. Also there usually is a way to get out of some of the bugs with in game items which is extremely helpful to say the least. A rune of recall is your best friend in this game because any time you fall into a whole or glitch into something else you can recall to you faction city.
PROS, It requires time and effort to build AND raid bases. None of this 4-5 weeks to wipe and 3-4 days to rebuild. It has seperated itself from ark with a different taming mechanic and by structuring tames in the same type of tiers as structures and having them interact with the world in pve in a different tier. Taming a mythical(about the same amount of effort as preparing for a Tek boss fight in ark) was both vastly rewarding and disappointing at the same time. For pve mythicals are the end game. Windrider/Fafnir can pick up flarehorns and you can fly the map and farm in safety for the most part using the windrider to clear mobs and then farming with the flarehorn till your full and heading back. Makes the end game expensive content much more achievable. The other mythicals are just as great for there roles, peragriff out puts damage at a high rate to dark mobs, the crystalline is great for raiding in pvp and dark mobs, the pegasus is a great healer(tame for mana and level up mana on it of course).
Cons, Manor work is nigh impossible to raid at the moment without a very large group dedicated to making one specific spell group. Still takes about 5x amount of resources to raid manor then it does to buiild manor. Mythicals aren't really doing anything to manor at all and i found that grossly disappointing. Farming in this game is pointless. The whole mechanic is broken without the treant buff as it takes several weeks in time to produce the items you need in a quantity necessary to accomplish a tame. Literally pointless and 100x faster to grind gold to buy the kibble/feed instead. The first progression cave of the game requires really exensive Blueprint crafted armor of legendary equivalent to just be able to survive the elements of the cave, whereas the cave that is supposed to be the next step of progression AFTER the ice cave only requires normal crafted items. I know its stilll early access and more then likely the cave will then require higher quality items to traverse but its just a glaring issue atm. Most of the tames in this game are completely useless outside of cuteness factors or coolness factors. Two tames pretty much covers all farming needs while the rest are liabilities and time sucks that constantly die to other low level wilds(even when the tame itself is high level and high HP/melee) in example. A 120 Tamed Kebo, with 5000 hp will die to a level 20 deathstalker. While your player/character can handle that level 20 deathstalker with ease as early as level 30 at only 500-600 hp. Same goes for any tame really including that same deathstalker after taming it.

INSTEAD PROGRESS PLAYERS INTO NEW SERVERS BY PROGRESSION AND OFFERING A BENEFIT TO TRANSFER TO THE NEW SERVERS/ZONES AS THEY ARE RELEASED. INSTEAD OF BREEDING CREATE A !!FRESH!! MECHANIC TO ENTICE PLAYERS TO CONTINUE TO TAME AND PLAY(maybe an affinity to your tames the more you use them or something like that). FTL is like the chess of space exploration. It is based on simple rules but allows a lot of variety, in the the gameplay and the 'story'. Therefore every game is different, with it's new challenges and surprises, only you get better with every each one of them.
It is a very deeply strategic game, with multiple ways to arrange your ship and your crew to win. For example you can buff up your ship with powerful weapons to deal with enemies faster than they deal with you (classic). Or you can play defensive and have a well crafted defense plan that no ship can go through, leaving you time to flee or even dish some damage overtime. Maybe you can specialize in boarding enemy ships with your crew of blood thirsty aliens, or even with drones. You can spy on the other ships to evaluate the best way to take them out. Hell, you can choose to make their oxygen supply room out-of-order, then breach the hull and let them die in the vacuum of space. You get it, the possibilities are numerous. But most importantly they are epic, making you feel like you are making your own science-fiction story.
FTL: deep and awesome strategies, exciting procedural narrative, great music and atmosphere. A+

Being a 40k fan and a Vidja gamer (and there has to be like a 90% overlap), puts one in an emotionally fragile position. For a member of that overlap, with the dearth of digital products available wearing the license, it has become so that life is indeed like a box of obscene novelty chocolates; you never know which is made of s#**.
When I found myself ignoring the 150 titles in my library and burning away all of my designated game time just rewatching early gameplay videos from Dawn of War 3, I finally heaved a begrudging sigh and picked this up to 'tide me over'.
Although I love 40k, my fandom has always been more... "adjacent" to it's naval setting. Drift back into Star Wars for that.
As hypocritical as it is I always thought 40k's ships  were rather silly looking, not having a proper context to mentally put them in, like a movie or game cutscene, etc.
But!.. it's an RTS, say's 40,000, has good reviews.. and I'm jones'n for the new DoW real bad. So....
....hash tag smitten.
Okay, let me tack a disclaimer on these next statements by saying: It's an exceptionally fun game in it's own right, on it's own merits. That said, human emotional response is tied quite intrinsically with connections to past, pleasent events, observe:
1. It's a PC adaptation of a miniature tabletop game set in a popular science fantasy franchise.
2. Choices impact the entire campaign.
3. Modifications, upgrades, and casualties are persistent. No take backsies
4. Despite the lovely graphics, the field of conflict is two dimensional.
5. (here's the big one), You can pause the game to issue orders, then watch them play out in real time.
To Me, Personally, this game is the spiritual successor to Battletech: The Crescent Hawk's Revenge!! Which is the title that introduced 8 year old me to; 'proper' PC gaming; the Real Time Strategy genre (which immediately spiralled off into Dune 2000 and then I was trapped in the C&C loop for a decade); and  made the Battletech/Mechwarrior franchise into an old, dear friend, (which indirectly led to MWO milking me for about $800 since the Founder's program... anyway).
Battlefleet also  does an excellent job of scratching the itch for list-building and tactics put in place by FFG's X-Wing Miniatures. A slow, tactical X-Wing video game wouldn't work at all, but translating that mindset into 40k capital ships goes together like cheese and grapes.
If you're enough of a fan of the franchise and/or genre to have made it far enough to be reading reviews, then go ahead and buy it, BFG:A is good people.

While I've been gaming a while, I never got into the original X-Com games when they were released. I certainly remembered them and heard good things, but turn-based strategy never appealed to me. Then I got to watching
playing through Xcom 2, which looks damned awesome. Finding this game on sale, I decided to give it a go.
Boy, am I ever glad I did, because this game is damned fantastic!
That said, the jokes and memes about this game are quite true. RNG-sus is a fickle god, and no matter how hard the player prays, he does not seem to play fair. I've had numerous soldiers miss on 88% to hit, while at the same time doing crits on 36%. Many tables will be flipped due to that♥♥♥♥♥♥ Your toopers will randomly panic and shoot your own guys when attacked. And there's nothing like having one of your top soldiers fall victim to a sudden Chryssalid gang-bang.
You will want to make liberal use of the save feature in this game. Like, a
.
Xcom also does not have a learning curve so much as a learning cliff, that you'll run into face first pretty quick. It took me about 4 tries to get enough experience enough to know what I was doing to not get totally trounced by the game. You'll want satellites as quickly as possible, and get at least one interceptor onto each continent as fast as you can in order to try and try and keep control of the countries and prevent them leaving. If you can make it through the first major story mission (the hidden base assault), things will get a lot smoother.
While some of the reviews do bring up glitches, I only had two minor ones during my playthroughs so far, and that was the game not recognizing that a soldier is able to be revived. Alas, that was a re-load or lose situation for that soldier, but I didn't have any of the game breaking bugs others have reported. It looks good, plays smooth, and I haven't had any real issues in all the hours I played. The movement animations and other recurring events like them can be switched off in the options menus to make things proceed faster.
Content wise, the base game is pretty good, but you
want the
DLC. Honestly, just get the Complete Pack. It adds a pile more content to the base game. The new human enemies, Exalt, are more dangerous as a swarm than individual enemies (Yes, their AI is rather single minded and dumb), but they are some of the tougher enemies. Price wise for the content, honestly wait for it to come up on sale. For a 5 year old game (at time of posting), this thing is too high IMO. That said, you can piecemeal it together from other sources (like I did) since Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within had physical releases and there's still a good deal of them floating around outside steam.
In the end, yeah, I liked Xcom
. The story is good, the characters well acted, graphics still pretty good given its age, and the just-one-more-turn/mission game play compelling. I look forward to replaying it again, probably trying some of the mods like The Long War, and most definitely getting the sequel!

The Room Two is a pretty good sequel to the original game. It has a lot of the same flavor that I loved about the original, but it also tries some new things. However, the new things are kind of a bittersweet addition.
As for what stays the same: You are still locked in a room trying to open weird puzzle boxes with hidden compartments and complicated mechanisms. The puzzles and their solutions still have that inimitable Myst-like quality that is so hard to find in other games.
As for what's different:
1. Instead of trying to solve one hugely complicated puzzle box in a single room, you are instead moved through a series of different rooms. Instead of each room having a single puzzle box to solve, there are instead different "points of interest" around the room that serve as sort of puzzle stations. This gives The Room Two much more of an "escape the room" or point-and-click adventure flavor than the original game. Some will consider this a positive, and in some ways I agree it adds an interesting newness. But it also introduces certain problems, because....
2. Due to the shift to a focus on "puzzle rooms" instead of a huge puzzle box, The Room Two introduces some classic point-and-click frustrations that it mostly managed to avoid in the original game. The biggest frustration of all is the dreaded pixel hunt. The Room allows you to click on points of interest to zoom in and interact, but you can't interact with things until you are fully zoomed in on them, and it is not always clear whether a point in the room can be clicked on to zoom in or not. Sometimes a point in the room is not a place you can zoom in on at first, but then later you can. Sometimes the "hit zone" of the area you have to click to zoom in can be kind of small. I won't say that it happens in every room or every puzzle, but there are definitely a few places in the game (and DEFINITELY on the last puzzle) where I felt like the game was only "difficult" because I was tediously clicking every pixel on the screen trying to find something I was missing rather than the more interesting difficulty of trying to solve an actual puzzle.
3. The Room Two introduces a "viewing lens" which functions as an eye/lens of truth (i.e. certain things are only visible when you are looking through the lens). I don't really mind the lens of truth idea in certain games, but I don't think it was a great addition to The Room. It just compounds that frustrating pixel-hunting feeling. Yes, you've searched everything, but have you looked at everything THROUGH THE LENS???? It's one more thing that turns the game into more of a "hidden object" type experience than a puzzle type experience. I wasn't super into this new idea.
But despite the new twists on the old formula being bittersweet, and despite the last puzzle room in particular making me especially grumpy with the level of pixel hunting, I have to say that all of the Myst-like things I loved about the original The Room are still there. 98% of the puzzles are fun, intuitive, and compelling.
If you played the original, expect some new additions that may or may not be to your liking, but the essential fun of the first game is still here and still fantastic.
7) A classic, essential, and/or must-buy game that is worth full price.
5) A pretty good game worth checking out--especially if discounted.
4) A fairly good game, but I'd recommend buying it discounted.
3) Not great, but a few redeeming qualities. Only buy if heavily discounted.
2) Only worth checking out if you are dangerously curious.
1) Avoid at all costs.

Inovation. Precision. Gorgeous. These are all of the words that came to mind upon loading up this masterpiece for the very first time. I got into a match right away, eager to try one of the hottest FPS titles of 2017, my hands trembling with excitement. As the screen faded in the first thing I saw was a fellow competitor spamming racial slurs in the chat box. "Now, I don't agree with such language but it is commendable of the developers to allow free speech in such a censorship heavy world.", I said to myself. Now, I'm primarely a controller user, and when I plugged in my Xbox 1 gamepad, I was greeted with one of the most groundbreaking control schemes I have ever had the pleasure of using. While "A" would typically make your avatar jump in traditional shooters, in this game it swaps weapons."What's so special about that?", you may ask. Well, dear reader, the genius of this shines only when you discover that the "Y" button also switches weapons! No longer are we oppressed by companies like Activision and Dice, telling use we can only have one weapon swapping button! If i want to press "Y", I do! If I want to press "A", I do! I must stress, my friends, that it only gets better. Most FPS games use the left trigger to aim, and the right trigger to fire your weapon. That is the pinacle of inconvenience. Why must I exaust myself pressing a trigger all the way down over and over? Well, thanks to Masked Shooters 2, this is a problem of the past. You see, you actually use the left bumper to aim, and the right bumper to shoot! Perfect for rapid firing the amazing 1 hit KO AR's and SMG's available to you from the very beggining. "So then, what do the triggers do then?", you ask once again, ignorant to this game's unrivaled layout. The answer is simple, the left trigger makes your soldier look down, and the right trigger makes you look up! Who needs joysticks? Not this gamer, I can assure you of that. Enough of the button layout, if you aren't sold yet then just you wait. This is hands down, the single most graphically impressive title I have ever played. 4K? Child's play. This game is real life. When I first booted it up, it felt like I was ripped from my plane of existance and placed into the world of the game. No longer was I a gamer in a wheelchair; I was a soldier. Ripping around the battlefield, quickscoping, no-scoping, 360 trickshots, I was doing it all. Never once did I realize I was in a game. The textures were so real, the audio so crisp. It may have been, in fact, too real. I lay awake most nights now. Flashbacks to the atrocities of war waking me up in terrified, cold sweats. Surley you must be thinking a game that looks that good would require a beastly PC, unafordable for most. I can, with upmost joy, deny this. How? It is the best optimized title in not only my steam library, but possibly on all of steam itself. My average FPS, on a foliage filled, expertly designed map with explosions and gunshots galore? Not 60. Not 144. 800. You read that right. 800FPS, sometimes peaking at over 1,000FPS. No other game will ever compare for the rest of my time on earth. I gathered up all of my favorite shooting games, MW3, BO2, battlefield 3, CSGO, games that were at one point my entire life; And I threw them into a fire. I do not need them any longer, for I am a proud owner of Masked Shooters 2.

Masked Shooters 2: A Diamond In The Rough
This game is a work of art, and the fact that it is looked over is appalling. I've never had more fun and been as impressed with a game in a long time. If this game was a museum, it would be The Louvre. Just like the Louvre, it's extremely difficult to see everything and figure everything out, while enjoying yourself. I have 1000+ hours in this game on my other steam account. I still haven't discovered every feature or have ever stopped having fun.
Graphically, this game is perfect. It's well optimized, which is a great plus, but with a great computer this game is an eye massage. It is like being surrounded by perfection 24/7 in this game, which makes the gameplay tougher. Sometimes you just want to look around, but the gameplay is so tantalizing you simply can't.
The gameplay of this game is phenomenal. This game has servers holding up to 75% of the playerbase, which makes playing with friends easy, and although the idea seems chaotic, it is really well controlled and proves that the creators of Masked Shooters 2 are geniuses. All the assortments of firearms are metaphors for the lives of the developers. These metaphors describe the different portions of the game perfectly, hence why the game revolves around the collection of different guns you can choose from.
If I could choose a single gun to use, it'd have to be the Desert Eagle. This gun was animated perfectly, and it requires a true master of mechanics to use. In a duel between two professionals using a Desert Eagle, I would say it could be a sport. I've never been so entertained with the click of my mouse, (with the help of my aim), than when I used this weapon. For any new players, try to avoid using this weapon. Instead, stick to the M4. This weapon requires a deep understanding of the game, and would give you a sense of difficulty that would drive you away from this masterpiece of a game. Don't let that happen, take my advice.
This game at such a low price is practically a steal. It's you paying a dollar for the experience of your life. This game, in my experienced opinion, was more important than friendships or relationships in general. I lost my girlfriend of 2 years because of this game. She hated that I would rather spend time developing my mechanics than spend time with her. It was too addicting, but I love it. Most of my friends (except for the 1 that plays with me) stopped inviting me to parties. I declined every invite anyways, because I wanted to become better. It's almost like a drug. It's addicting to get better and enjoy the game more and more. I haven't talked to my family in a couple years, and I haven't really talked to anyone in a few months. I don't need to, though, Masked Shooters 2 is enough for me. :)
In conclusion, this game is perfect. If you have any doubts after reading my review, this game isn't for you. It requires a decent amount of dedication to appreciate how great this game is, but it is all worth it. The learning curve is the hardest of any game I've witnessed, but it is possible to beat and once you beat it, it will be fun every single minute.
