As a player of the orginial version of the game and a fan of the books, i have to say this version became fantastic.
The atmosphere is great and very "book-like", so that bought me instantly.
As far as horrors go i can't find a game very scary when the player is able to use guns, and as a veteran horror game player all the jumpscares were predictable to me. However just a plain sight of your surrondings (dead explorers, skeletons, lots of blood, monster coprses, spiders, ghost, mutants, demons, nazis, soviets etc.)  and the fact that the story might become a possible future reality (not sure about the monsters of course) made it a prettyary game.
The game has 2 possible ways to play, first is survivor, the second is spartan. In survivor mode you depend on stealth and troughout exploration for ammo and other supplies because there aren't too many. The spartan modes provides a lot of ammo and a more classical FPS-shooter experience. Besides that there are 4 difficulty levels (normal, hardcore, ranger, ranger hardcore), so everyone should find a suitable one. I recommend ranger mode, because it gives a new, even more horrifying experience (no HUD, no hints, more damage for both sides, even less ammo), but only on second playthrough. As far as shooters go, you can choose from a wide vareity of weapons, and and all of them can be customized somehow (no visual upgrades only in effectiveness). You can carry 3 of them at the same time so you can be prepared for every occasion. Also you can have 3 types of grenades, throwing knives and a classical melee one.
For the assault rifles you can choose from 2 types of weapons, standard and military grade. However the latter should be used very mindfully, because it also serves as money, you can buy new weapons, upgrades from it, but also could save you in difficult situations.
The AI is not the best. The human enemies sometimes forget to get in cover, have trouble seeing you upclose when youre in the dark, and don't try to flank you which makes your job easier. The monsters very often will  treat you like the chosen one, and they only try to attack you even when you're a part of a big group, which caused me a lot of deaths, and also my teammates wasn't so eager to defend me.
The sound and the music fits well into the atmosphere, however the voiceacting is terrible. The characters have a frustrating, unnatural, farfetched russian accent in the english version which kinda murders the whole setup. Fortunately the game comes with a russian voiceover, which made the game more realistic, and a lot better. Although the russian voiceacting (with english subtitles!!) doesn't sound very good either. I don't speak russian, but still i had a much better experience like that.
Artyom, the hero.
Well unfortunately they made Artyom a silent hero, he never speaks in game, you can only hear his thoughts at loading screens, or read them via collectibles. This silence makes a lot of cutscene stupid, and unenjoyable. In my opinon the developers could've make  him a talkin character, because,they had every information about him from  the books, he had a fix personality. At least they put 51 collectable diary pages in the game (this is new in Redux version) which shines more light about Artyom and story. The story is great in general, but if you haven't read the book, you might not understand everything. That, the poster and the book copies in the game suggets you to buy it. This is a little forced advertisment, but it's only natural in a book based game, and well both of the books are great, so i suggest you to do the same.
The game is fairly long, and can be played over and over again, since it provides the mentioned two game modes, has a lot of achivements, and in the Redux version they made some more new areas that could be explored and some safes that could be opened if you find the proper keys, and of course the diary pages, they all worth to collect and read.
It's important to note that the game is not a sandbox, it leads you through in a big tunnel, but the great atmosphere, the events, and the action makes you almost forget that. However, i think they should've made the visitable stations bigger and  more exploreable, because they feel packed and unlife-like (given the current situation).
The graphics became great, and more creepy than before, the developers seems to fixed all the game breaking and frustrating bugs. Most of the achievements are easy to complete based on killing different types and number of enemies with different guns or methods, but there are some challenging ones also, even mission based. They can be completed to 100% in 2 playthroughs and some additional chapter selectin, but to achieve that you have to be extremly mindful for everything becasue of the "Enlightned" achievement, which is based on finding and triggering every flashbacks of Artyom's past, and additionaly making generous decisions all game long.
All in all it's a great game and recommended for everyone who is intrested in some horror based fps action with great story. Still enjoyable for those who haven't read the books.  The redux version also provides a lot of new experience for players who only played the original game.

Probably the most chilling experience I've had while gaming. The storytelling is simplistic and superb, the world is deep and vivid, and the level of freedom makes playing the game feel like I'm actually solving a mystery. well done!

Finally, a game that makes me want to be a better person. Somehow this game is able to completely make me want to avoid each turn in fear, all while helping me feel comfortable enough to do so. It is an introspective adventure that may be a moment of peace and emotional release for some, and a time of self-reflection and decision making for others. Sometimes you have to go through hell to find the truth and make it out on top, and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter invites you to do so.
Some of the higher points of this game are:
+   A story that is both touching and gripping, while at the same time remaining simple enough to pack a punch.
+   Control is never taken from the player for long if ever and as such I never feel disconnected from the experience of being Paul Prospero. Only at one time is control taken away from the player, but it needs to be taken, there is no other way. It is part of the experience that impacts the story in a powerful way.
+   Textures and Atmosphere that have to be seen to be believed. I found myself looking over every nook and cranny of the entire game. It never got old. Truly a masterpiece in game design. Never have I mistaken a video game environment with someplace that could exist. I found myself rethinking that concept at every corner within the game. Only complaint is that some of the mountain textures could have been more detailed. But I understand, how do you 3d scan a whole mountainside?
+   Graphics and gameplay flow that is new and revolutionary. At first I thought that when the Orange Sears across the screen I thought I was viewing an encoded video, but as I continued to play I realized it was an actually viewpoint that could change dynamically as I changed the scene. The door puzzle alone had me captivated and impressed with technically how the devs pulled it off. It stands out so much because it doesn't stand out to the player as a gimmick. It just works. This game is future proof.
+   An impressive soundtrack almost worth listening to on its own. But coupled with the game it is completely mesmerizing and adds to every moment of gameplay. Intriguing, Beautiful, Eerie, all with the feel of a AAA score.
+   Perfect amount of time to finish the game. Around 4 hours unless you cheat and look at guide. May take only a couple hours on subsequent play throughs. Not too long, not too short. The story is able to build and make its point all without overstaying its welcome.
+   Crime Solving I actually felt like I solved. As stated in the very beginning of the game "This game does not hold your hand" I haven't played to many mystery games, but the ones that I have played (like Murdered: Soul Suspect) all made me feel like I was just running around collecting evidence until something decided to happen. In this game I felt involved enough that I needed to know what happened, not just that the game needed me to solve something so I could move on further in the game. Because the game does not tell you what to do, true discovery happens. The little thoughts that pop up as you observe items are perfect and leading you slightly without getting in the way. When the thoughts congregate to pinpoint you to where a clue might be it feels natural and unobtrusive.
+   Very replay able. Not in the sense of Skyrim or Mass Effect where you can be something different each play through, but in the way a great movie with a moment of catharsis at the end makes you appreciate everything that came before even more, and even see it in a different light. It all keeps on adding up on itself each time you play again.
This is just a thought that is neither negative nor positive, but a note to those buying the game:
~   Some of the promo media advertising/screenshots/trailers never happens within this game. The screen shot above that shows the man crawling in front of the train, is never seen like shown, in the game. The picture of the ghostly lady standing outside the crypt is more accurate to what will happen. Personally I have mixed feelings that fully rendered play throughs of the entire crime scene events would have been better, compared to what the game offers, which is ghostly snippets broken up in chronological order.
Here are some of the few hang ups in this game that keep it from being a perfect game:
-   Some of the side quests broke the feel of the game flow. At only one point out of the whole 4+ hours of gameplay could you possibly die in this game and when it happens it really throws the whole game off since most of the game I felt secure in being an observer of the past. This wouldn't be so bad but since the game "doesn't hold your hand" you are left never knowing what to expect, which is just fine for a mystery game, that is unless you discover a part of the game that actually goes against the rest of the game’s standard even if just for a second.
-   The save system really stinks, you can't save at any point and it is really hard to understand when the game is saving for you. This leads to extra time playing over again the same part of the game catching up from when you quit the game last time. I know they devs wanted this to be one sitting gameplay experience or possibly 2, but I just didn't have time to play it in two sittings. I had about 6 times that I had to finish this game. Steam says it took 5 hours, but only about 4 of that was spent actively playing something new.
-   I felt downright confused by some of the mini side quests. And I don't mean normal confused like you are supposed to be in a mystery game, but one of them almost felt like an easter egg for the developer itself and until I understood how the game was flowing and how it fit into the story it seemed to be extremely distracting and took me out of the game. On the second play through it will not do that to me, but for sure on the first run though it really confused me.
-   Knowing when it is the actual end of the game could be confusing to some, and be possibly frustrating after realizing you missed something critical you didn't know you were supposed to discover.
But these negative points were all forgiven when I realized the worth of the impact of this game. Only one other game has actually left an impact on me (Spec Ops: The Line) for the better. Some things in life are not pretty and have to be faced upfront. This game is not just a pretty to play but flat experience, because I actually discovered I can have heartfelt feelings and play a video game at the same time. But this game ends up being very beautiful in my mind at the end of the day, and I'm not talking about the graphics.

The visuals in this game are stunning. This game flat out tells you that it does not hold your hand, and it doesn't. You're thrown into a highly immersive world with no instructions. One of the best adventure games I ever played.

The world in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter first appears as a beautiful yet sleepy backwoods town, but it quickly becomes apparent that not all is well. A more desolate, abandoned feel grows on Red Creek Valley, like it's been neglected by the outside world for decades, its prime time having long passed. This eerie view of our mundane world is also visible through the documents and newspaper clippings found throughout the valley, portraying an outside view of life in this rural neck of the woods. These external reports are starkly contrasted by Ethan Carter's own imagination, channeling the same goings-on into those of the supernatural, seen in stories scattered across the valley.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter shows an interesting and deep outlook on life—the mundane, sleepy world, against the fantastic imagination of a child. This powerful story combines with a beautiful, polished world together with an immersive music score and great voice acting yielding a top-notch game. But it is what you make of it, as you can beat it in a couple hours if you run from start to finish and skip most of the mysteries, but you will miss out on its deep story. On the other hand, if you explore the whole world and look for all its secrets, puzzles, and mysteries, the game will really shine its brightest.
Another unique and enjoyable part of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is its detective gameplay that reveals pieces of the story with each mystery solved. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is as close as you can get to making a detective novel into a game, and the result is something excellent. The game's succinct yet powerful, thought-provoking dialogue and story tied with its eerie, dark, supernatural premise makes it well worth the time of anyone that enjoys well-crafted mysteries and games with deeper meanings that will stay with players long after finishing.

This is one of the few games that is more a novel to play, no shooting, no questmarkers, no HUD about health, ammo and compass. Just a story and awesome graphics.
You can discuss about the price, but I highly recommend buying the game when it is on sale.
If you liked Alan Wake for the story (and not for the shooting) and think Dear Esther was too short (such story much cry very tears wow), then you should get The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.

FTL is like the chess of space exploration. It is based on simple rules but allows a lot of variety, in the the gameplay and the 'story'. Therefore every game is different, with it's new challenges and surprises, only you get better with every each one of them.
It is a very deeply strategic game, with multiple ways to arrange your ship and your crew to win. For example you can buff up your ship with powerful weapons to deal with enemies faster than they deal with you (classic). Or you can play defensive and have a well crafted defense plan that no ship can go through, leaving you time to flee or even dish some damage overtime. Maybe you can specialize in boarding enemy ships with your crew of blood thirsty aliens, or even with drones. You can spy on the other ships to evaluate the best way to take them out. Hell, you can choose to make their oxygen supply room out-of-order, then breach the hull and let them die in the vacuum of space. You get it, the possibilities are numerous. But most importantly they are epic, making you feel like you are making your own science-fiction story.
FTL: deep and awesome strategies, exciting procedural narrative, great music and atmosphere. A+

Quake Live is the most balanced iteration of what everybody refers too as "Quake 3 Arena". It's worth playing for free and if you like it, you can Subscribe to gain access to launch your own server in a specific location. These servers allow you to choose the gametype, maps and other misc settings such as timelimit, fraglimit, movement options and join password. Subscribers also receive extended stats, additional spectator features and the ability to create and join clans.Alongside the Steam release, loadouts were introduced into certain public gametypes to help cosey in new players. Quite simply, you can choose a primary and secondary weapon that you spawn with (rather than just the machine gun) and continue to play as you would before... picking up every other weapon, health and armor on the map whilst killing your opponent. Loadouts are fine to an extent, however the problem currently is that there's no easy transition for the new player into the Quake Live many competitive players want you to learn (there are some other differences such as weapon respawn times too). This is a non issue for Duel as the public gametype is the competitive gametype, it has remained unchanged. However for TDM or CTF you must have one player launch a gameserver via Subscription and enable the "Legacy Settings". This is a potential barrier as it requires free-to-play players be invited to such servers if they haven't yet subscribed. But please don't let this deter you as it's not a brick wall, easily overcome given the low cost per year if addicted. For new players to the franchise it should not matter, you'll find the grass can be greener and find your way into the competitive community and such servers in due time anyway.I played QL competitively under the TDM and CTF gametypes from 2009 to late 2011. I also competed for Team UK in numerous Nations Cups during this time. I may not play as much as i used too now but it's definitely worth picking up if you're new or returning to the franchise. It may miss some features present in the Quake III Arena modification CPMA (such as Clientside LAN Support and Multi POV Spectator), but it comes with ease of access and everything mentioned above. Tournament organisations can also contact the development team to obtain dedicated LAN servers for their offline events, this hasn't been an issue for ESL, DreamHack and others in the past.Quake Live is an extremely rewarding game on any skill level and is by far the best Arena Shooter on the market as of 2014. It's not perfect, but it does exactly what it says on the tin. With how easy it is to jump in and out of game you'll always find yourself going back. I could not recommend this game enough!

This is a sequel to another game whose name you can probably guess.  If you enjoyed the first one, you'll probably like this one almost as much.  It's easier, and shorter, but the extra variety and creepiness keeps it interesting.  If you didn't play the first one, go and play that instead.
The story seemed tacked-on and unnecessary in the first one, which was focussed on solving a series of ingeniously designed puzzle-boxes, but it works a lot better here, and leaves me wanting a further sequel.  I must admit I do miss the single-room nested box conceit of the first one though, and although the mechanics are reproduced here in a variety of smaller puzzle boxes and devices, they often left me wondering about the logic of it all, because sometimes a seemingly innocuous object is hidden under various locks and puzzles and just happens to be the exact thing you need at that moment.
The design work is the real draw of this series, and it's nice that this retains much of the style of the original.  As before, I much prefer the intricate mechanisms to the supernatural elements.  My favourite objects in both games are those which seem like they could be made in real life.  On the other hand, those latter elements are much expanded in the second game and are really very interesting and use very cool visual effects.
The price is fairly low, but be prepared for an abrupt and premature ending.

I'm reviewing this purely based on the 'Terrorist Hunt' mode; which could be a game in itself. To me, Rainbow Six Vegas 2 was the last great military FPS. In a market flooded with Call Of Duty and Battlefield and (to an extent) ARMA, Rainbow Six Vegas 2 stands out to me as the most fun, replayable game of all of them.
Playing Terrorist Hunt is a massively tense solo experience and a brilliantly funny multiplayer experience. No matter how you play, this game accommodates for your style.
It will make you think slowly and strategically about your actions, something that modern FPSs seem to have completely forgotten about. The innovative mechanics, such as rappelling, ropes and ladders add a degree of verticality to the maps, making them replayable to an almost infinite extent.
If you have (somehow) never played this game, you owe it to yourself to experience one of the greatest and most original first person shooters of this generation.

An atmospheric, sometimes scary Lovecraft-esque adventure game with stunning graphics.
Detective games are hard to do, since it is difficult to make the player feel like it is THEY who are performing the deductions/making the inferences. LA Noire and Murdered: Soul Suspect both failed to give the player this feeling, but The Vanishing of Ethan Carter IMO manages to nail it. The "crime scene chronology" mechanic is fantastic, elegant yet requires the use of your brain to make inferences from the clues. Having to return the scene of the crime back to how it was when the deceased was killed is also a nice touch and makes sense for a "psychic detective."
The graphics are frankly gorgeous, although unfortunately the performance isn't as stable as it should be.
The plot is good (although the ending can feel like a bit of an M. Night Shyamalan cop-out-twist-bordering-on-a-deus-ex-machina), the music is very appropriate and fitting, and I enjoyed my time with the game.
The big drawback is the game's length; it can easily be finished in less than four hours.
I'd advise buying the game if you love horror games, adventure/mystery/puzzle games, or just deeply atmospheric games in general. However, you may want to wait for a sale.
The gameplay mechanics for the investigation scenes, however, are excellent, and I hope The Astronauts is planning to make more games like this... if this game is intended as a "proof of concept" for their idea of how to make a detective game, then I'd say they've proven their concept with flying colors.
PROS:
+ Best investigation mechanics I've yet encountered in a detective game
+ Atmospheric
+ Incredible graphics
CONS:
- Brief
- Uneven graphical performance
Overall: Fans of horror and/or adventure games should certainly consider purchasing this game.

I have to write this review as it troubles me greatly the way that SEGA are distributing games.  I like Company of Heroes 2 and I like playing it just as I like the Total War series but I do not like the precedent that is being set through DLC and need to make others aware of it.
I am reviewing this game on the basis that it is full price and all the DLC is full price, which no sane person would pay!  Please, please wait until the game and all its content are on sale to buy it else you feel like you've had a raw deal.  I bought this game for £10 from a supermarket when it was on special offer and the deals Steam puts on can undercut that.  I felt I had got a good deal but if I had paid £29.99 I certainly would have felt cheated.
I'm from a generation of gamers who used to play on 4 colour 8-bit computers where you had to wait for games to load via a tape player that you bought from Tandy.  I've seen the development of PC games from Doom to the present day and it was a sad fact that the internet was double edged.  We had good things like forums, multiplayer servers, modders and the publisher could release updates for the game.  Then the bad like publishers releasing buggy, unfinished games which would then be patched later.  Now we can add to that the insidious practice of DLC (down loadable content) that we must pay for to use.  Now I'm a realist, some DLC such as extra levels or new units may be worth paying for where it adds to the game and its here to stay.  SEGA aren't the only distributors to sell DLC but in the case of Company of Heroes 2 they do let you know what you haven't got!
Let me explain.  So you've just paid £29.99 for this and checked out the DLC from the store page and see that there's some Theatres of War and an add on for Ardennes Assault (this is really a separate game and I won't cover that in detail here but it is a very good campaign).  So what do you get for £29.99?  You get a base Soviet campaign, one theatre of war and some commanders, skins and intel bulletins for skirmish/multiplayer (more on that later).  So you have a relativity engaging single player campaign but for multiplayer you quickly realise you've just been sold a 'starter pack' if you will and you're lacking a hell of a lot.  That doesn't mean it isn't there, it just you can't use it!
On the main menu screen you are hit with adverts for DLC - Theatres of War, Ardennes Assault and Fox company rangers to try and get you to purchase them.  It seems the game delights in showing you what you don't have.
So you click on the store page and you are taken to options you cannot see through Steam, you have to see them through the game, those are: Commanders, Skins and Faceplates, all with associated costs.  Then you thin, what have I actually paid for other than the short campaign?  A good Question and the answer raises more questions!
The theatres of war are like mini campaigns which take place on the maps from multiplayer and some are very challenging but they aren’t worth the full price of the game.  You look at the cost for all the Theatres of War DLC (Southern Fronts £2.99, Stalingrad £6.99 & Case Blue £6.99), total of £16.97.
Now comes the gut wrenching part, the cost for all those bits of DLC for multiplayer.  For those who aren’t familiar with the Company of Heroes games one of their traits is it allows you to select a commander  who has specific abilities that you can use to gain a tactical advantage during the game.  This can be the ability to call in airstrikes, off map artillery, special units or uniquely powerful armoured units such as Tiger tanks.  In the original game there were three commanders (Infantry, Airborne and Armoured).  In this game there are lots, I don’t know how many but there’s a forum about it somewhere.  Initially when you buy the game you get a basic number of commanders for the Soviets and the Werhmacht.  (I got a message that as a legacy player I’d unlocked some so I have a number that weren’t ‘unlocked’ with the base game).  These are critical for your experience on multiplayer and skirmish as the computer can use commanders you don’t have access to and it will.  Likewise, online players may have access to that German commander who can call in a Tiger Ace (a Tiger tank with full veterancy level) and you don’t have a commander who can call in an equally powerful unit.  This makes the game unbalanced.
OK, so I talked about ‘unlocking’ commanders and earlier on I mentioned intel bulletins.  Intelligence Bulletins change the mechanics of the game and you can select three from a vast number of options.  Some are subtle such as giving machine guns a 2% faster rate of fire and some have a greater impact such as giving tanks 20% greater accuracy.  You can’t buy these through DLC (that’s no loss as there’s already plenty of that) you have to ‘unlock’ them.  You unlock more commanders, intel bulletins, vehicle skins and other goodies via the war spoils system.  This essentially involves grinding away for hours on skirmish matches to ‘win’ random war spoils.  There’s no logic or pattern to what you get, when you get it or how many get.  For instance after one 20 minute game I won two war spoils and after one 1 hour game I got none.  Plus you can get repeats like trading cards except you can’t trade them with anyone.  So intel bulletins and commanders are classified as common, scarce and rare.  The rare types being the more useful and more powerful.
‘Rubbish’ you cry, I want the special commanders, can’t I download them?  Yes you can, at a price through that store page accessed via the game.  Now I’m not saying that anyone would buy all the commanders, or that you would even need to, especially as many just have different combinations of the same abilities.  But just say you’re a completest, well there are: 1 x starter bundle of four commanders at £6.49, 8 commanders at £2.79/each, 8 commanders at £2.99/each and 10 commanders at £1.99/each.  Total cost = £72.63.
I’m not finished with the DLC here though, no, you can also alter the cosmetic appearance of the game with vehicle skins (different camouflage paint jobs) and for a full set you need three (one for light vehicles, one for medium and one for heavy).  Now I’m not big on paying for cosmetic changes but just say you wanted to as they were there and you wanted them all.  There are two starter packs (one Soviet and one German) at £4.79/each.  There are then a whopping 40 extra skins at £1.59/each.  Total cost = £73.18
You can also change the control bar face plate if you so desired and there are four options at £1.59/each.  Total cost = £6.36
Then there are the Western armies (USA and OKW) at £14.99 that you will want for multiplayer.
Total cost of DLC = £184.13, yes £184.13!!!
But you say, surely you wouldn’t download all the cosmetic stuff, just what you want.  This is true, but it’s not the point.  You have paid £29.99 for a game that is missing fundamental aspects to make it playable in multiplayer and the only way to get it is to pay more, a lot more.  I would never part with my hard earned cash to buy commanders which should be in the game I’ve bought.  In fact they are in the game, I just can’t use them.  Fix the war spoils system, reward players who are very good and very skilful with the better commanders, don’t fleece us!
That’s why I can’t recommend this game, stuff the gameplay, it doesn’t matter, no game is worth £214.12 (DLC cost plus base game cost, all full price) to access all of its features, not one, ever!
Buy this game when it’s on offer, but please boycott paying for what’s in the game already.  Don’t buy the commanders, even those you really want or need.  £2.99 may not sound like a lot but you can often buy a FULL game for that on a Steam offer.  You’re paying to use a single special unit that the computer can use at will.  It sucks.

Just to put an end to the argument that this was copied from Ark, it was.  There were image files that didn't get changed right away that were clearly straight out of Ark.  That being said, they have been taking care of that and cleaning things up.  This game will always have a lot in common with Ark (blueprints, meteorites instead of beacons, grind, build, tame, etc).  The beauty of this game however is that it has its own "soul".  In Ark, you start totally alone and stay that way unless you join a tribe,, in DNL you start with a faction that you can keep coming back to with quests and vendors.  Over the short period of time they have already enhanced this portion of the game and it appears they intend to keep developing it.  This gives it a deeper feeling of immersion.
Fighting is ok, they have already made changes and improvements to that and I expect they will continue to enhance it.
Taming at times can be tedious and making iron hook arrows and magic essence appear to be the bane of everyone's existence but there are trade offs and ways of doing most things smarter.  What I have noticed is, because this is an EA a game, there aren't a lot of tutorials and guides out there walking people through how to do these things the most efficiently or "quick guides to leveling".  I know most people will say they don't use those but they typical have an awful lot of views and people subscribed to them considering "nobody" uses them.  My guess is most people don't know how to go about figuring out how to do a lot of this stuff on there own, they are all racing to get the biggest base or baddest tame or whatever and lose the fun along the way of truly exploring the world be it geographically or through its magic system, building system or tools.
Anyway, I'll get off my soap box now!  This game has developed its own flavor that is very distinct and unique.  The devs are doing a great job fixing bugs AND adding new content(not as fast as I'd like but I don't really want to pay more for a larger dev team) so I'll take it as it comes.
Two big potential draw backs however that could seriously limit this games growth and potential going forward-
1) No first person-they discussed in one of the dev q&a sessions that the animations weren't designed for first person and they most likely wouldn't do that.  They are missing the boat here-first person allows you to get really immersed in the game and that's when people really get in to it.  I've seen the petitions on the forums for it but I'm not sure the devs are going to cave on this based on what they said.  Too bad if that's the case.
2) At the start of the game you see a small island off of a much bigger land mass.  This is where the game currently takes place.  It looks awesome and promising, it looks like its going to be huge and sprawling.  During the same q&a above they said they probably wouldn't make the map that big for a bunch of reasons, my take away on this was the same as the one above, it'll be too hard.  As you could see on the master builder servers, the island is way too small if you have 40+ people playing on it and it doesn't take long to scout it all out.  Build the rest of the map, even if there are large expenses of plains or ridge lines that are cut and pasted.  Every single piece of the map doesn't have to be hand made, use the power of cut and paste then do some blending by hand and touch up work.
BLUF-This game is Early Access, get over the bugs or wait for full release, just quit your ♥♥♥♥♥ing about bugs.  The value in getting EA is the possibility to influence where the devs go with the game.  With full access you have ZERO chance to influence it with EA you have the possibility to impact the direction and outcome.  This game is worth it to me and I would recommend it to anyone who likes RPG, fantasy genre games and can be patient during the buggy development process.

XCOM is a well made Turn Based Tactics game. It features solid engaging mechanics, great level of challenge and replay-ability, good graphics and presentation, and is technically sound.
The game has a really challenging campaign. Played on Normal, I felt like the difficulty was quite balanced, it feels really hard compared to most games. Especially if you select missions with high threat level.
XCOM has a pattern-like flow to it: You play missions. You have break time in between. You can customize and develop your base, gear and technologies. Initiative researches and developments. Analyze captured enemies. Recruit and tend to soldiers. Level soldiers up and customize their load-outs. Build buildings giving resources or production capabilities. Launch fighter jets to attack or intercept attackers. And much more. There's plenty of strategy here and freedom of choice. Every upgrade feels substantial.
You are given occasional alerts of attacks worldwide. And you are given a choice - to select which country you are to save. Different events have different challenge levels and rewards.
There are also timed events for special requests, and of course story missions.
At the end of the game I managed to have all countries of the council supporting me and in high favor - giving extra benefits.
The gameplay is engaging. A rather fast paced turn based combat.
It still requires a lot of patience - as some levels can come into a crawl where every wrong step can be disastrous to your entire squad. Sometimes leading to a grind where you play hide and seek or seek and destroy with your enemies. But you can rarely ever rush in - less you get ambushed and wiped out.
There's a wide variety of weapons, skills, gear and machinery - which gives you flexibility between missions. Environment and cover also plays a significant role in combat.
There's also a large variety in enemies, with various strengths, weaknesses and behavior patterns.
The story, however is quite on the weak side.
XCOM combat has a lot of depth, it's both complex and simple enough, and there's great satisfaction to be gained here.
All in all - this is great game and a solid pick for the Tactics & Turn Based enthusiastic.

Do not buy if you're interested in singleplayer.
The AI blatantly cheats. No two ways around it. It will have fleet configurations that are impossible to buy under its point limit, which really stands out in a game like this to begin with. The AI also knows where hidden ships are, making the kind of stealth tactics available in MP useless, and will know in advance where "random" objectives will pop up. Play Planetary Assault - Defense against them and watch carefully, and you'll learn you can predict where bombardment objectives will appear based on where AI ships suddenly start running to 5-10 seconds before they appear. And that's when the objective doesn't just appear directly next to them - luck I assure you the player will never have! I gave up on the campaign after one too many losses due to this kind of impossible luck robbing me of a hard-won victory - not because I'm intolerant of losing ,but that I felt winning or losing wasn't a function of my skill in the game, but how generous or not the AI decided to be.
On the other hand, the AI is beyond stupid. I've seen them fly ships into asteroid fields until they died. I've seen enemy ships fly headfirst into minefields for no apparent reason simply because it was on the path between them and their goal. It seems to have no grasp of strategy beyond "fly at target and attack it." Once you learn how to exploit that, most game types vs. the AI are simple and a couple are just frustrating. You're playing against a hacker who's stoned - they may make dumb decisions, but they also make impossible plays and the game will consistently favor them.
There are other issues, as well. Bugs aren't super common, but they do happen. Especially obnoxious are bugs that end a battle out of nowhere. Startup takes
; the initial loading screen takes so long when I first played it, I thought it had crashed. After a victory or defeat condition is met, control is taken away for a 10-15 second cutscene before the endgame screen, during which the battle continues. It is possible to lose ships in battle while you stare helplessly at the victory screen. In Convoy - Defense, I even once reached the victory screen
because a transport was killed
That is unacceptable. Speaking of cutscenes, every last one is unskippable. The depictions of the WH40K ships are cool at first, but rapidly go from neat to obnoxious when you're treated to the exact same 15 second screen every single match. Oh, and the campaign's story is utterly generic 40k fare. Maybe you don't mind that, but they could've done better - other games in the franchise have.
Ship variety is low; most bigger ships are simply larger versions of smaller ships without representing any real change in how they're used. Maybe you could blame the source material for this, but it is disappointing. Upgrade and progression is pretty limited, as well; the ships all have identical upgrades available and most of them won't really matter. Skirmish, campaign, and multiplayer XP is all tracked separately, so you can't for instance build up your fleet in skirmish before taking on the world, or try new strategies versus the AI before taking them online.
Don't buy it for the singleplayer. If you think you'd play it in multiplayer a lot, go ahead. It's not a
game in that regard - the gameplay, minus a few bugs, is easy to grasp and flows well, if a little shallow.

Saints Row 2 was a well grounded & fun Action Sandbox game with clever writing. Saints Row 3 pretty much the same with a quirky twist. The fourth installment is just insane. No...really. This was supposed to be an expansion to Saints Row 3 with the fanfare of super powers (Apparently the community wanted a SR game with super powers). The plot here is that you are the President of the U.S and aliens abduct you and place you in a simulation.
Now, since this is Steam I'm going to keep this short. The real fun of this game is the sandbox itself with the superpowers. When that novelty wears thin, you got the main missions where you'd have a few laughs over the parodys and even self mimicry.
The main missions have some diversity to them in the sense that they again become parodys or mimic other genres.
I'll give an example, the mission where you have to rescue Gat from the simulation involves you playing the entire mission as a 2d Side Scrolling Beat Em Up game.
Another noticable parody is everytime you exit the simulation, you are on a ship which resembles Bioware's Mass Effect.
But beyond that everything else is thrown together half hazardly. Repetative side missions which mainly involve doing Events (Races, Mayhem etc.) rather than quests. Super powers that supress core aspects of the series i.e. Vehicles and Weapon Modifications.
Beyond the often humours parodies; the writing this time is subpar, often relating to nostalgia, meme references and popular culture. Don't expect SR2 style writing here.
Theres just too much going on in this game, so many ideas, very little actually doing any good to the overall game. The best way to enjoy it is to turn your mind off and use this game to de-stress yourself. It's a mess of a game, but a rather fun mess. It's like the "Scary Movies" of video games. Just don't pay full price for this.
If you have never played a Saints Row game before, Check out Part 2 and 3. Part 2 being the best in the series so far.

I played the first game, having bought it during the Steam Summer '16 sale, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. The puzzles flowed well together, and though you had to do a little lateral thinking, the challenge was there.
This game, I felt, deviated a little from what the first one was. The story aspect was far more prevalent in this one than the last, and it didn't deter from the game. Instead, what I felt lacking was the "flow." Pure and simple. A ship, a temple, etc....Things were disjointed until you realized they were matching the cards featured in a later level. But that jarring change from one thing to another broke the immersion of the puzzles. And the rooms....round and round you go, trying to remember what went where and what things did what.... It was too much all over the place.
Again, back to the flow... The puzzles were too abstract. Different types and formulas to keep you processing different things without repetition in each level which is a HUGE BONUS! But if I am trying to find a broken fuse, why the heck would I think to
While I might have stumbled onto that accidentally, it isn't something I would necessarily think about.
In the first game, it was a "big" box that split into smaller puzzle areas that, for the most part, once you were done with that area, you didn't have to worry about it. With this edition, it was a big room that split into several smaller areas that you weren't certain when or if you were done with it. You were forced to keep coming back to areas you weren't sure you needed to come back to or why you would need to. There wasn't the same level of satisfaction as there was in the first one.
Honestly, I wish there was a neutral button for this, because while the puzzles were challenging to figure out, I wasn't as satisfied with the outcome as I would have liked. The price is good for this quality of puzzle game, and you can comfortably play it on its own without having played the first one and still enjoy the puzzle aspect of it, though the story may be lost on you. But as one who played both the first and second game, the story feels to be the only thing connecting the two. The fact that the flow of the puzzles and the constant need to go around and around and the need to think TOO abstractly to solve the puzzles compared to the first game is the only reason I have to eke my opinion more towards not recommending the game.

A very tough one to review. In short this is a submarine warfare simulation, it's puts a strong emphasis on historical/engineering/physics accuracy. So if you're looking for a quick fix blow stuff up then this is not for you.
Pros:
- Challenging difficulty
- Realism
- 1960s and 1980s ships/weapons/missions
- Fast forward time, being stuck at 1/3 ahead becasue otherwise you'll cavitate in shallow waters means it can take agest to get somewhere
Cons:
- Lack of mission variety (biggest issue for me)
- Campaign seems to be the solo missions just randomised
- Tutorials need more detail, advanced turtorials maybe?
- Help sections need may more content
- Easy isn't that easy until you've made it up the learning curve a bit (you will die easily a few times at first)
- Graphical detail (dev effort clearly went mostly into mechanics rather than making it look shiny)
- Lots of functions (eg. noisemaker) tied to key combinations, it can be hard to remember some of them in a crisis
If you're into realism/simulators and like a challenge then I think you'll get on well with Cold Waters, and given that the game is still under development I can only hope that the negatives will be worked on over time and we'll ultimately get a polished game at the end. However in its current form there are issues which detract from the experience, mainly for me the lack of mission/scenarios and the fact that the game just servs up them up randomly to you in the campaign and when you combine this lack of variety with the slow paced nature of the game then things can easily get boring. If they just fix the lack of variety in missions the the replay-ability of the game goes through the roof for me.
tl;dr -> 6/10, in its current form don't buy at £30. If there's a sale and you can pick it up for closer to £10 then go for it.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a great example of what a game can be based on nothing but environment and story elements. It uses far-reaching landscapes and beautiful visual effects to bring you a great narrative experience. However, be warned, this game may not be for those of little patience.
__________
Synopsis:
You play as Paul Prospero, who seems to be a detective with paranormal abilities such as ESP. Receiving a letter from Ethan Carter, he learns Ethan has strong psychic connections, and that he has gone missing. Your job is to explore the village of Red Creek Valley and find Ethan. You quickly learn that something is amiss; the town is abandoned, no sign of Ethan's family, and mysterious occurrences.
Story: A short, but interesting tale shrouded in mystery. Perhaps too short, depending on how quickly you progress through the game. It doesn't suffer very much from ups and downs in the story, and it ends pretty well too.
Graphics: One of the most visually appealing games I've played in a long time. A wider, open world gives you plenty of room to stretch your legs and explore, taking in the sights and sounds as you go along.
Functionality: Controls are pretty linear and simple. Essentially a Sherlock Holmes-puzzle solving game. Pick stuff up, find where it goes, and solve problems.
Gameplay: Overall, it's not good. Again, it's basically a point-and-click mystery game akin to Sherlock Holmes. There is no combat mechanics, and every item falls into the one-use category. The real problem I encountered was spending obnoxiously long amounts of time searching the vast landscape for potential clues, which a majority of them felt arbitrary. This is where those of little patience may find the game frustrating.
______________________________
At the end of the day, you're buying this game for the story and the experience; but the experience tends to fall short when you're slowly crawling over a couple acres of land looking for that one last piece of the puzzle. I feel this may have been a better release under a different venue, like Heavy Rain, which offers great atmosphere, narritive, and incorporates at least DECENT gameplay elements.
I did enjoy it, but my advice would be to wait until this game goes on sale to purchase.

This game is pretty much the closest experience you can currently have to being a StarFleet captain barking orders at your subordinates.  Divert power from engines to the weapons systems! Vent oxygen from decks 2-12! Fire torpedos (missiles) at their shield systems! Lock phasers (lasers) on their weapons systems! Fire at will! Prepare to board! Plust plenty more less-StarTrek-y options for battle including teleporting bombs, attack and defense drones, mind control, hacking, etc. all wrapped up in a easy to figure out "rogue-lite" game engine that you can pause at any time, allowing you to play as tactically or as action-y as you'd like.
Lots of star systems to explore, strange new aliens to meet, ship systems to upgrade, and rebels to fight.  Plus the flow of the gameplay and the ability to pause make it a well suited to both focused intense FTL sessions, as well as a great game to play while surfing the net or watching netflix (though in this case, you will have to try extra hard to avoid yelling out all your commands in your best Jean-Luc Picard voice).  Hard to beat the value to price ratio of this game either, as my handful of dollars bought me a game I've ended up playing in excess of 100 hours.  All in all, highly recommended.

Nope this game has sub catagories that unlock different recipes at different levels for instance. At say level 5 you unlock a a few new recipes in each sub catagory (farming, armour crafting, tailoring, taming, enchanting, fire magic, earth magic, water magic, straw building, wood building etc etc to name but a few) but you also have to level those sub catagories up by making those items previously unlocked or harvesting items needed for those recipes. So take farming for instance, I can either try and harvest seeds, and get 1 xp per seed ish (roughly dont quote me) or I can make 10 compost bins (if youve unlocked those) for more xp (you can always demolish them for half your materials back)
Small things that really please me about the game - The first spell you learn is a faerie that lights your way (I love faeries). Grass is done in little swirls, like faerie circles (again faeries, love em) You can tame a Unicorn! (Yes Im into those too...before they were cool this year) You can apparently break barrels in villages for items (not seen any barrels yet but the christmas event is going on so they may have been replaced with all the presents) I saw a tree ent (treent?) You can turn into other creatures!!! I havnt got very far in the game yet but it appears to be my perfect type of game so far! Theres even a spell for being over encumbered (which I always am, So far ive managed to be so over encumbered I couldnt move even with the spell, ooops lol)
Things that I am concerned about. BUGS! I logged out of my game today and got the achievemnt for reaching level 20, 40 and 60! I have only just reached level 15! And yet I havnt even got the achievement for making a wand and using a spell (part of the tutorial) or creating my own house (what guilds/clubs/tribes etc are called) The one that really concerns me is the fact that faction titles arnt even implemeneted yet and this is suppose to be going to console this year. Factions play a big part in the game, you cant enter some cities if your faction score isnt high enough. One of the tasks (like quests you dont need to do them theyre only there to show you how to play and help you level (why else would you need to create 50 beds??? Im leaving those till later when materials are coming out my eye sockets and I dont care that I only get half my mats back when I destroy them) Anyway the problem is that one of the beginning quests (the ones you actually do to learn what your doing in the game) is donate gold to a vendor to raise your faction level and earn your first faction title (Vagabond, I think it is). DO NOT WASTE YOUR IN GAME MONEY! Faction titles arnt in it yet so you cant raise your faction levels. Of course donating to vendors does have a secondary out come in that it also allows them to sell more stock and buy more stock (selling stock to vendors is weird. Each vendor will only buy certain items and then only in set quantities. So for instance a smith will buy from you wood in quantities of 100 for 75 gold but you cant just sell all your junk to him. When was the last time you walked into your local second hand store and was like I need to make room in my bag, how much for this slightly used hankerchief, some squashed berries and a couple handfulls of grass?)
Another problem ive come across is that even with the wind spell for making my inventory lighter I cant make the huge bonfire from the survival sub catagory. This game is great and has potential to become even better. Dark and Light is a fabulous survival fantasy game. It reminds me of a cross between The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, and Ark: Survival Evolved. I'm a fan of the dragons and swords theme, which is why I prefer this over Ark. The game is in EA, which should tell you you'll need to overlook a few issues here and there. However, the game is still a joy to play. I will say, if you're not a fan of being raided by other players, potentially losing everything you've built up over hours of gameplay... stick to the PvE servers. I find alot of joy in building bases that are challenging for raiders to get into. If they can get past enough walls and fake treasure rooms, they deserve whatever they can find. Enough said about raiding though. The games AI functions similarly to enemies in Ark, in that they charge you and spam their attack until you're dead with no real mechanics to speak of. That said, you can still find clever ways to take down most enemy AI (I recommend a horse and spear in general though). The ability to buy land in the city is a plus as well as it keeps your stuff safe while you're away. I often rent a small home just to keep anything extremely valuable in. This game is a delight to play, and is worth trying even in EA, though you may want to have a (very) decent machine to run it on.

The basic survivalism in the game is great and fairly realistic. I had survival training as an infantryman (in the baracks, not basic/AIT) in the Army back in the late 70s and this game matches up in that respect. Your biggest enemies are the cold, heat as well as need for water and food. Beyond that you have to fashion weapons to beat the predators that come for you.

Update 2: And yeah, just got to play my first planetary bombardment mission. These guys are either idiots, or they were pushed way too hard to release early. Here's how it works: every couple minutes, a random point will appear that you need to race one of your ships to. Will you make it? Maybe one out of 5 times it's close enough to reach before the timer expires. You technically get 5 chances to reach 3 points, but you'll be lucky to have one functional ship left by the time the last point spawns. So what does that mean? It means you restart the mission repeatedly and watch the opening cutscene each time. Maybe buy this game if it's like $10. Almost a great game, but degenerates into a swirling cesspoool of aggravating mechanics and design once the novelty wears off.  I really valued the atmosphere and the constant state of tension which was created by the host of deadly opponents throughout the game, particularly at night.  However the scaling of ways to kill said opponents is entirely out of whack.  In the early game you are effectively encouraged to just run away from all opponents using your burgeoning skills of parkour.  This was actually quite satisfying as even against the most agile of enemies you could use the terrain to your advantage.  Deaths in this circumstance feel entirely the player's fault for not thinking clearly.  However, when you were inevitably forced to confront opponents directly, this really began to strain the enjoyment of the game.  The weapons you have access to are incredibly varied, compelling to build, entertaining to see in action, and damn near completely ineffective at handling swarms of zombies at any given time.  While there are numerous opportunities to use the environment and various combinations of effects to bring down your enemies, there were an absurd number of scenarios were this simply wasn't an option and you had to haphazardly hack at enemies with a weapon that should conceptually one shot your standard biters, but usually doesn't even trigger the elemental effect it boasts to any helpful extent before you have to repair it.  For myself, I had a period of elation where my skill unlocks were getting to the point where I could do some pretty heavy damage to zombies, and I was really excited about the design of the second main story zone I had just unlocked, but unfortunately the game suddenly scaled the difficulty (health for the most part) of all the zombies so my newfound skills basically kept me on par.  That in itself did not seem unreasonable, but the moment of unresistable urge to uninstall the game came when I went back to the first zone and discovered all the zombies inexplicably (both by lack of in game explanation and game design rationale) had ramped up much like the zombies in the second zone.  There was no opportunity to feel like a badass and hack down low level biters outside of the occasional weapon challenge which allowed you to use a weapon that did in fact one shot zombies (and incidentally does no appear to be accessible anywhere in game).  Add to the that the completely absurd waves of agile zombies attacking you when have done nothing to draw their attention (and you know you haven't because you've spent the rest of the game learning how to avoid their attention).  The constant stream of aggressive virals was possibly the most single most rage inducing aspect of the game.  They are not at all difficult to manage on their own, but when you are focused on another task, especially one that is timed, and they are constantly harassing you, it feels like a really really terrible strategy to increase challenge in the game.
This game had a few moments where I felt it was possibly the best of at least some of it's target genres (zombie,survival,open world), but the moments of mentally crippling rage overshadowed those.  Many players will likely find ways to overcome this, either by habituating a different set of tactics or simply accepting it for what it is, but there are a lot of other games I would rather play that don't have such extreme and frequent lows.
I should mention that I didn't touch multiplayer and that is perhaps a mode of play that for some consumers is the main reason to buy the game, but I cannot speak to that.  I will also mention that the game community appears to be thriving and the devs are very involved in the game.
Bottom line: only buy for single player if you enjoy multiple repeats on infuriating missions due to inconsistent design elements.

+ The devolopers surely deserve a praise for still supporting the game with both simple cosmetics, and more complicated things like new improvements, or new enemies.
- IMHO the combat feels clunky, to say at least.  Especially at the start of the game (which is understandable, you don't have high leveled gear), it gets a bit better later in the game, but still, despite having +1k dmg weapons, you will stumble upon that one enemy that takes a few hits and you seem like you're hitting a tree - no feeling of impact, and barely any reaction of the npc.
- Special zombies are more annoying, than intimidating. Bombers are often put inside rooms and walk out from the corner you're near, instakilling you on the explosion. I also encountered a few that just..popped out of nowhere behind me, or whatever you could call this - there surely wasn't a single room upstairs one could be hiding at, so he was just scripted to spawn at that horrible place for some reason. Virals on the other hand, are probably my most  hated enemies in the game. You get told they approach you if you are loud: shooting guns, blowing up explosives, or breaking some objects. That is true, but virals tend to spawn even without the player making any noise, either randomly, or because you're on high survivor level. And there are mostly 3-6 of them coming. And they're literally homing at you, because they have GPS in what remains of their brains. Especially annoying enemy type when you're in your buggy in the DLC. Other specials are less of a hassle, so not talking about them.
- The story in the main game is pretty mediocre, but still much more interesting and replayable  than the campaign in Skyrim.
- Quite big penalty upon death, based on how often you die NOT from your failure.
- The "Gaining Credence" quest in the Following will probably be a huge block for you when you start the DLC, especially when you happen to do it at the night. Riding the car to the valve will be your most hated thing of the evening. I'd suggest dying several times to fix that, since time (and car damage, eh) actually passes through reloading your saves, the night will eventually end, and you'll have 100x less volatiles and virals on your way.
- Boss battles are horrible - almost as bad as fighting the living bullet sponges in Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
Yes, there are less cons here than  the pros, but I consider these ones as more of core mechanics, hence why the game feels significialy less enjoyable for me, and why I have left a negative reccomendation.

Saints Row 2 was a well grounded & fun Action Sandbox game with clever writing. Saints Row 3 pretty much the same with a quirky twist. The fourth installment is just insane. No...really. This was supposed to be an expansion to Saints Row 3 with the fanfare of super powers (Apparently the community wanted a SR game with super powers). The plot here is that you are the President of the U.S and aliens abduct you and place you in a simulation.
Now, since this is Steam I'm going to keep this short. The real fun of this game is the sandbox itself with the superpowers. When that novelty wears thin, you got the main missions where you'd have a few laughs over the parodys and even self mimicry.
The main missions have some diversity to them in the sense that they again become parodys or mimic other genres.
I'll give an example, the mission where you have to rescue Gat from the simulation involves you playing the entire mission as a 2d Side Scrolling Beat Em Up game.
Another noticable parody is everytime you exit the simulation, you are on a ship which resembles Bioware's Mass Effect.
But beyond that everything else is thrown together half hazardly. Repetative side missions which mainly involve doing Events (Races, Mayhem etc.) rather than quests. Super powers that supress core aspects of the series i.e. Vehicles and Weapon Modifications.
Beyond the often humours parodies; the writing this time is subpar, often relating to nostalgia, meme references and popular culture. Don't expect SR2 style writing here.
Theres just too much going on in this game, so many ideas, very little actually doing any good to the overall game. The best way to enjoy it is to turn your mind off and use this game to de-stress yourself. It's a mess of a game, but a rather fun mess. It's like the "Scary Movies" of video games. Just don't pay full price for this.
If you have never played a Saints Row game before, Check out Part 2 and 3. Part 2 being the best in the series so far.

Masked Shooters 2 reminds me quite a bit of something from 2004-2006. It's a great thought with old graphics, old gameplay style, and less options than the advanced games. For some reason, though, it entices players to continue playing despite all the flaws I mentioned previously.
Masked Shooters 2 starts out with an older-style menu which lets you choose whether you want to play in Multiplayer, SIngleplayer, and there's an options tab for when you need to change things. The background is decent, however something a bit more interesting such as a tour of one of the maps, at least something that moves, might be a nice visual for the first thing players see when they purchase the game. As soon as you click an option, you have the ability to set up the map, the amount of bots you want to play with (this is assuming you clicked the singleplayer option), and whether you want a team battle, or a deathmatch type battle. You can then go right ahead and jump into the game after you pick your map (definite turn off for these kinds of games is the lack of maps. There are only 3 maps to choose from and no way to add/create your own.)
There are a few different guns, and I'll list them:
- MP5AK, Desert Eagle, M67 Grenade, M79 Grenade Launcher, M87T Shotgun, Knife, RPG, R93 Sniper, STW-25 Auto Sniper
For a game like this, I guess it's okay to be able to access all of the weapons by scrolling your mouse or pressing a button. However, the main issue I see is that pretty much everyone and anyone can and will use the rocket launcher to just destroy everybody, which makes it difficult to snipe or use the pistols. It would be a lot better if it had a tiered weapon system where players start with a knife and have to work their way up to get the RPG and better guns. Just as one gamemode though, as a lot of people probably enjoy using their RPG to massacre everyone.
One more thing that I must add, the bots are absolutely stupid. They won't detect me if I'm right behind them, and miss a shot. They have the tracking-type AI which will stop them from spotting me until they get their kill, or I kill them from behind. It makes it quite easy to get a lot of kills, as well as a lot of achievements easily. Achievement hunters, go ham on this game if you want the easiest 100% completion you can get.
I enjoy this game. Sometimes, it's nice to reminisce a bit in some classic games. That's why I have 2 arcade-type games in my purchased list that I play quite often. However, this game really isn't worth the cost that it has attached, unless you get a discount coupon. The only reason I bought Masked Shooters 2 was because of the 90% coupon I got from making a badge. Verdict is not recommended, unless you happen to stumble across a coupon that makes it cheaper. Might be worth the price for 2-3 hours of fun before you never play it again.

Cold Waters is a sub game that walks a fine line between realistic and action and does a pretty good job at it. The game centers around you taking control of a variety of US nuclear subs during the Cold War.  There are two campaigns that go with the "what if World War III happened" approach in either 1968 or 1984.  Both campaigns are dynamic and the war will be heavly influenced by your success or failures against the Soviet navy.
Overall the game is very easy to pick up and the controls are simple enough, but to truly master your sub and become an expert skipper requires some patience and practice.  You are directly controlling the sub's main systems which means you always need to be on your toes watching for enemy torpedos or depth charges while at the same time trying to sink your prey.  Simply put, if you are looking for an arcade type of experience you will probably end up very frustrated.
At the end of the day, Cold Waters is a fun game that I would recommend it to anyone looking for an entry level sub-sim game as well as anyone who enjoys this type of game in general.

The developers say this will be released in February, and I have no idea how they think that will be possible. The unmanned portion seems mostly complete, but the manned portion needs at least another year. It's full of bugs and glitches, there is absolutely no tutorial, explanation, or guide anywhere, and it's lacking a lot of immersion. The bugs range from being unable to attach a power cable properly to being flung across the Martian desert because you stood on said cable the wrong way. With no explanation in-game, on the walkthroughs through Steam, or on any forum for the game, every feature is hidden until you stumble across it and major components of the game are difficult to work out. It took me three hours to figure out how to assemble a structure, and I still have no clue what any of the various utilities do. The immersion problem is one they definitely won't fix, though, because they seem pretty happy with what they have: you can hear your astronaut's breath and heartbeat. All the time. Very loudly. Right in your ear. He also can't move any faster than a slow stroll, even on Earth, and can only run ten or twenty meters before getting winded. On the Moon, you would expect to do some cool Moon-style walking like in the NASA videos, but he just casually strolls from one place to another. I got to night-time on Mars (difficult because it's 1:1 timescale and there's no way to advance time, like sleeping or waiting) and expected some sort of awe inspiring view, but it was totally unimpressive. I was more impressed the first time I got a craft into orbit in Kerbal Space Program. I have the graphics all maxed out on a mobile GPU and I get 60 FPS - that means you're not trying hard enough.
From my previous experiences with this developer, I know what to expect: a game with countless flaws that showed promise and is occasionally, for very short periods, brilliant. Arma was like that, Take On Helicopters was like that, and DayZ is like that. They're very ambitious, and that's admirable, but they have no tenacity, patience, or follow-through.
If you get it on sale, like I did, you'll have a fun ten hours or so before deciding to just wait for the full release. But seeing as how they say that'll be in February, I'd say you should wait until the patch/update schedule has slowed a bit, because there should be a lot of them.

The following is the story of playing as Austria, on a Huge Earth map, beginning in the Ancient Era, Standard pace, with 11 other civilizations and 36 city states, on King difficulty...
We begin this tale on the Northern coastline of the continent of Africa. As the foundations of the Capital city are laid, our earliest scouting efforts show, that yes, there is in fact water to our immediate North and uninhabitable desert to our immediate South. Great.
The Austrian people struggle to found new cities along the mountainous coastline. With little arable land, the cities are slow-growing. A settlement founded South-Easternly from the Capital, intent on harvesting the abundant Incense resources in that area, are set upon by a small contingent of specialized Aztec Warriors. It seems the Aztecs had their eye on the Incense as well. They outnumber the Austrian forces 3 to 1. However, utilizing Ranged advantage, and their indigenous terrain, the Austrians were able to rally a sufficient response to put down the invaders. The Aztecs accept Peace flatly, and one can consider their formal introduction as Austria's neighbor across the Sahara, now complete.
Not a fortnight after the Peace with Montezuma, the Greeks ride in from the East across the Sinai. They too, set their sights on the abundant Incense resources, knowing they would provide both a needed luxury benefit domestically as well as fetch a worthy trade with other civilizations. The Greek Hoplites and specialized Horsemen come rushing in, but make one fatal error... they mobilized over half their forces across the Mediterranean Sea, where Austrian Composite Bowmen are able to sink their ships before they even make it ashore.
After an embarassing defeat, Alexander of the Greeks flatly accepts Peace. The scrappy little Austrian empire repelled two superior forces of aggressors, establishing itself in the process, but as a result, missing its opportunity to create a religion like many other civilizations already had. No matter, the Austrian empire will now continue to focus on its internal growth.
Many years pass, and it is becoming apparent that the Aztecs are aggressively colonizing across the continent with an army that is vastly superior to the Austrian empire's. The Austrian leadership sits back and allows the Aztec Catholic missionaries to spread their preposterous religion in their lands, all in hopes of averting direct confrontation with Montezuma's forces. The Aztecs later announce they will follow the ideology of Autocracy, and the Austrians follow suit, augmenting the fascade of comraderie.
The Austrians completely forgo any ambitions of scouting the world, or making relationships with its inhabitants. The Aztecs become the sole motivating factor for growth and survival of the empire. The Aztecs see the Austrians as their vassal, so offer a declaration of friendship, only to shortly after demand they declare war on the Greeks. Well, the Austrians agree, and the Aztec forces head to the East to engage their enemy. Austria does not send a single unit. Their entire contribution to the war is on paper. Yet, a crafty peace deal struck with Alexander as the Aztec forces closed in on Athens, granted the Austrians control of Argos, a Greek city that was founded at the entrance to the Red Sea, a fine strategic location. Soon Athens falls, and with that defeat, the Greeks are no more.
While the Aztecs fought ceaselessly in the East, the Austrians made a break across the Mediterranean into the area of Europe. Much to the explorers' surprise, it was only inhabited by two city states along the Eastern portion. Austrian forces set about colonizing as much of the European continent as possible. Through Diplomatic Marriage, the Austrian empire is able to acquire both of the city-states, and integrate them. Austria now controls all of Europe, all of the Mediterranean, and all of the North coast of Africa.
Austria spends the next several centuries building educational and transportation infrastructure. A network of trade and industry, focusing on implementing social policies such as Fortified Borders, Elite Forces, and Total War. While the Austrian standing army may be low in its membership, each unit that will be trained henceforth will be an unparalleled fighting machine. By this time, through the Aztecs, Austria meets the world, at the aptly named, World Congress.
Austria becomes the second civilization to complete their Manhattan Project. The Austrians begin to feverishly convert Uranium into Nuclear Bombs, then Nuclear Missiles. Upon utilizing all 16 deposits available domestically, the Austrians begin to trade for the Uranium of lesser civilizations. Pacal of the Maya gives up his Uranium for some Furs and Iron. (lol)
All civilizations are suddenly Afraid of the Austrians. The reserved, even-tempered folks with no opinions on anything, the world had known for a few centuries, were no more. Now a high tech, nuclear superpower, with a modern navy, the Austrians began to plot their world domination, and more importantly... their revenge on the Aztecs.
The year was 2011, and the world's top 3 civilizations are the Iroqois, the Aztecs, and the Austrians. Montezuma comes to the Austrian leadership with a proposal to wage war against Hiawatha and the Iroqois. The Austrians wisely request 10 turns to prepare. The next 10 turns are used to position nuclear-armed Missile Cruisers and Battleships. The war begins, and countless city-states pledging their allegiance to the Austrian empire become the frontline against the Iroqois who come from the area of Indo-China. The Aztecs journey great distances and engage the Iroqois, advancing on Onondaga. Heavy fighting ensues, and the world sees its first use of nuclear arms. Austria shows up as well, launching a tactical Nuclear Missile directly at the Iroqois capital. Direct hit. Population goes from 28 to 8.
The war waged for many more years, and through Gunboat Diplomacy, a monsterous economy, and social policies in the Patronage specialty, Austria is able to garner 40 of the 48 delegates it requires to win a Diplomatic Victory through the United Nations. By bribing long time ally Russia, to support their proposal in exchange for 2500 gold, the Diplomatic Victory is assured... but not before raining nuclear inferno upon the Aztec civilization. The missiles smite the war mongering heathens who threatened the Austrians' very existence millenia ago. And so the Aztec people and their cities, were reduced, ashes to ashes, and dust to dust, left to dance in the breeze amongst the dunes of the Sahara.
