X-Com starts out with a short cutscene depicting our first contact with alien life; meteor-like items streaking from the sky, bearing with them alien ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that you, as the commander of X-Com have been tasked with combating.You are dumped into your first mission in which you are introduced to the tiny, big-headed scumbags known as sectoids. So far I’ve beat the game on both normal and ironman mode, (ironman means you can’t reload saves for that playthrough, adding an extra layer of difficulty) and in those instances sectoids really are the little ♥♥♥♥♥ they’re meant to be. But now recently I’ve been trying classic ironman, the next step up in difficulty, and man, they pump those things up. You feel like you’re sitting pretty behind your cover on top of a two story building, but you’re not. You are still so indescribably boned, no one is safe from their herculean aim. You can be up there in this hypothetical scenario feelin’ pretty good with your height bonus to cover and aim, but little known to you, the aliens have decided to take you down several pegs, and a shot from an alien you can’t even see nails your guy and he’s down, forever. In reality this isn’t even a hypothetical, it’s happened to me twice in ironman classic. The first time I only lost one soldier, which sucked, but it wasn’t too bad, the second time a whole bloody mob of sectoids popped up and seal team sixed my whole squad, to say i became enamoured with the idea of dead aliens would certainly be an understatement.
Every other mission I’d find myself racking my brain for another insult to sling at my screen. The resentment X-Com makes you feel towards those rancid slimeball is so pure and justified that it feels all the better when you pull off a mission, keeping your squad just barely intact, which it gives you all the tools to do so with. The four core classes in the game: Assault, Support, Heavy, and Sniper offer some very fun and satisfying ways to cave in each individual alien’s skull. For example, a Heavy can use an ability to increase the aim bonus for your squad against an individual target, which then minimizes the risk of having your assault use an ability that allows them to fire twice for the price of decreased aim, which is only scratching the surface of the wonderful ways to weave your abilities.
It does, however, lead me to one of my gripes of the game, how exactly does my dude with shotgun, two feet from an alien miss his 98%  chance to hit shot while the aliens seem to be able to kill him just fine. I understand that the devs would be hard pressed to find a different way to go about that, but it is still definitely a nuisance, and if you’re like me you will invariably find yourself pushing onto the harder difficulty levels which do get, as previously mentioned, absurd. Although the game does tell you what you’re getting into, and  is also very polished, the base building and combat are intuitive, along with a rewarding research and development system.
But all of that is nothing compared to my favorite part of the game which I have not yet mentioned. There are mechs in the game, yes, you read that right, you can chop off an operator’s useless extremities and stuff them into a mech with a very, very big gun. The mach class can also be outfitted with different subsystems as you upgrade them, specifically in the beginning, a flame thrower or a giant punch apparatus strapped to the arm of the mech. Much later in the game the aliens adapt your use of mechs for their own soldiers, which is cool, because the whole game you’re using their technology for yourself as well. But what’s even cooler is that you can use said punching apparatus to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of their mechs, forever proving that yours are far, far superior. It even has a specialized animation that plays which in and of itself makes the game a must buy, awesome.

By now everyone knows how good this game is so I'll keep this as succinct as possible.
XCOM is an turn based Strategy RPG in the veign of Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, Disgaea, and Advanced Wars. But this is a Firaxis title, the company that also gives us Civilization. That being the case, rather than RPG elements outside of battles and cutscenes we get base building and production with budgeting and time management involved. And just as in Civilization, it's every bit as addicting here.
XCOM gives you the XCOM base which you must build up with your monthly funds provided by member nations of the XCOM project-an initiative tasked with fighting off the alien scourge. If you're short on funds you can sell off items attained in battle on the grey market, but be warned that these same items are used in manufacturing goods like weapons and upgrades. Increases in funding require sattelites to be launched over member nations, which necessitates building them and having the capacity to launch them into orbit, which requires building relays in your base. And building relays requires excavation, the pre-requisite number of engineers to take on the task, funding, and time for the task to be completed.
Short on engineers? Build a workshop to attain five! I think the picture is rather clear here: you want more money, better weapons, armor, and all manner of items but it takes time and money. Just as in Civilization, you want to have it all and the planning undertaken is the addictive aspect. It's not as complex as Civilization in that you are managing 1 base, rather than multiple cities and towns. But there is more complexity in managing one item here than one city in Civ.
To move time forward you go to the control room and "scan for activity". The globe spins dictating the passage of time and after a bit something occurs. Whether that be a mission given by the XCOM Council or reports of alien abductions. There are roughly 120 maps in the "Enemy Within" expansion and the missions tend to vary; either way one will pop up in due time and that's where the "SRPG" portion of the game emerges. A few times you'll be tasked with intercepting an alien craft with your own air fleet. This aspect is nothing more than seeing a 10 second animation of your craft and the alien craft fighting it out, but more is better than less even if it is an aspect that could have been fleshed out more. It's concise and functional.
You carry a maximum of 6 troops to battle; as this is all projectile based weaponry there are is no moving within 3 spaces of an enemy to land a specific attack. All attacks can hit an enemy provided they are within sight-you're using guns, afterall. The difference here is that the further away you are the more likely you are to miss, so you'll want to get a good vantage point or closer in order to strike enemies. Do take note that different weapons have different hit chances and ranges, so you'll have different troops at different optimal ranges.
Your squad, like any SRPG, has different classes each with specialized skill trees whereby you pick from 1 of 2 upgrade choices with every promotion earned. "Enemy Within" adds a Gene Upgrade tree that allows you to enhance soldiers with genetic upgrades, and there's also a psionic upgrade tree which is sadly lacking, but still rewarding in its own right. I assume this aspect is improved upon in the next title, but its worth noting that its a bit of a letdown.
The game itself follows a linear plot, but the way it all unfolds it always feels like the game is constantly moving forward and something is happening. Usually in any game the plot is detached from the gameplay in that you can take a rest from proceeding and either grind or do something else rather than proceed. But I found the plot here was tightly tied to the game so that you always felt like you were proceeding with a narrative even if it was just an alien abduction. The game does this through incredibly varied maps, succinct cutscenes that don't overstay their welcome but make every activity feel like it has importance and is moving something forward, and....I really love this ♥♥♥♥ing game, dude.
I could delve deeper but I'll end this by complimenting something this game deserves recognition for: the entire feel of the game delivers a fantastic package that makes you feel like a complete badass when doing anything. You *feel* like a commander and I think a good portion of the credit should go to the amazing voice acting by the representative of the council. The music as well really psyches you up for any upcoming missions. This game has presentation AND content; it does an amazing job of putting you in the mindset that you are Earth's elite force of alien eradicators. I felt like a kid again; I was excited and gleeful throughout, it was like playing make-believe. I *AM* the commander.
Strong recommendation; but make sure to play it with the "Enemy Within" Expansion pack. Just like Civilization, it adds content to the base game that I can't picture it going without.

For starters, it's amazing to me how much better DnL runs as an Early Access game than Ark as a fully released game. Seems Snail Games learned a thing or three from their development of Ark. Much smoother gameplay and "feels" better - at least to me. I find Ark annoying to play, by contrast.
Anyway!
Beyond that, I like other improvements they've made to DnL. The introduction is much better done. Starting in a city where you can get the hang of things in more relative safety is very very nice. Dying to a dinosaur seconds after you've loaded in, and no way to defend yourself or effectively fight back is very annoying. You're dying and you're not even sure what you were doing wrong - if you were in the first place.
The structuring of DnL feels better to me, too. Any question I had in Ark seemed difficult to find an answer to (without leaving the game and looking it up). DnL seems to have more information on-hand, right in-game. Not sure how to progress along a given skill line? No problem, you can look it up right in-game.
No pooping! Sounds silly, but that whole poop thing in Ark just seemed ridiculous to me. I mean, it's funny at first, and I realize it serves a function, but when you're in an area that's crowded with dinosaurs (everywhere that I went), it gets really annoying hearing that sound every few moments.
Also, I'm a much bigger fan of DnL's setting than Ark's. I love me some High Fantasty, so it's entirely subjective, but a major Plus for me.
All in all, I really like how things are progressing so far. We're only on a relatively tiny part of a massive map, and the available area is huge already.
If you're into a game like Ark, or other building/survival type games, with the caveat that it *is* in Early Access and so there *will* be issues along the way (it's weird how many people don't seem to understand this concept and complain about bugs, etc... something something reading comprehension...), I can comfortably recommend checking DnL out.

I've just finished the game and I really got to say ... well, I don't know what I got to say, or better "should" say, since reviews are for people that like to get a little insight in a game before hand, get a peek of what's in store for them and wether or not they should buy it. And to those: buy it! I just have to say it's better not to read any more and just enter the world of "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter". Its just one of these games that work best the less you know about it. The story really is something else, and for me, to experience this world and the love that clearly was put into it is something I don't want to miss. In thought, this game will stick with me for quite a while I'm sure.
On the more technical note, this game just looks amazing. The photographic technology they've used to create this world so rich in detail will surely be seen in more titles from lots of developers in the future. But for its debut, I'm glad it was used in a game like this and not a generic shooter.
To finish this game probably took me around 6 hours or so I guess ... I have to guess since my "hrs on record" seems to be off. Steam tells me 2.1 hrs on record, but that's kinda just what I've played today, so, not sure what happened there. All in all I have to say this game had exactly the right length for what the story was ... any longer would have been too much imho.
So from me, this game is a must have for everyone who loves atmospheric mystery/adventue games. It's money worth spending, because making games like this just should be rewarded.
A little advice: when you play the game, look around, don't blaze through it. Take your time and make sure not to miss anything. In the world there are riddles hidden aside the storyline of following ethan carter. It seems they are not "needed" since you can "follow" ethans trail without completing these riddles. But to get to the final ending, you will need to complete all of these riddles. Don't worry, you get your chance to complete and find these riddles later on and can always solve them at any time during the game, since it's an kinda open world ... but it just is more enjoyable to solve these riddles on your way, so you don't have to backtrack later on. But its not the backtracking that is annoying, it's just not that enjoyable doing them after you have followed the "ethan" storyline up to an almost-end ... because at that point, you just want to get to the ending ... going back and solving riddles then is just a hard "cut" in the atmosphere in my oppinion. So better get them on the road ;-) ... and to not make the mistakes I've made, there are 2 riddles to find before reaching the dam quite soon in the game. The others, later, are better to spot.

LEGO City Undercover was a fantastic release on the Wii U that used so many unique mechanics that to this day have not been re-used in a LEGO game. Everyone was sad it was a Wii U exclusive that didn't have the U because it was a really good game, but when it was announced for the new-gen consoles and PC, I was eager to get it from the start.
So let's start at the beginning.
LCU follows police officer Chase McCain after being on leave from LEGO City for 2 years, and when he comes back, things are not as he remembers. Dunby is now the chief of police, the former chief is now Mayor Gleeson, and most of the officers are not as up to their game as Chase, who now has to re-arrest the nefarious Rex Fury.
STORYLINE
The game's story is really well put together, and shows many locations that are based on the real world, or are completely original. A great feature is that since most of the story is hub-based, nearly the entire hub is explored during the course of the story. This is fantastic. People refer to this as a kid's GTA, and in many cases this does bear similarity to the franchise, but in a more light-hearted manner. The amount of references to other franchises or iconic movies during the story is great. The story itself is extremely well written, but sometimes the humor will be required to hold it together.
HUMOR
The humor of the game is very well written most times, and although some of it is based on crude kid jokes, the majority is just funny because it's a good joke. There are more kid jokes in the game but some jokes that older audiences find even funnier, whether be it about social security numbers or misnomers that are long-used phrases.
THE HUB
The hub world is a little harder to best than in most LEGO games because of the age it was made in, and that's the main con of this game. The hub as a whole is fantastic but some puzzles and mini objectives can be frustrating. Otherwise though, the design and overall gameplay are fantastic, and the amount of exploration that can be done is really fantastic.
COMBAT AND CONTROLS
The character controls in the game are pretty good, the auto-targeting can be a little fussy at times and the sprinting character speed really isn't as good as the other LEGO games while in-hub, making a vehicle the best option for movement. However, despite this, whilst on foot one can have a lot of fun, maybe more than they would on most vehicles, notably while wearing the space costume. The combat of the game is more polished than most other LEGO games aside from Ninjago Movie (which is no surprise, Fusion always delivers unique elements to their portion of the LEGO franchise), meaning that picking up robbers and tossing them into other robbers before arresting them can be done, or a Matrix jump and kick. It can be inconvenient at times when there are a lot of characters, but that's the combat flaw of a LEGO game in general, this isn't an issue that was new.
The game was one of the best LEGO experiences to date because it was unique. That's why it was really fun.

This is a truly wonderful sandbox game aimed at younger players. Both of my kids love playing it, the split screen co-op is a blast, there's tons of humor, hundreds of references to films (like the Arnold Schwarzenegger inspired construction worker who can't stop throwing out Arnold's most well known quotes "Get to the CHOPPER.... I mean crane!").
Then you have the 'Wonderboy the Dragon's Trap' style character swap where each of your different characters has a different ability and you'll need to utilize them all to navigate the world and reach secret areas, swapping them on the fly - speaking of which - the whole map is littered with hundreds of hard to reach nooks and crannies, actively encouraging you to explore every inch of the island to keep finding magical building blocks to unlock more and more of the 'master builder' locations.
My daughter has spent literally hours just riding around on the fairground attractions, of which there are many. The combat is visually striking but easy enough for young players not to get frustrated, death doesn't stop your progress, it just costs you a few Lego coins and you're right back in the action. There are a lot of missions, they are fun to play and just like the main map covered with hidden areas encouraging you to revisit them once you have unlocked more characters and abilities.
We've put in over fifty hours of play time already and there's no sign of the novelty wearing off. We have most of the Lego games and this is the only one requested by my kids time and time again. I'm genuinely surprised to see all the negative reviews, as I've seen no technical issues at all (one exception is that sometimes a controller being unplugged requires a re-load of the last save, but this affects all Lego games and at least in City Undercover it's only sometimes an issue, with all the other games it's every single time).
Lego City Undercover is packed to the rafters with detail, humor, secrets and wonderful gameplay. I can't recommend it enough.

After dropping the matchmaking system from when it was f2p, it has become just quake 3 refined and a little more accessible for newcomers.
That's only from UI and gameplay standpoint, because the playerbase is mostly formed by veterans and for those who don't like the steep learning curve it will be a frustrating experience (if all you have played in your life is modern tactical shooters you're gonna be thrashed hard for quite some time, and I mean REALLY hard).
I'm a returning quake 3 player who haven't touched online arena FPS for 7 years and I'm still struggling in keeping the same damage output that a mid-ELO player can display in Clan Arena mode after ~40h (which should be expected imho)
Haven't tried duel yet but it's gonna be even worse than other modes for sure.
Hopefully the next few rows of text will be helpful for those who want to try this game for the first time:
I suggest to play whith bots at first and learn maps and only then try some Online FFA to improve basic skills (for startes they're surprisingly good).
The first goal you should strive to achieve is learning how every weapon works and find a comfortable setup for mouse sensivity and weapon key bindings (don't keep the default confing because it's bad, also don't rely on mouse wheel for weapon switching), just bind weapons on keys around your movement ones (WASD and ESDF are the most common ones but even arrow keys are viable depending on your keyboard) and learn switching firearms for the right situation.
Many noobs that tried online quake FAA for 5h and pretend to have an informed opinion will state that this game is a mess all about twitch aiming and movement speed, but in reality decision making is a big factor, even in 1vs1 situations, and you got to think VERY fast if you want to survive.
For teamplay, I suggest to try Clan Arena (and CA variations of other modes like freezetag) on unranked servers to avoid some toxic behavior from players that are going to play in your team.
CA Capture The Flag is recommended when you learn how to move properly (which means strafejumping and rocketjumping fast without exposing yourself with predictable wide jump arcs or obvious routes).
Because of pickups, Classic Capture the flag, Team Deathmatch and especially Duel are really hardcore for new players so avoid them for some time.
Instagib is also recommended if you want to improve aiming with the railgun.
You have to enter this kind of game with the right mindset because you're litterally not going to kill anybody if you join a CA server for the first time with players that have years of experience behind them.
This game is rewarding to those willing to improve over time, short term satisfaction on the lucky "spray n' pray headshot kill" is nonexistent in Quake...you got skill or you don't, it's that simple.
If you're playing Clan Arena modes everyone will have tons of health and every weapon available from the start, so you need consistent aiming with hitscan weapons (google it if you don't know what they are) and movement prediction with projectile weapons plus good movement techinque for dodging enemy fire.
Classic modes with pickups are a little less demanding in the aiming department because managing your item "stack" is the most important thing but require even more prediction, really good map knowledge and movement skill to navigate the enviroments the fastest possible.
Quake is a game like none others, not even Unreal compares to its peculiar gameplay, and once you'll get good at it, other FPSs will feel really slow and less demanding skill-wise (even boring sometimes).

There's a hamfisted progression system that means you have to start with all the most generic and least interesting ships in each faction whenever you start a campaign, multiplayer profile, or vs AI profile (yeah that's a thing for some reason, having to level up to practice things against bots). This could maybe work if as you leveled up you unlocked interesting things and had to make meaningful choices about what you unlocked like in an RPG but every ship within each faction feels nearly identical aside from HP and they all have access to the same pool of passive and active upgrades. Most of those upgrades are as uninteresting as the differences between ship types, like 5 degree increased turning rate or a 25% increase in crit chance on a weapon with 0.625% base crit chance. Even across factions things feel too similar with maybe a third of the upgrades for each faction being unique and Eldar being the only faction who do anything but try to sit at broadsides at a range of their choosing.
The game runs really poorly as well, it takes upwards of 5 minutes to launch and there's then minute long loading screens to transition between almost everything like switching between the map and fleet outfitting in the campaign. It gets to the point where I'd rather play generic games against random AI than try and play through the campaign just so I dont have to waste time loading into and out of the map which doesn't really add anything to the game anyway. Every time I try to close it it also near locks up my computer for another 5-10 minutes.
It also doesn't feel sufficiently 40k in fluff, it's got all the right visuals, the ships look alright, the character profiles look fine, but all the voice acting is delivered in such bored monotones that sounds completely out of place. Inquisitors talk about chaos with emotion on the level of someone spilling the last inch of their coffee. The maps are all bland procedurally generated snorefests, warp travel is reduced to just a way to gg out of matches and the horrors of the warp are just a mechanic to force you to grind up redundant ships.
The whole thing feels like they were prototyping a digital version of the tabletop game as a Free-to-Play and then were told a month or two before release it needed singleplayer modes and to pull out the microtransactions so they grabbed whatever voice actors they could find to do one take each on some lines, hid the buttons to pay real money to skip grinding profiles up, and cut the optimization from the schedule entirely.

This game is amazing. All of the negative reviews are try harders crying about bugs and what not but it clearly states THIS IS AN EARLY ACCESS GAME AND A WORK IN PROGRESS. If you are not prepared to actually play the game with a playtest mindset then do not bother with it yet. If you can go into the game with the understanding there are going to be issues and report them as you find them then I would suggest you give it a try. It is a very nice survival game with some great mechanics and ideas. There are issues with the game especially with some of the player base on the PVE side of things where individuals want to pillar off the entire map to where new players cannot build or have to ask people to remove pillars in order to tame or build a base. I think this is the main reason for the 72 hour structure rule so that there is a way for others to tear pillars down and actually be able to build and play the game without being held hostage.
Pro's
-Visually stunning
-Great skill system (you gain skill by doing)
-Taming system is a great mechanic and if you find the right feed it helps to speed up the taming process
-The game is a challenge (you will die and lose your stuff, enjoy the struggle)
-Great private server options through third party sites are out there and you can enable and adjust things from resource gain to taming times, as well as damage dealt and resistances for both PC's and NPC's
Con's
-PVE player base can be crap with the way some players want to place pillar's to block other people from building and taming. This would not be an issue on PVP because there is recourse available but on the PVE servers it is tantamount to certain players basically holding the server hostage from everyone else. There is an anti-harassment clause about spamming the map to that effect but have not seen much enforcement.
-NPC Merchants will only buy certain things and in limited quantity so if you cannot be setting there at 8am game time each day to sale you will miss out.
-Server infastructure is not the best.
-Lag and rollback's can happen pretty regularly at times on certain servers
All in all for an early release game I think they have done a phenomenal job. There are bugs that need to be addressed and at times certain things should be made a priority in my opinion over other things that they choose to fix first, but when things have been reported I have seen them try to address it in most cases as quickly as possible. As I said above though, If you cannot play the game and understand what early release is about then do yourself a favor and do not play this yet. Otherwise if you understand early release and know you will lose things to bug's and challenges presented in game and you love the survivor genre and want amazing graphics and unique gameplay for the fantasy mythos then give it a try.

TLDR: Well made sub sim. Trades the anal, duller parts of Silent Hunter for stability, playability, and deeper, more enticing actual gameplay. Buy like a Wall Street floor trader on bath salts.
Fresh and well panned out sub sim. While it forgoes the at times anal details of e.g. Silent Hunter, this does serve to streamline the more trivial process of learning how to make the boat move, how to employ weapons, etc. and gives way to actually learning when to move the boat where, where to employ what weapon against what foe, and which enemy vessels are capable of what.
With the campaign using solely a 2D map for strategic movement and only spawning the player into the 3D world when encountering enemies, you escape the issues that would pop up in Silent Hunter where you might run aground and sink, get sniped with a depth charge by a passing plane, or constantly getting the fast forwarding interrupted for trivial reasons, considerably dragging out the non essential gameplay and making for more tedious long range travel. The only issues this currently causes (still in Beta stage) is that A, it's oftentimes fairly unclear at what speed and depth you will enter the 3D world, and B, in TLAM (Tomahawk strikes against land targets) missions, you won't enter the 3D world until you come within at maximum 25,000 yards of a ship. Currently these missions are always against ports, and so you're often forced by far too close to the target for your own good, and in shallow waters. This results in you either firing the TLAMs where you spawned in (this largely amounts to sneaking into someone's living room, slam firing a shotgun, and then attempting to leave unnoticed) which will result in helicopters, planes and rocket borne torpedoes and much more pouncing on you in waters where your ability to maneuver is restricted, or you spend a dull 10-20 minutes quietly making your way out to deep waters, where you can properly take advantage of the long range of your TLAMs before firing.
Judging by the state of the devs responding to the community thus far though, I feel confident that this will soon be remedied.
Enemy ships are spotted on the 2D map for you by friendly search planes, satellites, SOSUS in the GIUK Gap, etc. Likewise you can be spotted by similar assets of the Warsaw Pact. Hopefully a moderate number of NATO surface vessels will soon be introduced in the game world, or if they already are, then displayed on the map as you can sometimes get the impression that your own sub is the only thing representing the entire USN, RN and assorted other NATO navies in the game.
The missions are quite diverse and interesting. Comparing the game to Silent Hunter yet again, the campaign features more than basically just attacking merchantmen and the occassional task force. You are often tasked with intercepting and destroying specific wolfpacks as well as ambushing amphibious landing forces, attacking hostile submarine tenders, carrying out strategic TLAM strikes, covertly inserting Navy SEALs behind enemy lines, or stopping enemy subs from doing the same.
The game already features a large number of different surface ships, merchantmen, air assets, submarines and weapon systems of both sides to make few encounters similar and repetitive in nature, with more to come.
I'd very much recommend this game to anyone with an interest in submarines and/or the military aspects of the Cold War. It ought to suit people who primarily desire action as well as those (just sufficiently sane not be institutionalised) who print out medium sized libraries of technical aspects and details of cavitation, weapons, sensors, etc. and only play their sub sims wearing a custom made cap with their sub's name embroided on it.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter can only be described as an interactive, narrative driven vision of beauty telling a horrific tale that will grip you until the very moment the story ends.
From the moment Paul Prospero comes into this world, the Vanishing of Ethan Carter will strike you with its visual beauty and eerie atmosphere. Be it a stain of blood on the ground or a distant sound on the wind, you'll never feel completely safe in Red Creek Valley.
The first thing that came to my mind when I jumped into The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was that it did not look like an Unreal Engine game, especially not Unreal Engine 3. This is a technical achievement all on its own by the developers. The draw distance alone as well as lush environments show that The Astronauts succeeded where many AAA developers failed miserably. Naturally there are no loading screens.
Granted, the game requires a pretty powerful PC to run which is where I think the game has its biggest flaw. The game is decently optimized and I personally was getting solid frame-rates in outdoor areas with most of the settings set to High.
Is The Vanishing of Ethan Carter a game? No. Just as with many other "games" in this not-so-well-defined genre
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter only comes close to being a game during the crime scene investigation... let's call them puzzles.
It is a narrative driven experience which focuses on the story and immersing you in the world. It does so very well
it doesn't have guns or well defined gameplay mechanics such as skill trees and weapon upgrades. It will tell you it won't hold your hand and this is quite true.
This approach means you will have to figure out the mechanics for yourself and you have to do so in order to advance the story.
The crime scene investigation mechanic works in such a way that you have to find and restore objects to their original location and then linking a chain of events together by playing them back in the right order. This is where your supernatural powers come into play. My first experience with the crime scene investigation mechanic was for the most part looking around and clicking on objects it will draw your attention to. The way it does that is by hovering texts above the object in question. When you click on said text it shows you a thought process that in turn gives you clues as to what you are looking for.
It is a way of informing you what to do while not ruining the immersion with a HUD notification or by pausing the experience.
If only more game developers would take that approach.
Story-wise the game will show you various events that you access through investigating crime scenes. This is a tough game to describe. As someone who loves 40k, sci-fi, and games where you level up and upgrade your capital ships, I really enjoyed this game overall. The customization of your fleet is fun, although it would have been better to actually customize the ships (buy parts, switch weapons, modules, etc) instead you have to choose between "skills" or "upgrades" (which are not visually reflected) rather than equipment. There are also some serious gameplay flaws that make it extremely painful to continue playing the campaign: this game wastes the player's time over and over again. With the slow speed of ships, missions can take 15-20 minutes, which wouldn't be an issue except that it is extremely easy to arbitrarily lose these missions, especially early in the campaign. For example, data recovery missions: you are required to catch an enemy ship, take down its shields, board it and warp your ship off the map. You will spend the majority of the time simply chasing the target, and when you catch it, both teams are frantically beaming the data back and forth until someone can randomly escape. It's basically a coin toss if you are going to have the data when the timer is up, meaning that you might get unlucky and lose 2-3 times in a row, wasting 45+ minutes of uneventful time chasing an AI ship around. This ties in with another huge flaw with the campaign: you can make decisions/lose missions early in the campaign that will make it impossible to progress when you are 20 hours further in- so if you get bored of losing data recovery missions and decide to just accept the loss and move on, you might have just ruined your campaign but won't know until 20 turns later. I truly can't understand why game developers think this is a good idea. No gamer in the entire universe enjoys putting 20+ hours into a campaign and then reaching a point where they have to start over from square one. It's simple: don't ever include a mechanic in a game that causes a campaign to become unsalvageable.
To summarize, the game has fun moments and I would recommend it to those who like 40k and strategic capital ship battles, but be prepared: the developers decided to include a number of mechanics in this game that are incredibly frustrating. You will lose missions due to bugs/poor mission design/other factors outside of your control, and the game will let you continue with your campaign anyway, even though it may be doomed to fail.

It's a good game and fun, but needs some polish to address AI, campaign problems, and strange mission/scenario issues.
Pros:
-Good control scheme considering the requirements of maneuvering a submarine.
-Very satisfying when an attack goes off successfully.
-The interface provides most of the data you need and can be easily set to not allow for "cheating" by seeing undetected targets in your third-person cameras.
-Seems a very faithful rendition of the weapons and detection systems involved in undersea warfare. Thermal layers, detection radii, towed arrays and wire guidance factor in and feel well-implemented.
-Weapon evasion can get the blood pumping.
Cons:
-AI is still poorly tuned and suffering occasional serious problems. Subs dive past their implosion depth under attack rather than evading up and down in the shallow/deep cycle. Many of them turn into incoming torpedoes and don't use noisemakers. In shallow waters I often see them drive straight into the ground and never attempt to reverse off the mud. Torpedo evasion by AI subs is very poor in general, whereas surface ships seem to do a marginally better job overall at mission functions.
-The campaign has some major bugs, mainly around mission scheduling and allotted time intervals. For example, I got the Murmansk TLAM strike mission and immediately upon completion also received a SEAL insertion mission for the same port. Because my sub was still in proximity to Murmansk it immediately entered me into the second scenario without first giving me time to return to Holy Loch and board the SEALs, thereby forcing a mission failure. The campaign should also should be firing resupply tasks at a higher threshold so I'm less likely to blunder into a major mission with no weapons to use on the enemy.
-Sometimes the generated ambient noise is high enough that it renders Russian subs totally incapable of doing anything. In one SSBN scenario there was simply no method for me to make them hear my sub, even driving within 1000 yards at 20kt. Eventually I drove straight into the side of a Typhoon just to see what the ramming mechanics were like; only after the impact made some noise did they engage me at point blank range... which ultimately just led to the Typhoon dying to its own torpedoes. Meanwhile the Russian aircraft overhead seemed to be able to track me perfectly, even at ultra quiet beneath a layer, in 104db ambient noise. Strange.
Killerfish is a small studio, I'm sure this stuff will take time to work out. I do still highly recommend the game, it's great entertainment and suitably challenging if you want it to be - just expect to overlook the occasional frustration as you go about butchering Russian sailors. The studio appears to be very engaged with the community and talks regularly with current and former USN submariners (Jive Turkey in particular is a former sonar operator on 688 submarines, I highly recommend his stream) and technical professionals to ensure the simulation is as realistic as possible.

It's supposed to be a mixture of arcade and simulation, but instead it simply lacks features to qualify as either. It would be fine for an early access game but it's marketed as a complete product.
The calculation of firing solution you that some reviews mention is clicking on a blue circle. That's about all the complexity in this game.
Missions (even the campaign) are random and with very little variety.
The AI will ram into the ground on the first occasion.
If you encounter an enemy submarine in the campaign then a large section of the sea is loaded and you don't have any contacts on the sonar. You have to guess in which direction to search, and you may not find it for hours.
You don't know if the ships you're attacking in the campaign are your target so you can end up sinking a couple of ships and fail the objective. To make it worse you need to decide, often by random, between two or more convoys.
You'll never see the internals of any ship, there is only the outside view with 2 small HUD or a tactical screen.
You cannot set even the target depth or course so if you half of the game time is starting at the small HUD to see if your maneuver is completed - any distraction and you can end up surfacing or hitting the bottom.

One of the best sci-fi first person shooters out there. Being made in the source engine used for Half-Life 2, it does show it's age. But for it's limitations, it is not a bad looking game. The gameplay is solid, using elements from Counter Strike as well as incorporating a lean feature.  The mechanics that add a dynamic element to the gameplay is the classes, and their individual features.  Besides the obvious "scout is quick with low health, assault is balanced, support is slow and armored", vision is key.  The scout class has night vision, assault has motion sensitive vision, and support has thermal vision.  Why are these here, you might ask. Well, it has a dark atmosphere, support has smoke grenades paired with thermal vision and two of the three classes can activate camoflage, hence the motion sensitive vision.
Combine all of this with maps designed with realism in mind, original firearms that don't break physics laws, this is easily on of my top games.

An incredibly polished port of a really good mobile game.
In a similar style to the Myst series, you have a bunch of contraptions that aren't immediately clear how they interact, but as you look around and fiddle, all the pieces fall into place. The puzzles aren't THAT hard to figure out, and as there are no randomised elements, there is little replay value aside from playing with the switches and dials.
The controls are okay, not as immersive as touch controls on mobile, but still a reasonable amount of interaction with the pieces.
Instead of the better controls on mobiles, we get vastly superior graphics, which really enhance the atmosphere of this game which is eerie, borderline horror (though hopefully tame enough that those of a nervous disposition should still enjoy the thrill), and there are a few notes throughout to give a bit of context to the story although it's still quite mysterious up to this point.
Overall, it is basically an extremely high quality 'escape the room' type game. If you grew up enjoying that kind of flash game online, this will be right up your alley, and for those that enjoyed myst and similar puzzle games, again, you should enjoy it.
Obviously you should also play the first game, and indeed the sequel(s?) as and when they come out on steam. The games are relatively short, beatable in a couple of hours the first time, but for the price, you really can't argue, and it's great to support such respectable indie developers such as these.

I did find one area so far where you have to use stealth to avoid the baddies, but for the most part you are solving mysteries, mainly murders. Clues are marked as such, but it's up to you to look in the right places and put the pieces together. After you've found all the clues, you have to put them in proper order. And, of course, the main thing you are doing is putting together the larger story about what has happened to Ethan Carter. Story: Personally I like the mystery that surrounds the story that unfolds slowly as you explore. It's not a cutscene a minute sort of story telling, but more of a methodical unwrapping. Overall: It really is up to you. If you like this kind of story in general, then I really think that you will like this game. You'll see in other reviews I have made, I have a Pros and Cons section where I detail what I love and dislike.
This game is practically perfect.
- It's a turn-based squad game that gives you the creativity to put who you want on the battlefield and figure out what works best for you. Every move you make and decision you make affects your immediate game and late game as you defend the Earth from Extraterrestrial Life Forms.
- The story gets incredibly interesting and you, oddly, start to fall in love with your seemingly shallow squad members who you've had many missions with. You get pride when you have a character that lasts 80% of the game without dying.
- There are so many parts of the game that challenge your strategic placement of your soldiers. Some missions are easy and some are incredibly difficult. The payoff for the hard missions is there, in my opinion, if you don't lose a lot of soldiers.
- There is a high risk high reward system in this game as you play from the upgrades you give your base, your soldiers, research, and gear. You have to decide what needs to be a priority. Gives you personal control of what direction XCOM goes and their purpose/desire.
- I've put so many hours into this game and have considered another playthrough soon.
Buy it. You'll love it.

I'm a fan of the survival genre. I'm a fan of the science-fiction genre. Put those two together and you get Take on Mars.
While not completely finished, as denotes it's Beta Build, it is on it's way to becoming a remarkably accurate simulator (with obvious gameplay exceptions) of survival on Mars.
That being said... it does suffer similar problems to most Open World Sandbox games of the same ilk at the moment. Notably the 'nothing to do but survive' problem. At least in most scenarios. Take On Mars, however, seems to address this problem with the Scenario / Scenario Editor... you can utilise triggers, events, etc. to create a story arc style of play. From landing, base building, to extraction should you want it, and thus solve the major issues of the survive to survive most survival genre titles have.
What strikes me most about this game in either the Single or Multiplayer, is the emptiness. Some put it down as a Con, I put it down as a Pro... Mars is empty. There is very little to do there in reality, and this is refelcted somewhat by gameplay. However, the inclusion of science experiments, sampling, and more would add greatly to the overall experience.
You can 'fake' science with the previously mentioned Scenario Triggers, but this pales in comparison to what the developers could possibly do in terms of story arc.
Single Player - The Single Player Gameplay starts with what could be considered a 'modern space age' where you send probes, landers and rovers to Mars, Deimos, and even the Asteroid Belt. After 'completing' this portion of the campaign gathering all the outlined data under objectives, you are ready to launch your manned mission.
I don't want to spoil the storyline of this mission arc, but Mark Watney move over, there's a new King of Mars. And it is story driven, though limited in scope. Starting in one area, and moving to another. With no option to alter which starting area, nor where you head to.
If you're looking for a completely free-roam Open World Sandbox game, this one is not for you. If you're looking for a game that throws enough realism in your face to be accounted a 'true' survival game then this is the one for you.
The team seems dedicated to keeping updates flowing, and they do address problems with the product as they can.
The game has been in Early Access for a while, but this doesn't phase me in the slightest. Years in development is basically any title that has something unique about it, or needs to be built in a different way from previous titles. Comparing development times of a game like this to games such as Battlefield or Call of Duty wastes time, and mental energy. Building onto previously formulae (Battlefield, Call of Duty, <insert other franchise here>) will always be faster, easier, and more efficient than creating something new, and I prefer the effectiveness of Take On Mars to the fast development that would see it be a reskin of another title.
In conclusion, the game does have bugs, and some of its elements lack polish, but if the development team continues the way they are going it may well show a new way to experience survival that actually throws whatever it can at you to make you fail, without big green aliens, zombies, or other post apocalyptic horrors.

I'm loving this game and while it may not be complete, the potential is leagues above any similar games. A lot of people say it is just like ARK but I'd say that it's actually just similar to ARK.
That's really it from what I've seen. The similarities are basically limited to both being a semi-hardcore survival game with taming, crafting, and building. But the game changes things and makes large strides in improving ARK's system to where the game feels more like a standard MMORPG or an online Skyrim with Ark elements.
The cities are one of the biggest and best additions to the game. Solo players and new players can keep themselves relatively safe until they feel they can get themselves established by using the city for protection, housing, and can even gear themselves in fairly high quality equipment. Meanwhile groups of players can use the city to establish a seat of power. They can even become the owners of a city and change the rules of a city provided they have enough players to win the vote.
But the cities aren't the only great addition. The combat in Dark and Light feels like a third-person action game. Dodge rolls, power attacks, and spellcasting make combat really come to life. It adds a style to fighting that ARK just didn't have. A boar is charging at you? Dodge it. Enemy is sleeping and you've managed to sneak up on it? Power attack for high damage. Enemy a bit too strong for you to handle but you can almost do it? Cast the healing spell on yourself and watch your health go up while you battle. Really, if you don't enjoy building I feel like you could completely focus on just fighting and crafting gear for yourself the entire game and be perfectly fine.
Speaking of crafting, the way crafting works in this is much superior to ARK in my opinion. Instead of leveling your character by crafting a single item a billion times then putting your skill points into crafting it, instead you level yourself in whatever way you choose, then once you have unlocked the ability to learn a skill, you use that skill until you gain a level in it. For example, Survival can leveled by chopping trees. If you aren't able to learn the next tier of Survival crafts until level 10, then you first must level to 10 then once you have done so then you chop down trees to gain experience towards Survival. Once you have enough experience, Survival levels and you learn all the crafts at that tier. In this way, you can easily learn all the crafts in the game without having to worry about wasting your skill points just to build a house or craft gathering tools which, in my opinion, makes for a more enjoyable experience.
I'm not going to lie, this game is not for everyone. You will spend hours on some tames, then probably lose them because of a player or wild animal. You will build houses that players will destroy. You will probably have trouble finding resources or get killed to stupid things. This game isn't for everyone, but I think anyone can find something they enjoy in it whether it be crafting, fighting, building, or even just exploring. While this game may not be finished, it is already amazing and well worth the price. The potential it has is enormous and if done right, I think this game has the potential to be truly great.

Visually this game is utterly fantastic. I have rarely had the joy of seeing a game with as much attention to detail placed into nearly every environmental element. Everything from houses through to trees and down to rocks on the ground combine to produce a wonderfully immersive and beautiful world to explore. On top of the technical prowess the game displays, there is a clear and very effective aesthetic which together with the graphical fidelity generate something truly beautiful. The lighting and scene setting are also expertly done and there were many times where I simply stopped to admire what had been done.
At the same time as being beautiful to look at, it managed to convey a feeling of sadness, abandonment and menace that stuck with me throughout the whole game.
The soundtrack and sound design fit in with the visuals perfectly, very soft and low key. The environmental sounds were subtle and were effective in grounding the player in the scene and were very immersive.
In terms of gameplay, this game shares a lot of DNA with titles like Dear Esther and Gone Home in that it is mostly about exploration and has no action to speak of. Because of this, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is not something that everyone will like, however I do think it is one of the best entries I have played in this genre.
You play as a supernatural detective called Paul Prospero who has come to a quiet backwater town in response to a letter from Ethan Carter, something terrible has happened in this quiet and near abandoned town and it is down to you to investigate it. I will keep away from discussing plot points so as not to spoil the story as the game does rely somewhat on the player gradually unveiling what happened.
With Prospero’s medium like abilities, he is able to pick up an imprint of dramatic events that have occurred in an area – however it is sensitive to disorder, and to get a clear picture, he needs to find objects that played a vital role within the event and try arrange them as they were prior to the event to reset the area.
From here he gets an impression of events and once you have figured what order they go in, you can then see the ghostly playback of what happened.
These puzzles range in their effectiveness, with some being decidedly pedestrian in their difficulty, and one or two being very obscure. All however are quite effective in telling the story and for the most part they strike a good balance between pacing and difficulty.
Each of these story fragments form up the story of what happened in this town, and although some of the puzzles can be done out of order, the major plot points are cleverly obscured until it is appropriate, which helps ensure the player does not get lost, while still allowing flexibility in how you reveal the story for the most part.
The story was interesting and compelling enough to keep me going through till the end. Whilst the ending wasn’t quite what I had expected it was I felt a perfect ending for the narrative one that fit the tone that had permeated every aspect of the game.
Like Dear Esther and Gone Home, this game is very short and does not lend itself to being very replayable. That said I think the length was appropriate. It didn’t feel stretched out and I think a longer play time would be detrimental to the experience.
Dear Esther I felt was a dense poem ripe for critical analysis, Gone Home was a slice of life short story. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter I also feel is a short story in game form, a mystery novella. One that provided me with a great experience, well worth playing through.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a well-told tale in the vein of The Twilight Zone. Drawing clear inspiration from concepts such as Dear Esther, the Astronauts paint a scary, suspensful, and moving story as they draw out the player's emotions. Their love for their craft is evident in the excellent voice-acting and sumptuous graphics. The beautifully rendered Red Creek Valley makes an enjoyable canvas for the story.
It took me just over 5 hours to play through. Twice I came to points where I wasn't sure where to find my next clue. One item early on was pretty hard to find (in a pixel-hunting sense, though not exactly pixel-hunting) and another direction late in the game didn't stand out to me until I walked around a bit. Neither proved more than a slight delay.
I consider this game money well-spent for 6 hours of entertainment (try that at the movies)! I highly recommend The Vanishing of Ethan Carter as an engaging interactive story.

I have a lot of trouble with the "games are art" thing. I think games always contain art, but their purity of vision is usually hampered in some way: by gameplay mechanics, by economics, by a committee of creators. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter really doesn't feel like that, and I wouldn't hesitate for a second in describing it as art, perhaps the best piece of video game art I've experienced yet.
I've heard of this title being dismissed as a "walking simulator", which is crude as a pejoritive criticism (it's a long, long way advanced from Dear Esther) but it also backfires. The world in this game is so beautiful, I would happily have bought it just for the exploration. There is a lot more to it, however. I wouldn't say the scene investigations are exactly "puzzles", but they add an element to the storytelling that makes completing each chapter into a gentle addiction. There are a couple of decent problems to crack, and the easier stuff isn't insultingly simple. It's rewarding enough.

This game has two faces so bare with me for this one:
I love playing this game.
It's fun, exciting, descent graphics, good sound (their is a !!! large warning !!! about this though, more about that later)
Both the single player and multieplayer are fun to play with and things like terrorist hunt where you can multieplayer with up to 4 people with your friends to swipe a level of terrorist never gets old. Their are some minor annoyances of jittersish AI behavior: sometimes they react very slowly and other times they virtually 'teleport' around the corner and make an instant headshot. But it's more then workable, the game is beatable and enjoyable even through this.
You can customize your character a lot. Their are a whole range of skins, face features (mustaches, beards eyes) and that is just the face and body. You can equip different weapon sets per game and outfit your character with stuff you can unlock through gaining levels.
This leveling element has been flashed out well, their is a lot to unlock. It doesn't feel tedious because the game is well playable without a lot of unlocks. And it feels rewarding, it is just plain fun to see new stuff become available and show off your rank as well as your individual levels on assualt, CBQ and marksmen tactics.
The single player has a descent story and some interesting voice acting. It's no grande feast of fully inspired epic dialog and plot. But it's very enjoyable. Sometimes it takes a bit of good luck to get your AI colleges going and doing what they need to do, but again: it is more then workable and doesn't really halt the game in my opinion.
I would love to keep playing this game, although their one big BUT:
Their is a persistent sound bug that keeps popping up, mainly in multieplayer . The bug seams to trigger when their is full automatic gun fire (which their is almost constantly in a heated battle) and has a chance to keep looping.
Imagine the rattling of an M16 or AK rifle and that it just keeps stuck. Mostly it's a gun causing the problem laying on the ground, if you can find it and pick it up it mostly disappears.
But I also found a similar bug that isn't fixable through this and in general gets worse. The former bug is location bound, when you move away the sound is gone. This big however keeps going in any part of the game (in-agem, loading screen, main menu) and can even carry on inside your operating system. I am NOT kidding, I have tried to find the volume of the game in the Win7 volume control to mute it, disabled and enabled my sound card, but the only thing that works is rebooting your whole machine.
Now you might think, what does this rattling about a bug have to do in a review. Well, I am not the only one that has this bug. This bug is widely known and many, many users experience it. Their are a multietude of 'solutions' but nothing seams to stick. We have widely different system and have since we started playing all upgraded our machines or bought new ones, but the bugs stay. The internet is littered with forums etc that are filled with people with the same problem, but never a solid solution is provided.
I do not understand how they have been able to make a game based on the Unreal Engine that is this flawed in the audio department. You might argue that this game is a bit older, but I don't see it that way. This game has an active community and has a lot of stuff to unlock that you can only achieve by playing it a hell of a lot. In that regard I am very disappointing in both this game and Ubisoft for not providing the community with either a statement or a solution.
If this game didn't have said bug, it would be an instance classic and in my opinion can go through the decades like Unreal Tournament 2K4, Medal of Honor: Pacific Assualt, Quake 3 Arena and Battle Field 1942.
It's really a game you can pick up where you left off, have a whole lot of fun, but their is always room for improvement. A pure skill game that doesn't have game mechanics that just throw off the game balance like the new COD: Modern Warfare or the newer UT and Quake games that just didn't feel like anything we loved about the orginal format.
For me Rainbow Six was always a miss, because the AI was terribly stupid and the game very hard to learn in general. This game isn't, I really enjoy playing it and explore everything it has. But for some reason I have to accept that I will have to endure regular persistent automatic gun fire blazing through my headphones that NEVER STOP.

Personal Rating: 10/10
You'll see in other reviews I have made, I have a Pros and Cons section where I detail what I love and dislike.
This game is practically perfect.
- It's a turn-based squad game that gives you the creativity to put who you want on the battlefield and figure out what works best for you. Every move you make and decision you make affects your immediate game and late game as you defend the Earth from Extraterrestrial Life Forms.
- The story gets incredibly interesting and you, oddly, start to fall in love with your seemingly shallow squad members who you've had many missions with. You get pride when you have a character that lasts 80% of the game without dying.
- There are so many parts of the game that challenge your strategic placement of your soldiers. Some missions are easy and some are incredibly difficult. The payoff for the hard missions is there, in my opinion, if you don't lose a lot of soldiers.
- There is a high risk high reward system in this game as you play from the upgrades you give your base, your soldiers, research, and gear. You have to decide what needs to be a priority. Gives you personal control of what direction XCOM goes and their purpose/desire.
- I've put so many hours into this game and have considered another playthrough soon.
Buy it. You'll love it.

Finally, a 40k game aside from the Dawn of War series I can rely on to be enjoyable! Lots of replay value in this game, plenty of meaningful progression and one hell of a challenging learning curve. Each race has its own distinct tactical style and you'll have to learn them all back-to-front to consistently defeat them. The models are exceptional, and the game feels truly faithful to the Warhammer 40,000 fluff.
A good mix of objective-based gameplay and straight up interstellar slugfests keep things interesting, even in the skirmish mode which seems to be a break from RTS traditions. Skirmish features its own progression system and without any DLC gives you a choice of Imperial Navy, Eldar Corsairs, Ork Pirates and Chaos fleets to play with. You will also often battle against DLC factions such as the Tau Empire and Space Marines without owning those DLCs. Watching an Imperial Fists strike cruiser closing on your little Dauntless light cruisers with naught but violence in mind is certainly tense.
The campaign could use a lot more cinematic flair in my opinion. The focus seems to be very much on the gameplay, with only moderate concessions to cinematic storytelling. While this is definitely not a major issue by any means, I would have liked a little more characterisation and a story that followed specific characters more closely.
All-in-all, I heartily recommend this game to any fans of 40k and strategy games IN SPAAAAAAAAAAAAAACE! Well worth the original 30 quid price tag, and at half price right now it's a steal.

I've been playing Lego games since "Star Wars" (the one with the prequels) first came out.  I got it to introduce gaming to my wife.  Since then, I've kept up with most of the series as I had children and they've become gamers on their own.  Throughout, Lego has had more hits than misses and I would put "Lego City Undercover" in the former bracket.  Yes, there are some technical issues (I've had a few crashes), but it hasn't diminished the experience.  The plot is kiddie silliness with reference heavy humor; the gameplay is classic Lego with a heavier emphasis on exploration; and there are tons of collectibles.
The biggest positive is that it scratches that "Arkham" itch (now here me out).  Like Riddler trophies, the many collectibles around the map require you to utilize your platforming skills and use of your costumes to get them.  If you can get past the little glitches, there's quite a bit of fun to be had.  Pick it up on sale and share it with a family member.
